But first answer me this question of mine: Was the one who wrote the books and said how the world was created and that God does not foreknow a human being or not?” And I said, “A human being.” Peter replied, “Since he was a human being, then, how was it possible for him to know without error how the world was created and that God does not foreknow?”

Translator's notes for section 2.49 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: Εὐκόπως ἐλεγχθῆναι δυνάμενον προέτεινας ἡμῖν
Rendered as: You have put before us something that can easily be refuted
The substantival neuter participle leaves the object unnamed; “something” preserves that lack of specification rather than supplying “argument.”

2. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδὲν ἀγνοεῖ θεός, ἀλλὰ καὶ προγινώσκει
Rendered as: God is ignorant of nothing and even foreknows
The rendering preserves the contrast between lacking no knowledge and possessing knowledge in advance; “knows beforehand” is also possible for προγινώσκει.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὃ δὲ πυνθάνομαί σου; πρῶτον ἀπόκριναί μοι.
Rendered as: But first answer me this question of mine
The relative expression is taken with the following command. The editorial question mark could instead yield the more abrupt “But what I ask you? Answer me first,” but that is less natural English.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἰδέναι ἀψευδῶς
Rendered as: to know without error
ἀψευδῶς denotes knowing truly or infallibly; “without error” avoids implying merely personal honesty.

SECTION 2.50

And I, already perceiving the solution, said with a slight smile, “Because he was a prophet.” Peter said, “If, then, the prophet, though a human being, was ignorant of nothing because he had received foreknowledge from God, how could the very one who gave a human being the ability to foreknow, being God, have been ignorant?” And I said, “You spoke correctly.” Then Peter said, “Join me, then, in examining this very point further. Since we have agreed that God foreknows everything, it is absolutely necessary that the scriptures which say he is ignorant are false, while those which say he knows are true.” And I said, “It must be so.”

Translator's notes for section 2.50 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: αἰσθόμενος ἤδη τὴν ἐπίλυσιν ὑπομειδιῶν
Rendered as: already perceiving the solution, said with a slight smile
ἐπίλυσις is the solution or resolution of the difficulty, while ὑπομειδιῶν indicates a restrained or slight smile.

2. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τὸ ἀπὸ θεοῦ εἰληφέναι τὴν πρόγνωσιν
Rendered as: because he had received foreknowledge from God
The articular infinitive gives the reason, and πρόγνωσις denotes advance knowledge rather than a prediction uttered by the prophet.

3. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτὸς ὁ δεδωκὼς ἀνθρώπῳ τὸ προγινώσκειν
Rendered as: the very one who gave a human being the ability to foreknow
αὐτός emphasizes the giver himself, and the articular infinitive denotes the capacity or act of knowing in advance.

4. Translation choice — Greek: Ἔτι οὖν, ἔφη, εἰς αὐτὸ συνδιαπόρησόν μοι
Rendered as: Then Peter said, “Join me, then, in examining this very point further”
συνδιαπορέω invites joint consideration of a difficulty. “Join me in questioning” is possible, but “examining” is more idiomatic in context.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὰς δὲ γινώσκειν αὐτὸν λεγούσας
Rendered as: those which say he knows
αὐτόν is construed as the accusative subject of γινώσκειν in contrast with the preceding claim that he is ignorant. Its position also permits the formal alternative “say that someone knows him,” but that leaves the subject unstated and disrupts the explicit contrast.

SECTION 2.51

And Peter said, “If, then, some things in the scriptures are true and others false, our teacher had good reason to say, ‘Become approved money changers,’ since some of the statements in the scriptures are genuine while others are counterfeit. And to those being led astray by the false scriptures, he appropriately revealed the cause of their error by saying, ‘This is why you go astray: you do not know what is true in the scriptures; for this reason you are also ignorant of the power of God.’” And I said, “Very good.”

Translator's notes for section 2.51 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: μὲν-ἐστὶν
The supplied, image-checked reading prints a hyphen between μὲν and ἐστίν. It appears to be an editorial or typographic separator without semantic force; the translation construes the two printed words separately.

2. Greek: τῶν γραφῶν ἃ μὲν-ἐστὶν ἀληθῆ, ἃ δὲ ψευδῆ
If ἃ and ἀληθῆ directly modified the feminine γραφῶν, their neuter gender would be unexpected. They can defensibly be understood substantivally as “some things” or contents among the scriptures, especially in light of the following reference to λόγοι, so no correction is required.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν γραφῶν ἃ μὲν-ἐστὶν ἀληθῆ, ἃ δὲ ψευδῆ
Rendered as: some things in the scriptures are true and others false
The neuter forms ἃ and ἀληθῆ are read substantivally of contents or statements within the feminine γραφαί. “Some of the scriptures are true and others false” is contextually possible but would not preserve the printed gender distinction.

4. Translation choice — Greek: γίνεσθε τραπεζῖται δόκιμοι
Rendered as: Become approved money changers
τραπεζῖται are money changers or bankers, and δόκιμοι means tested, approved, or reliable. “Discerning money changers” would express the contextual function but less directly render the adjective.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τινῶν μὲν δοκίμων ὄντων λόγων, τινῶν δὲ κιβδήλων
Rendered as: some of the statements in the scriptures are genuine while others are counterfeit
λόγοι here are statements or passages. δοκίμων and κιβδήλων continue the coin-testing image with genuine versus counterfeit material.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν ψευδῶν γραφῶν πλανωμένοις
Rendered as: to those being led astray by the false scriptures
ἀπό marks the false writings as the source of the error; “because of the false scriptures” is an alternative.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ ἀληθῆ τῶν γραφῶν
Rendered as: what is true in the scriptures
The neuter substantive denotes the true contents or portions of the writings, not simply acquaintance with the writings as a whole.

SECTION 2.52

And Peter replied, “Therefore I have good reason to believe nothing against either God or the righteous people recorded in the law, taking reverent thought as my starting point. For, as I am convinced, Adam was not a transgressor, he who was gestated by the hands of God; nor was Noah a drunkard, he who was found righteous beyond the entire world; nor did Abraham live with three women at once, he who was deemed worthy of many children because of self-control; nor did Jacob have relations with four women, two of whom also happened to be sisters, he who, being the father of twelve tribes, also signaled that the presence of our teacher would come. Moses was not a murderer, and he did not learn to judge from a priest of an idol, he who prophesied God’s law for the entire age and, because of right understanding, was attested as a ‘faithful steward.’”

Translator's notes for section 2.52 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: οὔτε κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πιστεύω οὔτε κατὰ τῶν ἐν τῷ νόμῳ ἀναγραφέντων δικαίων
Rendered as: I have good reason to believe nothing against either God or the righteous people recorded in the law
With κατά and the genitive, πιστεύω concerns accepting something adverse to the named persons. “Nothing” supplies the object required by natural English without specifying a particular accusation.

2. Translation choice — Greek: εὐσεβῶς φρονεῖν προλαμβάνων
Rendered as: taking reverent thought as my starting point
προλαμβάνων presents reverent judgment as an antecedent presumption or principle. “Presupposing that one should think reverently” is also possible.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ ὑπὸ τῶν τοῦ θεοῦ χειρῶν κυοφορηθείς
Rendered as: he who was gestated by the hands of God
κυοφορέω ordinarily depicts carrying in the womb or gestation. The deliberately striking image is retained rather than reduced to the more general “formed.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ ὑπὲρ πάντα τὸν κόσμον δίκαιος εὑρεθείς
Rendered as: he who was found righteous beyond the entire world
ὑπέρ gives a comparative or surpassing sense. “Above the whole world” is more literal, while “more righteous than everyone in the world” makes the comparison explicit.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τρισὶν ἅμα συνῄει γυναιξίν
Rendered as: live with three women at once
σύνειμι with the dative can mean associate or cohabit and may carry a sexual or marital implication here. “Have relations with” is a possible stronger rendering.

6. Translation choice — Greek: οὔτε Ἰακὼβ τετράσιν ἐκοινώνει
Rendered as: nor did Jacob have relations with four women
κοινωνέω can mean share or associate with and, in this marital context, have relations with. “Women” is supplied from the preceding clause and confirmed by the feminine relative ὧν and ἀδελφαί.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν τοῦ διδασκάλου ἡμῶν παρουσίαν ἐσήμανεν ἐλθεῖν
Rendered as: signaled that the presence of our teacher would come
παρουσία is retained as “presence,” while ἐλθεῖν separately expresses its coming; translating only “the coming of our teacher” would collapse the source’s wording.

8. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ Μωϋσῆς φονεὺς ἦν, καὶ παρὰ ἱερέως εἰδώλου κρίνειν ἐμάνθανεν
Rendered as: Moses was not a murderer, and he did not learn to judge from a priest of an idol
The single οὐ is taken as governing both coordinated allegations, as required by the surrounding sequence of denials. A formally possible reading that affirms the second predicate would conflict with that structure.

9. Translation choice — Greek: παντὶ τῷ αἰῶνι τὸν τοῦ θεοῦ νόμον προφητεύσας
Rendered as: prophesied God’s law for the entire age
The dative is read temporally or as indicating the age for which the prophecy was given. “To the entire age” and, if αἰών is spatially extended, “to the whole world” are possible alternatives.

10. Translation choice — Greek: πιστὸς οἰκονόμος
Rendered as: faithful steward
οἰκονόμος denotes one entrusted with managing a household or its affairs; “manager” is a possible modern alternative.

SECTION 2.53

Nevertheless, at the proper time I will also give you an explanation of these matters together with similar ones. But for now, as you see, since evening has overtaken us, let the things said today be sufficient. On another occasion, if you wish, feel free to ask us about whatever you want, and we will gladly explain them without hesitation. After saying this, he got up. And so, after partaking of food, we turned to sleep, for night had overtaken us.

Translator's notes for section 2.53 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: καὶ οὕτως. τροφῆς μεταλαβόντες
The printed full stop leaves καὶ οὕτως as an elliptical sentence or separates an adverb naturally attachable to the following participial clause. The translation adopts the latter attachment; alternatively the print may be represented as “And so it was. After partaking of food ...” This is an editorial punctuation ambiguity, not unreadable or missing text.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἐπίλυσιν
Rendered as: an explanation
The noun can denote an explanation or solution; the context concerns resolving the hearer's questions.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ δὲ λοιποῦ
Rendered as: But for now
The phrase can mean “for the rest,” “for the remaining time,” or “henceforth.” The evening context supports taking it as a transition that closes the present session.

4. Translation choice — Greek: θαρρῶν ἡμῖν πυνθάνου
Rendered as: feel free to ask us
This expresses the participle’s call for confidence in idiomatic modern English while retaining the invitation to inquire.

5. Translation choice — Greek: χαίροντες ἀόκνως ἐπιλύσομεν
Rendered as: we will gladly explain them without hesitation
The participle χαίροντες conveys gladness, ἀόκνως readiness or lack of hesitation, and ἐπιλύσομεν the explaining or resolving of the matters raised.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἐγήγερται
Rendered as: he got up
The perfect is used in the narrative sequence for the completed action of rising.

7. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς ὕπνον ἐτράπημεν
Rendered as: we turned to sleep
This retains the source’s image of turning toward sleep rather than replacing it with the less transparent “went to bed.”

8. Translation choice — Greek: κατειλήφει γὰρ ἡ νύξ
Rendered as: for night had overtaken us
The rendering preserves both the pluperfect force and the image of night catching or overtaking the group; “us” is implicit from the context.

HOMILY 3

SECTION 3.1

So, when two days had passed and the third was beginning to dawn, I, Clement, awoke for the debate with Simon, and together with the companions who were with me, at the second calls of the roosters, we found the lamp still shining and Peter on his knees praying. When he had finished his petition, he turned, saw that we were ready to listen, and said:

Translator's notes for section 3.1 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τὸ διαλεχθῆναι τῷ Σίμωνι
Rendered as: for the debate with Simon
διαλέγεσθαι can denote discussion or debate; the planned public dispute supports “debate.”

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ τὰς δευτέρας τῶν ἀλεκτρυόνων φωνάς
Rendered as: at the second calls of the roosters
This preserves the reference to the second round of rooster calls rather than replacing it with a conventional time designation.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν δὲ Πέτρον γονυκλινῆ προσευχόμενον
Rendered as: Peter on his knees praying
γονυκλινής describes a kneeling posture.

SECTION 3.2

“I want you to know that those who, under our direction, associate with Simon so that, as they learn his plans, they may report them to us, enabling us to adapt ourselves to the variety of his wickedness, have themselves sent word and informed us, saying: ‘Today Simon, just as he arranged, is ready to come before everyone and demonstrate from the Scriptures that this one is not the highest God—he “who created heaven and earth” and all things in them—but that there is some other unknown and highest one, as one existing among secret mysteries, a God of gods. He sent two gods, of whom one is the one who created the world, while the other is the one who gave the law. Simon schemes to say these things so that he may undermine beforehand the right faith of those who are going to worship the one and only God, “who created heaven and earth.”’”

Translator's notes for section 3.2 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: μὴ τοῦτον εἶναι·θεὸν ἀνώτατον
The printed high point interrupts the infinitive construction between εἶναι and its predicate θεὸν ἀνώτατον. The surviving words permit a clear construction if the punctuation is provisionally disregarded.

2. Greek: τῶν τὸν ἕνα καὶ μόνον μελλόντων. σέβειν θεόν
The printed full stop separates μέλλειν from its complementary infinitive σέβειν. The translation provisionally treats this as intrusive editorial punctuation without changing the surviving words.

3. Translation choice — Greek: καθ’ ἡμετέραν πρόνοιαν
Rendered as: under our direction
In context πρόνοια refers to the deliberate arrangement by which the informants remain with Simon; “by our foresight” is also lexically possible.

4. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τὴν τῆς κακίας αὐτοῦ ποικιλίαν ἁρμόσασθαι
Rendered as: adapt ourselves to the variety of his wickedness
ποικιλία denotes variety or versatility, while ἁρμόζεσθαι expresses adjustment to it.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ἐν ἀπορρήτοις ὄντα θεὸν θεῶν
Rendered as: as one existing among secret mysteries, a God of gods
ἀπόρρητα can denote secrets, mysteries, or esoteric teachings. Here ὡς introduces the characterization attributed to Simon; alternatives include “supposedly existing among secret things as God of gods.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: προεκλύσει
Rendered as: may undermine beforehand
The compound verb indicates loosening or weakening in advance.

SECTION 3.3

“When I heard these things, how could I not have been disheartened? Therefore I also wanted you, the brothers who are with me, to know that my soul is in no small pain, as I observe that the evil one is vigilant for the testing of human beings, while human beings are utterly neglectful of their own salvation. For he has contrived to introduce notions of many other gods among those from the nations who are about to be persuaded that the earthly carved images are not gods, so that, if they cease from the polytheistic madness below, they will be deceived into speaking in another way—or even worse—against God’s sole sovereignty, so that, never having preferred what belongs to that sole sovereignty, they may never at any time be able to obtain mercy. For this audacious undertaking Simon approaches us for battle, armed with the false passages of the Scriptures. And what is worse, on the basis of prophets in whom he has not believed, he has not feared to teach such doctrines against the God who is truly God.”

Translator's notes for section 3.3 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: κατὰ τῆς· τοῦ θεοῦ μοναρχίας
The printed high point separates the article τῆς from its dependent genitive τοῦ θεοῦ and is syntactically intrusive. The translation provisionally reads the phrase as a continuous construction while preserving all surviving words.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς ἑαυτῶν σωτηρίας πάνυ ἀμελοῦντας
Rendered as: utterly neglectful of their own salvation
πάνυ intensifies the stated neglect and is retained rather than softened.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν ἐπιγείων ξοάνων
Rendered as: the earthly carved images
ξόανα are carved cult images; “earthly” preserves the contrast expressed by ἐπίγειος.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς κάτω πολυθέου μανίας
Rendered as: the polytheistic madness below
The spatial image of κάτω is retained; alternatives include “earthbound polytheistic madness” and “polytheistic madness down here.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς· τοῦ θεοῦ μοναρχίας
Rendered as: God’s sole sovereignty
μοναρχία here denotes the rule or sovereignty of the one God. The rendering provisionally disregards the printed high point but does not alter the surviving words.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἵνα μηδέποτε τὰ τῆς μοναρχίας προτιμήσαντες οὐπώποτε ἐλέους τυχεῖν δυνηθῶσιν
Rendered as: so that, never having preferred what belongs to that sole sovereignty, they may never at any time be able to obtain mercy
Both negative expressions, μηδέποτε and οὐπώποτε, are preserved rather than reducing their apparent repetition.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ ὄντως θεοῦ
Rendered as: the God who is truly God
ὄντως qualifies the designation θεός by marking this one as genuinely God. Alternatives include “the real God” and “the one who really is God”; the phrase is not treated as a separate assertion of existence.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἀφ’ ὧν οὐ πεπίστευκε προφητῶν
Rendered as: on the basis of prophets in whom he has not believed
The relative is attracted into the case of its antecedent προφητῶν. “From prophets whom he has not believed” is also possible.

SECTION 3.4

“As for us, who have inherited from our ancestors both the worship of the God who created everything and, further, the mystery of the books capable of deceiving, he will be able to accomplish nothing. But among those from the nations, who have the polytheistic conception as a companion from their upbringing and do not know the false elements in the Scriptures, he will be capable of much—not only he; even if someone else presents to those from the nations, against God, some empty, ornamented myth resembling a sumptuous dream, that person too will be believed, because from childhood their mind has been accustomed to accept the things said against God. Yet there will indeed be some rare ones among them—few out of a multitude—who, through good sense, will not be willing even so much as merely to hear an evil word against the God who created everything. For these alone, though they are from the nations, it will come about that they are saved. Therefore, let none of you blame Simon at all, or anyone else either, for nothing happens unjustly, seeing that even the false elements in the Scriptures turn out reasonably to serve as a test.”

Translator's notes for section 3.4 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: τὴν πολύθεον ὑπόληψιν· σύντροφον ἔχουσιν
The printed high point interrupts the construction in which σύντροφον is the complement of ἔχουσιν with τὴν πολύθεον ὑπόληψιν as its object. The translation provisionally repunctuates without changing the surviving words.

2. Greek: κακὸν. λόγον αὐτὸ κἂν ἀκοῦσαι μόνον
The printed full stop separates κακόν from λόγον and is syntactically intrusive. The neuter αὐτό is also unusual if taken as an adjective modifying masculine λόγον, but it can defensibly be read adverbially or intensively. The translation therefore provisionally repunctuates but adopts no lexical emendation.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν ἀπατᾶν δυναμένων βίβλων τὸ μυστήριον
Rendered as: the mystery of the books capable of deceiving
The rendering preserves both the books’ stated capacity to deceive and the unexplained “mystery” associated with them.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν πολύθεον ὑπόληψιν· σύντροφον ἔχουσιν
Rendered as: have the polytheistic conception as a companion from their upbringing
σύντροφος can describe something reared together with a person and thus ingrained from upbringing, not merely a temporary companion. The printed high point is provisionally treated as intrusive.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὅμοιον ὀνείρῳ πλουσίῳ, κεκοσμημένον
Rendered as: ornamented ... resembling a sumptuous dream
πλούσιος is rendered “sumptuous” to convey a richly furnished dream; “a rich dream” is the more literal alternative.

6. Translation choice — Greek: δι’ εὐγνωμοσύνην
Rendered as: through good sense
εὐγνωμοσύνη here denotes sound or fair-minded judgment; “upright-mindedness” is also possible.

7. Translation choice — Greek: κακὸν. λόγον αὐτὸ κἂν ἀκοῦσαι μόνον
Rendered as: even so much as merely to hear an evil word
The printed stop is provisionally treated as intrusive, and αὐτό is understood adverbially or intensively with “hear merely.” If it were construed as agreeing directly with λόγον, masculine αὐτόν would be expected.

8. Translation choice — Greek: παντελῶς μεμφέσθω
Rendered as: blame ... at all
With the negative imperative, παντελῶς can mean “at all”; “blame altogether” or “blame utterly” remains possible.

9. Translation choice — Greek: εὐλόγως πρὸς δοκιμὴν ἔχοντα τυγχάνει
Rendered as: turn out reasonably to serve as a test
The idiom presents the false elements as having a rationally explicable testing function.

SECTION 3.5

And when I, Clement, heard this, I said, “What do you mean, lord, by saying that even the false elements in the Scriptures reasonably serve to test human beings?” He answered, “The false elements of the Scriptures were permitted to be written, at wickedness’s request, for a certain just reason. Here is what I mean by ‘reasonably’: In matters concerning God, the evil one, though loving God no less than the good one does, falls short of the good one in only one respect: he does not pardon even those who act impiously because of ignorance; out of affection for what is being treated impiously, he desires the destruction of those who act impiously and does not even offer them healing. For the good one wants to heal everyone through changes of heart, but saves only those who have come to know God. Yet he does not heal those who do not know—not because he does not want to, but because it is not permissible to grant the good things prepared for the sons of the kingdom to those who, because of their lack of discernment, have been likened to irrational animals.”

Translator's notes for section 3.5 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: Τὰ ψευδῆ τῶν γραφῶν
Rendered as: The false elements of the Scriptures
The substantivized adjective refers to what is false within the Scriptures; “the falsehoods of the Scriptures” is possible but can imply that the Scriptures as a whole are characterized as false.

2. Translation choice — Greek: αἰτήματι κακίας
Rendered as: at wickedness’s request
The genitive presents wickedness as the source or possessor of the request; the personification is retained.

3. Translation choice — Greek: δικαίῳ τινὶ λόγῳ
Rendered as: for a certain just reason
λόγος here can denote reason, rationale, or account; the dative states the just rationale under which the writing was permitted.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν ταῖς θεολογίαις
Rendered as: In matters concerning God
The plural can denote discourses, teachings, or matters concerning God. “In theological discussions” is a more narrowly discursive alternative.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν ταῖς θεολογίαις ὁ πονηρὸς τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ τὸν θεὸν οὐκ ἔλαττον ἀγαπῶν ἑνὶ μόνῳ ἀπολείπεται τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ
Rendered as: In matters concerning God, the evil one, though loving God no less than the good one does, falls short of the good one in only one respect
The substantivized adjectives are retained as the labels “the evil one” and “the good one” without identifying their bearers. The possible continuity of ὁ πονηρός with “the evil one” in 3.3, together with the subsequent healing and saving actions, supports reading them as personal agents. The generic alternative “a wicked person ... a good person” remains grammatically possible, while specific identifications are not supplied by this wording.

6. Translation choice — Greek: στοργῇ τῇ πρὸς τὸ ἀσεβούμενον
Rendered as: out of affection for what is being treated impiously
The substantivized neuter participle denotes the object against which impiety is directed without explicitly identifying it as a person.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ γὰρ ἀγαθὸς ἰᾶσθαι πάντας θέλει ταῖς μεταμελείαις
Rendered as: For the good one wants to heal everyone through changes of heart
The deponent infinitive ἰᾶσθαι has active force here and presents the good one as the agent who wants to heal everyone. The plural μεταμέλειαι can denote regrets, reconsiderations, or changes of heart.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ταῖς μεταμελείαις
Rendered as: through changes of heart
μεταμέλεια can denote regret, reconsideration, or a change of mind or heart. “Changes of heart” fits the healing context while keeping this term distinct from μετανοέω and μετάνοια.

9. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τὸ ἀδιάκριτον
Rendered as: because of their lack of discernment
The substantivized adjective denotes an undiscerning condition or inability to distinguish rightly.

SECTION 3.6

The nature of the one and only God, who made the world, created us, and provided everything, is naturally such that, in the case of anyone who is never within the bounds of reverence for God and does not blaspheme his holy spirit, it carries that person’s soul toward him by affection for him, in the form of an innate longing for him. Even if that person is a sinner, after being punished as his deeds deserve, it is in his nature to be saved. If someone denies him or in some other way speaks impiously against him, then repents, he will indeed be punished for the ways in which he sinned against him, but he will be saved, because after turning back he loved him. Perhaps, however, if there is an extraordinary degree of reverence and supplication, he will even be released from punishment, having presented his ignorance together with his repentance as grounds for forgiveness of the sin. Those, however, who have not repented will also meet their end through the punishment of fire, even if they are most devout in every other respect. But, as I said, after being punished with age-long fire for one fifth of a measured age, they will be extinguished. For those who have acted impiously against the eternal and only God can no longer exist forever.

Translator's notes for section 3.6 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: παντὸς οὐδήποτε ἐντὸς ὅρων θεοσεβείας ὄντος
The selected confirmed print has smooth-breathed οὐδήποτε, ordinarily never, and that negative is translated in the main text. Substantival παντός supplies the person in a genitive absolute, while never modifies ὄντος: anyone who is never within the bounds of reverence for God. This is syntactically defensible, although the qualification is contextually difficult beside coordinated nonblasphemy and innate longing for God. A distinctly hypothetical contextual correction changes the breathing to genitive indefinite οὑδήποτε, of anyone whatsoever, producing a positive qualification such as anyone whatsoever who is within the bounds. That proposal would change the negative meaning and is not the supplied Greek or the main translation. It remains only a labeled alternative; no source alteration, newly verified corrected wording, or unique original recovery is claimed.

2. Greek: ἐμφύτου εἰς αὐτὸν ἔρωτος · ἰδέᾳ.
The confirmed printed raised dot interrupts the natural construction in which ἰδέᾳ governs the preceding genitive phrase. Treating it as sentence-final would leave ἰδέᾳ isolated before the full stop. The translation therefore provisionally treats the raised dot as anomalous internal editorial punctuation and attaches ἰδέᾳ to the preceding words.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τοιαύτη πέφυκεν φύσις
Rendered as: is naturally such
Preserves the repeated nature language of πέφυκεν and φύσις while allowing the following infinitive to express what this nature characteristically does.

4. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτοῦ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα
Rendered as: his holy spirit
Preserves the possessive expression and descriptive wording without using English capitalization to settle personhood beyond what the Greek itself marks.

5. Translation choice — Greek: μετὰ τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ὧν ἔπραξεν κολασθῆναι σώζεσθαι φύσιν ἔχει
Rendered as: after being punished as his deeds deserve, it is in his nature to be saved
κατ’ ἀξίαν expresses punishment corresponding to the worth or deserts of the deeds, while φύσιν ἔχει continues the passage’s emphasis on nature.

6. Translation choice — Greek: μετανοήσει
Rendered as: repents
The response follows denial or impious speech and precedes the stated turning back and love, supporting moral-spiritual repentance under the October13 contextual policy. The later noun and negated participle receive the same cognate repentance terminology. The distinct ἐπιστρέψας remains after turning back rather than being merged with repent. No destination or intensifier is added, and the historical author's stated punishment-and-salvation framework is left intact.

7. Translation choice — Greek: συγγνώμης τῆς ἁμαρτίας μετὰ τῆς μετανοίας δεδωκὼς τὴν ἄγνοιαν
Rendered as: having presented his ignorance together with his repentance as grounds for forgiveness of the sin
The compact construction presents ignorance and repentance in relation to pardon. It may alternatively be understood as offering ignorance as an excuse for the sin, but the chosen wording preserves both elements without making ignorance itself absolve him. Repentance reflects the morally responsive context rather than a mere change of opinion; no new condition or causal formula is supplied.

8. Translation choice — Greek: μεμετρημένου αἰῶνος τὸ πέμπτον πυρὶ αἰωνίῳ κολασθέντες
Rendered as: after being punished with age-long fire for one fifth of a measured age
“Age-long” preserves the relation between αἰωνίῳ and αἰῶνος and fits the explicitly measured duration. “Eternal fire” is a possible lexical alternative, in which case the fire rather than each person’s punishment would be described as eternal.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἀποσβεσθήσονται
Rendered as: they will be extinguished
Preserves the image of something being put out rather than replacing it with an interpretive abstraction such as “annihilated.”

10. Translation choice — Greek: παντὸς οὐδήποτε ἐντὸς ὅρων θεοσεβείας ὄντος καὶ μὴ βλασφημοῦντος αὐτοῦ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα
Rendered as: in the case of anyone who is never within the bounds of reverence for God and does not blaspheme his holy spirit
The supplied smooth-breathed negative adverb is retained as never, with substantival παντός and participle ὄντος forming a genitive absolute. The coordinated nonblasphemy is also retained. The positive indefinite οὑδήποτε would be a different proposed reading, not a meaning licensed by this supplied negative form; it appears only as an explicitly hypothetical alternative in the source note. The contextual difficulty is not resolved by deleting or reversing the negative or adding a new theological condition.

SECTION 3.7

Impiety toward him, then, is for a person who is within the discourse of reverence for God to die saying that there is another god besides the one who truly exists—whether speaking of that other as superior, as inferior, or in any way whatever. For the one who truly exists is this one, whose form the human body bears and for whose sake heaven and all the stars, though superior in essence, submitted to serve the one inferior in essence because of the superior one’s form. God has benefited the human being so greatly beyond all others that, having loved the benefactor because of the multitude of benefits, the human being might, by that very love, be able to be preserved even into the second age.

Translator's notes for section 3.7 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν τῷ τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγῳ ὄντα
Rendered as: a person who is within the discourse of reverence for God
λόγος may denote discourse, teaching, or profession. “Discourse” preserves the wording without reducing it solely to either private belief or formal religious office.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τελευτᾶν λέγοντα
Rendered as: to die saying
τελευτᾶν can mean “die” or “come to an end,” while a possible alternative is “end by saying” or “finally say.” The death sense is chosen because the surrounding argument concerns what a person maintains until death and the next section again speaks of dying under a charge.

3. Translation choice — Greek: οὗ τὴν μορφὴν τὸ ἀνθρώπου βαστάζει σῶμα
Rendered as: whose form the human body bears
μορφή is rendered “form” rather than harmonized with the more familiar theological term “image,” and βαστάζει retains the concrete idea of bearing.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οὗ τὴν μορφὴν τὸ ἀνθρώπου βαστάζει σῶμα, οὗ εἵνεκεν ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ πάντες οἱ ἀστέρες ὑπέμειναν δουλεύειν
Rendered as: whose form the human body bears and for whose sake heaven and all the stars ... submitted to serve
The main rendering takes both successive occurrences of οὗ as referring to God. The second οὗ may instead refer to the human being or the human body just mentioned, yielding “for the human being’s sake” or “for the sake of the human body.” That alternative is supported by the ensuing statement that the heavenly bodies serve the inferior recipient and by the account of God’s benefits to humanity.

5. Translation choice — Greek: κατ’ οὐσίαν κρείττονες ὄντες, τῷ κατ’ οὐσίαν χείρονι
Rendered as: though superior in essence, submitted to serve the one inferior in essence
The repeated κατ’ οὐσίαν is preserved symmetrically. The Greek leaves the inferior recipient grammatically substantive; the context identifies it with the human being, but the translation does not insert that identification into the phrase.

6. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὸ πλῆθος τῶν εὐεργεσιῶν
Rendered as: because of the multitude of benefits
The preposition εἰς marks the multitude of benefits as the ground or occasion for loving the benefactor; “in response to” is also possible.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ αὐτῆς ἀγάπης καὶ εἰς τὸν δεύτερον αἰῶνα διασωθῆναι δυνηθῇ
Rendered as: might, by that very love, be able to be preserved even into the second age
“Be able” explicitly represents δυνηθῇ, which governs the infinitive διασωθῆναι, “to be preserved.” The ascensive “even” represents καί before the destination and emphasizes that preservation extends into the second age; the less emphatic “also into the second age” remains possible.

SECTION 3.8

Affection for God on the part of human beings is therefore sufficient for salvation. The evil one, however, knowing this, while we are eager to sow in the souls of those from the nations who are about to believe the immortality-giving affection that human beings direct toward the one and only God, himself strives, while possessing against the ignorant a weapon sufficient for destruction, to sow the notion of many gods, or even of one as superior, so that, having conceived and become jointly convinced of things that are unlawful, after dying as though under a charge of adultery they may be cast out of his kingdom.

Translator's notes for section 3.8 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτάρκης οὖν εἰς σωτηρίαν
Rendered as: is therefore sufficient for salvation
αὐτάρκης denotes being sufficient or adequate in oneself; the rendering preserves the passage’s explicit claim about affection and salvation.

2. Translation choice — Greek: εἰδὼς δὲ ὁ πονηρός, ἡμῶν σπευδόντων
Rendered as: The evil one, however, knowing this, while we are eager
The genitive absolute ἡμῶν σπευδόντων is rendered circumstantially, while the unexpressed object of εἰδώς is supplied as “this,” referring to the preceding claim that affection for God is sufficient for salvation. Alternatively, the effort expressed by the genitive absolute may be understood as the inferred content of his knowledge: “knowing that we are eager.” The chosen rendering more directly preserves the circumstantial construction, but both interpretations are contextually viable.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς ἀπὸ ἐθνῶν πιστεύειν μέλλουσιν
Rendered as: those from the nations who are about to believe
Retains the source’s “from the nations” wording rather than automatically importing the conventional label “Gentiles.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἀθανατοποιὸν πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀνθρώπων στοργήν
Rendered as: the immortality-giving affection that human beings direct toward him
ἀθανατοποιός describes the affection as producing immortality, not merely as immortal in quality; πρὸς αὐτόν marks its direction.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πολλῶν θεῶν ἢ καὶ ἑνὸς ὡς κρείττονος
Rendered as: many gods, or even one as superior
The ellipsis after ἑνός is retained: one god is implied, but the Greek does not restate whom that one is superior to.

6. Translation choice — Greek: συλλαβόντες
Rendered as: having conceived
The verb can mean “grasped” or “accepted,” but “conceived” continues the preceding image of seed being sown and anticipates the adultery image.

7. Translation choice — Greek: συνπεισθέντες ἃ μὴ θέμις
Rendered as: become jointly convinced of things that are unlawful
The συν- element indicates shared persuasion, though the Greek does not specify whether the sharing is with the evil one or with others who accept the notion. “Come to share belief in” is a viable alternative.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς αὐτοῦ βασιλείας
Rendered as: his kingdom
The pronoun is preserved. The argument points to God’s kingdom, although the evil one is the nearest explicitly named masculine referent.

SECTION 3.9

Everyone, therefore, is worthy of exclusion who has so much as wished to hear anything of that kind against God’s sole rule. But if anyone, emboldened by the Scriptures, dares even to hear something directed against God, let him first reflect with me on this: if someone constructs for himself a plausible doctrine in whatever way he wishes and then studies them closely, he will be able to cite from them many testimonies in support of the doctrine he fashioned. How, then, can anyone confidently rely on these writings against God, when everyone’s chosen view can be found in them?

Translator's notes for section 3.9 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς θεοῦ μοναρχίας
Rendered as: God’s sole rule
μοναρχία denotes rule by one. “Sole rule” preserves its theological force more transparently than the modern political term “monarchy.”

2. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτὸ μόνον κἂν ἀκοῦσαί τι τοιοῦτον θελήσας
Rendered as: who has so much as wished to hear anything of that kind
The wording stresses that the mere willingness even to listen is enough for the stated condemnation.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς γραφαῖς τεθαρρηκὼς
Rendered as: emboldened by the Scriptures
γραφαί may be rendered generically as “writings,” but the continuing references to scriptural testimonies and passages support “the Scriptures” here.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εὔλογον ἑαυτῷ δόγμα ὡς βούλεται ἀναπλάσῃ
Rendered as: constructs for himself a plausible doctrine in whatever way he wishes
εὔλογον can mean reasonable or plausible. “Plausible” suits the argument that a person first fabricates a position and then seeks supporting texts.

5. Translation choice — Greek: αὐταῖς ἐνκύψῃ
Rendered as: studies them closely
ἐγκύπτω literally suggests bending over or peering into something and idiomatically denotes close examination.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν αἷς ἡ πάντων βουλὴ εἰσευρίσκεται
Rendered as: when everyone’s chosen view can be found in them
βουλή can mean counsel, purpose, will, or opinion. The context concerns finding textual support for whatever doctrine one wants, so “chosen view” is adopted; “everyone’s counsel” would be more formally literal but less clear in context.

SECTION 3.10

For instance, Simon, who is to debate with us tomorrow, dares to argue publicly against God’s sole rule, intending to bring forward many statements from the Scriptures themselves to the effect that there are many gods and that a certain one—not the one who created the world—is higher than the latter; and correspondingly he can furnish written proofs. We too can clearly point out many passages from the same Scriptures showing that this one, the one who created the world, is the one God, and that “there is no other except him.” Yet if anyone wishes to speak in some other way, he too will be able to provide proofs from them, in whatever way he wishes and about whatever he wishes. For the Scriptures say everything, so that none of those who search ungratefully may find the truth, but rather what he wants, while the truth is reserved for the grateful. Gratitude consists in preserving intact one’s affection for the one responsible for our existence.

Translator's notes for section 3.10 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτίκα γοῦν
Rendered as: For instance
The phrase introduces Simon as an immediate illustration of the preceding general claim; “at any rate, immediately” would preserve the particles more formally.

2. Translation choice — Greek: κατὰ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ μοναρχίας
Rendered as: against God’s sole rule
Renders μοναρχία as the rule of one rather than using a modern political label.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πολλὰς ἐξ αὐτῶν τῶν γραφῶν φωνὰς ἐνεγκεῖν
Rendered as: to bring forward many statements from the Scriptures themselves
φωναί literally means voices or utterances; “statements” fits citations taken from written texts while preserving their asserted content.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἷς δέ τις οὐχ ὁ τὸν κόσμον κτίσας τούτου ἀνώτερος
Rendered as: a certain one—not the one who created the world—is higher than the latter
The main text takes τούτου to refer to the world-creator. It could grammatically refer instead to the world, yielding “higher than this world.” The creator-reference is chosen because the surrounding argument contrasts the creator with an allegedly superior god, and the following sentence identifies the creator as the one God.

5. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ὁμῶς τὰς ἀποδείξεις ἐγγράφους ἔχει παρασχεῖν
Rendered as: and correspondingly he can furnish written proofs
The printed ὁμῶς means “equally” or “likewise,” hence “correspondingly.” “Nevertheless” would normally represent differently accented ὅμως and is not adopted.

6. Translation choice — Greek: πολλὰς περικοπὰς
Rendered as: many passages
περικοπαί are portions or sections cut from a larger text, naturally rendered here as scriptural passages.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν ἀγνωμόνως ζητούντων
Rendered as: those who search ungratefully
ἀγνωμόνως may also mean without judgment or unreasonably. The author’s immediate definition of εὐγνωμοσύνη as preserving affection for one’s benefactor supports the gratitude sense here.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἵνα μηδεὶς τῶν ἀγνωμόνως ζητούντων τὸ ἀληθὲς εὕρῃ, ἀλλ’ ὃ βούλεται
Rendered as: so that none of those who search ungratefully may find the truth, but rather what he wants
The main text takes τὸ ἀληθές as the object of εὕρῃ, in contrast with the second object, ὃ βούλεται. It is also grammatically possible to attach τὸ ἀληθές to ζητούντων and understand an unstated object for εὕρῃ: “those who search for the truth ungratefully may not find it, but rather what they want.” The explicit contrast between the two objects favors the chosen attachment.

9. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ ἀληθοῦς τοῖς εὐγνώμοσιν τετηρημένου
Rendered as: while the truth is reserved for the grateful
εὐγνώμων can mean right-minded, fair, or grateful. “Grateful” maintains the contrast with ἀγνωμόνως and anticipates the next sentence’s definition.

10. Translation choice — Greek: εὐγνωμοσύνη δέ ἐστιν τὸ τὴν πρὸς τὸν τοῦ εἶναι ἡμᾶς αἴτιον ἀποσώζειν στοργήν
Rendered as: Gratitude consists in preserving intact one’s affection for the one responsible for our existence
ἀποσώζειν conveys keeping or preserving safely and intact. “Gratitude” fits the benefactor relationship expressed by affection toward the cause of human existence, though “right-mindedness” remains a lexical alternative.

SECTION 3.11

Therefore, before everything else, one ought to know that one finds it nowhere except from a prophet of truth. A true prophet is one who always knows everything, including the thoughts of everyone, and is sinless, as one fully assured concerning God’s judgment. Therefore, we ought not to consider his foreknowledge superficially, but to ask whether his foreknowledge can subsist without any other basis. For physicians foretell things while having the sick person’s pulse as material laid before them; some do so by means of birds, others by means of sacrificial victims, and still others foretell while having many other different materials laid before them—and they are not prophets.

Translator's notes for section 3.11 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτὴν
Rendered as: it
The feminine pronoun’s antecedent lies outside the supplied passage; “it” preserves the unresolved reference, probably to truth.

2. Translation choice — Greek: προφήτου ἀληθείας
Rendered as: a prophet of truth
Retains the source’s genitive expression rather than replacing it with the interpretive “true prophet,” which appears explicitly in the next sentence.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς περὶ θεοῦ κρίσεως πεπληροφορημένος
Rendered as: as one fully assured concerning God’s judgment
πεπληροφορημένος denotes being fully convinced or assured; “fully informed concerning God’s judgment” is also possible.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἄνευ ἑτέρας προφάσεως
Rendered as: without any other basis
In context πρόφασις denotes an external ground, occasion, or means on which prediction depends; “pretext” is the more usual alternative in other contexts.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὑποβεβλημένην ὕλην
Rendered as: material laid before them
The phrase presents the pulse and divinatory objects as supplied material underlying the predictions.

SECTION 3.12

If someone should wish to say that what comes through predictions of this kind is like truly innate foreknowledge, he is greatly deceived. Such things disclose only what is present, and even that only if they speak truly. In another way, however, they too are useful to me, for they establish that foreknowledge exists. But the foreknowledge of the sole and true one knows not only the present; it extends prophecy without limit as far as the coming age itself, and needs nothing for understanding. He does not prophesy obscure and ambiguous things so as to make what is said require another prophet for understanding, but explicit and plain things, just as our teacher, being also a prophet, knew everything at all times through an innate and ever-flowing spirit.

Translator's notes for section 3.12 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: μὴ προφητεύων
The former Lagarde reading is exactly καὶ προφητειῶν. The selected reading μὴ προφητεύων is independently read from Dressel's 1853 main print. Dressel's apparatus attributes μὴ to Davisius: this is an editorial reading, not a newly collated manuscript or proof of uniquely recovered original wording. The selected negative and participle are translated, while their loose personal referent is disclosed separately.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν διὰ τῶν τοιούτων προρρήσεων τῇ ὄντως ἐνφύτῳ προγνώσει ὁμοίαν εἶναι
Rendered as: what comes through predictions of this kind is like truly innate foreknowledge
The first feminine article implies the foreknowledge claimed through such predictions. What comes through predictions represents that understood object without treating predictions themselves as the same thing as innate foreknowledge.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ δὲ τοῦ μόνου καὶ ἀληθοῦς πρόγνωσις
Rendered as: the foreknowledge of the sole and true one
The masculine substantivized adjectives identify a person, contextually the true prophet, whose foreknowledge is distinguished from the other predictions. The main text does not supply God as a uniquely established referent, and retains both sole and true.

4. Translation choice — Greek: μὴ προφητεύων ἀμαυρὰ καὶ ἀμφίβολα, ἵνα ἄλλου προφήτου χρείαν ἔχῃ τὰ λεγόμενα πρὸς ἐπίγνωσιν
Rendered as: He does not prophesy obscure and ambiguous things so as to make what is said require another prophet for understanding
The masculine nominative participle does not agree with feminine foreknowledge; it is read as resuming the person described by the genitive sole and true one, with a loose shift of construction. The later teacher-prophet is another possible contextual identification of that person. The negative governs obscure prophecy with its resulting need for another interpreter, not the existence of prophecy itself. No change to the selected Greek's case or gender is supplied.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἐνφύτῳ καὶ ἀεννάῳ πνεύματι
Rendered as: through an innate and ever-flowing spirit
Both adjectives describe the spirit through which the teacher knows. Ever-flowing preserves the continuous-flow image rather than replacing it simply with eternal or intermittent inspiration.

SECTION 3.13

Therefore, he confidently gave an account of what was going to happen—I mean sufferings, places, and limits. For, being an unerring prophet, surveying everything with the boundless eye of the soul, he knows it all while himself escaping notice. But if we too admit, as most people do, that even the true prophet has foreknowledge not always but only at times—when he has the spirit and, for that reason, foreknows, but when he does not have it, is ignorant—if we suppose this, we will both deceive ourselves and lay snares for others. For such a thing belongs to those madly inspired by a spirit of disorder, those becoming drunk beside altars and being filled with the reek of burnt fat.

Translator's notes for section 3.13 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: πάθη, τόπους, ὅρους
Rendered as: sufferings, places, and limits
ὅροι can denote boundaries, limits, or termini; “limits” preserves the term without conflating it with the explicitly named times in 3.15.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπείρῳ ψυχῆς ὀφθαλμῷ
Rendered as: with the boundless eye of the soul
Preserves both the singular eye image and ἄπειρος in its sense of boundless or unlimited.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπίσταται λανθάνων
Rendered as: he knows it all while himself escaping notice
λανθάνων most naturally describes the prophet as remaining unnoticed while knowing; “he knows secretly” is a possible but less formally precise alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἄλλους ἐνεδρεύσομεν
Rendered as: lay snares for others
ἐνεδρεύω denotes lying in wait for or entrapping someone, not merely leading someone into an intellectual error.

5. Translation choice — Greek: κνίσης ἐνφορουμένων
Rendered as: being filled with the reek of burnt fat
κνίσα is the smoke, steam, or odor of sacrificial fat; “being filled with sacrificial fumes” is a less vivid alternative.

SECTION 3.14

For if someone wishing to profess prophecy is allowed to have it believed, in the matters in which he is caught as a liar, that at that time he did not have the holy spirit of foreknowledge, he will not be easy to expose, though he is a prophet who is a liar. For in the cases where, while saying many things, he hits upon a few, he is then believed to have the spirit. Moreover, he speaks of first things as last and last things as first, things that have happened as things that will happen, and things that will happen as though they had already happened. He also says other, incoherent things, things stolen from others and transformed, and some things curtailed, shapeless, senseless, ambiguous, crooked, and unclear, all loudly proclaiming utter unintelligibility.

Translator's notes for section 3.14 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ τῆς προγνώσεως ἅγιον οὐκ εἶχεν πνεῦμα
Rendered as: he did not have the holy spirit of foreknowledge
Preserves the source’s attributive relation between the holy spirit and foreknowledge without imposing a later doctrinal identification.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς πολλὰ λέγων ὀλίγα ἐπιτυγχάνει
Rendered as: while saying many things, he hits upon a few
ἐπιτυγχάνει describes occasionally hitting the mark or obtaining a correct result among numerous claims.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐξ ἄλλων ὑφῃρημένα
Rendered as: things stolen from others
ὑφαιρέω can mean taking something away secretly; “appropriated from others” is a less pointed alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: μεμειωμένα
Rendered as: curtailed
The perfect passive describes things reduced, diminished, or mutilated; “curtailed” fits the treatment of allegedly defective predictions.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἀνείδεα
Rendered as: shapeless
The printed spelling supports ἀνειδής, “without form, shapeless, unsightly,” rather than ἀναιδής, “shameless.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: πάσης κεκραγότα δυσσυνειδησίας
Rendered as: all loudly proclaiming utter unintelligibility
The main text takes δυσσυνειδησία as difficulty of comprehension, continuing the immediately preceding descriptions senseless, ambiguous, crooked, and unclear. Utter expresses the totality of πάσης, while loudly proclaiming retains the statements' shouting image. The material moral alternative is all loudly proclaiming every kind of guilty conscience, reading the distorted and appropriated statements as exposing their speaker's fraudulent conscience; unscrupulousness is a related moral extension. The surrounding obscurity list favors the comprehension reading, but does not eliminate the moral one.

SECTION 3.15

But our teacher resorted to no such trickery. Rather, as I said earlier, being a prophet who always knew everything by an innate and ever-flowing spirit, he confidently set things out, clearly foretelling sufferings, places, fixed times, ways, and limits. For example, when foretelling about the sanctuary, he said, “Do you see these buildings? Amen, I tell you, not one stone upon another will be left here that will not be torn down,” and, “This generation will certainly not pass away, and the demolition will have its beginning. For they will come and encamp here and throw up an encircling stockade and slaughter your children here.” Likewise, he spoke what follows in a clear voice, things that we are able to see with our own eyes, so that, in the matters about which the word was spoken, the deed might also occur. For the prophet of truth frames the statement of proof to produce faith in those who hear.

Translator's notes for section 3.15 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδέν τι τοιοῦτο ἐγοητεύσατο
Rendered as: resorted to no such trickery
γοητεύω can denote practicing sorcery, bewitching, or deceiving as a charlatan; “trickery” preserves the polemical accusation without requiring a claim of literal magic.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐμφύτῳ καὶ ἀεννάῳ πνεύματι
Rendered as: by an innate and ever-flowing spirit
The same expression as in 3.12, apart from the printed spelling ἐμφύτῳ, is rendered consistently; “by an innate and unceasing spirit” is also possible.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐνπροθέσμους χρόνους
Rendered as: fixed times
The adjective describes times set or bounded in advance; “appointed times” is a viable alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: περὶ τοῦ ἁγιάσματος
Rendered as: about the sanctuary
ἁγίασμα denotes a holy place or sanctuary; “temple” would make the contextual identification more explicit than the source does.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἀμὴν ὑμῖν λέγω
Rendered as: Amen, I tell you
Retains the distinctive introductory formula rather than replacing it with the familiar interpretive rendering “Truly, I tell you.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: καθιοῦσιν ἐνταῦθα
Rendered as: encamp here
The future form conveys sitting or settling down; in the military context, “encamp” is natural, while “sit down here” is the more literal alternative.

7. Translation choice — Greek: περιχαρακώσουσιν
Rendered as: throw up an encircling stockade
The verb denotes enclosing with a palisade or stockade. The Greek supplies no explicit object, so the English likewise avoids specifying whom or what is enclosed.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ὁμῶς
Rendered as: Likewise
The adverb can mean “equally” or “all the same.” “Nevertheless” is possible, but continuation by similarity best fits the immediate context.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἵνα ἐφ᾽ ὧν ὁ λόγος ἐρρέθη, καὶ τὸ ἔργον γένηται
Rendered as: so that, in the matters about which the word was spoken, the deed might also occur
The main text takes ἐφ᾽ ὧν as neuter and topical, referring to the matters about which the statement was made. If ὧν is understood personally and interpreted temporally from the generational context, an alternative is “so that the deed too might occur in the days of those in whose days the word was spoken.” The topical reading avoids supplying an unexpressed noun meaning “days,” while the personal-temporal alternative remains contextually possible.

10. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς γὰρ πίστιν ἀκουόντων τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀποδείξεως ὁ τῆς ἀληθείας ποιεῖται προφήτης
Rendered as: For the prophet of truth frames the statement of proof to produce faith in those who hear
λόγον ποιεῖσθαι can mean formulating or delivering an account, while πρὸς πίστιν states its intended effect. “Gives an account of the demonstration for the faith of the hearers” is a more formal alternative.

SECTION 3.16

Nevertheless, there are many heralds of error, all having one leader of wickedness. For that reason there is one herald of the truth, himself also the leader of piety, who in their proper times will have as prophets all who are found pure. The chief reason people have gone astray has been this: they did not first understand the principle of pairing, which I will not cease setting out for you separately, on each occasion, in outline; for speaking point by point is a lengthy task. Therefore, be truth-loving judges for me of what is said.

Translator's notes for section 3.16 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἰδία
The image-checked edition prints ἰδία, a morphologically unexpected form in this adverbial position. The translation provisionally understands it as “separately” or “privately”; the printed form is preserved and is not treated as an OCR error.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ᾧ λόγῳ τῆς ἀληθείας εἷς
Rendered as: For that reason there is one herald of the truth
The singular noun is implicit from the preceding κήρυκες; “for that reason” renders the causal ᾧ λόγῳ.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν ἰδίοις καιροῖς
Rendered as: in their proper times
The phrase is taken with the prophets as referring to their respective times; attachment to the singular herald remains possible.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν τῆς συζυγίας λόγον
Rendered as: the principle of pairing
λόγος denotes an account or principle, while συζυγία is the work’s technical language for a paired relation; “doctrine of the pairs” is also possible.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἑκάστοτε
Rendered as: on each occasion
The adverb indicates recurrence on every relevant occasion, rather than merely occurring from time to time.

6. Translation choice — Greek: κεφαλαιωδῶς
Rendered as: in outline
The adverb indicates a summary treatment by principal points rather than a full exposition.

7. Translation choice — Greek: πολὺ γὰρ τὸ κατ᾽ εἶδος λέγειν
Rendered as: for speaking point by point is a lengthy task
κατ᾽ εἶδος means treating the matter specifically or item by item, while πολύ indicates its considerable extent.

SECTION 3.17

I will now begin speaking. If someone refuses to grant that the great and holy spirit of the foreknowledge of God, who made all things, was infused into the man brought to term by his hands, how does the person who assigns it to another—one born from a foul drop—not sin most gravely? I do not think that person obtains forgiveness, even if he is deceived by spurious scripture into thinking dreadful things against the father of all. For anyone who insults an image—and an eternal king’s image at that—commits that sin against the one in whose likeness the image happened to be. “But,” he says, “the divine spirit left him after he sinned.” Then it sinned along with him. And how is the one who says this not in danger? “No, he had received the spirit after he sinned.” Then it has been given to unrighteous people. And where is justice? “But it is supplied to righteous and unrighteous alike.” This is the most unjust thing of all. Thus every falsehood, even if supported by ten thousand contrivances, is bound to meet its refutation even within a short time.

Translator's notes for section 3.17 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ ὑπὸ χειρῶν αὐτοῦ κυοφορηθέντι ἀνθρώπῳ
Rendered as: into the man brought to term by his hands
κυοφορέω carries a gestational image, here paradoxically associated with God’s hands; “formed by his hands” would suppress that image.

2. Translation choice — Greek: δῴη τις ἐγχέναι
Rendered as: refuses to grant that ... was infused
The construction leaves the agency of the active infinitive ἐγχέναι implicit. The passive English keeps the spirit as what is infused without supplying an explicit agent; “grant that God infused” is a viable alternative.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ νόθου γραφῆς
Rendered as: by spurious scripture
νόθος marks the writing as illegitimate or inauthentic, and γραφή in this context can denote a purported scriptural writing; “spurious writing” is also possible.

4. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ταῦτα αἰωνίου βασιλέως
Rendered as: and an eternal king’s image at that
καὶ ταῦτα is an emphatic idiom highlighting the especially serious identity of the person represented by the image.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἁμαρτίαν εἰς ἐκεῖνον ἀναφερομένην ἔχει, οὗπερ καθ᾽ ὁμοίωσιν ἡ εἰκὼν ἐτύγχανεν οὖσα
Rendered as: commits that sin against the one in whose likeness the image happened to be
The sin is directed against the person represented by the insulted image; the wording does not transfer the offender’s culpability to that person. More literally, one “has the sin referred against that one.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: οὐκοῦν συνήμαρτεν
Rendered as: Then it sinned along with him
The compound verb presents the spirit as sharing in the man’s sin, which is the reductio advanced by the author.

7. Translation choice — Greek: κἂν μυρίαις ἐπινοίαις βοηθῆται
Rendered as: even if supported by ten thousand contrivances
The rendering preserves μυρίαις as “ten thousand,” though it can idiomatically mean “countless,” and takes ἐπίνοιαι as devised arguments or contrivances.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν ἔλεγχον κἂν ἐν μικρῷ χρόνῳ λαβεῖν ἔχει
Rendered as: is bound to meet its refutation even within a short time
ἔχει with the infinitive expresses an assured outcome, and ἔλεγχος here is exposure or refutation.

SECTION 3.18

Do not be deceived. Our father was ignorant of nothing, since even the law laid down publicly, while concealing him beneath a veil of allegory because of the unworthy, refers those who yearn for truth back to him, saying, “Examine your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will report to you.” It was this father one had to seek, these elders one had to seek out. But you did not seek to learn to whom the time of the kingdom belongs, or to whom the chair of prophecy belongs, even though he disclosed himself by saying, “The scribes and the Pharisees sat on Moses’ chair. Everything they tell you, listen to them.” He said “them” because they had been entrusted with the key of the kingdom, which is knowledge. It alone can open the gate of life, and through it alone it is possible to enter eternal life. “But yes,” he says, “they possess the key, yet they do not provide it to those who wish to enter.”

Translator's notes for section 3.18 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν
Rendered as: our father
The designation is retained without inserting a name or capitalizing it, since the immediate wording does not make the referent explicit.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἀλληγορίας ἐγκαλύμματι
Rendered as: beneath a veil of allegory
ἐγκάλυμμα is a covering or veil, and the law is depicted as concealing the father through allegorical presentation.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπ’ αὐτὸν ἀναπέμπει
Rendered as: refers ... back to him
ἀναπέμπω can mean sending or referring someone back to another person or authority.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τίνος ἐστὶν ὁ τῆς βασιλείας χρόνος, τίνος ἡ τῆς προφητείας καθέδρα
Rendered as: to whom the time of the kingdom belongs, or to whom the chair of prophecy belongs
The repeated genitive τίνος asks whose these prerogatives are; the English supplies “belongs” without identifying the person.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν κλεῖδα τῆς βασιλείας πεπιστευμένων
Rendered as: they had been entrusted with the key of the kingdom
The passive perfect of πιστεύω here means being entrusted with something, not merely believing it.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἥτις ἐστὶν γνῶσις, ἡ μόνη τὴν πύλην τῆς ζωῆς ἀνοῖξαι δύναται, δι’ ἧς μόνης
Rendered as: which is knowledge. It alone can open the gate of life, and through it alone
The repeated feminine forms are taken as referring to knowledge. Because πύλη is also feminine and nearer to δι’ ἧς, “through which gate alone” remains grammatically possible.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἀλλὰ ναί
Rendered as: But yes
The emphatic response concedes possession of the key before contrasting the refusal to provide it.

SECTION 3.19

For this reason, I say, he himself rose from the chair. Like a father acting on behalf of children, he proclaimed what had from eternity been handed down secretly to the worthy; he extended mercy even to the nations and had compassion on the souls of all, while disregarding his own blood. For he, having been deemed worthy to be king of the coming age, against the one who had now received the kingdom under a time-limited law.... And the greatest thing, which distressed him intensely, is this: those on whose behalf he waged the battle as for children were themselves fighting against him because of ignorance. And yet he loved even those who hated him, wept for those who disobeyed, blessed those who reviled him, and prayed for those who treated him as an enemy. He did not do only these things as a father, but also taught his own disciples to do similar things with the attitude they would have toward brothers. This is a father; this is a prophet; this is what is fitting: for him to reign over his own children, so that through the affection that goes from a father to children and the children’s heartfelt honor toward their father, eternal peace might be able to arise. For when the fitting ruler reigns, genuine joy concerning the ruler comes upon those who are ruled.

Translator's notes for section 3.19 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: τὴν βασιλείαν.... καὶ
The selected edition prints a lacuna of exactly four dots after βασιλείαν, leaving the preceding construction without its unavailable continuation. The English retains all four dots, and no restoration has been supplied.

2. Greek: ἐνπροθέσμῳ
The image-checked edition prints ἐνπροθέσμῳ, apparently an unassimilated or irregular spelling of the compound ordinarily written with μ before π. Its meaning remains recoverable, but this interpretation is provisional and the form is not treated as an OCR error.

3. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτὸς τῆς καθέδρας ἐγερθείς
Rendered as: he himself rose from the chair
The wording continues the chair imagery of the preceding section; ἐγερθείς is rendered as rising from it rather than merely being raised up.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ ἀπὸ αἰῶνος ἐν κρυπτῷ ἀξίοις παραδιδόμενα
Rendered as: what had from eternity been handed down secretly to the worthy
ἀπὸ αἰῶνος may also mean “from of old” or “from the beginning of the age”; the rendering retains its broad temporal force without supplying a starting event.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἰδίου αἵματος ἠμέλει
Rendered as: disregarding his own blood
The literal image is retained. It may refer to accepting the shedding of his blood or, more generally, neglecting his own life and safety.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἐνπροθέσμῳ ... νόμῳ
Rendered as: under a time-limited law
The compound denotes something governed by a fixed term or deadline; “under a law with a fixed term” is a more literal alternative.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπ’ αὐτῶν ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ ἐπολεμεῖτο
Rendered as: were themselves fighting against him because of ignorance
The passive verb depicts him as the object of their hostility, while ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ gives ignorance as its cause.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς αὐτοῦ μαθηταῖς ὡς πρὸς ἀδελφοὺς ἔχοντας τὰ ὅμοια ποιεῖν ἐδίδασκεν
Rendered as: taught his own disciples to do similar things with the attitude they would have toward brothers
The main rendering understands ἔχειν πρός relationally, with ὡς preserving the comparison to conduct toward brothers. Alternatively, ἔχοντας with the infinitive may express obligation: “taught his disciples that they had to do similar things as toward brothers.”

9. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦτο εὔλογον ... τοῦ γὰρ εὐλόγου βασιλεύοντος
Rendered as: this is what is fitting ... when the fitting ruler reigns
The repeated εὔλογος language can mean reasonable, fitting, or rightful. “Fitting” connects the claim that he should reign with the character of his rule; “when a reasonable ruler reigns” is also possible.

SECTION 3.20

Nevertheless, I return to the first argument concerning the truth. If someone does not grant that the man brought to term by God’s hands has the Messiah’s holy spirit, how is he not committing the greatest impiety by granting that some other person, born from a foul drop, has it? Rather, he acts with the greatest piety if he does not grant that another has it, but says that that one alone has it—the one who, from the beginning of the age, changing forms together with names, courses through the age until, having reached his own times and having been anointed by God’s mercy because of his labors, he will have rest forever. That one has been honored with ruling and exercising dominion over everything in air, on earth, and in waters. In addition, he received the breath of the very one who made man—an unbreakable covering for the soul—so that he might be able to be immortal.

Translator's notes for section 3.20 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ ἅγιον χριστοῦ ... πνεῦμα
Rendered as: the Messiah’s holy spirit
χριστός functions independently as a title, so it is rendered “Messiah.” The genitive relates the spirit to the Messiah without deciding whether possession, identity, or source is foremost; “the holy spirit of Christ” is an alternative form.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ ὑπὸ χειρῶν θεοῦ κυοφορηθέντι ἀνθρώπῳ
Rendered as: the man brought to term by God’s hands
The rendering retains the unusual gestational force of κυοφορηθέντι together with the explicit image of God’s hands.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς αἰῶνος ... τὸν αἰῶνα τρέχει
Rendered as: from the beginning of the age ... courses through the age
The repeated rendering preserves the source’s repetition of αἰών and its portrayal of movement throughout the age.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἅμα τοῖς ὀνόμασιν μορφὰς ἀλλάσσων
Rendered as: changing forms together with names
Both changing forms and corresponding names are retained without identifying particular manifestations not named here.

5. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τοὺς καμάτους θεοῦ ἐλέει χρισθείς
Rendered as: having been anointed by God’s mercy because of his labors
χρισθείς is rendered “anointed” to preserve its relation to the title Messiah, while διά with the accusative gives the labors as the reason; “on account of his toils” is an alternative.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἄρχειν τε καὶ κυριεύειν ... τετίμηται
Rendered as: has been honored with ruling and exercising dominion
The two infinitives preserve the distinction between governing and holding dominion as the honor granted to him.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν πνοὴν ἔσχεν, ψυχῆς ἄρρηκτον περιβολήν
Rendered as: he received the breath ... an unbreakable covering for the soul
The second phrase is taken in apposition to the breath. The genitive ψυχῆς may alternatively be rendered “an unbreakable covering of the soul,” but the context supports a covering bestowed upon and protecting the soul.

SECTION 3.21

This very man, who alone was a true prophet, appropriately assigned names to each living creature according to the worth of its nature, just as the one who made him did. For whatever he named, that was also the name given by the maker to what had come into being. Why, then, did he still need to partake of a plant so that he might know just what good or evil is? “He was commanded.” But the undiscerning believe these things, supposing that an irrational beast had become more beneficent than God, who created both them and everything.

Translator's notes for section 3.21 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: κατ᾿ ἀξίαν τῆς φύσεως
Rendered as: according to the worth of its nature
Preserves ἀξία as worth or corresponding value; “according to what was fitting for its nature” is a smoother possible rendering.

2. Translation choice — Greek: καθὼς ὁ πεποιηκὼς αὐτόν
Rendered as: just as the one who made him did
The masculine αὐτόν refers to the man, not to the neuter ζῷον. The comparison leaves its predicate implicit: it most naturally compares the man’s naming with the maker’s action, though it could compare the appropriateness of the naming with how the maker formed him.

3. Translation choice — Greek: εἴ τι γὰρ ἐπωνόμασεν
Rendered as: For whatever he named
The conditional wording literally permits “if he named anything,” but in context it functions as a general statement about every name he assigned.

4. Translation choice — Greek: φυτοῦ χρείαν εἶχε προσλαβεῖν
Rendered as: did he still need to partake of a plant
The partitive genitive φυτοῦ is retained without inserting an unattested fruit; προσλαβεῖν may denote taking or partaking.

5. Translation choice — Greek: „ἐνετέλλετο“
Rendered as: “He was commanded.”
Reads the middle-passive form passively, as an abrupt reply concerning the man. Since ἐντέλλομαι commonly functions as a deponent meaning “command,” the alternative “[the maker] was commanding” or “he commanded” remains grammatically possible.

SECTION 3.22

Nevertheless, a female nature was jointly created as a mate for this man, falling far short of him, as participation falls short of essence, the moon of the sun, and fire of light. She, ruling as a female over the present world, which resembles her, is believed to be the first prophetess, professing prophecy together with all those “among those born of women.” But the other, being male as “Son of Man,” also prophesies the superior things for the coming age as a male age.

Translator's notes for section 3.22 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἀποδέουσα -αὐτοῦ
The selected print places an anomalous hyphen immediately before αὐτοῦ. The translation provisionally treats it as nonlexical punctuation and takes αὐτοῦ as the genitive complement of ἀποδέουσα.

2. Greek: ὡς ἡλίου σελήνη; ὡς φωτὸς τὸ πῦρ
The selected print has a Greek question mark between two parallel comparisons. It may be deliberate editorial punctuation, but it interrupts the continuing comparative construction; the translation provisionally punctuates the sequence continuously.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς οὐσίας μετουσία
Rendered as: as participation falls short of essence
Carries forward the idea of falling short from ἀποδέουσα. The compact phrase literally juxtaposes participation and essence.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ νῦν κόσμου ὡς θήλεια ὁμοίου ἄρχουσα
Rendered as: ruling as a female over the present world, which resembles her
Takes ὁμοίου with κόσμου and understands her as the contextually supplied standard of likeness. “Ruling as a female over the corresponding present world” is also possible.

5. Translation choice — Greek: προφητείαν ἐπαγγελλομένη
Rendered as: professing prophecy
Here ἐπαγγέλλομαι can describe professing or laying claim to prophecy; “promising prophecy” remains possible.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ διαφέροντα
Rendered as: the superior things
διαφέροντα can denote things that excel, fitting the contrast between the present and coming ages. It can alternatively mean “the things that differ.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ τὰ διαφέροντα ὡς ἄρσενι τῷ μέλλοντι αἰῶνι προφητεύει
Rendered as: also prophesies the superior things for the coming age as a male age
The dative ἄρσενι agrees with τῷ μέλλοντι αἰῶνι, characterizing the coming age as male in contrast with the female present world; it does not merely state what befits the male prophet.

SECTION 3.23

Let there be, then, two generic prophecies for us: the masculine one (and let it be specified that the first, being male, has thereafter been placed second according to the principle of progression, whereas the second, being female, was appointed to come first in the procession of the pairs)—the one, then, who is “among those born of women,” professing prophecy as the female belonging to the present world, wants to be believed to be masculine. Therefore, stealing the male’s seeds and attending to them with her own seeds of the flesh, she brings forth the offspring together as though they were all her own—that is, the words. And she promises to give present earthly wealth as a dowry, wishing to exchange the slow for the quick, the brief for the greater.

Translator's notes for section 3.23 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: δύο οὖν ἡμῖν γενικαὶ ἔστωσαν προφητεῖαι
Rendered as: Let there be, then, two generic prophecies for us
