γενικαί describes prophecies belonging to broad kinds or classes; “universal prophecies” is another possible rendering.

2. Translation choice — Greek: κατὰ τὸν τῆς προόδου λόγον
Rendered as: according to the principle of progression
λόγος denotes the governing principle or rationale, while πρόοδος describes progression or procession.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν τῇ τῶν συζυγιῶν προελεύσει
Rendered as: in the procession of the pairs
συζυγίαι are paired counterparts, while προέλευσις can denote their procession or ordered sequence.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς ἰδίοις τῆς σαρκὸς σπέρμασιν ἐπισκέπτουσα
Rendered as: attending to them with her own seeds of the flesh
Retains the exact printed participle ἐπισκέπτουσα, from ἐπισκέπτομαι, which can mean inspecting, visiting, or attending to something; the stolen male seeds are understood as its implicit object. “Inspecting them with her own seeds” is lexically possible but less natural in context. The earlier rendering “covering them” would correspond more directly to a different form, ἐπισκέπουσα, which is not the supplied reading and is not adopted as a correction.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ὅλα ἴδια συνεκφέρει τὰ γεννήματα
Rendered as: she brings forth the offspring together as though they were all her own
Preserves both the claim that all the offspring are represented as hers and the συν- force of συνεκφέρει, which links what comes from the two sets of seeds.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ ταχεῖ τὸ βραδύ, τὸ βραχὺ τῷ μείζονι ὑπαλλάξαι
Rendered as: to exchange the slow for the quick, the brief for the greater
Treats the accusatives as what is exchanged for the dative counterparts. The direction of exchange can be construed in reverse with ὑπαλλάσσω.

SECTION 3.24

Yet she not only dares to speak and hear of many gods, but also gives assurance that she herself will become one; and in the hope of becoming what she does not possess by nature, she also destroys what she does possess. And as a female, when she comes into her menstrual periods, she is stained with blood under the pretext of sacrifices and so defiles those who touch her. And whenever, after conceiving, she gives birth to temporary kings who shed much blood, she stirs up wars. As for those who long to learn truth from her, by saying everything in contradictory ways and providing many and various services, she makes them keep seeking and find nothing until death itself. For from the beginning she has lain before blind people as an occasion of death; by prophesying deceptive, ambiguous, and crooked things, she deceives those who believe.

Translator's notes for section 3.24 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὴ γενέσθαι πιστοῦσα
Rendered as: but also gives assurance that she herself will become one
The active participle from πιστόω has the force of making certain, confirming, or assuring. “Confidently claiming that she herself will become one” is a viable contextual alternative, but ordinary “believing” would obscure this causative or confirmatory force.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐλπίδι τοῦ γενέσθαι ὃ μὴ ἔχει φύσιν καὶ ὃ ἔχει προσαπολλύουσα
Rendered as: in the hope of becoming what she does not possess by nature, she also destroys what she does possess
The parallel ὃ μὴ ἔχει and ὃ ἔχει supports taking her as the implicit subject of both and understanding φύσιν as an accusative of respect, “by nature.” Material alternatives are “in the hope of becoming what she lacks the nature or capacity to become, she also destroys what she possesses” and the impersonal “becoming what has no nature and destroying what does.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν ἐμμηνίοις γινομένη
Rendered as: when she comes into her menstrual periods
ἐμμήνια denotes menstruation or menstrual discharge; the rendering retains the author’s female-body imagery.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς προσκαίρους τίκτῃ βασιλεῖς, τοὺς αἷμα πολὺ χέοντας ἐγείρει πολέμους
Rendered as: she gives birth to temporary kings who shed much blood, she stirs up wars
Takes τοὺς αἷμα πολὺ χέοντας as an appositional description of the kings, which provides the more natural agents for shedding blood. Because the participle can also agree with πολέμους, the alternative is “she stirs up wars that shed much blood.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: πολλὰς καὶ διαφόρους παρέχειν ὑπουργίας
Rendered as: providing many and various services
ὑπουργία denotes service or assistance. If these are demands placed upon the seekers rather than services offered to them, “many and varied tasks of service” is possible.

6. Translation choice — Greek: θανάτου κεῖται πρόφασις
Rendered as: has lain ... as an occasion of death
πρόφασις can mean pretext, occasion, ostensible cause, or alleged reason. “Pretext for death” is more formally literal, while “occasion of death” better expresses the resulting harm in context.

SECTION 3.25

Therefore she imposed an equivocal name on her firstborn, calling him Cain, which admits a twofold interpretation; for it is interpreted both as “possession” and as “jealousy,” since in what was to come he was going to be jealous of either a wife or possessions or the parents’ affection toward him. But if none of these things actually came about, even so, calling him “possession” has hit the mark well; for she acquired him first, and this also proved useful to her. For he was a “murderer,” “and a liar,” and, amid sins, was unwilling to live quietly even while ruling. Moreover, those who came from his line became the first adulterers; they fashioned psalteries and lyres and became bronzesmiths of weapons of war. Therefore, how the prophecy of the descendants too, full of adulterers and psalteries, secretly stirs up wars through sensual pleasures!

Translator's notes for section 3.25 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἀμφοτερίζον ἐπέθηκεν ὄνομα
Rendered as: she imposed an equivocal name
ἀμφοτερίζον describes a name that goes in both directions or bears two senses, as the following clause explains.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὃ διχῇ ἔχει τῆς ἑρμηνείας τὴν ἐκδοχήν
Rendered as: which admits a twofold interpretation
The expression describes two possible outcomes or explanations of the name’s interpretation.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ζηλοῦν αὐτοῦ μέλλοντος ἐν τοῖς ἐσομένοις ἢ γυναῖκα ἢ κτήματα ἢ τὴν τῶν γονέων πρὸς αὐτὸν στοργήν
Rendered as: since in what was to come he was going to be jealous of either a wife or possessions or the parents’ affection toward him
The main rendering takes ὡς with the genitive absolute as an explanatory causal ground. Alternatively, ὡς may attribute an assumed reason to the namer: “on the assumption that in the future he would be jealous of either a wife or possessions or the parents’ affection toward him.” The following condition, εἰ δ’ ἄρα μηδὲν τούτων γένηται, leaves the anticipated jealousy contingent, so “was going to” avoids implying necessary fulfillment. αὐτοῦ is the subject of μέλλοντος, while the later αὐτόν may refer to Cain or to another contextually implied male; “toward him” preserves that referential uncertainty.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ „κτῆμα“ λέγεσθαι καλῶς ἐπιτέτευκται
Rendered as: calling him “possession” has hit the mark well
ἐπιτυγχάνω conveys attaining or hitting the mark; the infinitive phrase functions as the subject.

5. Translation choice — Greek: „φονεὺς“ γὰρ ἦν „καὶ ψεύστης“
Rendered as: For he was a “murderer,” “and a liar,”
Keeps καὶ within the second quoted expression, following the source’s quotation boundaries rather than placing “and” outside the quotation.

6. Translation choice — Greek: μετὰ ἁμαρτιῶν ἡσυχάζειν μηδὲ ἐπὶ τῷ ἄρχειν θέλων
Rendered as: amid sins, was unwilling to live quietly even while ruling
Takes μετά as accompaniment or surrounding circumstance and ἐπὶ τῷ ἄρχειν temporally. Alternatives include “unwilling to rest with his sins, even in ruling” or taking the final phrase as “even for the sake of ruling.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: ψαλτήρια καὶ κιθάρας ἡρμόσαντο
Rendered as: they fashioned psalteries and lyres
ἁρμόζω can mean fitting together, constructing, or tuning. “Fashioned” fits the account of originating instruments, while “tuned” remains possible.

8. Translation choice — Greek: χαλκεῖς ὅπλων πολεμικῶν ἐγένοντο
Rendered as: became bronzesmiths of weapons of war
χαλκεῖς specifically denotes workers in copper or bronze and, more broadly, metalworkers; the genitive identifies their products as weapons used in war.

9. Translation choice — Greek: λανθανόντως διὰ τῶν ἡδυπαθειῶν ὡς τοὺς πολέμους ἐγείρει
Rendered as: how ... secretly stirs up wars through sensual pleasures!
Takes ὡς before the finite clause as exclamatory, “how,” while λανθανόντως indicates that the effect operates unnoticed or secretly. A declarative reading such as “that it secretly stirs up wars” is also possible.

SECTION 3.26

But the one among the sons of humanity who possesses prophecy, innate and proper to the soul, plainly, as a male revealing the hopes of the coming age, named his own son Abel, a name that without any doubt is interpreted “mourning.” For he causes his sons to mourn for their deceived brothers, while promising them, without falsehood, consolation in the coming age. He says that one should petition only one God; he neither speaks of gods himself nor believes anyone else who does. He guards whatever good he has and increases it further. He hates sacrifices, blood, and libations. He loves the chaste, the pure, and the holy. He extinguishes the fire of altars. He abolishes wars and teaches peace. He commands self-control. He does away with sins. He sanctions marriage and permits continence; he leads everyone into purity. He makes people charitable. He establishes righteousness as law, seals the perfect among them, and reveals the word of rest. He prophesies definite things and speaks clearly. He frequently gives reminders of the eternal fire of punishment, continually proclaims the kingdom of God, announces heavenly wealth, promises glory that cannot be taken away, and demonstrates the forgiveness of sin by deed.

Translator's notes for section 3.26 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: προφητείαν ἔμφυτον ψυχῆς ἰδίαν
Rendered as: prophecy, innate and proper to the soul
Both adjectives characterize “prophecy”; the genitive presents it as something distinctive or proper to the soul.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ἄρσην
Rendered as: as a male
Preserves the passage’s explicit male–female contrast without replacing it with a theological title.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀψευστὶ αὐτοῖς ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι αἰῶνι τὴν παράκλησιν ὑπισχνούμενος
Rendered as: while promising them, without falsehood, consolation in the coming age
ἀψευστί characterizes the promise as truthful or free from falsehood, not merely as an act performed continually or unfailingly.

4. Translation choice — Greek: θεὸν ἕνα μόνον αἰτεῖν
Rendered as: one should petition only one God
The infinitive has an understood general subject, and αἰτεῖν here denotes directing requests to the one God.

5. Translation choice — Greek: γάμον νομιτεύει
Rendered as: sanctions marriage
The uncommon νομιτεύει presents marriage as recognized or established as lawful.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἐλεημονικοὺς ποιεῖ
Rendered as: makes people charitable
ἐλεημονικός can describe mercy or generosity expressed through almsgiving; “charitable” preserves the practical dimension without restricting it to a specific gift.

7. Translation choice — Greek: δικαιοσύνην νομιτεύει
Rendered as: establishes righteousness as law
The same uncommon verb used with marriage is retained here with legal or normative force.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν τῆς ἀναπαύσεως λόγον
Rendered as: the word of rest
Keeps λόγος as “word” and leaves open whether it denotes a message, teaching, or account concerning rest.

SECTION 3.27

And why is there any need to say more? The male is wholly truth, the female wholly error, while the one born from male and female speaks falsely in some things and truly in others. For the female, enclosing the male’s white seed in her own blood as in red fire, gives structure to what is weak in her with alien supports of bone. Giving pleasure through the flesh’s temporary bloom and secretly stealing away the strength of reason through brief pleasures, she leads most people into adultery and thus deprives them of the good bridegroom who is to come. For every human being is a bride whenever, being sown with the true prophet’s white word of truth, that person is enlightened in mind.

Translator's notes for section 3.27 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ ἄρσην ὅλος ἀλήθεια, ἡ θήλεια ὅλη πλάνη
Rendered as: The male is wholly truth, the female wholly error
Preserves the author’s stark gendered claim; πλάνη can also mean deception or wandering, but “error” fits the contrast with truth.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἀλλοτρίοις ἐρείσμασιν ὀστέων
Rendered as: with alien supports of bone
ἀλλοτρίοις means foreign or belonging to another, while ἐρείσμασιν retains the structural image of supports.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ λογισμοῦ τὴν ἰσχὺν ὑποσυλῶσα
Rendered as: secretly stealing away the strength of reason
ὑποσυλάω conveys covert deprivation, and λογισμός here is the faculty of reasoning rather than a particular calculation.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ μέλλοντος καλοῦ στερίσκει νυμφίου
Rendered as: deprives them of the good bridegroom who is to come
The genitive depends on the verb of deprivation; μέλλοντος may also be rendered “future.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος
Rendered as: every human being
The expression can formally suggest “the whole human being,” but the distributive sense fits the ensuing general condition.

6. Translation choice — Greek: φωτίζηται τὸν νοῦν
Rendered as: is enlightened in mind
The accusative marks the respect in which the person is enlightened.

SECTION 3.28

Therefore one must listen to the one and only prophet of truth, knowing that the word sown by someone else, having incurred a charge of adultery, is cast out of his kingdom as though by a bridegroom. But for those who know the mystery, even death results from adultery of the soul. Whenever the soul is sown by others, then, as one who has acted as a prostitute or committed adultery, she is abandoned by the spirit. Thus the ensouled body, after the life-giving spirit has separated, is dissolved into earth, and at the time of judgment the punishment proportionate to the sin is rendered to the soul after the dissolution of the body—just as among human beings a woman caught in adultery is first expelled from the household and then later judged for condemnation.

Translator's notes for section 3.28 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἡ ἐπὶ μοιχείᾳ. φωραθεῖσα
The selected edition’s printed full stop separates the article and prepositional phrase from the participle with which they naturally construe. The translation provisionally treats the words as one continuous noun phrase without altering the supplied Greek.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ παρ’ ἑτέρου σπαρεὶς λόγος
Rendered as: the word sown by someone else
Preserves λόγος as the grammatical subject and retains the sowing metaphor rather than substituting the person who receives the teaching.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ὑπὸ νυμφίου τῆς βασιλείας αὐτοῦ ἐκβάλλεται
Rendered as: is cast out of his kingdom as though by a bridegroom
The rendering preserves the attachment and referential ambiguity: αὐτοῦ may refer to the bridegroom, the true prophet, or another implied male authority.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ ψυχικῆς μοιχείας
Rendered as: from adultery of the soul
ψυχικός is rendered through its connection with ψυχή and the explicit soul imagery that follows; “psychic adultery” or “soulish adultery” would be more formally literal.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς πορνεύσασα ἢ μοιχευσαμένη
Rendered as: as one who has acted as a prostitute or committed adultery
Distinguishes the two sexual metaphors while allowing the middle form μοιχευσαμένη its contextually defensible intransitive sense.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ ἔμψυχον σῶμα
Rendered as: the ensouled body
Retains the explicit relation to ψυχή rather than reducing the phrase to the less specific “living body.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ κατ’ ἀξίαν κόλασις
Rendered as: the punishment proportionate to the sin
κατ’ ἀξίαν denotes punishment corresponding to what is deserved, while the preceding τοῦ ἁμαρτήματος supplies the sin to which it corresponds.

SECTION 3.29

While Peter was about to reveal this very mystical discourse fully to us, Zacchaeus arrived and said, “Now then, Peter, it is time for you to go out and hold the discussion. For a large crowd has gathered in the courtyard and is waiting for you. In its midst Simon stands like a general, with that crowd serving as his bodyguard.” When Peter heard this, he told me to withdraw for the sake of the prayer, since I had not yet received the baptism that leads to salvation. Then he said to those who were already perfect, “Rise, and let us pray that God, in his unfailing acts of compassion, may work with me as I press toward the salvation of the human beings created by him.” After saying this and praying, he went out into the large open-air area of the courtyard, where many had assembled in order to observe. His hesitation had made them more eager to hurry to hear him.

Translator's notes for section 3.29 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν μυστικὸν λόγον
Rendered as: the mystical discourse
λόγος here denotes the esoteric explanation Peter was giving; “mystical teaching” is also possible.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τὸ ἐκβάντα διαλεχθῆναί σε
Rendered as: for you to go out and hold the discussion
διαλέγεσθαι may mean converse, debate, or deliver an address; “hold the discussion” leaves the precise format open.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς πολέμαρχος ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ δορυφορούμενος
Rendered as: like a general, with that crowd serving as his bodyguard
The singular pronoun refers to the crowd, while δορυφορεῖν literally evokes attendance by spear-bearers and conventionally denotes an armed escort.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ πρὸς σωτηρίαν βάπτισμα
Rendered as: the baptism that leads to salvation
πρός expresses orientation or purpose; “baptism for salvation” is a more formally compact alternative.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς ἤδη τελείοις
Rendered as: those who were already perfect
τελείοις may contextually designate those already initiated or baptized, but the main text retains the source’s language of completion or perfection.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς διακρίσεως αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ σπεύδειν τοῦ ἀκούειν σπουδαιοτέρους πεποιηκυίας
Rendered as: His hesitation had made them more eager to hurry to hear him
διάκρισις can denote hesitation or doubt, as well as discernment or judgment and discussion, dispute, or disputation. “Hesitation” directly represents a lexical possibility and fits Peter’s intervening withdrawal and prayer without recasting the noun merely as elapsed delay; the other senses remain viable contextual alternatives.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τὸ σπεύδειν τοῦ ἀκούειν
Rendered as: to hurry to hear him
The nested infinitives express eagerness directed toward hastening in order to listen.

SECTION 3.30

So he stood and saw all the people gazing at him in deep silence, with Simon the magician standing in their midst, and began to speak as follows: “Peace be to all of you who stand ready to extend your right hands to the truth of God. This peace is his great and incomparable gift in the present world. The one who sent us, being an unerring prophet concerning what is supremely beneficial, commanded us to pronounce it to you in the form of a greeting before the words of instruction, so that, if anyone among you is a child of peace, peace may take hold of him through our teaching; but if any one of you does not wish to receive it, then, after shaking off as testimony the road dust from our feet—which we carried through our exertions and brought to you so that you might be saved—we may depart for the houses and cities of others.”

Translator's notes for section 3.30 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἡμῖν-ἐνετείλατο
The selected edition prints a hyphen between the dative pronoun and the verb. It has no defensible syntactic function here and is provisionally treated as typographic or editorial punctuation rather than as part of either word.

2. Translation choice — Greek: δεξιὰς διδόναι τῇ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀληθείᾳ
Rendered as: extend your right hands to the truth of God
The idiom depicts giving one’s right hand as a sign of agreement, pledge, or welcome; retaining the physical gesture preserves the image.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἣν αὐτοῦ μεγάλην τε καὶ ἀσύγκριτον ἐν τῷ νῦν κόσμῳ ὑπάρχουσαν δωρεὰν
Rendered as: This peace is his great and incomparable gift in the present world
The relative pronoun can refer either to the opening “peace” or, by proximity, to “truth.” The subsequent greeting, child of peace, and reception language favor “peace,” while “truth” remains a viable alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ ἐν ὑπεροχῇ συμφέροντος ἀψευδὴς ὑπάρχων προφήτης
Rendered as: being an unerring prophet concerning what is supremely beneficial
The genitive marks the subject matter of the prophet’s reliable proclamation; ἐν ὑπεροχῇ gives the benefit preeminent or surpassing force.

5. Translation choice — Greek: προφάσει προσηγορίας
Rendered as: in the form of a greeting
πρόφασις can mean occasion, outward form, or pretext, while προσηγορία can denote an address or salutation; the context does not require a deceptive “pretext.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: καταλάβῃ αὐτὸν ἡ εἰρήνη
Rendered as: peace may take hold of him
καταλαμβάνειν has the force of overtaking, reaching, or taking possession of someone.

7. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ δὲ ταύτην λαβεῖν ὑμῶν τις μὴ θέλοι, τότε ἡμεῖς ἀποτιναξάμενοι εἰς μαρτυρίαν τῶν ποδῶν ἡμῶν τὸν ἐκ τῶν ὁδῶν κονιορτόν, ὃν διὰ τοὺς καμάτους βαστάζαντες ἠνέγκαμεν πρὸς ὑμᾶς ὅπως σωθῆτε, εἰς ἑτέρων ἀπίωμεν οἰκίας καὶ πόλεις
Rendered as: but if any one of you does not wish to receive it, then ... we may depart for the houses and cities of others
The main rendering treats ἀπίωμεν as remaining under the preceding ἵνα, parallel to καταλάβῃ: the greeting is commanded so that peace may reach the receptive person and, in the contrary case, the messengers may depart. An independent hortatory construal, “then let us depart,” is also syntactically possible.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ὃν διὰ τοὺς καμάτους βαστάζαντες ἠνέγκαμεν πρὸς ὑμᾶς
Rendered as: which we carried through our exertions and brought to you
The relative pronoun refers to the road dust; διὰ τοὺς καμάτους can mean because of or through their toils.

SECTION 3.31

We truly tell you that on the day of judgment it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for you to remain in the place of disobedience. First, because you did not understand what is reasonable for yourselves; second, because, after hearing about us, you did not come to us; third, because you disobeyed us even when we came. Therefore, out of concern for you, we freely pray that our peace may come upon you. If you wish to have it, you must eagerly undertake not to do wrong and courageously bear being wronged. Human nature would not endure this unless it first gained knowledge of the surpassing benefit, which is to know the righteous nature of the one who surpasses everything: that, in avenging the wronged, he punishes, and that he benefits the reverent forever.

Translator's notes for section 3.31 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἢ τῷ τῆς ἀπειθείας τόπῳ ἐνδιατελεῖν
Rendered as: than for you to remain in the place of disobedience
The infinitive is read as remaining in the location designated by the dative, with the addressed listeners as its contextual subject. A rendering that treats the place itself as the object of judgment is also possible, but must still account for the expressed remaining infinitive rather than omit it.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἀδικουμένους ἐκδικῶν τιμωρεῖ
Rendered as: in avenging the wronged, he punishes
The wronged are the object of the avenging participle. The finite verb's punished object is unexpressed; the main text does not make the wronged people the ones punished, and leaves the implied wrongdoers unnamed.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς εὐσεβοῦντας
Rendered as: the reverent
The term describes those practicing reverence or piety, with the divine referent supplied by the surrounding argument. It is not replaced by a denominational group name.

SECTION 3.32

Therefore, as right-minded servants of God, recognizing for yourselves what is reasonable, adopt the way of life that pleases him, so that, by loving him in this way and being loved by him, you may possess forever what is beneficial. For he alone has the utmost ability to provide it—he who brought things that did not exist into being, fashioned heaven, compacted the earth, bounded the sea, stored away the things in Hades, and filled all things with air.

Translator's notes for section 3.32 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: θεοῦ δοῦλοι εὐγνώμονες
Rendered as: right-minded servants of God
εὐγνώμονες describes people of sound or appreciative judgment; “grateful” is also possible but is less closely tied to the following recognition of what is reasonable. δοῦλοι can also be rendered “slaves” or “bondservants”; here it conveys belonging and allegiance to God rather than merely hired service. “Servants” follows the POB reader-facing wording policy.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν αὐτῷ ἀρέσκουσαν ἀναδέξασθε πολιτείαν
Rendered as: adopt the way of life that pleases him
πολιτεία can denote conduct, manner of life, or commonwealth; personal conduct is demanded here.

3. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτῷ γὰρ μόνῳ τὸ παρασχεῖν δυνατώτατόν ἐστιν
Rendered as: he alone has the utmost ability to provide it
The impersonal Greek uses a superlative expression of capacity. The object “it” is supplied from the immediately preceding beneficial thing.

4. Translation choice — Greek: γῆν πιλώσαντι
Rendered as: compacted the earth
The verb depicts making dense or firmly packed. Renderings involving clay or mud are possible but would make the material more explicit than this wording does.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ ἐν ᾅδῃ ταμιεύσαντι
Rendered as: stored away the things in Hades
ταμιεύω presents the contents as kept or laid up in a store; the neuter plural object is preserved rather than reduced to souls alone.

SECTION 3.33

He alone transformed the single, primary, uniform substance fourfold and in opposite directions; then, by mixing them, he made countless blends from them, so that these blends, transformed into opposite natures and mixed together, might produce the pleasure of living through the coupling of opposites. Likewise, he alone created communities of angels and spirits by a nod of his purpose and filled the heavens, just as he also adorned the visible firmament with stars, for which he marked out paths and appointed a course. He compacted the earth for the growth of crops, but bounded the sea, setting habitation apart in waterless regions. He keeps in store the things in Hades, having named it a place of souls; and he filled all things with air, so that all living creatures might be able to breathe without fear in order to live.

Translator's notes for section 3.33 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἔπλησε τοὺς -οὐρανούς
The image-checked selected print has a hyphen-like mark immediately before οὐρανούς. Its function is uncertain, but it appears to be an editorial or typographical mark rather than a meaningful part of the word. Omitting it in continuous syntax is provisional and does not alter the confirmed supplied reading.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν μίαν καὶ πρώτην μονοειδῆ οὐσίαν τετραχῶς καὶ ἐναντίως ἔτρεψεν
Rendered as: transformed the single, primary, uniform substance fourfold and in opposite directions
μίαν, πρώτην, and μονοειδῆ respectively mark singleness, primacy, and uniformity. ἐναντίως may also be rendered “into opposites.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: μυρίας κράσεις
Rendered as: countless blends
κρᾶσις denotes a mixture or blending. “Mixtures” is equally possible, but “blends” distinguishes the products from the act of mixing.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ τῆς ἀντισυζυγίας
Rendered as: through the coupling of opposites
The compound denotes counter-pairing or reciprocal conjunction, here involving the previously mentioned opposite natures.

5. Translation choice — Greek: δήμους ἀγγέλων καὶ πνευμάτων
Rendered as: communities of angels and spirits
δήμους literally suggests peoples or organized populations. “Hosts” is possible but would introduce a potentially military nuance.

6. Translation choice — Greek: βουλῆς νεύματι
Rendered as: by a nod of his purpose
βουλή may mean counsel, will, or purpose, while νεῦμα depicts an authoritative nod or indication.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἔπλησε τοὺς -οὐρανούς· ὡς καὶ τὸ φαινόμενον στερέωμα ἄστροις ἐκόσμησεν
Rendered as: filled the heavens, just as he also adorned the visible firmament with stars
ὡς καί explicitly compares the filling of the heavens with angels and spirits to the adornment of the visible firmament with stars; it is therefore rendered as “just as he also” rather than merely “also.”

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν ἀνύδροις οἴκησιν ἀφορίσας
Rendered as: setting habitation apart in waterless regions
The clause associates the bounding of the sea with reserving dry places for habitation; no particular inhabitants are named.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἀδεῶς ἀναπνέειν
Rendered as: breathe without fear
ἀδεῶς literally means fearlessly or securely. “Breathe safely” would be more idiomatic but less directly preserve the image.

SECTION 3.34

Oh, the great hand of the wise God, which makes all things in all things! For a countless multitude of birds has been brought into being by him, and this multitude is diverse, each bird differing from another in every respect—I mean their colors, beaks, claws, eyes, dispositions, voices, and all the other features. And how many different forms of plants there are, distinguished by countless colors, qualities, and scents! And how many animals there are on dry land and in the waters! It is impossible to tell of their shapes, forms, locations, colors, ways of life, dispositions, natures, and multitude, and further of the multitudes and heights of mountains, the differences among stones, fearsome recesses, springs, rivers, lakes, seas, harbors, islands, forests, the whole inhabited world, and uninhabited places.

Translator's notes for section 3.34 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: πόσα δὲ τῆς χέρσου ζῷα καὶ τῶν ἐν ὕδασιν, ὧν ἀδύνατον, εἰπεῖν σχήματα, μορφάς, θέσεις, χρώματα, βίους, γνώμας, φύσεις, ὄχλον. ἔτι τε ὀρέων πλήθη καὶ ὕψη, λίθων διαφοράς, μυχοὺς φοβερούς, πηγάς, ποταμούς, λίμνας, θαλάσσας, λιμένας, νήσους, ὕλας, οἰκουμένην τε πᾶσαν καὶ ἀοικήτους τόπους.
The edition prints a full stop after ὄχλον, but the following catalogue contains explicitly accusative items, beginning with διαφοράς, that naturally continue or elliptically resume as objects of εἰπεῖν. The main translation therefore keeps the ensuing catalogue within the scope of “it is impossible to tell of.” Alternatively, the printed punctuation may be represented by an elliptical new catalogue: “And further: the multitudes and heights of mountains...” This is an interpretive question concerning the surviving syntax and editorial punctuation, not a missing or unreadable text.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς μεγάλης θεοῦ φρονίμου χειρός
Rendered as: the great hand of the wise God
Because φρόνιμος is a two-termination adjective, φρονίμου can qualify either θεοῦ or χειρός. The main text attaches it to the immediately preceding θεοῦ, yielding “the great hand of the wise God.” Alternatively, attaching it to χειρός gives “the great, wise hand of God,” an interpretation supported by the following description of the hand’s activity.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς ἐν πᾶσιν πάντα ποιούσης
Rendered as: which makes all things in all things
The rendering preserves the repeated πᾶς wording and its broad scope. “Which does everything in every sphere” is a possible interpretive alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ οὗτος ποικίλος, πρὸς τὸν ἕτερον κατὰ πάντα ἐξηλλαγμένος
Rendered as: and this multitude is diverse, each bird differing from another in every respect
The collective noun ὄχλος is masculine singular, and οὗτος and ἐξηλλαγμένος agree with it grammatically. The main rendering understands the comparison distributively among the birds because the following catalogue names their distinguishing features. Alternatively, the phrase may compare one collective group or kind of birds with another: “and this multitude is diverse, differing in every respect from the other group or kind.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: βλέμματα, γνώμας, φθέγματα
Rendered as: eyes, dispositions, voices
βλέμματα can mean looks, gazes, or eyes; γνώμαι denotes dispositions or traits of mind; φθέγματα denotes uttered sounds or voices.

6. Translation choice — Greek: θέσεις
Rendered as: locations
θέσις literally denotes placement or position. In this catalogue of animal differences, “locations” is cautious; “habitats” or “postures” are possible contextual alternatives.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ὀρέων πλήθη καὶ ὕψη
Rendered as: the multitudes and heights of mountains
The plural πλήθη denotes the quantity or numerousness of the mountains. “The numbers and heights of mountains” is a less formal alternative.

8. Translation choice — Greek: μυχοὺς φοβερούς
Rendered as: fearsome recesses
μυχός denotes an inner recess or depth. “Fearsome depths” is also possible.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ὕλας
Rendered as: forests
Although ὕλη can mean matter or material, the geographical catalogue supports its concrete sense “woods” or “forests.”

SECTION 3.35

And how many other things there are that remain unknown, having escaped human conjecture! But among the things that can be grasped, what human being knows even a single boundary? I mean: how heaven revolves; how the stars move; what forms they have and what constitution of life; what their airy paths are; from where the blasts of the winds are driven about and have their varied operations; from where the springs gush unfailingly, and perennial rivers, coming into being, make their way to the sea, while neither that from which they come is emptied nor that to which they depart is filled; how far the infinite depth of boundless Tartarus extends; on what, then, the heaven that encompasses everything is suspended; how clouds well up out of air and are drawn together into air; what the nature is of thunder, lightning, snow, hail, mist, ice, storms, rain, and hovering clouds; and how that nature molds plants and animals, continually completing them with countless differences and complete precision.

Translator's notes for section 3.35 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: συντίνεται
The selected print’s form is orthographically unusual. It may represent an itacistic or typographical form corresponding to συντείνεται, but that normalization and the word’s exact nuance remain uncertain. The surrounding description of clouds nevertheless permits a defensible rendering involving contraction, drawing together, or condensation.

2. Translation choice — Greek: στοχασμὸν ἀνθρώπων ἐκπεφευγότα
Rendered as: having escaped human conjecture
στοχασμός denotes conjecture, estimation, or speculative inquiry rather than certain knowledge.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν δὲ ἐν καταλήψει ὄντων τίς ἀνθρώπων ἕνα ὅρον οἶδεν
Rendered as: among the things that can be grasped, what human being knows even a single boundary?
κατάληψις concerns apprehension or comprehension, and ὅρος may denote a boundary, limit, definition, or determinate account. The following catalogue favors the broad image of a limit to human knowledge.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ ζῆν τὴν σύστασιν
Rendered as: what constitution of life
The phrase attributes a constitution or mode of living to the stars without explaining whether this is literal, cosmological, or analogical; the translation preserves that claim.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ ἀνέμων πνεύματα περιωθεῖται καὶ διαφόρους ἔχει τὰς ἐνεργείας
Rendered as: the blasts of the winds are driven about and have their varied operations
πνεύματα here denotes moving breaths or blasts, while ἐνέργειαι can mean activities, operations, powers, or effects.

6. Translation choice — Greek: μέχρι ποῦ τοῦ ἀπεράντου ταρτάρου τὸ ἄπειρον βάθος
Rendered as: how far the infinite depth of boundless Tartarus extends
The Greek is an elliptical question without an expressed verb; “extends” supplies the minimum required English syntax while preserving both terms of limitlessness.

7. Translation choice — Greek: πῶς νέφη ἐξ ἀέρος βρύει καὶ εἰς ἀέρα συντίνεται
Rendered as: how clouds well up out of air and are drawn together into air
βρύω supplies the image of gushing or welling up. The unusual συντίνεται is understood contextually as drawing or contracting together; “are condensed into air” is a possible alternative.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τίς φύσις βροντῶν καὶ ἀστραπῶν, χιόνων, χαλάζης, ὀμίχλης, κρυστάλλων, καταιγίδων, ὄμβρων, νεφῶν αἰωρουμένων καὶ πῶς φυτὰ καὶ ζῷα πλάσσει καὶ ταῦτα διαφοραῖς ἀναριθμήτοις πάσῃ ἀκριβείᾳ συνεχῶς ἀποτελουμένη
Rendered as: what the nature is of thunder, lightning, snow, hail, mist, ice, storms, rain, and hovering clouds; and how that nature molds plants and animals, continually completing them with countless differences and complete precision
The main rendering takes φύσις as the subject of πλάσσει, understands the formally middle/passive ἀποτελουμένη as a transitive middle agreeing with φύσις, and takes ταῦτα as referring to the plants and animals. This is supported by continuity with πλάσσει and by the accusative form ταῦτα. Alternatively, ἀποτελουμένη can be passive, yielding the sense “nature continually being brought to completion,” while καὶ ταῦτα can function adverbially as “and this too” rather than making ταῦτα the participle’s object. The supplied wording permits both analyses and has not been corrected.

SECTION 3.36

Nevertheless, if anyone surveys the whole accurately by reason, he will find that God has made it for the sake of humankind. For rainstorms occur for the sake of crops, so that a human may partake of them and animals may be fed so that they may serve humankind. The sun also shines and turns the air through four seasonal changes, so that each season may furnish humankind with what belongs to it. Springs also gush forth so that drink may be given to humans. Moreover, who, to the extent possible, exercises dominion over creation? Is it not the human being, who has received wisdom to cultivate the earth, sail the sea, hunt swimming creatures, flying creatures, and wild beasts, calculate the course of the stars, mine the earth, sift the sea, raise cities, appoint kings, establish laws, judge, conceive of an invisible God, know the names of angels, drive out demons, attempt to stop diseases with medicines, discover incantations against venomous reptiles, and devise natural counteragents?

Translator's notes for section 3.36 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ πᾶν ἀκριβῶς λογισμῷ συνίδῃ
Rendered as: surveys the whole accurately by reason
τὸ πᾶν denotes the whole created order under consideration, while λογισμός indicates rational reflection.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν ἀέρα εἰς τέσσαρας τροπὰς τρέπει
Rendered as: turns the air through four seasonal changes
The following reference to each καιρός supports understanding the four τροπαί as seasonal changes; “turns the air into four turnings” is the more literal alternative.

3. Translation choice — Greek: νηκτὰ πτηνὰ θηρία ἀγρεύειν
Rendered as: hunt swimming creatures, flying creatures, and wild beasts
The asyndetic accusatives name three classes of creatures subject to human hunting.

4. Translation choice — Greek: θάλασσαν σήθειν
Rendered as: sift the sea
σήθειν literally means to sift or strain; the unusual image of searching or working the sea is retained.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἀντιπαθείας ἐπινοεῖν
Rendered as: devise natural counteragents
In the context of venomous reptiles, ἀντιπάθειαι are opposing properties or remedies; “devise antipathies” is a more literal but less intelligible alternative.

SECTION 3.37

If you were grateful, human being, having recognized the God who benefited you in everything, you would also be immortal, with the things created for your sake possessing continued existence through gratitude. But even now you can become incorruptible, if you recognize the one you failed to notice, if you love the one you abandoned, and if you pray to him alone, who is able to punish and save your body and soul. Therefore, above all, consider that no one rules together with him and no one shares his designation—namely, that which is called “God.” For he alone is both called God and is God, and it is permitted neither to regard another as God nor to call another God. If anyone should dare to do so, that person’s soul is destined to be punished eternally.

Translator's notes for section 3.37 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ δὲ εὐγνωμόνεις
Rendered as: If you were grateful
The imperfect with ἂν ἦς forms a counterfactual condition; εὐγνωμονεῖν here denotes gratitude or proper acknowledgment toward a benefactor.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν διὰ σὲ κτισθέντων δι’ εὐγνωμοσύνην τὸ διαμένειν ἐχόντων
Rendered as: with the things created for your sake possessing continued existence through gratitude
The Greek does not expressly identify whose εὐγνωμοσύνη is meant, so the main wording leaves its possessor unstated. It may refer to the human addressee’s gratitude within the hypothetical condition, or to the created things’ own gratitude or good disposition, in which case their continuance supplies the comparison underlying “you would also be immortal.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐὰν ἐπιγνῷς ὃν ἔλαθες
Rendered as: if you recognize the one you failed to notice
The context contrasts recognizing God with previously abandoning him and supports the extended sense “failed to notice” or “overlooked.” The ordinary active construction of λανθάνω with an accusative can instead mean “the one whose notice you escaped”; that materially different reading remains grammatically possible, though it fits the immediate theological argument less readily.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδεὶς τῆς αὐτοῦ κοινωνεῖ ὀνομασίας
Rendered as: no one shares his designation
ὀνομασία denotes the designation or name subsequently identified as “God.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἄλλον δὲ οὔτε νομίσαι οὔτε εἰπεῖν ἔξεστιν
Rendered as: it is permitted neither to regard another as God nor to call another God
The preceding discussion supplies “God” as the complement of both verbs; νομίζειν can also be rendered “acknowledge” or “consider.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀιδίως τὴν ψυχὴν κολασθῆναι ἔχει
Rendered as: that person’s soul is destined to be punished eternally
ἔχει with the infinitive expresses an impending or necessary consequence rather than possession.

SECTION 3.38

When Peter had said these things, Simon, from outside the crowd, said in a loud voice, “Why do you wish, by lying, to deceive the uninstructed crowd standing by you, persuading it that it is permitted neither to regard any as gods nor to call them gods, when the public books among the Jews say that there are many gods? And now, moreover, together with everyone, I wish to debate with you from those very books about the need to acknowledge gods. But first I will demonstrate that the god of whom you spoke is not the highest power capable of everything, since he lacks foreknowledge, is incomplete, is needy, is not good, and is subject to many—indeed, countless—painful passions. Consequently, when this has been demonstrated from the Scriptures, as I maintain, there remains another, unattested in writing, who possesses foreknowledge, is perfect, needs nothing, is good, and is free from all painful passions. But the one whom you call the Creator proves to be subject to the opposites.”

Translator's notes for section 3.38 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἰδιώτην ὄχλον
Rendered as: uninstructed crowd
ἰδιώτης here characterizes the crowd as lacking specialist knowledge; “ordinary crowd” or “lay crowd” are possible alternatives.

2. Translation choice — Greek: θεοὺς μήτε νομίζειν μήτε λέγειν
Rendered as: neither to regard any as gods nor to call them gods
νομίζειν concerns acknowledgment or recognition, while λέγειν concerns naming or speaking of them as gods.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις δημοσίων βίβλων
Rendered as: the public books among the Jews
δημόσιοι presents the books as public or commonly recognized; “canonical books” would introduce a later technical category.

4. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ νῦν δὲ μετὰ πάντων
Rendered as: And now, moreover, together with everyone
μετὰ πάντων expresses association with everyone. It may portray everyone as participating in the discussion or, contextually, indicate that the debate occurs with everyone present; the Greek does not explicitly choose between those attachments.

5. Translation choice — Greek: περὶ τοῦ δεῖν θεοὺς νομίζειν
Rendered as: about the need to acknowledge gods
The articular infinitive presents the necessity of acknowledging gods as the subject for discussion; it does not itself introduce an open question about whether that necessity exists.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπρόγνωστός ἐστιν
Rendered as: he lacks foreknowledge
The active sense is favored by the explicit contrast with προγνωστικός and by the following accusations of ignorance. The adjective can also be read formally as passive, “he is not known beforehand,” but that reading fits the stated contrast less directly.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἕτερος ἀγράφως περιλείπεται εἶναι
Rendered as: there remains another, unattested in writing
The preceding god is said to be exposed by the scriptural accounts, after which Simon infers a contrasting other deity; this contrast favors taking ἀγράφως as marking that remaining deity as outside or unattested in those writings. Alternatively, the adverb may describe the manner of the inference: “another remains to be, apart from writing” or “is inferred without written testimony.”

8. Translation choice — Greek: πολλοῖς καὶ μυρίοις χαλεποῖς ὑποκείμενος πάθεσιν
Rendered as: subject to many—indeed, countless—painful passions
The rendering preserves both πολλοῖς and the intensifying μυρίοις, while πάθη can denote passions, experienced states, or afflictions.

SECTION 3.39

For example, Adam, who came into being according to his likeness, is created blind, is handed down as possessing no knowledge of good or evil, is found to be a transgressor, is expelled from Paradise, and is punished with death. Likewise, the one who formed him, since he does not see from every direction, says at the destruction of Sodom, “Come, and after going down let us see whether they are carrying matters through in accordance with their outcry that is coming to me; but if not, so that I may know,” and thereby shows himself to be ignorant. As for his saying about Adam, “Let us cast him out, lest perhaps, after stretching out his hand, he touch the tree of life and eat, and he will live forever”—his saying “lest perhaps” indicates ignorance, while his addition, “lest perhaps, after eating, he live forever,” also indicates envy. That it is written, “God considered that he had made the human being,” means that he both changes his mind and is ignorant. For “considered” is a reflection by which someone, through ignorance, wishes to determine precisely the outcome of what he intends, or the reflection of someone regretting something that did not turn out according to his intention. That it is written, “And the Lord smelled an odor of fragrance,” belongs to one who is needy, while taking pleasure in the fatty smoke of flesh belongs to one who is not good. Testing—as it is written, “And the Lord tested Abraham”—belongs to one who is evil and ignorant of the outcome of the endurance.

Translator's notes for section 3.39 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: πρὸς μὲ
The printed grave accent on μὲ is an apparent accentuation irregularity. The context clearly calls for the first-person pronoun “me,” so the wording remains translatable without supplying missing content.

2. Translation choice — Greek: γνῶσιν ἀγαθοῦ ἢ κακοῦ οὐκ ἔχων παραδέδοται
Rendered as: is handed down as possessing no knowledge of good or evil
The perfect passive παραδέδοται can describe how Adam is transmitted or represented in the received account; “is delivered over while possessing no knowledge” is possible but less coherent in this sequence.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπεὶ μὴ πανταχόθεν βλέπει
Rendered as: since he does not see from every direction
The literal spatial image of πανταχόθεν is retained rather than replaced with the interpretive abstraction “is not omniscient.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ κατὰ τὴν κραυγὴν αὐτῶν τὴν ἐρχομένην πρὸς μὲ συντελοῦνται
Rendered as: whether they are carrying matters through in accordance with their outcry that is coming to me
The main text takes συντελοῦνται in an action-oriented middle sense, referring contextually to conduct carried through in correspondence with the outcry; “matters” clarifies the implied object but is not expressed in Greek. A materially different passive reading is possible: “whether they are being brought to an end in accordance with their outcry that is coming to me.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ εἰπεῖν „μήπως“ ἀγνοεῖ
Rendered as: his saying “lest perhaps” indicates ignorance
When Simon isolates μήπως, he treats its expression of apprehension or uncertainty as evidence of ignorance. The word can be represented contextually by “lest,” while “perhaps” makes explicit the uncertainty on which his argument depends.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ δὲ ἐπαγαγεῖν „μήπως φαγὼν ζήσεται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα“ καὶ φθονεῖ
Rendered as: while his addition, “lest perhaps, after eating, he live forever,” also indicates envy
In the repeated clause μήπως retains its apprehensive and preventive force, connecting Adam’s possible eating and living forever with the accusation of envy; rendering it merely “perhaps” would obscure that connection.

7. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ μετανοεῖ καὶ ἀγνοεῖ
Rendered as: he both changes his mind and is ignorant
Here μετανοεῖ denotes alleged divine reconsideration or regret, not moral-spiritual reorientation toward God.

8. Translation choice — Greek: κνίσῃ σαρκῶν
Rendered as: the fatty smoke of flesh
κνίση is the steam, smoke, or savor produced by burning fat or flesh; the rendering retains the polemically physical image.

9. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ τέλος τῆς ὑπομονῆς
Rendered as: the outcome of the endurance
τέλος can denote either the outcome or the limit of endurance; “outcome” best fits the claim that testing seeks information about the eventual result.

SECTION 3.40

Similarly, Simon seemed to show from many things in the Scriptures that God is subject to every passion. In response Peter said, “Tell me whether an evil and utterly wicked person has no desire at all to expose himself regarding the things in which he sins.” Simon said, “He has no desire to.” Peter said, “How, then, can God be evil and wicked, if it was by his own will that the evils publicly written against him were added?” Simon replied, “It is possible that, contrary to his intention, the exposure against him was written by another power.” Peter said, “First, then, let us investigate this. If he exposed himself by his own counsel, as you just agreed, he is not wicked. But if it was done by another power, the matter must be investigated—and with all our strength. It must be examined whether someone implicated him, though he is nothing but good, in all the evil things.”

Translator's notes for section 3.40 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: λείμματι
The confirmed printed form ordinarily points to λείμμα, “remainder, deficiency, or omission,” but the immediate contrasts with “contrary to his intention” and “by his own counsel” strongly suggest an orthographic form of λήματι from λῆμα, “will” or “resolve.” This remains a contextual proposal rather than an alteration of the selected edition’s Greek.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὁμῶς
Rendered as: Similarly
ὁμῶς can mean “likewise” or “in the same way,” linking this summary to Simon’s preceding examples.

3. Translation choice — Greek: Εἰ μηδὲν ἀγαπᾷ ὁ κακὸς καὶ πάνυ μοχθηρὸς ἐφ’ οἷς ἁμαρτάνει ἑαυτὸν ἐλέγχειν, ἀπόκριναί μοι.
Rendered as: Tell me whether an evil and utterly wicked person has no desire at all to expose himself regarding the things in which he sins.
Here εἰ introduces the proposition Peter asks Simon to confirm or deny, as Simon’s reply Οὐκ ἀγαπᾷ indicates. Although εἰ can formally introduce a condition, the exchange supports an indirect question. ἀγαπᾷ with the infinitive concerns desire or willingness, while ἐλέγχειν means exposing or convicting one’s own wrongdoing.

4. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτοῦ λείμματι
Rendered as: by his own will
The immediate contrast with παρὰ προαίρεσιν αὐτοῦ and ὑπὸ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ βουλῆς supports interpreting the printed λείμματι as an orthographic form of λήματι from λῆμα, “will” or “resolve.” The ordinary sense of λείμμα, “remainder, deficiency, or omission,” does not readily sustain Peter’s argument.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν κατ’ αὐτοῦ γραφῆναι ἔλεγχον
Rendered as: the exposure against him was written
ἔλεγχος can mean refutation, censure, conviction, or exposure; “exposure” preserves the connection with the written disclosure of traits alleged to be blameworthy.

6. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτὸν μόνον ἀγαθὸν ὄντα
Rendered as: though he is nothing but good
The main rendering takes μόνον adverbially with ἀγαθόν, emphasizing the absence of evil in God; this is favored by the immediate contrast with the evil things attributed to him. Because μόνον formally agrees with αὐτόν, an alternative is “though he alone is good,” excluding goodness from others.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἐξεταστέον μή τις αὐτὸν μόνον ἀγαθὸν ὄντα ἐπὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς κακοῖς ὑπέβαλεν.
Rendered as: It must be examined whether someone implicated him, though he is nothing but good, in all the evil things.
μή introduces the matter to be examined. ὑποβάλλειν with ἐπί can describe putting someone under adverse things or charges and thus bringing that person under suspicion or implicating that person. Because the surrounding argument concerns evil statements publicly written against God and asks who authored them, “implicated him … in” is chosen as a false-attribution sense rather than as a claim that God was made to undergo actual evils. A more literal alternative is “whether someone subjected him, though he is nothing but good, to all the evil things,” which may suggest actual exposure to evils; in this context it can also be understood as subjection to allegations of those evils.

SECTION 3.41

And Simon said, “You are plainly avoiding hearing from the Scriptures the refutation directed against your God.”

And Peter said, “You yourself seem to me to be doing this. For whoever avoids an orderly course of inquiry does not want a true examination to take place. Therefore, by following the proper order and wishing the author to be identified first, I am plainly one who wishes to travel the straight road.”

And Simon said, “First acknowledge whether what has been written against the creator is indeed true, and whether he is not above all things but, according to the Scriptures, subject to every form of wickedness; afterward we will investigate the one who wrote it.”

And Peter said, “So that I may not seem unwilling to investigate because I oppose your disorderly procedure, I answer: I say that if what has been written against God were true, it would in that case show God to be wicked.”

And Simon said, “How can you establish this?”

Translator's notes for section 3.41 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: Πρόδηλος εἰ
The selected print has εἰ, normally the conjunction “if,” where the syntax strongly supports the second-person copula “you are.” Treating this as an accentual or orthographic error is contextually persuasive but remains a proposed interpretation of the confirmed printed wording.

2. Translation choice — Greek: φεύγων ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν τὸν κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ σου ἀκοῦσαι ἔλεγχον
Rendered as: avoiding hearing from the Scriptures the refutation directed against your God
Takes φεύγων with the infinitive in the sense “avoid doing” and attaches ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν to the source of what is heard. Alternatively, ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν could attach more directly to φεύγων: “fleeing from the Scriptures so as not to hear.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: πρῶτον τὸν συγγραφέα νοηθῆναι
Rendered as: the author to be identified first
In this dispute about who composed the writings, νοηθῆναι means that the author is to be recognized or ascertained, not merely understood abstractly.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν εὐθεῖαν ὁδεύειν
Rendered as: to travel the straight road
Preserves the source’s road image rather than reducing it to “proceed correctly.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: πάσῃ ὑποκείμενος μοχθηρίᾳ
Rendered as: subject to every form of wickedness
πάσῃ with the abstract noun is represented idiomatically by “every form of,” while retaining Simon’s sweeping accusation.

6. Translation choice — Greek: οὕτω τὸν θεὸν δείκνυσιν μοχθηρόν
Rendered as: it would in that case show God to be wicked
οὕτω points to the stated condition: if the hostile descriptions were true, they would show God in that way to be wicked.

SECTION 3.42

And Peter said, “Because contrary things have been written against the statements that speak badly of him, neither of the two can be confirmed.”

And Simon said, “How, then, when some scriptural statements call him evil and others good, can what is true be recognized?”

And Peter said, “All the statements of the Scriptures that agree with the creation made by him are true, while all that are contrary prove to be false.”

And Simon said, “How can you show that the Scriptures contradict themselves?”

And Peter said, “You say that Adam came into being blind, which he did not; for he would not have pointed it out to a blind man while commanding him, saying, ‘But from the tree of knowing good and evil, do not taste.’”

And Simon said, “He said that his mind was blind.”

And Peter said, “How could he have been blind even in mind, when, before tasting the plant, he assigned names proper to all the animals in agreement with the one who created him?”

And Simon said, “If Adam had foreknowledge, why did he not foresee the serpent that was going to deceive his wife?”

And Peter said, “If Adam did not have foreknowledge, how did he assign his sons, as soon as they were born, names corresponding to the deeds they would perform? He called the first Cain, which is interpreted ‘jealousy’; and Cain, having become jealous, killed his brother Abel, which is interpreted ‘mourning,’ for their parents mourned over him, the first to be murdered.”

Translator's notes for section 3.42 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ταῖς αὐτὸν κακῶς λεγούσαις φωναῖς τὰ ἐναντία γέγραπται
Rendered as: contrary things have been written against the statements that speak badly of him
The dative is taken as marking the statements against which contrary claims stand. φωναί here denotes textual statements or utterances, not merely audible voices.

2. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδ᾽ ὁπότερον βεβαιωθῆναι δύναται
Rendered as: neither of the two can be confirmed
ὁπότερον refers to either of the two opposing portrayals, one calling God evil and the other good.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ γενομένῃ κτίσει
Rendered as: the creation made by him
Preserves κτίσις as “creation” and the passive description of its having been brought into being by him.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἂν τυφλῷ ἐντελλόμενος ἐδείκνυεν
Rendered as: he would not have pointed it out to a blind man while commanding him
“Pointed it out” retains the showing or indicating force of ἐδείκνυεν separately from the command expressed by ἐντελλόμενος. The implied object is the tree in the quoted command; the wording does not require a particular physical gesture, and “shown it” is also possible.

5. Translation choice — Greek: συμφώνως τῷ κτίσαντι αὐτὸν οἰκεῖα πᾶσιν τοῖς ζῴοις ἐπιθεὶς ὀνόματα
Rendered as: assigned names proper to all the animals in agreement with the one who created him
οἰκεῖα describes names appropriate or proper to the animals, while συμφώνως expresses agreement or harmony with the creator.

6. Translation choice — Greek: Κάιν, ὃ ἑρμηνεύεται ζῆλος
Rendered as: Cain, which is interpreted ‘jealousy’
ζῆλος can mean “zeal” or “jealousy.” The following ζηλώσας and Cain’s killing of Abel favor “jealousy” here.

7. Translation choice — Greek: Ἄβελ, ὃ ἑρμηνεύεται πένθος
Rendered as: Abel, which is interpreted ‘mourning’
πένθος can denote grief or mourning; the following verb ἐπένθησαν supports “mourning” and preserves the lexical connection.

SECTION 3.43

But if Adam, being God’s work, had foreknowledge, much more did the God who created him. And the statement that is written, “God considered,” is false, as though he had resorted to reasoning because of ignorance. Furthermore, if “the Lord was testing Abraham,” it was so that he might know whether he would endure. And the written statement, “Let us go down and see whether they are bringing matters to completion in accordance with their outcry that is coming to me; but if not, so that I may know”—and, so that I do not greatly prolong the discussion, whatever statements speak of his ignorance or of anything else objectionable are overturned by other statements that say the opposite and are thereby exposed as false.

That he truly foreknows is shown when he says to Abraham, “Knowing, you will know that your offspring will be a sojourner in a land not its own, and they will enslave it, mistreat it, and humble them for four hundred years. But the nation to which they may be enslaved I myself will judge. After these things they will come out here with many possessions. You, however, will depart to your fathers in peace, having been sustained in a good old age. In the fourth generation they will return here, for up to now the sins of the Amorites have not yet reached their full measure.”

Translator's notes for section 3.43 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: πρὸς· μὲ
The selected print is confirmed as having a raised point between the preposition and pronoun, together with the printed accentuation μὲ. Reading the words continuously as “to me” is strongly supported by the syntax, but treating the punctuation and accentuation as editorial oddities remains a provisional interpretation rather than a change to the supplied Greek.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐνεθυμήθη ὁ θεός
Rendered as: God considered
ἐνθυμέομαι can mean consider, reflect, or take thought. “Considered” retains the alleged act of deliberation that the author connects with reasoning from ignorance.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς λογισμῷ χρησαμένου διὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν
Rendered as: as though he had resorted to reasoning because of ignorance
The genitive construction characterizes the quoted statement as implying that God used deliberative reasoning because he lacked knowledge.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἔτι μὴν καὶ εἰ „ἐπείραζεν κύριος τὸν Ἀβραάμ“, ἵνα γνῷ εἰ ὑπομενεῖ
Rendered as: Furthermore, if “the Lord was testing Abraham,” it was so that he might know whether he would endure
The purpose clause is retained as the consequence of the conditional wording. The sentence may alternatively be understood elliptically as identifying another written statement that the author regards as false.

5. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ κατὰ τὴν κραυγὴν αὐτῶν τὴν ἐρχομένην πρὸς· μὲ συντελοῦνται
Rendered as: whether they are bringing matters to completion in accordance with their outcry that is coming to me
This rendering preserves the completion or carrying-through component of συντελοῦνται while understanding the verb as describing conduct corresponding to the outcry. Alternatives include “whether they are carrying matters through according to their outcry” and, with a more passive sense, “whether they are being brought to completion according to their outcry.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὅσαι ποτὲ φωναὶ ἀγνοίας αὐτοῦ καταλέγουσιν ἢ ἄλλο τι χαλεπόν
Rendered as: whatever statements speak of his ignorance or of anything else objectionable
χαλεπόν can mean difficult, harsh, severe, or objectionable; here it denotes some other adverse claim about God.

7. Translation choice — Greek: γινώσκων γνώσῃ
Rendered as: Knowing, you will know
Preserves the emphatic repetition of the cognate participle and verb rather than replacing it with the familiar but less source-transparent “know for certain.”

8. Translation choice — Greek: δουλώσουσιν αὐτὸ καὶ κακώσουσιν καὶ ταπεινώσουσιν αὐτοὺς
Rendered as: they will enslave it, mistreat it, and humble them
The translation preserves the source’s shift from singular αὐτό, referring to the offspring collectively, to plural αὐτούς. Smoothing all the pronouns to either singular or plural would conceal the wording.

9. Translation choice — Greek: μετὰ ἀποσκευῆς πολλῆς
Rendered as: with many possessions
ἀποσκευή can denote baggage, equipment, or movable property. “Many possessions” conveys the property carried out without suggesting modern travel luggage.

10. Translation choice — Greek: οὔπω γὰρ ἀναπεπλήρωνται αἱ ἁμαρτίαι τῶν Ἀμορραίων
Rendered as: the sins of the Amorites have not yet reached their full measure
This idiomatic rendering represents the perfect form of ἀναπληρόω, literally indicating that the sins have not yet been filled up.

SECTION 3.44

What then? Does not Moses also indicate beforehand the people’s sins and reveal in advance their dispersion among the nations? If he himself gave Moses the ability to foreknow, how did he himself not have it? But he does have it. And if he has it, as we have shown, then the written phrases “he considered,” “he regretted,” and “I will go down and see,” and all such expressions are superfluous. These things, having been foreknown before they occurred just as they were going to turn out, receive, through wise administration, an outcome not to be regretted.

Translator's notes for section 3.44 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν διασπορὰν τὴν εἰς τὰ ἔθνη
Rendered as: their dispersion among the nations
εἰς literally presents movement into the nations; “among” expresses the resulting distribution without losing its destination.

2. Translation choice — Greek: περισσόν ἐστιν
Rendered as: are superfluous
περισσός here means unnecessary, redundant, or superfluous in light of divine foreknowledge. The plural English verb accommodates the listed expressions, though the Greek uses a singular predicate.

3. Translation choice — Greek: μετεμελήθη
Rendered as: he regretted
μεταμέλομαι denotes regret or a change of mind. “Regretted” fits the contrast with the later ἀμεταμέλητον and does not impose the separate reorientation terminology.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἅτινα πρὸ τοῦ γενέσθαι ὡς ἀποβαίνειν ἤμελλεν προγνωσθέντα
Rendered as: These things, having been foreknown before they occurred just as they were going to turn out
ἅτινα is taken as referring to the events represented by the preceding expressions. It could attach more loosely to “all such things,” but their occurrence and outcome favor an event reference.

5. Translation choice — Greek: οἰκονομίᾳ σοφῇ ἀμεταμέλητον λαμβάνει τὴν ἔκβασιν
Rendered as: receive, through wise administration, an outcome not to be regretted
οἰκονομία denotes ordering, management, or administration. “Not to be regretted” preserves the verbal relationship with the preceding “he regretted”; “irrevocable outcome” is another possible contextual rendering.

SECTION 3.45

That he did not desire sacrifices is apparent from the fact that those who craved meat were killed as soon as they tasted it and, after being buried, were called at their grave a “Hill of Desires.” The one who from the outset was angry at sacrificing animals and did not want them sacrificed did not command sacrifices as though he desired them, nor did he demand firstfruits; for without sacrificing animals, neither are sacrifices performed nor can firstfruits be given.

How, moreover, could darkness and gloom and tempest—for this too is written—coexist with the one who formed a pure heaven, created the sun to shine light for everyone, and fixed for the innumerable stars the unalterable order of their courses? Thus, Simon, God’s handwriting—I mean heaven—shows the intention of its maker to be pure and firm.

Translator's notes for section 3.45 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἀπαρχαὶ, δοθῆναι
The selected print is confirmed as having a comma between ἀπαρχαί and δοθῆναι. The translation provisionally treats it as nonsemantic editorial punctuation interrupting a subject-infinitive construction; no surviving word is omitted or replaced.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ δὲ θυσιῶν αὐτὸν μὴ ὀρεχθῆναι
Rendered as: That he did not desire sacrifices
The articular infinitive makes God’s not desiring sacrifices the claim demonstrated by what follows.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἅμα τῷ γεύσασθαι ἀναιρεθῆναι
Rendered as: were killed as soon as they tasted it
ἅμα with the articular infinitive indicates that their killing coincided with their tasting; “as soon as” gives this temporal force in natural English.

4. Translation choice — Greek: χωσθέντας ἐπὶ τῷ τάφῳ „βουνὸν ἐπιθυμιῶν“ προσαγορευθῆναι
Rendered as: after being buried, were called at their grave a “Hill of Desires”
The masculine plural participle refers to the people, while the singular predicate names them collectively as a burial mound. Alternatively, the phrase may be understood as compressed wording in which their burial place was called the “Hill of Desires.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ θύσει ζῴων χαλεπαίνων
Rendered as: was angry at sacrificing animals
χαλεπαίνω denotes anger or indignation, and θύσις here is the sacrificial slaughter of animals.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπαρχὰς
Rendered as: firstfruits
The conventional term preserves the cultic category. In this argument it may include offerings dependent on animal sacrifice, rather than referring only to produce.

7. Translation choice — Greek: σκότος καὶ γνόφος καὶ θύελλα
Rendered as: darkness and gloom and tempest
The three distinct images are retained in order: darkness, thick gloom, and a violent storm or tempest.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἀμεταμέλητον ὁρίσαντι τῶν δρόμων τὴν τάξιν
Rendered as: fixed ... the unalterable order of their courses
In relation to the stars’ courses, ἀμεταμέλητον denotes an order not withdrawn or revised; “unalterable” conveys that contextual force.

9. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ χειρόγραφον (λέγω δὲ τὸν οὐρανόν)
Rendered as: God’s handwriting—I mean heaven
Preserves the image of heaven as something written by God’s own hand rather than reducing χειρόγραφον to a generic “work.”

10. Translation choice — Greek: καθαρὰν καὶ βεβαίαν τὴν τοῦ πεποιηκότος δείκνυσιν γνώμην
Rendered as: shows the intention of its maker to be pure and firm
γνώμη may mean mind, judgment, disposition, or intention. “Intention” fits the argument that the ordered heaven reveals the maker’s settled purpose; “disposition” is also possible.

SECTION 3.46

Thus the voices that slander the God who created heaven are invalidated both by the opposing voices alongside them and by creation’s refutation; for they were not written by a prophetic hand, and consequently they also appear opposed to the hand of the God who created all things. And Simon said, “How can you demonstrate this?”

Translator's notes for section 3.46 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: αἱ τοῦ τὸν οὐρανὸν κτίσαντος θεοῦ διάβολοι φωναὶ
Rendered as: the voices that slander the God who created heaven
διάβολοι characterizes the voices as slanderous, while the genitive is understood objectively: their slander is directed against God.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ τῶν σὺν αὐταῖς ἐναντίων φωνῶν
Rendered as: by the opposing voices alongside them
This preserves both the opposition and the claim that the contrary voices occur together with the slanderous ones.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ τοῦ τὰ πάντα κτίσαντος θεοῦ χειρὶ ἐναντίαι
Rendered as: opposed to the hand of the God who created all things
The repeated image of a writing hand is retained rather than reduced to a general reference to divine action.

SECTION 3.47

And Peter said, “The law of God was given through Moses, unwritten, to seventy wise men to be handed down, so that it could be administered through succession. But after Moses’ taking up, it was written by someone, though certainly not by Moses; for in the law itself it is written, ‘And Moses died, and they buried him near the house of Phogor, and no one knows his burial place to this day.’ Was it possible for Moses, after dying, to write, ‘Moses died’? For in the period after Moses—perhaps some five hundred years or even more—it is found lying in the purified temple; and after roughly another five hundred years it is carried, and in the time of Nebuchadnezzar, after being burned in this way, it perishes. And yet, although written after Moses and repeatedly lost, this law too acknowledged Moses’ foreknowledge: because he foresaw its disappearance, he did not write it. Those who wrote it, however, were exposed as ignorant by their failure to foreknow its disappearance, and so were not prophets.”

Translator's notes for section 3.47 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: καθαιρισθέντι
The image-checked edition prints the uncommon form καθαιρισθέντι. The translation provisionally understands it in the purification sense and does not treat the confirmed printed form as an OCR defect or silently alter it; the equivalent rendering “cleansed” remains possible.

2. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ Μωϋσέως ἑβδομήκοντα σοφοῖς ἀνδράσιν ἀγράφως ἐδόθη παραδίδοσθαι
Rendered as: was given through Moses, unwritten, to seventy wise men to be handed down
διὰ Μωϋσέως explicitly identifies Moses as the intermediary; ἀγράφως indicates unwritten transmission, and the passive infinitive expresses the law’s continued handing down.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἵνα τῇ διαδοχῇ πολιτεύεσθαι δύνηται
Rendered as: so that it could be administered through succession
The law remains the natural singular subject. πολιτεύεσθαι may describe its administration or its regulation of communal life through an ordered succession.

4. Translation choice — Greek: μετὰ δὲ τὴν Μωϋσέως ἀνάληψιν
Rendered as: after Moses’ taking up
ἀνάληψις is rendered transparently without replacing the author’s expression with an explicit reference to death.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν τῷ καθαιρισθέντι ναῷ
Rendered as: in the purified temple
The uncommon printed form καθαιρισθέντι is provisionally understood in the cleansing or purification sense; “in the cleansed temple” is an equivalent rendering.

6. Translation choice — Greek: φέρεται καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ Ναβουχοδονόσορ οὕτως ἐνπρησθεὶς ἀπόλλυται
Rendered as: it is carried, and in the time of Nebuchadnezzar, after being burned in this way, it perishes
The passive φέρεται is rendered directly as “is carried,” without adding “away.” It could alternatively be read impersonally as “it is reported,” although the coordination with the finite ἀπόλλυται favors treating the law as the continuing subject.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν ἀφανισμὸν αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: its disappearance
The pronoun refers naturally to the law, while ἀφανισμός denotes its disappearance, loss, or removal from sight.

SECTION 3.48

And Simon said, “Since, as you said, the things concerning God can be understood by comparison with creation, how is it possible to recognize the remaining things in the law, which derive from Moses’ tradition, are in fact true, and are mixed with false things?” And Peter said, “A certain passage in the written law, by God’s providence, was recalled without error, so as to show clearly which of the things written are true and which are false.” And Simon said, “What is it? Disclose it to us.”

Translator's notes for section 3.48 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: τοῖς ψευδέσιν. μεμιγμένα
The printed period interrupts a single grammatical phrase, since μεμιγμένα agrees with the preceding neuter plural subject and takes τοῖς ψευδέσιν as its complement. The translation treats the confirmed punctuation as an editorial sentence break that does not control the syntax.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ τῆς πρὸς τὴν κτίσιν παραβολῆς
Rendered as: by comparison with creation
παραβολή here denotes comparison or setting one thing alongside another, not necessarily a narrative parable.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀληθῆ τυγχάνοντα
Rendered as: are in fact true
τυγχάνω with the participle emphasizes their actual state rather than chance.

4. Translation choice — Greek: Περικοπή τις
Rendered as: A certain passage
περικοπή denotes a bounded section or passage of text.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἄπταιστος ἐπεμνημονεύθη
Rendered as: was recalled without error
ἐπιμνημονεύω concerns remembering or mentioning, while ἄπταιστος marks the passage as free from error; “recalled” retains that wording without claiming an unattested act of textual restoration.

SECTION 3.49

And Peter said, “I will tell you at once. Near the end of the first book of the law it is written, ‘A ruler will not cease from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the one whose it is comes; and he is the expectation of nations.’ Therefore, if anyone can understand the one who has come after the ruler and leader from Judah ceased and who is destined to be awaited by nations, this person, from what has been fulfilled, the passage . . . . . to recognize as true the one who has come. Without being persuaded by the teaching, he will know which parts of the Scriptures are true and which are false.” And Simon said, “I understand that you mean your Jesus, as the very one prophesied by Scripture. Let it therefore be granted that this is so. Tell me, then, how he taught you to distinguish the Scriptures.”

Translator's notes for section 3.49 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: οὗτος τὴν περικοπὴν ἐκ τῶν ἀποτελεσθέντων . . . . . ἀληθῆ τὸν ἐληλυθότα ἐπιγνῶναι
The selected edition contains a clearly printed five-dot lacuna that interrupts the construction and leaves the surviving accusatives and infinitive without a complete governing syntax. The same five dots have been retained in the English, the unavailable content has not been recovered, and no restoration has been supplied.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ τῶν μηρῶν αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: from his thighs
The bodily image is retained rather than replaced by an interpretive term such as “descendants.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἕως ἂν ἔλθῃ οὗ ἐστιν
Rendered as: until the one whose it is comes
