The compressed relative expression is preserved. It may also be understood as “until the one to whom it belongs comes.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ ἐθνῶν προσδοκᾶσθαι μέλλοντα
Rendered as: who is destined to be awaited by nations
μέλλω marks the future expectation, and the passive construction leaves the nations as those doing the awaiting.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἀληθῆ τὸν ἐληλυθότα ἐπιγνῶναι
Rendered as: to recognize as true the one who has come
ἀληθῆ is attached predicatively to τὸν ἐληλυθότα, the nearest matching phrase. Because the printed gap disrupts the syntax, attachment to περικοπή—“to recognize the passage as true”—remains a viable alternative.

6. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ πειθόμενος γνώσεται
Rendered as: Without being persuaded by the teaching, he will know
The negated participle is taken as modifying the manner in which he will know, contrasting recognition from fulfilled events with persuasion by teaching.

SECTION 3.50

And Peter said, “As evidence that the true things are mixed with the false, I recall that somewhere, while reproaching the Sadducees, he said, ‘This is why you go astray: you do not know the true things in the Scriptures, and because of this you are ignorant of the power of God.’ Now if he implied that they were ignorant of the true things in the Scriptures, it is plain that false ones also exist. Moreover, by saying, ‘Become approved money changers,’ he indicated that there are both genuine and counterfeit sayings. And by saying, ‘Why do you not understand what is reasonable in the Scriptures?’ he makes the understanding of the person who exercises sound judgment by personal choice more secure.”

Translator's notes for section 3.50 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ ἀληθῆ τῶν γραφῶν
Rendered as: the true things in the Scriptures
The partitive expression distinguishes true contents within the writings rather than treating “the Scriptures” collectively as the direct object of knowing.

2. Translation choice — Greek: γίνεσθε τραπεζῖται δόκιμοι
Rendered as: Become approved money changers
τραπεζῖται retains the monetary image, while δόκιμοι describes persons proven competent or approved in testing what they receive.

3. Translation choice — Greek: δοκίμων καὶ κιβδήλων λόγων
Rendered as: genuine and counterfeit sayings
The contrast extends the coin-testing image: δόκιμος is genuine or approved, whereas κίβδηλος is adulterated or counterfeit.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ εὔλογον τῶν γραφῶν
Rendered as: what is reasonable in the Scriptures
The substantival adjective may denote the reasonable content, meaning, or portion of the writings; the chosen wording leaves those closely related possibilities open.

5. Translation choice — Greek: βεβαιότερον τοῦ αὐθαιρέτως εὐγνωμονοῦντος τίθησιν τὸν νοῦν
Rendered as: he makes the understanding of the person who exercises sound judgment by personal choice more secure
The genitive is taken possessively with τὸν νοῦν. Alternatively, it can be construed comparatively: “he establishes understanding more firmly than one who judges soundly on his own authority.”

SECTION 3.51

And it is evident that, even though the Scriptures lay open, he also sent people to scribes and teachers as people who knew the true things of the real law. And his also saying, “I did not come to annul the law,” while himself appearing to annul it, was the act of one indicating that the things he annulled were not part of the law. And by also saying, “Heaven and earth will pass away; one iota or a single stroke will certainly not pass away from the law,” he indicated that the things passing away before heaven and earth do are not part of the real law.

Translator's notes for section 3.51 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν γραφῶν προκειμένων
Rendered as: even though the Scriptures lay open
The genitive absolute describes the Scriptures as already lying before people or being available; “having been set forth” is also possible.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς τοῦ ὄντως νόμου εἰδότας τὰ ἀληθῆ
Rendered as: as people who knew the true things of the real law
The participle describes the scribes and teachers; ὄντως distinguishes the genuine or actual law from material merely attributed to it.

3. Translation choice — Greek: σημαίνοντος ἦν
Rendered as: was the act of one indicating
The genitive is naturally read as a genitive of characteristic, describing what his apparently contradictory conduct signified.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἰῶτα ἓν ἢ μία κεραία
Rendered as: one iota or a single stroke
κεραία denotes a small hornlike projection or written stroke; “serif” would be a more technical alternative.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ πρὸ οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς παρερχόμενα
Rendered as: the things passing away before heaven and earth do
πρό is temporal here: these things pass away earlier than the promised passing of heaven and earth.

SECTION 3.52

Since, then, while heaven and earth still remain, sacrifices, kingdoms, the “among those born of women” prophecies, and all such things have passed away because they were not commands of God—hence indeed he says, “Every planting that the heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted”—for this reason he himself, being a true prophet, said, “I am the gate of life; the one who enters through me enters into life,” since no other teaching capable of saving exists. Therefore he also cried out, saying, “Come to me, all who toil,” that is, those who seek the truth and do not find it; and again, “My sheep hear my voice”; and on another occasion, “Seek and find,” since the truth does not lie plainly exposed.

Translator's notes for section 3.52 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: αἱ „ἐν γεννητοῖς γυναικῶν“ προφητεῖαι
Rendered as: the “among those born of women” prophecies
The quoted prepositional phrase is retained without supplying an unstated agent or referent; it may characterize the prophecies by their place among those born of women.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πᾶσα φυτεία
Rendered as: every planting
φυτεία can denote either a planting or what has been planted; “every plant” is a viable smoother alternative.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ πύλη τῆς ζωῆς
Rendered as: the gate of life
πύλη denotes a gate or gateway; the genitive may be understood as a gate belonging or leading to life.

4. Translation choice — Greek: δεῦτε πρὸς μὲ πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες
Rendered as: Come to me, all who toil
κοπιάω emphasizes laboring or becoming weary through labor; “all who are weary” is also possible.

5. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ἄλλοτε
Rendered as: and on another occasion
ἄλλοτε is temporal, marking another time or occasion rather than another location or textual position.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ζητεῖτε καὶ εὑρίσκετε
Rendered as: Seek and find
Both forms can be read morphologically as indicatives or imperatives, but their setting as a direct exhortation supports imperatives; the Greek does not contain a future equivalent to “you will find.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς μὴ προδήλως κειμένης τῆς ἀληθείας
Rendered as: since the truth does not lie plainly exposed
ὡς with the genitive absolute is taken causally. It could instead be rendered “on the understanding that the truth does not lie plainly exposed.”

SECTION 3.53

But a voice bearing witness was also heard from the heavens, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I delighted; listen to him.” And besides these things, wishing to expose them as having gone still further astray, he declared that the prophets—from whom they indeed insisted they had learned—had died desiring truth and without having learned it, saying, “Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and to hear what you hear, and, amen, I tell you, they neither saw nor heard.” What is more, he said, “I am the one concerning whom Moses prophesied, saying, ‘The Lord our God raises up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me as well; listen to him in all things. But whoever does not listen to that prophet will die.’”

Translator's notes for section 3.53 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἐξ οὐρανῶν μάρτυς φωνὴ
Rendered as: a voice bearing witness … from the heavens
μάρτυς is a noun, literally presenting the voice as a witness; the rendering preserves that function without reducing it to merely “a heavenly voice.”

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ πλεῖον αὐτοὺς πεπλανημένους ἐλέγξαι θέλων
Rendered as: wishing to expose them as having gone still further astray
The main rendering attaches ἐπὶ πλεῖον to πεπλανημένους, expressing a greater degree of error. Alternatively, it may qualify ἐλέγξαι: “wishing to demonstrate more fully that they had gone astray.” Its position immediately before αὐτοὺς πεπλανημένους supports the chosen scope but does not make it certain.

3. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτοὺς πεπλανημένους ἐλέγξαι θέλων τοὺς προφήτας
Rendered as: wishing to expose them … he declared that the prophets
αὐτούς is taken as the object of ἐλέγξαι, while τοὺς προφήτας is taken as the object of ἀπεφήνατο later in the sentence. Alternatively, τοὺς προφήτας could stand in apposition to αὐτούς, making the prophets themselves those whom he wished to expose as having gone astray.

4. Translation choice — Greek: παρ’ ὧν δὴ μεμαθηκέναι ἐβεβαίουν
Rendered as: from whom they indeed insisted they had learned
βεβαιόω here means to maintain or affirm firmly; the object of “learned” remains implicit as in the Greek.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπιθυμοῦντας ἀληθείας καὶ μὴ μεμαθηκότας τελευτήσαντας
Rendered as: had died desiring truth and without having learned it
The participles characterize the prophets at death; “truth” supplies the natural object of “learned” from the immediately preceding genitive.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν
Rendered as: amen, I tell you
ἀμήν is retained rather than replaced with a harmonized familiar formula such as “truly I say to you.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: Προφήτην ἐγείρει ὑμῖν κύριος ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν
Rendered as: The Lord our God raises up for you a prophet
ἐγείρει is printed as a present-tense form. It could function as a prophetic present with future sense, but the main rendering preserves the selected edition’s observable tense.

SECTION 3.54

Therefore, without his teaching it is impossible to attain truth that saves, even if someone searches forever where the object of the search does not exist. But it was and is in the word of our Jesus. At any rate, knowing the true things of the law, when Sadducees asked on what grounds Moses had allowed seven to marry, he said, “Moses gave you permission because of your hardness of heart, for from the beginning it did not happen that way. For the one who created the human being from the beginning made him male and female.”

Translator's notes for section 3.54 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἀληθείᾳ σωζούσῃ ἐπιστῆναι
Rendered as: to attain truth that saves
ἐφίστημι with the dative here conveys arriving at or coming upon something; σωζούσῃ explicitly characterizes the truth as saving.

2. Translation choice — Greek: κἂν τὸν αἰῶνά τις ζητῇ
Rendered as: even if someone searches forever
The accusative τὸν αἰῶνα expresses extended duration; “for an age” would preserve the noun more formally.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἔνθα τὸ ζητούμενον οὐκ ἔστιν
Rendered as: where the object of the search does not exist
The substantival participle means “what is being sought”; the location introduced by ἔνθα is left general.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ ἡμῶν λόγῳ
Rendered as: in the word of our Jesus
λόγος may mean his word, discourse, or teaching. The rendering preserves the genitival attachment to “our Jesus” without identifying Jesus himself as “the Word.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: καθ’ ὃν λόγον Μωϋσῆς ἑπτὰ συνεχώρησεν γαμεῖν
Rendered as: on what grounds Moses had allowed seven to marry
καθ’ ὃν λόγον asks for the reason or principle. The indeclinable numeral ἑπτά is taken as the infinitive’s subject: “allowed seven [people] to marry,” a contextual reading of the Sadducees’ question. It could instead be the object: “allowed [someone] to marry seven [people].” The wording does not explicitly identify the seven as brothers, men, or women. Under the chosen subject reading, the object of “marry” remains unstated.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτόν
Rendered as: the human being … made him male and female
The selected wording has singular τὸν ἄνθρωπον and singular αὐτόν, followed by both “male and female”; the singular is preserved rather than changed to a plural familiar from other forms of the saying.

SECTION 3.55

To those who suppose, as the Scriptures teach, that God swears, he said, “Let your yes be yes and your no, no, for anything beyond these comes from the evil one.” And to those who say that Abraham and Isaac and Jacob died, he said, “He is not God of the dead but of the living.” To those who think that God “tempts,” as the Scriptures say, he said, “The evil one is the one who tempts,” the same one who also tempted him. To those who assume that God does not know beforehand, he said, “For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things before you petition him.” And to those who believe, as the Scriptures say, that he does not see everything, after saying, “Pray in secret,” he said, “And your Father, who sees secret things, will repay you.”

Translator's notes for section 3.55 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: Ἀβραὰμ καὶ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ Ἰακὼβ ἀπέθανεν
The selected text has the singular verb ἀπέθανεν after three coordinated names. This is a grammatical irregularity or singular agreement centered on the coordinated group; ordinary English requires the plural “died.”

2. Greek: τοῖς δὲ πιστεύουσιν (ὡς αἱ γραφαὶ λέγουσιν) ὅτι μὴ πάντα βλέπει, „ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ εὔχεσθε“ εἰπὼν „καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ βλέπων τὰ κρυπτὰ ἀποδώσει ὑμῖν“
The final construction uses the participle εἰπών but supplies no new finite speech verb before the second quotation. The preceding ἔφη is naturally understood by ellipsis, so the translation expresses it without emending the Greek.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ γὰρ περισσὸν τούτων
Rendered as: anything beyond these
τὸ περισσόν denotes what exceeds or goes beyond the stated yes and no; “the excess beyond these” would be more formally literal.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ
Rendered as: from the evil one
The genitive form can mean either “from evil” or “from the evil one.” The immediately following explicit ὁ πονηρός favors the personal rendering here.

5. Translation choice — Greek: οὐκ ἔστιν θεὸς νεκρῶν, ἀλλὰ ζώντων
Rendered as: He is not God of the dead but of the living
The implied subject is God from the preceding clause. The Greek describes the two groups substantivally as dead and living persons.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ πονηρός ἐστιν ὁ πειράζων
Rendered as: The evil one is the one who tempts
πειράζω can mean either test or tempt, but attribution to the evil one and the following reference to his tempting Jesus support “tempt.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ καὶ αὐτὸν πειράσας
Rendered as: the same one who also tempted him
The pronoun is retained as “him”; in context its most likely referent is Jesus, though the sentence does not rename him.

8. Translation choice — Greek: πρὶν αὐτὸν ἀξιώσητε
Rendered as: before you petition him
ἀξιόω most commonly concerns deeming worthy, but with a personal object it can carry the contextual sense of making a request or petition; “before you ask him” is a smoother alternative.

9. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ κρυπτὰ
Rendered as: secret things
The Greek is a substantival neuter plural, distinct from the preceding singular phrase ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ, “in secret.”

SECTION 3.56

To those who thought that he was not good (as the Scriptures say), he said, “Which of you will, if a son asks him for bread, give him a stone instead? Or if the son also asks for a fish, will he give him a snake instead? Therefore, if you, though evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him and to those who do his will?” To those who asserted that he was in a temple, he said, “Do not swear by heaven, because it is God’s throne, nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet.” To those who had assumed beforehand that God desires sacrifices, he said, “God wants mercy and not sacrifices, knowledge of him and not whole burnt offerings.”

Translator's notes for section 3.56 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: μήτε τὴν γῆν, ὅτι ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν αὐτοῦ ἐστίν. τοῖς δὲ προλαβοῦσιν
The supplied edition does not print a closing quotation mark after ἐστίν before the narrative resumes with τοῖς δὲ. The syntactic boundary is clear, so the English supplies the closing quotation mark without proposing missing words.

2. Greek: ἔφη „ὁ θεὸς ἔλεος θέλει καὶ οὐ θυσίας, ἐπίγνωσιν αὐτοῦ καὶ οὐχ ὁλοκαυτώματα.
The supplied edition opens this final quotation but prints no closing quotation mark after ὁλοκαυτώματα. The English supplies closure at the end of the intelligible quotation; this is an editorial-punctuation feature, not a restoration of wording.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τίνα ὑμῶν αἰτήσει υἱὸς ἄρτον, μὴ λίθον ἐπιδώσει αὐτῷ;
Rendered as: Which of you will, if a son asks him for bread, give him a stone instead?
The son is the subject of αἰτήσει, while the person addressed by τίνα ὑμῶν is the understood subject of ἐπιδώσει. The conditional English expresses the paratactic relationship, and the rhetorical question preserves μή’s expectation of a negative answer.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς αἰτουμένοις αὐτὸν
Rendered as: those who ask him
The middle-form participle is rendered idiomatically as requesting something from him.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς δὲ αὐτὸν διαβεβαιουμένοις ἐν ναῷ εἶναι
Rendered as: To those who asserted that he was in a temple
διαβεβαιόομαι conveys confident assertion; the pronoun’s referent remains as implicit as it is in the Greek.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς δὲ προλαβοῦσιν ὅτι θυσιῶν ὀρέγεται ὁ θεός
Rendered as: To those who had assumed beforehand that God desires sacrifices
Here προλαμβάνω presents a prior assumption or preconception. Unlike the preceding διαβεβαιουμένοις, it does not by itself establish that they voiced a confident assertion.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπίγνωσιν αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: knowledge of him
The genitive is taken objectively, referring to knowledge of God; “recognition of him” remains a viable lexical alternative.

SECTION 3.57

To those who had been persuaded that he was evil (as the Scriptures say), he said, “Do not call me good, for the one who is good is one.” And again, “Become good and compassionate like the Father who is in the heavens, who makes the sun rise upon the good and the evil and brings rain upon the righteous and the unrighteous.” To those who had been deceived into supposing that there are many gods (as the Scriptures say), he said, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord, is one.”

Translator's notes for section 3.57 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: μή με λέγε ἀγαθόν· ὁ γὰρ ἀγαθὸς εἷς ἐστίν
Rendered as: Do not call me good, for the one who is good is one
The masculine singular substantive ὁ ἀγαθός and masculine εἷς refer to a personal singular, “the one who is good.” The rendering preserves the unusual numerical predication without adding “God” or substituting a familiar canonical formula.

2. Translation choice — Greek: γίνεσθε ἀγαθοὶ καὶ οἰκτίρμονες
Rendered as: Become good and compassionate
γίνεσθε denotes becoming, while οἰκτίρμονες emphasizes compassion or mercy.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ πατὴρ ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς
Rendered as: the Father who is in the heavens
The attributive article and phrase are represented explicitly, and the plural οὐρανοῖς is retained as “heavens.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: φέρει τὸν ὑετὸν
Rendered as: brings rain
This preserves the verb φέρει rather than assimilating it to the wording of a familiar parallel.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πολλοὺς θεοὺς ὑπονοεῖν
Rendered as: supposing that there are many gods
ὑπονοέω denotes supposing or imagining; English supplies “there are” to express the predicate construction naturally.

6. Translation choice — Greek: κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν κύριος εἷς ἐστίν
Rendered as: the Lord your God, the Lord, is one
The rendering retains both occurrences of κύριος and the plural possessive ὑμῶν. An alternative syntactic presentation is “The Lord, your God, is one Lord,” but the main wording more visibly preserves the repeated title and final numerical predicate.

SECTION 3.58

All the same, Simon, recognizing that Peter was compelling him to use the Scriptures as Jesus had taught, did not want an examination of the discourse about God to take place, although Peter had changed the examination, as Simon himself had demanded, so that it would proceed by question and answer. Nevertheless, the inquiry continued for three days. As the fourth day began to dawn, Simon set out by night for Tyre in Phoenicia. Not many days later, some of those who had gone ahead came and told Peter, “Simon, performing great wonders in Tyre, has astounded many of the people there and, through many slanders, has caused you to be hated.”

Translator's notes for section 3.58 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ὁμῶς ὁ Σίμων
The image-checked edition prints ὁμῶς, which can mean “similarly” or “in the same way.” The context permits the adversative force normally written ὅμως, “nevertheless.” “All the same” is a provisional contextual rendering, while the printed form remains unchanged and its interpretation is not certain.

2. Translation choice — Greek: Πέτρος αὐτὸν συνάγει ταῖς γραφαῖς χρῆσθαι
Rendered as: Peter was compelling him to use the Scriptures
συνάγει can express constraint or compulsion in this construction; “bringing him to use” is a possible but weaker alternative.

3. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὸν περὶ θεοῦ λόγον ἐξέτασιν γενέσθαι
Rendered as: an examination of the discourse about God to take place
λόγος may mean discourse, teaching, or argument; “discourse” preserves the broad sense without identifying it with a particular doctrine.

4. Translation choice — Greek: μεταθεμένου τοῦ Πέτρου
Rendered as: although Peter had changed the examination
The implicit object of μετατίθημι is supplied from ἐξέτασιν, and the following phrase identifies the new question-and-answer format.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ ζήτησις τριῶν ἐπεκράτησεν ἡμερῶν
Rendered as: the inquiry continued for three days
ἐπικρατέω literally suggests holding sway, but with the duration expressed by τριῶν ... ἡμερῶν it indicates that the inquiry persisted throughout that period.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τινες τῶν προόδων
Rendered as: some of those who had gone ahead
The substantival expression denotes people preceding the main party; “members of the advance party” and “forerunners” are viable alternatives.

7. Translation choice — Greek: σὲ πολλαῖς διαβολαῖς μισεῖσθαι ἐποίησεν
Rendered as: through many slanders, has caused you to be hated
The dative πολλαῖς διαβολαῖς expresses the means by which Simon caused hostility toward Peter.

SECTION 3.59

When Peter heard this, on the following night he had the crowd of hearers assemble. All the same, when they had assembled, he said, “Since, as I was setting out toward the nations that declare that there are many gods, to proclaim and teach that God is one, ‘who created heaven and earth’ and everything in them, so that by loving him they might be able to be saved, evil got there first and, by the law of pairing, sent Simon ahead, so that, if people cease declaring that there are many gods, they may condemn those called gods on earth but suppose that there are many gods in heaven, so that, having never honored the good of sole rule, they may perish completely after punishment. And what is most terrible, because the true word possesses incomparable strength, by getting there first with his slanders he persuades them not to accept it from me at all, lest the slanderer himself be exposed as a devil in reality and the true word, once shown forth, be able to be believed. I must therefore overtake him quickly, so that the slander, if allowed to persist, does not gain complete control of everyone.”

Translator's notes for section 3.59 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ὁμῶς συνελθοῦσιν ἔφη
The image-checked edition again prints ὁμῶς. It can be read as “similarly,” but the context permits the adversative force “all the same,” normally written ὅμως. The main rendering is provisional, and the printed form is not treated as an OCR defect.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν ἀκροατῶν τὸν ὄχλον συνελθεῖν ἐποίησεν
Rendered as: he had the crowd of hearers assemble
The causative construction with ἐποίησεν and the infinitive indicates that Peter caused or arranged for the gathering.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ ἔθνη τὰ πολλοὺς θεοὺς λέγοντα
Rendered as: the nations that declare that there are many gods
λέγειν with πολλοὺς θεούς conveys asserting the existence of many gods, not merely pronouncing the words.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ τῆς συζυγίας νόμῳ
Rendered as: by the law of pairing
συζυγία denotes conjunction, yoking, or pairing and here evokes the work’s paired-agent framework; “law of conjunction” remains a viable alternative.

5. Translation choice — Greek: καταγνόντες τῶν ἐπὶ γῆς λεγομένων
Rendered as: they may condemn those called gods on earth
“Gods” is supplied from the immediately preceding πολλοὺς θεοὺς λέγειν. The more formally elliptical “those spoken of on earth” is possible but obscures the contextual referent.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ τῆς μοναρχίας τιμήσαντες καλὸν
Rendered as: having honored the good of sole rule
μοναρχία denotes rule by one or sole sovereignty. The preceding μηδέποτε negates the participle: they never honor this good.

7. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτὸ μηδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἀναδέξασθαί μου
Rendered as: not to accept it from me at all
αὐτό most naturally refers to the true word, while μηδὲ τὴν ἀρχήν is idiomatic for “not at all.” The more temporally explicit “not to accept it from me even at the outset” remains possible.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ διαβάλλων αὐτὸς τῷ ὄντι διάβολος
Rendered as: the slanderer himself be exposed as a devil in reality
Rendering διαβάλλων as “slanderer” and διάβολος as “devil” preserves the source’s wordplay.

9. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτὸν ἐπικαταλαβεῖν
Rendered as: overtake him
ἐπικαταλαμβάνω here means catching up with someone who has gone ahead.

SECTION 3.60

“Since, then, it is necessary to appoint someone in my place, one who will fill my position, let us all pray to God with one resolve, so that he himself may make evident the best of those among us, in order that, seated upon the Messiah’s chair, he may administer his church devoutly. Who, then, will be appointed? For by God’s counsel that man is shown to be blessed whom his lord will appoint over the service of his fellow servants, to give them their provisions at their proper time, neither thinking nor saying in his heart, ‘My lord is delaying his coming,’ nor beginning to beat his fellow servants while eating and drinking with both prostitutes and drunkards. And the lord of that servant will come at an hour that he does not expect and on a day that he does not know, and he will cut him in two and place the unfaithful part of him with the hypocrites.”

Translator's notes for section 3.60 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: μὴ ἐννοούμενον καὶ λέγοντα ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ Χρονίζει ὁ κύριός μου ἐλθεῖν καὶ ἄρξηται τύπτειν τοὺς συνδούλους αὐτοῦ, ἐσθίων καὶ πίνων μετά τε πορνῶν καὶ μεθυόντων
The construction begins with accusative participles connected to ὃν, shifts to the finite subjunctive ἄρξηται, and then uses the nominative participles ἐσθίων and πίνων. The scope of μή is also uncertain. The main text takes it broadly over the coordinated misconduct because the surrounding clause identifies the appointed man as blessed and charges him with timely provision. A narrower scope, in which only ἐννοούμενον is negated and the saying and abuse are affirmative, remains possible and better prepares for the following punishment. The sentence is anacoluthic, but both readings arise from the supplied wording and no conjectural restoration is required.

2. Translation choice — Greek: μιᾷ προαιρέσει
Rendered as: with one resolve
προαίρεσις denotes deliberate purpose or resolve; the phrase calls for united intention in prayer.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν ὄντων ἐν ἡμῖν τὸν κρείττονα
Rendered as: the best of those among us
The comparative κρείττονα selects the superior member from the group and therefore functions contextually as “the best”; “the one who is better among us” is a more formally comparative alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τῆς χριστοῦ καθέδρας
Rendered as: upon the Messiah’s chair
χριστός functions independently as a title and is rendered “Messiah”; καθέδρα denotes an authoritative seat or chair.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν αὐτοῦ ἐκκλησίαν εὐσεβῶς οἰκονομῇ
Rendered as: he may administer his church devoutly
οἰκονομέω denotes managing or administering, while εὐσεβῶς describes reverent or devout conduct. The pronoun’s precise antecedent remains implicit in English as in Greek.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τῆς θεραπείας τῶν συνδούλων αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: over the service of his fellow servants
θεραπεία may denote service, attendance, care, or a body of household attendants. “Over the care of his fellow servants” and “over the household of his fellow servants” are contextual alternatives.

7. Translation choice — Greek: μὴ ἐννοούμενον καὶ λέγοντα ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ Χρονίζει ὁ κύριός μου ἐλθεῖν καὶ ἄρξηται τύπτειν τοὺς συνδούλους αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: neither thinking nor saying in his heart, ‘My lord is delaying his coming,’ nor beginning to beat his fellow servants
The main rendering takes μή broadly over the coordinated misconduct, keeping it within the characterization or warning attached to the appointed man. English “neither ... nor” expresses that broad negative scope. A narrower reading—“not taking thought, and saying ... and beginning”—is grammatically possible and more directly anticipates the ensuing punishment, but it turns the latter actions into affirmative narrative and fits the description of the blessed appointee less readily.

8. Translation choice — Greek: Χρονίζει ὁ κύριός μου ἐλθεῖν
Rendered as: My lord is delaying his coming
χρονίζειν with an infinitive means taking a long time or delaying the action. Lowercase “lord” preserves the servant-master imagery without deciding whether a divine referent is foregrounded.

9. Translation choice — Greek: διχοτομήσει αὐτόν
Rendered as: he will cut him in two
This preserves the literal and violent image of διχοτομέω rather than weakening it to “punish severely.”

10. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ ἀπιστοῦν αὐτοῦ μέρος μετὰ τῶν ὑποκριτῶν θήσει
Rendered as: place the unfaithful part of him with the hypocrites
The neuter participle ἀπιστοῦν directly qualifies μέρος, producing the unusual image of an unfaithful or unbelieving part of the servant. The rendering does not replace it with the textually different idea of assigning the servant a portion.

SECTION 3.61

But if any of those present, though able to manage people’s unreasonableness, draws back, caring only for his own rest, let him too expect to hear, “Wicked and lazy servant, you should have put my silver before the bankers, and when I came I would have collected what was mine. Cast the useless servant into the outer darkness.” And rightly so. “For it was your responsibility,” he says, “human being, to put my words before bankers like silver and to test them like currency.” Therefore, the multitude of believers must obey one particular person, so that in this way it may be able to continue in harmony. For a system that culminates in the rule of a single authority, as an image of monarchy, puts those who submit in a position to enjoy peace because of good order; but when all are eager to rule and unwilling to yield to one alone, they are also certain to fall because of division.

Translator's notes for section 3.61 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: χρήματα;δοκιμάσαι
The selected edition prints a Greek question mark between χρήματα and δοκιμάσαι, interrupting two coordinated infinitives. The translation follows the defensible syntactic coordination while disclosing the punctuation rather than treating it as missing wording.

2. Greek: τὸ δὲ πάντας φιλαρχοῦντας ἑνὶ μόνῳ ὑπεῖξαι μὴ θέλειν, καὶ αἰτίᾳ διαιρέσεως πάντως καὶ πεσεῖν ἔχουσιν
The sentence begins with a neuter substantivized infinitival construction but shifts to the plural finite verb ἔχουσιν, with the semantic plural πάντας supplying the sense. This is intelligible as an anacoluthon, so no restoration is required.

3. Translation choice — Greek: διοικεῖν δυνάμενος τὴν ἀγνωμοσύνην τῶν ἀνθρώπων
Rendered as: though able to manage people’s unreasonableness
Here ἀγνωμοσύνη denotes deficient judgment or unreasonable conduct; “ingratitude” is lexically possible but fits the governing context less well.

4. Translation choice — Greek: δοῦλε πονηρὲ καὶ ὀκνηρέ
Rendered as: Wicked and lazy servant
Following the supplied policy, δοῦλος is rendered “servant”; the context still carries the subordinate status of a servant answerable to his lord.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἔπραξα τὸ ἐμόν
Rendered as: I would have collected what was mine
πράσσω here means exacting or recovering what is due, rather than merely “doing” what belongs to the speaker.

6. Translation choice — Greek: σοῦ γὰρ (φησίν), ἄνθρωπε
Rendered as: For it was your responsibility, he says, human being
The genitive σοῦ with the following infinitives is understood as an elliptical expression of obligation: “it was your part” or “it was your responsibility.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς χρήματα;δοκιμάσαι
Rendered as: to test them like currency
δοκιμάζω evokes testing or assaying currency; “them” refers to the preceding λόγους, though the Greek does not repeat the object.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ γὰρ εἰς ἀρχὴν μιᾶς λῆγον ἐξουσίας
Rendered as: a system that culminates in the rule of a single authority
The substantivized neuter phrase describes an arrangement or system ending in one governing authority.

9. Translation choice — Greek: μοναρχίας εἰκόνι
Rendered as: as an image of monarchy
The dative εἰκόνι characterizes the single-authority arrangement as a likeness or representation of monarchy.

10. Translation choice — Greek: πάντως καὶ πεσεῖν ἔχουσιν
Rendered as: they are also certain to fall
ἔχειν with an infinitive expresses what lies ahead or is inevitable; “they must also fall” is a viable alternative.

SECTION 3.62

But furthermore, let what happens before our eyes persuade us: now, with many kings throughout the whole earth, wars happen continually. For each has the other’s rule as a pretext for war. But if one person is leader of the whole, having nothing for which to wage war, he has perpetual peace. Ultimately, then, for those deemed worthy of eternal life, God appoints one king over the whole in that age, so that, because of monarchy, unfailing peace may come about. Therefore, everyone must follow one person as guide, honoring him as an image of God, while the guide must know the entrance leading into the holy city.

Translator's notes for section 3.62 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἀλλ᾽ .ἔτι
The selected edition prints a period between the elided ἀλλ᾽ and ἔτι. It appears to be stray editorial punctuation rather than a lacuna marker; no wording has been supplied in its place.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πειθέτω τὰ παρ᾽ ὀφθαλμοῖς γινόμενα
Rendered as: let what happens before our eyes persuade us
The verb has no expressed object; “us” represents the assembled hearers, while “persuade the observer” or “be persuasive” remains possible.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἔχει γὰρ ἕκαστος πρόφασιν εἰς πόλεμον τὴν ἑτέρου ἀρχήν
Rendered as: each has the other’s rule as a pretext for war
πρόφασις may mean a pretext, occasion, or stated reason; “pretext” preserves the author’s critical force.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οὗ εἵνεκεν πολεμεῖ οὐκ ἔχων
Rendered as: having nothing for which to wage war
The relative expression is understood impersonally as the absent reason or occasion for war; “having no one against whom to wage war” is a contextual alternative.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πέρας γοῦν
Rendered as: Ultimately, then
πέρας functions adverbially as “at last,” “in the end,” or “as the final outcome,” introducing the eschatological arrangement.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἄπτωτος εἰρήνη
Rendered as: unfailing peace
ἄπτωτος literally describes what does not fall or collapse; “secure peace” or “unshakable peace” are viable alternatives.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς εἰκόνα θεοῦ προτιμῶντας
Rendered as: honoring him as an image of God
προτιμάω conveys assigning precedence or special honor; “preferring him” would be more literal but less clear in this context.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν πόλιν εἰσούσης εἰσόδου
Rendered as: the entrance leading into the holy city
The rendering preserves the source’s repeated entrance-and-entering image without reproducing an awkward English cognate construction.

SECTION 3.63

“Whom else among those present shall I choose except Zacchaeus, to whom our Lord also went in and rested, judging him worthy to be saved?” After saying this, he laid his hand on Zacchaeus, who was standing there, and pressed him to sit in his chair. But Zacchaeus fell at his feet and begged him to release him from governing, while making this promise and saying, “Whatever a leader must do, I will do; only grant me not to bear this name. For I am wary of putting on the name of office, for it is full of bitter envy and danger.”

Translator's notes for section 3.63 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς ὃν καὶ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν εἰσιὼν ἀνεπαύσατο
Rendered as: to whom our Lord also went in and rested
The wording says that the Lord entered or went in to Zacchaeus and rested; it does not explicitly name a house.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ σώζεσθαι κρίνας ἄξιον εἶναι
Rendered as: judging him worthy to be saved
The genitive articular infinitive depends on ἄξιον and identifies that of which Zacchaeus was judged worthy.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐβιάζετο ἐπὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ καθεσθῆναι καθέδραν
Rendered as: pressed him to sit in his chair
The middle verb can mean compel, constrain, or strongly urge. “Pressed” preserves the insistence without necessarily implying physical force.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ καθεσθῆναι καθέδραν
Rendered as: to sit in his chair
αὐτοῦ most naturally refers to Zacchaeus, though Peter remains a grammatically possible referent; the English pronoun preserves that ambiguity.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ ἄρχειν αὐτὸν ἀπολύσῃ
Rendered as: release him from governing
The genitive infinitive names the responsibility from which Zacchaeus asks to be released.

6. Translation choice — Greek: εὐλαβοῦμαι
Rendered as: I am wary
The verb may express caution, apprehension, or reverential fear; “I am afraid” is possible but somewhat stronger.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ τῆς ἀρχῆς ἐνδύσασθαι ὄνομα
Rendered as: putting on the name of office
The translation retains the clothing image of ἐνδύομαι and renders ἀρχή as governing office in this context.

SECTION 3.64

And Peter said, “If this is what you are wary of, do not be called a ruler, but ‘the one appointed,’ since the Lord permitted this expression to be used when he said, ‘Blessed is that man whom his lord will appoint over the care of his fellow servants.’ If, however, you do not want it known at all that you have authority to administer, you seem to me not to realize that the acknowledged authority of the one presiding has considerable power to inspire deference in the multitude. For each person obeys one who has received the authority, since he regards his conscience as a powerful constraint. What then? Do you not also know for certain that you are to rule, not as the rulers of the nations do, but as a servant (ministering to them), as a father (to those being wronged), as a physician (attending to them), as a shepherd (guarding them)—in short, I say, having every concern for their salvation? Do you think I am unaware what sort of toils I am pressing you to undertake when I require you to be judged by crowds whom it is impossible for anyone to please? Yet one who acts well is fully able to win God’s favor. Therefore I ask you to undertake it willingly, for God’s sake, for the Messiah’s sake, for the salvation of the brothers, for their proper ordering, and for your benefit.”

Translator's notes for section 3.64 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἄρχων μὲν μὴ καλοῦ, ἀλλὰ ὁ καθεστώς
Rendered as: do not be called a ruler, but ‘the one appointed’
ὁ καθεστώς is a perfect participial title meaning the person who has been established or appointed, deliberately distinguished from ἄρχων.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦτο τοῦ κυρίου δεδωκότος λέγεσθαι
Rendered as: since the Lord permitted this expression to be used
The genitive absolute says that the Lord granted or allowed this designation to be spoken; “gave this to be said” would be more formally literal.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τῆς θεραπείας τῶν συνδούλων αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: over the care of his fellow servants
θεραπεία can denote care, service, attendance, or a body of attendants. “Over the company of his fellow servants” is therefore possible, but “care” fits the ensuing description of pastoral duties.

4. Translation choice — Greek: συνδούλων
Rendered as: fellow servants
Following the supplied policy, δοῦλος and its compound are rendered with “servant”; the compound stresses shared subordination to the same lord.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς δυσωπίαν τοῦ πλήθους
Rendered as: to inspire deference in the multitude
δυσωπία concerns restraint produced by respect, shame, or awe. “To overawe the multitude” is possible but gives the phrase a harsher tone.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς μεγάλην ἀνάγκην τὴν συνείδησιν ἔχων
Rendered as: since he regards his conscience as a powerful constraint
The participle most naturally continues with ἕκαστος as its subject; conscience supplies the compelling reason to obey recognized authority.

7. Translation choice — Greek: οὐχ ὡς οἱ ἄρχοντες τῶν ἐθνῶν ἄρχειν ἔχεις
Rendered as: you are to rule, not as the rulers of the nations do
ἔχεις with the infinitive expresses what Zacchaeus is expected or obliged to do.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ὅτι οἴει ἀγνοεῖν με
Rendered as: Do you think I am unaware
The initial ὅτι introduces an elliptical rhetorical question; “Is it because you think I am unaware?” is a more explicit alternative.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ ὄχλων κρίνεσθαί σε ἀξιῶν
Rendered as: when I require you to be judged by crowds
ἀξιόω with an infinitive can mean require, expect, or deem appropriate, rather than necessarily “consider worthy.”

10. Translation choice — Greek: θεὸν δὲ εὖ πράττοντα πείθειν δυνατώτατον
Rendered as: Yet one who acts well is fully able to win God’s favor
The person acting well is taken as the subject of πείθειν and God as its object. More literally, “to persuade God” or “to prevail upon God” is possible; context favors the idiom of gaining divine approval.

11. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ χριστόν
Rendered as: for the Messiah’s sake
Χριστός functions independently as a title here, so it is rendered “the Messiah” under the supplied policy.

12. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὲρ τῆς αὐτῶν οἰκονομίας
Rendered as: for their proper ordering
οἰκονομία can denote administration, management, arrangement, or stewardship. The genitive may be understood as the proper ordering or administration of the brothers.

SECTION 3.65

Also consider this other point: to the degree that administering the Messiah’s church involves toil and danger, the reward is that much greater. But furthermore, the punishment is also greater for one who is capable and disobeys. Therefore, knowing that you are more learned than those present, I want you to lend out the good counsels with which you have been entrusted by the Lord, so that you may hear, “Well done, good and faithful servant,” and not, like the one who hid the single talent, be found liable to punishment after receiving an accusation. But if you do not wish to become a good guardian of the church, identify someone else in your place, more learned and more faithful than you. But you will not provide one. For you were with the Lord, gave an account of the marvelous deeds, and learned how to administer a church.

Translator's notes for section 3.65 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ τὴν χριστοῦ ἐκκλησίαν οἰκονομεῖν
Rendered as: administering the Messiah’s church
οἰκονομεῖν denotes managing or administering, and Χριστός is rendered as the independently functioning title “Messiah.”

2. Translation choice — Greek: τοσούτῳ μείζων ὁ μισθός
Rendered as: the reward is that much greater
τοσούτῳ supplies the proportional counterpart to the preceding toil and danger: the greater the burden, the greater the reward.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ δυναμένῳ καὶ ἀπειθήσαντι
Rendered as: for one who is capable and disobeys
The substantival participles describe someone able to accept the responsibility who nevertheless refuses or disobeys.

4. Translation choice — Greek: δανείζειν καλὰς γνώμας
Rendered as: to lend out the good counsels
The rendering retains the financial metaphor of δανείζειν. γνώμαι may also be rendered “teachings,” “judgments,” or “principles.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἃς παρὰ τοῦ κυρίου πεπίστευσαι
Rendered as: with which you have been entrusted by the Lord
The perfect passive treats the counsels as a trust committed to Zacchaeus by the Lord.

6. Translation choice — Greek: εὖ δοῦλε ἀγαθὲ καὶ πιστὲ
Rendered as: Well done, good and faithful servant
The isolated εὖ implies commendation, conventionally expressed in English as “Well done”; δοῦλος follows the supplied “servant” policy.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἔγκλημα λαβὼν κολάσει ὑπεύθυνος ἀναφανῇς
Rendered as: be found liable to punishment after receiving an accusation
ἔγκλημα is a charge, accusation, or ground of blame, and ἀναφανῇς means being shown or found to occupy the stated condition.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἕτερον ἀντὶ σοῦ μήνυσον
Rendered as: identify someone else in your place
μηνύω here means disclose, point out, or name a suitable alternative.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἀλλὰ οὐ δώσεις
Rendered as: But you will not provide one
The object is unexpressed but is supplied by the previously requested alternative person; “you will not produce one” is also possible.

10. Translation choice — Greek: τὰς θαυμασίους πράξεις ἱστόρησας
Rendered as: gave an account of the marvelous deeds
ἱστορέω can mean recount or report what one has learned, supporting the narrative rendering chosen here. In view of the preceding statement that Zacchaeus was with the Lord, the experiential alternatives “observed the marvelous deeds,” “witnessed the marvelous deeds,” or “became acquainted with the marvelous deeds” are also contextually viable.

11. Translation choice — Greek: τὰς θαυμασίους πράξεις
Rendered as: the marvelous deeds
θαυμασίους may be analyzed as the feminine accusative plural of a two-termination adjective agreeing with πράξεις; the printed form therefore does not require correction.

12. Translation choice — Greek: διοίκησιν ἐκκλησίας μεμάθηκας
Rendered as: learned how to administer a church
The Greek uses the noun “administration” with “church”; the verbal English form expresses the acquired practical knowledge without adding a new claim.

SECTION 3.66

And your task is to command what is necessary, while the brothers’ task is to submit and not disobey. Those who submit, then, will be saved, but those who disobey will be punished by the Messiah, because the one presiding has been entrusted with the Messiah’s place. Therefore, either honor or insult shown to the one presiding is carried to the Messiah, and from the Messiah it is referred to God. I have said this so that the brothers themselves may not be unaware of their own danger from disobedience toward you: whoever disobeys when you command disobeys the Messiah, and one who has disobeyed the Messiah provokes God to anger.

Translator's notes for section 3.66 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: σοῦ μὲν ἔργον ἐστὶν κελεύειν ἃ δεῖ, τῶν ἀδελφῶν ὑπείκειν
Rendered as: your task is to command what is necessary, while the brothers’ task is to submit
The second clause elides ἔργον ἐστίν, which is supplied in English without adding a new claim.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ προκαθεζόμενος χριστοῦ τόπον πεπίστευται
Rendered as: the one presiding has been entrusted with the Messiah’s place
The passive πεπίστευται presents the presider as entrusted with a representative position; it does not identify him as the Messiah.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἤτοι τιμὴ ἢ ὕβρις τοῦ προκαθεζομένου
Rendered as: either honor or insult shown to the one presiding
The genitive is understood objectively in context: the honor or insult is directed toward the presider. A less likely formal alternative is “the presider’s honor or insult.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: χριστοῦ
Rendered as: Messiah
Χριστός functions independently as a title throughout the passage rather than as part of a personal-name construction.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς πρὸς σὲ ἀπειθείας τὸν κίνδυνον αὐτῶν
Rendered as: their own danger from disobedience toward you
The placement of αὐτῶν is awkward but defensibly identifies the danger as belonging to the brothers; the genitive ἀπειθείας indicates the disobedience from which that danger arises.

SECTION 3.67

The church, therefore, like a city built on a height, must have a God-loving order and good administration. Above all, let the bishop, as ruler, be listened to in the matters about which he speaks. Let the elders be diligent to see that what is commanded is done. Let the deacons, going all around among the brothers, look after their bodies and souls and confer with the bishop. Let all the other brothers accept being wronged; but if they want their cases concerning the wrongs done to them to be judged, let them be brought to agreement before the elders. The elders are then to report the settlement also to the bishop.

Translator's notes for section 3.67 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς πόλιν ἐν ὕψει ᾠκοδομημένην
Rendered as: like a city built on a height
This preserves both the city comparison and its elevated location without turning the image into a quotation from another text.

2. Translation choice — Greek: φιλόθεον ἔχειν τάξιν
Rendered as: have a God-loving order
The adjective φιλόθεον directly characterizes the community’s τάξις as devoted to or loving God.

3. Translation choice — Greek: περὶ ὧν λέγει ἀκουέσθω
Rendered as: let ... be listened to in the matters about which he speaks
The passive of ἀκούω can imply being heeded or obeyed; “be listened to” preserves that force without making obedience more explicit than the wording requires.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκπεριερχόμενοί τῶν ἀδελφῶν τὰ σώματα καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἐπισκεπτέσθωσαν καὶ τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ ἀντιβαλλέτωσαν
Rendered as: going all around among the brothers, look after their bodies and souls and confer with the bishop
Ἐπισκέπτομαι includes visiting, inspecting, and caring for. The uncommon ἀντιβάλλω may indicate conferring with, reporting back to, or laying the findings before the bishop; “confer with” leaves the precise exchange open.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων συμβιβαζέσθωσαν
Rendered as: let them be brought to agreement before the elders
The passive or middle συμβιβάζεσθαι can denote reconciliation or the settlement of a dispute; the following συμβιβασμόν supports an agreed settlement.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν δὲ συμβιβασμὸν ... τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ προσαναφερέτωσαν
Rendered as: report the settlement also to the bishop
Προσαναφέρω here denotes referring or reporting the elders’ settlement upward or additionally to the bishop.

SECTION 3.68

Let them expedite the marriages not only of the young but also of those advanced in years, lest seething desire bring a plague upon the church through an occasion of sexual immorality or adultery. For above every sin, the impiety of adultery is hated by God, because it destroys not only the sinner himself but also those who share his table and strive alongside him. It resembles rabies, for by nature it imparts its own madness. For chastity’s sake, therefore, let not only the elders but everyone be eager to complete marriages. The sin of the adulterer forces its way upon everyone. Therefore, urging the brothers to live chastely is the first act of mercy, for it is care for the soul; food for the body is relief.

Translator's notes for section 3.68 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἀλλὰ-καὶ
The selected print joins the two particles with a hyphen. This is an orthographic or editorial feature and does not alter the ordinary construction “but also.”

2. Greek: τοῦτο πρώτῃ ἐλεημοσύνη
The dative πρώτῃ does not agree with the predicate noun ἐλεημοσύνη. The intended predicate sense is nevertheless clear, and the translation represents it as “the first act of mercy.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: κατεπειγέτωσαν τοὺς γάμους
Rendered as: let them expedite the marriages
The verb calls for actively hastening the marriages rather than merely recommending them.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν προβεβηκότων
Rendered as: those advanced in years
The perfect participle describes people who have progressed in age; “older people” is also possible.

5. Translation choice — Greek: προφάσει πορνείας ἢ μοιχείας
Rendered as: through an occasion of sexual immorality or adultery
Πρόφασις can mean pretext, occasion, or ostensible cause. “Through an occasion” best fits the warning that seething desire may bring the stated plague; a more literal but less clear alternative is “under a pretext of sexual immorality or adultery.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς συνεστιωμένους καὶ συναμιλλωμένους
Rendered as: those who share his table and strive alongside him
The two participles depict people dining with the offender and engaging alongside him. The second can also be understood more generally as associating or sharing his pursuits.

7. Translation choice — Greek: λύσσῃ γὰρ ἔοικεν
Rendered as: It resembles rabies
Λύσσα can denote rabies or raging madness; the following image of contagious madness supports the disease sense while retaining its association with frenzy.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ οὖν σπεύδειν σωφρονεῖν τοὺς ἀδελφούς
Rendered as: urging the brothers to live chastely
Σπεύδειν is taken transitively as hastening or urging the brothers toward σωφροσύνη. The syntax also permits “the brothers’ being eager to live chastely.”

9. Translation choice — Greek: ψυχῆς γὰρ ἐστὶν θεραπεία
Rendered as: for it is care for the soul
Θεραπεία can mean care, treatment, or healing; “care” preserves the contrast with bodily nourishment without asserting a specific medical image.

SECTION 3.69

Nevertheless, if you love your brothers, you will take nothing away from them, but you will share what you have. You will feed the hungry, provide drink for the thirsty, clothe the naked, visit the sick, help those in prisons as far as possible, eagerly welcome strangers into your own lodgings, and hate no one. As for how you must act devoutly, your own understanding will teach you, since you are discerning. Above all—even if it is necessary to tell you—meet together more frequently; would that it were every hour, but at least on the customary days of assembly. For if you do this, you are within walls of refuge, since desertion from the ranks is the beginning of destruction. Accordingly, let no one be absent from meeting together on the pretext of petty resentment toward a brother. For if anyone among you is absent from gathering, that person will be counted among those who scatter the Messiah’s church and will be punished as one who has become one of those opposed to the Messiah’s disciples. That person will be cast out with adulterers. For, like an adulterer, he has separated himself on some pretext under the influence of the spirit within him, and has given the evil one room against himself to seize a sheep as one found outside the folds.

Translator's notes for section 3.69 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: συνεχέστερον συνέρχεσθε, εἴθε καθ’ ὥραν, ἐπεί γε ἐν ταῖς νενομισμέναις τῆς συνόδου ἡμέραις
The wish εἴθε καθ’ ὥραν is followed by a verbless ἐπεί γε phrase. The translation treats the latter as an elliptical minimum—“but at least on the customary days of assembly.” The more formally connective alternative “since at least on the customary days of assembly” leaves the same gathering verb implicit. No missing wording has been restored.

2. Greek: ὡς γὰρ μοιχὸς ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ πνεύματος προφάσει τινὸς ἑαυτὸν ἀφώρισεν
The opening comparison and the agent phrase permit more than one attachment: the absent person may be compared with an adulterer, or ὡς μοιχός may characterize him directly as one. The main rendering takes it as a comparison and attaches “by the spirit within him” to his self-separation.

3. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδὲν αὐτῶν ἀφαιρήσεσθε
Rendered as: you will take nothing away from them
The middle form can mean taking something from others for oneself or depriving them; the following promise to share one’s possessions supplies the contrast.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εὐγνωμονοῦντας ὑμᾶς
Rendered as: since you are discerning
Εὐγνωμονέω can describe being sensible, fair-minded, or well-disposed. Here it concerns the readers’ capacity to recognize how piety should be practiced.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἐντὸς τειχῶν ἀσυλίας ἐστέ
Rendered as: you are within walls of refuge
The rendering preserves the enclosing-wall image and takes ἀσυλία as safety, immunity, or inviolable refuge.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀρχὴ γὰρ ἀπωλείας λειποταξία
Rendered as: desertion from the ranks is the beginning of destruction
Λειποταξία is a military term for abandoning one’s assigned position, here applied metaphorically to absence from the assembly.

7. Translation choice — Greek: προφάσει μικροψυχίας τῆς πρὸς ἀδελφὸν
Rendered as: on the pretext of petty resentment toward a brother
Μικροψυχία literally suggests smallness or faintness of spirit and can denote pettiness or discouragement. In this interpersonal setting, “petty resentment” is contextually defensible; “discouragement concerning a brother” remains possible.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν χριστοῦ ἐκκλησίαν
Rendered as: the Messiah’s church
Χριστός is used independently as a title, not within a personal-name construction.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ πνεύματος
Rendered as: under the influence of the spirit within him
The phrase identifies the spirit as the agent of his self-separation but does not explicitly identify it as his own spirit, the Holy Spirit, or an evil spirit; lowercase wording preserves that uncertainty.

10. Translation choice — Greek: πρόβατον ἁρπάσαι ὡς μανδρῶν ἔξω εὑρεθέν
Rendered as: to seize a sheep as one found outside the folds
The absent person is depicted through the sheep image. The ὡς with the participle presents the sheep as regarded or found outside, while μανδρῶν is plural, “folds.”

SECTION 3.70

However, listen to your bishop, and do not grow weary in rendering him every honor, knowing that, though ostensibly directed to him, it is carried to the Messiah; from the Messiah it is referred to God, and it is repaid many times over to the one who offered it. You will therefore honor the Messiah’s throne, since you were also commanded to honor Moses’ seat, even if those who preside are regarded as sinners. These things have been said to you sufficiently. But as for how he must live blamelessly, I consider it superfluous to speak, since he is a proven disciple of the one who taught even me.

Translator's notes for section 3.70 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ ἐπισκόπου ὑμῶν ἀκούετε
Rendered as: listen to your bishop
The genitive with ἀκούετε can include heeding or obeying; “listen to” preserves that range while the surrounding commands establish the authoritative setting.

2. Translation choice — Greek: προφάσει τῇ πρὸς αὐτὸν εἰς χριστὸν φέρεται
Rendered as: though ostensibly directed to him, it is carried to the Messiah
The implied subject is the honor just mentioned. Πρόφασις marks its outward or apparent direction toward the bishop, while the author says its ultimate recipient is the Messiah.

3. Translation choice — Greek: χριστὸν
Rendered as: Messiah
Χριστός functions independently as a title throughout the passage rather than as part of a personal name.

4. Translation choice — Greek: πολυπλασίως ἀνταποδίδοται
Rendered as: it is repaid many times over
The adverb indicates a multiplied return rather than merely an equivalent repayment.

5. Translation choice — Greek: θρόνον ... χριστοῦ ... Μωϋσέως καθέδραν
Rendered as: the Messiah’s throne ... Moses’ seat
Distinct English terms preserve the source’s distinction between θρόνος and καθέδρα rather than harmonizing both as “seat” or “chair.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: δόκιμος ὑπάρχει μαθητής
Rendered as: he is a proven disciple
Δόκιμος describes someone tested and found approved or dependable; “proven” conveys that evaluative force.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ κἀμὲ διδάξαντος
Rendered as: of the one who taught even me
The crasis κἀμέ means “me also” or, with rhetorical emphasis, “even me”; the latter suits the speaker’s appeal to the bishop’s teacher.

SECTION 3.71

Nevertheless, brothers, there are some things you should not wait to hear, but should also recognize for yourselves what is reasonable. Is Zacchaeus alone to labor for you? Having given himself over entirely to being occupied, since he has a belly and has no leisure for himself, how can he obtain the necessary food? Is it not reasonable for all of you to take thought for his livelihood, without waiting for him to ask you? For that is the act of a beggar, and he would die of hunger rather than undertake to do this. How, then, will you yourselves not incur punishment if you fail to consider that “the worker is worthy of his wages”? And let no one say, “So then, is the word that was provided freely being sold?” By no means. For if someone who has the means to live should accept support, that person is selling the word. But if someone without the means to live receives food in order to live—as the Lord also received food both at dinners and among friends, possessing nothing though he is the one who will possess everything hereafter—he does not sin. Accordingly, honor elders, catechists, useful deacons, widows who have lived well, and orphans as children of the church. Moreover, whenever a need for some resource for a necessary purpose arises, all of you should contribute together. Act piously toward one another, not hesitating to endure anything at all for the sake of your own salvation.

Translator's notes for section 3.71 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: Ζακχαῖος μόνος ὑμῖν;
The confirmed editorial question punctuation leaves the clause without an expressed predicate. The main rendering supplies the idea of labor from the immediately following occupation language; alternatively, the words may be represented more literally as “Is Zacchaeus alone for you?” or ὑμῖν may be understood closely with the following infinitive despite the punctuation. No textual correction is required.

2. Greek: Ζακχαῖος
The selected edition spells the name here with one χ but uses Ζαχχαίῳ in 3.72. This is an orthographic variation; both are represented by the conventional English name “Zacchaeus,” without altering the supplied Greek.

3. Translation choice — Greek: Ζακχαῖος μόνος ὑμῖν;
Rendered as: Is Zacchaeus alone to labor for you?
The printed question is elliptical. “To labor” is supplied contextually from the following description of his complete occupation; a more formally literal but obscure alternative is “Is Zacchaeus alone for you?”

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὅλος ἑαυτὸν ἀσχολεῖν ἀποδεδωκώς
Rendered as: Having given himself over entirely to being occupied
The phrase depicts complete dedication to an occupation or lack of leisure, without specifying a separate office or activity.

5. Translation choice — Greek: κοιλίαν ἔχων
Rendered as: since he has a belly
This preserves the source’s concrete bodily image rather than reducing it to the abstract statement that he has needs.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ ζῆν αὐτοῦ πρόνοιαν ποιεῖν
Rendered as: to take thought for his livelihood
The construction calls for active provision or care concerning the means by which he lives.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦτο γὰρ προσαιτοῦντός ἐστιν
Rendered as: For that is the act of a beggar
The genitive denotes conduct characteristic of one who begs or solicits alms.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἔν τε δείπνοις καὶ φίλοις
Rendered as: both at dinners and among friends
The two coordinated expressions differ slightly in sense—one denotes occasions and the other company—but both can be retained without emendation.

9. Translation choice — Greek: τιμᾶτε
Rendered as: honor
The immediate context includes material provision, but the verb itself means to honor; the translation does not restrict it to payment alone.

10. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς ἀλλήλους εὐσεβεῖτε
Rendered as: Act piously toward one another
The verb denotes the practice of piety or dutiful reverence, here directed toward fellow members of the community.

SECTION 3.72

After saying these things, he laid his hand on Zacchaeus and said, “Sovereign and Lord of all, the Father and God, you yourself preserve the shepherd together with the flock. You are the cause; you are the power. We are those who receive help; ‘you are the helper’, ‘the physician’, ‘the Savior’, ‘the wall’, the life, ‘the hope’, ‘the refuge’, the joy, the expectation. You are rest. To sum it up, I will say: you are everything to us. Work with us toward the eternal possession of salvation; rescue us; guard us. You can do all things, for you are ruler of rulers and Lord of lords, master of kings. Give the one who presides authority to loose what must be loosed and to bind what must be bound. Make him wise. Through him as through an instrument, preserve the church of your Messiah as a beautiful bride. For yours is eternal glory, the praise of Father and Son and Holy Spirit, throughout all the ages. Amen.”

Translator's notes for section 3.72 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἡμεῖς τὸ βοηθούμενον, „σὺ ὁ βοηθός“, „ὁ ἰατρός“, „ὁ σωτήρ“, „τὸ τεῖχος“, ἡ ζωή, „ἡ ἐλπίς“, „ἡ καταφυγή“, ἡ χαρά, ἡ προσδοκία. ἡ ἀνάπαυσις,
The selected edition marks six expressions as quotations and places a full stop after προσδοκία. The translation preserves the quotation distinctions and treats ἡ ἀνάπαυσις as an elliptical predicate, “You are rest.” It could instead be punctuated as a continuation of the preceding enumeration. No textual correction is proposed.

2. Greek: πρὸς αἰώνιον ὕπαρξιν σωτηρίας συνέργησον
The relation between ὕπαρξιν and σωτηρίας is interpretively open: the phrase may mean “eternal possession of salvation,” “an eternal state of salvation,” or “eternal existence in salvation.” The main rendering is grammatically and contextually defensible, so no conjecture is needed.

3. Greek: σοῦ γὰρ ἐστὶν δόξα αἰώνιος, ὕμνος πατρὸς καὶ υἱοῦ καὶ ἁγίου πνεύματος
The syntax allows ὕμνος to stand in apposition to δόξα, as in the main translation, or to function as a second predicate: “For yours are eternal glory and the praise of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” The supplied wording supports either construction.

4. Greek: Ζαχχαίῳ
The selected edition spells the name here with two χ letters, whereas 3.71 has Ζακχαῖος. This nonblocking orthographic variation is represented by the same conventional English name, “Zacchaeus.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: Δέσποτα καὶ κύριε τῶν ὅλων
Rendered as: Sovereign and Lord of all
“Sovereign” conveys the authority of δεσπότης while distinguishing it from the following κύριος, “Lord.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: σὺ ἡ πρόφασις
Rendered as: You are the cause
In this prayer πρόφασις is read as the originating cause or ground, rather than its frequent negative sense “pretext.” “You are the ground” is also possible.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἡμεῖς τὸ βοηθούμενον
Rendered as: We are those who receive help
The singular neuter participial expression is treated collectively as the party being helped.

8. Translation choice — Greek: „σὺ ὁ βοηθός“, „ὁ ἰατρός“, „ὁ σωτήρ“, „τὸ τεῖχος“, ἡ ζωή, „ἡ ἐλπίς“, „ἡ καταφυγή“, ἡ χαρά, ἡ προσδοκία
Rendered as: ‘you are the helper’, ‘the physician’, ‘the Savior’, ‘the wall’, the life, ‘the hope’, ‘the refuge’, the joy, the expectation
The six expressions separately marked as quotations in the selected edition retain distinct inner quotation boundaries, while the intervening unquoted attributes remain outside them.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ ἀνάπαυσις
Rendered as: You are rest
The noun names rest or repose as a divine attribute. The predicate “you are” is carried forward from the surrounding enumeration so that “rest” cannot be mistaken for an unspecified remainder.

10. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς αἰώνιον ὕπαρξιν σωτηρίας συνέργησον
Rendered as: Work with us toward the eternal possession of salvation
ὕπαρξις can denote possession, state, subsistence, or existence. “Eternal possession of salvation” gives a coherent objective-genitive sense; “an eternal state of salvation” is a viable alternative.

11. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ προκαθεζομένῳ
Rendered as: the one who presides
The participle literally describes the person seated in front and contextually denotes the community’s presiding leader.

12. Translation choice — Greek: σὺ σόφισον
Rendered as: Make him wise
The unexpressed object is understood from the immediately preceding presiding leader.

13. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ χριστοῦ σου
Rendered as: the church of your Messiah
χριστός functions independently as a title possessed by God, so its titular meaning is rendered rather than treated as part of a personal name.

14. Translation choice — Greek: σοῦ γὰρ ἐστὶν δόξα αἰώνιος, ὕμνος πατρὸς καὶ υἱοῦ καὶ ἁγίου πνεύματος
Rendered as: For yours is eternal glory, the praise of Father and Son and Holy Spirit
The rendering takes ὕμνος as an appositional description of the glory. It leaves “praise of” able to express either praise associated with or praise directed toward Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

SECTION 3.73

After saying these things, he then said, “All of you who wish to be baptized, begin fasting tomorrow, have hands laid on you each day, and inquire about whatever you wish. For I want to remain with you for ten more days.” After three days, when he had begun baptizing, he called me, Aquila, and Nicetas and said, “Since I intend to set out for Tyre after seven days, I want you, after leaving this city, secretly lodging as guests with Bernice the Canaanite, Justa’s daughter, and learning from her precisely the matters concerning Simon, to write to me. For this is of great help to me, so that I may adjust myself accordingly. Therefore, depart from this city in peace.” And so, leaving him baptizing just as he had commanded, we went ahead of him to Tyre in Phoenicia.

Translator's notes for section 3.73 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἐξ αὐτῆς
The phrase occurs twice. Tyre is an explicit feminine antecedent candidate immediately before the first occurrence, while the main translation instead supplies an implicit reference to the current city. At both occurrences, ἐξ αὐτῆς may also function idiomatically as “at once.” The ensuing journey to Tyre is compatible both with departure from the current city and with immediate departure, so it does not by itself decide between those readings. No source correction is proposed.

2. Greek: πρὸς αὐτὸ ἁρμόσωμαι
The neuter singular pronoun does not directly refer to the masculine Simon and does not formally agree with the preceding neuter plural τὰ. It can nevertheless refer collectively to the matter or situation concerning Simon, yielding “adjust myself accordingly” or “adapt myself to it.” No emendation is necessary.

3. Translation choice — Greek: Ὅσοι ποτὲ βαπτισθῆναι θέλετε
Rendered as: All of you who wish to be baptized
Here ποτε gives an indefinite force comparable to “whoever”; it does not require a separate temporal phrase in English.

4. Translation choice — Greek: καθ’ ἡμέραν χειροθετεῖσθε
Rendered as: have hands laid on you each day
In the preparation of baptismal candidates, the passive verb naturally refers to receiving the laying on of hands; “be appointed” is contextually less likely.

5. Translation choice — Greek: μεθ’ ἡμέρας ἑπτὰ
Rendered as: after seven days
The phrase marks the intended interval before the departure for Tyre.

6. Translation choice — Greek: Μέλλων ἐπὶ τὴν Τύρον ὁρμᾶν μεθ’ ἡμέρας ἑπτὰ βούλομαι ἐξ αὐτῆς ὑμᾶς ἀπελθόντας
Rendered as: Since I intend to set out for Tyre after seven days, I want you, after leaving this city
Tyre immediately precedes the first ἐξ αὐτῆς and is formally a feminine antecedent candidate. The main rendering instead understands an implicit reference to the current city. The phrase may also be idiomatic and temporal, “at once,” rather than spatial.

7. Translation choice — Greek: λανθανόντως ἐπιξενωθέντας
Rendered as: secretly lodging as guests
The adverb conveys remaining unnoticed or concealed, while the participle denotes receiving or taking guest lodging.

8. Translation choice — Greek: παρ’ αὐτῆς τὰ κατὰ τὸν Σίμωνα ἀκριβῶς μαθόντας
Rendered as: learning from her precisely the matters concerning Simon
τὰ κατά with a person denotes the facts, circumstances, or matters concerning that person.

9. Translation choice — Greek: πολὺ γὰρ μοι συμβάλλεται, ἵνα πρὸς αὐτὸ ἁρμόσωμαι
Rendered as: For this is of great help to me, so that I may adjust myself accordingly
The neuter singular αὐτό is taken collectively as the matter or situation disclosed by the requested report. A more formally explicit alternative is “so that I may adapt myself to it.”

10. Translation choice — Greek: διὸ ἐξ αὐτῆς πορεύεσθε μετὰ εἰρήνης
Rendered as: Therefore, depart from this city in peace
The main rendering again supplies the current city as the spatial referent of αὐτῆς. An idiomatic temporal rendering, “Therefore, depart at once in peace,” is also viable.

11. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς Τύρον αὐτὸν προήξαμεν τῆς Φοινίκης
Rendered as: we went ahead of him to Tyre in Phoenicia
With the personal object αὐτόν, προάγω here means to precede or go ahead of him rather than to lead him.

HOMILY 4

SECTION 4.1

Leaving Caesarea of Strato, I, Clement, together with Nicetas and Aquila, arrived at Tyre in Phoenicia. At the instruction of Peter, who had sent us, we were received as guests by Berenice, daughter of Justa the Canaanite. She welcomed us most gladly. She exerted herself greatly in the honor she showed me and in her affection for Aquila and Nicetas; in her joy she treated us warmly, speaking freely as though she were an old acquaintance, and hospitably pressed us to care for our bodies. Perceiving, then, that she was allowing us to make a brief postponement, I said, “You do well to hasten to fulfill the duties of love. But fear of our God must be preferred to this. For, since we are engaged in a struggle on behalf of many souls, we are afraid to prefer our own rest to their salvation.”

Translator's notes for section 4.1 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: Καισαρείας δὲ τῆς Στράτωνος
Rendered as: Leaving Caesarea of Strato
The genitive identifies the city historically; “Strato’s Caesarea” or “Caesarea Stratonis” would also be possible.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς συνήθης παρρησιαζομένη
Rendered as: speaking freely as though she were an old acquaintance
συνήθης can describe someone familiar or intimate, while παρρησιαζομένη denotes speaking with freedom or frankness.

3. Translation choice — Greek: βραχεῖαν ἡμῖν ὑπέρθεσιν ποιεῖσθαι
Rendered as: allowing us to make a brief postponement
The object of the postponement is left implicit in Greek, so the English does not specify whether it was their mission, inquiry, or departure.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ἡμῶν φόβος
Rendered as: fear of our God
The placement of ἡμῶν naturally permits attachment to θεόν, yielding “our God”; “our fear toward God” remains grammatically possible.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὲρ πολλῶν ψυχῶν τὸν ἀγῶνα ἔχοντες
Rendered as: since we are engaged in a struggle on behalf of many souls
ἀγών retains the image of a contest or struggle rather than merely denoting responsibility.

SECTION 4.2

“We hear that Simon the magician, after being defeated in the debate at Caesarea with our lord Peter, immediately fled and is committing many evils here. For by reviling Peter with every kind of charge contrary to the truth, he sweeps away the souls of the multitude. Though he is a magician himself, he calls that man a magician; though he is a deceiver himself, he publicly denounces that man as a deceiver. And though he himself came off worse in the debates before everyone and fled, he claims to have won. He repeatedly instructs people not to listen to Peter, supposedly out of concern that they might be bewitched by a formidable magician.”

Translator's notes for section 4.2 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τῆς ἐν Καισαρείᾳ πρὸς τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν Πέτρον ζητήσεως
Rendered as: in the debate at Caesarea with our lord Peter
ζήτησις here denotes a formal dispute or debate. κύριος is retained as the honorific “lord” for Peter rather than being treated as a divine title.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πᾶσι γὰρ τοῖς ὑπεναντίοις παρὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν λοιδορῶν τὸν Πέτρον
Rendered as: by reviling Peter with every kind of charge contrary to the truth
The dative plural τοῖς ὑπεναντίοις is taken as substantivized neuter, referring to hostile allegations or means of abuse. A possible alternative is to take it as masculine recipients: “reviling Peter before all his opponents, contrary to the truth.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: πλάνος
Rendered as: deceiver
The word can mean a deceiver, impostor, or one who leads others astray; “deceiver” fits the reciprocal accusation here.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ ἧττον ἀπενεγκάμενος
Rendered as: came off worse
This idiom means to emerge as the inferior or defeated party, not literally to carry away something lesser.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς δῆθεν κηδόμενος
Rendered as: supposedly out of concern
δῆθεν marks the stated concern as pretended or merely alleged.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ δεινοῦ καταγοητευθῶσιν μάγου
Rendered as: might be bewitched by a formidable magician
δεινός may mean formidable, terrible, or highly skilled; “formidable” preserves the threatening ability implied by Simon’s warning.

SECTION 4.3
