“Having learned these things, our lord Peter sent us ahead to investigate what had been reported to him, so that, if matters were so, once we had written he himself might learn; and when he comes, he will expose Simon in the very presence of those before whom Simon had slandered him. Since, then, danger involving many souls lies before us, for this reason we have set aside our bodily rest for a little while and wish to learn truthfully from you, since you live here, whether what we have heard is in fact true. So now please tell us every detail.”

Translator's notes for section 4.3 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: προἀπέστειλεν ἡμᾶς ἐξεταστὰς τῶν λεχθέντων αὐτῷ ἐσομένους
Rendered as: sent us ahead to investigate what had been reported to him
ἐξεταστάς identifies them as investigators or examiners; the English verbalizes that role without adding a separate office.

2. Translation choice — Greek: γραψάντων ἡμῶν αὐτὸς μάθοι
Rendered as: once we had written he himself might learn
The Greek leaves the recipient and contents of the writing implicit, so neither a letter nor a formal report is specified.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐξελέγξει αὐτὸν
Rendered as: he will expose Simon
ἐλέγχω can mean expose, convict, or refute. “Expose” accommodates both the personal accusations and the anticipated public confrontation.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκείνων ἄντικρυς ἐφ’ ὧν αὐτὸν διέβαλλεν
Rendered as: in the very presence of those before whom Simon had slandered him
ἐκείνων and ὧν are taken as referring to the people before whom Simon had spoken against Peter. The repeated αὐτόν has different contextual referents, made explicit in English to prevent confusion.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς τοῦ σώματος ἡμῶν ἀναπαύσεως πρὸς βραχὺ ἀμελήσαντες
Rendered as: we have set aside our bodily rest for a little while
ἀμελέω literally means to neglect or disregard; “set aside” expresses the temporary, deliberate forgoing of rest indicated by πρὸς βραχύ.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀψευδῶς μαθεῖν
Rendered as: to learn truthfully
The adverb denotes learning without falsehood or deception; “reliably” would be another contextual rendering.

SECTION 4.4

Having been called upon, Berenice said, “These matters are as you heard. But listen to the other things concerning Simon himself, which perhaps you do not know. For by making apparitions and phantom-images appear in the middle of the marketplace in broad daylight, he astonishes the whole city. When he goes out, statues move and many shadows go before him, which he himself says are the souls of the dead. Having soon afterward won over to himself many who were trying to expose him as a sorcerer, he sacrificed an ox under the pretext of a banquet and feasted them, then beset them with various diseases and subjected them to demons. And—to keep from saying too much—after harming many, he has been regarded as a god; besides being fearsome, he has also been held in special honor.”

Translator's notes for section 4.4 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ Βερνίκη δὲ ἀξιωθεῖσα
Rendered as: Having been called upon, Berenice said
Although the passive of ἀξιόω can literally mean “having been deemed worthy,” it can contextually introduce someone who has been requested or invited to speak.

2. Translation choice — Greek: φαντάσματά τε γὰρ καὶ ἰνδάλματα
Rendered as: apparitions and phantom-images
The paired nouns both concern visual manifestations; the differentiated rendering preserves the source’s two terms rather than collapsing them into one.

3. Translation choice — Greek: προϊόντος αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: When he goes out
The participle can describe going out, coming forward, or proceeding in public; the surrounding moving statues and preceding shadows suggest a public appearance or procession.

4. Translation choice — Greek: διαλλάξας πρὸς ἑαυτὸν εὐθύστερον
Rendered as: Having soon afterward won over to himself
διαλλάσσω denotes reconciling or winning people over. εὐθύστερον is taken temporally as indicating prompt succession; it could instead qualify the manner as “more directly” or “more readily.” The supplied reading is retained without emendation.

5. Translation choice — Greek: διαφόροις νόσοις περιέβαλεν
Rendered as: beset them with various diseases
περιβάλλω literally evokes surrounding or enveloping; with diseases as its instrument, “beset” preserves more of that image than the generic “afflicted.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: δαίμοσιν ὑπέβαλεν
Rendered as: subjected them to demons
ὑποβάλλω here presents the victims as being placed under the power or influence of demons.

7. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τῷ φοβερὸν εἶναι καὶ προτετίμηται
Rendered as: besides being fearsome, he has also been held in special honor
φοβερός actively means fear-inspiring, while the perfect προτετίμηται indicates an established state of exceptional esteem or preference.

SECTION 4.5

“Therefore I do not think anyone will be able to extinguish so great a fire that has been kindled. For no one doubts what that man claims; rather, each person emphatically maintains that it is so. Therefore, so that you may not be put in danger, I urge you not to attempt anything against him before Peter comes, who alone will be able to contend against so great a power (being the most proven disciple of our Lord Jesus Christ). For I have become so afraid of the man that, if he had not on another occasion also debated with my lord Peter and come off worse, I would have advised you to persuade even Peter himself not to attempt a counter-debate with Simon.”

Translator's notes for section 4.5 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τοσοῦτον ἀναφθὲν πῦρ σβέσαι
Rendered as: extinguish so great a fire that has been kindled
The attributive participle describes the fire as already kindled; the rendering retains both that existing state and the explicit fire metaphor.

2. Translation choice — Greek: περὶ ὧν ἐκεῖνος ἐπαγγέλλεται
Rendered as: what that man claims
ἐπαγγέλλομαι may mean promise, profess, or claim; here it concerns Simon’s asserted powers and representations.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀλλὰ τοῦτο οὕτως ἔχειν διαβεβαιοῦται ἕκαστος
Rendered as: rather, each person emphatically maintains that it is so
With its accusative-and-infinitive complement, διαβεβαιοῦται expresses emphatic affirmation. This preserves a distinction from the preceding οὐδὲ ἐνδοιάζει τις: the people not only do not doubt but positively maintain the claim.

4. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τοσαύτην δυναστείαν
Rendered as: against so great a power
δυναστεία can denote power, dominion, or potent authority; “power” best fits Simon’s feared magical capacity in context.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ δοκιμώτατος ὑπάρχων μαθητής
Rendered as: being the most proven disciple of our Lord Jesus Christ
δοκιμώτατος is formally superlative and can be comparative, “the most proven disciple,” or elative, “a highly approved” or “well-proven disciple,” without ranking Peter above every other disciple. The main rendering adopts the comparative force because the surrounding clause says that Peter alone can contend with Simon, but the elative reading remains viable.

6. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τὸν κύριόν μου Πέτρον διαλεχθεὶς τὸ ἧττον ἀπηνέγκατο
Rendered as: debated with my lord Peter and came off worse
διαλέγομαι denotes discussion or debate here, and τὸ ἧττον ἀπηνέγκατο is the idiom for emerging as the defeated or inferior party. “Lord” is lowercased because κύριος is an honorific for Peter in this clause.

7. Translation choice — Greek: μὴ πειρᾶσθαι ἀντεξετάζεσθαι τῷ Σίμωνι
Rendered as: not to attempt a counter-debate with Simon
ἀντεξετάζομαι denotes engaging in examination or disputation in opposition to another; “counter-debate” preserves that reciprocal adversarial force.

SECTION 4.6

And I said, “If our lord Peter did not know that he alone can prevail over that man’s power, he would not have sent us ahead with instructions to learn in detail, without attracting notice, what concerned Simon and to write it to him.” All the same, since evening had overtaken us, we partook of salt and slept. In the morning, someone acquainted with Bernice came and said that Simon had sailed away to Sidon but had left behind some of his disciples: Appion the many-times victor, an Alexandrian man and a grammarian by training, whom I recognized as a friend of mine through my father; Annubion the Diospolitan, a certain astrologer; and Athenodorus the Athenian, who approved of the teaching of Epicurus. After learning what concerned Simon, we wrote everything down at dawn and sent it on to Peter, and then went off for a walk.

Translator's notes for section 4.6 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ὁμῶς
The printed accentuation gives ὁμῶς, ordinarily associated with “alike,” while the context supports the concessive force of ὅμως, “nevertheless” or “all the same.” The supplied form can still be represented contextually as “All the same.”

2. Translation choice — Greek: Ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν Πέτρος
Rendered as: our lord Peter
The human honorific κύριος is retained as “lord” rather than recast as a theological title.

3. Translation choice — Greek: λανθανόντως τὰ κατὰ Σίμωνα διαμανθάνοντας
Rendered as: to learn in detail, without attracting notice, what concerned Simon
διαμανθάνω conveys thorough learning, while λανθανόντως indicates that it was to be done secretly or unnoticed.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἁλῶν μεταλαβόντες
Rendered as: we partook of salt
The wording literally invokes sharing salt and can idiomatically denote taking food; the concrete image is preserved.

5. Translation choice — Greek: Ἀππίωνα τὸν πλειστονίκην
Rendered as: Appion the many-times victor
πλειστονίκης is treated as an epithet meaning one who has won very many victories; it could alternatively be presented as the title or name “Pleistonikes.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὃν πρὸς πατρός μοι φίλον ὄντα ἐπέγνων
Rendered as: whom I recognized as a friend of mine through my father
πρὸς πατρός indicates a paternal connection. Possible nuances include “a paternal family friend” or “my father’s friend.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ Ἐπικούρου ἀρεσκόμενον λόγῳ
Rendered as: who approved of the teaching of Epicurus
ἀρεσκόμενον expresses being pleased with or approving Epicurus’s λόγος; “approved of” avoids implying the stronger allegiance suggested by “devoted.”

SECTION 4.7

And Appion met us, not only with the two companions already mentioned but also with about thirty other men. As soon as he saw me, he greeted me, kissed me warmly, and said, “This is Clement, about whose noble birth and freeborn dignity I have spoken to you at length, telling you that, although he is a man of the family of Tiberius Caesar and has been trained in every branch of Greek education, he has been deceived by a certain barbarian named Peter into doing and saying the things of the Jews. I therefore ask you to join me in the effort to correct him. And in your presence I question the man himself. Let him tell me this: since he thinks he has devoted himself to being pious, how is he not committing the gravest impieties by abandoning his ancestral customs and turning aside to barbarian ways?”

Translator's notes for section 4.7 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἑτέρων’ ἀνδρῶν
The raised apostrophe after ἑτέρων is syntactically inert and appears to be anomalous editorial punctuation. It does not affect the sentence’s meaning.

2. Greek: τὰ πάτρια,’ ἀποκλίνας
The apostrophe beside the comma after πάτρια appears to be an extraneous editorial mark. The participial construction remains clear.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπηντᾶτο ἡμῖν
Rendered as: met us
The imperfect can describe Appion encountering or coming to meet the group.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς τε εὐγενείας καὶ τῆς ἐλευθεροπρεπείας
Rendered as: his noble birth and freeborn dignity
εὐγένεια concerns distinguished birth, while ἐλευθεροπρέπεια denotes dignity or conduct befitting a free person; “generosity” or “magnificence” is also possible for the latter.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πολὺν ἐποιούμην λόγον, ὅτι
Rendered as: I have spoken to you at length, telling you that
ὅτι is taken as introducing the content of Appion’s prior account and is therefore explicitly connected to λόγον. It could alternatively be causal—“I spoke at length because …”—but the reporting attachment provides a natural transition into what Appion had said about Clement.

6. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς γένους Τιβερίου Καίσαρος ὢν
Rendered as: he is a man of the family of Tiberius Caesar
The phrase presents Clement as related to or descended from Tiberius Caesar’s family.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ Ἰουδαίων ποιεῖν καὶ λέγειν
Rendered as: doing and saying the things of the Jews
The elliptical τὰ Ἰουδαίων is preserved broadly rather than narrowed to particular Jewish rites or doctrines.

8. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ἐφ’ ὑμῶν αὐτοῦ πυνθάνομαι
Rendered as: And in your presence I question the man himself
ἐφ’ ὑμῶν means “before/in the presence of you,” and the genitive αὐτοῦ is naturally taken with πυνθάνομαι as the person questioned.

9. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τὸ εὐσεβεῖν ἑαυτὸν ἀποδεδωκέναι
Rendered as: he thinks he has devoted himself to being pious
ἀποδίδωμι with the reflexive expresses giving or devoting oneself to an undertaking.

SECTION 4.8

And I answered, “I welcome your good intention toward me, but I reject your ignorance. The intention is good, because you want me to be among those things you regard as good; but your understanding, being unsound, strives under the pretext of friendship to set an ambush for me.” Appion said, “Does it seem to you to be ignorance for someone who observes his ancestral customs to hold the beliefs of the Greeks?” And I answered, “One who chooses to be pious need not invariably observe ancestral customs. He should observe them if they are pious, but cast them off if they prove impious. For someone born of an impious father may wish to be pious and therefore not wish to follow the object of his father’s worship.” Appion replied, “What then? Are you saying that your father lived a wicked life?” And I said, “His life was not wicked, but his belief was.” Appion said, “What was this wicked notion of his? I want to hear.” And I said, “He believed the false and wicked myths of the Greeks.” Appion asked, “Which are these myths of the Greeks that are both false and wicked?” And I said, “The wrong conception of gods, which, if you are patient, you will hear about together with those who are eager to learn.”

Translator's notes for section 4.8 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν δὲ ἀγνωσίαν ἀποσείομαι
Rendered as: but I reject your ignorance
ἀποσείω literally suggests shaking something off and here expresses firm rejection.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ δὲ γνῶσις οὐκ ὀρθῶς ἔχουσα
Rendered as: but your understanding, being unsound
γνῶσις contrasts with ἀγνωσία and denotes Appion’s understanding or judgment, which Clement considers incorrectly disposed.

3. Translation choice — Greek: φιλίας προφάσει ἐνεδρεύειν ἀγωνίζεται
Rendered as: strives under the pretext of friendship to set an ambush for me
The martial image of lying in ambush is retained; “for me” supplies the contextually evident target.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ πάτρια ἔθη φυλάττοντα τὰ Ἑλλήνων φρονεῖν
Rendered as: for someone who observes his ancestral customs to hold the beliefs of the Greeks
τὰ Ἑλλήνων is elliptical, literally “the things of the Greeks,” and in this argumentative context denotes Greek beliefs or opinions.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ τοῦ πατρὸς ἀκολουθεῖν σεβάσματι
Rendered as: to follow the object of his father’s worship
σέβασμα can denote an object of reverence or worship; “his father’s religion” is a broader possible rendering.

6. Translation choice — Greek: Κακοῦ μὲν οὐκ ἦν βίου, κακῆς δὲ ὑπολήψεως
Rendered as: His life was not wicked, but his belief was
The compact nominal contrast between βίος and ὑπόληψις is expressed idiomatically while preserving the repeated evaluation as wicked.

7. Translation choice — Greek: Ἡ περὶ θεῶν οὐκ ὀρθὴ δόκησις
Rendered as: The wrong conception of gods
δόκησις denotes an opinion or conception; the phrase does not itself specify one particular doctrine about the gods.

SECTION 4.9

“Therefore, before the discussions, let us now withdraw to some quieter place; there I will converse with you. This is the reason I have wished to speak in private: neither the many nor even all those who practice philosophy approach the judgment of things that exist sincerely. For we know many, even among those who take great pride in philosophy, who seek empty glory or have put on the coarse cloak for the sake of making money rather than for virtue itself. If they do not find what they practice philosophy for, they turn to scoffing. Because of such people, then, let us choose a place suitable for being by ourselves.”

Translator's notes for section 4.9 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ δὲ ἰδιολογεῖσθαί με βούλεσθαι
Rendered as: I have wished to speak in private
ἰδιολογέομαι denotes holding a private or separate conversation.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ τῶν ὄντων κρίσει
Rendered as: the judgment of things that exist
The philosophical expression may also be rendered “the examination of realities”; the more source-transparent wording preserves τὰ ὄντα.

3. Translation choice — Greek: κενοδοξοῦντας
Rendered as: who seek empty glory
The compound describes vainglorious conduct or pursuit of baseless prestige.

4. Translation choice — Greek: χρηματισμοῦ χάριν περιβεβλημένους τὸν τρίβωνα
Rendered as: have put on the coarse cloak for the sake of making money
The τρίβων is the worn cloak conventionally associated with philosophers; the image is retained rather than replaced with a general reference to pretending to be philosophers.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἐὰν μὴ εὕρωσιν δι’ ὃ φιλοσοφοῦσιν
Rendered as: If they do not find what they practice philosophy for
The wording leaves the desired objective implicit; it may refer to empty prestige, financial gain, or either motive just mentioned.

6. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τὸ ἰδιάζειν
Rendered as: suitable for being by ourselves
ἰδιάζω here means withdrawing from the public or remaining in private, in parallel with the preceding wish for private conversation.

SECTION 4.10

And a certain wealthy man among them, who also always possessed around himself a certain tract of all-accomplished leaves, said, “Since the heat is blazing fiercely, let us withdraw a short distance from the city, into my gardens.” And so, after going on, they seated themselves where there were clear streams of cool spring water and a green canopy of trees of every kind. There I gladly sat down, with the rest around me. As they remained silent, in place of the voice that was about to make a request of me, they showed by staring at me that they were demanding the fulfillment of the promise. And so I began to speak in this way.

Translator's notes for section 4.10 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: καὶ διὰ παντὸς χῶρόν τινα περὶ ἑαυτὸν κεκτημένος παμμούσων φύλλων
The image-checked supplied reading literally describes the man as continually possessing around himself “a certain tract of all-accomplished leaves.” The application of παμμούσων, denoting accomplishment in all the arts, to φύλλων, “leaves,” is contextually anomalous and may reflect corruption, but that possibility is not established. The main text therefore preserves a defensible literal representation of the selected edition. A possible conjecture is χορόν, “company,” for χῶρόν and φίλων, “friends,” for φύλλων, yielding a company of friends accomplished in every art; this conjecture has not been substituted into the translation.

2. Translation choice — Greek: σφόδρα καῦμα ἐπιφλέγει
Rendered as: the heat is blazing fiercely
ἐπιφλέγω presents the heat as burning or blazing upon them, and σφόδρα supplies the intensity.

3. Translation choice — Greek: βραχὺ τῆς πόλεως
Rendered as: a short distance from the city
The accusative βραχύ expresses a small extent of distance.

4. Translation choice — Greek: καθαρὰ ψυχρῶν ναμάτων ῥεύματα
Rendered as: clear streams of cool spring water
νάματα denotes flowing or spring water, while ῥεύματα emphasizes its streams or currents.

5. Translation choice — Greek: δένδρων παντοίων χλοερὰ σκέπη
Rendered as: a green canopy of trees of every kind
σκέπη is shelter or covering; in the garden setting, “canopy” conveys the trees’ green overhead cover.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀντὶ τῆς μελλούσης ἀξιοῦν με φωνῆς
Rendered as: in place of the voice that was about to make a request of me
The voice is personified as about to appeal to Clement. The wording is elliptical about the requested action, which the following clause identifies as fulfillment of the promise.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς ὑποσχέσεως τὴν ἀπόδειξιν
Rendered as: the fulfillment of the promise
ἀπόδειξις literally denotes demonstration or proof; here it is the promised exposition whose delivery the listeners demand.

SECTION 4.11

There is a great difference, men of Greece, between truth and custom. Truth, when genuinely sought, is found; but a custom, whatever form it has when received, whether true or false, is uncritically reinforced by itself. The person who has received it neither delights in it because it is true nor is distressed because it is false. For such a person has believed not through judgment but through preconception, entrusting his own hope, with the outcome uncertain, to the opinion of those before him. And it is not easy to strip off the ancestral garment, even if it is shown to him quite plainly to be foolish and ridiculous.

Translator's notes for section 4.11 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἀληθείας τε καὶ συνηθείας
Rendered as: truth and custom
συνήθεια can denote familiarity, habit, or customary practice; the ensuing discussion of inherited ἔθος supports “custom.”

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ δὲ ἔθος, ὁποῖον ἂν παραληφθῇ
Rendered as: but a custom, whatever form it has when received
The rendering preserves both the indefinite quality of ὁποῖον and the idea of receiving an established custom.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀκρίτως ὑφ’ ἑαυτοῦ κρατύνεται
Rendered as: is uncritically reinforced by itself
The reflexive agent is retained rather than assigning the reinforcement to an unstated external authority.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ γὰρ κρίσει, ἀλλὰ προλήψει
Rendered as: not through judgment but through preconception
πρόληψις here is a belief accepted in advance rather than a conclusion reached by critical judgment; “presupposition” or “prejudice” are possible alternatives.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν πάτριον περιβολήν
Rendered as: the ancestral garment
The concrete clothing image of περιβολή is preserved rather than flattened to “ancestral tradition.”

SECTION 4.12

For example, then, I say that the entire education of the Greeks is a most pernicious scheme of an evil demon. Some of them introduced many gods, and these evil and subject to every passion, so that anyone wishing to do similar things might not even feel shame—shame being characteristic of a human being—since he has as his example the evil and indecent lives of the gods spoken of in myth. And by not even feeling shame, such a person does not even show hope of repentance. Others introduced fate, the so-called nativity, contrary to which no one can experience or do anything. So this too is likewise the same as the first position. For when someone has come to believe that no one is able either to experience or to do anything contrary to nativity, he readily comes to sin—and after sinning he does not regret what he has done impiously, offering as a defense that he was forced by nativity to do these things—and, since he is unable to correct his nativity, he is not even capable of feeling shame for the ways in which he sins.

Translator's notes for section 4.12 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν πᾶσαν Ἑλλήνων παιδείαν κακοῦ δαίμονος χαλεπωτάτην ὑπόθεσιν
Rendered as: the entire education of the Greeks is a most pernicious scheme of an evil demon
παιδεία denotes the Greek system of education or culture, while ὑπόθεσις here is understood as an underlying scheme or design; “most grievous undertaking” is also possible.

2. Translation choice — Greek: παντοπαθεῖς
Rendered as: subject to every passion
The word characterizes the gods as undergoing or being governed by every kind of passion, not merely as suffering greatly.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἀνθρώπου ἴδιον
Rendered as: shame being characteristic of a human being
ὅπερ is taken as referring to the immediately relevant act of feeling shame; reference to the broader preceding clause is grammatically possible but less fitting in context.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ δὲ μηδὲ αἰδεῖσθαι οὐδὲ ἐλπίδα μετανοίας ὁ τοιοῦτος ἐμφαίνει
Rendered as: And by not even feeling shame, such a person does not even show hope of repentance
The paired μηδέ and οὐδέ remain the repeated not even. Prospective μετάνοια concerns a moral-spiritual response to wrongdoing, so repentance follows the October13 contextual policy without reducing it to shame alone. No Godward destination is inserted. The later distinct μεταμελεῖται remains regret, preserving the different expression rather than imposing a blanket substitution.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν λεγομένην γένεσιν
Rendered as: the so-called nativity
In this argument γένεσις is the astrologically determined condition associated with one’s birth, not simply the event of birth; “birth-destiny” is an explanatory alternative.

6. Translation choice — Greek: παρ’ ἣν μηδένα πάσχειν τι ἢ ποιεῖν δύνασθαι
Rendered as: contrary to which no one can experience or do anything
παρά with the accusative is read as “contrary to” or “outside the determination of”; “apart from which” is a viable alternative.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν γένεσιν κατορθῶσαι μὴ δυνάμενος
Rendered as: since he is unable to correct his nativity
κατορθόω can mean set right, correct, or successfully master. “Correct” preserves the text’s deliberately impossible task without replacing it with an explanatory paraphrase.

SECTION 4.13

Others propose a motion devoid of providence, as though all things revolved spontaneously, with no master presiding over them. To think this way about these matters, as we have said, is in fact the most pernicious of all beliefs. For, as though there were no one presiding, exercising providence, and assigning to each person what is deserved, someone will readily do everything he can because of his lack of fear. Hence those who think such things are not easily—or perhaps not at all—brought to self-restraint, for they do not foresee the danger that would turn them back. But the teaching of the barbarian Jews, as you call them, is most pious, proposing one Father and Creator of this universe, good and just by nature: good, in that he forgives the sins of those who regret them; and just, in that after the repentance he proceeds against each person according to what the things done deserve.

Translator's notes for section 4.13 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ὡς. αὐτομάτως
The image-checked printed period after ὡς interrupts a construction in which ὡς appears to introduce the following description. The translation provisionally treats the stop as editorial punctuation rather than as the end of an independent sentence.

2. Greek: ταῦτα δὲ οὕτω νομίζειν, ὡς εἰρήκαμεν, πασῶν δοξῶν τυγχάνει οὖσα χαλεπωτάτη
The feminine forms οὖσα χαλεπωτάτη do not formally agree with the neuter infinitival clause ταῦτα ... νομίζειν. The sentence remains intelligible as an anacoluthon or as attraction to an understood feminine δόξα, “belief,” but no unique grammatical repair is certain.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπρονόητον φορὰν
Rendered as: a motion devoid of providence
φορά can denote motion, course, or movement; the following description of everything revolving spontaneously favors cosmic “motion.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τὴν ἀφοβίαν
Rendered as: because of his lack of fear
This avoids the potentially positive connotations of English “fearlessness” and expresses the absence of deterrent fear intended by the argument.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν γὰρ ἐπιστρέφοντα κίνδυνον
Rendered as: the danger that would turn them back
ἐπιστρέφοντα is taken transitively, with the affected persons understood. “The returning danger” or “the danger coming back upon them” is also grammatically possible.

6. Translation choice — Greek: μεταμελομένοις χαριζόμενον τὰ ἁμαρτήματα
Rendered as: he forgives the sins of those who regret them
χαρίζομαι with sins means freely remit or forgive them. The distinct μεταμέλομαι remains regret, rather than being homogenized with the repentance rendering chosen for μετάνοια in the following clause.

7. Translation choice — Greek: μετὰ τὴν μετάνοιαν
Rendered as: after the repentance
The morally responsive context supports repentance under the October13 policy. The temporal after is retained even though the author's wording creates tension with the preceding forgiveness statement. Alternatives include after the change of mind and after the reorientation; it is not rewritten as if there is no repentance. No new Godward formula, condition of reform, or resolution of the historical author's framework is added.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἑκάστῳ μετὰ τὴν μετάνοιαν κατ’ ἀξίαν τῶν πεπραγμένων ἐπεξιόντα
Rendered as: he proceeds against each person according to what the things done deserve
ἐπεξέρχομαι with the dative can mean proceed against, pursue, or call someone to account. “Proceeds against” retains its judicial and potentially punitive force without supplying a different verb such as “reward.”

SECTION 4.14

This teaching, even if it happens to be a myth, would nevertheless, since it is at least pious, not be unprofitable for life. For each person, in expectation of being judged by the all-seeing God, receives a stronger impulse toward self-restraint. And if the teaching should also be true, it has delivered the one who has lived with self-restraint from eternal punishment and has additionally benefited him through the everlasting and ineffable good things provided by God.

Translator's notes for section 4.14 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: κριθήσεσθαι. ὑπὸ
The image-checked printed period separates the passive infinitive κριθήσεσθαι from its apparent agent phrase ὑπὸ τοῦ παντεπόπτου θεοῦ. The syntax supports construing them together, so the translation provisionally does not reproduce the disruptive stop.

2. Translation choice — Greek: οὗτος ὁ λόγος
Rendered as: this teaching
λόγος here denotes the religious account or doctrine described in the preceding section, not merely a spoken word.

3. Translation choice — Greek: εὐσεβής γε ὢν
Rendered as: since it is at least pious
γε gives concessive emphasis: even if the teaching were a myth, its pious character would still make it beneficial.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ παντεπόπτου θεοῦ
Rendered as: the all-seeing God
παντεπόπτης describes one who observes everything; “all-observing God” is a close alternative.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τὸ σωφρονεῖν
Rendered as: toward self-restraint
σωφρονεῖν here concerns morally disciplined conduct. “Sound-mindedness” or “temperance” would preserve other aspects of the term.

6. Translation choice — Greek: προσευεργέτηκεν δὲ τοῖς ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀιδίοις τε καὶ ἀπορρήτοις γιγνομένοις ἀγαθοῖς
Rendered as: has additionally benefited him through the everlasting and ineffable good things provided by God
The dative τοῖς ... ἀγαθοῖς is taken instrumentally, and the beneficiary is supplied from the preceding τὸν σωφρόνως βεβιωκότα. “Has further bestowed benefit on him with” is a more formal alternative.

SECTION 4.15

Nevertheless, I return to the first belief of the Greeks, the one that tells the myth that there are many gods subject to every passion. And so that I may not spend much time on settled matters by setting out the impious deeds of each of the so-called gods, I would not, for my part, recount all their love affairs: those of Zeus and Poseidon, Pluto and Apollo, Dionysus and Heracles, and of every one of them individually. Not even you yourselves are ignorant of their lives, since you proceed from a Greek education—the lives in which you were instructed so that, as emulators of the gods, you might do similar things,

Translator's notes for section 4.15 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: πράττοτε
The image-checked printed reading πράττοτε is morphologically unexpected in this ἵνα purpose clause and is not the regular subjunctive or optative form ordinarily anticipated here. The intended action remains contextually defensible from ἵνα, the πράττ- stem, and the surrounding syntax, but whether the printed form is a typographical irregularity and what correction, if any, should be adopted remain uncertain.

2. Greek: ἵνα ὡς ζηλωταὶ τῶν θεῶν τὰ ὅμοια πράττοτε,
The selected section ends with a printed comma and therefore closes while the larger sentence or rhetorical sequence is still continuing. The English retains an open-ended close and supplies no continuation from outside the requested passage.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν πρωτίστην τῶν Ἑλλήνων δόξαν
Rendered as: the first belief of the Greeks
πρωτίστην is read contextually as the first position previously listed, namely belief in many gods. “Foremost belief” or “earliest belief” is also lexically possible.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν πολλοὺς καὶ παντοπαθεῖς θεοὺς εἶναι μυθολογοῦσαν
Rendered as: the one that tells the myth that there are many gods subject to every passion
The participle μυθολογοῦσαν characterizes the belief as narrating or asserting through myth, while παντοπαθεῖς retains the gods’ subjection to every passion.

5. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὰ ἀσφαλῆ
Rendered as: on settled matters
ἀσφαλής here describes matters treated as certain or already established, not physically safe things.

6. Translation choice — Greek: πάντας ... αὐτῶν τοὺς ἔρωτας
Rendered as: all their love affairs
In the context of the gods’ indecent lives, ἔρωτες denotes their erotic involvements rather than love in a general sense.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ παιδείας Ἑλληνικῆς ὁρμώμενοι
Rendered as: since you proceed from a Greek education
ὁρμάομαι ἐκ marks one’s starting point or basis. “Being grounded in Greek education” is a smoother alternative.

8. Translation choice — Greek: οὓς ἐπαιδεύθητε βίους
Rendered as: the lives in which you were instructed
The compressed construction can describe lives or ways of life received as the content of education. Alternatives include “the lives you were taught” and “the ways of life in which you were trained.”

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἵνα ὡς ζηλωταὶ τῶν θεῶν τὰ ὅμοια πράττοτε
Rendered as: so that, as emulators of the gods, you might do similar things
The purpose force comes from ἵνα, while the recognizable πράττ- stem supplies the action. The modal “might” expresses the purpose clause without claiming that the irregular printed πράττοτε is a regular subjunctive or optative form.

SECTION 4.16

I will begin with Zeus himself, the most royal of all. His father Cronus, by swallowing his own children, as you say, and harvesting the private parts of his father Uranus with an adamantine sickle, showed those zealous for the gods' mysteries the pattern of reverence toward parents and love toward children. Zeus himself bound his own father and imprisoned him in Tartarus, and he punishes the other gods. For those who wish to do unspeakable things, he begot Metis and swallowed her. Metis was semen, for it is impossible to swallow an infant. To provide a defense for lovers of boys, he abducts Ganymede. Coming to the aid of adulterers on behalf of adultery, he himself is often found to be an adulterer. He encourages the seduction of sisters, having had relations with his sisters Hera, Demeter, and heavenly Aphrodite, whom some call Didone. For those who wish to have relations with daughters, he becomes an evil example from the myths by having had relations with Persephone. Indeed, he has committed countless acts of impiety, so that the impious might pronounce this abomination a god because of his excessive lack of self-control.

Translator's notes for section 4.16 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ δὲ τοῦ βασιλικωτάτου Διὸς
Rendered as: with Zeus himself, the most royal of all
The superlative describes Zeus as supremely kingly or royal. The rendering preserves its degree rather than replacing it with an unexpressed formal title.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ ἐξ ἀδάμαντος ἅρπῃ τοῦ πατρὸς Οὐρανοῦ τὰ μόρια θερίσας
Rendered as: harvesting the private parts of his father Uranus with an adamantine sickle
The harvesting verb and sickle image are retained, while private parts follows the source's euphemistic noun in this context. Adamant denotes the mythic hard material; steel or diamond would be more specific than the supplied wording.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς τὰ μυστικὰ τῶν θεῶν ζηλοῦσιν τὸν ὑπογραμμὸν ἔδειξεν
Rendered as: showed those zealous for the gods' mysteries the pattern
The noun can denote mysteries, secret rites, or secret practices, and the verb can express zeal for or emulation of them. The main text retains the mysteries language without deciding whether specific initiation rites are intended. The favorable-sounding pattern of filial reverence and parental love is preserved as the speaker's irony, not replaced by an explanatory moral label.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς δὲ ἀρρητουργεῖν θέλουσιν τὴν Μῆτιν γεννήσας κατέπιεν· ἦν δὲ ἡ Μῆτις γονή· βρέφος γὰρ καταπιεῖν ἀδύνατον
Rendered as: For those who wish to do unspeakable things, he begot Metis and swallowed her. Metis was semen, for it is impossible to swallow an infant
The active participle explicitly says begot, not impregnated. Γονή can refer to reproductive seed, generation, or offspring; semen best fits the stated contrast with an infant and the surrounding accusation. This preserves the ancient speaker's explanation without substituting a more familiar myth or adding physical detail.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὲρ δὲ ἀπολογίας παιδεραστῶν Γανυμήδην ἁρπάζει
Rendered as: To provide a defense for lovers of boys, he abducts Ganymede
The phrase states the apologetic purpose attributed to the mythic act. Lovers of boys renders the historical sexual category without embellishment, and abducts retains the force of seizing or carrying off.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀδελφοφθορεῖν δὲ προτρέπει ἀδελφαῖς συνελθών
Rendered as: He encourages the seduction of sisters, having had relations with his sisters
The compound verb carries a morally condemnatory sexual sense, while the participle supplies Zeus's own conduct as the inducement. Sexual corruption of sisters is a more literal alternative; the rendering does not specify coercion where the verb alone does not establish it.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἣν τινες Διδώνην λέγουσιν
Rendered as: whom some call Didone
The printed name is transliterated as Didone. It is not silently changed to Dione or equated with Dido on the basis of a more familiar name.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἵν’ ὑπὸ τῶν δυσσεβῶν διὰ τὴν ὑπερβάλλουσαν ἀκρασίαν θεὸς εἶναι τὸ μύσος δογματισθῇ
Rendered as: so that the impious might pronounce this abomination a god because of his excessive lack of self-control
The contemptuous neuter noun calls Zeus an abomination. The purpose construction and the stated reason for treating him as divine are retained as the speaker's polemical claim, rather than recast as a neutral statement about Greek belief.

SECTION 4.17

You might reasonably be moderately indignant with the uneducated over such beliefs. But as for those whose starting point is education, what does one even need to say? Some of them claim to be grammarians and sophists and affirm that such acts are worthy of gods. For, lacking self-control themselves, they seize on this mythical pretext and are bold in committing indecent acts, supposedly imitating those superior to them.

Translator's notes for section 4.17 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἰδιώταις ἔχοις περὶ τῶν τοιούτων ὑπολήψεων ἀγανακτεῖν μετρίως εὔλογον
Rendered as: You might reasonably be moderately indignant with the uneducated over such beliefs
The potential expression is retained. The main text attaches moderately to be indignant, giving restrained indignation in the contrast between uneducated and educated people. A material alternative attaches μετρίως to εὔλογον: You might be moderately justified in being indignant with the uneducated over such beliefs. That limits the justification rather than the intensity of indignation. Ἰδιῶται can mean ordinary people or non-specialists; uneducated follows the contrast without implying low intelligence.

2. Translation choice — Greek: γραμματικοὶ καὶ σοφισταὶ ἀξιοῦντες εἶναι
Rendered as: claim to be grammarians and sophists
The claim to professional learned status is retained. Grammarians here are literary-language scholars as well as teachers of grammar; sophists denotes the historical learned profession rather than simply deceptive arguers.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὰς τοιαύτας πράξεις θεῶν ἀξίας. εἶναι βεβαιοῦσιν
Rendered as: affirm that such acts are worthy of gods
The infinitive construction is read across the printed punctuation: acts is the subject of being worthy, and affirm is the governing verb. No surviving wording is omitted or a missing clause supplied.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς δὴ μιμηταὶ τῶν κρειττόνων ἄσεμνα διαπραττόμενοι παρρησιάζονται
Rendered as: are bold in committing indecent acts, supposedly imitating those superior to them
The verb expresses confident openness or boldness, here accompanying conduct. Speak freely is a more speech-specific alternative. The qualification supposedly reflects ὡς δή, and the superior beings are not renamed in the main text where this clause leaves them implicit.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς δὲ ἐκ παιδείας ὁρμωμένοις τί δεῖ καὶ λέγειν;
Rendered as: But as for those whose starting point is education, what does one even need to say?
The rhetorical question preserves δεῖ as need or necessity rather than ability. The preceding contrast with the uneducated remains explicit. What must one even say is a more compact alternative; the chosen wording retains the question about what needs saying without replacing it with what can be said.

SECTION 4.18

For this reason, those who live in the countryside sin much less than they do. They have not been wickedly instructed through the things used to instruct those who dare such deeds, who learned from a bad education to act impiously. For those who learn their letters through such myths from childhood, while their souls are still tender, ingrain the impious deeds of the so-called gods in their own minds. As a result, when they grow older, these deeds bear fruit like bad seeds sown in the soul. Worst of all, these deeply rooted acts of impiety cannot even be cut out easily when, as grown men, they recognize them as harmful. For everyone delights in remaining in the things to which they have been accustomed from childhood. Thus, since habit has almost as much power as nature, it becomes hard for them to change toward the good things that were not sown in their souls from the beginning.

Translator's notes for section 4.18 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: οὐκ εἰσηγμένοι πονηρῶς δι’ ὧν εἰσήχθησαν οἱ ταῦτα τολμῶντες, ἐκ παιδείας κακῆς ἀσεβεῖν μεμαθηκότες
Rendered as: They have not been wickedly instructed through the things used to instruct those who dare such deeds, who learned from a bad education to act impiously
The countryside dwellers are contrasted with those who dare the acts, and the final learned participle describes the latter. The repeated verb of introduction is rendered consistently as instruction; initiation is possible, but need not imply formal mystery initiation in this educational context.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὰς τῶν λεγομένων θεῶν ἀσεβεῖς πράξεις εἰς τὸν αὑτῶν συνφύουσι νοῦν
Rendered as: ingrain the impious deeds of the so-called gods in their own minds
The verb depicts the deeds growing together with or into the learner's mind. Ingrain conveys deep incorporation, while the following English retains the explicit seed, fruit, and root images. A more literal alternative is cause the deeds to grow into their own minds.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὅθεν ἐπαυξηθείσης τῆς ἡλικίας ὡς κακὰ σπέρματα καταβληθέντα τῇ ψυχῇ τελεσφοροῦσιν
Rendered as: As a result, when they grow older, these deeds bear fruit like bad seeds sown in the soul
The preceding impious deeds supply the contextually inferred subject of bear fruit, with seeds as the explicit comparison. The learners' increasing age is retained. An alternative foregrounds the learners as producing the fruit, but the seed comparison favors the ingrained deeds as what comes to fruition.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὁπόταν ἀνδρωθεῖσιν αὐτοῖς χαλεπὰ εἶναι νοῆται
Rendered as: when, as grown men, they recognize them as harmful
The impious practices remain the things recognized, and the grown men the persons doing the recognizing. Grievous or troublesome is a material alternative to harmful for χαλεπά. The main rendering does not turn this into recognition merely that uprooting the practices is difficult.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς συνηθείας οὐ πολὺ ἔλαττον πρὸς τὴν φύσιν δυναμένης
Rendered as: since habit has almost as much power as nature
The source says habit's power is not much less than nature's, rather than identical to it or greater. Almost as much preserves that comparison in accessible English.

6. Translation choice — Greek: δυσμετάβλητοι γίνονται πρὸς τὰ μὴ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς αὐτοῖς καταβληθέντα τῇ ψυχῇ καλά
Rendered as: it becomes hard for them to change toward the good things that were not sown in their souls from the beginning
Their resistance concerns a change toward goods not planted from the outset. The rendering retains the direction of change and the planting image without claiming that such change is impossible.

SECTION 4.19

Therefore, young people should not be trained in corrupting lessons, and those in their prime should carefully refrain from listening to Greek mythology. For their teachings are far worse than ignorance, as we demonstrated from those who live in the countryside, who sin less because they have not been educated in Greek teachings. One must therefore avoid their myths of this kind, their theaters, and their books—if only it were possible, their cities too. For they are full of evil teachings and breathe what is like a frenzy upon their associates; they pass on to those nearby what they themselves have suffered. Worst of all, whoever has received more education among them has strayed far from thinking in accordance with nature.

Translator's notes for section 4.19 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς ἐπὶ τῆς ἀκμῆς ὄντας ἐπιμελῶς ὑποστέλλεσθαι τῆς Ἑλλήνων ἐπακούειν μυθολογίας
Rendered as: those in their prime should carefully refrain from listening to Greek mythology
Those at their prime are distinguished from the young people just mentioned. Refrain preserves the caution or withdrawal expressed by the middle verb without adding an external enforcer or extending the statement to all Greek learning.

2. Translation choice — Greek: εἴθε δυνατὸν ἦν καὶ τὰς πόλεις
Rendered as: if only it were possible, their cities too
The phrase is a wish that avoiding even the cities were possible, not an unqualified claim that it is possible. Avoid is understood from the preceding obligation and is not repeated in Greek.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πνέοντες τοῖς συναμιλλωμένοις ὥσπερ λύσσαν
Rendered as: breathe what is like a frenzy upon their associates
The breath and contagion-like comparison are retained. Λύσσα can mean raging madness or rabies; frenzy avoids specifying a medical condition, while what is like preserves ὥσπερ rather than making the comparison a literal diagnosis.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὅστις παρ’ αὐτοῖς πλεῖον πεπαίδευται, πολλῷ τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν οὗτος φρονεῖν ἐκτέτραπται
Rendered as: whoever has received more education among them has strayed far from thinking in accordance with nature
The greater extent of education and the great extent of deviation are both retained, without turning them into a precise proportional scale. The measure is the speaker's thinking in accordance with nature, not an added claim about a particular modern concept of normality.

SECTION 4.20

Some among them, even claiming to be philosophers, treat such sins as morally indifferent and call those who are angry at such acts foolish. For, they say, such things are not sins by nature: they were prohibited by laws enacted by the wise men who lived in the beginning because those men knew that people, with their easily swayed souls, are greatly distressed over such things and start wars against one another. For these reasons, the wise men established a law and prohibited such acts as sins. But it is ridiculous to think this way. For how are things that cause disturbances, murders, and every kind of turmoil not sins? Do not defrauding people of their livelihoods, the ruin of households, sorcery, deceit, hardship, and many other evils arise from adultery?

Translator's notes for section 4.20 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ τοιαῦτα ἁμαρτήματα ἀδιάφορα τίθενται
Rendered as: treat such sins as morally indifferent
Indifferent is used in the philosophical sense of neither morally good nor morally bad, not a lack of emotional interest. The speaker's own description of the acts as sins is retained even though the reported philosophers deny that description by nature.

2. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν (φασί) τὰ τοιαῦτα τῇ φύσει ἁμαρτήματα, ὅσα θετοῖς ἀπηγόρευται νόμοις ὑπὸ τῶν κατ’ ἀρχὰς γενομένων σοφῶν
Rendered as: For, they say, such things are not sins by nature: they were prohibited by laws enacted by the wise men who lived in the beginning
The relative description identifies the acts prohibited by established law, contrasting enacted law with nature. The colon divides the long construction for English readability without changing the prohibition into a natural one. Those in the beginning is retained without specifying a historical period or identifying particular lawmakers.

3. Translation choice — Greek: εὐριπίστῳ ψυχῇ ἐπὶ τοῖς τοιούτοις μεγάλως ἀχθόμενοι πρὸς ἀλλήλους πόλεμον αἴρονται
Rendered as: with their easily swayed souls, are greatly distressed over such things and start wars against one another
The adjective describes a soul readily tossed or shifted about; fickle or unstable are material alternatives. The rendering preserves both the strong distress and the resulting interpersonal warfare rather than treating the claim as merely disagreement.

4. Translation choice — Greek: βίων περιγραφαί
Rendered as: defrauding people of their livelihoods
Βίος can denote livelihood or property as well as life, and περιγραφή can denote fraudulent deprivation. The economic sense fits the ensuing household ruin and hardship. Cutting short of lives or loss of property are material alternatives if life or possessions, respectively, are foregrounded. The main text does not add a specific legal or financial mechanism.

5. Translation choice — Greek: οἴκων ἀναστάσεις, μαγεῖαι, δόλοι, ἀπορίαι
Rendered as: the ruin of households, sorcery, deceit, hardship
The source lists the overturning of households, magical practices, deception, and want or difficulty. Hardship preserves the breadth of ἀπορίαι rather than restricting it to financial destitution; household ruin preserves the destructive force of ἀναστάσεις.

SECTION 4.21

“But why,” he says, “if a man does not know that his own wife is committing adultery, does he not become jealous, grow angry, cause an uproar, or wage war? Thus such things are not evils by nature; rather, irrational human opinion makes them terrible.” But I say that, even if these terrible things do not happen, it is possible for the wife, through her intimacy with the adulterer, either to abandon her husband, or, even while living with him, to plot against him, or to give the adulterer what her husband acquired through toil. And while her husband is away, she may conceive by the adulterer and, because she is ashamed of being exposed, wish to destroy what is in her womb and become a child-killer, or, while destroying it, perish along with it. But if she conceives by an adulterer while her husband is living with her and then gives birth, the child, once reared, does not know his father but takes the man who is not his father to be his father. And so, when the man who is not his father dies, he leaves his own estate to someone else’s child. And how many other evils naturally tend to spring from adultery! We do not know the hidden things belonging to these evils. For just as a rabid dog kills those whom it touches by transmitting its utterly unseen rabies, so also the hidden evil of adultery, even when it remains unknown, brings about the severing of succession.

Translator's notes for section 4.21 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: συνφθαρῆναι
The printed form has unassimilated συν- before φ. It remains intelligible as an orthographic form of the compound meaning “to be destroyed together,” so no content is uncertain.

2. Greek: ὁ -παῖς
The prefixed hyphen is present in the supplied image-checked reading but has no evident syntactic or morphological function. It is provisionally treated as a typographical feature rather than as part of the noun.

3. Translation choice — Greek: κἂν μὴ τὰ δεινὰ ταῦτα συμβαίνῃ
Rendered as: even if these terrible things do not happen
The phrase may refer particularly to the husband’s jealousy, anger, uproar, and conflict, or more generally to the harmful consequences just discussed; the English preserves that breadth.

4. Translation choice — Greek: συνηθείᾳ τῇ πρὸς τὸν μοιχὸν
Rendered as: through her intimacy with the adulterer
συνήθεια can denote familiarity, association, or intimacy; the adulterous context supports “intimacy,” while the wife remains the understood subject of the following infinitives.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ κατὰ γαστρὸς φθεῖραι
Rendered as: to destroy what is in her womb
The idiom τὸ κατὰ γαστρός denotes what is in the womb. “Destroy” preserves φθείρω without replacing the author’s wording with a modern technical term.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν ἑαυτοῦ καταλείπει βίον
Rendered as: he leaves his own estate
Here βίος most naturally means one’s means of living or property left at death, rather than biological life; “livelihood” or “possessions” are possible alternatives.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς διαδοχῆς τὴν ἐκκοπὴν
Rendered as: the severing of succession
διαδοχή may denote succession, inheritance, or continuation of a family line. The context of misidentified paternity and inheritance favors “succession” while leaving the precise dimension open.

SECTION 4.22

But let that now be passed over by us. This, however, we all know: as a rule, men are uncontrollably indignant over it; wars have been stirred up over it, households have been overthrown, cities have been captured, and countless other things have occurred. For this reason I took refuge with the Jews’ holy God and their law, having placed my confidence in the firm judgment that, from God’s just judgment, both law has been laid down and the soul, wherever it may be, certainly receives what its deeds deserve.

Translator's notes for section 4.22 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ἐπίπαν
Rendered as: as a rule
The expression indicates what happens generally or for the most part, not an exceptionless claim.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἀνεπισχέτως δυσχεραίνοντας
Rendered as: are uncontrollably indignant
ἀνεπισχέτως conveys lack of restraint, while δυσχεραίνω can mean to be displeased, distressed, or indignant; the ensuing wars and destruction support the stronger contextual wording.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀποδεδωκὼς τὴν πίστιν ἀσφαλεῖ τῇ κρίσει
Rendered as: having placed my confidence in the firm judgment
πίστις here denotes confidence or credence given to a conclusion. An alternative is “having entrusted my faith to the sure judgment,” but that can suggest a more technical religious use than the construction requires.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ὧν ἔπραξεν
Rendered as: what its deeds deserve
Literally, the soul receives “what is according to the worth of the things it did”; the rendering expresses proportionate recompense without specifying reward or punishment beyond the Greek.

SECTION 4.23

After I said this, Appion added to the argument, saying, “What then? Do not the laws of the Greeks also forbid base acts and punish adulterers?”

I said, “Then the gods of the Greeks, since they have acted contrary to the laws, owe a penalty. Moreover, how will I be able to discipline myself if I suppose that the gods themselves were the first to commit every grievous act along with adultery and have paid no penalty, although they owe it all the more for this very reason, since they are not enslaved to desire? But if they were subject to it, how could they be gods?”

Appion said, “Then let our objects of attention no longer be gods, but the judges; with our eyes on them, we will be afraid to sin.”

I replied, “The cases are not alike, Appion. A person who keeps a human being in view will dare to sin in the hope of escaping notice. But one who has settled in his own mind that God sees everything, knowing that he cannot escape God’s notice, will refrain even from sinning in secret.”

Translator's notes for section 4.23 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: πῶς· δὲ καὶ σωφρονίζειν
The image-checked edition prints a middle dot between πῶς and the postpositive δέ. That punctuation interrupts what is otherwise a coherent question, so the translation provisionally construes the words together without altering the supplied Greek wording.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπήνεγκεν τῷ λόγῳ
Rendered as: added to the argument
The expression means to bring or add something to the ongoing discourse; “responded to the argument” is also possible.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ταύτῃ μᾶλλον ὀφείλοντες διδόναι
Rendered as: they owe it all the more for this very reason
ταύτῃ points forward to their not being enslaved to desire: freedom from compulsion makes the gods, on the speaker’s reasoning, more accountable.

4. Translation choice — Greek: Ἔστωσαν ἡμῖν σκοποὶ
Rendered as: let our objects of attention be
σκοποί can mean goals, marks, or objects kept in view. The following εἰς οὓς ἀφορῶντες supports the visual and exemplary sense rather than “goals” alone.

5. Translation choice — Greek: θεὸν παντεπόπτην τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ψυχῇ ὁρισάμενος
Rendered as: one who has settled in his own mind that God sees everything
The construction can be rendered more formally as “one who has defined God in his soul as all-seeing.” The chosen wording gives a defensible modern English expression of the internal conviction.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ λάθρα ἁμαρτεῖν παραιτήσεται
Rendered as: will refrain even from sinning in secret
παραιτέομαι here means to decline, avoid, or refrain from an action; καί adds the force “even” in context.

SECTION 4.24

When Appion heard this, he said, “Ever since I heard that you were associating with Jews, I knew that your outlook had changed. For someone has aptly said, ‘Bad associations corrupt good character.’”

I replied, “Then good associations correct worthless character.”

Appion said, “Today I had fully resolved to ascertain your position; that is why we allowed you to speak first. But tomorrow—here, if it pleases you—when the same friends have assembled, I will demonstrate that our gods are neither adulterers nor murderers nor destroyers of children, and that they did not have sexual relations with sisters or daughters. Rather, the ancients, wishing only lovers of learning to know the mysteries, veiled them in myths of the kind you have described. For in their account of nature they say that Zeus is the boiling substance, Cronus is time, and Rhea is the ever-flowing nature of water. Nevertheless, as I promised, tomorrow at dawn, when you have assembled, I will interpret each particular form allegorically and reveal to you the truth about what exists.”

In response I said, “Tomorrow do just as you have promised. But now, beginning from this point, listen also to what bears on the very things you are going to say.”

Translator's notes for section 4.24 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἠλλοιῶσθαι τὴν γνώμην
Rendered as: your outlook had changed
γνώμη can denote mind, judgment, opinion, or outlook. The passive ἠλλοιῶσθαι indicates that it had been altered.

2. Translation choice — Greek: φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί
Rendered as: Bad associations corrupt good character
ὁμιλίαι denotes associations or company, and ἤθη denotes habits, morals, or character. The wording preserves the maxim and its reversal in the next sentence without making a familiar rendering from another work controlling.

3. Translation choice — Greek: Σήμερον πεπληροφορήμην τὴν σὴν ἐπιγνῶναι ἔνστασιν, διὸ σοὶ πρώτῳ εἰπεῖν συνεχωρήσαμεν
Rendered as: Today I had fully resolved to ascertain your position; that is why we allowed you to speak first
The pluperfect πεπληροφορήμην places the settled resolve before the permission expressed by συνεχωρήσαμεν, while ἐπιγνῶναι can denote learning or ascertaining the position. This sequence favors a prospective reading: Appion had resolved to ascertain the position and therefore let the other speaker go first. A materially possible alternative is “Today I had become fully assured that I understood your objection,” taking πεπληροφορήμην as achieved assurance and ἐπιγνῶναι as recognition already attained; ἔνστασις may mean “objection,” “position,” or “contention.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: παίδων φθορεῖς
Rendered as: destroyers of children
φθορεύς can denote a destroyer or corrupter. In a list with adultery and murder and in the context of myths about the gods, “destroyers” is the more direct choice, though “corrupters of children” is lexically possible.

5. Translation choice — Greek: οὐχ ἀδελφαῖς ἢ θυγατράσιν πλησιάσαντες
Rendered as: they did not have sexual relations with sisters or daughters
πλησιάζω literally means to approach or associate closely, but with these dative objects and the surrounding accusations of sexual misconduct it has a sexual sense.

6. Translation choice — Greek: Ζῆνα γὰρ τὴν ζέουσαν οὐσίαν εἶναι φυσιολογοῦσιν
Rendered as: in their account of nature they say that Zeus is the boiling substance
φυσιολογοῦσιν introduces a natural-philosophical explanation. The Greek also makes an etymological sound association between Ζῆνα and ζέουσαν that cannot be reproduced naturally in English.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ καθ’ ἕκαστον εἶδος
Rendered as: each particular form
The phrase may refer to each divine figure, each mythic form, or each individual feature of the allegory. “Form” preserves the expression without selecting one referent too narrowly.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἐντεῦθεν καὶ πρὸς αὐτὰ ἃ μέλλεις λέγειν, ἄκουσον
Rendered as: beginning from this point, listen also to what bears on the very things you are going to say
The Greek elliptically commands Appion to hear something directed toward or bearing upon his forthcoming claims. “Listen to a reply to the very things you are going to say” is another possible way to supply the English relation.

SECTION 4.25

If the deeds of the gods, though good, were veiled in evil myths, great wickedness is revealed in the one who covered them, because he hid honorable things beneath evil narratives so that no one might become an imitator of them. But if they truly committed impious acts, those acts should instead have been covered with good narratives, so that people, looking up to them as their superiors, would not attempt sins like theirs.

After I said this, those present were plainly beginning to feel love for the arguments I had made. Indeed, after repeatedly and earnestly urging me to come without fail on the following day, they departed.

Translator's notes for section 4.25 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: τῆς πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ λεχθέντας λόγους · ἀγάπης
The image-checked edition prints a middle dot between λόγους and ἀγάπης, although the surrounding words support the continuous genitive construction “love for the arguments spoken by me.” The translation provisionally adopts that defensible syntax while preserving disclosure of the printed punctuation.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πολλὴ τοῦ σκεπάσαντος δείκνυται κακία
Rendered as: great wickedness is revealed in the one who covered them
The genitive identifies the person responsible for concealing the deeds; “is demonstrated on the part of the one who covered them” is a more formal alternative.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ σεμνὰ
Rendered as: honorable things
σεμνός can mean venerable, august, solemn, or honorable. Here it describes supposedly good divine deeds that would merit imitation.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἀγαθοῖς αὐτὰ ἐπισκέπειν
Rendered as: those acts should instead have been covered with good narratives
ἐπισκέπειν is understood here in the sense of covering over, corresponding to the earlier language of veiling. The substantival ἀγαθοῖς takes its contextual content from the preceding “myths” and “narratives.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς εἰς κρείττονας ἀφορώντες
Rendered as: looking up to them as their superiors
κρείττονας may mean those who are better, stronger, or superior. The gods function here as supposedly higher examples whom humans observe and imitate.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀρχὴν λαμβάνοντες τῆς πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ λεχθέντας λόγους · ἀγάπης
Rendered as: beginning to feel love for the arguments I had made
ἀρχὴν λαμβάνειν with the genitive means to make a beginning of something. λόγοι may be words, statements, or arguments; the argumentative setting favors “arguments,” while the printed middle dot is provisionally treated as editorial punctuation that does not prevent ἀγάπης from completing the construction.

7. Translation choice — Greek: πάντως με τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ ἐλθεῖν
Rendered as: me to come without fail on the following day
πάντως expresses insistence that the visit occur in any event or by all means.

HOMILY 5

SECTION 5.1

So, on the following day in Tyre, I went to the quiet place as we had arranged. After seeing and greeting the others, together with some additional people, but not seeing Appion, I asked why he was not present. Someone said that he had been physically unwell since that very evening. When I said that it was reasonable for us to set out immediately and visit him, almost everyone requested that I first hold a discussion with them and that then, in that way, I would be able to visit him as well. Once everyone had come to a single decision, I began to speak:

Translator's notes for section 5.1 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: κἀκεῖνον ἐπισκέψασθαι δύνασθαι αὐτόν
The main rendering analyzes κἀκεῖνον as the object of ἐπισκέψασθαι and αὐτόν as the accusative subject of δύνασθαι, contextually referring to Clement with a shift from the preceding first-person με to the participants’ third-person perspective. Alternatively, κἀκεῖνον and αὐτόν may be understood as an emphatic or resumptive double reference to Appion, yielding the sense “visit that man himself.” The construction is unusual but does not require deleting either accusative.

2. Translation choice — Greek: δυσαρρώστως αὐτὸν ἀπ’ αὐτῆς ἑσπέρας ἐσχηκέναι τὸ σωμάτιον
Rendered as: he had been physically unwell since that very evening
The idiom describes the poor condition of his body. The diminutive σωμάτιον need not imply literal smallness and is represented naturally by “physically,” while “that very evening” preserves the intensive force of αὐτῆς.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πρότερον διαλεχθῆναί με αὐτοῖς
Rendered as: that I first hold a discussion with them
διαλέγομαι can mean converse, discourse, or debate; “hold a discussion” suits the requested address without predetermining its degree of formality.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἶθ’ οὕτως κἀκεῖνον ἐπισκέψασθαι δύνασθαι αὐτόν
Rendered as: and that then, in that way, I would be able to visit him as well
The rendering takes κἀκεῖνον as the object of ἐπισκέψασθαι and αὐτόν as the accusative subject of δύνασθαι, referring to Clement from the participants’ perspective. English naturally returns that third-person reference to the narrator’s first person.

5. Translation choice — Greek: μιᾶς οὖν πάντων γνώμης γενομένης
Rendered as: Once everyone had come to a single decision
Literally, “when one opinion of all had come about”; the rendering expresses their resulting unanimity.

SECTION 5.2

“Yesterday, when I left this place, friends, I admit that I could not get to sleep, because I was deeply preoccupied with the discussion that was going to take place with Appion. As I lay awake, the stratagems I had devised against him in Rome rushed into my mind. They were as follows. From childhood I, Clement, had loved truth, had sought the things that matter to the soul, and had spent my time on refutations and demonstrations; but because I could find nothing definitive, under the strain of my thoughts I ran aground in illness. And indeed, while I lay ill, Appion arrived in Rome. He was a friend of my father and stayed as my guest. When he learned that I was bedridden, he came in to see me, since he was not unversed in medicine, and asked why I had taken to bed. I was well aware that the man held Jews in deep hatred—so much so that he had written many books against them—and that he had now taken Simon himself as a friend, not out of a love of learning, but because he knew him to be a Samaritan, a Jew-hater, and someone who had come forward against the Jews. For that reason he had drawn him close, so that he could learn from him something to use against the Jews—

Translator's notes for section 5.2 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἵνα δύνατο κατὰ Ἰουδαίων τι παρ’ αὐτοῦ μανθάνειν
The form δύνατο after ἵνα is morphosyntactically unusual by classical standards but can be understood as late or nonclassical use of a past indicative in a purpose clause. The proposed optative is only a possible normalization, not the supplied reading.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς πρὸς Ἀππίωνα μελλούσης ἔσεσθαι ζητήσεως
Rendered as: the discussion that was going to take place with Appion
ζήτησις can denote an inquiry, dispute, or debate. “Discussion” leaves its precise character open while the wider narrative supplies its adversarial aspect.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ ἐν Ῥώμῃ πρὸς αὐτόν μοι μεμηχανημένα
Rendered as: the stratagems I had devised against him in Rome
μηχανάομαι denotes contriving or devising, while πρὸς αὐτόν is contextually adversarial rather than merely relational.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς ἀνασκευὰς καὶ κατασκευὰς
Rendered as: on refutations and demonstrations
The paired terms denote arguments that respectively dismantle and establish a position; alternatives include “disproofs and proofs” or “negative and positive arguments.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ τῆς συνοίας ἐξώκειλα εἰς νόσον
Rendered as: under the strain of my thoughts I ran aground in illness
σύνοια can denote intense thought, anxiety, or distress arising from reflection. The rendering “strain of my thoughts” preserves that range, while “ran aground” retains the nautical image in ἐξώκειλα rather than reducing it to a generic transition into illness.

6. Translation choice — Greek: πατρικὸς ὢν μοι φίλος
Rendered as: He was a friend of my father
πατρικὸς φίλος can mean a paternal or inherited family friend. The immediate first-person construction most naturally indicates a friend connected with Clement’s father.

7. Translation choice — Greek: σαμαρέα αὐτὸν οἶδεν μισοϊουδαῖόν τε ὄντα
Rendered as: he knew him to be a Samaritan, a Jew-hater
The ethnic designation and the compound μισοϊουδαῖος are retained distinctly rather than treating Samaritan identity itself as equivalent to hatred of Jews.

SECTION 5.3

Knowing these things beforehand about Appion, as soon as he asked the cause of my illness, I answered in pretense, “I suffer what young men suffer, and my soul aches.” He replied, “Child, trust me as you would a father and tell me: what is the illness of your soul?” Once again I sighed in pretense, as though ashamed to speak about being in love. By my silence and by lowering my head, I gave him grounds to suspect what I wanted to suggest. Convinced that I was truly in love with a woman, he said, “There is nothing in life that cannot receive help. For when I myself was young, I fell in love with a most distinguished woman. Not only did I consider it impossible to obtain her; I did not even hope ever to address her. Nevertheless, I happened to meet an Egyptian who was highly accomplished in the practices of magicians. After he befriended me, I disclosed my passion, and he not only placed himself at my disposal for everything I wanted, but, endeavoring to be even more lavish toward me, did not begrudge teaching me also the incantation through which I obtained her. Persuaded by that secret instruction of his and by the unstinting generosity of the man who taught me, after I had succeeded once, I stopped being in love.”

Translator's notes for section 5.3 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: δαψιλέστερον πρὸς μὲ φιλοτιμούμενος
The confirmed print has μὲ with a grave accent. The context provisionally supports understanding it as the pronoun με, “me,” rather than as an incomplete μέν; the proposed reading regularizes the accent but is not the supplied text.

2. Translation choice — Greek: Τὰ νέων πάσχω
Rendered as: I suffer what young men suffer
The compact expression literally refers to “the things of young men.” The rendering preserves Appion’s intended inference of youthful erotic distress without adding it directly to Clement’s words.

3. Translation choice — Greek: διά γε τῆς σιωπῆς καὶ τοῦ κάτω νεύειν
Rendered as: By my silence and by lowering my head
κάτω νεύειν describes the visible gesture of inclining or lowering the head, here conveying affected embarrassment.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ δὲ ἐρᾶν με γυναικὸς ἀληθῶς ἀναπεισθεὶς ἔφη
Rendered as: Convinced that I was truly in love with a woman, he said
ἀληθῶς can qualify either ἐρᾶν (“truly in love”) or ἀναπεισθείς (“truly convinced”). The main rendering attaches it to the supposed love because Appion interprets Clement’s affected behavior as evidence of a real passion; the alternative is “Truly convinced that I was in love with a woman.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ μόνον αὐτῆς τυχεῖν ἡγούμην ἀδύνατον εἶναι, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ προσαγορεῦσαί ποτε ἤλπιζον
Rendered as: Not only did I consider it impossible to obtain her; I did not even hope ever to address her
The coordinated clauses express an escalation from regarding possession of her as impossible to lacking even the hope of ever speaking to her.

6. Translation choice — Greek: πάνυ τὰ μάγων ἀκριβοῦντι
Rendered as: highly accomplished in the practices of magicians
ἀκριβόω here signifies exact mastery or thorough knowledge; τὰ μάγων denotes the matters or practices belonging to magicians.

7. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ φιλωθεὶς ἐκφαίνω μου τὸν ἔρωτα
Rendered as: After he befriended me, I disclosed my passion
The passive φιλωθείς can mean being loved or treated as a friend. “Befriended” fits the ensuing disclosure, while ἐκφαίνω is represented according to the sense of its vivid historical present.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἐπαοιδήν, δι’ ἧς ἔτυχον
Rendered as: the incantation through which I obtained her
ἐπαοιδή is a sung spell or incantation. Although the object of ἔτυχον is implicit here, the earlier αὐτῆς τυχεῖν supplies the woman as its contextual object; an alternative is “through which I succeeded.”

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ δὲ τῆς ἐκείνου λαθραίας ὑποδείξεως πεισθεὶς τῇ τοῦ διδάξαντος ἀφθονίᾳ
Rendered as: Persuaded by that secret instruction of his and by the unstinting generosity of the man who taught me
The dative τῇ … ἀφθονίᾳ is taken instrumentally alongside ἐκ τῆς … ὑποδείξεως. An alternative is “persuaded by that secret instruction of his to trust in the teacher’s unstinting generosity.”

10. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ἅπαξ ἐπιτυχών, ἐπαυσάμην τοῦ ἔρωτος
Rendered as: after I had succeeded once, I stopped being in love
Placing “once” after “succeeded” explicitly preserves the numerical force of ἅπαξ rather than reducing it to a temporal conjunction meaning merely “after.”

SECTION 5.4

“Therefore, if you too have suffered something of this kind, as humans do, put your confidence in us and set your mind at ease, for within seven days I will make you obtain her without fail.” When I heard this, I kept my own purpose in view and said, “Forgive me for not fully believing that magic is real, for I have already had experience of many people making many promises and then failing to fulfill them. Still, your promise presses me and leads me to hope. Yet I am afraid when I consider whether demons may sometimes fail to obey magicians in the things they are commanded to do.”

Translator's notes for section 5.4 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ καὶ σὺ τοιοῦτόν τι πέπονθας ἀνθρωπίνως
Rendered as: if you too have suffered something of this kind, as humans do
ἀνθρωπίνως marks the experience as human or natural to humanity, not as morally commendable.

2. Translation choice — Greek: θάρσησον ἡμῖν πρὸς τὸ ἀμέριμνον
Rendered as: put your confidence in us and set your mind at ease
The text has the plural ἡμῖν, “in us,” although Appion is speaking. It may be an inclusive or self-referential plural; the translation preserves it rather than silently changing it to “me.” πρὸς τὸ ἀμέριμνον expresses the intended freedom from worry.

3. Translation choice — Greek: μαγείαν ὑφεστάναι
Rendered as: that magic is real
ὑφίστημι in this construction concerns actual existence or reality, not merely the practice of magic.

4. Translation choice — Greek: πολλῶν γὰρ πολλὰ ἐπαγγελλομένων καὶ διαψευσαμένων ἤδη πεπείραμαι
Rendered as: I have already had experience of many people making many promises and then failing to fulfill them
διαψεύδομαι can denote proving false, disappointing expectations, or failing in a claim. “Failing to fulfill them” makes the relation to the promises explicit without alleging a particular motive.

5. Translation choice — Greek: δυσωπεῖ με καὶ εἰς ἐλπίδας ἄγει ἡ σὴ ὑπόσχεσις
Rendered as: your promise presses me and leads me to hope
δυσωπέω may mean shame, constrain, move, or win someone over. “Presses me” retains Clement’s affected reluctance without implying that he already believes Appion.

SECTION 5.5

Appion said, “Concede that I know more about these matters than you do. Yet, so that you may not think you have heard nothing from me in answer to what you said, learn how it is that demons are compelled to submit to magicians in the matters about which they receive commands.
