Just as it is impossible for a soldier to contradict his commander, and the commanders themselves cannot disobey a king—for if anyone contradicts those set over him, he is certainly judged deserving of punishment—so it is impossible for demons not to serve their angelic commanders. When adjured by appeal to those angels, they shudder and yield, knowing well that if they disobey, they will certainly be punished. But even the angels themselves, when magicians adjure them by the one who is superior, obey, for fear that they may be judged guilty of disobedience and perish. For if all beings that possess life and reason did not foresee the punishment coming from the superior one, confusion would have arisen, with all of them rebelling against one another.”

Translator's notes for section 5.5 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: καθ’ ὧν ὁρκιζόμενοι φρίττοντες· εἴκουσιν
The confirmed edition prints a high stop after φρίττοντες. The translation provisionally reads the participle with εἴκουσιν as a continuous construction, while preserving the marked editorial break in this disclosure; no replacement wording is required for a defensible translation.

2. Translation choice — Greek: Ταῦτα ἐμοὶ σοῦ μᾶλλον συγχώρει εἰδέναι
Rendered as: Concede that I know more about these matters than you do
συγχωρέω here asks Clement to concede or grant Appion’s asserted superior knowledge, not to give Appion permission to acquire knowledge.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πῶς ἀνάγκην ἔχουσιν οἱ δαίμονες τοῖς μάγοις ὑπείκειν
Rendered as: how it is that demons are compelled to submit to magicians
Literally, the demons “have necessity” to yield. “Are compelled” expresses the asserted necessity without introducing a distinct external agent.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς αὐτῶν ἡγουμένοις ἀγγέλοις
Rendered as: their angelic commanders
The participial noun ἡγουμένοις identifies angels who lead or command the demons; the phrase need not imply that the demons possess the angels.

5. Translation choice — Greek: καθ’ ὧν ὁρκιζόμενοι φρίττοντες· εἴκουσιν
Rendered as: When adjured by appeal to those angels, they shudder and yield
In adjuration language, κατά with the genitive identifies the authority invoked. The participle φρίττοντες is rendered together with εἴκουσιν despite the printed high stop. An alternative is “being adjured by them, they yield with trembling.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: κατὰ τοῦ κρείττονος ὑπὸ μάγων ὁρκιζόμενοι
Rendered as: when magicians adjure them by the one who is superior
κρείττων is comparative and may mean the greater, stronger, or higher-ranking one. “The one who is superior” preserves the hierarchy without identifying the referent beyond what the passage states.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἐκ τοῦ κρείττονος δίκην
Rendered as: the punishment coming from the superior one
δίκη can denote justice, judgment, or penalty. The repeated warnings of punishment and destruction favor “punishment” here, while κρείττων is rendered consistently with the preceding clause.

SECTION 5.6

And I said, “Then are the things said by poets and philosophers correct: that in Hades the souls of the impious, after being judged for what they dared to do, are punished—such as the souls of Ixion, Tantalus, Tityus, Sisyphus, the daughters of Danaus, and all the others who ever acted impiously here? And if these things are not so, how could magic have any reality?” When he said that matters in Hades were indeed so, I asked, “Why, then, have we ourselves not feared magic, since we are convinced of the punishment in Hades for adultery? For I do not agree that it is right to use magic to force a woman who is unwilling. But if someone promises to persuade her, I am quite ready for that and to acknowledge my gratitude as well.”

Translator's notes for section 5.6 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: δυνατὸν ἂν μαγείαν ὑφεστάναι
Rendered as: how could magic have any reality
ὑφεστάναι has an existential sense here: magic could not subsist or be real if the premises about Hades were false.

2. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ αὐτοὶ μαγείαν οὐ πεφοβήμεθα
Rendered as: have we ourselves not feared magic
The first-person plural is retained as an inclusive rhetorical question; αὐτοί adds emphasis, ‘we ourselves.’

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ μοιχείας πεπεισμένοι τὴν ἐν ᾅδου δίκην
Rendered as: since we are convinced of the punishment in Hades for adultery
ἐπὶ μοιχείας identifies adultery as the ground for the punishment; πεπεισμένοι governs the conviction expressed by τὴν ... δίκην.

4. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τοῦτο μετὰ τοῦ καὶ χάριν ὁμολογεῖν ἑτοίμως ἔχω
Rendered as: I am quite ready for that and to acknowledge my gratitude as well
ἑτοίμως ἔχω expresses readiness, while χάριν ὁμολογεῖν means to acknowledge gratitude or indebtedness.

SECTION 5.7

And Appion said, “Do you not think it amounts to the same thing whether you obtain her by magic or by persuading her with words?” I said, “They are not at all alike; each is far removed from the other. The man who compels an unwilling woman by magic’s force incurs the harshest punishment as one who has schemed against a chaste woman. But the man who persuades her by speech and makes his appeal depend on her own freedom and choice has used no force. Still, I think the persuader will be punished less than the man who used force. So if you can persuade her, I will be grateful if I succeed; otherwise, I would rather die than forcibly compel a woman who does not consent.”

Translator's notes for section 5.7 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτῆς ἐπιτύχοις
Rendered as: you obtain her
With a person as the genitive object in this erotic context, ἐπιτυγχάνω means to attain or succeed in obtaining that person.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τῇ αὐτῆς ἐξουσίᾳ καὶ βουλῇ ποιησάμενος τὴν παράφασιν
Rendered as: makes his appeal depend on her own freedom and choice
παράφασις can denote an appeal, exhortation, or persuasion. The ἐπί phrase makes her own authority and will the basis on which the appeal succeeds; the defensible alternative ‘makes the persuasion subject to her own freedom and will’ preserves the same contrast with force.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἧττον δὲ οἶμαι κολασθήσεσθαι τὸν πεπεικότα τοῦ βιασαμένου
Rendered as: I think the persuader will be punished less than the man who used force
The genitive τοῦ βιασαμένου supplies the standard of comparison after ἧττον.

4. Translation choice — Greek: χάριν ἕξω ἐπιτυχών
Rendered as: I will be grateful if I succeed
Literally, the speaker will ‘have gratitude’ upon succeeding; English expresses this naturally as being grateful.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἥδιόν μοι τεθνάναι μᾶλλον ἢ
Rendered as: I would rather die than
The comparative wording is emphatic in Greek; idiomatic English expresses the preference with ‘rather ... than.’

SECTION 5.8

And Appion, genuinely at a loss, said, “What am I to say to you? At one moment, as a man tormented by love, you wish to obtain her; at another, as if you were not in love, you put fear before desire. You imagine that after persuading her you will be free from liability as though sinless, but that if you obtain her by the force of magic, you will incur punishment. Yet you fail to understand that what is judged in every action is its outcome—the fact that it happened—not how it happened. And if you commit adultery, surely you will not be judged to have acted impiously if you manage it by magic, yet be absolved of the sin involved in adultery if you persuade her.” I said, “Because I am in love, obtaining the woman I love is in any case my settled aim. I must therefore choose one of the two, and, if possible, I will choose to flatter rather than use magic. But it is not easy to persuade her even with flattery, for the woman is thoroughly a philosopher.”

Translator's notes for section 5.8 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἀληθῶς διαπορῶν
Rendered as: genuinely at a loss
διαπορέω conveys serious perplexity or uncertainty about how to proceed.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς ἐπιθυμίας προτιμᾷς τὸν φόβον
Rendered as: you put fear before desire
The genitive marks the thing over which fear is preferred; ‘prefer fear to desire’ is an equivalent alternative.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ἀναμάρτητος ἔσεσθαι ἀνεύθυνος
Rendered as: you will be free from liability as though sinless
ἀνεύθυνος means not liable or not accountable, while ὡς ἀναμάρτητος presents the supposed basis for that exemption.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ τέλος παντὸς πράγματος κρίνεται ὅτι γέγονεν
Rendered as: what is judged in every action is its outcome—the fact that it happened
τέλος denotes the resulting end or outcome. The following ὅτι γέγονεν clarifies that the occurrence itself, rather than its manner, is in view.

5. Translation choice — Greek: μαγείᾳ μὲν δυνηθεὶς
Rendered as: if you manage it by magic
The participle δυνηθείς leaves the action implicit; the context supplies succeeding in the adultery through magic.

6. Translation choice — Greek: πάνυ γὰρ ἐστὶν ἡ γυνὴ φιλόσοφος
Rendered as: the woman is thoroughly a philosopher
πάνυ intensifies the predicate φιλόσοφος; ‘very much a philosopher’ is more literal but less idiomatic.

SECTION 5.9

And Appion said, “For that very reason I am more confident that I will be able to persuade her as you yourself wish, if indeed we can speak with her.” I answered, “Impossible.” Appion asked whether it was possible to write to her. I said, “That is possible.” Then Appion said, “Before this night is over, I will compose a book, an encomium to adultery. You will take it from me and send it on to her, and I hope that, once persuaded, she will consent.” Appion composed that book and gave it to me. It was about this book that I thought during this night, and at just the right time I was reminded that I had it among the other books I carry with me. After relating these things, I showed the book to those present and read it aloud when they wished to hear it. And then, after reading it, I said, “Gentlemen, this is the education of the Greeks, with a noble theme for sinning without fear.” The book ran as follows:

Translator's notes for section 5.9 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: οἷς μεθ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιφέρομαι
The confirmed printed wording has the third-person reflexive ἑαυτοῦ with the first-person verb ἐπιφέρομαι. Later Greek can extend ἑαυτοῦ beyond strict third-person reference, so the supplied wording remains intelligible as ‘with me’; the classically expected first-person reflexive would be ἐμαυτοῦ. The proposed reading is therefore only a conjectural normalization, not a correction to the selected edition.

2. Translation choice — Greek: Ταύτῃ μᾶλλον εὔελπίς εἰμι
Rendered as: For that very reason I am more confident
Ταύτῃ is taken causally as referring to the woman’s being a philosopher. It could more formally be rendered ‘in this respect,’ but the causal connection is contextually stronger.

3. Translation choice — Greek: Ἔτι τῇ νυκτὶ ταύτῃ
Rendered as: Before this night is over
ἔτι with the temporal dative indicates that the composition will occur while the present night still lasts; ‘this very night’ is an equivalent alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: πεισθεῖσα συνθήσεται
Rendered as: once persuaded, she will consent
συντίθεμαι here means to agree or consent to the proposed relationship.

5. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ εὐκαίρως ἔχειν αὐτὸ ὑπεμνήσθην
Rendered as: at just the right time I was reminded that I had it
εὐκαίρως is taken with the act of being reminded. A possible alternative attachment is ‘I was reminded that I conveniently had it,’ but the temporal reading is more natural in context.

6. Translation choice — Greek: σὺν ἄλλοις βιβλίοις οἷς μεθ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιφέρομαι
Rendered as: among the other books I carry with me
The relative οἷς is understood by case attraction to βιβλίοις, and the reflexive phrase is interpreted contextually with the first-person verb.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ τῶν Ἑλλήνων παιδεία
Rendered as: the education of the Greeks
παιδεία may also mean Greek culture or intellectual formation; ‘education’ preserves the immediate connection with the philosophical book just read.

8. Translation choice — Greek: γενναίαν ὑπόθεσιν ἔχουσα πρὸς τὸ ἀδεῶς ἐξαμαρτάνειν
Rendered as: with a noble theme for sinning without fear
The wording is ironic: γενναίαν calls the book’s ὑπόθεσις ‘noble,’ while the purpose or tendency expressed by πρός is fearless wrongdoing.

SECTION 5.10

The Lover to His Beloved
(Anonymously, because of the laws originating from foolish people)

At the commands of Love—the oldest of all—for the sake of a child. I have learned that you devote yourself to philosophy and, for virtue’s sake, emulate the life of those who are superior. And who among all beings could be superior to the gods, and who among human beings could be superior to the philosophers? For philosophers alone know which actions are evil or good by nature, and which, though they are not so, are regarded as such through the enactment of laws. Take, for example, the act called adultery: some have supposed it to be evil, although it is good in every respect, for it takes place at Love’s commands for the multiplication of life. Love is the oldest of all gods. For without Love no mingling or generation can take place—of elements, of gods, of human beings, of irrational animals, or of all the remaining things. Indeed, we are all instruments of Love. But the craftsman himself, working through us and present in the souls of every being that is generated, is Mind. Consequently, it is not of our own volition that we desire to do his will, but when we are commanded by him. And if, while desiring by his will, we attempt for the sake of so-called self-control to restrain our desire, how will we not commit the greatest acts of impiety by opposing the oldest of all gods and human beings?

Translator's notes for section 5.10 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: Ὁ ἐρῶν τῇ ἐρωμένῃ
Rendered as: The Lover to His Beloved
The nominative sender and dative recipient form an epistolary heading. ἐρωμένη denotes the woman loved or desired.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἀνωνύμως διὰ τοὺς ἐκ τῶν ἀνοήτων ἀνθρώπων νόμους
Rendered as: Anonymously, because of the laws originating from foolish people
ἐκ marks the foolish people as the source of the laws; ‘because of the laws made by foolish people’ is an equivalent contextual rendering.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπιταγαῖς Ἔρωτος τοῦ πάντων πρεσβυτάτου παιδὸς χάριν
Rendered as: At the commands of Love—the oldest of all—for the sake of a child
The main rendering takes Ἔρωτος with ἐπιταγαῖς, treats τοῦ πάντων πρεσβυτάτου as describing Love, and construes παιδὸς χάριν as the separate phrase ‘for the sake of a child.’ Because the compressed heading permits competing attachment, τοῦ πάντων πρεσβυτάτου παιδός could alternatively be understood together as ‘the oldest child of all,’ though that leaves the function of χάριν less clear.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τίνες δὲ ἂν εἶεν κρείττονες ἢ θεοὶ μὲν ἁπάντων, ἀνθρώπων δὲ οἱ φιλόσοφοι;
Rendered as: And who among all beings could be superior to the gods, and who among human beings could be superior to the philosophers?
The rendering takes ἤ after comparative κρείττονες as ‘than’ and understands ἁπάντων and ἀνθρώπων partitively, expanding the elliptical second half to preserve the parallel rhetorical comparison. A viable alternative takes ἤ as ‘except’ or ‘other than’: ‘And who could be superior except the gods among all and the philosophers among human beings?’ Another possible construal treats the genitives comparatively, making the gods superior to all and philosophers superior to other humans.

5. Translation choice — Greek: οὗτοι γὰρ μόνοι ἴσασιν
Rendered as: For philosophers alone know
The demonstrative most naturally resumes the immediately preceding philosophers, who possess the claimed philosophical discernment. It could grammatically encompass both gods and philosophers, but the argument is directed to the recipient’s philosophical learning.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ποῖα δὲ τῇ τῶν νόμων θέσει (οὐκ ὄντα) νομίζεται
Rendered as: which, though they are not so, are regarded as such through the enactment of laws
The omitted predicate is supplied from ‘evil or good’; the parenthetical οὐκ ὄντα denies that the actions possess by nature the qualities assigned by law.

7. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς γὰρ τὴν τοῦ βίου πολυγονίαν
Rendered as: for the multiplication of life
πολυγονία denotes abundant generation or production of offspring. ‘For life’s abundant procreation’ is a more literal alternative.

8. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ ζῴων ἀλόγων
Rendered as: of irrational animals
ἄλογος contrasts nonhuman animals as lacking reason; ‘non-rational living creatures’ is an equivalent alternative.

9. Translation choice — Greek: παντὸς τοῦ γεννωμένου ψυχαῖς ἐπιδημῶν
Rendered as: present in the souls of every being that is generated
ἐπιδημέω literally denotes residing, sojourning, or being present among; here it describes Mind’s presence in the souls of generated beings.

10. Translation choice — Greek: ἐστὶ νοῦς
Rendered as: is Mind
νοῦς is capitalized because the passage identifies it as the craftsman operating through all beings; ‘intellect’ or lowercase ‘mind’ would preserve the lexical sense but less clearly convey the personified cosmic role.

11. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελευσθῶμεν, τὸ ἐκείνου βούλημα
Rendered as: we are commanded by him ... his will
The pronouns immediately follow the identification of the craftsman as Mind, while the argument also closely identifies that craftsman with Love’s activity. The English preserves the masculine referent without forcing a sharper distinction between Love and Mind than the passage supplies.

12. Translation choice — Greek: χάριν τῆς λεγομένης σωφροσύνης κρατεῖν τῆς ἐπιθυμίας
Rendered as: for the sake of so-called self-control to restrain our desire
σωφροσύνη can mean self-control, moderation, or chastity. ‘Self-control’ suits the immediately following attempt to master sexual desire, while ‘so-called chastity’ remains a viable context-specific alternative.

SECTION 5.11

But let every door be opened to him, and let all the wretched, enacted laws be dissolved, laws laid down for jealous people. Dominated by folly and unwilling to understand what is reasonable, and also looking suspiciously at the so-called adulterers, these people are reasonably made sport of by Zeus himself through Minos and Rhadamanthys, by means of enacted laws. For Love cannot be restrained once he has taken up residence in souls. The passion of lovers is not voluntary. Indeed, Zeus himself, the lawgiver of these people, had relations with countless women. Some wise men praise him as a benefactor in childbearing, granting human beings union with himself. But among those who, he knew, did not recognize him in connection with the favor, he changed his appearance, so that he would neither distress them nor seem to act against the laws he himself had established. Therefore, for the sake of a good life, you must devote yourself to philosophy and imitate those acknowledged to be superior, whose unions have been countless.

Translator's notes for section 5.11 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: θετοὶ
Rendered as: enacted
The laws are instituted or laid down, contrasting humanly established prohibition with the speaker's account of irresistible love. Arbitrary is a possible evaluative reading, but enacted does not add that judgment to the adjective itself.

2. Translation choice — Greek: εὐλόγως θετοῖς παίζονται νόμοις
Rendered as: are reasonably made sport of ... by means of enacted laws
The passive verb describes the jealous people as being played with or mocked, not as themselves playing. The positive judgment reasonably is the letter writer's, and is not silently reversed to match the surrounding narrative's moral position.

3. Translation choice — Greek: παρ’ οἷς δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ χάριτι ἠπίστατο ἀγνοούμενος
Rendered as: among those who, he knew, did not recognize him in connection with the favor
The passive participle describes Zeus himself as unrecognized or misunderstood, not the favor as unrecognized. The main text takes the former sense while retaining the respect in which he was unrecognized. A material alternative is among those by whom he knew he was misunderstood with respect to the favor; both leave the personal recipients general rather than naming a particular husband or woman.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ φιλοσοφίᾳ προσανέχουσαν
Rendered as: you must devote yourself to philosophy
The feminine participle addresses the female recipient. The main English does not need a gendered pronoun, but retains the instruction to attend to philosophy rather than treating philosophy as an external agent.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ Ζεὺς αὐτὸς ὁ τούτων, νομοθέτης
Rendered as: Zeus himself, the lawgiver of these people
These is taken as referring to the jealous people just discussed, since the laws are said to have been laid down for them. The lawgiver of these laws is a material alternative, taking the genitive as referring to the previously mentioned enacted laws. The main wording does not claim this referent is grammatically unique.

SECTION 5.12

And so as not to waste time needlessly on further proofs, I will begin with Zeus himself, the father of gods and humans, and disclose some of his unions; recalling them all is impossible because of their number. Listen, then, to the unions of great Zeus himself that were concealed through changes of form because of foolish men's jealousy. First, wishing to remove for the wise the supposed sin of adultery arising from different unions, when he was about to marry, and knowing that, as at a first bed, he was not becoming an adulterer according to most people, he obtained a sinless marriage through the supposed sin, as I said. For he marries Hera, his own sister, having made himself resemble the plumage of a cuckoo. From her Hebe and Eileithyia were born. For he gives birth to Metis without union with anyone, just as Hera gives birth to Hephaestus.

Translator's notes for section 5.12 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς διαφόρου μίξεως
Rendered as: different unions
The adjective can indicate differing or varied unions. The context presents the writer's attempt to remove the charge of adultery from multiple unions, but the phrase is not expanded to specify particular partners not named here.

2. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ὡς ἐπὶ πρώτῃ εὐνῇ κατὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς μοιχὸς εἰδὼς οὐ γινόμενος
Rendered as: and knowing that, as at a first bed, he was not becoming an adulterer according to most people
The unusual first-bed comparison and the appeal to most people's judgment are both preserved. Bed is a sexual or marital union here. The nominative participles are read as Zeus's knowledge of his own not becoming an adulterer; an alternative takes knowing and not becoming as parallel descriptions. The main text does not resolve the argument into an unstated rule about either partner's previous marital status.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὁμοιωθεὶς κόκκυγος πτερῷ
Rendered as: having made himself resemble the plumage of a cuckoo
The dative literally names a cuckoo's feather or plumage. Plumage preserves that expressed image rather than simply replacing it with the whole bird; a cuckoo's feather is a narrower alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν Μῆτιν γὰρ χωρὶς τῆς πρὸς τινὰ μίξεως ἀποκυΐσκει
Rendered as: For he gives birth to Metis without union with anyone
The active verb assigns the birth to Zeus. The supplied name and unusual parentage are retained rather than harmonized with other versions of the myth.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Διὸς τοῦ πατρὸς θεῶν τε καὶ ἀνθρώπων ἄρξομαι τὰς ἐνίων μηνύειν κοινωνίας
Rendered as: I will begin with Zeus himself, the father of gods and humans, and disclose some of his unions
The genitive some has an unexpressed referent. The main text follows the immediate focus on Zeus and the next sentence about his hidden unions, treating the selection as unions with some partners. A more source-literal alternative is I will begin with Zeus himself and disclose the unions of some of them, with some potentially referring to the divine beings under discussion. Unions with some partners is another explicit alternative; the English selection of his unions is contextual rather than a claim that the genitive uniquely modifies Zeus.

SECTION 5.13

He also has relations with a sister born to him from Uranus and Sea through Cronus's castration, .... Eros and Cypris, whom they also call Didone. He also has relations with Antiope, daughter of Nycteus, having made himself like a satyr; from her Amphion and Zethus were born. He unites with Alcmene, Amphitryon's wife, resembling Amphitryon her husband; from her Heracles was born. He also approaches Aegina, daughter of Asopus, becoming an eagle; from her Aeacus is born. He lies with Amalthea, daughter of Phocus, resembling a bear. He flowed down upon Danae, daughter of Acrisius, as gold; from her Perseus flew forth. For Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, he became a fierce lion, and she bears another, Arcas. He united with Europa, daughter of Phoenix, through a bull; from her Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Sarpedon sprang forth. With Eurymedusa, daughter of Achelous, he became an ant; from her came Myrmidon. With the nymph of Hersaeus he became a vulture; from her came the Palici in Sicily. He united with earth-born Himalia in Rhodes through rain; from her came Spartaeus, Cronius, and Cytus. He took Cassiopeia as a bride, resembling Phoenix her husband; from her Atymnius sprang forth for him. With Nemesis, daughter of Thestius, who was also considered Leda, he became a swan or a goose and fathered Helen; and again, becoming a star, he brought forth Castor and Polydeuces. For Lamia he changed into a hoopoe.

Translator's notes for section 5.13 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἐκτομῆς, . . . . Ἔρως καὶ Κύπρις
The selected edition prints a four-dot gap. The English retains exactly four dots and the following fragment Eros and Cypris, without inventing the lost connection or restoring a missing birth statement. The surviving passage is not represented as an unbroken original.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς Κρόνου ἐκτομῆς
Rendered as: through Cronus's castration
The genitive can describe a castration associated with Cronus as agent or as the person castrated. Castration carried out by Cronus is a material alternative. The possessive English preserves the association without supplying an otherwise unnamed victim in this clause.

3. Translation choice — Greek: Ἔρως καὶ Κύπρις, ἣν καὶ Διδώνην λέγουσιν
Rendered as: Eros and Cypris, whom they also call Didone
The two names after the printed gap remain a fragment, without an invented verb or genealogical connection. The feminine relative refers to Cypris. Didone transliterates the printed name rather than silently correcting it to Dione.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐξ ἧς Περσεὺς ἀνέπτη
Rendered as: from her Perseus flew forth
The verb's flight image is retained. Sprang forth would be a more idiomatic birth expression but would conceal the explicit flying verb.

5. Translation choice — Greek: Καλλιστοῖ τῇ Λυκάονος ἠγριώθη λέων, καὶ ἄλλον τίκτει Ἀρκάδα
Rendered as: For Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, he became a fierce lion, and she bears another, Arcas
The supplied lion form and the word another are retained without harmonizing other accounts. The main text infers Callisto as the subject of bears from the childbearing context, assuming an unmarked change of subject. Continuing Zeus as subject is also viable, since τίκτω can describe male begetting: and he begets another, Arcas. The masculine name identifies the child but does not itself determine which parent is the verb's subject.

6. Translation choice — Greek: Ἑρσαίου νύμφῃ
Rendered as: the nymph of Hersaeus
The genitive relationship is left broad. Νύμφη can also mean bride or young wife, so bride of Hersaeus is a material alternative. The text is not expanded into a specific genealogy or a different familiar myth.

7. Translation choice — Greek: Νεμέσει τῇ Θεστίου, τῇ καὶ Λήδᾳ νομισθείσῃ, κύκνος ἢ χὴν γενόμενος
Rendered as: With Nemesis, daughter of Thestius, who was also considered Leda, he became a swan or a goose
Both the alternative bird forms and the source's identification of Nemesis with Leda are preserved rather than choosing a single familiar version.

SECTION 5.14

Resembling a shepherd, he makes Mnemosyne the mother of the Muses. He marries Semele, daughter of Cadmus, while blazing, and from her brings forth Dionysus. He himself takes his daughter Persephone as a bride, having made himself like a serpent; she was also considered the wife of his brother Pluto. He has relations with many other women even without changing form, their husbands feeling no jealousy as though over a sin, but knowing well that by freely sharing in union with their wives he fathers children, granting them Hermeses, Apollos, Dionysuses, Endymions, and all the others we have mentioned, outstanding in beauty from union with him.

Translator's notes for section 5.14 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: πυρσέων
Rendered as: while blazing
The participle describes Zeus as flaming or blazing. The translation does not supply a specific material body or explain the event using a different familiar account.

2. Translation choice — Greek: Περσεφόνην αὐτὸς ἐκνυμφεύει τὴν θυγατέρα
Rendered as: He himself takes his daughter Persephone as a bride
The verb can concern marrying off or taking in marriage. The reflexive emphasis and the sexual sequence favor Zeus himself as the participant taking his daughter as a bride; the alternative of his giving her in marriage remains lexically possible.

3. Translation choice — Greek: Ἑρμεῖς, Ἀπόλλωνας, Διονύσους, Ἐνδυμίωνας
Rendered as: Hermeses, Apollos, Dionysuses, Endymions
The source prints these names in the plural. The English preserves that conspicuous pattern rather than normalizing them to singular named children; it can characterize children of the named divine types.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἀφθόνως
Rendered as: freely
The adverb may express abundance or the absence of jealousy or grudging. Freely keeps both generosity and lack of restraint available without adding the claim that every husband consented.

SECTION 5.15

So that I do not spend my time on an endless account, you will find ungrudging unions among all the gods along with Zeus—unions that foolish people call adulteries of the gods. The gods do not even avoid unions with males as shameful, but practice this too as something becoming. Thus Zeus himself loves Ganymede; Poseidon, Pelops; Apollo, Cinyras, Zacynthus, Hyacinthus, Phorbas, Hylas, Admetus, Cyparissus, Amyclas, Troilus, Branchus, Atymnius, Parus, Potnieus, and Orpheus; Dionysus, Adonis, Ampelus, Hymenaeus, Hermaphroditus, and Achilles; Asclepius, Hippolytus; Hephaestus, Peleus; Pan, Daphnis; Hermes, Perseus, Chrysus, Thersus, and Odrysus; and Heracles, Abderus, Dryops, Iocastus, Philoctetes, Ilas, Polyphemus, Haemon, Diomus, and Pirithous.

Translator's notes for section 5.15 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: πάντων μετὰ Διὸς θεῶν ἀφθόνους εὑρήσεις κοινωνίας
Rendered as: ungrudging unions
The source separates this adjective and noun with the verb. The adjective can mean abundant or free from jealousy and grudging; the argument against jealousy supports ungrudging, while abundant unions is a material alternative.

2. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτὸς ὁ Ζεὺς Γανυμήδους ἐρᾷ
Rendered as: Zeus himself loves Ganymede
The stated erotic love supplies the understood verb for the ensuing series of gods and their named male beloveds. The English preserves every listed person and does not add ages or acts beyond the source.

3. Translation choice — Greek: Ὕλα
Rendered as: Hylas
This name in Apollo's list begins with upsilon and a rough breathing. It is distinguished in transliteration from the printed Ἴλα in Heracles' list rather than silently treating the two spellings as identical.

4. Translation choice — Greek: Ἴλα
Rendered as: Ilas
The printed iota spelling in Heracles' list is retained as Ilas. Identification with the Hylas in Apollo's list is possible but is not imposed on the source text.

SECTION 5.16

I have therefore set before you some of the loves of all the more prominent gods, dearest, so that you may know that only foolish human beings experience jealousy over this. That is also why they are mortal and pass their lives in sorrow: because, through their own jealousy, they have declared evil the things that seemed good to the gods. From now on, then, you will be blessed if you imitate gods rather than humans. For when people see you preserving what is considered chastity, they praise you because of their own passion, but do not benefit you. But when the gods see you becoming like themselves, they will both praise and benefit you.

Translator's notes for section 5.16 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ μέρους τοὺς ἔρωτας
Rendered as: some of the loves
The phrase signals partial coverage of each set of loves, not an exhaustive account. Loves can also be rendered love affairs in this context.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν νομιζομένην σωφροσύνην
Rendered as: what is considered chastity
The qualifier marks the letter writer's skeptical treatment of conventional sexual restraint. It is not removed to make the writer endorse chastity, nor does the English adopt his skepticism as the translator's own judgment.

3. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τὸ ἴδιον πάθος
Rendered as: because of their own passion
The noun can indicate emotion or a condition of suffering; the surrounding jealousy makes a possessive passion the likely reference. The main text leaves its precise emotional identity implicit rather than inserting a new named motive.

SECTION 5.17

For consider for me how many beloved women they rewarded: some they made into constellations, and they benefited both the children and the helpers of some of them. Thus Zeus made Callisto into a constellation, the one called the Little Bear, which some also call the Dog's Tail. Poseidon placed Dolphin in heaven because of Amphitrite, and counted Orion, born of Euryale daughter of Minos, worthy of the stars because of Euryale his mother. Dionysus did so with Ariadne's crown. Zeus assigned the eagle that helped in the abduction of Ganymede, and Ganymede himself, a place with the honor of Aquarius; and he honored the bull because of Europa. Moreover, as a favor to Leda, he made Castor, Polydeuces, and Helen into stars; Perseus because of Danae; Arcas because of Callisto; the Maiden, also called Justice, because of Themis; and Heracles because of Alcmene. I will not go on any longer. It would take a long time to detail how many others the gods have benefited because of their many beloved women, through their unions with humans. Foolish people forbid these unions as evil acts, not knowing that pleasure is the great enjoyment among humans.

Translator's notes for section 5.17 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: Γανυμήδους.ἁρπαγῇ
The selected print places a full stop between the possessive Ganymede and the noun abduction. The English follows their grammatical relationship continuously. This is disclosed editorial punctuation treatment, not a lacuna, restoration, or allegation of OCR error; the supplied Greek remains unchanged.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν λεγομένην ἄρκτον μικράν, ἣν καὶ κυνὸς οὐρὰν προσαγορεύουσίν τινες
Rendered as: the one called the Little Bear, which some also call the Dog's Tail
Both constellation designations and their attribution to Callisto are retained exactly, without harmonizing the passage with a different astronomical identification.

3. Translation choice — Greek: Διόνυσος τὸν Ἀριάδνης στέφανον
Rendered as: Dionysus did so with Ariadne's crown
The source is an elliptical clause, carrying over the preceding placement among the stars. Did so supplies only that established predicate, not a new celestial act.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν Ὑδροχόου τιμῇ ἔταξεν
Rendered as: assigned ... a place with the honor of Aquarius
Aquarius translates the constellation title Water-Pourer by its conventional English name. The wording attaches the honor to Zeus's assignment; the extent to which the eagle shares the Aquarius description is not resolved by adding a different constellation for it.

5. Translation choice — Greek: παρθένον τὴν καὶ.Δίκην
Rendered as: the Maiden, also called Justice
The feminine designation is translated as the Maiden, with Justice retaining the meaning of Dike. The source's stray full stop is not treated as a lost-word marker or expanded into an extra gap.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἡδονή ἐστιν ἡ μεγάλη ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἀπόλαυσις
Rendered as: pleasure is the great enjoyment among humans
The near repetition of pleasure and enjoyment belongs to the source's maxim. It is retained rather than replaced by a stronger claim that pleasure is the only good or purpose of human life.

7. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ Ὠρίωνα τὸν ἐξ Εὐρυάλης τῆς Μίνω δι’ Εὐρυάλην τὴν μητέρα τῶν ἄστρων κατηξίωσεν
Rendered as: and counted Orion, born of Euryale daughter of Minos, worthy of the stars because of Euryale his mother
The main text attaches stars as the genitive complement of deemed worthy, a verb that can govern what someone is worthy of. The mother refers to Orion's mother, supported by the preceding identification of him as born of Euryale. A material alternative attaches the genitive stars to mother: he deemed Orion worthy because of Euryale, the mother of the stars. That reading leaves the celestial object of worthiness implicit in the context. The main attachment is defensible but not grammatically unique.

SECTION 5.18

What then? Do not even the celebrated wise men prefer pleasure, and did they not have relations with whichever women they wished? First among them is the teacher of Greece, about whom Phoebus himself said, ‘Of all men, Socrates is wisest.’ Does he not propose that women be held in common in the best-governed city, Lacedaemon, and cover the handsome Alcibiades beneath his cloak? The Socratic Antisthenes also writes that one should not reject so-called adultery. And does not his pupil Diogenes openly have relations with Lais, in return for carrying her publicly on his shoulders? Does not Epicurus prefer pleasure? Does not Aristippus, after being perfumed, give his whole self to Aphrodite? Does not Zeno, hinting at treating things as indifferent, say that the divine is present through everything, so that intelligent people may recognize that, with whomever someone has relations, he has relations as with himself, and that forbidding so-called adulteries or unions with a mother, daughter, sister, or children is superfluous? Chrysippus, in his love letters, also mentions the image in Argos, placing Hera's face at Zeus's genitals.

Translator's notes for section 5.18 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: κοινὰς προτίθησι τὰς γυναῖκας
Rendered as: propose that women be held in common
The claim is assigned to Socrates in the source and retained as the letter writer's claim. It is not silently reassigned to another philosopher or rewritten into a historically corrected account.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ μισθῷ τοῦ φέρειν αὐτὴν ἐπ’ ὤμων δημοσίᾳ
Rendered as: in return for carrying her publicly on his shoulders
The infinitive specifies the payment or recompense as carrying Lais. The rendering does not add money, identify a fee amount, or reverse who carries whom.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀδιαφορεῖν αἰνισσόμενος
Rendered as: hinting at treating things as indifferent
Indifference is the philosophical treatment of the acts as morally neither good nor bad, not simply emotional unconcern. The source presents this as an indirect implication, retained as hinting rather than an explicit quotation from Zeno.

4. Translation choice — Greek: μίξεις μητρὸς ἢ θυγατρὸς ἢ ἀδελφῆς ἢ παίδων
Rendered as: unions with a mother, daughter, sister, or children
Children preserves the broad age and relationship range of παῖδες. Boys is possible in this sexual context, but the adjacent family categories also support children; the source does not name particular ages.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τῷ τοῦ Διὸς αἰδοίῳ φέρων τῆς Ἥρας τὸ πρόσωπον
Rendered as: placing Hera's face at Zeus's genitals
The participle concerns the writer's description of the image. The precise position is retained without adding an act not expressly named in the supplied wording.

6. Translation choice — Greek: οὐκ Ἀρίστιππος μυρισθεὶς ὅλον αὐτὸν Ἀφροδίτῃ χαρίζεται;
Rendered as: Does not Aristippus, after being perfumed, give his whole self to Aphrodite?
The main rendering takes whole self with the finite giving verb, foregrounding his complete self-dedication to Aphrodite after perfuming. The alternative Does not Aristippus, perfumed all over, give himself to Aphrodite takes whole self as an accusative of respect with perfumed and foregrounds the extent of perfuming. Both attachments are viable; the chosen one keeps the full accusative expression as what is given rather than leaving the giving object to inference alone.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἵνα γνώριμον τοῖς συνετοῖς γένηται ἵνα ᾧ ἂν τις μιγῇ, ὡς ἑαυτῷ μίγνυται
Rendered as: so that intelligent people may recognize that, with whomever someone has relations, he has relations as with himself
The supplied wording repeats ἵνα. The first clause is purposive; the main text reads the second clause loosely as the content of the intended recognition, which the phrase become known calls for in this context. A material alternative preserves the repeated purpose force, so that it may become known to the intelligent ... so that, with whomever someone has relations, he has relations as with himself. Their exact syntactic relationship remains uncertain. No substitution of an unprinted ὅτι or other Greek emendation has been supplied.

SECTION 5.19

I know that these things appear terrifying and utterly shameful to those uninitiated in the truth, but not to the gods and philosophers of the Greeks, nor to the mysteries of Dionysus and Demeter. But, after all this, so that I do not waste time recounting the lives of every god and philosopher, let two be your greatest models: Zeus among gods, and Socrates among human philosophers. Having understood the rest from what I have reminded you of in writing, take care never to distress a lover of yours. For if you act against gods and lovers, you will be judged impious and undergo the appropriate punishment. But if you offer yourself to every lover, then, as an imitator of the gods, you will obtain their beneficence. For the rest, dearest, remember the mysteries I have disclosed to you and show me your decision in writing. Farewell.

Translator's notes for section 5.19 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς ἀληθείας ἀμυήτοις
Rendered as: those uninitiated in the truth
The initiation image is explicit and continues into the reference to mysteries. Uninformed would be smoother but would erase the writer's claim to privileged initiatory knowledge.

2. Translation choice — Greek: δύο ἔστωσάν σοι μέγιστοι σκοποί
Rendered as: let two be your greatest models
The noun can mean marks, aims, or objects of attention. The two exemplary figures and the subsequent imitation argument favor models; the rendering does not make them legal authorities or assign a new office.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐὰν δὲ παντὶ ἐραστῇ ἑαυτὴν παράσχῃς
Rendered as: if you offer yourself to every lover
The universal every and reflexive yourself are retained as the letter writer's demand. The translation reports his coercive argument without adopting it or adding detail.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ ἐξ ὧν σοι γράψας ὑπέμνησα συνεῖσα ἔπεχε, μήποτε ἐραστήν σου λυπήσῃς
Rendered as: Having understood the rest from what I have reminded you of in writing, take care never to distress a lover of yours
The main text takes the rest as the object of understanding and the written reminders as its basis, explicitly preserving ἐξ as from. An alternative treats the rest adverbially, for the rest, while still requiring an understanding drawn from those reminders. The prior wording made the reminders themselves the direct object and has been corrected.

SECTION 5.20

So I took this document from Apion as though I really intended to send it to the beloved woman. I fabricated a reply as though she had written back to these things, and when Apion came the next day, I gave it to him as her supposed reply. It read as follows:

Translator's notes for section 5.20 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπλασάμην ὡς ἐκείνης πρὸς ταῦτα ἀντιγραψάσης
Rendered as: I fabricated a reply as though she had written back to these things
The narrator explicitly claims authorship of the fictional response. It is not presented as an authentic letter from the woman or as a mere transcription of one.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ βιβλίον τοῦτο
Rendered as: this document
The object is the preceding written letter, not necessarily a codex or full-length book. Document preserves the written artifact without imposing a modern book format.

SECTION 5.21

Copy of a letter to Apion, supposedly from the beloved woman. I am amazed that, after praising me for wisdom, you write to me as though I were foolish. For, wishing to persuade me into your passion, you drew your examples from myths about the gods, not afraid to blaspheme Love—the oldest of all, as you said, and above all gods and humans—so that you might corrupt my soul and outrage my body. For the love involved in desires is not the originator of the gods. If he desires willingly, he himself is his own passion and punishment, and one who suffers willingly would not be a god. But if he unwillingly desires union and, passing through our souls, is carried through our bodies as through instruments into unions with intelligible beings, the one who makes him love and carries him is greater than he is. And again, if that very one who carries him is carried by another longing, another, greater one is found who carries that one, and an endless regress of lovers results, which is impossible. Thus there is neither one who carries nor one who is carried; rather, it is the lover's own desiring passion, increasing through hope and diminishing through despair.

Translator's notes for section 5.21 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἐπὶ πάντων θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων
The former Lagarde phrase is exactly ἐπὶ τῆς πάντων θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων. The selected phrase ἐπὶ πάντων θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων is Dressel's independently image-read main print, not a newly collated manuscript. It is not the separate marginal proposal ἐπιθεὶς, and no participle from that proposal has been adopted or silently added. The main interpretation and its alternative attachment are explained in the lexical note; no unique original wording is claimed.

2. Translation choice — Greek: Ἀντίγραφον ἐπιστολῆς πρὸς Ἀππίωνα ὡς παρὰ τῆς ἐρωμένης
Rendered as: Copy of a letter to Apion, supposedly from the beloved woman
The heading's supposedly marks the letter's presented rather than certified authorship. It is retained without turning the heading into an authentic attribution.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἔρωτα τὸν πάντων πρεσβύτατον (ὡς ἔφης) ἐπὶ πάντων θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων
Rendered as: Love—the oldest of all, as you said, and above all gods and humans
The selected ἐπὶ with the genitive is read as a relation of superiority, above or over all, describing Love alongside oldest of all. English and links the two descriptors without supplying a Greek participle meaning set or place. A material alternative attaches the prepositional phrase to blaspheme: before or in the presence of all gods and humans. The age and universal scope are retained in either reading; the superiority interpretation fits the ensuing denial that desire-based love originates the gods but is not claimed as uniquely established.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἔρως γὰρ θεῶν οὐκ ἔστιν ἀρχηγέτης ὁ ἐν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις
Rendered as: For the love involved in desires is not the originator of the gods
The qualification limits this denial to love associated with desires. Originator preserves the founding or originating force of ἀρχηγέτης; leader is a viable alternative stressing rule rather than origin.

5. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὰς τῶν νοητῶν φέρεται συνουσίας
Rendered as: is carried ... into unions with intelligible beings
The supplied adjective concerns beings or things apprehensible to thought. With intelligible beings takes the genitive as partners of union; unions of intelligible beings is a material alternative leaving their relation broader. The unusual wording is not silently replaced with mortal or bodily partners.

6. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς ἀπέραντον ἐπαναφορὰ τῶν ἐρώντων γίνεται
Rendered as: an endless regress of lovers results
The argument repeatedly seeks a greater bearer behind each bearer. Regress denotes that unending backward sequence rather than a finite recurring cycle.

SECTION 5.22

Those unwilling to master shameful desire tell lies about the gods, so that, by pointing to the gods as having done first the things they themselves do, they may escape blame. For if the so-called gods committed adulteries for the sake of having children and not sexual excess, why did they also have relations with males? ‘But,’ he says, ‘as a favor to their beloved women, they made them into constellations.’ So were there no stars before this, until heaven was adorned with stars by adulterers on the pretext of sexual excess? And how is it that the descendants of those made into constellations are punished in Hades: Atlas weighed down, Tantalus tormented by thirst, Sisyphus pushing a rock, Tityus having his entrails dug into, and Ixion rolling endlessly around a wheel? And how is it that the lovers, being gods, made those whom they defiled into constellations, without granting this favor to themselves?

Translator's notes for section 5.22 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἀσελγείας
Rendered as: sexual excess
The term describes unrestrained or shameless sexual conduct in this argument. The same rendering is maintained in the two occurrences rather than replacing the second by an invented account of how constellations were formed.

2. Translation choice — Greek: οἱ τῶν κατηστερισμένων ἔκγονοι
Rendered as: the descendants of those made into constellations
The relationship and direction of descent are retained as the speaker's claim. They are not changed to ancestors or to the constellated figures themselves to harmonize the list with other myths.

3. Translation choice — Greek: Τιτυὸς τὰ σπλάγχνα διορυττόμενος
Rendered as: Tityus having his entrails dug into
The passive suffering and the body part are retained. No animal, instrument, or additional violent detail absent from this clause is supplied.

SECTION 5.23

They were not gods, then, but veiled representations of tyrants. For a tomb of Cronus is shown in the Caucasian mountains—not in heaven but on earth—the tomb of a savage man who devoured his children. A tomb of the sexually unrestrained Zeus of myth, who likewise swallowed his daughter Metis, is also seen in Crete. There is also Pluto's tomb at the Acherusian lake, Poseidon's on Tenos, the Sun's at Atroi and the Moon's at Carrhae, Hermes' at Hermopolis, Ares' in Thrace, Aphrodite's on Cyprus, Dionysus' at Thebes, and those of others in other places. In any case, the tombs of the very gods mentioned are visible. For they were humans, and wicked ones and sorcerers at that. They could not otherwise have become absolute rulers—I mean the Zeus of myth and Dionysus—unless, through transformation into whatever they themselves wished, they held sway over whomever they wished.

Translator's notes for section 5.23 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τυράννων αἰνίγματα
Rendered as: veiled representations of tyrants
The noun denotes enigmatic or figurative representations. The claim identifies the mythic gods as disguised presentations of human tyrants, not merely difficult riddles that tyrants posed.

2. Translation choice — Greek: Ἡλίου δὲ ἐν Ἄτροις καὶ Σελήνης ἐν Κάρραις
Rendered as: the Sun's at Atroi and the Moon's at Carrhae
The divine names are rendered by their transparent celestial meanings; Helios and Selene are conventional name alternatives. Atroi follows the supplied place-name spelling without silently identifying it with another city.

3. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ μὴ τῇ μεταμορφώσει ὧν ἤθελον ἐπεκράτουν εἰς ὅπερ αὐτοὶ ἤθελον
Rendered as: unless, through transformation into whatever they themselves wished, they held sway over whomever they wished
The main text attaches into whatever they themselves wished to transformation, retaining the explicit changing-form image that matches the preceding accounts of assumed forms. The material alternative unless through transformation they gained control over whomever they wished for whatever purpose they themselves wished takes the final phrase as the intended end of domination. The source does not expressly settle whose form changes, so no otherwise unnamed magical mechanism is supplied.

SECTION 5.24

If we must emulate their lives, let us imitate not only their adulteries but also their tables. For Cronus swallowed his own children, and Zeus likewise his own daughter. And what need is there to say more? Pelops became a dinner for all the gods. So let us too, before our unlawful marriages, hold a dinner like the gods'. Then the dinner would be worthy of the marriages. But you would never bear to do this, just as I would never bear to commit adultery. Besides all this, you threaten me with the wrath of Love as though he were a powerful god. Love is not a god such as he is thought to be, but a desire arising from the constitution of the living being for the succession of life, according to the providence of the one who brought everything into being. This is so that the whole race may never fail, but, on the pretext of pleasure, another may again come into being from the substance of the one who is going to die, sprung from a lawful marriage, so that he may know his own father in order to support him in old age. Those born from adultery would not be able to do this, lacking a natural affection toward those who begot them.

Translator's notes for section 5.24 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ τί δεῖ λέγειν;
Rendered as: And what need is there to say more?
The rhetorical question concerns what needs saying, not what one is able to say. More is supplied from the movement toward the final example, rather than changing the question into an appeal to ability.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ τῆς τοῦ ζῴου κράσεως
Rendered as: from the constitution of the living being
The noun refers to the mixture or constitution of the organism. Animal is another literal rendering of ζῷον, but living being preserves its applicability to humans in this explanation.

3. Translation choice — Greek: προφάσει ἡδονῆς
Rendered as: on the pretext of pleasure
The same pretext language used in the polemic is retained in the positive account of generation. For the sake of pleasure would flatten the distinction between the reproductive purpose and the pleasure that provides its occasion.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὅπως πρὸς τὸ γηροτροφεῖν τὸν αὐτοῦ πατέρα γνώσῃ
Rendered as: so that he may know his own father in order to support him in old age
The child is the inferred subject of knowing, with the father its expressed object and support in old age the purpose. The source's ensuing assertion about children born from adultery is retained as the fictional letter writer's claim, not presented as an established psychological fact.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὅθεν καὶ ἡμεῖς πρὸ τῶν ἀθεμίτων γάμων ὅμοιον δεῖπνον τοῖς θεοῖς ἐπιτελέσωμεν
Rendered as: So let us too, before our unlawful marriages, hold a dinner like the gods'
The dative gods is read comparatively because the preceding instruction explicitly calls for imitation of the gods' tables. A material alternative reads it as beneficiaries: let us too, before our unlawful marriages, hold a similar dinner for the gods. That alternative would propose a banquet offered to them rather than only a banquet modeled on theirs; the main text does not claim to exclude it grammatically.

SECTION 5.25

Since, then, erotic desire arises for the sake of succession and legitimate increase, as I said, parents should take thought for chastity and educate their children in advance, before desire arises, through books that teach self-restraint. They should accustom them beforehand to better teachings, because habit is a second nature. In addition, they should frequently remind them of the punishments imposed by the laws, so that, using fear like a bridle, they do not rush along with improper pleasures. It is also fitting to satisfy through marriage the natural passion of their age before desire reaches its height, having first persuaded them not to fix their eyes on the figure of a courtesan.

Translator's notes for section 5.25 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: γνησίας ἐπαυξήσεως
Rendered as: legitimate increase
The adjective concerns legitimate descent in the contrast with adultery. Genuine growth is a more literal lexical alternative, but would obscure the explicitly marital context.

2. Translation choice — Greek: σωφροσύνης προνοουμένους, τοὺς αὐτῶν παῖδας πρὸ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας διὰ τῶν σωφρονιζόντων βιβλίων
Rendered as: take thought for chastity ... through books that teach self-restraint
The shared word-family concerns restraint, here especially sexual chastity. The English varies the cognate forms for natural readability while disclosing their connection; books that teach chastity is a narrower alternative.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸ τοῦ τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν ἐπακμάσαι γάμῳ τὸ φυσικὸν τῆς ἡλικίας πληροφορεῖν πάθος
Rendered as: satisfy through marriage the natural passion of their age before desire reaches its height
The ancient recommendation and its timing are retained without turning them into present-day guidance or adding an age not stated in the source. The verb denotes filling or satisfying the passion, not merely recognizing it.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς εἶδος ἑταίρας γυναικὸς μὴ ἀτενίζειν
Rendered as: not to fix their eyes on the figure of a courtesan
The supplied ἑταίρας is read as the noun courtesan, not silently changed to ἑτέρας, another. Figure renders visible form or appearance without adding the adjective beautiful.

SECTION 5.26

For our mind, whenever at the outset it takes an impression of the beloved woman’s appearance under the influence of pleasure, is tormented through memory, as though always gazing at her form in a mirror; and when it does not attain its desire, it devises the paths to attainment, but when it does attain it, it grows still more, like a fire amply supplied with fuel, and especially when fear has not already been impressed on the lover’s soul before the passion. For just as water extinguishes fire, so fear too is an extinguisher of irrational desire. Therefore, since I learned from a certain Jew both to think and to do what befits God, I am not made easy prey to adultery by false myths. But may God help you, as you wish and strive to be self-controlled while your soul is inflamed with erotic passion, and may he provide the cure.

Translator's notes for section 5.26 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ εἶδος τῆς ἐρωμένης ἀπομάξηται
Rendered as: takes an impression of the beloved woman’s appearance
ἀπομάσσομαι can describe taking or receiving an impression, fitting the following mirror image; “copies” or “imprints upon itself” are also possible.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπιτυχὼν δὲ μᾶλλον αὔξεται
Rendered as: but when it does attain it, it grows still more
The English pronouns preserve the referential tension: νοῦς is the formal subject, while the context may make the growing element the desire or passion.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ πῦρ τῆς ὕλης εὐποροῦν
Rendered as: a fire amply supplied with fuel
ὕλη can mean material or wood; in the fire image it denotes available fuel.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εὐἄλωτος πρὸς μοιχείαν
Rendered as: easy prey to adultery
εὐάλωτος literally describes what is easily captured, so the rendering preserves the predatory image rather than merely saying “easily persuaded.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: φλεγμαινούσῃ ψυχῇ πρὸς ἔρωτα
Rendered as: while your soul is inflamed with erotic passion
ἔρως here denotes erotic love or desire, while φλεγμαίνω continues the preceding fire imagery.

SECTION 5.27

On hearing the feigned written reply, Appion said, “Do I hate Jews without reason? Now, at any rate, a certain Jew once encountered this woman, brought her over to his religion, and persuaded her to be self-controlled; and from now on it is impossible for her to enter into intimacy with anyone else, because such people, having set God before themselves as the all-seeing observer of actions, steadfastly persist in strict self-control, since they are unable to go unnoticed.”

Translator's notes for section 5.27 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς ὑποκρίτου ἀντιγραφῆς
Rendered as: the feigned written reply
ἀντιγραφή is a written response, while ὑπόκριτος marks it as assumed, acted, or feigned.

2. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὴν θρησκείαν μεταγαγὼν
Rendered as: brought her over to his religion
μετάγω expresses transfer to another position, and θρησκεία may denote religion, worship, or religious observance. The possessive is contextually supplied by the preceding Jewish agent, though it is not explicit in Greek.

3. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς κοινωνίαν ἑτέρου τινὸς συνελθεῖν
Rendered as: to enter into intimacy with anyone else
κοινωνία can mean association or participation, but the surrounding discussion of adultery supports sexual intimacy or union here.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν θεὸν ὡς παντεπόπτην τῶν πράξεων προθέμενοι
Rendered as: having set God before themselves as the all-seeing observer of actions
παντεπόπτης presents God as seeing everything; προτίθημι depicts placing that awareness before oneself.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς λαθεῖν μὴ δυνάμενοι
Rendered as: since they are unable to go unnoticed
The infinitive λαθεῖν means escaping notice; the one from whom they cannot remain hidden is implicit from the preceding reference to God.

SECTION 5.28

Having heard this, I said to Appion, “Now I will confess the truth to you. I did not fall in love with a woman, nor with any other person, because my soul was entirely expended upon other longings and upon the discovery of true doctrines. And up to the present, after scrutinizing many opinions of philosophers, I inclined toward none of them except only that of the Jews, when a certain merchant of theirs, who sold linen cloths and was staying here in Rome, through a fortunate encounter set before me in simpler terms the belief in one sovereign.”

Translator's notes for section 5.28 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδὲ ἄλλου τινός
Rendered as: nor with any other person
The genitive form can be masculine, “anyone else,” or neuter, “anything else.” The personal sense fits the statement about falling in love, but the broader alternative remains grammatically possible.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πάνυ μου τῆς ψυχῆς δεδαπανημένης
Rendered as: because my soul was entirely expended
δαπανάω conveys spending or consuming resources; here the soul is portrayed as having its energies consumed or devoted elsewhere.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς οὐδένα αὐτῶν ἔνευσα ἢ πρὸς τὸ Ἰουδαίων μόνον
Rendered as: I inclined toward none of them except only that of the Jews
νεύω literally means nodding or inclining toward something and here denotes assent. The neuter τὸ Ἰουδαίων leaves the Jewish opinion, position, or doctrine implicit.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὀθόνας πιπράσκοντος
Rendered as: who sold linen cloths
ὀθόνη denotes a linen cloth, sheet, or similar piece of fabric; “linen cloths” retains the commercial object without narrowing its use.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ μοναρχικὸν φρόνημα
Rendered as: the belief in one sovereign
Literally a “monarchic conviction,” the phrase in this theological context concerns sole sovereignty, commonly understood as the sole rule of God; “monotheism” would flatten its wording.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἁπλούστερόν μοι ... παραθεμένου
Rendered as: set before me in simpler terms
παρατίθημι means placing or presenting something before another, while the comparative ἁπλούστερον can mean “more simply” or, idiomatically, “quite simply.”

SECTION 5.29

But when Appion heard the truth from me—he who irrationally hates what is Jewish and neither knows nor wishes to know what their belief actually is—he grew angry without examination and, in silence, at once departed from Rome itself. And now, having met him for the first time since then, I reasonably suspect that his anger dates from that time. Nevertheless, in your presence I will ask him what he might have to say about the so-called gods, whose lives—mythologized as subject to every passion—are deliberately sung in public to encourage imitation of such things, and whose tombs are also pointed out in their respective places, in addition to their human passions, as I said.”

Translator's notes for section 5.29 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ Ἰουδαίων
Rendered as: what is Jewish
The substantivized neuter expression can denote the Jewish position, doctrine, cause, or way; the broad rendering avoids replacing it with the Jewish people themselves.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τί ποτε ἐστὶν αὐτῶν τὸ πιστὸν
Rendered as: what their belief actually is
τὸ πιστόν may denote their belief, faith, or what they hold as trustworthy; the interrogative τί ποτε adds the force of “what exactly” or “actually.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀκρίτως ὀργισθεὶς τῇ σιωπῇ
Rendered as: he grew angry without examination and, in silence
ἀκρίτως indicates acting without judgment or examination. The dative τῇ σιωπῇ is read as manner, “silently,” though attachment as anger “at the silence” is grammatically conceivable but contextually less natural.

4. Translation choice — Greek: πλὴν ἐφ᾽ ὑμῶν αὐτοῦ πεύσομαι
Rendered as: Nevertheless, in your presence I will ask him
ἐφ᾽ ὑμῶν means “before you” or “in your presence,” while αὐτοῦ is taken as the genitive personal complement of πεύσομαι, supplying “him.” This is syntactically straightforward and identifies Appion as the person questioned. Alternatively, αὐτοῦ may be adverbial, “there” or “on the spot,” with “him” inferred from context.

5. Translation choice — Greek: παντοπαθεῖς εἶναι μυθολογούμενοι
Rendered as: mythologized as subject to every passion
παντοπαθής can describe undergoing every kind of passion, experience, or suffering; the repeated πάθεσιν and the moral context favor “every passion.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τὴν τοῦ ὁμοίου μίμησιν ἐπίτηδες ᾄδονται δημοσία
Rendered as: are deliberately sung in public to encourage imitation of such things
ἐπίτηδες makes the singing purposeful, and πρὸς with μίμησις expresses its intended movement toward imitation of like conduct.

7. Translation choice — Greek: οἱ κατὰ τόπον δείκνυνται τάφοι
Rendered as: their tombs are also pointed out in their respective places
κατὰ τόπον can mean place by place, locally, or in the respective locations; the rendering preserves the claim that identifiable tombs are shown.

SECTION 5.30

The others, having heard these things from me beforehand and longing to learn what came next, joined me, intending to visit Appion. And indeed we found him already bathed at a table that had been made ready; therefore . we went into only a few details concerning the discussion about gods. But he, I think, perceived our purpose and promised that on the following day he would have something to say about gods; and he indicated the same place to us in advance, intending to converse there. With that promise, after expressing our thanks to him, we each departed for home.

Translator's notes for section 5.30 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: διόπερ . ὀλίγα
The selected image-checked edition prints one isolated dot after διόπερ as a gap marker. The content represented by the gap is unavailable; the translation retains exactly one dot and supplies no restoration. This faithful representation of the selected edition’s printed lacuna does not itself block publication.

2. Translation choice — Greek: προακούσαντες ἐμοῦ
Rendered as: having heard these things from me beforehand
The prefix in προακούω indicates hearing in advance, and the genitive identifies the narrator as the source.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ἐπισκεψόμενοι Ἀππίωνα
Rendered as: intending to visit Appion
ὡς with the future participle expresses the companions’ purpose or intention.

4. Translation choice — Greek: λελουμένον αὐτὸν ἤδη κατελαμβάνομεν ἐφ᾽ ἑτοίμῳ τραπέζῃ
Rendered as: we found him already bathed at a table that had been made ready
λελουμένον depicts Appion as having bathed, while ἐφ᾽ ἑτοίμῳ τραπέζῃ places him at a prepared or ready table.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὀλίγα ἠκριβολογησάμεθα
Rendered as: we went into only a few details
ἀκριβολογέομαι denotes speaking or discussing with precision; ὀλίγα limits the discussion to a few matters or a small amount.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν αὐτὸν προεδήλωσεν ἡμῖν τόπον
Rendered as: he indicated the same place to us in advance
προδηλόω marks advance indication or notification, and τὸν αὐτὸν τόπον most directly means “the same place.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: σὺν τῇ ὑποσχέσει, χάριν ὁμολογήσαντες αὐτῷ
Rendered as: With that promise, after expressing our thanks to him
χάριν ὁμολογεῖν means acknowledging or expressing gratitude; σύν retains the promise as the circumstance accompanying their departure.

HOMILY 6

SECTION 6.1

On the third day I went with my closest companions to the appointed place in Tyre. There I found Apion sitting between Anubion and Athenodorus, waiting for us with many other educated men. Nevertheless, I was not at all intimidated. I greeted him and sat down opposite Apion, who soon began to speak: ‘I want to begin first and move quickly from here to the question at issue. Before you joined us, my child Clement, this Anubion and Athenodorus, who heard you speaking yesterday along with the others, told me how, when I associated with you in Rome on the assumption that you were in love, I told many lies about the gods. I said they were lovers of boys, sexually unrestrained, having relations with mothers, sisters, and daughters, and involved in countless adulteries. But you should have known, my child, that I did not write these things because I held such views about the gods. Rather, out of affection for you, I held back from telling the truth. If you now wish, hear that truth from me.’

Translator's notes for section 6.1 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: Ἀννουβίωνός τε καὶ Ἀθηνοδώρου
The first occurrence spells Anubion's name with doubled nu, while the same passage later has Ἀνουβίων. The English uses the conventional name Anubion for both occurrences; no second person is inferred.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ἐρῶντι
Rendered as: on the assumption that you were in love
The dative participle refers to Clement, with whom Apion associated. The phrase presents the supposition under which Apion acted; it does not name the object of Clement's supposed love. ‘As with someone in love’ is a closer but less natural alternative.

3. Translation choice — Greek: παιδεράστας, ἀσελγεῖς
Rendered as: lovers of boys, sexually unrestrained
The first term names the gods' alleged sexual interest in boys, and the second their lack of sexual restraint in this context. The rendering preserves the historical accusation without adding details.

4. Translation choice — Greek: στοργῇ τῇ πρὸς σὲ τὰ ἀληθῆ λέγειν ἀπεκρυπτόμην
Rendered as: out of affection for you, I held back from telling the truth
The middle verb and infinitive express Apion's concealment or withholding of his truthful account. ‘I concealed the truth from you out of affection’ is also possible, but loses the explicit reference to speaking.

SECTION 6.2

‘The wisest men of old learned the whole truth themselves through hard work, but kept those who were unworthy and had no desire for divine teachings from receiving this knowledge. For twelve children were not born to Uranus and his mother Earth, as the myth lists them: the males Oceanus, Coeus, Crius, Hyperion, Iapetus, and Cronus; and the females Theia, Themis, Mnemosyne, Demeter, Tethys, and Rhea. Nor did Cronus cut off the genitals of his father Uranus with an adamantine sickle, as you say, and throw them into the depths. Nor did Aphrodite come into being from drops of blood that flowed from Uranus's severed part. Nor, again, did Cronus have relations with Rhea and, after fathering Pluto first, swallow him, fearing because of some pronouncement of Prometheus that a child born to him might prove nobler than he was and strip him of his kingship. He did not father Poseidon second and swallow him in the same way. After these, when Zeus was born, his mother Rhea did not hide him and give Cronus a stone instead when he demanded him to swallow. That stone did not, when swallowed, squeeze those swallowed earlier and force them out, so that Pluto, the first swallowed, came out first, Poseidon after him, and Zeus third. Nor, as they say, did Zeus, saved by his mother's foresight, ascend into heaven and depose his father from his kingship. He did not punish his father's brothers. He did not come down out of desire for mortal women. He did not have shameful relations with sisters or daughters, with brothers' wives, or with boys. Nor did he beget Metis and swallow her ...., so that he might cause Athena from Metis to grow out of his brain and give birth from his thigh to Dionysus, whom they say the Titans tore apart. He does not hold a feast at the wedding of Thetis and Peleus. He did not exclude Strife from the wedding. This Strife, dishonored, did not devise conflict and faction among the guests. She did not take a golden apple from the gardens of the Hesperides and inscribe on it, “A gift for the beautiful one.” Then they tell the myth that Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite find the apple and, quarreling over it, come to Zeus. He did not judge between them himself, but sent them through Hermes to the shepherd Paris to have their beauty judged. Yet the goddesses were not judged, nor did Paris award the apple to Aphrodite. Aphrodite, thus honored, did not honor him in return with marriage to Helen. For the goddess's honor would not have become the occasion for a war involving every people, and that to the destruction of the man who had received the honor and was closely related to Aphrodite's family. But, as I said, my child, such stories have an appropriate philosophical explanation, capable of being expressed through allegory, so that you will marvel when you hear it.’ I said, ‘Please do not torment me by delaying.’ He replied, ‘Have no fear. I will not put it off, but will begin speaking now.’

Translator's notes for section 6.2 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: κατέπιεν ...., ἵνα
The selected edition prints a gap of four dots after ‘swallowed.’ The English retains exactly four dots at the corresponding point. Its unavailable content has not been restored, and the sentence must not be represented as an unbroken original.

2. Greek: ὡς προελθεῖν πρῶτον μὲν τὸν πρῶτον καταποθέντα Πλούτωνα, ἐπ’ αὐτῷ δὲ Ποσειδῶνα καὶ τρίτον τὸν Δία
This enumeration includes Zeus third among those coming out, although the preceding account has Rhea hide him. The translation retains the supplied names and order instead of reconciling the narrative with itself or with other versions of the myth.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ ἐξ ἀδάμαντος ἅρπῃ
Rendered as: with an adamantine sickle
Adamant names the exceptionally hard material of the mythic weapon. ‘A sickle of adamant’ is equally close; specifying steel or diamond would identify a material more precisely than the Greek warrants.

4. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τινὰ Προμηθέως θεσμὸν
Rendered as: because of some pronouncement of Prometheus
The noun can denote an ordinance or decree, here a pronouncement that supplies the reason for Cronus's fear. ‘Decree’ preserves its authoritative force more explicitly; ‘prophecy’ fits the story but narrows the noun beyond what is stated.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὃς οὐ καταποθεὶς τοὺς προκαταποθέντας θλίψας ἐξῶσεν
Rendered as: That stone did not, when swallowed, squeeze those swallowed earlier and force them out
The negative is taken with the finite verb, within Apion's repeated denials of mythic events, rather than as ‘not swallowed’ attached only to the participle. The swallowed participle and the stone as subject are both retained.

6. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδὲ Μῆτιν γεννήσας κατέπιεν
Rendered as: Nor did he beget Metis and swallow her
The supplied active participle says ‘having begotten,’ with Metis as its expressed object. The translation preserves that wording rather than substituting a familiar myth about impregnation or swallowing an already pregnant Metis.

7. Translation choice — Greek: δῶρον τῇ καλῇ
Rendered as: A gift for the beautiful one
The adjective is positive, not superlative. ‘For the fairest’ would introduce a degree not expressed in this wording.

8. Translation choice — Greek: λόγον τὰ τοιαῦτα οἰκεῖον καὶ φιλόσοφον, ἀλληγορίᾳ φρασθῆναι δυνάμενον
Rendered as: such stories have an appropriate philosophical explanation, capable of being expressed through allegory
The account is both fitting to its subject and philosophical, and allegory is the means of expressing it. ‘An explanation proper to them and philosophical in character’ is more explicit but heavier English.

SECTION 6.3

‘There was once a time when nothing existed except chaos and an undifferentiated mixture of elements still heaped together without order. Nature itself acknowledges this, and great men have understood that this was so. I will give you Homer himself as a witness, the greatest in wisdom among great men. Speaking of the original confusion, he says, “But may you all become water and earth,” since everything originated from that state and, after the dissolution of its moist and earthy substance, is restored again to its first nature, which is chaos. Hesiod says in his Theogony, “Indeed, first of all chaos came into being.” Clearly, “came into being” signifies having originated, as things that come into being do, not always existing, as things without origin do. Orpheus, too, compares chaos to an egg, in which the first elements were mixed together. What Hesiod proposes as chaos, Orpheus calls an egg that came into being, brought forth from boundless matter. It came about in this way:’

Translator's notes for section 6.3 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: χάος καὶ στοιχείων ἀτάκτων ἔτι συντεφορημένων μίξις ἀδιάκριτος
