Rendered as: chaos and an undifferentiated mixture of elements still heaped together without order
The rendering retains both the named chaos and the description of the mixture, including the elements' disorder and lack of differentiation. ‘An unseparated mixture’ is another possible rendering of the last adjective.

2. Translation choice — Greek: γεγενῆσθαι ὡς γενητὰ σημαίνει, οὐ τὸ ἀεὶ εἶναι ὡς ἀγένητα
Rendered as: signifies having originated, as things that come into being do, not always existing, as things without origin do
The distinction concerns coming into existence versus existing without an origin. ‘Created’ and ‘uncreated’ could introduce a maker not specified in these terms; ‘begotten’ could imply biological generation too narrowly.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐξ ἀπείρου τῆς ὕλης προβεβλημένον
Rendered as: brought forth from boundless matter
The verb describes the egg's being projected or brought forth, while the adjective qualifies matter as unlimited. The translation does not identify a personal agent where none is supplied.

SECTION 6.4

‘The fourfold matter was alive, and an entire boundless deep was forever flowing and moving without differentiation, bringing up countless incomplete mixtures, now one and now another, and so dissolving them in its disorder. It gaped open, unable to be bound together so as to generate a living being. At some point, as the boundless sea itself was driven around by its own nature, it happened to flow in an orderly way, by a natural movement, from the same point back to that same point, like a whirlpool, and to mix the substances. Thus, from what was audible, the richest part of everything, which was particularly suited to generating a living being, flowed through the middle of the whole as through a funnel. Driven by the whirlpool that carried everything, it moved into the depths and drew in the surrounding breath; and, gathered together as into something supremely fertile, it formed a structure capable of differentiation. For just as a bubble tends to form in liquid, so a spherical cavity took shape, enclosed on every side. Then, having been gestated within itself and being lifted by the sulfurous breath that had received it, this enormous offspring emerged into the light: a living work brought forth, as it were, from the entire boundless deep, resembling the roundness of eggs and the swiftness of flight.’

Translator's notes for section 6.4 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἐξ ἀκουστοῦ
The supplied wording literally supports ‘from what was audible’ or ‘from what was heard,’ but its role in this physical account is obscure. The English retains the audible sense openly rather than conjecturally replacing the printed Greek. This is not a claim that the cosmological referent has been identified; no alternative source wording has been supplied.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς τετραγενοῦς ὕλης ἐμψύχου οὔσης
Rendered as: The fourfold matter was alive
The matter comprises four kinds and is described as possessing life or soul. ‘The matter of four kinds was ensouled’ is more technical; ‘alive’ keeps the assertion accessible without replacing it with a modern physical explanation.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐξ ἀκουστοῦ τῶν πάντων τὸ νοστιμώτατον
Rendered as: from what was audible, the richest part of everything
The supplied ἀκουστοῦ is rendered according to its ordinary sense ‘audible’ or ‘heard’; the resulting unusual phrase is not silently changed to ‘from it’ or a different cosmological expression. The superlative νοστιμώτατον is read as the choicest or richest portion, clarified by the following statement of its suitability for generating life. See the separate source issue.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς εἰς γονιμώτατον συλληφθὲν ποιεῖν κριτικὴν σύστασιν
Rendered as: gathered together as into something supremely fertile, it formed a structure capable of differentiation
The phrase ὡς εἰς is retained as an analogical qualification, “as into,” rather than reduced to an unqualified description of an actual condition. The neuter superlative γονιμώτατον is rendered substantivally as “something supremely fertile”; the Greek does not expressly name a state, mass, or receptacle. The participle can evoke conception as well as gathering. For κριτικὴν σύστασιν, “a discerning constitution” is a material alternative if the adjective points to a living being's discriminating faculty rather than physical differentiation. “A structure capable of differentiation” preserves a capacity to distinguish without importing a particular physiological mechanism.

5. Translation choice — Greek: σφαιροειδὲς πανταχόθεν συνελήφθη κύτος
Rendered as: a spherical cavity took shape, enclosed on every side
Κύτος can denote a hollow container, cavity, or enclosing body; the bubble analogy favors a cavity enclosed on all sides. The translation does not identify a shell material.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ τοῦ παρειληφότος θειώδους πνεύματος ἀναφερόμενον
Rendered as: being lifted by the sulfurous breath that had received it
The active perfect participle παρειληφότος agrees with πνεύματος: the breath is the agent that has received something. The developing body is supplied as its contextually inferred object, not made the receiving agent. Θειώδης can mean sulfurous; divine-like is a material lexical alternative. The physical account of the rising enclosed breath supports sulfurous here. Πνεῦμα is rendered breath in this physical account, with wind or spirit as alternatives. The following section's explicit θεῖον πνεῦμα is separately rendered divine spirit rather than automatically homogenized with this adjective.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ περιφερείᾳ τῶν ὠῶν προσεοικὸς καὶ τῷ τάχει τῆς πτήσεως
Rendered as: resembling the roundness of eggs and the swiftness of flight
The coordinated datives supply two comparisons: the roundness of eggs and the swiftness of flight. The genitive τῶν ὠῶν modifies roundness, not flight. This rendering does not attribute flight to eggs or invent a particular flying creature or mechanism.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἔπειτα αὐτὸ ἐν ἑαυτῷ κυηθέν
Rendered as: Then, having been gestated within itself
The passive participle κυηθέν explicitly continues the conception and birth imagery. Its unusual reflexive phrase is retained, rather than generalized to development or resolved into a new biological mechanism.

SECTION 6.5

‘Understand Cronus, then, as time, and Rhea as the flowing of moist substance, because all matter, carried along in time, gave birth, like an egg, to the spherical heaven that contains everything. At first this was full of generative marrow, capable of producing elements and colors of every kind. Yet from one substance and a single color it presented an appearance of every kind. For just as in the offspring of a peacock the egg appears to have one color, but potentially contains within itself the countless colors of the creature that will reach full development, so the living egg brought forth from boundless matter, moved by the underlying, ever-flowing matter, reveals changes of every kind. For within its circumference a male-and-female living being takes shape through the providence of the divine spirit present in it. Orpheus calls him Phanes, because, when he appeared, the whole universe shone from him through the brilliance of fire, the most radiant of the elements, which reached full development in the moisture. This is not unbelievable, since nature has also granted us a sight of moist light in glowworms as an example.’

Translator's notes for section 6.5 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: Κρόνον οὖν τὸν χρόνον μοι νόει, τὴν δὲ Ῥέαν τὸ ῥέον τῆς ὑγρᾶς οὐσίας
Rendered as: Understand Cronus, then, as time, and Rhea as the flowing of moist substance
The allegory associates Cronus with χρόνος, time, and Rhea with ῥέον, flowing. The English translates the explanations while retaining the names; their Greek sound associations cannot be fully reproduced in English.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ γονίμου μυελοῦ
Rendered as: generative marrow
The bodily term marrow and its life-producing quality are both preserved. ‘Fertile core’ would be smoother but would obscure the explicit bodily image.

3. Translation choice — Greek: παντοδαπὴν ἐκ μιᾶς οὐσίας τε καὶ χρώματος ἑνὸς ἔφερε τὴν φαντασίαν
Rendered as: from one substance and a single color it presented an appearance of every kind
The rendering keeps the contrast between the single substance and color and the manifold appearance. ‘A variegated appearance’ is more idiomatic but could make the statement concern visible colors alone, while the next comparison expressly distinguishes visible color from potential colors.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ζῷόν τι ἀρρενόθηλυ εἰδοποιεῖται
Rendered as: a male-and-female living being takes shape
The compound describes one living being as both male and female. It does not describe two separate creatures or introduce a modern identity category.

5. Translation choice — Greek: Φάνητα Ὀρφεὺς καλεῖ, ὅτι αὐτοῦ φανέντος τὸ πᾶν ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἔλαμψεν
Rendered as: Orpheus calls him Phanes, because, when he appeared, the whole universe shone from him
The conventional name Phanes is retained, with the source's explanatory connection to appearing and shining. The explanation is the speaker's ancient account, not a claim of established etymology.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ φέγγει τοῦ διαπρεπεστάτου τῶν στοιχείων πυρὸς ἐν τῷ ὑγρῷ τελεσφορουμένου
Rendered as: through the brilliance of fire, the most radiant of the elements, which reached full development in the moisture
The genitive participle agrees with fire, so its reaching full development in moisture is retained. The superlative explicitly supports ‘most radiant’; the translation does not attribute the development only to light.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ λαμπυρίδων δείγματος ἕνεκα
Rendered as: in glowworms as an example
The noun denotes luminous insects. ‘Fireflies’ is a viable familiar alternative; the Greek does not specify a modern species.

SECTION 6.6

Thus the egg that first formed, warmed from below by the living creature within, bursts. Then, having taken form, it comes forth, of a kind that Orpheus also describes: “when the hard, very capacious egg was split.” And thus, once he himself—the one who has come forth—has appeared with great power, the mass receives its cohesion and obtains its ordered arrangement. He himself sits as though at the summit of heaven, while, amid secret things, shining all around the boundless age. As for the fertile matter left inside the mass: it lay underneath over a long period, until the heat, naturally seething beneath, separated the substances of all things. For its lowest part first sank downward under its weight like sediment. Because of its heaviness, and because the quantity of the underlying substance was weighty and large, they named it Pluto, declaring him king of Hades and of the dead.

Translator's notes for section 6.6 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ὑποκειμένη ἕως φυσικῶς
This candidate follows the human-authorized, independently image-checked public-domain Dressel 1853 reading, printed page 160, PDF page 173, associated with O/Ottobonianus 443. The former selected Lagarde reading is preserved here exactly: ὑποκειμένης ἕως φυσικῆς. Dressel’s apparatus also records that genitive reading under C; the nominative/adverb variant is not a recovery of an undisputed original. The source curation changes only the two documented forms, not ἕως. The marked syntax and English verbal resumption are explained in the lexical note; a missing Greek predicate is not restored. Fresh independent source-and-translation review remains mandatory.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὑποθερμανθὲν ὑπὸ τοῦ ἔσωθεν ζῴου
Rendered as: warmed from below by the living creature within
The compound heating verb retains the under/beneath nuance. The living creature is explicitly the agent of the warming; no separate fire source is added.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἔπειτα δὲ μορφωθὲν προέρχεται ὁποῖόν τι καὶ Ὀρφεὺς λέγει
Rendered as: Then, having taken form, it comes forth, of a kind that Orpheus also describes
The subject of the neuter participle and verb is not newly named. It is contextually the inner creature that appears, but the previous egg is also neuter; the main text leaves “it” while the subsequent masculine description represents the emerging figure. ὁποῖόν τι characterizes its kind or form, rather than introducing a newly specified shape.

4. Translation choice — Greek: κραναίου σχισθέντος πολυχανδέος ὠοῦ
Rendered as: when the hard, very capacious egg was split
The printed κραναίου is unusual; “hard” is a contextual interpretation associated with the Greek κραναός family’s hard/rugged sense, not a claim that this precise form has been uniquely established as that lemma. “Rugged” is a less interpretive alternative, but less natural for an egg. The Greek is not normalized to κραναοῦ or replaced with an editor’s conjectural epithet. πολυχανδέος denotes capacity to contain much, expressed as “very capacious”; no literal stone material or lost shell noun is supplied.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ μὲν κύτος τὴν ἁρμονίαν λαμβάνει καὶ τὴν διακόσμησιν ἴσχει
Rendered as: the mass receives its cohesion and obtains its ordered arrangement
κύτος can denote a hollow body, enclosing bulk, or cavity; “mass” refers to the enclosing whole in this cosmogony, not a newly named universe. ἁρμονία is its joining/cohesion; “harmony” is a more literal alternative, and διακόσμησις is its arrangement or ordering.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν ἀπορρήτοις τὸν ἄπειρον περιλάμπων αἰῶνα
Rendered as: amid secret things, shining all around the boundless age
The masculine participle retains the emerging figure as its subject. ἀπορρήτοις can denote secret or unspeakable things, with “in mysteries” a contextual alternative. αἰών can be an age, duration, or cosmic world-order; the main text keeps “age” and the surrounding illumination without uniquely selecting an eternal duration or a named realm.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ δὲ τοῦ κύτους ἔνδοθεν γόνιμος ὑπολειφθεῖσα ὕλη, ὡς ἐν πολλῷ τῷ χρόνῳ ὑποκειμένη ἕως φυσικῶς ὑποζέουσα ἡ θερμότης, τὰς πάντων διέκρινεν οὐσίας.
Rendered as: As for the fertile matter left inside the mass: it lay underneath over a long period, until the heat, naturally seething beneath, separated the substances of all things
The selected nominative ὑποκειμένη can agree with the initial ὕλη. I read that initial noun phrase and the ὡς-plus-participle circumstance as a suspended topic: the matter as lying underneath over a long period. The sentence then shifts to heat as the subject of διέκρινεν inside a temporal ἕως-clause. φυσικῶς qualifies ὑποζέουσα, the nominative participle agreeing with ἡ θερμότης. English resumes the topic with “it lay,” converting the surviving participial description into a finite predicate, rather than claiming that a lost Greek verb has been found. ὡς contributes the circumstance in which the matter is presented; the English topic-and-resumption structure does not claim that ὡς itself literally means “as for.” The Greek remains marked anacoluthon, with no independent finite predicate for the initial matter-topic. This is a proposed contextual analysis, not a regular-syntax proof or uniquely established reading. “Until” preserves ἕως without deletion or emendation. If the independent reviewer finds this verbal resumption unsupported, the candidate remains unresolved.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ὃ διὰ τὴν ὁλκότητα καὶ διὰ τὸ ἐμβριθὲς καὶ πολὺ τῆς ὑποκειμένης οὐσίας πλῆθος Πλούτωνα προσηγόρευσαν
Rendered as: Because of its heaviness, and because the quantity of the underlying substance was weighty and large, they named it Pluto
Both expressions of weight are represented: ὁλκότης and ἐμβριθές. πολὺ preserves the great quantity. “Pluto” is the conventional name; the lower substance’s naming as a personal ruler is the author’s own shift and is not harmonized away.

9. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ οὕτω μεγάλῃ δυνάμει αὐτοῦ τοῦ προεληλυθότος φανέντος, τὸ μὲν κύτος τὴν ἁρμονίαν λαμβάνει καὶ τὴν διακόσμησιν ἴσχει
Rendered as: And thus, once he himself—the one who has come forth—has appeared with great power, the mass receives its cohesion and obtains its ordered arrangement
The genitive absolute φανέντος presents the emerging figure’s manifestation as the circumstance accompanying or preceding the mass’s cohesion. μεγάλῃ δυνάμει characterizes that appearance, “with great power,” rather than being directly attached as the means by which the mass receives cohesion. The perfect προεληλυθότος is represented as “who has come forth”; the aorist φανέντος is represented as completed manifestation, “has appeared,” before the historical-present receives/obtains clauses. αὐτοῦ supplies the personal emphasis, “he himself.” A causal understanding of the absolute is also possible, approximately “because he himself, the one who has come forth, has appeared with great power”; it would make the manifestation as a whole causal, not the power alone. The main temporal-circumstantial analysis does not uniquely exclude that alternative.

SECTION 6.7

This first and abundant, foul and rough substance, then, they say was swallowed by Cronus—that is, Time—in a natural sense, because of its downward descent. After the first sediment, they named the water that had flowed together and floated upon the first deposit Poseidon. The remaining third portion, the purest and uppermost, since it was transparent fire, they named Zeus because of the boiling nature within it. For since fire rises upward, it was not swallowed in the regions below by Time, Cronus; rather, as I said, the fiery substance, being life-giving and upward-moving, flew up into the air itself, which is also the most intelligent because of its purity. By his own heat, therefore, Zeus—that is, the boiling substance—draws up the most rarefied and divine breath left within the underlying moisture, which they called Metis.

Translator's notes for section 6.7 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ Κρόνου τοῦ χρόνου
Rendered as: by Cronus—that is, Time
The rendering preserves the author’s identification and wordplay between Κρόνος and χρόνος rather than treating τοῦ χρόνου as an unrelated genitive.

2. Translation choice — Greek: φυσικῶς
Rendered as: in a natural sense
The adverb signals the physical or natural-philosophical interpretation of the myth; “by natural processes” is also possible.

3. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τὴν κάτω ὑπονόστησιν αὐτῆς
Rendered as: because of its downward descent
ὑπονόστησις denotes movement or return downward; “downward retreat” would preserve its etymological coloring but is less natural here.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν πρώτην ὑποστάθμην
Rendered as: the first sediment
ὑποστάθμη denotes matter settled at the bottom; the related ὑποστάσει later in the sentence is rendered “deposit.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: Ζῆνα ὠνόμασαν διὰ τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ ζέουσαν φύσιν
Rendered as: they named Zeus because of the boiling nature within it
The conventional name “Zeus” is used while the explicit sound association between Ζῆνα and ζέουσαν is retained through “boiling.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ ἰσχνότατον καὶ θεῖον ἀνιμᾶται πνεῦμα
Rendered as: draws up the most rarefied and divine breath
In this physical account, ἀνιμᾶται describes drawing up or vaporizing, and ἰσχνότατον means exceedingly fine or tenuous rather than literally lean.

SECTION 6.8

When that breath reaches the crown of the ether itself and is drunk up by it, like liquid mixed with heat, it produces an ever-moving pulsation and gives birth to understanding, which they also call Pallas because it pulses: a most skillful intelligence, by whose use the etherial craftsman fashioned the entire cosmos. From Zeus himself, who permeates everything—the hottest ether—the air reaches as far as the regions here; this they call Hera. And since it has descended beneath the purest substance of the ether and is feminine in purity by comparison with what is superior, it was reasonably regarded as Zeus’s sister, since it had been generated from the same substance, but as his wife because it lies beneath him as a woman does.

Translator's notes for section 6.8 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ὁ ἀὴρ μέχρι τῶν ἐνταῦθα διικνεῖται τόπων, ἣν ἐπονομάζουσιν Ἥραν
The masculine antecedent ὁ ἀήρ is followed by the feminine relative ἣν. This can defensibly be understood as an anticipatory shift to the personified feminine name Hera rather than as omitted content, so the translation uses the gender-neutral demonstrative “this” without emendation.

2. Translation choice — Greek: κατὰ κορυφῆς δὲ αὐτοῦ ἐλθὸν τοῦ αἰθέρος
Rendered as: When that breath reaches the crown of the ether itself
The implicit subject is the divine πνεῦμα from 6.7. κορυφή can denote the top, crown, or head, preserving both cosmological height and the mythic head imagery.

3. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ συμπωθὲν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: and is drunk up by it
συμπωθέν carries an ingestion or drinking image, here depicting the breath’s uptake by the ether; rendering it as physical compression would lose that image.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν ἀεικίνητον παλμὸν ἐνποιῆσαν
Rendered as: it produces an ever-moving pulsation
παλμός denotes a throbbing, quivering, or pulsation; this wording also supports the following association with Pallas.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἣν καὶ Παλλάδα ἐπονομάζουσιν διὰ τὸ πάλλεσθαι
Rendered as: which they also call Pallas because it pulses
The translation preserves the author’s wordplay between Παλλάδα and πάλλεσθαι without asserting that it is a historical etymology.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ αἰθέριος τεχνίτης
Rendered as: the etherial craftsman
The adjective identifies the craftsman with or as belonging to the ether; “craftsman of the ether” is possible but may imply that ether is merely his material.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ διήκοντος Διὸς
Rendered as: Zeus himself, who permeates everything
διήκω means to extend or pass through; “permeates everything” reflects the description of Zeus as universally diffused.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς θήλεια τὴν καθαρότητα, πρὸς σύγκρισιν τοῦ κρείττονος
Rendered as: is feminine in purity by comparison with what is superior
The accusative τὴν καθαρότητα marks respect: the air is characterized as female with respect to purity relative to the superior ether. “Less pure, and therefore female” would make the implication more explicit than the Greek does.

9. Translation choice — Greek: γαμετὴ δὲ διὰ τὸ ὡς γυναῖκα ὑποκεῖσθαι
Rendered as: but as his wife because it lies beneath him as a woman does
γαμετή means a wedded woman or wife, and ὑποκεῖσθαι retains both the physical placement of air beneath ether and the author’s gendered analogy.

SECTION 6.9

Hera is taken to represent a temperate balance of airs, and for that reason she is also exceedingly fertile. Athena, whom they also call Pallas, was regarded as a virgin because, on account of the extreme heat, she could not produce the generation of anything. Artemis is interpreted similarly: they take her to represent the lowest recess of the air and, because she is barren through the extremity of the cold, they likewise called her a virgin. As something that clouds the mind, they name the turbid and intoxicating compound of vapors from above and below Dionysus. The water beneath the earth, though one in nature, passes through all the channels in the land and is divided into many parts—as though cut into pieces—so they called it Osiris. They also take Adonis to represent ripe fruits, Aphrodite sexual union and generation, Demeter the earth, Kore seeds, and some take Dionysus to represent the vine.

Translator's notes for section 6.9 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: Ἀφροδίτην εἰς μίξιν καὶ γένεσιν
The noun μίξις permits both physical “mixture” and “sexual union.” The pairing with Aphrodite and generation supports the sexual rendering adopted in the text, while the surrounding natural-philosophical interpretation leaves physical mixture as a viable alternative. This is ordinary lexical ambiguity and does not require emendation.

2. Translation choice — Greek: παραλαμβάνεται δὲ ἡ μὲν Ἥρα πρὸς ἀέρων εὐκρασίαν
Rendered as: Hera is taken to represent a temperate balance of airs
παραλαμβάνεται introduces an allegorical identification, while εὐκρασία is a well-balanced or temperate mixture rather than merely pleasant weather.

3. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τὸ ἄκρως θερμὸν γένεσίν τινος ποιῆσαι μὴ δυναμένη
Rendered as: because, on account of the extreme heat, she could not produce the generation of anything
The rendering preserves both the extreme heat and the explicit inability to cause γένεσις; “bring anything into being” is a smoother alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὸν κατώτατον μυχὸν τοῦ ἀέρος
Rendered as: to represent the lowest recess of the air
μυχός is an innermost or remote recess; “lowest depth” is possible, but “recess” preserves the spatial image.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς φρενῶν θολωτικὸν
Rendered as: As something that clouds the mind
φρένες can denote the mind, understanding, or faculties, and θολωτικός means making turbid or confused.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἀπὸ τῶν ἄνω τε καὶ κάτω ἀτμῶν θολερὰν καὶ μεθύουσαν σύστασιν
Rendered as: the turbid and intoxicating compound of vapors from above and below
σύστασις here is a combination or compound; μεθύουσαν may describe it as intoxicating or as itself drunken.

7. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ πάντων τῶν χερσαίων πόρων διείρον
Rendered as: passes through all the channels in the land
διείρον depicts passage or threading through, and χερσαίων specifies channels belonging to the land.

8. Translation choice — Greek: λαμβάνουσι δὲ καὶ Ἄδωνιν εἰς ὡραίους καρπούς
Rendered as: They also take Adonis to represent ripe fruits
ὡραῖος means produced in its proper season and hence ripe; “seasonal fruits” is an equally possible rendering.

9. Translation choice — Greek: Ἀφροδίτην εἰς μίξιν καὶ γένεσιν
Rendered as: Aphrodite sexual union and generation
μίξις can denote mixture generally or sexual union. Its association here with Aphrodite and generation favors “sexual union,” while “mixture” remains possible within the passage’s physical allegory. The same sexual sense is explicit in the plural μίξεις with males in 6.10.

SECTION 6.10

Understand all such things for me as likewise possessing some such allegory. Regard Apollo as the sun that makes its circuit, an offspring of Zeus, which they also called Mithras, completing the circuit of a year. Let these transformations be understood by you as the many changes of Zeus, who permeates everywhere, and conceive of his countless women as years or generations. For the power that passes through the air from the ether itself, consorting with every year and generation, changes it in different ways and thus produces or destroys the things of the season. The ripe fruits are called children, while the unions with males are the periods of barrenness that occur at certain seasons.

Translator's notes for section 6.10 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: νόει μοι
Rendered as: Understand ... for me
The ethical dative μοι adds a personal appeal such as “take it from me”; retaining “for me” preserves it without making the phrase overly colloquial.

2. Translation choice — Greek: Ἀπόλλωνα δὲ ἥλιον τὸν περιπολοῦντα εἶναι νόμιζε
Rendered as: Regard Apollo as the sun that makes its circuit
περιπολεῖν denotes going around or patrolling a circuit, fitting the sun’s recurring course.

3. Translation choice — Greek: γονὴν ὄντα τοῦ Διός
Rendered as: an offspring of Zeus
γονή can mean birth, offspring, or generative seed; the personal genealogy favors “offspring,” though “product of Zeus” is possible in the physical allegory.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὃν καὶ Μίθραν ἐκάλεσαν
Rendered as: which they also called Mithras
The masculine relative most naturally refers to the sun identified with Apollo, though its proximity to Zeus permits momentary grammatical ambiguity.

5. Translation choice — Greek: αἱ πολλαὶ νοείσθωσάν σοι τροπαί
Rendered as: be understood by you as the many changes
τροπαί can be turnings, changes, or seasonal revolutions; “changes” distinguishes it from the preceding μεταμορφώσεις while retaining the sense.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὰς δὲ μυρίας αὐτοῦ γυναῖκας ἐνιαυτοὺς ἢ γενεὰς ἐπινόει
Rendered as: conceive of his countless women as years or generations
μυρίας means countless or innumerable, and γενεάς may denote generations, ages, or successive periods.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἑκάστῳ ἐνιαυτῷ καὶ γενεᾷ συνουσιάζουσα διαφόρως αὐτὸν τρέπει
Rendered as: consorting with every year and generation, changes it in different ways
συνουσιάζουσα preserves the sexual language underlying Zeus’s unions. The masculine αὐτόν can refer to the air or to each year; “it” retains that referential ambiguity.

8. Translation choice — Greek: γεννᾷ ἢ φθείρει τὰ ὡραῖα
Rendered as: produces or destroys the things of the season
τὰ ὡραῖα denotes things belonging to or ripening in their proper season, including seasonal produce; “ripe things” would be narrower.

SECTION 6.11

While Appion was interpreting these things allegorically, I was deep in thought and appeared not to be following what he was saying. So he broke off his discourse and said to me, “If you are not following what I am saying, why am I even having this discussion in the first place?” I replied, “Do not suppose that I am insensible to what you are saying, for I understand it very well, since this is not the first time I have heard it. To let you know that I am not ignorant of what you are saying, I will summarize what you have stated; and as for what you have omitted, I will complete the allegories in sequence, just as I heard them from others.” Appion said, “Do as you say.”

Translator's notes for section 6.11 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: σύννους ὢν
Rendered as: I was deep in thought
σύννους describes being absorbed or pensive, which explains why Clement merely appeared not to be following.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ λεγομένοις μὴ παρακολουθεῖν
Rendered as: not to be following what he was saying
παρακολουθέω here denotes following or comprehending the course of an argument.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ μὲν σοι ῥηθέντα ἐπιτεμοῦμαι
Rendered as: I will summarize what you have stated
ἐπιτέμνομαι means to abridge or summarize; the dative σοι is understood as identifying the person by whom the preceding statements were made.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν δὲ παραλειφθέντων σοι κατ’ ἀκολουθίαν
Rendered as: as for what you have omitted, I will complete the allegories in sequence
κατ’ ἀκολουθίαν is taken as describing an orderly continuation; “by logical consequence” is also possible.

SECTION 6.12

And I replied, “I now pass over giving a detailed account of the living egg brought forth from the chance blending of boundless matter. When it burst, according to some, a male-and-female being, Phanes, sprang out. I also summarize all those matters up to the point when the ruptured shell assumed its harmonious structure, while marrow-like matter from it remained; then, in outline, I run through the account of the things produced inwardly by that matter, together with what follows. For, as you say, from Cronus and Rhea—that is, by time and matter—were born first Pluto, as the sediment that settled below; second Poseidon, who is the middle, moist substance floating above the nature with the strongest downward pull; and third the highest substance, which is aether, namely Zeus. This third substance was not swallowed, but, being a hot force and having a nature that rises upward, it flew up, as if driven by some gust, into the most sovereign aether above.”

Translator's notes for section 6.12 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: κἀγὼ ἀπεκρινάμην
Rendered as: And I replied
The narrative introduction explicitly identifies the following account as Clement’s reply and is retained before the direct speech.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ ἐκ τῆς ἀπείρου ὕλης κατὰ ἐπιτυχίαν κράσεως ἀποκυηθὲν ἔμψυχον ὠόν
Rendered as: the living egg brought forth from the chance blending of boundless matter
ἔμψυχον is rendered “living” rather than the more technical “ensouled”; κατὰ ἐπιτυχίαν presents the blending as occurring by chance.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀρρενόθηλυ ἐξέθορεν, Φάνης
Rendered as: a male-and-female being, Phanes, sprang out
The neuter compound ἀρρενόθηλυ denotes an androgynous or male-and-female entity, while ἐξέθορεν conveys a sudden springing forth.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ ῥαγὲν κύτος τὴν ἁρμονίαν ἔλαβεν
Rendered as: the ruptured shell assumed its harmonious structure
κύτος can denote a hollow vessel, casing, or shell; τὴν ἁρμονίαν ἔλαβεν indicates acquiring an ordered or harmonious arrangement.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ κάτω παραχωρήσασα ὑποστάθμη
Rendered as: the sediment that settled below
ὑποστάθμη denotes sediment or dregs, and παραχωρήσασα depicts it giving way or moving to the lower position.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ κάτω ὀλκοτάτῃ φύσει
Rendered as: the nature with the strongest downward pull
The unusual ὀλκοτάτῃ is understood from the idea of drawing or pulling, while κάτω specifies a downward tendency. “The lowest, most attractive nature” is a possible alternative.

7. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὸν ἄνω ἡγεμονικώτατον ἀνέπτη αἰθέρα
Rendered as: it flew up into the most sovereign aether above
ἡγεμονικώτατον characterizes the upper aether as ruling or preeminent; “most ruling” would be less idiomatic English.

SECTION 6.13

Cronus’s bonds are the fastening together of heaven and earth, as I have also heard from others who give allegorical interpretations. The cutting off of his parts is the separation and differentiation of the elements, because all things were cut away from their own natural substance and set apart, each to be arranged by itself. Time no longer begets; instead, the things begotten through it carry on the succession by nature’s law. Aphrodite, who rose from the depth, is the generative substance arising from moisture. When the hot spirit mingles with it, it produces the desire for their union and brings the beauty of the world to completion.

Translator's notes for section 6.13 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ σύμπηξις οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς
Rendered as: the fastening together of heaven and earth
σύμπηξις denotes a joining, compacting, or solid fastening together.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ δὲ ἀποκοπὴ τῶν μορίων
Rendered as: the cutting off of his parts
μορίων is the source’s euphemistic “parts”; the possessive “his” refers contextually to Cronus.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πάντα ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀπετμήθη
Rendered as: all things were cut away from their own natural substance
ἐκ is retained as marking source or separation. “Were divided according to their respective natures” is contextually possible but renders ἐκ less directly.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ γεννηθέντα δι’ αὐτοῦ νόμῳ φύσεως ποιεῖται τὰς διαδοχάς
Rendered as: the things begotten through it carry on the succession by nature’s law
The neuter plural subject takes a singular verb; διαδοχάς may denote successive generations or succession more generally.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν τῆς μίξεως ποιεῖται ἔρωτα
Rendered as: it produces the desire for their union
ἔρως can mean desire or erotic impulse, while τῆς μίξεως may describe either desire for the mixture or desire generated by it; the former fits the generative context.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τελεσιουργεῖ τοῦ κόσμου τὸ κάλλος
Rendered as: brings the beauty of the world to completion
τελεσιουργέω means to accomplish, perfect, or bring something fully into effect.

SECTION 6.14

The wedding banquet, where Zeus was holding the feast for the Nereid Thetis and the beautiful Peleus, has the following allegory—so that you may know, Appion, that we have heard such things even without you. The banquet, then, is the world; the twelve are the Fates’ heavenly encircling supports, which they call zodiacal signs; Prometheus is forethought, through which all things came to be; Peleus is mud, conceived from earth for the making of a human being and mixed with the Nereid—that is, with water. From the mixture of the two, water and earth, the first human was not begotten but molded, and was complete; because he had not brought his lips to breasts, he was called Achilles. He himself also represents the prime of life. If that prime desires Desire—Polyxena—who is alien and foreign to truth, it is killed by serpent venom, by an arrow to the heel, as death creeps in along the footprint.

Translator's notes for section 6.14 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἔστι δὲ αὐτὸς καὶ ἀκμήν, ἥτις
The printed ἀκμήν is formally accusative or adverbial, whereas a predicate after ἔστι and the feminine nominative relative ἥτις would ordinarily call for ἀκμή. The context supports reference to the prime of life, but that interpretation remains provisional and is disclosed rather than treated as though the supplied Greek already contained the nominative form.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ δεῖπνον ἐτέλει Ζεὺς ὑπέρ τε τῆς Νηρηΐδος Θέτιδος καὶ τοῦ καλοῦ Πηλέως
Rendered as: Zeus was holding the feast for the Nereid Thetis and the beautiful Peleus
τελεῖν a feast means to conduct or celebrate it; ὑπέρ identifies those for whom or in whose honor it is held.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ οὐράνια τῶν Μοιρῶν περιστηρίγματα
Rendered as: the Fates’ heavenly encircling supports
περιστηρίγματα is rare and denotes structures set or supporting something around a circumference; “surrounding fixtures” is another possible rendering.

4. Translation choice — Greek: Προμηθεὺς ἡ προμήθεια
Rendered as: Prometheus is forethought
The translation preserves the explicit etymological wordplay between Προμηθεύς and προμήθεια.

5. Translation choice — Greek: Πηλεὺς πηλὸς ὁ ἀπὸ γῆς εἰς ἀνθρώπου γένεσιν περινοηθεὶς
Rendered as: Peleus is mud, conceived from earth for the making of a human being
πηλός preserves the wordplay with Peleus. περινοηθείς is taken in its mental sense, “conceived” or “devised,” though “selected” is also contextually possible.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ πρῶτος οὐ γεννηθεὶς ἀλλὰ πλασθεὶς τέλειος
Rendered as: the first human was not begotten but molded, and was complete
The masculine ὁ πρῶτος resumes the preceding ἀνθρώπου. τέλειος can mean complete, perfect, mature, or full-grown.

7. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τὸ μαζοῖς χείλη μὴ προσενεγκεῖν Ἀχιλλεὺς προσηγορεύθη
Rendered as: because he had not brought his lips to breasts, he was called Achilles
The source supplies an allegorical etymology linking Achilles with the absence of nursing at the breast; the explanation is preserved without replacing it with a modern etymology.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἥτις ἐὰν ἐπιθυμίαν (Πολυξένην) ὡς ἀληθείας ἀλλοτρίαν οὖσαν καὶ ξένην ἐπιθυμῇ
Rendered as: If that prime desires Desire—Polyxena—who is alien and foreign to truth
The main text takes ὡς with οὖσαν descriptively, characterizing Desire as alien and foreign to truth. More explicitly it could be rendered “desires Desire as being alien and foreign to truth”; ὡς with the participle can also present this characterization as the represented reason or ground, yielding a causal sense such as “because she is alien and foreign to truth.”

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἰῷ ὄφεως ἀναιρεῖται βέλει κατὰ πτέρναν καὶ κατὰ ἴχνος ἐνέρποντος τοῦ θανάτου
Rendered as: it is killed by serpent venom, by an arrow to the heel, as death creeps in along the footprint
The main text reads both ἰῷ and βέλει instrumentally, attaches κατὰ πτέρναν to the arrow, and takes ἴχνος as a footprint or track with death’s creeping entrance. The instruments may instead be appositional or describe venom conveyed by the arrow. Moreover, ἴχνος can mean the sole or foot, and both coordinated κατὰ phrases may go with death’s entrance: “with death creeping in at the heel and at the sole of the foot.”

SECTION 6.15

Hera, then, and Athena and Aphrodite and Eris and the apple and Hermes and the judgment and the shepherd hint at some such meaning: Hera is dignity; Athena, courage; Aphrodite, pleasures; Hermes, interpreting reason; and Paris the shepherd, the unreasoning and barbarous impulse. So if, at the prime of life, the reasoning faculty that shepherds the soul happens to be barbarous and, passing over what is beneficial—thrusting aside both courage and self-control—chooses pleasures alone and awards victory to desire alone, as though receiving delightful things from her in return, then the one who judged wrongly will receive enjoyment to the destruction of both himself and all that is his. Eris is contentious vice. The golden apple of the Hesperides would be wealth, which sometimes knows how to lead even the self-controlled—as Hera—toward idleness, makes the courageous—as Athena—more contentious over things unfitting for them, and, under the pretext of luxury, destroys beauty of soul—as Aphrodite. I will put it briefly: wealth provokes everyone to evil strife.

Translator's notes for section 6.15 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: Ἑρμῆς ὁ ἑρμηνευτικὸς λόγος
Rendered as: Hermes, interpreting reason
λόγος here belongs to the psychological allegory and is therefore rendered “reason”; ἑρμηνευτικός also sustains the wordplay with Hermes. “Interpretive discourse” is possible.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ ποιμὴν Πάρις ἡ ἀλόγιστος ὁρμὴ καὶ βάρβαρος
Rendered as: Paris the shepherd, the unreasoning and barbarous impulse
ὁρμή denotes impulse or drive, while ἀλόγιστος marks it as lacking rational deliberation.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ τὴν ψυχὴν ποιμαίνων λογισμὸς
Rendered as: the reasoning faculty that shepherds the soul
The rendering preserves the shepherd image in ποιμαίνων and distinguishes λογισμός as the faculty of calculation or reasoning.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς παρ’ αὐτῆς τὰ τέρποντα ἀντιλαμβάνων
Rendered as: as though receiving delightful things from her in return
ἀντιλαμβάνων expresses receiving something in exchange or return; ὡς allows the motivation to be presented as the reasoner’s supposition.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπ’ ὀλέθρῳ ἑαυτοῦ τε καὶ τῶν αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: to the destruction of both himself and all that is his
The substantival τῶν αὐτοῦ is broad. In the Paris allegory it may refer to his people or household, but it can also denote his possessions; “all that is his” is intended to leave both personal and nonpersonal referents open.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ φιλονεικοῦσα κακία
Rendered as: contentious vice
φιλονεικοῦσα characterizes vice as loving disputes or strife.

7. Translation choice — Greek: προφάσει τρυφῆς
Rendered as: under the pretext of luxury
πρόφασις is a pretext or professed ground, while τρυφή denotes luxury, indulgence, or soft living.

SECTION 6.16

But the Heracles who killed the serpent, the ruler and guardian of wealth—the true Heracles—is also the philosophical mind. Naked of every vice, it ranges throughout the world, visiting souls and bringing those it meets to sound judgment; I mean people resembling bold lions, cowardly deer, wild boars, or many-sided hydras. Likewise, all the other things Heracles is said to have accomplished as labors are riddles of intellectual virtue. For now, let what has been said suffice, for not even all of time will be enough to speak about each one.

Translator's notes for section 6.16 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: Ἡρακλῆς ὁ γνήσιος καὶ φιλόσοφός ἐστι νοῦς
The attachment of ὁ γνήσιος and force of καί are interpretively ambiguous. The main rendering attaches “true” appositionally to Heracles and understands καί as “also,” but ὁ γνήσιος καὶ φιλόσοφος may instead jointly characterize νοῦς, yielding “Heracles is the genuine and philosophical mind.” This is an attachment ambiguity, not evidence of a defective source.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν τοῦ πλούτου ἡγεμόνα καὶ φύλακα ὄφιν
Rendered as: the serpent, the ruler and guardian of wealth
Preserves both roles attributed to the serpent and the genitive relation to wealth.

3. Translation choice — Greek: Ἡρακλῆς ὁ γνήσιος καὶ φιλόσοφός ἐστι νοῦς
Rendered as: the true Heracles—is also the philosophical mind
Takes ὁ γνήσιος as identifying the true Heracles and καὶ φιλόσοφος with νοῦς, with καί represented by “also.” A material alternative coordinates γνήσιος and φιλόσοφος as qualifications of νοῦς: “Heracles is the genuine and philosophical mind.” The main rendering is retained because the article in ὁ γνήσιος naturally permits an appositional identification of Heracles, while the surrounding allegory identifies the genuine Heracles with mind.

4. Translation choice — Greek: σωφρονίζων τοὺς ἐντυγχάνοντας
Rendered as: bringing those it meets to sound judgment
σωφρονίζω can mean making someone prudent, self-controlled, or sound-minded; this wording suits the philosophical context.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὕδραις πολυτρόποις
Rendered as: many-sided hydras
πολύτροπος can mean manifold, versatile, devious, or many-natured; “many-sided” preserves its breadth without choosing only the moral sense “wily.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: νοερᾶς ἀρετῆς
Rendered as: intellectual virtue
νοερός concerns mind or intellect, matching the passage’s allegory of the philosophical mind.

SECTION 6.17

Still, I wonder how those who concealed these things in oblique riddles and veiled them over with wicked myths are called intelligent and wise by you, when the things could have been disclosed clearly, reverently, and beneficially by the uncovered, straight way. As though driven on by an evil demon, they laid snares for almost all humanity. For either these are not riddles but true sins of the gods—in which case they ought not to have exposed the gods or, in the first place, set those sins before human beings for imitation—or the things falsely presented as having been done by the gods were told in riddling form. And the men you call wise sinned, Appion, because by covering solemn things with indecent myths they encouraged human beings to sin, and did this while insulting those whom they even believed to be gods.

Translator's notes for section 6.17 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν θεῶν ψευδῶς πεπραγμένα
ψευδῶς may be heard as modifying the alleged performance itself (“falsely done”) or the presentation of the deeds as divine. The surrounding contrast between true sins and riddling falsehood supports “falsely presented as having been done.”

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἀκαλύπτῳ τῇ εὐθείᾳ
Rendered as: by the uncovered, straight way
Preserves the source’s contrast between an unveiled direct route and oblique, concealing riddles.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐνήδρευσαν ἀνθρώπους
Rendered as: laid snares for ... humanity
ἐνεδρεύω evokes lying in ambush or entrapping, rather than merely misleading.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐλέγχειν αὐτοὺς
Rendered as: to have exposed the gods
ἐλέγχω can mean expose, convict, or censure; “exposed” fits the argument that their sins should not have been publicized.

5. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν
Rendered as: or, in the first place
Under negation, τὴν ἀρχήν idiomatically means “at all” or “in the first place,” not merely “at the beginning.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν θεῶν ψευδῶς πεπραγμένα
Rendered as: the things falsely presented as having been done by the gods
The context contrasts actual divine sins with false mythic representations. A more formally literal alternative is “the things falsely done by the gods.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ σεμνὰ
Rendered as: solemn things
σεμνός may mean solemn, venerable, august, or dignified; the contrast is with indecent myths.

SECTION 6.18

Therefore regard such people not as wise men but as evil demons, for they put forward wicked storylines for noble deeds, so that those wishing to become imitators of their betters might emulate the actions of the so-called gods. When speaking on the previous day I did not conceal those actions: I mean patricides, murders of children, impious unions with mothers, daughters, and sisters, unseemly adulteries, male-male intercourse, and defiled acts unfit to name, besides ten thousand other unlawful unions of this kind. Still more impious are those who want these things to be regarded as true, so that they may do the like without shame. In this matter, if they had really wished to act reverently, they ought—as I just said—even if the gods had in fact committed the evils sung about them, out of honor for the gods to have covered the indecent things with myths of a more seemly kind, and not the reverse: as you claim, when good deeds had been performed by them, to wrap them in evil and indecent forms. Such forms, when allegorized, can be understood only with labor and scarcely at that; and whenever some people understand them, they have given those people, in exchange for their great toil, the benefit of not being led astray, though the toil could have been avoided, while they have utterly destroyed those who were led astray. Nevertheless, I approve those who allegorize them toward the more dignified sense, such as those who intimated in a riddle that practical wisdom sprang from the head of Zeus. But perhaps this is more plausible to me: once wicked men had won the reputation of gods, those outrages were dared.

Translator's notes for section 6.18 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ὧν ἀσεβέστεροι οἱ ταῦτα ἀληθῆ δοκεῖν εἶναι θέλοντες
The antecedent and force of comparative ὧν are not fully explicit. It may mean “more impious than these” or introduce a subgroup, “among whom the more impious are.” The main text uses the defensible contextual sense “still more impious” without forcing an antecedent.

2. Greek: τοὺς εἰς τὸ σεμνότερον ἀλληγοροῦντας αὐτὰς
The feminine pronoun αὐτάς may refer back to the actions or accounts implicit in the argument; its precise antecedent is not explicit. The English “them” preserves that referential openness.

3. Translation choice — Greek: κακὰς ὑποθέσεις ἔργων καλῶν
Rendered as: wicked storylines for noble deeds
ὑπόθεσις may denote a subject, underlying premise, or dramatic plot; “storylines” fits myths that clothe supposedly good deeds in wicked narratives.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν κρειττόνων
Rendered as: their betters
The comparative can refer to those superior to the imitators, here especially the beings called gods.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἀρρενομιξίας
Rendered as: male-male intercourse
The compound directly denotes sexual intercourse between males; the rendering avoids importing a broader modern identity category.

6. Translation choice — Greek: μιαρὰς ἀρρητουργίας
Rendered as: defiled acts unfit to name
μιαρός marks pollution or defilement, while the rare ἀρρητουργία denotes the doing of things that are unspeakable or not to be named.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τιμῇ τῇ πρὸς θεοὺς
Rendered as: out of honor for the gods
The dative phrase expresses the honor owed or directed toward the gods.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκείνοις μὲν ἀντὶ τοῦ πολλοῦ μόχθου παρέσχον τὸ μὴ πλανηθῆναι, ἐξὸν μὴ μοχθῆσαι
Rendered as: they have given those people, in exchange for their great toil, the benefit of not being led astray, though the toil could have been avoided
The benefit is identified as not being led astray, while μέν sets up the contrast with those who were led astray; the Greek does not expressly make this their only benefit.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἀναπηδῆσαι τὴν φρόνησιν
Rendered as: that practical wisdom sprang
φρόνησις is prudent or practical understanding, while ἀναπηδάω supplies the vivid image of springing forth.

10. Translation choice — Greek: δόξαν θεῶν ἀπενεγκαμένων
Rendered as: had won the reputation of gods
ἀποφέρομαι with δόξαν can mean carrying off, gaining, or winning a reputation.

SECTION 6.19

But we do not find the poetic allegory concerning all the gods consistent. To take an immediate example, in the ordering of the universe the poets say at one time that nature became the originator of the whole creation, and at another that mind did. For they say that the first motion and mingling of the elements arose from nature, but that this was ordered by the providence of mind. Although they declare that the universe was fashioned by nature, because they cannot demonstrate this beyond objection on account of the artistry of creation, they also interweave the providence of mind, thinking themselves able to sweep along even those who are very discerning. But we say to them: If the world came into being from spontaneous nature, how has it acquired proportion and order? These can be brought about only by surpassing intelligence and can be comprehended by knowledge, which alone is capable of determining these things precisely. But if all things received their combination and ordering through intelligence—which necessarily cannot be otherwise—how could these things then possibly have happened to come into being spontaneously?

Translator's notes for section 6.19 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ποιητικὴν ἀλληγορίαν
Rendered as: the poetic allegory
ποιητικός can mean poetic or belonging to poets; “the poets’ allegory” is a viable alternative, but the adjective is preserved directly.

2. Translation choice — Greek: φύσιν ... νοῦν ἀρχηγὸν
Rendered as: nature ... mind ... the originator
The passage contrasts nature and mind as competing explanatory first principles; lowercase English avoids imposing personification beyond the context.

3. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τὸ τῆς δημιουργίας ἔντεχνον
Rendered as: on account of the artistry of creation
ἔντεχνος denotes what is artful, skillfully made, or governed by craft.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς πάνυ σαφοὺς
Rendered as: even those who are very discerning
σαφής applied to people can describe those who are clear-minded, perspicacious, or discerning, while πάνυ marks a high degree, represented by “very” rather than a superlative.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ μόνης ὑπερβαλλούσης φρονήσεως
Rendered as: only by surpassing intelligence
Here φρόνησις concerns the intelligence responsible for cosmic proportion and order, while μόνης restricts what can bring them about.

6. Translation choice — Greek: καταληφθῆναι ὑπὸ ἐπιστήμης τῆς μόνης ταῦτα ἀκριβοῦν δυναμένης
Rendered as: can be comprehended by knowledge, which alone is capable of determining these things precisely
The second μόνης belongs to the attributive phrase describing knowledge as alone capable of precise determination; it does not directly restrict the passive verb “can be comprehended.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ τοῦ αὐτομάτου
Rendered as: spontaneously
The phrase can also be rendered “by chance” or “of itself”; “spontaneously” maintains the connection with ἐξ αὐτομάτου φύσεως earlier in the argument.

SECTION 6.20

Therefore, those who wished to allegorize divine matters in the more shameful direction—for example, that Metis was swallowed by Zeus—have fallen into perplexity. They do not understand that those who gave oblique accounts of nature concerning the gods have also abolished their very existence as gods, dissolving their forms by allegory into the substances of the world. It is more plausible, then, to say that the gods celebrated by them were certain evil magicians. Though wicked human beings, they assumed different forms by magic, broke up marriages, and ruined lives; yet to people of old, who did not know what magic even was, they seemed to be gods because of what they did. In city after city, both their deaths and their tombs are evident.

Translator's notes for section 6.20 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: φυσιολογήσαντες ·περὶ θεῶν
The supplied, image-checked print has a raised point before περὶ. This verified editorial punctuation leaves περὶ θεῶν capable of being associated either with the oblique account of nature or more loosely with the following claim about abolishing the gods. The translation provisionally takes it with the participial phrase while retaining the supplied reading; the punctuation is not treated as an OCR defect.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τὸ αἴσχιον ἀλληγορῆσαι
Rendered as: to allegorize ... in the more shameful direction
The comparative phrase describes the direction or resulting sense of the allegorical interpretation, not simply its method.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν Μῆτιν
Rendered as: Metis
In the mythic example Μῆτις is the conventional name Metis, although the name itself also means counsel or cunning intelligence.

4. Translation choice — Greek: πλαγίως φυσιολογήσαντες
Rendered as: gave oblique accounts of nature
φυσιολογέω means discoursing or theorizing about nature, while πλαγίως marks the indirect or oblique manner.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ εἴδη αὐτῶν ... εἰς τὰς τοῦ κόσμου οὐσίας
Rendered as: their forms ... into the substances of the world
Preserves the philosophical contrast between the gods’ forms or identities and the cosmic substances into which allegory resolves them.

6. Translation choice — Greek: κακοί τινες γεγόνασιν μάγοι
Rendered as: were certain evil magicians
μάγος here denotes practitioners of magic; the following μαγείᾳ confirms that sense.

7. Translation choice — Greek: μεταμορφούμενοι
Rendered as: they assumed different forms
The middle or passive participle can mean transforming themselves or being transformed; the context presents magical changes of appearance.

8. Translation choice — Greek: οἱ μόροι
Rendered as: their deaths
μόρος can mean death, doom, or allotted fate; its pairing with tombs favors “deaths,” though “fates” remains possible.

SECTION 6.21

Indeed, to take an immediate example (as I also said on another occasion), in the Caucasus Mountains the tomb of a certain Cronus, a man, is pointed out—the tomb of a savage tyrant and killer of his children. His son, named Zeus, became worse; appearing as ruler of the world by the power of magic, he breaks up many marriages and punishes his father together with his uncles. When he then died, the Cretans point out his tomb. In Mesopotamia, a certain Helios lies at Hatra and a certain Selene at Carrhae; a certain Hermes, a human being, lies in Egypt; Ares in Thrace; Aphrodite in Cyprus; and Asclepius in Epidaurus. Tombs of many other such figures are also visible.

Translator's notes for section 6.21 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: καὶ οὕτως τελευτήσαντος τὸν τάφον Κρῆτες ἐπιδεικνῦσιν
The genitive absolute does not explicitly identify the person who died. The continuing focus and the Cretan tomb tradition favor Zeus; Cronus is grammatically possible but contextually less likely.

2. Translation choice — Greek: Κρόνου τινὸς σῆμα ἀνθρώπου δείκνυται
Rendered as: the tomb of a certain Cronus, a man, is pointed out
Although σῆμα can mean a sign or monument, the burial context and the subsequent τάφον and τάφοι support “tomb.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: μαγείας δυνάμει κοσμοκράτωρ ἀναφανεὶς
Rendered as: appearing as ruler of the world by the power of magic
Preserves both the alleged magical means and ἀναφανείς, which presents his world-rule as an appearance or emergence.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν πατέρα σὺν τοῖς θείοις κολάζει
Rendered as: punishes his father together with his uncles
The family and mythological context supports the substantival sense “uncles,” with the father and uncles as joint objects. “Punishes his father together with the divine ones” is lexically possible.

5. Translation choice — Greek: Ἥλιος μὲν τις ἐν Ἄτροις
Rendered as: a certain Helios lies at Hatra
Ἄτροις is treated as the dative plural place-name referring to Hatra in Mesopotamia.

6. Translation choice — Greek: Ἑρμῆς ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ τις ἄνθρωπος
Rendered as: a certain Hermes, a human being, lies in Egypt
The apposition explicitly identifies Hermes as a human being; the verb “lies” is carried forward from κεῖνται.

SECTION 6.22

Thus it has been plainly acknowledged by those who think correctly that they were human beings. Those who were their contemporaries, perceiving that they had proved mortal, paid less attention to them after they died; but the long passage of time clothed them with the reputation of gods. Do not be amazed if those who lived in the days of Asclepius and Heracles were deceived, or those in the days of Dionysus or anyone else of that period, since the people in those places worship even Hector at Ilium and Achilles on the island of Leuce, the Opuntians worship Patroclus, and the Rhodians worship Alexander the Macedonian.

Translator's notes for section 6.22 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἄνθρωποι γεγενῆσθαι ὡμολόγηνται
Rendered as: it has been plainly acknowledged that they were human beings
The implied subjects are the allegedly divine figures discussed in the preceding section; the perfect construction identifies them as having been human.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπαισθόμενοι αὐτοὺς θνητοὺς γεγονέναι
Rendered as: perceiving that they had proved mortal
The verb can express noticing, apprehending, or suspecting, while the completed deaths demonstrate the figures’ mortality.

3. Translation choice — Greek: δόξαν θεῶν αὐτοῖς περιέθηκεν
Rendered as: clothed them with the reputation of gods
Retains the image of time placing divine repute around them without asserting that they truly became gods.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οἱ κατὰ Ἀσκληπιὸν καὶ Ἡρακλέα γενόμενοι
Rendered as: those who lived in the days of Asclepius and Heracles
The surrounding argument concerns contemporaries and the effect of elapsed time. “Those associated with Asclepius and Heracles” is also possible.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὅπου καὶ Ἕκτορα
Rendered as: since the people in those places worship even Hector
Here ὅπου introduces a striking supporting circumstance; the worshipers are supplied later by οἱ ἐκεῖ.

SECTION 6.23

But among the Egyptians, even now, a man is worshiped as a god before his death. This, at least, is a lesser act of impiety, because the Egyptians accord divine honors while a man is alive; but the most ridiculous thing of all is that they worship birds and reptiles and all animals. For most human beings neither understand nor do anything with judgment. Now observe what is most shameful of all: the one who, by their account, is father of gods and humans, whom most people call Zeus, they depict on a panel as a goose coupled with Leda and set up publicly. As retribution for this outrage, I would have liked it if they had portrayed their present king in a shameful coupling and, having done the same thing they have dared to do in Zeus’s case, had set it up publicly, so that, even if only through the anger of their temporary king—and he a human being—they might learn through punishment how due honor must be rendered. I tell you these things not as one who has already recognized the God who truly is, but, being fair-minded, I confess: Though I do not know what God is, still I think I know clearly that God exists.

Translator's notes for section 6.23 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἤθελον εἰ
The construction continues with aorist indicatives and is compressed. It defensibly expresses an unreal wish, “I would have liked it if they had ...”; “I wanted to see whether they had ...” is grammatically conceivable but fits the argument less well. No textual correction is required.

2. Translation choice — Greek: θείας τιμὰς νομίζουσιν Αἰγύπτιοι
Rendered as: the Egyptians accord divine honors
Νομίζω can denote customary observance or acknowledgment; here it concerns treating a living person as entitled to divine honors.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν δι’ αὐτῶν ὄντα πατέρα θεῶν τε καὶ ἀνθρώπων
Rendered as: the one who, by their account, is father of gods and humans
The phrase δι’ αὐτῶν is literally “through them.” In context it can mark Zeus’s status as established through their own representation or claim; “through their agency” remains possible.

4. Translation choice — Greek: Λήδᾳ συνεσχηματισμένον χῆνα
Rendered as: as a goose coupled with Leda
Χῆνα explicitly means “goose,” not the familiar “swan.” The participle describes Zeus as joined or correspondingly formed with Leda and, in this sexual context, is rendered “coupled with.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ αἰσχρᾶς πλοκῆς
Rendered as: in a shameful coupling
Πλοκή can denote entwining or entanglement; the preceding sexual image involving Zeus and Leda supports “coupling.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ προσκαίρου βασιλέως
Rendered as: their temporary king
Πρόσκαιρος emphasizes that the earthly ruler lasts only for a limited time.

7. Translation choice — Greek: Εἰ καὶ τί θεὸς οὐκ οἶδα, ἀλλ’ οὖν γε σαφῶς ὅτι θεός, νομίζω εἰδέναι
Rendered as: Though I do not know what God is, still I think I know clearly that God exists
The contrast is between not knowing what God is and knowing that God exists. “What sort of god” and “that he is God” are grammatically possible but fit the immediate contrast less directly.

SECTION 6.24

To take an immediate example, the first four elements—things brought into being by another—cannot be God; neither can mixing, blending, coming-to-be, the visible vessel that encompasses the whole, the sediment collecting in Hades, the water floating on top, the boiling substance, or the air extending from it as far as the things here. For whether the four elements had stood apart from one another—in which case they could not have been mixed for the generation of a living creature without some great craftsman—or had always been joined to one another, even so they are fitted together by a craftsman mind to suit what belongs properly to the limbs and parts of the living creature, so that it may be able to preserve the proportion of each to each and may possess a well-bounded constitution, and so that all the things within may receive the appropriate harmony. Likewise, the craftsman mind precisely fashions the proper places of each with complete beauty. To sum up: of all the other things that a living creature must ever have, nothing was lacking in this great living creature of the whole circuit.

Translator's notes for section 6.24 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἵνα τὴν ἑκάστου πρὸς ἕκαστον ἀναλογίαν ἀποσώζειν δύνηται καὶ τὴν ἕξιν εὐπερίγραφον ἔχῃ
The singular verbs leave their subject implicit. The resulting organized whole or living creature is the best contextual referent; the neuter plural elements can also govern singular verbs in Greek, so they remain a grammatical alternative.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ πρῶτα τέσσαρα στοιχεῖα θεὸς εἶναι οὐ δύναται τὰ ὑπὸ ἄλλου γενόμενα
Rendered as: the first four elements—things brought into being by another—cannot be God
The final participial phrase characterizes the four elements and supplies the reason they cannot themselves be God.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ πᾶν περιέχον ὁρατὸν κύτος
Rendered as: the visible vessel that encompasses the whole
Κύτος denotes a hollow body, cavity, or vessel. “Vessel” preserves the cosmological container image without identifying it more specifically.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ ἐν τῷ ᾄδῃ συρρέουσα ὑποστάθμη
Rendered as: the sediment collecting in Hades
Ὑποστάθμη denotes sediment, dregs, or what settles at the bottom, while συρρέουσα presents it as flowing or gathering together.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ ἐξ αὐτῆς μέχρι τῶν ἐνταῦθα διήκων ἀήρ
Rendered as: the air extending from it as far as the things here
The feminine pronoun most naturally refers to the immediately preceding “boiling substance,” though another feminine item in the list is grammatically possible.

6. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τὸ οἰκεῖον τῶν τοῦ ζῴου μελῶν καὶ μερῶν συναρμόζεται
Rendered as: are fitted together to suit what belongs properly to the limbs and parts of the living creature
The phrase describes an intelligent fitting of the elements to the proper constitution or requirements of the creature’s members and parts.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἕξιν εὐπερίγραφον ἔχῃ
Rendered as: may possess a well-bounded constitution
Ἕξις here denotes condition or constitution, while εὐπερίγραφος suggests being readily circumscribed or clearly bounded. “A well-defined constitution” is also possible.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ μεγάλῳ τούτῳ ζῴῳ τῆς ὅλης περιφορᾶς
Rendered as: in this great living creature of the whole circuit
The cosmos is presented as a great living creature. Περιφορά can denote revolution, circular motion, or the circuit produced by it; “of the whole revolution” is also possible.

SECTION 6.25

Thus there must be some unoriginated craftsman mind that either gathered the elements when they were apart or, when they were together with one another, skillfully blended them for the generation of a living creature and completed a single work from them all; for it is impossible for an exceedingly wise work to be completed without some greater mind. Nor indeed can love be the craftsman of all, nor desire, nor force, nor anything else of that kind, since such things are passions and naturally come and go. Nor is whatever is borne by another a god, nor indeed whatever is altered by time or nature and dissolved into no longer existing.

Translator's notes for section 6.25 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: νοῦν ἀγέννητον τεχνίτην
Rendered as: unoriginated craftsman mind
Ἀγέννητος means not generated or not brought into being. “Unoriginated” suits the contrast with elements produced by another; “unbegotten” is possible but carries stronger traditional theological associations.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς ζῴου γένεσιν τεχνικῶς ἐκέρασεν
Rendered as: skillfully blended them for the generation of a living creature
The adverb emphasizes artful or craftsmanlike arrangement, while the prepositional phrase states its purpose.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πάνυ σοφὸν ἔργον
Rendered as: an exceedingly wise work
The phrase presents the work as embodying extraordinary wisdom or skill; “a work of surpassing skill” is an idiomatic alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἔρως εἶναι δύναται πάντων τεχνίτης
Rendered as: love can be the craftsman of all
Ἔρως can denote love as a cosmic principle and may evoke personified Eros. Lowercase “love” avoids requiring personification.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πάθη ὄντα συμβαίνειν καὶ ἀποβαίνειν πέφυκεν
Rendered as: such things are passions and naturally come and go
The paired verbs describe the proposed principles as contingent passions that arise and depart.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ ὑφ’ ἑτέρου φερόμενόν ἐστιν θεὸς
Rendered as: whatever is borne by another is a god
The translation is negated by the preceding οὐδὲ. Φέρω in the passive can mean carried, borne, or moved; “moved by another” is also viable.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ ὑπὸ χρόνου ἢ φύσεως ἀλλοιούμενον καὶ εἰς τὸ μηκέτι εἶναι ἀναλυόμενον
Rendered as: whatever is altered by time or nature and dissolved into no longer existing
Preserves both the alteration, the image of dissolution, and its stated outcome of nonexistence.

SECTION 6.26

While I was discussing these things with Appion, Peter arrived from Caesarea, and crowds converged in Tyre, hurrying to meet him and thank him for coming. Appion withdrew with only Anubion and Athenodorus, but all the rest of us set out to meet Peter. I was the first to welcome him in front of the gates, and I led him to the lodging. When we arrived there, we dismissed the crowds. When he asked me to tell him what had happened, I held nothing back; instead, I reported Simon’s slanders, the monstrous apparitions he had produced, how many illnesses he had sent after the feast arising from the ox sacrifice, and that, of those who were ill, some had remained right there in Tyre, while the others had gone away with Simon to Sidon at the same time as my arrival, in expectation of being healed by him. I also reported that I had learned that none of them had obtained healing from him, and I recounted to Peter the discussion I had had with Appion. Then, to show affection and offer encouragement, he praised and blessed me. After partaking of salt, because of the exertions of the journey, he gave himself over to the most necessary rest of sleep.

Translator's notes for section 6.26 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: συνδρομαὶ τῶν ὄχλων
Rendered as: crowds converged
The phrase describes crowds running or gathering together, not merely static assemblies.

2. Translation choice — Greek: χάριν τῇ ἐπιδημίᾳ ὁμολογεῖν
Rendered as: thank him for coming
ἐπιδημία can denote an arrival, presence, or visit; the immediate context favors Peter’s coming to Tyre.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τὴν ξενίαν
Rendered as: to the lodging
ξενία may denote hospitality or guest quarters; here it functions as the destination where Peter would stay.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὰς τερατώδεις φαντασίας ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ γεγενημένας
Rendered as: the monstrous apparitions he had produced
φαντασίαι can be appearances, apparitions, or illusions; “apparitions” preserves their presented visual character without deciding whether they were real or deceptive.

5. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ὅσας ἔπεμψεν νόσους
Rendered as: how many illnesses he had sent
ὅσας preserves the emphasis on their number or extent; it could also be rendered “all the illnesses that he had sent.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: μετὰ τὴν ἐκ τῆς βουθυσίας ἑστίασιν
Rendered as: after the feast arising from the ox sacrifice
βουθυσία is an ox sacrifice, while ἐκ presents the feast as proceeding from or resulting from it; “the feast from/of the ox sacrifice” is also possible.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἅμα τῷ ἐμὲ ἐλθεῖν
Rendered as: at the same time as my arrival
The construction expresses simultaneity; the alternative “as soon as I arrived” would give it a stronger sequential force.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ θεραπευθησόμενοι
Rendered as: in expectation of being healed by him
ὡς with the future participle presents the travelers’ purpose or expectation rather than endorsing the expected healing as fact.

9. Translation choice — Greek: στοργῆς καὶ προτροπῆς χάριν
Rendered as: to show affection and offer encouragement
χάριν marks the purpose of Peter’s praise and blessing; προτροπή may also be rendered “exhortation.”

10. Translation choice — Greek: ἁλῶν μεταλαβών
Rendered as: after partaking of salt
The translation preserves the explicit salt image; the phrase may contextually imply sharing or eating food more generally.

11. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ ἀναγκαιοτάτῃ ἡσυχίᾳ τοῦ ὕπνου ἑαυτὸν ἐπέτρεπεν
Rendered as: he gave himself over to the most necessary rest of sleep
This retains the superlative force of ἀναγκαιοτάτῃ and the image of entrusting or yielding oneself to sleep.

HOMILY 7

SECTION 7.1

On the fourth day of our stay in Tyre, toward dawn, when Peter had come forward, not a few inhabitants of the neighboring places and very many from Tyre itself met him and cried out, saying, “May God have mercy on us through you; may he heal us through you.” Peter stood on a certain high stone so that he could be seen by everyone and, after greeting them in accordance with the law that reveres God, began as follows:

Translator's notes for section 7.1 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς ἐν Τύρῳ ἡμῶν ἐπιδημίας
Rendered as: of our stay in Tyre
Here ἐπιδημία denotes a temporary residence or stay, not an epidemic or an official visitation.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ τὸν ὄρθρον
Rendered as: toward dawn
The phrase locates the event near the approach of daybreak.

3. Translation choice — Greek: προεληλυθότι τῷ Πέτρῳ
Rendered as: when Peter had come forward
The perfect participle presents Peter as having gone out or come forward; “come forward” fits his subsequent public address without specifying an unmentioned building.

4. Translation choice — Greek: προσαγορεύσας θεοσεβεῖ νόμῳ
Rendered as: after greeting them in accordance with the law that reveres God
προσαγορεύω means greet or address, while the dative θεοσεβεῖ νόμῳ expresses the God-revering rule or manner governing the greeting; “with a God-revering greeting” is also possible.

SECTION 7.2

God, who created heaven and the universe, does not lack an occasion for the salvation of those who wish to be saved. Therefore, no one should rashly accuse him of lacking benevolence toward humanity, even on account of things that appear bad. For the outcomes of what happens to a human being are unknown to humans and are suspected of tending toward evil, but they are known to God as things that will turn out well. Take Simon as an immediate example: being God’s left-hand power and holding authority over those who do not know God for the purpose of doing harm, he was able to surround you with diseases. These diseases, having been permitted to arise through God’s good providence, compelled you, after you had looked around for and found the one able to heal, to accept, on the pretext of treatment of the body, the things that seem good to God and to be persuaded to set your minds on them, so that in this way, together with your bodies that are to be saved, you might also have your souls safe.

Translator's notes for section 7.2 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ λείπει πρόφασις πρὸς σωτηρίαν
Rendered as: does not lack an occasion for the salvation
“Occasion” preserves πρόφασις as grounds or an opportunity for action and also makes visible its lexical connection with the later προφάσει. In the later occurrence, bodily treatment is the ostensible basis on which the hearers accept divine instruction, so the context supports the more pointed rendering “pretext” there.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὅθεν μηδὲ ἐπὶ τοῖς δοκοῦσιν φαύλοις ὑπὸ προπετείας τις αὐτὸν ὡς μὴ φιλάνθρωπον αἰτιάσθω
Rendered as: Therefore, no one should rashly accuse him of lacking benevolence toward humanity, even on account of things that appear bad
The rendering treats ὑπὸ προπετείας as the rash manner or impulse behind the accusation and preserves the emphatic force of μηδέ with “even.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς μὴ φιλάνθρωπον
Rendered as: of lacking benevolence toward humanity
φιλάνθρωπος describes one who is humane or benevolent toward people; the rendering preserves the negation without importing a specialized theological title.

4. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτίκα γοῦν Σίμων ἀριστερὰ τοῦ θεοῦ δύναμις ὢν
Rendered as: Take Simon as an immediate example: being God’s left-hand power
αὐτίκα γοῦν introduces a concrete immediate example, and ἀριστερὰ τοῦ θεοῦ δύναμις directly identifies Simon as the left-hand power of God.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν τὸν θεὸν οὐκ εἰδότων ἐπὶ κακοποιΐᾳ τὴν ἐξουσίαν ἔχων
Rendered as: holding authority over those who do not know God for the purpose of doing harm
The genitive marks those over whom the authority operates, while ἐπὶ κακοποιΐᾳ states its harmful purpose or function.

6. Translation choice — Greek: προφάσει τῆς τοῦ σώματος θεραπείας
Rendered as: on the pretext of treatment of the body
This repeats the πρόφασις wording used earlier.
