A materially different nominal reading takes ὄναρ adverbially and denies the whole dream-apparition predicate: Thus that is no longer an apparition in a dream. This changes what is denied and affirmed and remains viable if the preceding question concerns disagreement. The unusual ἐπιφανείη is read as a noun; an optative verbal reading might appear is another morphological alternative but fits the copular sequence less readily. English interpretive punctuation does not alter the supplied spelling or punctuation of the Greek, and no missing Greek word has been restored.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ψυχῆς τὰ ἐπιγενήματα τοῖς παροῦσι φόβοις καὶ ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἀποδιδούσης τὰς ἰδέας
Rendered as: the soul's, the soul reproducing as images the effects arising from present fears and desire
The effects and images are taken as two expressions of the dream products, with present fears and desire as the circumstances generating them. A material alternative foregrounds the returning of images in response to those fears and desire: the soul giving back images of their ensuing effects. The main text preserves both the effects and the images rather than collapsing the first accusative into the fears themselves. The selected present adjective directly agrees with fears, while desire is coordinated with them.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἢ γὰρ φόβῳ τὸν νοῦν πληγεῖσα
Rendered as: Or, indeed, struck by fear in its mind
The initial or is retained as another explanatory turn rather than silently deleted. The feminine participle continues the soul, and mind expresses the respect in which fear strikes it.

6. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ δὲ ἔσται, οὕτω τὸ τοιοῦτο θεός ἐστιν
Rendered as: But if it does happen, is such a thing thereby a god?
The next demon-finger and worm examples support a rhetorical question denying that movement alone establishes divinity. The source has a full stop, so the question punctuation is interpretive. An assertion such a thing is then a god is a formal alternative, but runs against the ensuing counterexamples; the Greek words have not been changed.

7. Translation choice — Greek: πόσοις κατ’ ὄναρ ὁμοίως ἄλλοις ὤφθησαν καὶ ὕπαρ συναντήσαντες ἀλλήλοις πρὸς τὸ κατ’ ὄναρ ἀντιβάλλοντες οὐ συνεφώνησαν;
Rendered as: To how many other people have they similarly appeared in dreams—and, when those people met one another while awake and compared their dream experiences, did those people not agree?
The appearing beings are the subject of appeared; the subsequent meeting, comparing, and agreement are read with their human recipients as an understood changed subject. The main text makes that change explicit. The negative question is taken rhetorically to invite assent that the recipients agreed. A material alternative asks how many recipients did not agree, treating οὐ as actual disagreement rather than an assent-seeking question. Neither rhetorical interpretation nor the unmarked subject shift is presented as grammatically unique.

SECTION 9.16

That each person’s soul, in accordance with its preconceptions, depicts forms of demons, and that the so-called gods do not appear, is clear from the fact that they do not appear to Jews. But someone will say, “How, then, do they deliver oracles foretelling the future?” This too is false. Yet grant that it is true: does that therefore make such a thing a god? For something is not a god merely because it foretells the future. Python mediums also foretell the future, but when adjured by us as demons, they are driven away. But someone will say, “They prescribe treatments for some people.” That is false. Yet grant that this is so: does that therefore make such a thing a god? Physicians also heal many people, and they are not gods. “But,” someone says, “physicians do not invariably heal those for whom they care, whereas these both deliver an oracle and heal.” Demons, however, know the remedies actually suited to each particular ailment. Consequently, they are knowledgeable physicians capable of healing—even these ailments that human beings are capable of healing—but they are also divinatory beings and know when each ailment is cured spontaneously; at that time they prescribe the treatments, so that they may claim the credit for themselves.

Translator's notes for section 9.16 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: μαντικὰ ὄντα καὶ εἰδότα
The printed text shifts to neuter plural participial forms after the masculine subjects οἱ δαίμονες and ἰατροὶ ... δυνάμενοι. This may be an anacoluthon or may reflect an implicit neuter referent such as δαιμόνια. The translation follows the demons as the continuing semantic subject, but that interpretation remains provisional.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τὰς προλήψεις
Rendered as: in accordance with its preconceptions
πρός with the accusative indicates correspondence to each soul’s prior conceptions, according to which it depicts the demonic forms.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πύθωνες
Rendered as: Python mediums
The term denotes persons or agencies associated with a Python spirit and divination. Alternatives include “Python spirits” and “those possessed by Python.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: δεδόσθω δὲ ἀλήθειαν εἶναι, οὕτω τὸ τοιοῦτο θεός ἐστιν
Rendered as: Yet grant that it is true: does that therefore make such a thing a god?
Although the last clause is printed as a statement, the immediately following denial supports taking it as a rhetorical question: even genuine prediction would not establish divinity.

5. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ταῦτα τὰ ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων ἰαθῆναι δυνάμενα
Rendered as: even these ailments that human beings are capable of healing
The neuter ταῦτα is understood as referring to the ailments under discussion and emphasizes that they also fall within the reach of human medicine.

6. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ εἰδότα πότε ἕκαστον ἐξ αὐτομάτου θεραπεύεται
Rendered as: and know when each ailment is cured spontaneously
The neuter ἕκαστον most naturally resumes the earlier ἕκαστον πάθος, “each ailment.” A patient-focused alternative, “when each person recovers spontaneously,” is contextually possible but less directly reflects the grammatical gender and antecedent.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἵνα ἑαυτοὺς ἐπιγράψωσιν
Rendered as: so that they may claim the credit for themselves
Literally, they seek to “inscribe” themselves upon the cure, idiomatically attaching their own name or credit to it.

SECTION 9.17

For why do they announce healings by oracle only after a long time? Why, if they can do everything, do they not bring about healing without an offering? Why do they prescribe treatments for some who pray, but sometimes deliver no oracle to others who are even more closely connected with them? It is in this way: whenever a spontaneous recovery is about to occur, they make a promise so that they may claim the credit for themselves. Others fell ill and prayed, and when they recovered spontaneously, they credited those whom they had invoked and made votive offerings. Those who died after prayer, however, cannot dedicate their failures. Yet if the relatives of the dead, or some from among them, had jointly investigated the failures, you would have found the failures more numerous than the successes. But no one already prepossessed in their favor wants to expose the case against them, being ashamed or afraid. On the contrary, they join in concealing their well-attested absurdities.

Translator's notes for section 9.17 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: συνκρύβουσιν
The image-checked print has the unassimilated compound spelling συνκρύβουσιν, where συγκρύβουσιν would be the standard assimilated spelling. The printed form still yields the clear sense “conceal together” or “join in concealing.”

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἄνευ τοῦ προσφέρειν τι
Rendered as: without an offering
The substantivized infinitive means presenting something, naturally an offering in this cultic context. The more literal alternative is “without presenting anything.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: οἰκειοτέροις οὖσιν
Rendered as: who are even more closely connected with them
The comparative describes a closer relationship or affiliation, though whether familial, cultic, or generally intimate is not specified.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οἱ μέντοι γε μετὰ εὐχὴν διαφωνήσαντες
Rendered as: Those who died after prayer, however
διαφωνέω ordinarily denotes disagreement, discrepancy, or an outcome contrary to expectation, so a broader rendering would be “those whose cases turned out otherwise after prayer.” The following reference to “the relatives of the dead” strongly supports understanding it here as a euphemistic reference to those whose failed treatment ended in death.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πλὴν εἰ οἱ συγγενεῖς τῶν τεθνεώτων ἢ ἐξ αὐτῶν τινὲς συνεζήτησαν τὰς ἀποτυχίας, πλείονας ἂν εὑρήκειτε τὰς ἀποτυχίας τῶν ἐπιτευγμάτων
Rendered as: Yet if the relatives of the dead, or some from among them, had jointly investigated the failures, you would have found the failures more numerous than the successes
The aorist indicative in the condition and the pluperfect with ἄν in the result form a retrospective contrary-to-fact construction. The referent of ἐξ αὐτῶν remains open; it may indicate some among the unsuccessful supplicants or among a broader previously mentioned group.

6. Translation choice — Greek: συνεζήτησαν τὰς ἀποτυχίας
Rendered as: had jointly investigated the failures
The verb can mean jointly examine, investigate, or discuss. “Had compiled the failures” is possible in view of the subsequent numerical comparison, but “jointly investigated” more directly preserves the verb.

7. Translation choice — Greek: προειλημμένος αὐτοῖς
Rendered as: already prepossessed in their favor
The perfect participle describes someone whose judgment has already been captured or prejudiced by them. “Previously taken in by them” is an alternative.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ πιστὰ αὐτῶν ἀτοπήματα
Rendered as: their well-attested absurdities
πιστά can mean credible, reliable, or firmly established. Here it presents the absurdities as attested evidence rather than as conduct worthy of trust.

SECTION 9.18

How many also falsely claim oracular responses and cures accomplished by these images, and confirm them with oaths? How many have hired themselves out, undertaking through certain contrivances to suffer something and proclaiming it in that way, then, having been restored from their affliction by a counteracting treatment, say that the cure was revealed by an oracle, so that they may label the unfeeling thing an object of worship? How many of these objects were consecrated from the beginning by magical art, so that they might dream and give oracles? Yet over a long time these too proved discordant. How many now practice sorcery, wishing to strengthen such things? Nevertheless, if something has powers of divination or healing, that does not make it a god.

Translator's notes for section 9.18 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ὀνειροπολῇ
The former Lagarde reading is exactly ὑνερπολῇ. The selected independently image-read Dressel main-print reading is ὀνειροπολῇ, concerning dreaming or dream activity, not the unresolved former form. This is an explicitly documented public-domain primary-print variant; it is not adopted or relicensed upstream XML, a new manuscript collation, or an autograph claim. The contextual lexical alternatives remain disclosed.

2. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτῶν τὸ πάθος ἀντιπαθείᾳ ἀποκατασταθέντες
Rendered as: having been restored from their affliction by a counteracting treatment
The restoration concerns the people in respect of their affliction, not a strengthening or restoration of the affliction itself. The counteraction opposes the contrived suffering; the text does not identify a substance, remedy, or procedure, so none is supplied.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἵνα τὸ ἀναίσθητον ἐπιγράψωσιν σέβασμα
Rendered as: so that they may label the unfeeling thing an object of worship
The insensate thing is what is labeled, and object of worship is its assigned designation. The translation does not add a physical inscription or a particular dedication text.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἵνα ὀνειροπολῇ καὶ χρηματίζῃ
Rendered as: so that they might dream and give oracles
The selected first verb concerns dreaming or dealing in dreams; the second concerns giving oracular responses. Dream preserves the lexical activity as attributed to the consecrated objects without inventing a mechanism. Deal in dreams or provide dream manifestations is a material contextual alternative in the preceding account of images appearing to dreamers. The source's singular verbs with the neuter plural things are rendered by normal English plural agreement.

5. Translation choice — Greek: μακρῷ χρόνῳ καὶ ταῦτα διεφώνησεν
Rendered as: over a long time these too proved discordant
The lack of agreement or consistency is retained, without inventing a specific prediction, date, or measurable error rate.

SECTION 9.19

For God can do everything. He is good and just, showing patience toward everyone now, so that those who are willing, after regretting the evil deeds they committed and living accordingly, may, on the day when everything is judged, receive what they deserve. Therefore begin now, obeying God, the cause of good knowledge, to oppose your evil desires and thoughts, so that you may recover for yourselves the original saving religion handed down to humanity. In this way good things will immediately spring up for you; once you have received them, you will thereafter leave behind your experience of evils. But give thanks to the one who gave them, reigning forever with the King of Peace over the inexpressible good things. At present, after washing yourselves in an ever-flowing river or spring, or indeed even in the sea, with the thrice-blessed invocation, you will not only be able to drive away the spirits lurking in your innermost recesses, but—if you yourselves no longer sin and believe God without wavering—you will drive out other people’s evil spirits and fierce demons, together with their dreadful afflictions. Sometimes, however, they will flee when you merely yield. For they recognize those who have given themselves to God, and therefore, showing them honor, they flee in fear. Just as yesterday you saw how, when I had put off praying for those who were suffering until after the discourse, the afflictions themselves cried aloud because of the honor paid to the religion, unable to endure for even a short time.

Translator's notes for section 9.19 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: μεταμεληθέντες
Rendered as: after regretting
The verb denotes regret or a changed concern regarding the evils committed. It is kept distinct from the μετανοέω terminology governed by the reorientation policy.

2. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ πολιτευσάμενοι
Rendered as: and living accordingly
πολιτεύομαι concerns conducting one’s life. “Accordingly” expresses the contextual connection with regret; the more formally literal alternative is “and having conducted their lives.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀγαθῆς γνώσεως αἰτίᾳ θεῷ πειθόμενοι
Rendered as: obeying God, the cause of good knowledge
The dative αἰτίᾳ is taken in apposition to θεῷ, identifying God as the cause of good knowledge. Other possible attachments are “because of good knowledge, obeying God” and “for the sake of good knowledge, obeying God.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν πρώτην τῇ ἀνθρωπότητι παραδοθεῖσαν σωτήριον θρησκείαν
Rendered as: the original saving religion handed down to humanity
πρώτην characterizes the religion as first or original, while σωτήριον describes it as saving. The wording preserves the author’s historical claim without harmonization.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἅτινα λαβόντες πεῖραν τῶν κακῶν τοῦ λοιποῦ καταλείψετε
Rendered as: once you have received them, you will thereafter leave behind your experience of evils
The chosen attachment takes ἅτινα, referring to the good things, as the object of λαβόντες and πεῖραν τῶν κακῶν as the object of καταλείψετε. A grammatically possible alternative joins λαβόντες πεῖραν τῶν κακῶν, “having experienced evils,” and takes ἅτινα as the object of καταλείψετε: “which, after experiencing evils, you will thereafter leave behind.” That alternative would make the promised good things what is abandoned and is therefore contextually difficult.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τῇ τρισμακαρίᾳ ἐπονομασίᾳ
Rendered as: with the thrice-blessed invocation
ἐπονομασία can mean naming, designation, or invocation. In the washing context, “invocation” conveys an enacted naming formula without supplying words not quoted in the source.

7. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ μόνον τὰ ἐνδομυχοῦντα ὑμῖν πνεύματα ἀπελάσαι δυνήσεσθε, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτοὶ μηκέτι ἁμαρτάνοντες καὶ θεῷ ἀνενδοιάστως πιστεύοντες τὰ ἄλλων κακὰ πνεύματα καὶ δαιμόνια χαλεπὰ σὺν τοῖς δεινοῖς πάθεσιν ἀπελάσετε
Rendered as: you will not only be able to drive away the spirits lurking in your innermost recesses, but—if you yourselves no longer sin and believe God without wavering—you will drive out other people’s evil spirits and fierce demons, together with their dreadful afflictions
The first member explicitly expresses ability with ἀπελάσαι δυνήσεσθε, whereas the second uses the direct future ἀπελάσετε. The English therefore does not extend “be able” over the second expulsion.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ ἐνδομυχοῦντα ὑμῖν πνεύματα
Rendered as: the spirits lurking in your innermost recesses
ἐνδομυχέω depicts dwelling or hiding deep within and preserves the source’s spatial image.

9. Translation choice — Greek: μόνον ἐνδόντων ὑμῶν
Rendered as: when you merely yield
The genitive absolute uses ἐνδίδωμι in the intransitive sense “yield” or “give way.” In context it may mean yielding oneself to God, as the following clause about self-dedication suggests; “when you merely consent” or “when you merely permit it” remains possible.

10. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτὰ τὰ πάθη τῇ πρὸς τὴν θρησκείαν τιμῇ ἀνέκραγεν
Rendered as: the afflictions themselves cried aloud
The neuter plural subject takes a singular verb, a regular Greek construction. The personification, or identification of the afflictions with their spiritual agents, is preserved rather than explained away.

11. Translation choice — Greek: ἐμοῦ ἀναθεμένου μετὰ τὴν προσομιλίαν εὔξασθαι ὑπὲρ τῶν πασχόντων
Rendered as: when I had put off praying for those who were suffering until after the discourse
The main text takes ἀναθεμένου as postponing or reserving the prayer and attaches after the discourse to its intended time. This fits the following inability of the afflictions to endure even the brief delay. A material alternative takes the verb as undertaking: when after the discourse I undertook to pray for those who were suffering. That places the undertaking after the discourse rather than depicting the prayer as deferred. Both lexical and temporal choices are disclosed; the verified Greek has not been corrected.

12. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτὰ τὰ πάθη τῇ πρὸς τὴν θρησκείαν τιμῇ ἀνέκραγεν
Rendered as: the afflictions themselves cried aloud because of the honor paid to the religion
The main causal dative leaves the source of the honor unexpressed. A material alternative is cried aloud out of respect for the religion, taking the afflictions or their spiritual agents themselves as showing reverence, supported by the immediately preceding demons showing honor. Neither identifies a new explicit honor-giver, and the personification of the afflictions remains intact.

SECTION 9.20

Therefore, do not suppose that we are unafraid of demons because we are of a different nature. For we are of the same nature as you, though not of the same religion. Consequently, being superior to you not merely by much but altogether, we do not begrudge your becoming such people; on the contrary, we counsel you to do so, knowing that all these beings, in an uncomprehending way, hold in special regard and fear those who have become closely allied with God.

Translator's notes for section 9.20 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἡμεῖς ἄλλης φύσεως ὄντες κατὰ τοῦτο δαίμονας οὐ φοβούμεθα
Rendered as: we are unafraid of demons because we are of a different nature
The warning rejects a proposed explanation of their fearlessness, not necessarily the claim that they are unafraid: their freedom from fear comes from religion rather than a different nature.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς γὰρ αὐτῆς ὑμῖν ἐσμὲν φύσεως, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ θρησκείας
Rendered as: For we are of the same nature as you, though not of the same religion
The second genitive is elliptical, contrasting shared human nature with differing religion or worship.

3. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ πολύ, ἀλλὰ τὸ πᾶν κρείττονες
Rendered as: superior to you not merely by much but altogether
The compressed expression is literally “not much, but the whole/altogether.” The rendering treats it as a rhetorical escalation beyond superiority by degree to comprehensive superiority. “Not by much, but in every respect superior” is a more formally literal but potentially contradictory-sounding alternative; no correction of the printed πολύ is warranted.

4. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ὑμᾶς τοιούτους γενέσθαι οὐ φθονοῦμεν
Rendered as: we do not begrudge your becoming such people
τοιούτους refers to becoming people of the religious standing just described, while φθονέω means begrudging or envying another’s acquisition of that standing.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς θεῷ προσοικειωθέντας
Rendered as: those who have become closely allied with God
προσοικειόω denotes being brought into close relationship or affinity. Alternatives include “those made God’s own” and “those who have drawn near to God.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: ταῦτα πάντα ἀγνώστως προτιμᾷ καὶ φοβεῖται
Rendered as: all these beings, in an uncomprehending way, hold in special regard and fear
The neuter plural collectively refers to the demonic beings or powers under discussion and takes singular Greek verbs. ἀγνώστως may mean “unknowingly,” “without understanding,” or “in an inexplicable manner.” The chosen wording allows the beings to recognize God’s people, as stated previously, without necessarily understanding their standing or authority.

SECTION 9.21

For just as the soldiers subordinate to one of Caesar’s commanders of a thousand know, because of the authority of the one who granted it, to honor the person who received it—so fully that those set over them can say to one, “Come,” and he comes, and to another, “Go,” and he goes—so also the person who has given himself to God—faithful as he is—merely speaks to demons and afflictions and is obeyed; and demons withdraw, though they are much stronger than those commanding them. For by an inexpressible power God subjects each person’s mind to whomever he wishes. For just as many governors, together with all their camps and cities, have feared Caesar, although he is a man, while each person’s heart hastens to give precedence to the image of all things (for all things, enslaved by God’s will, do not know the cause because of fear), so all the spirits that produce affliction honor and flee the person who takes refuge in God and carries righteous faith in his own heart as though it were God’s image, having become afraid through some natural way.

Translator's notes for section 9.21 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: (πιστὸς ὢν δαίμοσίν τε καὶ πάθεσιν) μόνον λέγων ἀκούεται
The printed parentheses group δαίμοσίν τε καὶ πάθεσιν with πιστός, which could yield the contextually difficult sense “faithful/trustworthy to demons and afflictions.” The translation instead construes those datives with λέγων across the editorial parenthesis: the faithful person speaks to demons and afflictions and is obeyed. Another possible reading is that he is recognized as trustworthy by them.

2. Translation choice — Greek: Καίσαρος χιλιάρχῳ
Rendered as: one of Caesar’s commanders of a thousand
χιλίαρχος literally denotes a commander of a thousand; the expanded rendering translates the office rather than merely transliterating it.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς ἐφεστῶτας
Rendered as: those set over them
The participle can denote people placed in authority; “those standing by” is also lexically possible, but the command structure favors the former.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἀφράστῳ γὰρ δυνάμει τὸν ἑκάστου νοῦν ὁ θεὸς ὑποτάσσει ᾧ βούλεται
Rendered as: For by an inexpressible power God subjects each person’s mind to whomever he wishes
The dative relative ᾧ is taken personally as “whomever”; “to whatever he wishes” remains grammatically possible but fits the comparison with delegated personal authority less well.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν τῶν ὅλων εἰκόνα
Rendered as: the image of all things
The referent of the image is not explicitly identified. The genitive may also be represented as “of the whole” or “of the universe,” so the translation does not identify the image specifically with Caesar or with God.

6. Translation choice — Greek: θεοῦ γὰρ βουλῇ τὰ πάντα δεδουλωμένα φόβῳ τὴν αἰτίαν οὐκ οἶδεν
Rendered as: for all things, enslaved by God’s will, do not know the cause because of fear
θεοῦ βουλῇ is taken instrumentally with δεδουλωμένα and φόβῳ causally with οὐκ οἶδεν. Alternatively, φόβῳ could mean that all things are “enslaved to fear.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ παθοποιὰ πνεύματα
Rendered as: the spirits that produce affliction
πάθος can denote suffering, illness, or passion. “Affliction” retains a range broad enough for the surrounding healing and demonic context.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ὥσπερ εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ ἐν τῇ αὐτοῦ βαστάζοντα καρδίᾳ
Rendered as: carries righteous faith in his own heart as though it were God’s image
The first αὐτοῦ is understood as referring to God and the second reflexively to the person taking refuge in God; the Greek itself uses the same pronoun for both.

SECTION 9.22

But nevertheless, even if all demons together with all afflictions flee from you, you must not rejoice in this alone, but in the fact that, because you have proved pleasing, your names have been inscribed in heaven as those of people who live forever. Thus the divine Holy Spirit too rejoices because a human being has conquered death; for the expulsion of demons takes place for someone else’s healing. We say these things, however, not as people who deny the claim that there is no need to help others, but because one must not grow conceited over this and neglect oneself. Sometimes demons flee some lawless men because of an honored name, and both the one who drove them away and the one who witnessed what happened are ambushed. The one who drove them away is ambushed as though he had been favored because of righteousness, not knowing the demon’s villainy (for the demon has both honored the name and, by its flight, wrapped the impious man in a conceit of righteousness and deceived him into not repenting); but the one who witnessed what happened, having associated with the one who drove them away as with a devout man and having hastened toward the same way of life, perishes. At times they also pretend to flee oaths not connected with God, so that, after deceiving them, they may destroy them whenever they wish.

Translator's notes for section 9.22 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἀλλ᾽. ὅμως
The printed period separates the elided conjunction ἀλλ᾽ from ὅμως, leaving ἀλλ᾽ abruptly isolated. The translation reads the two together as “But nevertheless” while retaining both words.

2. Greek: οὐχ ὡς ἀρνούμενοι τὸ μὴ δεῖν ἄλλοις βοηθεῖν
As printed, the nested negatives mean “not as denying the claim that there is no need to help others,” and that sense is retained in the translation. It is contextually awkward because the following clause warns only against neglecting oneself, and an intrusive μή may be suspected. The surviving wording nevertheless permits a defensible literal translation.

3. Translation choice — Greek: δι᾽ εὐαρεστίαν
Rendered as: because you have proved pleasing
εὐαρεστία denotes being pleasing or acceptable. God is the likely implied evaluator, but the Greek does not state the referent explicitly.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ θεῖον ἅγιον πνεῦμα
Rendered as: the divine Holy Spirit
The article and paired adjectives present the spirit as the divine holy spirit in view; capitalization reflects the personal theological referent without adding a title absent from the wording.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ ἱστορήσας
Rendered as: the one who witnessed what happened
ἱστορέω can mean to observe, investigate, inquire about, visit, or recount. Here it denotes the person who learns of or observes the expulsion and consequently treats the exorcist as devout.

6. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς οἴησιν δικαιοσύνης περιβαλὼν
Rendered as: wrapped the impious man in a conceit of righteousness
The rendering preserves the clothing or enveloping image of περιβάλλω; οἴησις may mean an opinion, supposition, or conceited belief.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ μὴ μετανοεῖν ἠπάτησεν
Rendered as: deceived him into not repenting
The articular infinitive expresses the result sought by the deception: the impious man’s conceit of righteousness keeps him from the moral response he needs. Repenting fits that context under the October 13 policy, with the negative retained; this is not an adverse change of mind that calls for a reconsideration exception. Repentance here implies changed disposition and conduct, not mere remorse, but no stronger requirement or Godward formula is added. The earlier reorienting wording is preserved in its prior record.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς μὴ θεῷ προσκειμένους ὅρκους
Rendered as: oaths not connected with God
The participle grammatically modifies ὅρκους and describes oaths not attached or devoted to God. Context may imply “oaths used by people not devoted to God,” but those people are not explicitly named in this phrase.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἵν’ ἀπατήσαντες αὐτοὺς ὅτε θελήσωσιν ἀνέλωσιν
Rendered as: so that, after deceiving them, they may destroy them whenever they wish
The repeated masculine pronoun is preserved without supplying an explicit antecedent. It most plausibly concerns the people relying on the oaths, though grammatically it can refer back to the masculine plural ὅρκους.

SECTION 9.23

So then, we want you to know this too: unless someone willingly gives himself over as a servant to demons (as I said earlier), the demon has no authority against him. Therefore, having chosen to worship one God, having abstained from the “table of demons,” having embraced self-control together with benevolence and righteousness, and having been baptized with the thrice-blessed invocation for the forgiveness of sins, by devoting yourselves as much as you can toward the perfection of purity, you can, once rescued from everlasting punishment, become heirs of eternal good things. After saying this, he ordered those troubled by afflictions to come forward. And so many, having gathered together on the evidence of those who had been healed the day before, came forward. He laid his hands on them and prayed, healing them at once; then, after instructing them and the others to assemble earlier in the morning, he himself bathed, took food, and went to sleep.

Translator's notes for section 9.23 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἑαυτὸν δαίμοσιν δοῦλον ἐκδῴη
Rendered as: gives himself over as a servant to demons
δοῦλος is rendered “servant” under the supplied policy, while ἐκδίδωμι conveys voluntary surrender into the demons’ ownership and control.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς τάχιον εἶπον
Rendered as: as I said earlier
The comparative adverb τάχιον can mean “more quickly,” but in references to prior speech it naturally means “earlier” or “a little while ago.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: σωφροσύνην μετὰ φιλανθρωπίας καὶ δικαιοσύνης
Rendered as: self-control together with benevolence and righteousness
σωφροσύνη can include sound-minded restraint, temperance, or chastity; φιλανθρωπία denotes humane love or benevolence; δικαιοσύνη can also be rendered “justice.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: τρισμακαρίᾳ ἐπονομασίᾳ
Rendered as: the thrice-blessed invocation
ἐπονομασία can denote an invocation, naming, or appellation. “Invocation” fits baptismal use, but the Greek does not spell out the invoked wording.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ ὅσον δύνασθε ἐπὶ τὸ τέλειον τῆς ἁγνείας ἑαυτοὺς ἐπιδιδόναι
Rendered as: by devoting yourselves as much as you can toward the perfection of purity
The articular infinitive is taken instrumentally with δύνασθε. ἁγνεία may denote purity generally or chastity specifically.

6. Translation choice — Greek: κολάσεως αἰδίου ῥυσθέντες αἰωνίων ἀγαθῶν κληρονόμοι
Rendered as: once rescued from everlasting punishment, become heirs of eternal good things
Different English terms preserve the source’s distinction between ἀΐδιος, “everlasting,” and αἰώνιος, “eternal,” without asserting that the author intended sharply different durations.

7. Translation choice — Greek: πείρᾳ τῶν ἐχθὲς θεραπευθέντων
Rendered as: on the evidence of those who had been healed the day before
πείρᾳ can refer to experience, proof, or the evidentiary effect of what was experienced; the healed people supplied the reason others gathered.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ὀρθριαίτερον συνεδρεύειν
Rendered as: to assemble earlier in the morning
ὀρθριαίτερον is a comparative referring to an earlier morning hour, while συνεδρεύω literally means to sit together and can denote meeting or assembling.

HOMILY 10

SECTION 10.1

On the third day in Tripolis, then, Peter rose from sleep rather early and entered the garden, where there was a large reservoir into which abundant water flowed continuously. There he bathed; then, after praying in this way, he sat down. Realizing that we were sitting around him and gazing intently at him as though we wanted to hear something, he said:

Translator's notes for section 10.1 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὀρθριαίτερον
Rendered as: rather early
The comparative adverb indicates an earlier-than-usual or notably early hour; “earlier in the morning” is also possible.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὑδροχοεῖον μέγα
Rendered as: a large reservoir
The noun denotes a receptacle or reservoir for water; “large water basin” is a viable alternative.

3. Translation choice — Greek: εἶθ’ οὕτως εὐξάμενος
Rendered as: then, after praying in this way
οὕτως most naturally qualifies the praying as “thus/in this way,” though it may function more loosely as a sequential “thereupon.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἡμᾶς δὲ περικαθεζομένους
Rendered as: we were sitting around him
The participle portrays the group seated around Peter; the object “him” is supplied from the immediate context.

SECTION 10.2

“There seems to me to be a great difference between the ignorant and those who have gone astray. For the ignorant person seems to me to resemble a man who chose not to set out for a flourishing city because he did not know the good things there, whereas the person who has gone astray resembles one who learned of the city’s good things but, while setting out along the road, turned aside from the path and therefore wanders. In the same way, then, there seems to me to be a great difference between those who worship idols and those who wander in the worship of God. For those who worship idols are ignorant of eternal life (and for that reason they do not even desire it, since they cannot love what they do not know); but those who have chosen to worship the one God and have learned that eternal life is given to the good, if they either believe or do anything contrary to what God approves, resemble those who have left the city of punishment but to come to the flourishing city ... and who, while on the road, have strayed from the straight way.”

Translator's notes for section 10.2 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: εἰς τὴν εὐθηνουμένην ... καὶ
The selected image-checked edition prints exactly three dots here, marking a lacuna that disrupts the construction after “to come to the flourishing city.” The unavailable content has not been restored, and the three printed dots are retained in the translation.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν ἀγνοούντων πρὸς τοὺς πεπλανημένους
Rendered as: between the ignorant and those who have gone astray
The contrast is between lack of knowledge and deviation after acquiring knowledge; “those who have been misled” is also grammatically possible for the perfect passive form.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπ’ εὐθηνουμένην πόλιν
Rendered as: for a flourishing city
The participle describes a city prospering or thriving; “prosperous city” is an alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τρίβον παραλλάξαντι
Rendered as: turned aside from the path
The phrase depicts deviation from or missing the traveled track; “passed by the path” is more formally possible but less suitable to the ensuing wandering.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς ἐν θεοσεβείᾳ ἀλωμένους
Rendered as: those who wander in the worship of God
θεοσέβεια can denote worship of God, reverence for God, or piety; “worship of God” best preserves the contrast with idol worship.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ δοκοῦντα τῷ θεῷ
Rendered as: what God approves
The expression denotes what seems right or acceptable to God; “what seems right to God” is a more formally transparent alternative.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ τῆς εὐθείας πλανηθεῖσιν
Rendered as: who, while on the road, have strayed from the straight way
The genitive τῆς εὐθείας is taken with πλανηθεῖσιν as what they strayed from, while ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ supplies the setting. An attachment yielding “on the road of the straight way” is possible but less idiomatic.

SECTION 10.3

While he was discussing these things with us, one of our people came in—the man appointed to report such matters to him—and said, “Large crowds, my lord Peter, are standing before the doors.” When he gave permission, a large crowd came in. Peter rose, took his place on the platform used the day before, greeted them according to the custom of reverence for God, and said: “The human being, having come into being in the image and likeness of God—the God who created heaven and earth and made everything in them, as the true prophet told us—was appointed to rule and exercise dominion. I mean over the things in the air, on the earth, and in the waters. From the fact itself one can perceive that by his own intelligence he brings down the things in the air, brings up the things in the depths, and captures the things on the earth, even though they are far stronger than he is—I mean elephants, lions, and things like them.”

Translator's notes for section 10.3 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ ἐπὶ τῷ ἀπαγγέλλειν αὐτῷ τὰ τοιαῦτα καθεστηκὼς
Rendered as: the man appointed to report such matters to him
καθεστηκώς indicates that this person had been assigned or established in the reporting role.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ ἐχθὲς βάσει
Rendered as: the platform used the day before
βάσις may denote a base, stand, or raised platform; the context of public speaking favors “platform.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ τῆς θεοσεβείας ἔθει προσαγορεύσας
Rendered as: greeted them according to the custom of reverence for God
προσαγορεύω denotes addressing or greeting, while θεοσέβεια may also be rendered “piety” or “worship of God.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: κατ’ εἰκόνα καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν γεγονὼς
Rendered as: having come into being in the image and likeness of God
κατά expresses correspondence to an image and likeness; “according to the image and likeness” is a more formally literal alternative.

5. Translation choice — Greek: κατ’ ἀλκὴν αὐτοῦ πολλῷ μείζονα ὄντα
Rendered as: even though they are far stronger than he is
Literally, the animals are “much greater than he in strength”; the chosen wording gives that comparison idiomatic English without reducing its force.

SECTION 10.4

“Yet when he was righteous, he was also above every suffering, since, with an immortal body, he was incapable of experiencing pain. But when he sinned (as we showed yesterday and the day before), he became a servant of sin and fell under every suffering, deprived by a just judgment of all good things. For it was not reasonable that, when the giver had been abandoned, the things given should remain with the ungrateful. Therefore, out of his surpassing compassion, so that, along with the original good things, we might also receive the eternal good things to come, he sent his prophet. The prophet commanded us to speak to you—to tell you what you must think and do. Make your choice, then; that lies within your power. What you must think, then, is this: to worship the God who made everything. If you apprehend him with your mind, you will receive from him, along with the original good things, the eternal good things to come.”

Translator's notes for section 10.4 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: πάντων παθημάτων ἀνώτατος
Rendered as: above every suffering
πάθημα here denotes suffering or affliction, as the following reference to pain indicates; “beyond all sufferings” is an alternative.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς δοῦλος γεγονὼς τῆς ἁμαρτίας
Rendered as: he became a servant of sin
The wording portrays subjection and belonging to sin. “Slave of sin” makes the ownership nuance more explicit, while the stipulated default renders δοῦλος as “servant.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἅμα τοῖς πρώτοις
Rendered as: along with the original good things
The substantivized adjective refers to the former or first good things of which humanity had been deprived; “the former good things” is also possible.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐλέσθε οὖν, ὃ ἐπὶ τῇ ὑμετέρᾳ κεῖται ἐξουσίᾳ
Rendered as: Make your choice, then; that lies within your power
The relative clause is taken as referring to the act of choosing. It could instead be construed as “choose what lies within your power.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν πάντα πεποιηκότα σέβειν θεόν
Rendered as: to worship the God who made everything
The delayed θεόν is taken with the substantival participle. The syntax can also be represented as “to worship as God the one who made everything.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὃν ἂν ἀπολάβητε τῷ νῷ, ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ ἀπολήψεσθε
Rendered as: If you apprehend him with your mind, you will receive from him
The first ἀπολαμβάνω is understood as mentally grasping or apprehending because of τῷ νῷ, while the second means receiving from God. “When you take hold of him with your mind” is a viable alternative.

SECTION 10.5

“You will therefore be able to persuade yourselves to do what benefits you if, as though chanting an incantation to the fearsome serpent nesting in your heart, you say, ‘You shall fear the Lord God, and you shall serve him alone.’ By every line of reasoning, then, it is beneficial to fear him alone, not as unjust, but as just. For one fears an unjust person lest one be unjustly killed, and the just one lest, after being caught in sin, one be punished. Through fear of him, then, you can be freed from many harmful fears. For if you do not fear the one Lord and Maker of all, you will be servants of all evils, to your own harm—I mean demons, sufferings, and everything capable of causing harm in any way whatever.”

Translator's notes for section 10.5 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ᾡδήτινι
The selected edition prints this as a single, unusually accented and undivided sequence. In context it is defensibly understood as the relative-plus-particle expression meaning “in any way whatever”; this is an orthographic or word-division issue rather than an unreadable construction.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πεῖσαι οὖν ἑαυτοὺς πρὸς τὰ συμφέροντα
Rendered as: persuade yourselves to do what benefits you
The πρός phrase expresses movement toward beneficial things. “Bring yourselves around to what is beneficial” is a closer structural alternative but less direct in English.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ ἐμφωλεύοντι ἐν τῇ ὑμετέρᾳ καρδίᾳ δεινῷ ὄφει
Rendered as: the fearsome serpent nesting in your heart
ἐμφωλεύω depicts making a lair or dwelling within, while δεινός here conveys the serpent’s fearsome or terrible character.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὥσπερ ἐπᾴδοντες
Rendered as: as though chanting an incantation
ἐπᾴδω refers to singing or reciting a charm over or to someone or something; “casting a spell” is a possible but less source-transparent rendering.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν δίκαιον
Rendered as: the just one
In context this most naturally refers to God as the just one, contrasting him with an unjust person. Grammatically, “a just person” remains possible.

6. Translation choice — Greek: πάντων τῶν κακῶν δοῦλοι
Rendered as: servants of all evils
The phrase expresses subjection to every evil. “Slaves of all evils” would foreground the ownership and bondage force of δοῦλοι.

7. Translation choice — Greek: δαιμόνων καὶ παθημάτων
Rendered as: demons, sufferings
πάθημα continues the sense of suffering or affliction found in the preceding section; “passions” is lexically possible but less consistent with the immediate discussion of harmful experiences.

SECTION 10.6

Take courage, then, and approach God—you who were made at the beginning to rule and exercise lordship over everything, who have his image in the body and likewise possess in the mind the likeness of will. Since, then, by doing things resembling irrational animals you lost from your soul the soul of a human being, you became like pigs and became what demons ask for. If, then, you accept God’s law, you become human beings. For it is not possible to say to irrational animals, “You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal,” and the rest. Therefore, do not begrudge yourselves entering your original nobility when you are called back to it. For it is possible. If you become like God through good deeds, then, having been reckoned his sons because of the likeness, you will be able to be restored as masters of everything.

Translator's notes for section 10.6 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἐκ τῆς ψυχῆς τὴν ἀνθρώπου ψυχὴν ἀπωλέσατε
The repetition of ψυχή produces the semantically unusual statement “you lost from your soul the soul of a human being.” The supplied reading is translatable and has been preserved rather than silently changed, though rhetorical paradox or textual disturbance remains possible.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐπὶ τῷ πάντων ἄρχειν καὶ κυριεύειν γεγενημένοι
Rendered as: made at the beginning to rule and exercise lordship over everything
Treats τὴν ἀρχήν temporally and preserves the distinction between ἄρχειν and κυριεύειν.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν τῷ νῷ τῆς γνώμης τὴν ὁμοιότητα
Rendered as: possess in the mind the likeness of will
γνώμη can denote will, disposition, purpose, or judgment. “Will” fits the contrast between bodily image and mental or volitional likeness without adding an explicit possessive absent from the phrase.

4. Translation choice — Greek: δαιμόνων αἰτήματα ἐγένεσθε
Rendered as: became what demons ask for
Literally, “became requests of demons.” The contextual rendering treats αἰτήματα as the objects requested, likely invoking demons’ request concerning pigs; “became demons’ demands” is another possible rendering.

5. Translation choice — Greek: μὴ φθονέσητε ἑαυτοῖς
Rendered as: do not begrudge yourselves
Preserves the reflexive force and the sense of withholding a good from oneself.

6. Translation choice — Greek: πάντων δεσπόται ἀποκαταστῆναι
Rendered as: be restored as masters of everything
Takes πάντων with δεσπόται and retains the restoration motif established earlier in the section.

SECTION 10.7

Begin, then, to strip off the harmful fears of empty idols, so that you may escape unjust slavery. For they have become your masters, though they are useless to you even as servants. I mean the material of the lifeless statues, which are of no use even in serving you. For it neither hears nor sees nor perceives; indeed, it cannot even move. Or does any of you wish to see as it sees, to hear as it hears, and to perceive and move? But far be it to insult any human being at all with such an insult, one who carries God’s image around, even if he has lost the likeness.

Translator's notes for section 10.7 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἀποδύεσθαι τῶν κενῶν εἰδώλων τοὺς ἐπιβλαβεῖς φόβους
Rendered as: strip off the harmful fears of empty idols
Preserves the clothing metaphor in ἀποδύεσθαι and allows the genitive to identify the idols that occasion or receive the fears.

2. Translation choice — Greek: οἳ καὶ εἰς δούλους ὑμῖν ἄχρηστοι τυγχάνουσιν
Rendered as: though they are useless to you even as servants
The idols are contrasted with the mastery wrongly granted to them: they would be useless even in the subordinate role of servants.

3. Translation choice — Greek: λέγω δὲ περὶ ὕλης
Rendered as: I mean the material
The singular pronouns in the following sentence naturally refer to ὕλη, the statue’s inert material, rather than to the preceding plural statues.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οὕτως ὁρᾶν ὡς ὁρᾷ καὶ ἀκούειν ὡς ἀκούει
Rendered as: to see as it sees, to hear as it hears
Retains the deliberately absurd comparison with the sight and hearing of insensible material.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπείη τοιαύτῃ λοιδορίᾳ λοιδορεῖν πάνθ’ ὁντινοῦν ἄνθρωπον
Rendered as: far be it to insult any human being at all with such an insult
Preserves the emphatic repudiation, the repetition of the λοιδορία word group, and the comprehensive force of πάνθ’ ὁντινοῦν.

SECTION 10.8

Restore, at any rate, your gods—those of gold and silver, or those made from any other material—to their original nature: to bowls, I mean, and basins and all the other things that can be useful in serving you. And these good things, given to you from the beginning, will be able to be restored to you. But perhaps you will say, “The laws of those in authority do not permit us to do this.” Good! It is laws, and not the nonexistent power of the vain objects of worship themselves. How, then, have you regarded as gods those who are defended by human laws, guarded by dogs, and secured by bars? And this is so if they are of gold, silver, or bronze; for the stone or earthenware ones are protected by their lack of value, because no human being desires to steal a stone or earthenware god. Thus your gods made from more costly material are exposed to great danger. How, then, are they even gods when they are stolen, melted down, weighed, and hammered?

Translator's notes for section 10.8 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὴν πρώτην αὐτῶν φύσιν ἀποκαταστήσατε
Rendered as: restore ... to their original nature
The statues’ materials are to be returned to their prior, useful forms, preserving both φύσις and the restoration language.

2. Translation choice — Greek: εἴς τε φιάλας λέγω καὶ λεκάνας
Rendered as: to bowls, I mean, and basins
φιάλη denotes a broad or shallow bowl, while λεκάνη denotes a basin; λέγω marks the author’s clarification.

3. Translation choice — Greek: οἱ τῶν ἐφεστώτων νόμοι
Rendered as: the laws of those in authority
ἐφεστῶτες are those standing over others, hence rulers or authorities; the less specific rendering preserves the source’s formulation.

4. Translation choice — Greek: καλῶς ὅτι Νόμοι, καὶ οὐκ αὐτῶν τῶν εἰκαίων σεβασμάτων ἡ μὴ οὖσα δύναμις
Rendered as: Good! It is laws, and not the nonexistent power of the vain objects of worship themselves
The compressed retort contrasts the actual restraint of civil laws with the nonexistent power of the objects being revered. εἰκαῖος can mean vain, idle, or groundless.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ ἀνθρωπίνων νόμων ἐκδικουμένους
Rendered as: defended by human laws
ἐκδικέω in the passive can mean avenged, vindicated, or protected. “Defended” best fits laws preventing the statues’ destruction or removal.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ γὰρ λίθινα ἢ ὀστράκινα
Rendered as: the stone or earthenware ones
ὀστράκινος denotes material made from fired clay or earthenware, not merely an object shaped like a shell.

7. Translation choice — Greek: κλεπτόμενοι, χωνευόμενοι, σταθμιζόμενοι, σφυρούμενοι
Rendered as: stolen, melted down, weighed, and hammered
Preserves all four passive participles and the sequence of actions to which valuable metal images are subjected.

SECTION 10.9

Ah, the minds of wretched human beings, afraid of things deader than corpses! For I cannot even call things that have never lived dead—unless, that is, they are tombs of ancient people. Sometimes someone arriving in unfamiliar places does not know whether the temples he sees are memorials of dead men or of the so-called gods. But after asking and hearing that they belong to gods, he worships, without being ashamed that, if he had not learned by inquiry, he would have passed one by as a dead man’s monument because of the exact resemblance. Still, I need not contribute toward an extensive demonstration concerning superstition of this kind. For anyone willing to understand can easily grasp that it is nothing—unless someone does not see. Nevertheless, at least now hear that it does not hear, and understand that it does not understand. For the hands of a man who died “made” it. And if the one who made it came to his end, how will what came into being through him not be dissolved? Why, then, do you worship a mortal’s work, when it is entirely without sensation and people who possess reason do not even worship animals or pay court to the elements made by God—I mean heaven, sun, moon, stars, earth, sea, and everything in them—but correctly judge that they should not worship the things made by him, but should revere God, the creator and provider of these things? For these things themselves also rejoice in this: that no one has attached to them the honor belonging to the one who made them.

Translator's notes for section 10.9 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: εἰ μὴ ἐκτὸς τάφοι ἀρχαίων ἀνθρώπων εἰσίν
The combination εἰ μὴ ἐκτός is unusually redundant as an exceptive expression. A defensible emphatic reading is available, so the supplied text is retained without conjectural correction.

2. Greek: πλὴν οὐ χρή με πρὸς τὴν τῆς τοιαύτης δεισιδαιμονίας πολλὴν παρέχειν ἀπόδειξιν
The printed order places πρός before an accusative phrase extending through ἀπόδειξιν, although παρέχειν can elsewhere take ἀπόδειξιν directly as its object. The translation provisionally takes παρέχειν absolutely, “contribute,” with the πρός phrase expressing the goal. The syntax is compressed and alternative construals such as “contribute toward an extensive exposition concerning this kind of superstition” remain possible, but no correction of the supplied text is required for a defensible translation.

3. Translation choice — Greek: νεκρῶν νεκρότερα
Rendered as: deader than corpses
The comparative image is retained; νεκροί here naturally denotes dead persons or corpses rather than abstractly “the dead.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ μὴ ἐκτὸς τάφοι ἀρχαίων ἀνθρώπων εἰσίν
Rendered as: unless, that is, they are tombs of ancient people
Treats the stacked exceptive wording εἰ μὴ ἐκτός as emphatic. The alternative “unless perhaps” gives a similar contextual sense.

5. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τὸ ἴσον τῆς ὁμοιότητος
Rendered as: because of the exact resemblance
Literally referring to the equality of the likeness, the phrase stresses that a temple and a tomb are indistinguishable in appearance.

6. Translation choice — Greek: πλὴν οὐ χρή με πρὸς τὴν τῆς τοιαύτης δεισιδαιμονίας πολλὴν παρέχειν ἀπόδειξιν
Rendered as: Still, I need not contribute toward an extensive demonstration concerning superstition of this kind
Takes παρέχειν absolutely as “contribute” and πρὸς with the accusative phrase ending in ἀπόδειξιν as expressing the goal. The genitive τῆς τοιαύτης δεισιδαιμονίας identifies the demonstration’s subject matter. “Contribute toward an extensive exposition of superstition of this kind” is a viable alternative; the construction does not explicitly express proof “against” superstition.

7. Translation choice — Greek: πλὴν κἂν νῦν ἄκουσον
Rendered as: Nevertheless, at least now hear
In this exhortation κἄν has the concessive-minimal force “at least,” rather than introducing a full conditional clause.

8. Translation choice — Greek: χεῖρες γὰρ αὐτὸ θανόντος ἀνθρώπου „ἐποίησαν“
Rendered as: the hands of a man who died “made” it
Preserves the source’s quotation marking around the rendering of ἐποίησαν alone, while rendering the singular object αὐτό outside the quotation marks.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ὁπότε οἱ λογισμοὺς ἔχοντες
Rendered as: when ... people who possess reason
The clause is attached to the preceding rhetorical question as a contrasting circumstance. It could instead be presented as a loosely independent “seeing that” or “whereas” sentence; the edition’s punctuation does not require emendation.

10. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδὲ στοιχεῖα τὰ ὑπὸ θεοῦ γεγενημένα κολακεύουσιν
Rendered as: do not ... pay court to the elements made by God
στοιχεῖα denotes cosmic elements or constituent parts of the world, while κολακεύω literally evokes flattering or courting them.

11. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν τούτων δημιουργὸν καὶ πάροχον σέβειν θεόν
Rendered as: revere God, the creator and provider of these things
πάροχος can denote a provider, supplier, or giver. “Provider” preserves its distinction from δημιουργός, “creator.”

SECTION 10.10

For glory worthy of honor belongs to him alone, the only unoriginated one, since everything else has come into being. Just as being God, then, belongs uniquely to the unoriginated one, so anything at all that has come into being is not truly God. Above all, therefore, you must understand the malicious scheme of the serpent that is deceiving you from within. It cleverly deceives you with the promise of better reasoning, crawling from your brain into your spinal marrow and regarding your being deceived as a great gain.

Translator's notes for section 10.10 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ ἔντιμος δόξα
Rendered as: glory worthy of honor
ἔντιμος describes something honored, esteemed, or worthy of honor. The rendering avoids turning the adjective and noun into two separate source claims.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ μόνου ἀγενήτου
Rendered as: the only unoriginated one
ἀγένητος is contrasted here with γενητός and γενόμενον, so “unoriginated” preserves the coming-into-being contrast more precisely than “unbegotten.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: πᾶν ὁτιοῦν γενόμενον θεὸς τῷ ὄντι οὐκ ἔστιν
Rendered as: anything at all that has come into being is not truly God
πᾶν ὁτιοῦν is emphatically comprehensive, while τῷ ὄντι means “in reality” or “truly.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἀπατῶντος ὄφεως κακοῦργον ἐπίνοιαν
Rendered as: the malicious scheme of the serpent that is deceiving you from within
ἐν ὑμῖν may describe either the serpent’s location or the sphere of its deception. “From within” preserves both possibilities without identifying the serpent with a specific anatomical structure.

5. Translation choice — Greek: φρονίμως ὑμᾶς ἀπατᾷ ὑποσχέσει κρείττονος λογισμοῦ
Rendered as: cleverly deceives you with the promise of better reasoning
φρονίμως is ironic here and means intelligently or shrewdly; λογισμός may mean reasoning, calculation, or thought.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἕρπων ὑμῶν ἐκ τοῦ ἐγκεφάλου εἰς τὸν νωτιαῖον μυελὸν
Rendered as: crawling from your brain into your spinal marrow
Retains the anatomical image and the serpent’s downward movement from the brain into the spinal cord or marrow.

7. Translation choice — Greek: μέγα κέρδος ἡγούμενος τὴν ὑμετέραν ἀπάτην
Rendered as: regarding your being deceived as a great gain
ὑμετέραν ἀπάτην could formally mean “your deception,” including deception practiced by you, but the repeated claim that the serpent deceives the audience favors the objective sense, their being deceived.

SECTION 10.11

For, knowing the law from the beginning—that if he merely brings you to entertain the notion of any beings called gods, so that you sin against the good of sole rule, your destruction becomes gain for him (and this is because, having been condemned to eat earth, he has authority to eat the person who through sin has dissolved into earth and become earth, while your souls pass into the belly of his fire)—he therefore, so that you may suffer these things, suggests to you every notion directed against you.

Translator's notes for section 10.11 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς νόμον
Rendered as: the law from the beginning
Preserves the temporal phrase; “the original law” is possible but would make its characterization less explicit.

2. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς ὑπόνοιαν ὡνδήποτε λεγομένων θεῶν ἐνέγκῃ
Rendered as: brings you to entertain the notion of any beings called gods
ὑπόνοια denotes a notion or supposition here, while λεγομένων marks them as beings designated or said to be gods.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ τῆς μοναρχίας ἀγαθὸν
Rendered as: the good of sole rule
μοναρχία refers contextually to the rule of one God; “sole rule” preserves that claim without importing a familiar theological formula.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὴν τοῦ πυρὸς αὐτοῦ γαστέρα
Rendered as: into the belly of his fire
Retains the source’s unusual image and possessive attachment rather than replacing it with the smoother “fiery belly.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: πᾶσαν τὴν καθ’ ὑμῶν ὑμῖν ὑποβάλλει οἴησιν
Rendered as: suggests to you every notion directed against you
καθ’ ὑμῶν describes the notions as working against their recipients; οἴησις may also be rendered “opinion” or “supposition.”

SECTION 10.12

For all the deceptive suppositions opposed to sole rule are sown by him into your mind for your harm. First, so that after hearing the words concerning reverence for God you may not drive away ignorance, the cause of evils, he lies in ambush under the pretext of false knowledge. At first he uses one preconception applied to everyone: the idea that one has decided wisely because, if someone does not hear the message concerning reverence for God, he is not “liable to judgment.” Therefore some, deceived in this way, do not wish to listen, so that they may remain ignorant, not knowing that ignorance is itself, on its own, enough of a deadly poison. For it is not the case that, if someone takes deadly poison unknowingly, he does not die. In the same way, sins by their nature destroy the sinner, even if in ignorance he does what he ought not to do.

Translator's notes for section 10.12 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: αἱ ἁμαρτία ἀναιροῦσιν
The supplied ἁμαρτία is singular in form, while the article αἱ and verb ἀναιροῦσιν are plural. The English follows the plural agreement required by the surrounding construction; the proposed reading adds the expected final iota but is not the supplied reading.

2. Translation choice — Greek: αἱ κατὰ τῆς μοναρχίας ἀπατηλοὶ ... ὑπολήψεις
Rendered as: the deceptive suppositions opposed to sole rule
ὑπολήψεις are received notions or suppositions, and κατὰ marks their opposition to divine sole rule.

3. Translation choice — Greek: προφάσει γνώσεως ἐνεδρεύει ψευδοῦς
Rendered as: he lies in ambush under the pretext of false knowledge
ψευδοῦς grammatically modifies γνώσεως; “under the pretext” conveys the instrumental dative προφάσει.

4. Translation choice — Greek: μιᾷ τῇ κατὰ πάντων προλήψει
Rendered as: one preconception applied to everyone
κατὰ πάντων may indicate universal application or direction against everyone; the rendering adopts universal application in this context.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ νομίζειν καλῶς βεβουλεῦσθαι ὅτι
Rendered as: the idea that one has decided wisely because
The middle perfect βεβουλεῦσθαι can describe having formed a supposedly wise resolution; alternatively, the phrase may be understood impersonally as “thinking it has been wisely determined that.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ γάρ, εἴ τις προσλάβοι θανασίμου φαρμάκου ἀγνοῶν, οὐκ ἀποθνήσκει
Rendered as: For it is not the case that, if someone takes deadly poison unknowingly, he does not die
The expanded English preserves the emphatic negative construction and the analogy between unknown poison and unwitting sin.

SECTION 10.13

But if judgment comes on account of disobedience to words, much more will God destroy those who have refused to accept the worship directed toward him. For the one who does not wish to learn in order not to be liable is already judged as one who knows. For the one who does not wish to listen has understood; thus no contrivance can serve as a defense before God, the “knower of hearts.” Therefore flee the crafty thought that the serpent insinuates into your mind. But even if someone actually ends the present life in ignorance, he will face the charge that, though he lived for a time, he did not know who had been his benefactor and the source of the provisions supplied to him, and that he is rejected from the kingdom of God as an insensible, ungrateful, and very unworthy servant.

Translator's notes for section 10.13 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἔγνω γὰρ ὁ μὴ ἀκοῦσαι θέλει
In the supplied reading, ὁ precedes the finite verb θέλει rather than a participle, producing an irregular construction under standard Greek syntax. The main text adopts a contextually defensible subject-reading in parallel with the preceding sentence. An orthographic normalization of ὁ to the neuter relative ὃ would instead yield the object-reading “For he has come to know what he is unwilling to hear.” The normalization is conjectural, not the supplied reading.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ παρακοῇ λόγων
Rendered as: on account of disobedience to words
παρακοή can denote failure to hear or disobedience; the context concerns a culpable refusal to listen, so “disobedience” preserves that moral force.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν εἰς αὐτὸν θρησκείαν ἀναδέξασθαι
Rendered as: to accept the worship directed toward him
θρησκεία denotes religious observance or worship, while εἰς αὐτόν explicitly supplies its direction.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἔγνω γὰρ ὁ μὴ ἀκοῦσαι θέλει
Rendered as: For the one who does not wish to listen has understood
The rendering treats the supplied ὁ as introducing the person characterized by the finite clause, in contextual parallel with the preceding ὁ μὴ θέλων. If ὁ is instead normalized to the neuter relative ὃ, the materially different rendering would be “For he has come to know what he is unwilling to hear.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς „καρδιογνώστην“ θεόν
Rendered as: before God, the “knower of hearts”
The rendering retains the source’s quotation marks around the descriptive compound καρδιογνώστης.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἵνα δὲ καὶ ὄντως ἀγνοήσας τις τὸν παρόντα βίον τελευτήσει
Rendered as: But even if someone actually ends the present life in ignorance
The unusual ἵνα with the future indicative is understood as introducing an argumentative concession or supposition; “suppose that someone actually ends” is a viable alternative.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τίς αὐτῷ τε καὶ τῶν αὐτῷ ἐπιχορηγηθεισῶν τροφῶν ὑπῆρξεν εὐεργέτης
Rendered as: who had been his benefactor and the source of the provisions supplied to him
The Greek coordinates the personal beneficiary and the supplied provisions unevenly. “Source” conveys the beneficent provision without positing a second benefactor.

8. Translation choice — Greek: δοῦλος
Rendered as: servant
The policy-default rendering is used; the term still presents the person as belonging to and accountable to a superior.

SECTION 10.14

Again, the formidable serpent suggests to you that you should think this and say this very thing, which, roughly speaking, most of you say: “We too know that the Lord of all is one, but these also are gods. For just as Caesar is one but has administrators under him—consular officials, prefects, commanders of a thousand, commanders of a hundred, and commanders of ten—in the same way, since the great God is one, like Caesar, they too are gods by analogy with the subordinate authorities: they are subject to him but administer us.” Listen, then, you who have been smeared by him with this supposition as with a terrible poison—I mean the evil implication of the example—so that you may know what is good and what is evil. For you have not yet regained your sight, since you do not even look closely into the things you yourselves put forward.

Translator's notes for section 10.14 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: οὕπω γὰρ ἀνεβλέψατε
The supplied print reads οὕπω, with rough breathing and an acute; the negative adverb is conventionally written οὔπω, with smooth breathing and an acute. The English renders the contextual negative sense “not yet.” The proposed form is an orthographic normalization, not the supplied reading.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ δεινὸς ὄφις
Rendered as: the formidable serpent
δεινός can mean formidable, terrible, or fearsome; “formidable” fits the serpent’s dangerous cunning without weakening the description.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὃ σχεδὸν οἱ πλεῖστοι ὑμῶν λέγουσιν
Rendered as: which, roughly speaking, most of you say
σχεδόν explicitly qualifies the attribution with approximation. Its position permits the sense “roughly speaking, most of you”; “which nearly all of you say” is another possible idiomatic rendering of the combined expression.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπατικούς, ἐπάρχους, χιλιάρχους, ἑκατοντάρχους, δεκαδάρχους
Rendered as: consular officials, prefects, commanders of a thousand, commanders of a hundred, and commanders of ten
The transparent numerical renderings preserve the descending administrative or military hierarchy; ὑπατικοί denotes persons of consular standing rather than necessarily serving consuls.

5. Translation choice — Greek: κατὰ τὸν τῶν ὑποκειμένων ἐξουσιῶν λόγον
Rendered as: by analogy with the subordinate authorities
λόγος here expresses the proposed correspondence or analogy, though “according to the status of the subordinate authorities” is also possible.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς δεινῷ ὑπαλειφθέντες ἰῷ
Rendered as: smeared ... as with a terrible poison
Retains the physical image of ὑπαλείφω, “smear” or “anoint,” and the comparison of the supposition to poison.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ παραδείγματος τὴν κακὴν ὑπόνοιαν
Rendered as: the evil implication of the example
Here ὑπόνοια is understood as the underlying implication carried by the Caesar analogy; “evil supposition arising from the example” is also possible.

8. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδὲ τοῖς προβαλλομένοις ὑφ’ ὑμῶν ἐνορᾶτε
Rendered as: you do not even look closely into the things you yourselves put forward
The wording preserves the distinction between advancing an argument and discerning what lies within or follows from it.

SECTION 10.15

For if you say that God, on the analogy of Caesar, has subordinate authorities—the beings called gods—even so you do not follow your own example. For if you did follow it, you ought to know this: just as it is not permissible to give Caesar’s name to another—I mean, to a consul, a prefect, a commander of a thousand, or anyone else—because the giver will not live and the receiver will be put to death, so, by your own example, it is not permissible for the name “God” to be given to another, since even the person persuaded either to receive it or to give it perishes. And if an affront in a human case incurs punishment, much more will those who call others gods, as people who have insulted God, be subject to eternal punishment. And rightly so, because you have subjected the name entrusted to you to honor with regard to his sole rule to every insult of which you were capable. For “God” is not his true name. Rather, having received it for the present, you insulted what was given to you for this purpose: that however you might use it, it might be reckoned as treatment of his true name; but you subjected it to every insult.

Translator's notes for section 10.15 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὸν τοῦ Καίσαρος λόγον
Rendered as: on the analogy of Caesar
λόγος refers to the proposed correspondence between divine and imperial administration; “according to Caesar’s model” is a viable alternative.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ Καίσαρος ὄνομα
Rendered as: Caesar’s name
ὄνομα may also mean title or designation here, but “name” is retained because the passage explicitly compares it with the name “God.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ πεισθεὶς εἴτε λαβεῖν εἴτε δοῦναι
Rendered as: the person persuaded either to receive it or to give it
The passive participle is preserved; the unnamed object is contextually the disputed name or designation.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ ἀπ’ ἀνθρώπου ὕβρις
Rendered as: an affront in a human case
The ἀπό phrase is compact and may describe an insult involving a human being, an insult committed by one, or punishment at human hands. The contextual rendering preserves the human-versus-divine comparison without deciding the phrase’s exact direction.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ εἰς τὴν αὐτοῦ μοναρχίαν παραδοθὲν ὑμῖν τιμᾶν ὄνομα
Rendered as: the name entrusted to you to honor with regard to his sole rule
The name remains the object of τιμᾶν: it was entrusted to the recipients for them to honor. The phrase εἰς τὴν αὐτοῦ μοναρχίαν may qualify either the entrusting or the honoring; “with regard to his sole rule” preserves that attachment uncertainty.

6. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ γὰρ τὸ ὄντως ἐστὶν αὐτοῦ ὄνομα θεός
Rendered as: For “God” is not his true name
The clause distinguishes the designation θεός from God’s actual or true name; quotation marks clarify that the designation itself is under discussion.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τέως παρειληφότες
Rendered as: having received it for the present
τέως may mean “for the present” or “up to now.” The former suits the contrast between the provisionally received designation and the true name, while the temporal alternative remains possible.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ὃ ἐδόθη ὑμῖν, ἵνα ὡς ἂν αὐτῷ χρήσῃσθε, εἰς τὸ ὄντως αὐτοῦ ὄνομα λογισθῇ
Rendered as: what was given to you for this purpose: that however you might use it, it might be reckoned as treatment of his true name
The purpose clause is understood as explaining why the designation was given: its use would count as treatment of the true name it represents. Attachment of ἵνα to ὑβρίσατε is syntactically possible, yielding “you insulted what was given to you so that ...,” but that would make the reckoning the purpose of their insult and is less suitable contextually.

SECTION 10.16

For example, the leaders among your Egyptians—those who boasted of their study of phenomena aloft and professed to distinguish the natures of the stars—because of an evil suspicion lurking deep within them, subjected it to every dishonor, as far as lay in their power. For some of them handed down the worship of an ox called Apis, others of a male goat, others of a cat, others of a serpent, and even of a fish, onions, winds from bellies, sewers, and limbs of irrational animals, along with countless other utterly shameful absurdities.

Translator's notes for section 10.16 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτίκα γοῦν
Rendered as: For example
Here the phrase introduces the Egyptians as an immediate illustrative case rather than asserting that their conduct occurred at once; a temporal rendering such as “immediately, then” is possible in other contexts.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν Αἰγυπτίων ὑμῶν οἱ ἀρχηγέται
Rendered as: the leaders among your Egyptians
This takes the adjacent τῶν Αἰγυπτίων ὑμῶν together as “your Egyptians.” Alternatively, ὑμῶν can qualify ἀρχηγέται, yielding “your leaders from among the Egyptians.” The noun ἀρχηγέται can denote leaders, originators, or founders; “leaders” preserves their authoritative role without specifying that they were historical founders.

3. Translation choice — Greek: οἱ περὶ μετεωρολογίας αὐχοῦντες
Rendered as: those who boasted of their study of phenomena aloft
μετεωρολογία denotes inquiry or discourse concerning phenomena aloft, including astronomical and atmospheric matters. “Study of phenomena aloft” preserves both the field-of-study sense and its broader ancient scope, which modern “meteorology” would narrow.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ κακῆς αὐτοῖς ἐνδομυχούσης ὑπονοίας
Rendered as: because of an evil suspicion lurking deep within them
ἐνδομυχέω depicts something dwelling or lurking in the innermost recesses, while ὑπό expresses cause or agency.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πάσῃ αὐτὸ ἀτιμίᾳ ὅσον τὸ κατ’ αὐτοὺς ὑπέβαλαν
Rendered as: subjected it to every dishonor, as far as lay in their power
The neuter αὐτό has no explicit antecedent within this section, so the translation retains the pronoun rather than identifying its referent in the main text; in the preceding context it most naturally refers to the name under discussion.

6. Translation choice — Greek: οἱ δὲ τράγον
Rendered as: others of a male goat
τράγος specifically denotes a male goat; the elliptical English continues “handed down the worship” from the preceding clause.

7. Translation choice — Greek: γαστρῶν πνεύματα καὶ ὀχετοὺς
Rendered as: winds from bellies, sewers
πνεύματα preserves the bodily-wind image, while ὀχετοί denotes drains or sewers in this deliberately degrading list.

SECTION 10.17

When Peter had said these things, the crowd standing there laughed. In response to their laughter Peter said, “You laugh at their practices, not knowing that you yourselves are being laughed at far more by them. Yet you laugh at one another’s practices, for you do not see your own, having been led into deception by evil custom. I agree that you do indeed rightly ridicule the Egyptians, since, although they are rational beings, they worship irrational animals—things certain to die. But hear how those people in turn speak while ridiculing you: ‘Although we worship things that die,’ they say, ‘they at least were once alive, whereas you venerate things that have never been alive.’ In addition, they say, ‘Wanting to honor the form of the one God, and not discovering what it is like, we chose to honor every form.’ Similarly, by saying certain things of this sort, they suppose that their thinking is sounder than yours.”

Translator's notes for section 10.17 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: Γελᾶτε ὑμεῖς τὰ ἐκείνων
Rendered as: You laugh at their practices
Γελᾶτε can be indicative or imperative. The accompanying participle “not knowing” supports describing the audience’s conduct, though “Laugh at their practices” remains grammatically possible.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πλὴν τὰ ἀλλήλων γελᾶτε· τὰ γὰρ ἴδια ὑπὸ συνηθείας κακῆς εἰς ἀπάτην ἀχθέντες οὐ βλέπετε
Rendered as: Yet you laugh at one another’s practices, for you do not see your own, having been led into deception by evil custom
The explanatory γάρ connects their reciprocal ridicule with their failure to perceive their own practices; the participial phrase identifies evil custom as what led them into deception.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὅτι δὲ ὄντως ὀρθῶς καταγελᾶτε τῶν Αἰγυπτίων, σύνφημι
