Rendered as: I agree that you do indeed rightly ridicule the Egyptians
“Do indeed” preserves the explicit emphasis of ὄντως, “rightly” renders ὀρθῶς, and “I agree” represents σύνφημι.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἡμεῖς (φησίν)
Rendered as: ‘Although we ...,’ they say
The singular parenthetical φησίν functions as a quotation formula within a response introduced as what the Egyptians say, even though the quoted speakers use the plural.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πᾶσαν μορφὴν προτιμᾶν
Rendered as: to honor every form
Although προτιμάω can mean “prefer” or “honor especially,” “honor” fits the claim that every form was selected as an object of reverence.

6. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ὁμῶς
Rendered as: Similarly
The printed ὁμῶς is the adverb “alike” or “similarly,” not the more familiar ὅμως, “nevertheless.”

SECTION 10.18

“Therefore you too should answer them: ‘You are lying, for it is not out of honor directed toward the God who truly is that you venerate these things. For then all of you would be worshiping every form, which is not what you have been doing. Some of you, having supposed the divine to be an onion and venerating winds from a belly, wage war; and similarly all of you, having singled out one thing for honor, fault the objects of others. With divergent judgment, one person venerates one limb of the same animal and another person another.’ Yet some of them, still breathing sentiments of sound reason and ashamed of the manifest disgrace, attempt to turn these things into allegories, wishing through another kind of weakness to fortify what is deadly in their deception. Nevertheless, we would have refuted the allegories as well, had we been there—the allegories of those whom so foolish a passion has mastered as to produce the greatest sickness in their imagination. For the plaster must not be applied to the healthy part of the body, but to the part that is suffering. Since, then, by laughing at the Egyptians’ practices you showed that you had not suffered what they suffer, it was reasonable, regarding the condition from which you yourselves suffer, for me, being here, to provide you with a cure for the condition within you.”

Translator's notes for section 10.18 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: πρὸς· αὐτοὺς
The selected print places a high stop between the preposition πρὸς and its object αὐτούς. The syntax requires the words to be construed together; this is treated provisionally as an editorial punctuation anomaly, not as missing wording.

2. Greek: ἐνποιῆσαι
The selected print has the unassimilated compound spelling ἐνποιῆσαι, where the normalized assimilated spelling ἐμποιῆσαι is common. The printed form remains intelligible and has not been silently normalized.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τιμῇ τῇ πρὸς τὸν ὄντως θεὸν
Rendered as: out of honor directed toward the God who truly is
The phrase describes honor oriented toward the genuinely existing God; “the true God” is possible but would make the existential wording less visible.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οὐχ ὡς ἐποιεῖτε
Rendered as: which is not what you have been doing
The imperfect ἐποιεῖτε points to their established conduct, which contradicts their claim to honor every form.

5. Translation choice — Greek: οἱ μὲν γὰρ ὑμῶν κρόμμυον ὑπονοήσαντες εἶναι τὸ θεῖον καὶ γαστρὸς πνεύματα σέβοντες πολεμοῦσιν
Rendered as: Some of you, having supposed the divine to be an onion and venerating winds from a belly, wage war
The main rendering takes both participles as describing the shared subject introduced by οἱ μὲν. A material alternative distributes them between rival groups: “Some among you—the ones supposing the divine to be an onion and the ones venerating winds from a belly—wage war.” The ensuing account of each group preferring one object supports that distributive possibility. The Greek does not state an object for “wage war,” so none is supplied.

6. Translation choice — Greek: κρόμμυον ὑπονοήσαντες εἶναι τὸ θεῖον
Rendered as: having supposed the divine to be an onion
The construction presents τὸ θεῖον as the subject of the infinitive and κρόμμυον as its predicate.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἕν τι προτιμήσαντες
Rendered as: having singled out one thing for honor
The rendering preserves both selection or preference and the religious honor implied by προτιμάω.

8. Translation choice — Greek: διαφόρῳ δὲ γνώμῃ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ζῴου μελῶν ὃς μὲν ἄλλο σέβει, ἕτερος δὲ τὸ ἕτερον
Rendered as: With divergent judgment, one person venerates one limb of the same animal and another person another
The genitive μελῶν is represented partitively through “one limb ... another,” while διαφόρῳ γνώμῃ marks the worshipers’ differing judgments.

9. Translation choice — Greek: πλὴν αὐτῶν ἔτι τὰ τοῦ ὀρθοῦ λογισμοῦ πνέοντες
Rendered as: Yet some of them, still breathing sentiments of sound reason
The partitive αὐτῶν is understood with an omitted “some,” while πνέοντες retains the metaphor of breathing or exuding what belongs to sound reasoning.

10. Translation choice — Greek: δι’ ἑτέρας ἀτονοίας τὰ τῆς ἀπάτης αὐτῶν θανάσιμα κρατύνειν
Rendered as: through another kind of weakness to fortify what is deadly in their deception
ἀτονία denotes weakness or lack of strength, while the substantival τὰ ... θανάσιμα refers generally to the deadly features or effects belonging to their deception.

11. Translation choice — Greek: ὧν τὸ τοσοῦτον μωρὸν ἐπεκράτησεν πάθος
Rendered as: those whom so foolish a passion has mastered
ὧν is taken as the genitive object of ἐπεκράτησεν. It could alternatively be possessive—“whose exceedingly foolish passion became strong enough”—without materially changing the accusation.

12. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἔμπλαστρον
Rendered as: the plaster
The expression supplies the image of a medicinal plaster being applied specifically to the diseased part.

SECTION 10.19

The one who chooses to worship God ought first of all to know what alone is distinctive of God’s nature, something that cannot belong to another, so that, by looking to his distinctive property and not finding it in anyone else, he may never be deceived into assigning to another the status of being God. God’s distinctive property is that he alone, as maker of all things, is also superior to all. With respect to power, what makes is greater than what is made; with respect to magnitude, the infinite is greater than the finite; with respect to form, what is most beautiful; with respect to blessedness, what is most blessed; and with respect to intellect, what is most perfect. Likewise, in all other respects he himself possesses superiority beyond comparison. Since, then, as I said, it is distinctive of God that he is superior to all things, and since the world that contains everything has come into being through him, it is absolutely necessary to say that nothing that has come into being through him can stand in equal comparison with him.

Translator's notes for section 10.19 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τί μόνον τῆς θεοῦ φύσεως ἴδιόν ἐστιν
Rendered as: what alone is distinctive of God’s nature
ἴδιον denotes a uniquely proper or distinguishing characteristic, not merely a common attribute.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἑτέρῳ τὸ θεῷ εἶναι μὴ ἀπατηθῇ δοῦναί ποτε
Rendered as: he may never be deceived into assigning to another the status of being God
The infinitive phrase literally concerns giving “being God” to another; “status” makes the construction intelligible without reducing it to a divine quality.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦτον μόνον εἶναι, ὡς πάντων ποιητήν, οὕτως καὶ κρείττονα
Rendered as: that he alone, as maker of all things, is also superior to all
κρείττονα is the predicate of the infinitive, while πάντων explicitly accompanies “maker” and is contextually carried into the comparison. A more structurally literal alternative is “that he alone is, just as maker of all, so also superior.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ ποιοῦν τοῦ ποιητοῦ
Rendered as: what makes is greater than what is made
τοῦ ποιητοῦ is read as the substantivized verbal adjective ποιητός, “made,” rather than the identically formed genitive of ποιητής, “maker,” since the resulting maker-made contrast fits the argument and the parallel comparisons.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς εἶδος τὸ εὐμορφότατον
Rendered as: with respect to form, what is most beautiful
The comparative idea “is greater” is carried forward elliptically from κρείττόν ἐστιν, while the Greek supplies no explicit second term for this comparison.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἴσην ἔχειν σύγκρισιν
Rendered as: stand in equal comparison
The expression denies that anything created can bear a comparison that places it on equal terms with God.

SECTION 10.20

But if one who does not possess incomparability, unsurpassability, and freedom from need in every way and on every side cannot himself be God, and if the whole world cannot be this insofar as it has come into being, would it not be all the more irrational for its parts to be called God? By “parts” I mean those you call gods, made from gold and silver, bronze and stone, or indeed from any other material whatsoever—and these fashioned by a mortal hand. Nevertheless, in answer to these points, let us see what kinds of poison the terrible serpent, through a human mouth, administers with his hissings to those who are being deceived.

Translator's notes for section 10.20 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ ἀπαράβλητον καὶ ἀνυπέρβλητον καὶ πάντῃ πάντοθεν ἀνενδεὲς
Rendered as: incomparability, unsurpassability, and freedom from need in every way and on every side
The substantivized adjectives name qualities required of God; πάντῃ πάντοθεν emphatically expresses completeness from every direction or standpoint.

2. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτὸς εἶναι οὐ δύναται
Rendered as: cannot himself be God
The predicate “God” is supplied from the surrounding argument and is stated explicitly later in the same sentence; “cannot himself be” would be unintelligibly incomplete in English.

3. Translation choice — Greek: καθὸ γεγένηται
Rendered as: insofar as it has come into being
καθό gives the respect or ground on which the world fails the stated criterion: it is something generated.

4. Translation choice — Greek: πόσῳ γε μᾶλλον τὰ μόρια αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἂν ἀλόγως κληθείη θεός;
Rendered as: would it not be all the more irrational for its parts to be called God?
The main rendering takes οὐκ as framing a rhetorical negative question and ἀλόγως as characterizing the act of calling the parts God. The sequence οὐκ ἂν ἀλόγως can alternatively be parsed as “would not unreasonably,” but that reading would reverse the argument developed in the surrounding sentences. The neuter plural subject can take the singular verb κληθείη in Greek.

5. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ταῦτα ὑπὸ θνητῆς χειρὸς δεδημιουργημένα
Rendered as: and these fashioned by a mortal hand
καὶ ταῦτα adds emphatic indignation: the alleged gods are not merely material but are manufactured by mortal agency.

6. Translation choice — Greek: οἷα δι’ ἀνθρώπου στόματος ὁ δεινὸς ὄφις φαρμάσσει τοῖς συριγμοῖς τοὺς ἐξαπατωμένους
Rendered as: what kinds of poison the terrible serpent, through a human mouth, administers with his hissings to those who are being deceived
φαρμάσσω can mean to drug, poison, or bewitch. “Administers poison” preserves the serpent’s venom image and the instrumental hissings; a less imagistic alternative is “how the terrible serpent drugs or bewitches those who are being deceived.”

SECTION 10.21

For most people say, “In our objects of worship, we venerate not the gold, nor the silver, nor wood or stone (for we too know that these are nothing other than lifeless matter and the craftsmanship of a mortal human), but the spirit dwelling in them; this is what we call a god.” See, then, the dishonesty of those who say this. For since what is visible is easily exposed as nothing, they have fled for refuge to the invisible, as though they could not be refuted about something uncertain. Nevertheless, such people agree with us in part that one half of the cult images among them is not a god but unfeeling matter. It remains for them to show how we are to believe that it has a divine spirit. Yet such a person cannot demonstrate to us that it exists, since it does not—and we do not believe that they have seen it themselves. We will provide them with proofs that it does not have a divine spirit, so that lovers of truth, on hearing the refutation of this rabid supposition, may turn away from thinking that these things are animate.

Translator's notes for section 10.21 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: Τῶν σεβασμάτων ἡμῶν
Rendered as: In our objects of worship
σεβάσματα denotes things treated as sacred or worthy of veneration; “objects of worship” preserves the cultic sense without assuming that they are divine.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ ἥμισυ τῶν παρ’ αὐτοῖς ἱδρυμάτων
Rendered as: one half of the cult images among them
ἱδρύματα refers here to erected cult objects. “One half” preserves the argument that their alleged material-and-spirit composite is already conceded to be partly mere matter.

3. Translation choice — Greek: λοιπὸν δὲ περιλείπεται δεῖξαι αὐτοῖς πῶς πιστεύομεν ὅτι· θεῖον ἔχει πνεῦμα.
Rendered as: It remains for them to show how we are to believe that it has a divine spirit.
The main rendering construes αὐτοῖς with περιλείπεται and the infinitive as identifying those responsible for demonstrating the claim. Alternatively, αὐτοῖς may be the recipient of δεῖξαι: “it remains to show them how we believe that it has a divine spirit.” The main reading better anticipates the demand that follows for an opponent to demonstrate the spirit’s existence. πῶς πιστεύομεν could also be rendered indicatively as “how we believe,” but “how we are to believe” gives it deliberative or challenging force consistent with the speaker’s stated disbelief.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἀλλ’ ἐπιδεῖξαι ἡμῖν οὐ δύναται ὅτι ἔστιν, ἐπεὶ μὴ ἔστιν — καὶ αὐτοῖς ἑωρακέναι οὐ πιστεύομεν.
Rendered as: Yet such a person cannot demonstrate to us that it exists, since it does not—and we do not believe that they have seen it themselves.
The singular δύναται is taken as referring to a representative opponent, while the following αὐτοῖς resumes the opposing group in the plural. Because the subject of δύναται is unstated, an image or the alleged spirit could instead be understood as the subject: “Yet it cannot demonstrate to us that it exists.” The confirmed singular has not been regularized as a plural.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς λυσσώδους ὑπονοίας
Rendered as: this rabid supposition
ὑπόνοια can mean suspicion, notion, or supposition; here it is the hostile characterization of the belief that the images are animate. λυσσώδης supplies the forceful image of rabid madness.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἔνπνοα
Rendered as: animate
The adjective means possessing breath or life, in contrast with the objects’ lifeless material.

SECTION 10.22

First, then, if you venerate them as animate, why do you also bow down before the tombs of ancient people, who admittedly did not even possess a divine spirit? Thus you are not telling the truth in this respect either. Yet if your objects of worship really were animate, they would move by themselves, would have a voice, would shake off the cobweb on them, would repel those who wish to plot against them and who steal from them, and would easily seize those stripping away the votive offerings. But now they do none of these things. Instead, like condemned prisoners—and especially the more valuable among them—they are kept under guard, as we said at the outset. Again, do not the rulers demand taxes and duties from you on their account, on the ground that you derive great profit from the things there? And have they not often been plundered by enemies and, after being smashed, divided up? And do not the priests themselves, even more than those who worship from outside, having passed judgment against themselves over their useless worship, secretly remove many of the votive offerings?

Translator's notes for section 10.22 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: τί καὶ ἀνθρώπων; ἀρχαίων τάφους προσκυνεῖτε
The selected edition’s question mark separates ἀνθρώπων from the agreeing genitive adjective ἀρχαίων, although the surviving words form the coherent phrase “tombs of ancient people” when read continuously. This is treated provisionally as an editorial-punctuation irregularity, not as missing wording.

2. Greek: τῶν ἐκεῖ;.
The selected edition prints both a Greek question mark and a period at the end of the question. The duplicated punctuation does not affect the recoverable syntax or wording.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀνθρώπων; ἀρχαίων τάφους
Rendered as: the tombs of ancient people
ἀρχαίων agrees with ἀνθρώπων in the genitive plural; together they identify whose tombs are meant. The English reads the wording continuously across the selected edition’s question mark, as disclosed in the punctuation note.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς αὐτοῖς ἐπιβουλεῦσαι θέλοντας καὶ κλέπτοντας
Rendered as: those who wish to plot against them and who steal from them
The first participle expresses hostile intent and the second actual theft. The object of κλέπτοντας is unstated; “from them” fits the surrounding discussion of images and their offerings, while “who steal them” is also possible.

5. Translation choice — Greek: οἱ τιμιώτεροι αὐτῶν
Rendered as: the more valuable among them
τίμιος can mean honored or costly. The need to guard the objects from theft makes material value the more immediate sense, though “the more honored” remains possible.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς πολλὰ καρπιζομένους τῶν ἐκεῖ
Rendered as: on the ground that you derive great profit from the things there
καρπίζομαι denotes enjoying or reaping proceeds. τῶν ἐκεῖ is elliptical, referring to the things or resources located at the cult sites.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν ἔξω θρησκευόντων
Rendered as: those who worship from outside
The phrase distinguishes the priests from worshipers outside the priestly group; “lay worshipers” is a contextual alternative but is more interpretive.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τῇ ἀχρήστῳ θρησκείᾳ ἑαυτῶν κατεγνωκότες
Rendered as: having passed judgment against themselves over their useless worship
The perfect participle presents the priests as having reached, or as standing in, an adverse judgment against themselves concerning their worship before or while they secretly remove the offerings. It does not state that the theft itself produces that judgment.

SECTION 10.23

“Yes,” he says, “but they were detected through the gods’ providence.” This is false. For how many of them have gone undetected? If, because some have been caught, they say that those gods possess power, they are mistaken. Some tomb robbers too are discovered, while others escape notice, and surely those who are caught were not detected by the power of the dead. We can understand something similar about the gods that are stolen and despoiled. “But,” he says, “the gods within them have no concern for their own carved images.” Why, then, do you yourselves tend them—scrubbing, washing, and cleaning them, crowning them, and offering sacrifices to them? Therefore recognize from this that you are not acting with sound reasoning either. For just as you weep over the dead, so you also offer sacrifices and pour libations to your gods.

Translator's notes for section 10.23 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ναί φησιν, ἀλλὰ προνοίᾳ αὐτῶν ἐφωράθησαν.
Rendered as: “Yes,” he says, “but they were detected through the gods’ providence.”
The first plural referent is the thieves, while αὐτῶν refers contextually to the gods or cult images credited with providential action. The nouns are made explicit in English to prevent the two pronouns from being confused.

2. Translation choice — Greek: δύναμιν αὐτοὺς ἔχειν
Rendered as: that those gods possess power
The accusative αὐτούς resumes the gods credited with detecting thieves, not the thieves who were caught.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τοιοῦτόν τι καὶ περὶ τοὺς κλεπτομένους καὶ συλωμένους θεοὺς ἔστιν ἡμῖν νοεῖν.
Rendered as: We can understand something similar about the gods that are stolen and despoiled.
ἔστιν with the dative and infinitive expresses the possibility or availability of understanding the analogous situation, rather than an obligation or recommendation. Both passive participles modify the gods themselves.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν ξοάνων αὐτῶν
Rendered as: their own carved images
ξόανον originally denotes a carved, especially wooden, cult image and can more broadly denote an idol or statue. “Carved images” preserves that material sense without requiring that every object be wooden.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τημελεῖτε σμήχοντες καὶ πλύνοντες καὶ καθαίροντες, στεφανοῦντες, ἐπιθύοντες
Rendered as: tend them—scrubbing, washing, and cleaning them, crowning them, and offering sacrifices to them
The sequence lists the physical and ritual care supplied by the worshipers. ἐπιθύω here means to offer sacrifice, not merely to desire.

SECTION 10.24

Yet calling them administrators no longer accords even with the analogy of Caesar and the authorities under him, when you yourselves take all care of them, as I said before, tending your cult images in every respect. For, capable of nothing, they do nothing. So tell us: what do they administer? What do they do comparable to what the rulers in each locality do? What do they accomplish comparable to God’s stars? Unless perhaps they shine like the sun—the very ones for whom you yourselves light lamps? Can they, just as the clouds bring rains, also bring downpours—they who cannot even move themselves unless people take hold of them? Or do they provide fruits in the same way as the earth—they for whom you supply sacrifices? Thus they can do nothing.

Translator's notes for section 10.24 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: διοικητὰς αὐτοὺς λέγειν
Rendered as: calling them administrators
διοικητής denotes one who manages, governs, or administers. “Administrators” maintains the comparison with Caesar’s subordinate authorities.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ ἱδρύματα
Rendered as: cult images
The erected objects are the material images being tended, illuminated, and physically moved; “cult images” conveys this setting better than the broader “institutions” or “establishments.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: οἱ κατὰ τόπον ἡγούμενοι
Rendered as: the rulers in each locality
The phrase denotes leaders or governors assigned to particular places, continuing the administrative analogy.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ μήτι φαίνουσιν ὡς ὁ ἥλιος, οἷς λύχνους ὑμεῖς ἅπτετε;
Rendered as: Unless perhaps they shine like the sun—the very ones for whom you yourselves light lamps?
εἰ μήτι introduces an ironic possible exception. The emphatic ὑμεῖς sharpens the contrast between supposedly shining gods and worshipers who must provide their light.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἐὰν μὴ ἄνθρωποι ἐπιλάβωνται
Rendered as: unless people take hold of them
The middle verb means to grasp or take hold of something; here people must handle the immobile images before they can move.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν αὐτὸν τῇ γῇ τρόπον
Rendered as: in the same way as the earth
The dative τῇ γῇ marks the earth as the standard of comparison for providing fruit.

SECTION 10.25

And even if they were able to do something, you would not rightly call them gods, since even the elements, through which good things are supplied, may not be called gods. But only the one who ordered them to carry out everything for our use and commanded them to serve humankind—him alone do we rightly call God. Unaware of his beneficence, you proclaimed that the elements assigned to you as servants were to rule over human beings. And why is there any need to speak about the elements, when you even make lifeless statues and not only bow down before them but also think it proper to be subjected to them in every respect as servants? For this reason, you yourselves, through the things by which you lost your senses, have become subject to demons. Nevertheless, through recognition of God himself, you can by good deeds become masters again, give orders to demons as servants, and, as sons of God, be established as heirs of an eternal kingdom.

Translator's notes for section 10.25 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: τὰ ὑμῖν δοῦλα ἀπονεμηθέντα στοιχεῖα καθ’ αὐτῶν δεσπόζειν ἀνηγορεύσατε
The plural αὐτῶν has no nearby plural human antecedent; its nearest explicit plural antecedents are the elements or the good things, neither of which gives the expected contrast. The translation defensibly treats it as a notional resumption of generic ἀνθρώπῳ, but καθ’ ὑμῶν, “over you,” is a plausible conjecture and is not the supplied reading.

2. Greek: διὰ τοῦτο ἑαυτοὺς δι’ ὧν παρεφρονήσατε, δαίμοσιν ὑποχείριοι γεγόνατε.
The accusative ἑαυτούς does not formally agree with the nominative predicate ὑποχείριοι and the second-person subject of γεγόνατε. It can be read as a pendent accusative emphasizing the people addressed, which supports the main rendering; nominative αὐτοί would be a possible conjectural regularization.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ στοιχεῖα
Rendered as: the elements
The term denotes the constituent powers or elements of the natural order through which benefits are supplied; the argument denies that their usefulness makes them gods.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν μόνον τάξαντα αὐτὰ πρὸς τὴν ἡμετέραν χρῆσιν ἐκτελεῖν τὰ πάντα
Rendered as: only the one who ordered them to carry out everything for our use
τάσσω expresses appointing or ordering the elements to perform their assigned functions for human use.

5. Translation choice — Greek: κελεύσαντα ἀνθρώπῳ ὑπηρετεῖν
Rendered as: commanded them to serve humankind
The singular ἀνθρώπῳ is generic, referring to humanity rather than one particular man.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ ὑμῖν δοῦλα ἀπονεμηθέντα στοιχεῖα καθ’ αὐτῶν δεσπόζειν
Rendered as: that the elements assigned to you as servants were to rule over human beings
The main rendering takes αὐτῶν as a notional plural resumption of the preceding generic ἀνθρώπῳ, “humankind.” Taking it as referring to the elements themselves or to the good things would produce a much less coherent claim.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς δοῦλοι κατὰ πάντα αὐτοῖς ὑποτετάχθαι
Rendered as: to be subjected to them in every respect as servants
δοῦλοι marks complete subordinate status. “Servants” follows the supplied wording policy, while “slaves” would more explicitly foreground ownership and coercive subjection.

8. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τοῦτο ἑαυτοὺς δι’ ὧν παρεφρονήσατε, δαίμοσιν ὑποχείριοι γεγόνατε
Rendered as: For this reason, you yourselves, through the things by which you lost your senses, have become subject to demons.
The accusative ἑαυτούς is treated as a pendent emphatic expression resumed by the second-person verb. δι’ ὧν refers to the cult objects as the means or occasion of their loss of reason.

9. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τῆς εἰς αὐτὸν τὸν θεὸν ἐπιγνώσεως ἐκ τῶν καλῶν πράξεων
Rendered as: through recognition of God himself, you can by good deeds
The main rendering attaches ἐκ τῶν καλῶν πράξεων to becoming masters again, while διὰ τῆς ... ἐπιγνώσεως gives the broader means. It could alternatively describe recognition of God as arising from good deeds.

10. Translation choice — Greek: δαίμοσιν ὡς δούλοις ἐπιτάξαι
Rendered as: give orders to demons as servants
The dative phrase identifies the demons as the servants being commanded, reversing the preceding subjection to them.

11. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς υἱοὶ θεοῦ αἰωνίου βασιλείας κληρονόμοι καταστῆναι
Rendered as: as sons of God, be established as heirs of an eternal kingdom
The main rendering attaches αἰωνίου to βασιλείας. Grammatically it could instead modify θεοῦ, yielding “as sons of the eternal God, be established as heirs of a kingdom,” but the chosen attachment gives the more natural division of the two genitive phrases.

SECTION 10.26

After saying these things, he ordered those possessed by demons and those gripped by diseases to be brought to him. When they had been brought, he laid his hands on them and prayed, then sent them away in good health, reminding them and the rest of the crowds to remain there in attendance for however many days he might stay there and speak. After the others had withdrawn, Peter bathed in the reservoir there together with those who wished to do so. He ordered the meal to be laid out on the ground beneath a dense canopy of trees for the sake of the shade, and had each person recline according to his rank; and so we partook of food. Then, after offering a blessing and further thanking God for the refreshment received, in accordance with the Hebrews’ customary faith, while much time still remained, he allowed us to ask about whatever we wished. And although there were twenty of us, he answered each one as each asked in turn. When evening had now come upon us, we all entered the most spacious room of the lodging together with him and slept there.

Translator's notes for section 10.26 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἀπέλυσεν αὐτοὺς· ὑγιαίνοντας,
The selected edition prints a high stop between αὐτοὺς and ὑγιαίνοντας. The accusative participle naturally construes with αὐτούς, yielding “sent them away in good health.” The punctuation is editorial and does not require alteration of the Greek wording.

2. Greek: χαμαὶ στρωθῆναι
The wording does not explicitly identify what was spread on the ground. The banquet context supports “the meal to be laid out,” while “couches or coverings to be spread” and “the table to be set” remain viable alternatives. This is ordinary contextual ellipsis, not evidence of omitted text.

3. Greek: κατὰ τὴν Ἑβραίων συνήθη πίστιν
Both the attachment of the phrase and the contextual range of πίστις admit alternatives. It is rendered as describing the manner of the blessing and thanksgiving, with πίστις retained as “faith”; “according to the Hebrews’ customary observance/practice” is also defensible.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς δαιμονῶντας καὶ νόσοις ἐγκατειλημμένους
Rendered as: those possessed by demons and those gripped by diseases
The coordinated participles are rendered as two contextually natural classes. Grammatically, they could instead describe a single group suffering both conditions.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἐνταῦθα παρεδρεύειν
Rendered as: to remain there in attendance
παρεδρεύω denotes staying close by or waiting in attendance, not merely sitting.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὅσων ἂν ἡμερῶν ἐπιδημῶν διαλέγηται
Rendered as: for however many days he might stay there and speak
ἐπιδημέω describes remaining in a place, while διαλέγομαι may mean speak, converse, or deliver discourse.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν τῷ ἐκεῖ ὑδροχοείῳ
Rendered as: in the reservoir there
ὑδροχοεῖον denotes a place where water is collected or held; “reservoir” fits the bathing context.

8. Translation choice — Greek: χαμαὶ στρωθῆναι
Rendered as: the meal to be laid out on the ground
The passive infinitive leaves what was spread unstated. The meal context supports this rendering, though couches, coverings, or a table setting are also possible.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ τινὰ πυκνὴν τῶν δένδρων κόμην
Rendered as: beneath a dense canopy of trees
κόμη literally denotes hair or foliage and here forms an image of the trees’ thick leafy canopy.

10. Translation choice — Greek: κατ’ ἀξίαν ἕκαστον κατακλιθῆναι
Rendered as: had each person recline according to his rank
κατ’ ἀξίαν indicates arrangement according to worth, dignity, status, or rank.

11. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπευχαριστήσας τῷ θεῷ ἐπὶ τῷ εὐφρανθῆναι
Rendered as: further thanking God for the refreshment received
The wording denotes additional thanksgiving for being gladdened or refreshed; “for having enjoyed the meal” is another contextually possible expression.

12. Translation choice — Greek: κατὰ τὴν Ἑβραίων συνήθη πίστιν
Rendered as: in accordance with the Hebrews’ customary faith
The rendering retains πίστις as “faith” and attaches the phrase to the blessing and thanksgiving. In this context πίστις could alternatively denote customary religious observance or practice.

13. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν μέρει ἑκάστῳ πυθομένῳ ἐπέλυσεν
Rendered as: he answered each one as each asked in turn
ἐν μέρει means “in turn,” and ἐπιλύω here means to resolve or explain what each person asked.

14. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν εὐρύτατον τῆς ξενίας οἶκον
Rendered as: the most spacious room of the lodging
οἶκος can denote a room or chamber, and ξενία here refers to the place of lodging or guest accommodation.

HOMILY 11

SECTION 11.1

On the fourth day in Tripolis, then, Peter got up and found us awake. After greeting us, he went out to the water basin to wash and pray, and we followed his example. After we had prayed together and sat down before him, he spoke about the need to keep pure. When it was now daylight, he allowed the crowds to enter. Once the crowd had come in, he greeted many of them as usual and began to speak:

Translator's notes for section 11.1 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὑδροχοεῖον
Rendered as: water basin
The noun denotes a place or vessel supplying water, not necessarily a modern bathroom. Washing precedes prayer.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν περὶ τοῦ δεῖν ἁγνεύειν ἐποιεῖτο λόγον.
Rendered as: he spoke about the need to keep pure
ἁγνεύειν can concern ritual or moral purity; the discourse develops both and neither is excluded here.

SECTION 11.2

“Because of your great neglect of yourselves, your mind has sprouted the many harmful notions associated with religious worship, and you have become like land left uncultivated for lack of a farmer. You need much time for cleansing, so that your mind, receiving the true word imparted to you like good seed, may not choke it with evil thoughts and make it fruitless in the deeds that can save. Therefore those concerned for their own salvation must listen more continually, so that the wrongs multiplied over long periods may be brought into proportion, for cleansing, with the short time remaining through sustained .. effort. Since each person does not know the end of his own time, hurry to pull out the many thorns from your hearts, not little by little. For you will not be able to be cleansed that way, since you have lain uncultivated for so long.

Translator's notes for section 11.2 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: συνεχεῖ.. σπουδῇ
The supplied text contains exactly two dots between the adjective and noun. They remain as two dots in English; no unavailable wording is reconstructed.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὰς πολλὰς καὶ βλαβερὰς τῶν θρησκειῶν ὑπονοίας
Rendered as: the many harmful notions associated with religious worship
Retains religious practices in the plural conceptual background; notions can also be suspicions or suppositions.

3. Translation choice — Greek: συνεχεῖ.. σπουδῇ
Rendered as: through sustained .. effort
The supplied edition has two consecutive dots after συνεχεῖ. Exactly two dots remain in the main text; unavailable content is not restored.

4. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς κάθαρσιν ἀναλογῆσαι δυνηθῇ.
Rendered as: may be brought into proportion, for cleansing
The proportionality concerns accumulated errors and the short remaining time, with sustained effort as means; the wording is not replaced by a claim of automatic cleansing.

SECTION 11.3

You will not otherwise endure undertaking the great effort needed for your cleansing unless you become angry with them and rebuke them for the ways in which, like useless servants, you were ambushed by agreeing with your evil desires, so that you may be able to apply your righteous anger to your mind like fire to a field left uncultivated. So if you do not have righteous fire—I mean anger against evil desires—learn what good things you have been ambushed and deprived of, what punishment you have been prepared for, and by whom you have been deceived. In this way your mind, becoming clear-minded and kindled to anger like fire by the teaching of the one who sent us, may be able to consume the things that are against desire. Believe me: if you are willing, you will be able to set everything right.

Translator's notes for section 11.3 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: τὰ κατὰ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀναλῶσαι δυνηθῇ.
The formal grouping the things that are against desire is defensible from the supplied article and genitive construction, but its fit with the surrounding fire-and-desire argument is difficult. This translation does not claim to resolve that difficulty or emend the Greek. The previous adverbial attachment is not retained, because an independent object for τὰ was not adequately established.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ἀχρεῖοι δοῦλοι
Rendered as: like useless servants
Uses the POB servant gloss; the comparison retains the underlying bonded-status and master-accountability sense of δοῦλοι.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ κατὰ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀναλῶσαι δυνηθῇ.
Rendered as: may be able to consume the things that are against desire.
τὰ substantivizes the following prepositional phrase, and κατά with the supplied genitive τῆς naturally means against. The formal grouping preserves that syntax without silently replacing the genitive with an accusative or moving opposition to qualify the consuming action. Its precise intended sense remains difficult in the surrounding fire-and-desire argument; things belonging to desire would require a textual or syntactic account not established by this wording.

4. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτοῖς ὀργισθέντες ἐπιπλήξητε
Rendered as: become angry with them and rebuke them
The supplied αὐτοῖς is third-person them, not reflexive αὑτοῖς. The English retains the anaphoric pronoun without independently naming its antecedent. The prior self-directed rendering is not retained because the supplied spelling and context do not establish it; a reflexive reading would require separate grammatical or textual support, not silent accent alteration.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἵνα τὴν δικαίαν ὑμῶν ὀργὴν τῷ νῷ ὡς πῦρ χερσευσάσῃ ἀρούρῃ ἐπαφεῖναι δυνηθῆτε.
Rendered as: so that you may be able to apply your righteous anger to your mind like fire to a field left uncultivated
So that explicitly keeps the purpose or intended-result link of ἵνα with the preceding anger and rebuke, not an independent assured future result. The fire/uncultivated-field comparison remains intact.

SECTION 11.4

You are an image of the invisible God. Therefore those who wish to practice reverence must not say that idols are an image of God and that they must therefore be revered. For the human being is God’s image. Whoever wishes to show reverence toward God does good to a human being, because the human body bears God’s image. But not everyone bears the likeness: that belongs to the pure mind of a good soul. Nevertheless, since we know that the human being was made “according to the image and according to the likeness” of God, we tell you to show reverence toward this human being, so that the gratitude may be credited to God, whose image he is. You must therefore offer honor to God’s image—that is, the human being—in this way: food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the unclothed, care to the sick, shelter to the stranger, and visits and whatever help is possible to the prisoner. Not to speak item by item: whatever good things someone wishes for himself, let him likewise provide for another who needs them. Then a good reward can be credited to him for having shown reverence toward God’s image. By the same reasoning, if he does not undertake to do these things, he will be punished for having neglected the image.

Translator's notes for section 11.4 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν δὲ ὁμοιότητα οὐκέτι πάντες, ἀλλὰ ἀγαθῆς ψυχῆς ὁ καθαρὸς νοῦς.
Rendered as: But not everyone bears the likeness: that belongs to the pure mind of a good soul.
Retains the author’s image/likeness distinction rather than harmonizing them.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἵνα εἰς θεόν, οὗπέρ ἐστιν εἰκών, ἡ χάρις λογισθῇ.
Rendered as: so that the gratitude may be credited to God, whose image he is
χάρις can be gratitude, favor, or the benefit; gratitude is preferred in the transfer of honor to the one represented. The benefaction being reckoned as directed to God is another viable construal.

SECTION 11.5

What can it mean, then, to say that you revere every form for the sake of reverence toward God, when in every way you abuse the human being who truly is God’s image—murdering, committing adultery, stealing, and dishonoring him in many other ways? You ought not to do any evil that causes a person grief. But now you do everything that makes a person lose heart. For injustice and discouragement come through being murdered, having one’s property taken away, and all the other things you know you do not want to suffer. But you, deceived into evil by a certain malicious serpent through a notion of knowledge of many gods, show irreverence toward the true image—that is, the human being—while imagining that you show reverence toward insensible things.

Translator's notes for section 11.5 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἑρπετῷ τινὶ κακούργῳ
Rendered as: a certain malicious serpent
ἑρπετόν is a creeping creature; serpent follows the recurring figure explicitly called ὄφις nearby without adding its identity as a name.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπονοίᾳ πολυθέου γνώσεως
Rendered as: through a notion of knowledge of many gods
Keeps the claim to knowledge and its many-gods qualification; it is not presented as the translator’s own true knowledge.

SECTION 11.6

Some say, “If he did not want them to exist, they would not exist, but would have been destroyed.” I too say that this certainly will happen when everyone has displayed his own choice toward him; then the present world will be changed. Yet even if you wanted him to act in this way, so that none of the things worshiped existed, tell us: which existing thing have you not worshiped? Do not some of you worship the sun, others the moon, others water, others earth, others mountains, others plants, others seeds, and others even a human being, as in Egypt? Then God would have had to leave nothing, not even us, so that there would be neither anything worshiped nor anyone worshiping. Truly, this is what the terrible serpent lurking within you wants to happen; he does not spare you. But it will not be so. For the thing worshiped commits no sin: it suffers violence at the hands of the person who wants to worship it. Even if all human beings judge unjustly, God does not. For it is not just for the one who suffers and the one who inflicts it to receive the same punishment—unless the former himself willingly accepts the honor belonging to the one who alone is most worthy of honor.

Translator's notes for section 11.6 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν αὐτῶν πρὸς αὐτὸν δείξωσιν προαίρεσιν
Rendered as: has displayed his own choice toward him
Retains human choice and its orientation toward God without inserting a doctrine of predestination.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ αὐτὸς ἑκὼν ἀναδέξηται τὴν τοῦ μόνου τιμιωτάτου τιμήν.
Rendered as: unless the former himself willingly accepts the honor belonging to the one who alone is most worthy of honor
The exception concerns a recipient of worship willingly accepting divine honor. No named example is added.

SECTION 11.7

“But,” someone says, “the worshipers themselves ought to be destroyed by the true God, so that no one else does this.” But you are not wiser than God, so as to offer him advice as someone more intelligent. He knows what he is doing. For he is patient with all who live in impiety, like a merciful father who loves humanity, knowing that even impious people become reverent. Many of the very people who revere shameful and insensible things have become clear-minded, stopped revering them and sinning, and taken refuge in the true God; through prayers and good deeds they have been saved.

Translator's notes for section 11.7 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: νήψαντες
Rendered as: have become clear-minded
Uses the POB clear-minded rendering for awakening from religious error, not an exclusively literal sobriety claim.

2. Translation choice — Greek: εὐχαῖς καὶ καλοῖς ἔργοις ἐσώθησαν.
Rendered as: through prayers and good deeds they have been saved
Preserves the author’s explicit linkage of salvation, prayers, and good deeds without imposing a denominational explanation.

SECTION 11.8

“But from the beginning he ought to have made us not even think about such things at all.” In saying this, you do not know what freedom of choice is or how it is possible to be truly good. For the person who is good by his own choice is truly good; the person made good by someone else’s compulsion is not truly so, because he is not what he is by his own choice. Since each person’s freedom produces what is truly good and reveals what is truly evil, God has arranged, through the circumstances, for becoming an enemy or a friend to lie within each person. “No,” someone says, “rather, he himself makes us think everything that we think.” Stop! What further blasphemy are you speaking when you say this? For if, in everything we may think, we are moved by him, you are calling him the cause of sexual immoralities, shameless acts, greed, and every blasphemy. Stop speaking ill of him, you who ought to speak well of him and assign him every honor. And do not say, “God does not claim honor.” Even if he claims nothing, we still ought, with an eye to what is just, to repay with a thankful voice the one who has benefited us in every way.

Translator's notes for section 11.8 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ αὐτεξούσιον
Rendered as: freedom of choice
Literally self-determination or being in one’s own power; the paragraph explicitly contrasts personal choice and external compulsion.

2. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τῶν ὑποθέσεων
Rendered as: through the circumstances
ὑποθέσεις can denote situations, underlying conditions, or proposed matters; circumstances fits the arrangements in which choice operates without specifying their exact mechanism.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πορνειῶν, ἀσελγειῶν, πλεονεξιῶν
Rendered as: sexual immoralities, shameless acts, greed
Preserves distinct vice categories without embellishing sexual content or reducing all three to a generic evil.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ γὰρ πᾶν ὅ,τι ἂν ἐνθυμηθῶμεν, ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ἐνεργούμεθα
Rendered as: For if, in everything we may think, we are moved by him
We remains the subject of ἐνεργούμεθα. Moved or actuated concerns the alleged divine agency in our thinking; it does not make thoughts into actions implemented by God.

SECTION 11.9

“But,” someone says, “we do better by thanking him and everyone else together.” In saying this, you do not know the plot against you. For suppose many physicians promise to treat one sick person but can do nothing, while one who really can heal does not administer his remedy, reasoning that if he heals the patient, others will take the credit. In the same way, when God is esteemed along with many who can do nothing, he does not bestow benefits. “What then?” someone says. “Is God indignant about this, if someone else gets the credit when he heals?” I say that even if he is not indignant, he still does not wish to become an accomplice in deception. For when he does good, the idol that has done nothing is also confirmed as having power. I too say that if the person infatuated with insensible things were not harmed in his nature, perhaps God would have put up even with this. So become clear-minded for the sake of salvation and think what is reasonable. For God, being without need, himself needs nothing and is not harmed. It is we who benefit or are harmed. Just as Caesar is neither harmed when he is reviled nor benefited when he is thanked, but safety belongs to the one who thanks him and destruction to the one who reviles him, so those who speak well of God do not benefit him at all but save themselves. Likewise, those who blaspheme do him no injury but are themselves destroyed.

Translator's notes for section 11.9 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ μὴ φυσικῶς ἠδίκητο πρὸς ἀναίσθητα ἐπτοημένος, ἴσως ἂν καὶ τοῦτο ὑπομεμενήκει
Rendered as: if the person infatuated with insensible things were not harmed in his nature, perhaps God would have put up even with this
The subject of being harmed and infatuated is understood as the worshiper, while the subject of putting up with this is God, who immediately afterward is explicitly said not to suffer harm. φυσικῶς can also mean naturally. The Greek leaves these subjects implicit, so this contextual subject differentiation is disclosed.

2. Translation choice — Greek: Καῖσαρ
Rendered as: Caesar
Retains the imperial name/title without identifying a particular emperor.

SECTION 11.10

“But,” someone says, “it is not the same with a human being and God.” I agree that it is not the same. For the punishment is greater for having shown irreverence toward one who is greater, and less for the one who has sinned against someone lesser. Thus, just as God is greater than all, the person who has shown irreverence toward him will undergo greater punishment for having sinned against someone greater. It is not that God retaliates with his own hand; rather, all creation is indignant at this and pursues the offender by its nature. For neither will the sun give the blasphemer light, nor the earth its fruits, nor a spring its water, nor the ruler established in Hades give the soul there rest, since even now, while the world’s allotted term still stands, all creation shares in the indignation. Therefore neither does heaven provide rain in full nor the earth its fruits, and most people are consequently brought to ruin. Even the air itself, inflamed with anger, changes to act as a pestilence. Yet whatever good things we enjoy, he compels creation by his mercy to act with love toward us. This is how all creation is angry with you who dishonor the maker of all.

Translator's notes for section 11.10 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: οὐκ ἐν ᾅδῃ τῇ ψυχῇ ὁ ἐκεῖ καθεστὼς ἄρχων τὴν ἀνάπαυσιν
Rendered as: nor the ruler established in Hades give the soul there rest
Retains Hades as the source’s named realm; it is not replaced by a later, more specific doctrine of hell.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου προθεσμίας ὑφεστώσης
Rendered as: while the world’s allotted term still stands
The stated time-limit belongs to the world; the text does not supply its length.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ αὐτοῦ ἐλέῳ εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν φιλανθρωπίαν βιάζεται τὴν κτίσιν.
Rendered as: he compels creation by his mercy to act with love toward us
The reflexive/possessive references are retained contextually: God compels creation toward humane treatment of us. The active force of βιάζεται is not softened into permission.

SECTION 11.11

For even if you escape punishment through the dissolution of the body, how will you be able through destruction to escape your soul, which is indestructible? For even the soul of the impious is immortal; it would have been better for them not to have it indestructible. Punished by unquenchable fire with unending punishment and not dying, it cannot come to an end, to its own hurt. But perhaps one of you will say, “You frighten us, Peter.” Then teach us how we are to state things as they are while remaining silent, for we cannot make them known to you otherwise. If we remain silent, you are ambushed by evils through ignorance; if we speak, we are suspected of frightening you on a false premise. How, then, are we to examine the evil lurking within you and cunningly sowing in you notions hostile to God under the pretext of friendship with God? Be reconciled with yourselves: taking refuge in him with good deeds is for your salvation. Irrational desire within you is a kind of enmity toward God; for through supposed understanding, it strengthens ignorance.

Translator's notes for section 11.11 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν κακῷ ἐνδομυχοῦντι
Rendered as: the evil lurking within you
The possessive phrase τὴν ὑμετέραν has no expressed feminine noun in the supplied wording. Within you preserves the contextual location of the lurking evil without inventing a named organ or restoring Greek words.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ κακῷ τῷ αὐτῆς τέλος λαβεῖν οὐκ ἔχει.
Rendered as: it cannot come to an end, to its own hurt
Retains endless survival as harmful to the punished soul; the author’s claim is not harmonized with annihilation.

3. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ πανούργως ὑποσπείροντι ὑμῖν τὰς θεῷ ἐχθραινούσας ὑπονοίας
Rendered as: and cunningly sowing in you notions hostile to God
In you explicitly preserves ὑμῖν as the recipients of the sowing, separately from the earlier location of the lurking evil.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπονοίᾳ γὰρ φρονήσεως τὴν ἄγνοιαν κρατύνει.
Rendered as: for through supposed understanding, it strengthens ignorance.
ὑπόνοια is a supposition, notion, or suspicion; supposed understanding preserves that cognitive claim rather than introducing a deliberate display or pretension. For retains the explanatory γάρ.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πῶς οὖν ἐτάσωμεν τῷ εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν κακῷ ἐνδομυχοῦντι
Rendered as: How, then, are we to examine the evil lurking within you
Examine preserves the testing, scrutiny, or questioning force of ἐτάσωμεν instead of general deal with. Its dative complement is understood as the target or concern of the examination, with the lurking/sowing participles describing that evil. The English object construction makes this contextual relation readable without changing the printed dative or diagnosing an OCR defect. Question or put to the test are viable lexical alternatives.

6. Translation choice — Greek: διαλλάγητε ἑαυτοῖς·
Rendered as: Be reconciled with yourselves:
The main text reads plural ἑαυτοῖς reflexively because the surrounding argument concerns evil, ignorance, and irrational desire within the hearers. Be reconciled with one another is the material reciprocal alternative, also possible with the plural reflexive. Neither reading is presented as uniquely established.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἔχθρα τις ἐστὶν θεῷ ἐν ὑμῖν ἄλογος ἐπιθυμία·
Rendered as: Irrational desire within you is a kind of enmity toward God;
ἔχθρα is the noun enmity, not adjective ἐχθρά. A kind preserves the indefinite τις and the nominal classification of desire as enmity, rather than introducing only the existence of a hostile desire.

SECTION 11.12

Others say, “God has not cared about us.” This too is false. For if he truly did not care, he would not make his sun rise on good and evil people or send his rain on the righteous and unrighteous. Others say, “We are more reverent because we revere both him and the statues.” I do not think so—if someone who says this tells a king, “I assign you the same honor as I do the dead and discarded dung,” I do not think he will come off well. But someone will say, “Do you call our objects of reverence dung?” Yes, I say. For you made them useless to yourselves by counting them among objects of worship, although their substance might have served some other purpose, even the use of dung. But now it is not useful even for this, since you have reshaped it and worship it. How can you, the most impious of all, also claim to be more reverent? For this one incomparable sin alone you truly owe the destruction of your soul, if you persist. Just as a son who receives many benefits from his father and gives someone else, who is not his father, the honor owed to his father certainly becomes disinherited, so, when he lives according to his father’s judgment and gives thanks for the benefits, he reasonably becomes an heir.

Translator's notes for section 11.12 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς οὐσίας αὐτῶν ἴσως εἰς ἄλλο τι (εἰς χρῆσιν κόπρου) εὐχρηστησάσης.
Rendered as: although their substance might have served some other purpose, even the use of dung
Retains the parenthetical comparison with useful dung rather than upgrading the idols into useful objects of worship.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ταύτῃ αὐτῇ τῇ μιᾷ καὶ ἀσυγκρίτῳ ἀμαρτίᾳ ψυχῆς ὄλεθρον ὀφείλοντες
Rendered as: For this one incomparable sin alone you truly owe the destruction of your soul
Preserves the severe stated consequence, with the following if-you-persist condition retained in the main text.

3. Translation choice — Greek: οὐκ οἶμαι, εἰ τοῦτο λέγων τις ἐρεῖ βασιλεῖ Τὴν ἴσην σοι ἀπονέμω τιμήν, οἵαν καὶ τοῖς νεκροῖς καὶ τῇ ἐρριμμένῃ κοπρίᾳ· οὐκ οἴομαι εἰ καλῶς ἀπαλλάξει.
Rendered as: I do not think so—if ... I do not think he will come off well.
The selected edition repeats the negative assertion οὐκ οἶμαι / οὐκ οἴομαι around a conditional and syntactic restart. Both assertions remain, rather than being compressed into one; the restart is a supplied feature, not alleged OCR corruption.

SECTION 11.13

Others say, “We shall be acting impiously if we abandon the objects of reverence handed down to us from our fathers, for it is like keeping something entrusted to us.” By this reasoning, then, even if someone is the child of a robber, or of a father, or of a man who lives shamefully, is the son, once he has become clear-minded, not to choose the better course, lest he act impiously and sin by not doing the same things as his parents? How senseless are those who say, “We worship these things so as not to trouble him himself,” as though God were troubled by being praised but not troubled by being blasphemed through ingratitude! Why, then, when rain is withheld, do you look to heaven for everything and offer prayers and entreaties? And when you succeed, why do you forget so quickly? For after reaping or gathering the vintage, you immediately assign the firstfruits to idols that are nothing, quickly forgetting the God who did you good. Then you go into sacred groves and temples and feast while performing sacrifices. For this reason some of you say, “These things have been well devised for comfort and feasting.”

Translator's notes for section 11.13 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: κἂν λῃστοῦ τις ἢ πατρὸς ἢ αἰσχροβίου
Rendered as: even if someone is the child of a robber, or of a father, or of a man who lives shamefully
Both printed ἢ disjunctions remain. The child relationship is inferred from the ensuing explicit son, not restored from missing text; the redundant father remains the supplied reading. Taking the first ἢ as conjectural ᾖ would create a smoother alternative, but that conjecture is not adopted.

2. Translation choice — Greek: οὐκ ὀφείλει ὁ υἱὸς νήψας τὸ κρεῖττον ἑλέσθαι, ἵνα μὴ ἀσεβήσῃ καὶ μὴ τὰ ἴσα τοῖς γονεῦσιν ποιῶν ἀμαρτάνῃ;
Rendered as: is the son, once he has become clear-minded, not to choose the better course, lest he act impiously and sin by not doing the same things as his parents?
Once clear-minded keeps νήψας circumstantial. The main text reads the question as a reductio of the proposed obligation to preserve ancestral practices and attaches the second μή to ποιῶν: not repeating parental conduct would be treated as sin under that argument. The full material alternative reads οὐκ ὀφείλει as a rhetorical obligation question and the second μή as negating the clause ending in ἀμαρτάνῃ: Is the son, once clear-minded, not obliged to choose the better course, so that he does not act impiously and does not sin by doing the same things as his parents? That reading instead makes repeating the parents’ conduct the sin to avoid. Both scope decisions are disclosed; neither implies a source-corruption claim.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς οὐρανὸν τὰ πάντα ἀφορῶντες
Rendered as: look to heaven for everything
The neuter accusative τὰ πάντα qualifies the scope of looking, not the nominative people looking. Looking wholly toward heaven is another viable adverbial rendering; for everything is selected in the petition-for-rain context.

SECTION 11.14

Senseless people, become just judges of what is being said. For even if one ought to give oneself over to bodily enjoyment here, which feast is better: one by rivers and woods and groves, where there are banquets and drinking parties and shaded places, or one where there is the frenzy of demons, cutting of hands, cutting off of genitals, fits of fury and madness, clipping of hair, boasts, possession, shrieks, and all those things done theatrically to astound the senseless, so that you offer their owed prayers and thanksgivings to things deader even than the dead?

Translator's notes for section 11.14 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: χειρῶν τομαὶ καὶ αἰδοίων ἀποκοπαὶ
Rendered as: cutting of hands, cutting off of genitals
Preserves both named ritual injuries soberly without euphemism or added detail.

2. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ νεκρῶν νεκροτέροις
Rendered as: to things deader even than the dead
Retains the pointed comparative and its rhetorical excess.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὅπως τὰς αὐτῶν ὀφειλομένας εὐχὰς καὶ εὐχαριστίας καὶ νεκρῶν νεκροτέροις προσενέγκητε;
Rendered as: so that you offer their owed prayers and thanksgivings to things deader even than the dead?
Their preserves the printed third-person αὐτῶν alongside second-person you offer. It can refer to the previously mentioned senseless people, potentially including the audience. Your is a contextual identification alternative, but the main text does not silently harmonize the pronouns.

SECTION 11.15

And why do you do these things gladly? Since the serpent nesting within you, who sowed fruitless desire in you, does not want to tell you, I will remind you by explaining. It is like this: in the worship of God it is proclaimed that one must be clear-minded, exercise self-control, master anger, not appropriate what belongs to others, live justly, reasonably, steadily, and gently, and discipline oneself in deprivation rather than, when lacking something, take it unjustly from someone else and be filled. But among the so-called gods, the opposite happens. Some commands are also given to inspire awe at righteousness; yet even if you perform all the commands, ignorance of God alone is sufficient for your punishment. Nevertheless, you gather at the places you have assigned to them, gladly become drunk, and kindle altars. Their drifting sacrificial smoke, through the power, brings even the blind and deaf spirits to the place where they smell it. Thus, of those there, some are filled with possession, others with strange foods, while others turn to shameless conduct and others to thefts and murders. For the vapor of the blood there and the libation of wines set even the impure spirits themselves dancing. Lurking within you, they make you take pleasure in what goes on there, surround you through dreams with false visions, and punish you with countless afflictions. For under the pretext of the so-called sacrificial offerings you are filled with fierce demons, who also kill you while cunningly escaping your notice, so that you do not understand the plot against you. For under the pretext of some abuse, necessity, passion, anger, or grief, they remove you from life by hanging, by drowning you in water, by throwing you from a cliff, by your own hand, by a stroke, or by some other affliction.

Translator's notes for section 11.15 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ἔνια εἰς κατάπληξιν δικαιοσύνης παραγγέλλεται
Rendered as: Some commands are also given to inspire awe at righteousness
The phrase relates certain commands to an impressive effect associated with righteousness. An impressive display of righteousness is another viable rendering; the main text does not decide that all such commands are merely fraudulent.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ κνίσα ῥεμβομένη καὶ τὰ τυφλὰ καὶ κωφὰ πνεύματα διὰ τῆς ἐξουσίας ἄγει εἰς τὸν τῆς ὀσφρήσεως αὐτῶν τόπον.
Rendered as: Their drifting sacrificial smoke, through the power, brings even the blind and deaf spirits to the place where they smell it.
Smoke is the grammatical subject, but the possessor or source of ἐξουσία is not stated. The power leaves it unspecified. Its power, assigning power to the smoke, is a defensible contextual alternative, not an explicit Greek possessive. No divine or demonic source of the power is independently added.

3. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ αὐτὰ χοροῖ τὰ ἀκάθαρτα πνεύματα
Rendered as: set even the impure spirits themselves dancing
Preserves the dancing image, not merely attraction.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἢ αὐτοχειρίᾳ ἢ ἀποπληξίᾳ
Rendered as: by your own hand, by a stroke
By your own hand understands the demons as inducing the victims’ self-killing, supported by the listed pretexts and means of death. αὐτοχειρία can also be killing with one’s own hand, so direct killing by the demons themselves is a material alternative given the surrounding demonic subjects. Stroke preserves the separate ἀποπληξία without adding clinical detail.

SECTION 11.16

But none of us can suffer anything of this kind. Rather, they are themselves punished by us when, after entering someone, they beg us to let them come out slowly. But perhaps someone will say, “Some who revere God also fall into such afflictions.” I say that this is impossible. For the God-revering person is the one I mean, the one who truly reveres God, not someone merely called so. The one who truly is such carries out the commands of the law given him. If someone acts impiously, he is not reverent. In the same way, if a foreigner practices the law, he is a Jew; a Jew who does not practice it is a Greek. For the person who believes God practices the law, and through this faith also removes the other afflictions that resemble mountains and weigh him down. But the person who does not practice the law plainly deserts his post because he does not believe God. Thus, as a sinner who is not a Jew, because of sin he is overpowered by the afflictions appointed to punish sinners. By God’s will, determined from the beginning, punishment justly follows those who revere him on account of their transgressions. This happens so that, after exacting the sin like a debt through torment, it may present those who have turned back clean at the judgment of all. For just as luxury here becomes for the wicked a loss of eternal good things, so punishments are sent to Jews who transgress as an exaction, so that, after receiving the due for their transgression here, they may be released from the eternal punishment there.

Translator's notes for section 11.16 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: βραδέως ἐξιέναι ἡμᾶς παρακαλοῦσιν.
Rendered as: they beg us to let them come out slowly
Takes us as the object of beg and demons as the implied subject of coming out. Permission is implicit. Beg us to withdraw slowly is another grammatical grouping, but the expulsion context favors the former.

2. Translation choice — Greek: μὴ πράξας δὲ Ἰουδαῖος Ἕλλην
Rendered as: a Jew who does not practice it is a Greek
Preserves the author’s explicit Jew/Greek categories defined here through observance. Greek can function as Gentile in the religious argument; no literal change of ancestry is added.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς ἐπιστρέψαντας
Rendered as: those who have turned back
Keeps the turning verb distinct from μετανοέω/reorient.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς ἔκπραξιν
Rendered as: as an exaction
Retains the debt-collection image of punishment.

SECTION 11.17

But you cannot say these things, for you do not believe that things there are as we say—I mean the place where everyone receives repayment. Therefore, ignorant of what benefits you, you are ambushed by temporary pleasures so as not to receive eternal things. We therefore try to demonstrate what benefits you, so that, fully assured about the promises of reverence toward God, through good actions you may be able to inherit with us the age without sorrow. Until you come to know us, then, do not be angry with us as though we were lying about the good things we want for you. For we have not begrudged bringing you what we consider true and good; on the contrary, we have been eager to make you fellow heirs of the good things we believe in. For this is how one must speak to unbelievers. But that we really speak truth about what we say you will not be able to know unless you first obey with a love of truth.

Translator's notes for section 11.17 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: φιλαλήθως ὑπακούσητε.
Rendered as: obey with a love of truth
ὑπακούω can be listen or obey; obey retains the demanded response while the adverb retains love of truth.

SECTION 11.18

For the present, therefore, even if the serpent lurking within you wishes to ambush you in countless ways, putting evil thoughts and distractions into you, you must contend against him all the more in this way: listen to us continually. For you who have been so greatly deceived must sit together and learn how to chant against him. Otherwise it is impossible. By chanting against him, I mean resisting his evil counsels with reason, remembering that from the beginning he brought death into the world through a promise of knowledge.

Translator's notes for section 11.18 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: πῶς χρὴ ἐπᾴδειν αὐτῷ
Rendered as: how to chant against him
Retains the incantation metaphor that the author immediately defines as rational resistance, not a newly supplied magical formula.

SECTION 11.19

Therefore the prophet of truth, knowing that the world was greatly deceived and seeing that it had agreed with evil, did not love peace with it, since that peace arose from error. Setting out that it ultimately brings death upon all who agree with evil, in place of error he cast into those who had become clear-minded an anger against the one who had ambushed them, like fire and resembling a sword. Holding out the word, he does away with ignorance through knowledge, as though cutting and separating the living from the dead. So, as evil was overcome by knowledge in accordance with the law, war gripped everything. For the sake of salvation a son who yielded separated from a disobedient father, or a father from a child, or a mother from a daughter, or a daughter from a mother—in short, relatives from relatives and friends from companions.

Translator's notes for section 11.19 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ὅτι εἰς τέλος ἐπιφέρει πᾶσιν τοῖς πρὸς κακίαν ὁμογνωμονοῦσιν παραθεὶς
The object of brings upon is implicit. Death in the main text is inferred from the immediately preceding death-language and ensuing living/dead contrast. The antecedent can be error-based peace or its sustaining error.

2. Greek: ἀπὸ τῶν. νεκρῶν.
The selected, image-checked edition prints a period between the article τῶν and noun νεκρῶν. English reads them together as from the dead despite this intervening punctuation. This is a supplied print feature, not assumed OCR corruption; no replacement Greek has been introduced.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὅτι εἰς τέλος ἐπιφέρει πᾶσιν τοῖς πρὸς κακίαν ὁμογνωμονοῦσιν παραθεὶς
Rendered as: Setting out that it ultimately brings death upon all who agree with evil
The object brought is implicit. Death is inferred from the end of 11.18 and the ensuing living/dead contrast. The it can be the peace founded on error or its sustaining error; no new punishment is specified.

4. Translation choice — Greek: υἱὸς ὑπείξας
Rendered as: a son who yielded
The recipient of yielding is not explicit. The saving instruction is contextual, but the English does not insert that recipient.

SECTION 11.20

And let no one say, “How is this just, for parents to be separated from children and children from parents?” It is entirely just. For if by staying with them they not only did them no good but also perished with them, how is it not just for the one who wants to be saved to be separated from the one who does not want to be saved but wants to perish together? Moreover, those who had understood what is better did not themselves want to be separated, but to remain with them and benefit them by teaching better things. Therefore the disobedient, unwilling to listen to them, themselves fought against them, separating them, persecuting them, and hating them. But those who suffered these things pitied them as people ambushed by ignorance and, taught to understand, prayed for those who mistreated them, having learned that ignorance is the cause of sin. For the teacher himself, when nailed up, prayed to the Father that the sin of those killing him might be forgiven, saying, “Father, forgive them their sins, for they do not know what they are doing.” Becoming imitators of the teacher themselves, in their sufferings they prayed for those who inflicted them, as they had been taught. Thus they did not separate because they hated their parents, since they even offered prayers for those who were not their parents but had become enemies, and try to love them as they were commanded.

Translator's notes for section 11.20 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: διδασκαλίᾳ φρονήσεως
Rendered as: taught to understand
The dative connects instruction in understanding with the prayerful response, not with a newly supplied revelation.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐχωρίζο[ντο]
Rendered as: they ... separate
Bracketed letters are already supplied by the selected edition; no new restoration has been made.

3. Translation choice — Greek: μ[ὲν ὄντ]ων
Rendered as: who were not their parents
Follows the supplied bracketed reading and preserves the contrast with enemies.

4. Translation choice — Greek: προσηλωθεὶς
Rendered as: when nailed up
Preserves the physical nail-language.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ μὴ θέλοντος, συναπολέσθαι δὲ βουλομένου;
Rendered as: from the one who does not want to be saved but wants to perish together?
The person described by βουλομένου remains the subject of co-perishing. To be saved repeats the contextual object of willing in the prior clause, not a new wish for other people’s destruction.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὅθεν οἱ ἀπειθεῖς ἐπακούειν αὐτῶν μὴ θέλοντες αὐτοὶ αὐτοὺς ἐπολέμουν, χωρίζοντες, διώκοντες, μισοῦντες.
Rendered as: themselves fought against them, separating them, persecuting them, and hating them.
The expressed αὐτούς is taken as the shared object of the parallel participles, giving the disobedient people agency in imposing separation. Separating from them is an intransitive alternative, but it is less source-transparent after the statement that the instructed people did not want separation.

SECTION 11.21

But tell me: how do you love your parents? If you do so with a constant regard for what is just, I join in your prayer; but if merely as it happens, I do not, for even on a small pretext you can become their enemies. If you love with knowledge, tell us what “parents” means. You will say, “Founders of a family line.” Why, then, have you not loved the origin of all things, if you have undertaken to do this with a just mind? But even now you will say, “We have not seen him.” Why, then, do you flatter insensible things without having searched? And what of this? Even if it was difficult for you to know what God is, you could not fail to know what is not God, so that you might reason that God is not wood, not stone, not bronze, or anything else made of perishable matter.

Translator's notes for section 11.21 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ τῶν ὅλων γένος
Rendered as: the origin of all things
γένος links the argument to lineage and parentage. Origin or source here refers to God; progenitor of all is a viable more explicitly personal alternative.

2. Translation choice — Greek: συνεύχομαι
Rendered as: I join in your prayer
Retains the prayer compound; join in wishing this is also possible, rather than bare agreement.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τί δέ;
Rendered as: And what of this?
Preserves the separate rhetorical question introducing the final argument.

SECTION 11.22

Were they not shaped on a lathe by iron—and was not the iron that shaped them on a lathe softened by fire—and is not fire itself extinguished by water? Does not water get its motion from wind, and does not wind have the origin of its movement from the God who made all things? For this is what the prophet Moses said: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and God’s Spirit was borne over the water.” And when God speaks, this Spirit, like his hand, fashions everything, separating light from darkness and spreading out the visible heaven after the invisible one, so that the regions above may be inhabited by the angels of light, while those below may be administered by the human being together with all things made for his sake.

Translator's notes for section 11.22 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ δὲ ὕδωρ οὐχ ὑπὸ πνεύματος τὴν κίνησιν ἔχει
Rendered as: Does not water get its motion from wind
πνεῦμα can be wind or spirit. Wind fits the physical water-motion argument; the same word recurs as God’s Spirit in the quotation, preserving an important lexical link in these notes.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς ἐκστάσεως
Rendered as: the origin of its movement
Here displacement or movement is intended, not religious ecstasy.

3. Translation choice — Greek: μετὰ τὸν ἀόρατον οὐρανὸν τὸν φαινόμενον ἐφαπλῶσαν
Rendered as: spreading out the visible heaven after the invisible one
Retains the visible/invisible distinction and after without supplying numbered heavens.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἢ γὰρ οὐχ ὑπὸ σιδήρου ἐτορνεύθησαν, — καὶ ὁ τορνεύσας σίδηρος ὑπὸ πυρὸς ἐμαλάχθη —
Rendered as: Were they not shaped on a lathe by iron—and was not the iron that shaped them on a lathe softened by fire—
Both forms of τορνεύω retain turning or lathe-working workmanship. Shaped alone is broader and would conceal the particular working image.

SECTION 11.23

For it was for you, the human being, that God commanded the water on the face of the earth to withdraw, so that the earth could offer you fruits. He made openings so that it might provide springs for you, streams of rivers might appear, and animals might be cast up. To put it briefly, so that everything could be at your service. Is it not for you that winds blow for the production of fruits, rains are brought, and seasonal turnings occur? Indeed, the sun and moon, together with the other stars, carry out their risings and settings for you, and rivers and lakes, together with all the springs, serve you. Therefore, just as greater honor was given to you, insensible though you are, so greater punishment through fire has been prepared for you in your ingratitude, because you were unwilling to know the one whom you ought to have known before all others.

Translator's notes for section 11.23 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ τρηδόνας ἐποίησεν
Rendered as: He made openings
