The main text interprets the continuation adversatively: after contrasting the two teachings he nevertheless gives the example. Non-adversative alike or together is a lexical alternative for the printed form. This interpretation is not a change to the source or a claim that the Greek has been normalized to ὅμως.

SECTION 15.6

Peter answered, ‘But you judged unjust what is most just. If you wish, listen.’ The father said, ‘I very much wish to.’ Peter said, ‘Suppose there are two hostile kings, each with a separate territory. If one king's subject is discovered in the other's country and thereby owes death, but is released from punishment with a slap rather than death, does not the one who released him appear humane?’ The father said, ‘Very much so.’ Peter said, ‘What, then, if this same man takes from someone something of that person's own, or even something belonging to someone else, and is caught for it? If he gives double, although he owes fourfold and death because he was caught within the enemy's borders, does it not seem to you that the one who took double and released him from death is humane?’ The father said, ‘It appears so.’ Peter said, ‘What then? Should not someone in another's kingdom, and that of a wicked enemy at that, for the sake of staying alive, flatter everyone, yield beyond what is demanded by those who compel service, greet those who do not greet him, reconcile enemies, avoid quarreling with angry people, freely provide his possessions to everyone who asks, and do other things of this sort?’ The father said, ‘I would all the more reasonably endure everything, if indeed he puts staying alive before these things.’

Translator's notes for section 15.6 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἴδιόν τι τινὸς αὐτὸς οὗτος ἀφέληται ἢ καὶ ἀλλότριον
Rendered as: this same man takes from someone something of that person's own, or even something belonging to someone else
The contrast is read as the victim's own property versus another person's property in the victim's possession. An alternative takes own in relation to the person doing the taking. The main rendering makes the contextual property relations intelligible without changing the two expressed categories into a single generic theft.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἀγγαρεύουσιν ἐπὶ πλεῖον ὑπείκειν
Rendered as: yield beyond what is demanded by those who compel service
The verb refers to impressed or compulsory service, with yielding to a greater extent. The rendering retains the excess compliance without introducing a specific journey or distance into this general instruction.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ἀδεῶς παντὶ αἰτοῦντι παρέχειν
Rendered as: freely provide his possessions to everyone who asks
Ἀδεῶς can mean without fear or hesitation. Freely is read as unhesitating willingness, not a claim that the hostile country is safe or that the possessions carry no monetary value.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἴπερ τούτων τὸ ζῆν προκρίνει
Rendered as: if indeed he puts staying alive before these things
The source moves from the father's first-person willingness to an expressed third-person verb. He retains the hypothetical person as its subject rather than silently replacing it with I; the comparison is preference for life over the burdens just listed.

SECTION 15.7

Peter said, ‘Is it not, then, the case that those whom you said were being wronged are themselves trespassers, since they are in another's kingdom, and are taking more than their due to the extent that they possess anything? Those thought to be doing wrong grant each person on the opposing side as much as they allow that person to have. For these things belong to those who have chosen the present. They are so humane as even to permit them to live. That is how the illustration stands; now hear the actual matter. When the prophet of truth was present, he taught us that the creator and God of all assigned two kingdoms to two beings, a good one and an evil one. He gave the evil one the kingdom of this present world, together with a law, so that he might have authority to punish wrongdoers; to the good one, the coming eternal age. He made each human being free, with authority to assign himself to whichever he wishes: either the present evil or the future good. Those who have chosen the present have authority to be rich, live luxuriously, enjoy themselves, and do whatever they can, for they will have none of the good things to come. But those who have decided to receive the things of the future kingdom may not consider any of the things here their own, since they belong to another king, except only water and bread—and these obtained with sweat to sustain life, since voluntary death is not permitted—and also a single covering. For one is not allowed to stand naked because of heaven, which sees everything.’

Translator's notes for section 15.7 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτοὶ παρορισταὶ τυγχάνουσιν, καθὰ ἐν ἑτέρου εἰσὶν βασιλείᾳ, καὶ τοσοῦτον πλεονέκται εἰσίν
Rendered as: trespassers ... taking more than their due
These words occur in the clause about being in another's kingdom. The first denotes crossing a boundary, the second grasping or claiming an excessive share. The rendering does not replace their property-based accusation by a general description of sinful attitudes.

2. Translation choice — Greek: δυσίν τισιν ἀπένειμεν· βασιλείας δύο, ἀγαθῷ τε καὶ πονηρῷ
Rendered as: assigned two kingdoms to two beings, a good one and an evil one
The two recipients are distinct from the creator assigning their realms. The English supplies beings for the substantivized adjectives without naming either as a second creator or as a particular named angel.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἢ τῷ παρόντι κακῷ ἢ τῷ μέλλοντι ἀγαθῷ
Rendered as: either the present evil or the future good
These substantivized adjective forms permit reference to the present evil and future good as conditions or realms, alongside the preceding recipients of the kingdoms. The translation retains the broad evil/good antithesis instead of forcing every occurrence to name an individual being; the inflected forms themselves do not settle masculine versus neuter reference.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἕνεκεν τοῦ πάντ᾽ ἐφορῶντος οὐρανοῦ
Rendered as: because of heaven, which sees everything
Heaven is the expressed all-seeing subject. It may function as a reverential reference to heavenly observation, but the main text does not silently replace it with God or infer a particular observer.

SECTION 15.8

‘If, then, you wish to hear the precise account of the matter, those whom you said a little earlier were being wronged are, rather, themselves doing wrong. For they, having chosen what is to come, live in the present among the wicked, sharing many of the same things with them: life itself, light, bread, water, clothing, and some other things of that kind. But those whom you thought were doing wrong share nothing with the good men in the things to come.’ The father answered, ‘Now that you have persuaded me that those doing wrong are themselves being wronged, while those being wronged are instead taking more than their due, the whole matter seems to me even more utterly unjust. Those who seem to be doing wrong permit many things to those who chose the future; those who seem to be wronged themselves do wrong, because there they do not provide equivalent things to those who permitted them here what they themselves permitted them.’ Peter said, ‘This is not unjust either, because each person has authority to choose the present or the future, whether small or great. A person who has chosen by his own judgment and will is not wronged—not even, I say, if he chooses the small things, since the great things lay before him; for the small things too lay before him.’ The father said, ‘You have spoken rightly. For one of the Greek sages has also said, “Responsibility belongs to those who choose; God is not responsible.”’

Translator's notes for section 15.8 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: οἱ δὲ ἀδικεῖν ὑπὸ σοῦ νομισθέντες ἐν τοῖς ἐσομένοις ἀγαθοῖς ἀνδράσιν οὐδὲν συνυπάρχουσιν
Rendered as: those whom you thought were doing wrong share nothing with the good men in the things to come
Good men is read together as the persons with whom no future sharing occurs. A possible alternative takes good with future good things; the supplied masculine ἀγαθοῖς ἀνδράσιν supports the main attachment.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἃ αὐτοὶ αὐτοῖς συνεχώρησαν
Rendered as: what they themselves permitted them
The repeated pronouns return to the present-world benefactors and the recipients. The English retains the repetition of granting rather than adding a new category of compensation absent from the clause.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπεὶ προέκειτο τὰ μεγάλα· προέκειτο γὰρ αὐτῷ καὶ τὰ μικρά
Rendered as: since the great things lay before him; for the small things too lay before him
Both statements about available choices, in their printed order, are retained. The repetition is not silently rewritten into a different conditional argument.

4. Translation choice — Greek: αἰτία ἑλομένων, θεὸς ἀναίτιος
Rendered as: Responsibility belongs to those who choose; God is not responsible
The contrast concerns accountability or blame for choice. The Greek sage remains unnamed because this passage does not identify him.

SECTION 15.9

‘But explain this argument to me as well. I remember Clement telling me that we suffer wrongs and sufferings for the forgiveness of sins.’ Peter said, ‘That too is right. For we who have chosen the future, when we possess things in excess—whether clothes, food, drink, or anything else—possess sins, because we ought to have nothing, as I explained a little earlier. For all, possessions are sins. Their deprivation, however it happens, is a removal of sins.’ The father said, ‘It follows, as you have distinguished two territories of the two kings, leaving each of those under their authority to choose what he wishes. But what about sufferings? Do we suffer these justly too?’ Peter said, ‘Most justly. Since the rule for those being saved is, as I said, that no one should possess anything, yet many possess many things—which are, in other words, sins—for this reason, out of God's surpassing love for humanity, sufferings are brought upon those who do not live with complete sincerity. This is so that, because of their measure of love for God, they may be saved from eternal punishments through temporary penalties.’

Translator's notes for section 15.9 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: πᾶσι τὰ κτήματα ἁμαρτήματα
Rendered as: For all, possessions are sins
The dative all and the wordplay between possessions and sins are retained as Peter's claim within this argument. The categorical wording is not softened into merely a warning against excessive attachment.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ τῶν σωζομένων ὅρος
Rendered as: the rule for those being saved
Ὅρος can mean a boundary, definition, or determining rule. Here the following infinitive gives a rule of possession; territorial boundary remains a live echo of the preceding kingdoms illustration.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τοῖς μὴ εἰλικρινῶς πολιτευομένοις
Rendered as: those who do not live with complete sincerity
The adverb concerns purity or sincerity of conduct. Completely is not an invented moral intensifier but expresses the adverb's undiluted quality; live purely is a concise alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τὸ ποσῶς φιλόθεον προσκαίροις τιμωρίαις αἰωνίων σωθῶσιν κολάσεων
Rendered as: because of their measure of love for God, they may be saved from eternal punishments through temporary penalties
The limited degree of God-love is retained, as is the contrast between temporary and eternal punishment. The translation does not add a named intermediate place or impose a later doctrinal account of the mechanism.

SECTION 15.10

The father said, ‘What then? Do we not see many impious people who are poor? Are these too among those being saved just because of that?’ Peter said, ‘Not necessarily. Poverty is not acceptable if someone desires what he ought not. Thus some are rich in their intention while poor in money, and are punished as people desiring to grasp more than their due. Nor is someone necessarily righteous simply because he is poor. He may be destitute in money yet desire or even do what he ought above all not to do. He may worship idols, blaspheme, engage in sexual immorality, or live indifferently, whether swearing falsely, lying, or living unfaithfully. Nevertheless, our teacher pronounced the faithful poor blessed—not because they had provided anything, for they had nothing, but because, committing no sin, they cannot be condemned solely for not giving alms because they have nothing.’ The father said, ‘Truly, the facts seem entirely consistent with the premise. That is why I have decided to hear the whole account in order.’

Translator's notes for section 15.10 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ προαιρέσει πλουτοῦσιν πενόμενοι χρήμασιν
Rendered as: are rich in their intention while poor in money
The contrast is between chosen desire and actual means, not a claim that the poor secretly possess wealth. Intention preserves the volitional force of προαίρεσις.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἢ γὰρ εἴδωλα σέβει ἢ βλασφημεῖ ἢ πορνεύει ἢ ἀδιαφόρως ζῇ, ἢ ἐπιορκῶν ἢ ψευδόμενος ἢ ἀπίστως βιούς.
Rendered as: live indifferently, whether swearing falsely, lying, or living unfaithfully
Indifference concerns disregard for moral distinctions, not merely lack of strong emotion. The main wording groups the final participles as explanations of living indifferently; the transition from finite verbs to participles supports that attachment. A material alternative takes the repeated ἢ phrases as continued coordinate alternatives in the wrongdoing list: or swearing falsely, or lying, or living unfaithfully. The repeated or supports that reading, so the main grouping is not presented as uniquely established.

3. Translation choice — Greek: μηδὲν ἁμαρτάνοντες, ἐπὶ μόνῳ τῷ τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην μὴ ποιεῖν διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν καταδικασθῆναι οὐκ ἔχουσι
Rendered as: committing no sin, they cannot be condemned solely for not giving alms because they have nothing
The participial qualification is retained; the argument concerns the faithful poor who do not otherwise sin, not a declaration that every poor person is sinless. The two negatives concern not giving and inability to condemn on that sole ground, and are both represented.

SECTION 15.11

Peter said, ‘Since, then, you are now eager to learn about our worship, I owe you an orderly account, beginning with God himself and showing that he alone must be called God, and that no others should be called or considered gods. Whoever acts otherwise must be punished eternally, as one who has committed the greatest impiety against the very Master of all.’ After saying this, he laid his hands on those troubled by afflictions, the sick, and those possessed by demons, prayed, healed them, and dismissed the crowds. Then he went inside, partook of his customary salt, and slept.

Translator's notes for section 15.11 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτὸν μόνον δεῖ λέγειν θεόν, ἑτέρους δὲ μήτε λέγειν μήτε νομίζειν
Rendered as: he alone must be called God, and ... no others should be called or considered gods
Both naming and regarding others as gods are prohibited. The rendering does not narrow the claim merely to verbal forms of address.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν συνηθεστέρων ἁλῶν μεταλαβὼν
Rendered as: partook of his customary salt
The plural salt expression may function as a reference to simple customary fare or a shared table. The main text keeps the expressed salt rather than supplying bread or a detailed meal not named here; customary fare is a smoother metonymic alternative.

HOMILY 16

SECTION 16.1

At dawn Peter went out and stood at his usual place for discussion, where he saw a large crowd assembled. Just as he was about to speak, one of his attendants came in and said, ‘Simon has arrived from Antioch. Having learned as early as last evening that you had promised to give a discourse on sole sovereignty, he is ready, together with Athenodorus the Epicurean, to come upon you while you speak and publicly oppose everything you say in any way in support of sole sovereignty.’ While the attendant was saying this, look—Simon himself was coming in with Athenodorus and some other companions. Before Peter could say anything, Simon spoke first:

Translator's notes for section 16.1 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: περὶ μοναρχίας
Rendered as: on sole sovereignty
The discussion concerns the rule of the one God, not a particular human monarchy. Sole sovereignty retains the political-rule image without replacing it everywhere by the broader modern term monotheism.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν αὐτοῦ διακόνων
Rendered as: of his attendants
The noun denotes one who serves Peter. An ecclesiastical deacon is possible, but a formal office is not established by this occurrence alone.

SECTION 16.2

‘I learned that yesterday you promised Faustus to demonstrate today, presenting your discourse in order and beginning with the Master of all himself, that he alone must be called God, that no others should be called or considered gods, and that whoever acts otherwise must be punished eternally. Above all, I am truly astounded at your recklessness in hoping to persuade a wise man, an old man at that, to your own wishes. But you will not achieve your designs, especially with me present here to expose your false arguments. Perhaps, had I not been present, the wise old man would have been deceived, since he is unfamiliar with the books publicly credited among the Jews. For now I will pass over lengthy arguments so as to expose your promise more quickly. Therefore begin to say what you promised in our own presence, for we know the scriptures. If, however, ashamed of exposure, you wish to pass over your promise in our presence, that too is sufficient proof that you are lying, because you did not dare to speak before those who know the scriptures. And why am I now waiting for you to speak, when I have the greatest witness to your promise in the old man standing here?’ Having said this, he looked directly at our father and said, ‘Tell me, most honored of all men, did not this man promise to demonstrate to you today that there is one God, that one should not call or consider anyone else a god, and that whoever acts otherwise, as someone sinning most grievously, must be punished eternally? Or will you not answer me?’

Translator's notes for section 16.2 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτὸν μόνον δεῖ λέγειν, ἄλλους δὲ μήτε λέγειν μήτε νομίζειν
Rendered as: he alone must be called God, that no others should be called or considered gods
God is the understood predicate supplied by the discourse and explicitly repeated later in the same passage. Both calling and regarding are retained.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις δημοσίᾳ πεπιστωμένων βίβλων
Rendered as: the books publicly credited among the Jews
The books' accepted authority is attributed to the Jewish community in Simon's speech. Credited or held trustworthy is the sense, not a claim that their contents have already been proved in this debate.

SECTION 16.3

Our father said, ‘You would rightly demand testimony from me, Simon, if Peter had first denied it. As things stand, I will not be ashamed to say what needs saying. I think you want to debate while cut through by anger, which is unfitting for you to do and for us to listen to. It means witnessing a quarrel, not being helped toward truth. Knowing from Greek education how inquirers should proceed, I will now remind you. Let each of you set out his own doctrine, and let your arguments be directed against the other. If Peter alone sets out his view while you keep yours silent, an argument you put forward might press against both his view and yours. Although both of you were defeated by the argument, you would not both appear defeated: the one who set out his view would, but the equal defeat of the one who did not set out his view would not be evident. He might even be thought to have won.’ Simon answered, ‘I will do as you say, but I fear that, having already been won over by his words, you will not be a truth-loving judge.’

Translator's notes for section 16.3 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὀργῇ πεπρισμένον
Rendered as: cut through by anger
The participle preserves the image of being cut or sawn through. The main text does not substitute a fire image; sawn through by anger is a more specific lexical alternative.

2. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ εἰς ἕτερον οἱ λόγοι γενέσθωσαν
Rendered as: and let your arguments be directed against the other
The reciprocal contrast of two speakers supports each directing argument toward the other. It does not require appointing an unnamed third interlocutor.

3. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ἀμφοτέρους ὑμᾶς ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου ἡττηθέντας μὴ φαίνεσθαι ἡττημένους
Rendered as: Although both of you were defeated by the argument, you would not both appear defeated
The next clauses specify that only the openly stated position would visibly lose. Both actual defeat and asymmetric appearance are retained, without changing the hidden position into a victorious one.

SECTION 16.4

Our father answered, ‘Do not force me to agree with you without judgment so that I may seem a truth-loving judge. If you wish to hear the truth, I am more predisposed toward your view.’ Simon said, ‘How are you predisposed when you do not know what I think?’ Our father said, ‘That is easy to know; listen to how. You promised to expose Peter as lying when he says there is one God. It is entirely clear that someone promising to convict the speaker of one God of falsehood does not, if he speaks truly, say the same thing. For if he says the same thing as the one speaking falsely, he too is lying. But if he says the opposite and proves it, then he speaks truly. You cannot, then, call the man who says there is one God a liar unless you believe there are many gods. I too say there are many gods. Since I say the same thing as you before the inquiry, I am more predisposed toward you. In this respect you have no need to be anxious about me; Peter does, since I still think the opposite of him. After your inquiry, I hope, as a truth-loving judge who has stripped off preconception, to agree with the prevailing argument.’ When our father had said this, a subdued cry of praise arose from the crowds because he had argued in this way.

Translator's notes for section 16.4 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ καταψευδομένῳ
Rendered as: the one speaking falsely
The main text takes the participle in a middle sense concerning false speech, since the conditional argument compares two speakers making the same supposedly false assertion. A material passive alternative is the one being falsely accused or lied about. That passive sense does not itself establish the accused person as actually false; neither reading is presented as uncontested, and the conditional remains hypothetical.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πρόληψιν ἀποδυσάμενος
Rendered as: who has stripped off preconception
The clothing-removal image and the need to set aside a prior opinion are both retained, rather than changing the father's initial shared belief into an already completed conversion.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ δὲ τὸν ἕνα λέγοντα ψεύσματος ἐλέξαι ἐπαγγελλόμενος
Rendered as: someone promising to convict the speaker of one God of falsehood
The supplied print has ἐλέξαι. Convict follows the context, especially the preceding explicit ἐλέγξειν and the charge of falsehood, rather than treating the form as choosing a speaker. Normalization to ἐλέγξαι would be a proposed Greek change, not the supplied reading. No OCR error or independently verified corrected print is claimed.

SECTION 16.5

And Peter likewise said, ‘I am ready to do as the mediator of our discussion has said, and now, without any further delay, I will set out my view about God. I too say that there is one God, who made heaven, earth, and everything in them. It is not permitted to call or consider anyone else a god.’ Simon said, ‘But I say that the scriptures trusted among the Jews speak of many gods, and that God is not angry at this, because he himself has spoken of many gods through his scriptures.’

Translator's notes for section 16.5 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἄλλον. δὲ οὔτε λέγειν οὔτε νομίζειν ἔξεστιν.
The selected print places a full stop after ἄλλον before δὲ. The English treats the surviving words as one intelligible construction. This is disclosed punctuation treatment, not a lacuna, a supply of missing words, or an allegation that a corrected Greek print has been verified.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ τῶν λόγων μεσίτης
Rendered as: the mediator of our discussion
The role concerns moderation of the exchange, not a theological mediator between God and humanity.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ αὐτὸν διὰ τῶν γραφῶν αὐτοῦ πολλοὺς θεοὺς εἰρηκέναι
Rendered as: because he himself has spoken of many gods through his scriptures
The divine subject and possessive scriptures are retained as Simon's stated reason. They do not represent an independent translator's conclusion about scriptural authorship or polytheism.

4. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ὁμῶς ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη
Rendered as: And Peter likewise said
The selected print reads ὁμῶς, ordinarily alike or likewise, and that sense is preserved. It does not itself mean the adversative nevertheless normally spelled ὅμως; no accentual normalization has been supplied. Likewise concerns Peter's joining the exchange and does not assert that his doctrine agrees with the father's preceding many-gods view.

SECTION 16.6

‘Indeed, in the law's first utterance he even appears to speak of them as like himself. For it is written that the first human had received God's command to eat from every tree in the garden, but not to eat from the tree of knowing good and evil. The serpent, through the woman, persuaded them to eat on the promise that they would become gods, and caused them to see. Then, when they had come to see, God said to them, “Look, Adam has become like one of us.” Thus the serpent, saying, “You will be like gods,” appears to have spoken as though gods exist, all the more so since God too testified, saying, “Look, Adam has become like one of us.” So the serpent, who said that there are many gods, did not lie. Again, the writing, “You shall not speak evil of gods, and you shall not speak badly of the rulers of your people,” indicates many gods, of whom he does not even wish evil to be spoken. Elsewhere too it is written, “Has another god dared to go in and take for himself a nation from the midst of a nation, as I, the Lord God, have?” In saying, “Has another god dared,” he spoke as though others exist. And elsewhere, “Gods who did not make heaven and earth, let them perish,” as those who did not make them are going to perish. Somewhere else it says, “Watch yourself, lest you go and worship other gods whom your fathers did not know,” as though other gods exist, whom he also tells them not to follow. And again, “The names of other gods shall not rise upon your lips.” Here too he speaks of many gods, whose names he does not wish to be named. Again it is written, “The Lord your God, he is God of gods.” And again, “Who is like you, Lord, among gods?” And again, “God of gods, the Lord.” And again, “God stood in an assembly of gods, and in their midst he judges gods.” So I wonder how, when so many utterances testify in writing that there are many gods, you do not firmly assert that one must neither call them gods nor believe that they exist. For the rest, if you have anything to say in response to these clear statements, speak before everyone.’

Translator's notes for section 16.6 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: [οὐκ ἐποίησαν, ἀπολέσθωσαν“ ὡς τῶν]
This wording is supplied within editorial square brackets in the selected edition. The English translates that supplied wording, including the negative and the destruction clause; it is not an independent recovery or proof that the bracketed words survive unbroken in the underlying witness. There is no printed dotted gap here to invent or fill.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἀναβλέψαι ἐποίησεν
Rendered as: caused them to see
The verb can mean look up or regain sight. The ensuing Adam quotation and the related form ἀναβλέψασιν support their coming to sight or awareness here; opened their eyes is an idiomatic alternative but supplies an unexpressed anatomical object.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ταύτῃ μᾶλλον ἢ καὶ θεὸς ἐπεμαρτύρησεν
Rendered as: all the more so since God too testified
The awkward comparative sequence is read as reinforcing the serpent's statement with God's corroboration. More literally, all the more in this respect—or even God testified. The main text makes the evidentiary link intelligible without changing who speaks or testifies.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ διαβεβαιοῦσαι μὴ δεῖν μήτε λέγειν μήτε εἶναι νομίζειν
Rendered as: you do not firmly assert that one must neither call them gods nor believe that they exist
Both the printed οὐ and the subsequent prohibition's negatives are retained. The resulting question is rhetorically awkward in Simon's argument; the initial negative is not silently deleted or changed into a different Greek word to resolve the difficulty.

5. Translation choice — Greek: κύριος ὁ θεός
Rendered as: the Lord God
The quoted Greek title is translated Lord, not replaced by Yahweh, since this is the wording quoted by the ancient author rather than a fresh translation from a Hebrew divine-name occurrence.

SECTION 16.7

Peter said, ‘Hear a briefer reply to what you have said. The law itself, which has often spoken of gods, itself says to the Jewish multitude, “Look, to the Lord your God belong the heaven of heaven and everything in them.” This includes the point that, even if gods exist, they are under him, that is, under the God of the Jews. Again, “For the Lord your God, he is God in heaven above and on earth below, and there is no other besides him.” Somewhere else scripture says to the Jewish multitude, “The Lord your God, he is God of gods,” as though to say that even if gods exist, they are under the God of the Jews. Elsewhere scripture says of him, “The great and true God, who shows no partiality and will accept no gift, rendering justice to orphan and widow.” In calling the God of the Jews great, true, and one who renders justice, scripture indicated that the others are small and not true. Elsewhere too scripture says, “As I live, says the Lord, there is no other god besides me. I am first; I am after these things; besides me there is no god.” Again, “You shall fear the Lord your God and worship him alone.” And again, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord.” Indeed, many utterances seal with an oath that God is one and that there is no god besides him. So I wonder how, when so many utterances testify that there is one God, you say there are many.’

Translator's notes for section 16.7 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ οὐρανὸς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ πάντα ὅσα ἐστὶν ἐν αὐτοῖς
Rendered as: the heaven of heaven and everything in them
The singular heaven of heaven and the ensuing plural pronoun are preserved as quoted, rather than harmonized with a different scriptural form.

2. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ λαμβάνει πρόσωπον οὐδὲ μὴ λάβῃ δῶρον
Rendered as: shows no partiality and will accept no gift
The first idiom concerns favoritism rather than literally taking a face. The second names a gift in a judicial context, where bribe is a plausible explanatory alternative; the main wording keeps the source's expressed noun.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐγὼ πρῶτος, ἐγὼ μετὰ ταῦτα
Rendered as: I am first; I am after these things
The supplied expression after these things is translated rather than replaced with the familiar but unprinted title last.

4. Translation choice — Greek: κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν κύριος εἷς ἐστίν
Rendered as: the Lord your God is one Lord
The quoted word order permits the traditional one-Lord rendering or the Lord is one. The main rendering keeps the repeated Lord and the explicit numerical one, without importing a different creed or Hebrew wording.

SECTION 16.8

Simon said, ‘My argument with you from the beginning was to expose you from the scriptures as lying when you say one must not speak of many gods. That is why I showed many written utterances: the divine scriptures themselves speak of many gods.’ Peter said, ‘The very scriptures that speak of many gods themselves also brought this before us, saying, “The names of other gods shall not rise upon your lips.” So I did not speak against what is written, Simon.’ Simon said, ‘Listen to a reply to that too, Peter. You seem to me to sin in speaking against them, since scripture says, “You shall not speak evil, and you shall not speak badly of a ruler of your people.”’ Peter said, ‘I do not sin, Simon, in foretelling their destruction in agreement with the scriptures. For it is written, “Gods who did not make heaven and earth, let them perish.” This does not mean, as you interpreted it, that some did make them and will not perish. For the maker is shown to be one by what is written from the beginning: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” It did not say “the gods.” Somewhere else it says, “The firmament announces the work of his hands.” And in another place it is written, “The heavens themselves will perish, but you will remain forever.”’

Translator's notes for section 16.8 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: παρήγεσαν ἡμῖν εἰποῦσαι
Rendered as: themselves also brought this before us, saying
The printed form is treated as a form of παράγω, bringing forward or passing by. The main text preserves its presentation sense, with this pointing to the following quotation. A material intransitive alternative is passed before us, saying. The quoted prohibition functions as instruction, but that function is not substituted for the movement or presentation verb; no Greek correction is supplied.

2. Translation choice — Greek: στερέωμα
Rendered as: firmament
The term denotes the established heavenly expanse in the quoted cosmological language. It is not modernized into a scientifically specified atmosphere or an otherwise unexpressed material dome.

SECTION 16.9

Simon said, ‘To show that there are many gods, I presented clear utterances from the scriptures. You have brought as many, or even more, utterances from those same scriptures to show that there is one God, the God of the Jews. In answer to my saying that one must not speak evil of gods, you added, to show that there is one maker, that those who did not make must perish. In answer to my saying that one must speak of gods, since the scriptures also speak of them, you showed that one must not utter their names, because the same scripture says not to utter the names of other gods. Since, then, the scriptures themselves say that there are many gods and at other times that there is only one, and sometimes say not to speak evil of them and at other times to speak evil of them, what must we conclude from this except that the scriptures themselves mislead us?’

Translator's notes for section 16.9 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τί δεῖ λογίσασθαι
Rendered as: what must we conclude
The question is about the inference required by the stated premises, retaining the necessity expressed by δεῖ rather than substituting mere ability.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πλανῶσιν
Rendered as: mislead
The term means leading astray or deceiving, not merely presenting a neutral diversity of views. Its accusation is retained as Simon's argument.

SECTION 16.10

Peter said, ‘They do not mislead; they expose, bringing into the open the evil intention against God that lurks like a serpent within each person. For they lie before us resembling many different impressions. Each person, having his own intention like wax, looks over them and finds everything in them. Whatever kind of god he wants to exist, he presses upon them his intention, which, as I said, resembles wax, and takes its impression. Since, then, anyone finds in them whatever he wishes to think about God, one person takes impressions of many gods from them. We, however, have taken the image of the one who truly exists, recognizing the true impression from our own form. Moreover, the soul within us is clothed in his image for immortality. If I abandon the begetter of this image, it too must abandon me by a just judgment, recognizing me as unjust from that very act of audacity. Coming from a just one, it will justly abandon me, and thus I shall perish in soul after punishment, when the help from it has departed. If there is another god, let him first clothe me in another appearance, another form, so that through the body's new form I may recognize the new god. But even if he changes the form, will he also change the soul's substance? If he changes that too, I am no longer myself, having become another in both form and substance. Let him therefore fashion others, if there is another. But there is not. If there were, he would have fashioned them. Since he has not fashioned them, being nonexistent, let him leave the one who truly exists alone. For there is no such one except in Simon's opinion alone. I accept no other God besides the one who created me.’

Translator's notes for section 16.10 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τύποις
Rendered as: impressions
The scriptures' differing patterns are likened to forms that stamp wax. Impressions keeps the molding image that develops in the verbs of pressing and taking an imprint; types or models are lexical alternatives.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ταύτης τὸν γεννήτορα ἐὰν καταλίπω, δικαίᾳ κρίσει καὶ αὐτή με καταλιπεῖν ἔχει
Rendered as: If I abandon the begetter of this image, it too must abandon me by a just judgment
The feminine pronouns are read as referring to the immediately preceding image in which the soul is clothed. The soul itself is a grammatically possible alternative, but the ensuing loss of assistance and destruction as to the soul favors the protecting image as what departs.

3. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ὡς ἀπὸ δικαίου δικαίως καταλείψει με
Rendered as: Coming from a just one, it will justly abandon me
The phrase from a just one is read as the image's provenance from the righteous creator. A more literal alternative is and, as from a just one, it will justly abandon me; the main text does not make the unjust person just in order to remove the tension.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ψυχὴν μετὰ κόλασιν, τῆς ἀπ’ αὐτῆς ἀπολειφθείσης βοηθείας, φθαρήσομαι
Rendered as: I shall perish in soul after punishment, when the help from it has departed
The accusative soul is taken as the respect in which destruction occurs, and it continues the image as the help's source. This conditional destruction is not softened into bodily death alone or harmonized with the later description of souls as immortal.

5. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἔστιν ἢ μόνῃ γνώμῃ. Σίμωνος
Rendered as: For there is no such one except in Simon's opinion alone
The negative concerns the proposed other god. The genitive Simon's completes opinion across the printed punctuation; no second speaker or missing sentence is invented.

SECTION 16.11

Simon said, ‘Since I see you speaking more frequently on behalf of the God who fashioned you, learn from me how you are impious even toward him. Those who fashioned you appear to be two, as scripture says, “And God said, Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness.” “Let us make” indicates two or more, but certainly not one.’

Translator's notes for section 16.11 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ’ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν
Rendered as: Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness
The plural deliberative form and our are central to Simon's inference and retained. The second phrase does not repeat an expressed possessive, so the English does not add a second our.

2. Translation choice — Greek: οἱ πλάσαντες δύο φαίνονται
Rendered as: Those who fashioned you appear to be two
Fashioned repeats the preceding πλάσαντός, preserving Simon's shared wording and its distinction from make in the quotation. You is understood from the preceding God who fashioned you, rather than identifying an additional created object not in the context.

SECTION 16.12

Peter answered, ‘There is one who said to his own wisdom, “Let us make a human.” Wisdom, with which he himself always rejoiced as with his own spirit, is united with God like a soul, but extends from him like a hand, creating the whole. For this reason one human also came into being, and from him the female came forth. Though one in kind, it is a pair. For through extension and contraction the one is considered two. Thus I act rightly in rendering all honor to one God as to parents.’ Simon said, ‘What then? Even if the scriptures speak of other gods, will you not accept them?’

Translator's notes for section 16.12 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἥνωται μὲν ὡς ψυχὴ τῷ θεῷ, ἐκτείνεται δὲ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ὡς χείρ
Rendered as: is united with God like a soul, but extends from him like a hand
Both soul and hand comparisons are retained as the author's own account of wisdom. The rendering does not convert these comparisons into a later creedal definition or a separate independent creator.

2. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ μία οὖσα τῷ γένει δυάς ἐστιν
Rendered as: Though one in kind, it is a pair
The feminine one and the noun pair can concern the human kind represented by male and female, with a possible continuing analogy to wisdom. The English leaves the collective referent broad instead of introducing a second named divine person.

3. Translation choice — Greek: κατὰ γὰρ ἔκτασιν καὶ συστολὴν ἡ μονὰς δυὰς εἶναι νομίζεται
Rendered as: For through extension and contraction the one is considered two
The numerical unity and duality are translated into accessible English while preserving both spatial-process terms. A unit is considered a pair is a more technical alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἑνὶ θεῷ ὡς γονεῦσιν
Rendered as: to one God as to parents
The singular one God and plural parents are both retained. The comparison is not silently normalized to one parent or expanded into two gods.

SECTION 16.13

Peter answered, ‘Whether scriptures or prophets speak of gods, they speak to test their hearers. For it is written: “If a prophet arises among you, giving you signs and wonders, and that sign and wonder comes to pass, but he says to you, ‘Let us go and worship other gods whom your fathers did not know,’ you shall not listen to that prophet. Your hands shall be the first to stone him, for he tempted you to turn away from the Lord your God. If you say in your heart, ‘How did he perform that sign or wonder?’ you shall surely know that the tempter was testing you to see whether you fear the Lord your God.” It was said that the tempter was testing, but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon. For God, who knows everything (as can be shown from many passages), would not test in order to learn for himself, since he knows everything beforehand. If you wish, we will discuss this, and I will show that God has foreknowledge. The claim that he is ignorant has been shown to be false and itself written as a test. Thus, Simon, we cannot be made to stumble either by scriptures or by anyone else; neither are we deceived into accepting many gods, nor do we agree with any statement spoken against God.’

Translator's notes for section 16.13 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἀπὸ ·γραφῶν
The selected image-checked print places a middle dot immediately before γραφῶν. The English translates the surviving wording without assigning the point lexical content. No letters are corrected, no wording restored, and no OCR error or established lacuna is inferred from this apparent print feature.

2. Translation choice — Greek: γινώσκων γνώσῃ
Rendered as: you shall surely know
The participle plus finite verb repeats the knowing root for emphasis. The main rendering expresses that assurance without adding a new source of knowledge.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ πειράζων ἐπείραζεν
Rendered as: the tempter was testing
The agent is a substantivized participle, the one who tests or tempts, not a separately supplied Greek noun. The main English varies the lexical roots as tempter and testing; it does not reproduce the Greek's repeated root. A neutral, root-transparent alternative is the one who tests was testing, or the tester was testing. Tempter is chosen because the preceding act tempts toward apostasy and Peter argues against identifying the agent with an omniscient God who needs to learn. The neutral testing interpretation remains a viable lexical alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἑτέρως δὲ μετὰ τὴν εἰς Βαβυλῶνα μετοικεσίαν φαίνεται
Rendered as: but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon
The clause asserts a difference in presentation after the Babylonian displacement. It does not specify a scribe, manuscript, or exact replacement wording, so none is supplied.

SECTION 16.14

‘For we ourselves know from the scriptures that angels have been called gods: I mean the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob, as well as the one born as Emmanuel and the one called Mighty God. Moreover, Moses became a god to Pharaoh, though in reality he was a human. So too the idols of the nations. But for us there is one God, one: the one who made created things and ordered everything, whose son the Messiah also is. In obedience to him, we recognize the false things in the scriptures. Moreover, supplied by the fathers with the true things of the scriptures, we know only one who made the heavens and the earth, the God of the Jews and of all who choose to worship him. The fathers, declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God, handed him down to us, so that we might know that anything said against God is false. But I will say something even beyond this: if things are not as I have said, may it be my lot, and that of those who love the truth, to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us.’

Translator's notes for section 16.14 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἔτι .δὲ
The selected print has a point immediately before δὲ. The English translates the surviving words as a continuous construction, without assigning the point lexical content. No letters are corrected or missing wording restored; the apparent print feature is not labeled an OCR error or an established lacuna.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἀγγέλους θεοὺς λεχθέντας
Rendered as: angels have been called gods
The following examples remain within Peter's statement about appellations. Their inclusion is retained without imposing or repairing the author's classification to fit a later theological system.

3. Translation choice — Greek: οὗ καὶ ὁ χριστὸς υἱός, ᾧ πειθόμενοι
Rendered as: whose son the Messiah also is. In obedience to him
Christos functions independently as a title, so Messiah follows the supplied policy. Also preserves the additive καὶ but does not by itself establish other sons. The relative him is grammatically compatible with the Messiah or God; the main text leaves that pronoun unexpanded rather than resolving its antecedent silently.

4. Translation choice — Greek: θεοφιλεῖ λογισμῷ ἀληθὲς ὂν δογματίσαντες
Rendered as: declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God
The adjective can mean God-loving or beloved by God. The argument's insistence on reverent thinking supports the active sense; reasoning dear to God is a material alternative. The truth qualification is retained without adding a new creed.

5. Translation choice — Greek: περὶ εὐφημίας τοῦ πεποιηκότος ἡμᾶς θεοῦ κινδυνεύειν
Rendered as: to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us
The willingness to risk being wrong is explicitly tied to reverent speech about the creator. The translation does not turn it into a denial that any risk exists.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς βάτου λαλήσας καὶ τῷ Ἰακὼβ παλαίσας
Rendered as: the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob
The first two participles share the single article ὁ, which motivates a shared-subject rendering. This differs from the repeated articles before the subsequent Emmanuel and Mighty God designations. The English preserves that grammatical pattern without independently assigning the subject a later theological identity.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ᾧ πειθόμενοι ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν τὰ ψευδῆ ἐπιγινώσκομεν
Rendered as: In obedience to him, we recognize the false things in the scriptures
The main text takes from the scriptures as identifying the source material in which false things are recognized. The following contrast with the scriptures' true things supports this material-source reading. A material alternative attaches the phrase to recognition as its evidentiary basis: In obedience to him, we recognize what is false from the scriptures, meaning by scriptural evidence. Neither attachment is claimed to be uniquely established.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦτον καὶ θεοφιλεῖ λογισμῷ ἀληθὲς ὂν δογματίσαντες οἱ πατέρες παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν
Rendered as: The fathers, declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God, handed him down to us
The main rendering understands the neuter phrase ἀληθὲς ὂν as characterizing the preceding assertion about the one creator, while masculine τοῦτον identifies the God handed on. A material alternative takes ὂν substantivally as being: having affirmed this one as a true being through God-loving reasoning, the fathers handed him on to us. The supplied gender distinction is retained and disclosed, not corrected or diagnosed as OCR corruption.

SECTION 16.15

When Simon heard this, he said, ‘Since you say that one must not believe even a prophet who gives signs and wonders but speaks of another god, knowing that he also deserves death, then your teacher too, who gave signs and wonders, was reasonably put to death.’ Peter answered, ‘Our Lord neither declared that gods exist besides the one who created everything nor proclaimed himself to be God. But he reasonably pronounced blessed the person who said that he was the son of the God who ordered everything.’ Simon answered, ‘Does it not seem to you, then, that one who comes from God is God?’ Peter said, ‘Tell us how this can be. We cannot tell you this, because we did not hear it from him.’

Translator's notes for section 16.15 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: οὔτε ἑαυτὸν θεὸν εἶναι ἀνηγόρευσεν
Rendered as: nor proclaimed himself to be God
The denial is retained as the author's Peter states it. It is not corrected or softened to conform to a denominational account of Christ's identity.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν ἀπὸ θεοῦ θεὸν εἶναι
Rendered as: one who comes from God is God
The origin phrase is rendered openly. God versus a god is a material English article alternative; the Greek argument concerns application of the divine designation rather than a newly specified rank in a pantheon.

SECTION 16.16

‘Besides, it belongs to the Father not to have been begotten, but to the Son to have been begotten. What is begotten is not comparable with what is unbegotten or even self-begotten.’ Simon said, ‘Even if it is not the same in respect of generation?’ Peter said, ‘One who is not in every respect the same as another cannot have all the same designations as that one.’ Simon said, ‘That is assertion, not demonstration.’ Peter said, ‘Why do you not understand that the one is self-begotten or even unbegotten, whereas the other, being begotten, cannot be called the same, not even if the begotten one is of the same substance as the begetter .... But learn this too: human bodies have immortal souls clothed in God's breath. Having come forth from God, they are of the same substance, but are not gods. If they are gods, then by that reasoning the souls of all humans—those who have died, those living, and those yet to be born—are gods. But if, persisting in your argument with me, you say that they too are gods, what great distinction remains even for the Messiah in being called God? For he has what everyone also has.’

Translator's notes for section 16.16 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: τῷ γεγεννηκότι .... ἀλλὰ
The edition prints four dots after the begetter clause. The English preserves exactly four dots, without supplying a missing verb or continuation. Its rendering of is in the preceding conditional clause provides ordinary English copular syntax and does not claim to restore the unavailable wording after the clause.

2. Translation choice — Greek: γεννητὸν δὲ ἀγεννήτῳ ἢ καὶ αὐτογεννήτῳ οὐ συγκρίνεται
Rendered as: What is begotten is not comparable with what is unbegotten or even self-begotten
The three generation terms and their distinctions are retained. Self-begotten is not silently collapsed into unbegotten, and the comparison is not rewritten to assert a later creedal formula.

3. Translation choice — Greek: Εἰ καὶ τῇ γενέσει οὐ ταὐτόν ἐστιν;
Rendered as: Even if it is not the same in respect of generation?
The main text takes εἰ καί concessively in response to the preceding distinction and preserves οὐ as actual nonidentity. A material alternative interprets the utterance as a negative question seeking assent: Is it not the same even in respect of generation? That alternative remains a negative question, not an affirmative conditional. Generation can mean coming-to-be or birth and is not silently replaced by substance.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς αὐτῆς οὐσίας
Rendered as: of the same substance
The phrase is retained both in the conditional argument about the begotten one and the subsequent account of souls. The passage's own distinction between shared substance and the title God is not harmonized with another theological position.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ θεῷ λέγεσθαι
Rendered as: in being called God
The supplied dative form occurs in the title-ascription expression. The English preserves the intended naming construction without supplying a further predicate or claiming to correct the printed Greek.

SECTION 16.17

‘We call God the one whose distinctive property cannot belong to another. For just as he is called boundless because he is infinite in every direction, and it is altogether necessary, since another cannot likewise be infinite, that being called boundless not be a property of another—if anyone says this is possible, he lies, for two things infinite in every direction cannot coexist, since each is bounded by the other—so it is natural for the unbegotten to be one. Even if he has a shape, in this way too the incomparable is one. For this reason he is also called Most High, because, being above all, he has everything subject to himself.’

Translator's notes for section 16.17 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: μὴ εἶναι ἴδιον τὸ καλεῖσθαι ἀπέραντος
Rendered as: that being called boundless not be a property of another
The negative is retained, and of another is inferred from the immediately preceding statement that another cannot likewise be infinite. If distinctive property is instead attached to God without that contextual complement, the clause appears to deny the distinctiveness it argues for. The main reading preserves the negation and supplies the contextually available referent, not a conjectural alteration of the Greek.

2. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ δὲ ἐν σχήματί ἐστιν
Rendered as: Even if he has a shape
The conditional concession is retained. The phrase does not deny shape in order to impose a different doctrine of divine incorporeality.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὕψιστος
Rendered as: Most High
The superlative title is translated and immediately explained by the source's claim of superiority over all.

SECTION 16.18

Simon said, ‘Surely “God,” which everyone says, is not his unutterable name, that you insist so strongly even about the name, so that it may not be given to another?’ Peter said, ‘I know that this is not his unutterable name, but the one spoken by human convention. If you give this to another, you will attach the unspoken one to another too. In terms of intention, the spoken name is an advance toward the unspoken one. On this account the insult is reckoned also against what has not yet been spoken, just as honor directed toward what is known is referred to what is not yet known.’

Translator's notes for section 16.18 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπόρρητον ὄνομα
Rendered as: unutterable name
The adjective can denote a name not to be divulged or spoken. Secret name is another possible emphasis; the subsequent spoken/unspoken contrast supports unutterable without specifying the hidden name's letters.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ λεγόμενον ὄνομα τοῦ μὴ λεγομένου πρόοδός ἐστιν
Rendered as: the spoken name is an advance toward the unspoken one
Advance toward reads the movement from the public designation to the unspoken name, because the preceding conditional traces giving the spoken name to another into consequently attaching the unspoken name to another. A materially different genitive reading is the spoken name is a going-forth of the unspoken one, or its outward expression, in which the movement originates in the unspoken name. Both directions are disclosed; the main text is contextual rather than a claim that the genitive uniquely means toward. No hidden name or magical utterance is supplied.

SECTION 16.19

Simon said, ‘I wished to know, Peter, whether you truly believe that the human form has been patterned after his form.’ Peter said, ‘Truly, Simon, I am fully convinced that this is so.’ Simon said, ‘How can death dissolve the body when it is patterned by the greatest seal?’ Peter said, ‘It is the form of a righteous God. When it begins to do wrong, the image within it flees, and so the body dissolves, in order that the form may disappear and an unrighteous body may not possess the form of a righteous God. The dissolution, however, concerns not the seal but the body that was sealed. The sealed thing is not dissolved without the one who sealed it. Thus it is not permitted even to die without judgment.’ Simon said, ‘What need was there, then, to give the form of such a one to the human raised from the earth?’ Peter said, ‘This happened because of the creating God's love for humanity. For in respect of substance everything is superior to human flesh—I mean the ether, the sun, the moon, the stars, air, water, fire, in a word, everything else too. These things, having come into being for human service and being superior in substance, gladly endure serving what is inferior in substance because of the form of the superior one. For just as those honoring a clay statue of a king have their honor referred to the one whose form the clay bears, so all creation gladly serves the human made from earth, looking toward that one's honor.’

Translator's notes for section 16.19 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὰν οὖν ἀδικεῖν ἄρξηται, ἡ ἐν αὐτῷ ἰδέα φεύγει
Rendered as: When it begins to do wrong, the image within it flees
It refers to the body or embodied person under discussion. The distinction between the departing image and the dissolving sealed body is maintained, rather than replacing image with a named material organ.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἄνευ δὲ τοῦ σφραγίσαντος τὸ σφραγισθὲν οὐ λύεται
Rendered as: The sealed thing is not dissolved without the one who sealed it
The phrase does not explicitly name permission, presence, or action as the sense of without. The English leaves that relation broad; without the sealer's permission is a contextual explanatory alternative but adds an unexpressed noun.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ κατ’ οὐσίαν λόγῳ
Rendered as: in respect of substance
The comparison concerns what things consist of, not their moral worth. Its repetition distinguishes superior substance from the honor attached to the inferior human body's divine form.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὴν ἐκείνου ἀφορῶσα τιμήν
Rendered as: looking toward that one's honor
The king-statue comparison points to the superior original whose form the human bears. That one preserves the pronoun while the note identifies its contextual direction; it does not claim that earth itself is the king.

SECTION 16.20

‘See, Simon, what kind of God you wish to persuade us to be ungrateful toward! The earth still carries you, perhaps wishing to see who would dare to think as you do. For you were the first to dare what no one had dared, the first to utter what we heard for the first time. We were the first and only ones to witness God's boundless patience in the face of such impiety from you—not that of some other god, but of the one who created the world, against whom you dared to be impious. No chasms opened in the earth, no fire was sent down from heaven or advanced to burn people, no rain was withheld, no multitude of wild beasts was sent from the thickets, and God's destructive wrath did not begin even against us because of one sinner, as in the case of spiritual adultery, which is worse than adultery according to the flesh. For is not the one who then punished sins the God who created heaven and earth? For even now, most grievously blasphemed, he would have inflicted the greatest punishment. But, on the contrary, he is patient and calls us to repentance. He has destructive arrows stored in his treasuries for the destruction of the impious, which he will release like living creatures when he takes his seat to repay his enemies with judgment. Therefore let us fear the righteous God whose form the human body bears as an honor.’

Translator's notes for section 16.20 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἴσως δὲ ἰδεῖν βουλομένῃ τίς σοι τὰ ὅμοια φρονεῖν τολμήσοι
Rendered as: perhaps wishing to see who would dare to think as you do
The feminine participle is read as continuing the personified earth, despite its oblique inflection beside the nominative earth. Perhaps qualifies the conjecture; the English does not replace the earth with an unexpressed masculine observer.

2. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν ὁ τότε ἐπεξελθὼν τὰ ἁμαρτήματα οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς κτίστης θεός;
Rendered as: For is not the one who then punished sins the God who created heaven and earth?
The printed negative question is retained rather than turned into a categorical identification or categorical denial. Its relation to the following counterfactual punishment and contrasting patience is rhetorically difficult. A reading that challenges the attribution of the earlier punishments to the creator is materially possible; the main text preserves the question rather than deleting the negative or resolving the theology by emendation.

3. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς μετάνοιαν καλεῖ
Rendered as: calls us to repentance
The creator’s patient invitation contrasts with the preceding impiety against him, supporting repentance as a moral-spiritual response under the October 13 contextual policy. It is not reduced to sadness or a change of opinion. Us remains the previously disclosed contextual addressee, not an expressed Greek object and not a claim that God must repent. Toward God is not retained as a formula: the Greek names repentance as the object of the call but does not print an additional Godward phrase. The older reorientation toward God wording remains in its historical record.

4. Translation choice — Greek: συντελοῦντα βέλη πρὸς συντέλειαν τῶν ἀσεβῶν
Rendered as: destructive arrows ... for the destruction of the impious
The repeated completion or ending root describes final, destructive force. The English retains the destructive aim and the arrows image without supplying a specific weapon technology.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ζῷα ἔμψυχα
Rendered as: like living creatures
The life-bearing comparison is explicit; it does not say that the arrows are literally a named species of animal or angel.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ἐπὶ μοιχείας πνευματικῆς τῆς κατὰ σάρκα χείρονος ὑπαρχούσης
Rendered as: as in the case of spiritual adultery, which is worse than adultery according to the flesh
The main reading takes adultery according to the flesh as the genitive of comparison and attaches worse being to spiritual adultery. It is favored by the surrounding rebuke, which presents Simon's impiety as especially serious. A material alternative takes adultery according to the flesh as subject of a genitive absolute: adultery according to the flesh being worse. That reverses the comparison and is not excluded by morphology alone. This is a disclosed attachment ambiguity, not an unverified printing defect.

SECTION 16.21

After Peter had said this, Simon answered, ‘Since I see you cleverly hinting that the things written against the creator in the books are not true, tomorrow I will show from your teacher's words that he says the creator is not the highest God.’ Having said this, Simon went out. Peter said to the crowds standing there, ‘Even if Simon can harm us in no other way concerning God, at least he prevents you from hearing the words that can purify the soul.’ At these words from Peter, much murmuring arose among the crowds, who said, ‘What necessity is there to let him come in here and speak his blasphemies against God?’ Peter heard and said, ‘May speech against God for the testing of human beings find its sufficient limit in Simon. For, as the Lord said, “There will be false apostles, false prophets, sects, and ambitions for rule.” These, as I conjecture, will take their beginning from Simon, who blasphemes God, and cooperate in saying the same things against God as Simon does.’ Having said this with tears, he beckoned the crowds with his hand. As they came forward, he laid his hands on them, prayed, and dismissed them, telling them to assemble earlier in the morning. Having said this, and groaning, he went inside and slept without even taking food.

Translator's notes for section 16.21 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: [ὅτι]
The selected edition supplies this conjunction in editorial brackets. Its sense is translated as that, without claiming independent recovery of an unbroken witness.

2. Greek: [ἐν ταῖς βί]βλοις
The selected edition supplies the beginning of in the books within brackets, including part of the noun. The English translates the supplied complete expression; it does not invent additional lost wording or a dotted gap.

3. Greek: αὔ[ριον ἀπὸ]
The selected edition brackets the completion of tomorrow and the following from. These supplied words are translated as printed; the translation is not a new reconstruction of their underlying witness.

4. Greek: ἐὰν
The supplied print accents this as ἐὰν. The English follows the permissive infinitive sense allow, supported by accusative αὐτόν and infinitive λέγειν, rather than treating it as a conditional conjunction. The usual infinitive accent ἐᾶν would be a proposed accentual normalization, not the supplied reading. No OCR error or independently verified corrected accent is claimed.

5. Translation choice — Greek: αὔ[ριον ἀπὸ] τῶν τοῦ διδασκάλου σου λόγων δείξω τὸν δημιουργὸν μὴ ἀνώτατον λέγοντα εἶναι θεόν.
Rendered as: tomorrow I will show from your teacher's words that he says the creator is not the highest God
The main text infers the teacher as the unexpressed object of show and subject of saying from the explicit reference to the teacher's words; the creator is the subject of the being infinitive. A materially different direct attachment makes λέγοντα agree with τὸν δημιουργόν: I will show from your teacher's words the creator saying that he is not the highest God. The reference to the teacher's words motivates the main inference but does not make it explicit or uncontested.

6. Translation choice — Greek: Γένοιτο μέχρι Σίμωνος ἀρκετὸν γενέσθαι τὸν κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πρὸς πειρασμὸν ἀνθρώπων λόγον
Rendered as: May speech against God for the testing of human beings find its sufficient limit in Simon
The wish concerns the sufficiency and limit of the testing discourse in Simon. May it suffice as far as Simon is a more literal alternative; the English does not change the wish into a prediction that no later blasphemy will occur.

7. Translation choice — Greek: αἱρέσεις, φιλαρχίαι
Rendered as: sects, and ambitions for rule
The first noun can mean factions or schools and the second loves of ruling or power-seeking. Sects and ambitions for rule preserve both social division and desire for control, without assigning later denominational names.

HOMILY 17

SECTION 17.1

On the next day, then, Peter, who was about to debate with Simon, woke rather early and prayed. Just as he finished, Zacchaeus came in and said, “Simon is sitting outside, speaking with some of his own people, about thirty of them.” Peter said, “Let him speak until a crowd gathers, and then let us begin the debate. In this way we can hear what he says, prepare ourselves to address it, and go out and speak.” And that is what happened. Zacchaeus went out and, not long afterward, came back in and reported to Peter the statements Simon had made against Peter.

Translator's notes for section 17.1 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἀντέβαλλεν τῷ Πέτρῳ
Rendered as: reported to Peter
The verb can denote comparison or putting statements before someone; reported fits the messenger’s relay of Simon’s speech, not a second debate with Peter.

SECTION 17.2

He said, “He accuses you, Peter, of being a servant of evil, of having great power in magic, and of filling people’s souls with images in a way worse than idolatry. He seemed to offer this as proof that you are a magician, saying: ‘I know about myself that I think things through when I am alone, but when I come to debate with him, I do not remember a single argument. For while he is speaking, my mind is occupied with recalling the things I had thought of saying to him when I came, and I do not hear anything at all that he says. Since I do not experience anything like this with anyone else, but only with him, how am I not being bewitched by him? That whatever he teaches is worse than idolatry will be clear to anyone with understanding once I explain it. For there is no other benefit than for the soul to become free of idols of every kind. When it imagines a form, it is bound by fear; it withers with anxiety about suffering something, and, being altered, becomes possessed. Yet in its possession it seems to most people to be sound-minded.

Translator's notes for section 17.2 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: κακίας ὄντα ὑπηρέτην
Rendered as: being a servant of evil
This is Simon’s reported accusation, not the narrator’s verdict. ὑπηρέτης is an assistant or subordinate.

2. Translation choice — Greek: φαντασιοῦντα
Rendered as: filling ... with images
Preserves the mental-image vocabulary that structures Simon’s criticism, not generic deception alone.

3. Translation choice — Greek: εἰδώλων παντοδα[πῶν]
Rendered as: idols of every kind
The bracketed letters already belong to the supplied edition’s reading. No new restoration is made.

4. Translation choice — Greek: δαιμονοῦσα
Rendered as: in its possession
Retains the demon/possession language; raves or acts like one possessed is a possible phenomenological rendering.

SECTION 17.3

This is what Peter gives you under a promise of making you sound-minded. For under the pretext of one God he seems to free you from many lifeless idols. These do not do their worshipers much harm, because with their very eyes they can see that they are stone, bronze, gold, or some other lifeless material. Therefore, knowing that what is seen is nothing, the soul cannot be haunted by fear in the same way through the visible thing. But when, through deceptive teaching, it looks toward a fearsome God, it is uprooted from its natural condition. I say these things not because I advise you to revere idols, but because Peter, while seeming to free your souls from fearsome images, makes each of your minds possessed by a more fearsome image, introducing a God with a form—and, moreover, supremely just. With this comes terror, and shuddering for the soul that thinks of it, capable even of loosening the tension of sound reasoning. For the mind, placed in such a storm, has its brightness muddied like deep water by a violent wind. Therefore, if he comes for your benefit, let him not, while seeming to dissolve your relatively mild fears arising from lifeless forms, introduce in their place a fearsome form of God. But does God have a form? If he does, he has a shape. If he has a shape, how is he not bounded? If bounded, he is in a place. If in a place, he is less than the place containing him. If less than something, how is he greater, stronger, or higher than all? So much for these matters.

Translator's notes for section 17.3 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς φοβερὸν θεὸν ἀποβλέπουσα τῶν κατὰ φύσιν ἐκβαθρεύεται.
Rendered as: when ... it looks toward a fearsome God, it is uprooted from its natural condition
Retains the upheaval/derangement image and the author’s contrast with nature; this remains Simon’s reported position.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν ὀρθῶν λογισμῶν ἐκλῦσαι τοὺς τόνους
Rendered as: loosening the tension of sound reasoning
Preserves the tension image rather than merely saying it makes thinking difficult.

3. Translation choice — Greek: μορφὴν δὲ ἔχει θεός;
Rendered as: form ... shape ... bounded
Keeps distinct vocabulary in the chain of argument. Bounded denotes spatial delimitation, not simply weakness.

4. Translation choice — Greek: φοβερῶν ἰδεῶν δοκῶν ἀπαλλάσσειν ὑμῶν τὰς ψυχάς, φοβερωτέρᾳ ἰδέᾳ τὸν ἑκάστου ὑμῶν ἐνθουσιᾶν ποιεῖ νοῦν
Rendered as: while seeming to free your souls from fearsome images, makes each of your minds possessed by a more fearsome image
ἰδέα can denote form, appearance, or a mental representation. Images preserves the visual thread through idols, imagined forms, and God in a form without asserting that every image is a physical statue. Ideas or conceptions is a material cognitive alternative but would conceal the unqualified visual sense in modern English.

SECTION 17.4

It is also obvious that he does not truly believe even the things said by his own teacher, for he proclaims the opposite of them. For, as I learn, his teacher said to someone, “Do not call me good, for the good one is one.” But when he says “good,” he no longer means that just one whom the scriptures proclaim, who kills and gives life—kills those who sin and gives life to those who live according to his judgment. That he really did not call the maker good is clear to anyone able to think it through. For the maker was known to Adam, whom he formed; to Enoch, who pleased him; to Noah, whom he saw to be righteous; likewise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and also to Moses, the people, and the whole world. Yet Peter’s teacher Jesus came and said, “No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father, and those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” Therefore, if the one present was himself the Son, from his coming he revealed to those he wished the one unknown to all. Thus the Father was unknown to everyone before him, not being this one who was known to all.

Translator's notes for section 17.4 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: μή με λέγε ἀγαθόν, ὁ γὰρ ἀγαθὸς εἷς ἐστίν
Rendered as: Do not call me good, for the good one is one
Keeps the wording actually quoted here, not a familiar expanded Gospel form. Simon’s distinction between good and just is retained as his argument.

2. Translation choice — Greek: δημιουργοῦ
Rendered as: the maker
δημιουργός denotes creator or maker, not automatically an evil demiurge; the speaker’s proposed distinction is not editorially endorsed.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ δικαίῳ ὁραθέντι Νῶε
Rendered as: to Noah, whom he saw to be righteous
δικαίῳ is taken predicatively, righteous being what God perceived in Noah, fitting the list of people pleasing or accepted by the maker. To righteous Noah, whom he saw is the material attributive alternative: righteousness is then Noah’s epithet rather than the content of the seeing. Both retain Noah as the person seen by God; neither reverses the action into Noah seeing God.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν πατέρα, εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱός, ὡς οὐδὲ τὸν υἱόν τις οἶδεν εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ
Rendered as: No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father
Preserves the distinct Greek knew/knows forms instead of homogenizing the quoted tenses.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἀγαθὸν δὲ εἰπὼν οὐκέτι ἐκεῖνον λέγει τὸν δίκαιον
Rendered as: But when he says “good,” he no longer means that just one
No longer retains the additional οὐκέτι force. It can express the logical consequence under the good designation—no longer under that description—rather than necessarily a chronological change of belief. The clause remains Simon’s argument, not a narrator’s endorsement.

SECTION 17.5

And in saying this, Jesus does not even agree with himself. For sometimes, in other statements drawn from the scriptures, he establishes a fearsome and just God, saying, “Do not fear the one who kills the body but can do nothing to the soul. Fear the one who can cast both body and soul into the Gehenna of fire. Yes, I tell you, fear this one.” That he really said to fear this one as a just God, to whom he also says the wronged should cry out, is shown when he gives a parable on this and adds its explanation, saying, “If, then, the unjust judge acted in this way because he was petitioned repeatedly, how much more will the Father bring vindication for those who cry to him day and night? Or do you think that because he is patient with them, he will not do it? Yes, I tell you, he will do it, and quickly.” But whoever says that God vindicates and repays establishes him as just by nature, and not good. Further, he also gives thanks to the Lord of heaven and earth. If he is Lord of heaven and earth, he is acknowledged as maker; and being maker, he is just. Calling him good at one time and just at another, he does not agree even in this way. Thirdly, his wise disciple insisted yesterday that direct perception is more adequate than an apparition, not knowing that direct perception can be human, whereas an apparition is acknowledged to belong to divinity.’

Translator's notes for section 17.5 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν γέενναν τοῦ πυρὸς
Rendered as: the Gehenna of fire
Retains the named place and fire qualification, not the distinct Hades term.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἐκδίκησιν
Rendered as: vindication
ἐκδίκησις can be vengeance or the securing of justice. Vindication fits the wronged petitioners while retaining the punitive repayment explained afterward.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐνάργειαν ὀπτασίας ἱκανωτέραν εἶναι
Rendered as: direct perception is more adequate than an apparition
