ἐνάργεια here is direct evident encounter, contrasted with ὀπτασία, an apparition. The polemical wise disciple is not softened into neutral description.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐνίοτε γὰρ ἄλλαις φωναῖς τῶν ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν φοβερὸν καὶ δίκαιον συνίστησι θεὸν
Rendered as: For sometimes, in other statements drawn from the scriptures, he establishes a fearsome and just God
The main text takes τῶν ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν partitively, other statements among those derived from scripture. The subsequent fear, judgment, and Lord-of-heaven-and-earth material continues Simon’s contrast with the scriptural just maker, favoring this reading. The comparative-genitive alternative is with statements different from those from the scriptures; that would distinguish rather than include the statements’ scriptural derivation. The supplied wording permits both and is not emended.

SECTION 17.6

“By these and similar statements, Peter, Simon, standing outside and speaking to the crowds, seems to me to be disturbing most of them. So go out immediately and dissolve his false arguments by the power of truth.” After Zacchaeus said this, Peter prayed as usual and went out. He stood in the place of the previous day, greeted the crowds in the customary manner of reverence toward God, and began to speak as follows: “Our Lord Jesus, being a true prophet—as I will also give assurance about this at the proper time—made concise declarations about matters important to the truth, for these two reasons. First, he addressed people who revered God and knew to believe what he uttered as a declaration, for what was said was not foreign to their customary practice. Second, because he had a limited time to proclaim, he did not employ demonstrative argument, so that he might not spend all his allotted time on arguments. Otherwise he would have been occupied with explaining a few statements that could be understood through effort of soul, and would thus not have presented the arguments important to truth more extensively. For he declared what he wished as to a people able to understand, among whom we too belong. Whenever, on a rare occasion, we did not understand something he said, we asked him privately, so that none of what he said would remain unintelligible to us.

Translator's notes for section 17.6 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὸν πρὸ μιᾶς τόπον
Rendered as: in the place of the previous day
The elliptical before one refers to one day before; no new location is invented.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ τῆς ἀποδείξεως οὐκ ἐχρῆτο λόγῳ
Rendered as: he did not employ demonstrative argument
Distinguishes concise pronouncement from developed proof, not truthful from untruthful speech.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν ὑπὸ πόνου ψυχῆς νοεῖσθαι δυναμένων
Rendered as: that could be understood through effort of soul
Retains the intellectual effort supplied by the source rather than rendering the matters permanently incomprehensible.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς ἀληθείᾳ διαφέροντας μὴ ἐπὶ πλεῖον εἰσφέρειν λόγους
Rendered as: would thus not have presented the arguments important to truth more extensively
λόγους expressly denotes arguments or discourses presented, distinguished from the earlier matters about which declarations were made. Presented retains introducing them into discussion, not simply naming their topics.

SECTION 17.7

Knowing, then, that we knew everything he had said and could supply the proofs, when he sent us to the uninstructed nations to baptize them for forgiveness of sins, he commanded us to teach them first. Of these commands, this is the first and great one: to fear the Lord God and serve him alone. The God he said to fear is the one whose angels belonging to the least of the believers among us stand in heaven continually beholding the Father’s face. For he has a form for the sake of primary and sole beauty, and all his members, not for use. He does not have eyes in order to see from there, for he sees from every side, being in body incomparably brighter than the seeing spirit within us and more radiant than every light, so that compared with him the sun’s light is reckoned darkness. Nor does he have ears in order to hear, for from every side he hears, understands, moves, acts, and makes. He has the most beautiful form for the human being’s sake, so that the pure in heart may be able to see him and rejoice in that for which they endured these things. For with his form, as with a most magnificent seal, he stamped out the human being, so that the human being might rule and have dominion over all and everything might serve him. Therefore, judging him to be the whole and the human being his image—he himself invisible, but his image, the human being, visible—the one who wishes to revere him honors his visible image, namely the human being. Whatever someone does to a human being, whether good or evil, is referred to him. Therefore judgment from him will go forth to all, assigning to each what is deserved, for it vindicates his form.

Translator's notes for section 17.7 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: μορφὴν γὰρ ἔχει διὰ πρῶτον καὶ μόνον κάλλος
Rendered as: he has a form for the sake of primary and sole beauty
Preserves the unusual first/only qualification of beauty. For beauty first and alone is another possible grouping, treating first adverbially; neither reading makes the form a merely metaphorical appearance.

2. Translation choice — Greek: λαμπρότερος ὢν τὸ σῶμα
Rendered as: being in body ... brighter
Retains the author’s explicit bodily attribution to God without conforming it to a later account of divine incorporeality.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ γὰρ αὐτοῦ μορφῇ ὡς ἐν μεγίστῃ σφραγῖδι τὸν ἄνθρωπον διετυπώσατο
Rendered as: with his form, as with a most magnificent seal, he stamped out the human being
Preserves the form/seal/imprint sequence and its relation to human dominion.

4. Translation choice — Greek: κρίνας εἶναι τὸ πᾶν αὐτὸν καὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ εἰκόνα τὸν ἄνθρωπον
Rendered as: judging him to be the whole and the human being his image
Attaches κρίνας to the following worshipper, whoever wishes to revere him. The worshipper judges God, not himself, to be the whole. Continuing God as subject of a determination from the preceding sentence is a possible contextual alternative: God determined himself to be the whole and the human being his image. The main text chooses the more direct attachment to the following grammatical subject, avoiding a dangling divine determination. The precise God/whole relation is left at the source’s abstract wording, without a later metaphysical explanation.

SECTION 17.8

But someone will say, “If he has a form, he also has a shape and is in a place. And if he is in a place and contained by it as something lesser, how is he great above all? And how can he also be everywhere while having a shape?” To the person saying this, one can first say: those around Simon persuade people to believe such thoughts about him; but we know to be true the things attested by our Lord Jesus Christ. Proofs that this is so must be supplied to you, not on the basis of a command. But first I will speak about place and God. Place is what does not exist, whereas God is what exists; and what does not exist cannot be compared with what exists. For how can place have existence, unless it is a second region, such as heaven, earth, water, air, and any other body, if there is one, which would also fill the void there? It is called void for this reason: because it is nothing. For ‘nothing’ is a more suitable name for it. For what is the so-called void—some sort of vessel that contains nothing? Yet the vessel itself, being empty, is not itself place; rather, place is that in which the void itself is, if indeed it is a vessel. For what exists must necessarily be in what is nothing. But this is what I mean by what does not exist, which some call place: it is nothing. But how can what is nothing be compared with what exists, except as opposites, so that what exists is not [place], but what does not exist is called place? But even if it is something, although many examples press to come forth from me as proof, I wish to use just one, to show that what contains is not invariably stronger than what is contained. The sun is a circular shape and is wholly contained by air, but it illuminates the air, heats it, and cuts through it. And if the sun is absent from it, the air is enveloped in darkness, and wherever a part of it becomes bright, it grows cold as though dying. But by the sun’s rising it is illuminated again, and wherever it is warmed by the sun it is also adorned with greater beauty. And the sun does these things by its presence, although its substance is bounded. What, then, still prevents God, as the maker and master of this and all things, while he himself has shape, form, and beauty, from having the presence proceeding from him extended infinitely?

Translator's notes for section 17.8 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: καὶ οὗ ἂν αὐτοῦ μέρους λαμπρὸν γένηται, ὡς νεκρούμενον ψύχεται
The wording associates becoming bright with cooling, which is puzzling in this analogy. Bright is nevertheless what the supplied text says; no emendation to dark has been made.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀληθεῖς γινώσκομεν τὰς μαρτυρουμένας
Rendered as: we know to be true the things attested
The feminine plural has no expressed noun; things or statements attested expresses the ellipsis without adding an extra source claim.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ μὲν ὂν μὴ ᾖ, τὸ δὲ μὴ ὂν τόπος λέγηται
Rendered as: what exists is not [place], but what does not exist is called place
The first member has copular ᾖ, be, while only the second has λέγηται, be called; the main text preserves that distinction. Place in the first member is an understood predicate drawn from the second member, not an expressed Greek noun there. Its English brackets disclose this interpretive ellipsis, not a printed lacuna, recovered wording, or restoration of Greek. The surrounding comparison of opposites and the explicit place predicate in the second member favor the elliptical reading. A material non-elliptical alternative is so that what exists should not exist, while what does not exist is called place, potentially functioning as a paradoxical reductio. That existential reading remains available; the main preference does not disprove it. Ceases to exist is not offered as that alternative because it would introduce a temporal change absent from μὴ ᾖ.

4. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ οὗ ἂν αὐτοῦ μέρους λαμπρὸν γένηται, ὡς νεκρούμενον ψύχεται
Rendered as: wherever a part of it becomes bright, it grows cold as though dying
The supplied wording says bright, not dark. The resulting physical description is puzzling, but the main text preserves that printed adjective rather than silently emending it to fit the argument. Its referent is understood as a part of the air.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ μετουσίαν ἀπείρως ἐκτεταμένην ἔχειν
Rendered as: from having the presence proceeding from him extended infinitely
μετουσία can be presence, participation, or communicated influence. Presence preserves the analogy with the bounded sun’s effects without adding a second bodily substance.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὃ ἂν καὶ αὐτοῦ πληροῦν τὸ κενόν
Rendered as: which would also fill the void there
Takes αὐτοῦ locatively, there, referring to the discussed place or region. It is not nominative emphatic αὐτό, itself. A genitive alternative is which would also fill its void, with the precise possessive referent drawn from the surrounding body/region discussion; no replacement Greek is adopted.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τί οὖν ἔτι κωλύει τὸν θεὸν ὡς τούτου καὶ πάντων δημιουργὸν καὶ δεσπότην ὄντα, αὐτὸν μὲν ἐν σχήματι καὶ μορφῇ καὶ κάλλει ὄντα, τὴν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ μετουσίαν ἀπείρως ἐκτεταμένην ἔχειν;
Rendered as: What, then, still prevents God, as the maker and master of this and all things, while he himself has shape, form, and beauty, from having the presence proceeding from him extended infinitely?
The participial descriptions present God as maker/master and as himself being in shape, form, and beauty. The infinitive governed by prevents concerns his having the presence proceeding from him infinitely extended. The revised question preserves that grammatical focus rather than making the shape itself the prevented action and the extension merely circumstantial.

8. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ κατὰ κέλευσιν τὰς ἀποδείξεις ὑμῖν τοῦ οὕτως ἔχειν ἀνάγκη παρέχειν
Rendered as: Proofs that this is so must be supplied to you, not on the basis of a command.
The main text gives οὐ narrow scope over κατὰ κέλευσιν, leaving the obligation ἀνάγκη παρέχειν affirmative. The immediate placement of the negative before the command phrase favors this source-transparent scope, and the following developed proofs fit an obligation to supply demonstration rather than an appeal to command. A materially different broad scope denies obligation on command: We are not obliged to provide you at a command with proofs that things are so. The latter is a possible contextual construal, but the main text does not insert a negative before ἀνάγκη or claim the two scopes are equivalent. The source does not identify whose command is meant.

9. Translation choice — Greek: πλὴν αὐτὸ τὸ σκεῦος κενὸν ὂν οὐκ αὐτό ἐστι τόπος, ἀλλ’ ἐν ᾧ ἐστὶν αὐτὸ τὸ κενόν, εἴπερ σκεῦός ἐστιν.
Rendered as: Yet the vessel itself, being empty, is not itself place; rather, place is that in which the void itself is, if indeed it is a vessel.
The main text renders substantival αὐτὸ τὸ κενόν as the void itself, preserving the recurring κενόν earlier called void and tested hypothetically as a vessel. If indeed it is a vessel retains that conditional uncertainty rather than affirming that the void is a physical container. A contextual ellipsis can instead supply vessel from the preceding σκεῦος: Yet the vessel itself, being empty, is not itself place; rather, if it is a vessel, place is that in which the empty vessel itself is. The final vessel proviso supports that alternative, but the repeated substantive void is more source-transparent and no unprinted second vessel noun is required. The precise conditional referent remains open between the hypothesized void/container and the vessel already under discussion.

10. Translation choice — Greek: οἷον οὐρανός, γῆ, ὕδωρ, ἀὴρ καὶ εἰ ἄλλο τι ἐστὶν σῶμα
Rendered as: such as heaven, earth, water, air, and any other body, if there is one
The final item retains the separate καὶ εἰ existential condition, if there is another body, not merely an open-ended or-list. The following relative clause remains attached to the body/region discussion, including its existing locative-versus-genitive αὐτοῦ alternatives.

11. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦτο γὰρ αὐτῷ (τὸ οὐδέν) οἰκειότερον ὄνομα
Rendered as: For ‘nothing’ is a more suitable name for it.
Quotation marks identify nothing as the proposed name in the source’s parenthesis τὸ οὐδέν, not an indefinite denial that any suitable name exists. For explicitly preserves the explanatory γάρ; more suitable retains the comparative οἰκειότερον.

12. Translation choice — Greek: πῶς δὲ καὶ πανταχῇ εἶναι δύναται, ἐν σχήματι ὤν;
Rendered as: And how can he also be everywhere while having a shape?
And retains the discourse link δέ and also separately preserves the additive καί introducing the further everywhere claim. The shape condition is unchanged.

13. Translation choice — Greek: κἂν ἀπῇ αὐτοῦ, σκότῳ περιβάλλεται
Rendered as: And if the sun is absent from it, the air is enveloped in darkness
κἄν contracts καὶ ἐάν; and if preserves the link and conditional force rather than giving only temporal when. The subject shift is contextual: the sun is absent, while the air is enveloped in darkness. An even if emphasis is possible for the contracted particle, but the sequential account of the sun’s effects favors and if here; no absent Greek word or changed print is introduced.

14. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ δὲ τῆς αὐτοῦ ἀνατολῆς πάλιν φωτίζεται
Rendered as: But by the sun’s rising it is illuminated again
By makes the causal or agency force of ὑπό explicit, not only temporal coincidence at the rising. But and again retain δέ and πάλιν; the air remains the contextual subject.

SECTION 17.9

There is therefore one true God, who sits presiding in a superior form, being twice the heart of what is above and below. From him, as from a center, a substance wells forth with vital, incorporeal power and passes through all things, together with stars and the things belonging only to heaven, air, water, earth, fire, and anything else that exists. It is infinite in height, unbounded in depth, immeasurable in breadth, extending in three directions to infinity the life-giving and intelligent nature proceeding from him. This reality that proceeds from him and is infinite on every side must therefore have as its heart the one who truly is above all in shape. Wherever he may be, he is in the middle, as in something infinite, being the boundary of the whole. Therefore the extensions, beginning from him, have a nature drawn from what is boundless. Of these, one takes its beginning from him and reaches into height above, another into depth below, another to the right, another to the left, another in front, and another behind. Looking toward these as a number equal on every side, he completes the world in six intervals of time, himself being rest and having the coming boundless age as an image, being beginning and end. For the six infinities terminate in him and receive from him their extension into infinity.

Translator's notes for section 17.9 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: σὺν τε ἄστροις καὶ μόνοις οὐρανοῦ, ἀέρος, ὕδατος, γῆς, πυρὸς
The relation of substantival μόνοις to the following element genitives is compressed. The main rendering understands things belonging only to those elements, preserving every supplied element and the only restriction; no conjectural replacement is adopted.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ ἄνω τε καὶ κάτω δὶς ὑπάρχων καρδία
Rendered as: being twice the heart of what is above and below
δὶς literally means twice. Its precise link to above and below is compressed; the main text retains twice rather than replacing it with an unprinted cosmological term.

3. Translation choice — Greek: σὺν τε ἄστροις καὶ μόνοις οὐρανοῦ, ἀέρος, ὕδατος, γῆς, πυρὸς
Rendered as: together with stars and the things belonging only to heaven, air, water, earth, fire
The adjective μόνοις is taken substantivally with an implicit things, qualified by the following genitives. The phrase is syntactically compressed; the main text preserves its only restriction and the complete element list, without changing μόνοις to another conjectured word.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οὐσία ἄπειρος εἰς ὕψος, ἀπέραντος εἰς βάθος, ἀμέτρητος εἰς πλάτος
Rendered as: a substance ... infinite in height, unbounded in depth, immeasurable in breadth
Retains the three distinct spatial measures and their distinct adjectives.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἀνάγκη εἶναι καρδίαν, ἔχον τὸν ὄντως ὑπὲρ πάντα ἐν σχήματι
Rendered as: must ... have as its heart the one who truly is above all in shape
Takes εἶναι with ἔχον as a having construction, καρδίαν as what is had, and the person as its identifying complement. A more formally segmented rendering is must be a heart, containing the one, but the center-and-extensions argument favors having him as heart.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν ἐσόμενον ἄπειρον αἰῶνα εἰκόνα ἔχων
Rendered as: having the coming boundless age as an image
Keeps the future age and image relationship without substituting an unprinted doctrine of the seventh day.

SECTION 17.10

This is the mystery of the sevenfold order. For he himself is the rest of all things, so that to those who imitate his greatness on a small scale he grants himself as rest. He alone is in one respect graspable and in another ungraspable, in one respect bounded and in another unbounded, having the extensions from him reaching into infinity. For he is graspable and ungraspable, near and far, being here and there, existing alone and possessing the communicating presence of the mind that is infinite on every side. By breathing this, the souls of all have life. Even if they are separated from the body, if they are found to possess longing for him, they are carried immortal into his embrace, just as in winter the vapors of the mountains, drawn by the sun’s rays, are carried toward the sun. What affection, then, can we conceive if we behold the beauty of his form with our mind? Otherwise it is impossible: for beauty cannot exist without form, nor can anyone be drawn toward love of him or even imagine seeing God if he has no form.

Translator's notes for section 17.10 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἑβδομάδος μυστήριον
Rendered as: mystery of the sevenfold order
ἑβδομάς is a group of seven or a week. Sevenfold order retains the six extensions plus rest discussed just before; mystery of the week is a viable more familiar alternative.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ πανταχόθεν ἀπείρου νοὸς τὴν μετουσίαν ἔχων
Rendered as: possessing the communicating presence of the mind that is infinite on every side
μετουσία can be participation, presence, or shared influence. Communicating presence retains its life-imparting reach in the breathing clause, without silently identifying a second deity.

3. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὸν αὐτοῦ κόλπον φέρονται
Rendered as: they are carried ... into his embrace
κόλπος is bosom or lap; embrace makes the intimate image readable while retaining a personal destination.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ἐν χειμῶνι ὥρας οἱ ἀτμοὶ τῶν ὀρῶν
Rendered as: just as in winter the vapors of the mountains
Retains the vapor simile and its mountain origin, without a modern scientific correction.

5. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὸν αὐτοῦ κόλπον φέρονται, ὡς ἐν χειμῶνι ὥρας οἱ ἀτμοὶ τῶν ὀρῶν ὑπὸ τῶν τοῦ ἡλίου ἀκτίνων ἑλκόμενοι φέρονται πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀθάνατοι.
Rendered as: they are carried immortal into his embrace, just as in winter the vapors of the mountains, drawn by the sun’s rays, are carried toward the sun
The main text attaches immortal to the souls because the paragraph concerns their continued life after separation from the body. ἀθάνατοι can grammatically agree with feminine souls or masculine vapors, and its printed position after the simile permits the local alternative the vapors ... are carried toward the sun, immortal. Moving the adjective to the souls is a disclosed attachment choice, not uniquely established by morphology.

SECTION 17.11

But some, being strangers to the truth and allies of evil, say under the pretext of glorifying him that he is without shape, so that, being formless and without appearance, he may be visible to no one and thus not become an object of longing. For a mind that does not see God’s form is empty of him. How can someone even pray without having anyone in whom to take refuge or on whom to lean? Having nothing solid to meet it, the mind is thrown off its footing into a void. “Yes,” someone says, “one should not fear God, but love him.” I too say this. But a good conscience about every good deed will bring this about, and doing good arises from fear. “But fear,” he says, “stuns the soul.” Yet I say it does not stun it, but awakens it and turns it back. Perhaps it would rightly be said that one ought not to fear God if we human beings did not fear many other things—I mean plots from our fellows, as well as wild animals, creeping creatures, diseases, afflictions, demons, and countless other things. Let the one who demands that we not fear God rescue us from these, so that we need not fear them either. But if he cannot, why does he begrudge our being released from countless fears through one fear directed toward the just one, and becoming able through a little faith in him to remove countless afflictions from ourselves and others, while also expecting a reward of good things and, by doing no evil through fear of the God who sees everything, continuing in peace even in the present?

Translator's notes for section 17.11 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἀντιτυπίαν γὰρ οὐκ ἔχων εἰς κενὸν ἐκβαθρεύεται.
Rendered as: Having nothing solid to meet it, the mind is thrown off its footing into a void.
ἀντιτυπία denotes resistance or solidity encountered; the spatial image of a supportless mind is retained rather than a modern psychological diagnosis.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐξυπνίζει καὶ ἐπιστρέφει
Rendered as: awakens it and turns it back
The turning verb is kept distinct from the reorientation terminology for μετανοέω.

3. Translation choice — Greek: βραχείᾳ τῇ πρὸς αὐτὸν πίστει
Rendered as: through a little faith in him
Retains the small/little qualification instead of adding great faith.

SECTION 17.12

Thus grateful servitude to the true master sets all the rest free. So if it is possible for someone not to sin without fearing God, let him not fear. For it is possible, through love for him, not to do what does not meet with his approval. For both fearing him is written and loving him is commanded, so that each person may use a medicine suited to his own constitution. One can therefore fear him because he is just. Whether you fear or love, then, do not sin. May someone who fears be able to master unlawful pleasures, not desire what belongs to others, practice love of humanity, exercise self-control, and act justly. For I see some whose fear of him is incomplete committing very many sins. Let us therefore fear God not only because he is just: for in mercy toward those who have been wronged he punishes those who have wronged them. As water extinguishes fire, so fear does away with desire for evils. The person who teaches fearlessness does not himself fear; and the person who does not fear does not believe that there will be a judgment, increases his desires, practices magic, and slanders others for the things he himself does.”

Translator's notes for section 17.12 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ πρὸς τὸν ὄντως δεσπότην εὐγνώμων δουλεία
Rendered as: grateful servitude to the true master
δουλεία denotes bonded service or slavery. Servitude retains the paradox that subjection to the true master frees from other masters; grateful also allows well-disposed.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς λοιποὺς πάντας ἐλευθέρους τίθησιν
Rendered as: sets all the rest free
Retains the plural all the rest; the scope may be everyone else affected or all remaining people, rather than silently replacing it with a different direct object such as all fears.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τὴν αὐτοῦ ἕκαστος κρᾶσιν ἐπιτηδείῳ χρήσηται φαρμάκῳ
Rendered as: may use a medicine suited to his own constitution
Retains the medicine/constitution analogy and different appropriate responses rather than deleting fear or love.

SECTION 17.13

Hearing this, Simon interrupted and said, “I know whom you are addressing with these things. But so that I do not myself spend time on things I do not wish by saying the same things to refute you, you promised to answer the matters set before us. You said that you had adequately understood your teacher’s teachings because you were present to see him by direct perception and hear him, and that no one else could have the like through a vision or an apparition. But I will show that this is false. Someone who hears a person directly is not entirely assured about what is said, for his mind can reason: perhaps the figure before me, being human, is lying. An apparition, however, as soon as it is seen, gives the one seeing it assurance that it belongs to divinity. Answer me about this first.”

Translator's notes for section 17.13 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὁράματι ἢ ὀπτασίᾳ
Rendered as: a vision or an apparition
ὅραμα and ὀπτασία are kept distinguishable in this argument; direct perception represents ἐνάργεια, the opposed category.

2. Translation choice — Greek: μὴ ἄρα ψεύδεται (ἄνθρωπος ὢν) τὸ φαινόμενον.
Rendered as: perhaps the figure before me, being human, is lying
The neuter the appearing thing/figure is the source’s way of referring to the visible speaker, not necessarily a supernatural apparition in this clause.

SECTION 17.14

Peter said, “You proposed to speak to one point but answered another. For you proposed that someone is better able to understand more ...... by hearing from an apparition than, indeed, from direct perception ... But then you went on to persuade us that the person hearing from an apparition is more secure than the one hearing from direct perception itself. Indeed, this was why you asserted that you knew Jesus’ teachings more adequately than I, as someone who had heard the word from him through an apparition. Nevertheless I answer the point proposed at the beginning. Once the prophet has first given assurance that he is a prophet, he is securely believed concerning what he says directly; having first been recognized as truthful, he answers after being examined and questioned as the learner wishes. But someone who trusts an apparition, a vision, or a dream is in danger, for he does not know whom he trusts. It is possible that this is an evil demon or a deceptive spirit, pretending in its speech to be what it is not. If someone should wish to inquire who the one appearing is, the apparition can say whatever it wishes about itself. Thus, flashing like an evil being and remaining as long as it wishes, it is extinguished, without staying for the questioner’s examination as long as the questioner wanted. Someone who sees through dreams cannot even inquire about what he wishes, for the sleeper’s reasoning is not under his own control. This is why, though we desire to learn many things while awake, in a dream we ask about other things, or, without even asking, hear about things of no concern to us. On waking we are discouraged that we neither heard about nor examined what we desired to learn.”

Translator's notes for section 17.14 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: μᾶλλον δύνασθαί τινα πλεῖον νοεῖν ...... παρ’ ὀπτασίας ἀκούοντα, ἢ γὰρ παρὰ τῆς ἐναργείας ...
Six dots and then three dots mark two printed gaps. Both exact counts remain, without restoring the missing wording or hiding the interrupted syntax.

2. Translation choice — Greek: μᾶλλον δύνασθαί τινα πλεῖον νοεῖν ...... παρ’ ὀπτασίας ἀκούοντα, ἢ γὰρ παρὰ τῆς ἐναργείας ...
Rendered as: someone is better able to understand more ...... by hearing from an apparition than, indeed, from direct perception ...
Better able separately represents μᾶλλον with δύνασθαι, while understand more represents πλεῖον with νοεῖν. Exactly six and three printed gap dots remain; no missing words are restored. The comparison is retained, with indeed representing γάρ in the interrupted construction.

3. Translation choice — Greek: δύναται λέγειν ἑαυτῷ ὃ βούλεται.
Rendered as: the apparition can say whatever it wishes about itself
The subject of δύναται is unstated. The main text takes the apparition as subject, interpreting the dative as speaking on its own behalf, with self-description inferred from the preceding identity question. About itself is not claimed as the literal meaning of ἑαυτῷ. A materially different reading takes the questioner as subject and the reflexive as to himself: If someone wishes to inquire who the appearing figure is, he can tell himself whatever he wishes. The following evanescent apparition favors the main subject continuation, but does not eliminate the alternative.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἢ δαίμονα κακὸν εἶναι ἢ πνεῦμα πλάνον
Rendered as: an evil demon or a deceptive spirit
Both alternatives remain distinct.

SECTION 17.15

Simon said, “If you say that apparitions do not always speak truth, nevertheless visions and dreams, being sent by God, do not lie about whatever he wishes to say.” Peter said, “You said correctly that, being sent by God, they do not lie. But it is unclear whether the person who saw it has seen a God-sent dream.” Simon said, “If the person who saw it is righteous, he has seen something true.” Peter said, “You said correctly. But who is righteous if he needs a vision to learn what he ought to learn and to do what he ought to do?” Simon said, “Grant me this, that only the righteous person can see a true vision, and I will answer you on that point. For I have decided that an impious person does not see a true dream.” Peter said, “This is false, and I can demonstrate it both without writing and from writing, though I do not promise to persuade you. For a man who has inclined toward love of a wicked woman does not transfer his mind to lawful life together with another who is good in every way. Sometimes, even knowing in themselves which is better, because they are already captivated they love the worse one. You too are suffering something like this without knowing it.” Simon said, “Leave these things aside and speak to what you promised. For it seems impossible to me for impious people to be given dreams by God in any manner.”

Translator's notes for section 17.15 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἀγράφως καὶ ἐγγράφως
Rendered as: both without writing and from writing
The contrast is between proof apart from written texts and proof from them, not between illiteracy and literacy.

2. Translation choice — Greek: προειλημμένοι
Rendered as: because they are already captivated
Preoccupation or prior capture explains the persistence in an inferior attachment; no explicit compulsion beyond the source is added.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀλλ’ οὖν γε τὰ ὁράματα καὶ τὰ ἐνύπνια θεόπεμπτα ὄντα οὐ ψεύδεται, περὶ ὧν ἂν εἰπεῖν θέλῃ.
Rendered as: nevertheless visions and dreams, being sent by God, do not lie about whatever he wishes to say
He understands God as the subject of θέλῃ, chosen because God is the sender encoded in θεόπεμπτα. The subject is not expressly named. About whatever they wish to say is a material alternative with visions and dreams as subject, since a neuter plural can take a singular verb, as the immediately preceding ψεύδεται does. Neither reading requires correcting the supplied text.

SECTION 17.16

Peter said, “I remember that I promised to show this and supply proof both without writing and from writing. Now listen as I speak. We know many people—if you are fair-minded; in any case I have those present as judges—who revere idols, commit adultery, and sin in every way, yet see visions and true dreams, some even apparitions of demons. For I do not say that anyone can see the fleshless form of Father or Son, because mortal eyes are dazzled by the greatest light. Therefore God’s not being seen by the human being who has been turned into flesh is not because he begrudges it, but because he is merciful. For the one who sees cannot live. The excess of light dissolves the flesh of the viewer, unless by God’s ineffable power the flesh is transformed into the nature of light so that it can see light, or the substance of light is transformed into flesh so that it can be seen by flesh. For seeing the Father without transformation belongs to the Son alone. The righteous do not see in the same way: at the resurrection of the dead, when their bodies have been transformed into light and they become equal to angels, then they will be able to see. Indeed, even if one of the angels attempts to appear to a human being, he turns into flesh so that he can be seen by flesh. For no one can see a fleshless power, not only that of the Son but not even that of an angel. But if someone sees an apparition, let him understand it to be that of an evil demon.

Translator's notes for section 17.16 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν γὰρ ἄσαρκον ἰδέαν
Rendered as: the fleshless form
Retains form without flesh, not shapelessness, since the argument distinguishes the two.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ εἰς σάρκα τετραμμένῳ ἀνθρώπῳ
Rendered as: the human being who has been turned into flesh
Preserves the transformation wording without replacing it with a philosophical assumption about human origins.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ γὰρ ἀτρέπτως πατέρα ἰδεῖν υἱοῦ μόνου ἐστίν.
Rendered as: For seeing the Father without transformation belongs to the Son alone.
Without transformation can concern the conditions of the seeing encounter or the viewer/seen; English leaves the qualification unassigned rather than claiming explicitly which party remains unchanged.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἰσάγγελοι
Rendered as: equal to angels
Retains equality to angels, not an assertion that human beings become angels.

SECTION 17.17

Nevertheless, that even impious people see true visions and dreams is clear, and I can prove it from writing. For it is written in the law that Abimelech—being impious and having wished to defile the wife of righteous Abraham through intercourse—heard from God in sleep, as the scripture says, not to touch her because she was living with a husband. Pharaoh too, an impious man, saw a dream about abundance and scarcity of wheat; Joseph, explaining it to him, said that the dream had come from God. Nebuchadnezzar, who revered idols and ordered those who revered God to be thrown into fire, saw a dream concerning an age’s whole length. And let no one say, “But no impious person beholds a vision while awake.” That is false. Nebuchadnezzar himself, after ordering three men to be thrown into fire, saw a fourth in the furnace and said, “I see the fourth as a son of God.” Yet although they saw true apparitions, visions, and dreams, they were impious. Such a person is not necessarily reverent simply because he sees visions, dreams, and apparitions. For to the reverent person truth wells up in an inborn and pure mind, not pursued through a dream, but given to good people through understanding.

Translator's notes for section 17.17 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν τέταρτον ὁρῶ ὡς υἱὸν θεοῦ
Rendered as: I see the fourth as a son of God
Retains the anarthrous son of God in the quoted statement without identifying the figure as a particular later doctrinal person.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὄνειρον ὅλου μήκους αἰῶνος
Rendered as: a dream concerning an age’s whole length
Retains the broad age-duration wording rather than identifying an unprinted historical timetable.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ γὰρ εὐσεβεῖ ἐμφύτῳ καὶ καθαρῷ ἀναβλύζει τῷ νῷ τὸ ἀληθές
Rendered as: to the reverent person truth wells up in an inborn and pure mind
The adjectival grouping can also be taken as in the reverent, inborn, and pure mind; both emphasize inward truth and do not make the dream the source of it.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐνιδὼν τῇ καμίνῳ τέταρτον ἔφη
Rendered as: saw a fourth in the furnace and said
τέταρτον remains the object of seeing in the narrator’s construction, not merely the subject matter of the subsequent speaking. The following quotation is retained as a separate reported statement.

SECTION 17.18

For this is how the Son was revealed to me too by the Father. Therefore I know the power of revelation, having learned from my own experience. For as soon as the Lord asked who people said he was, and I had heard different people saying different things about him, it rose in my heart. I do not know, then, how I said, “You are the Son of the living God.” He pronounced me blessed and told me that the one who had revealed it was the Father. From then on I learned that learning without being taught, without an apparition or dreams, is revelation. And this truly is so. For in the thing placed within us by God in seed form ...., all truth resides. It is covered and uncovered by God’s hand, the one who brings this about knowing what accords with each person’s worth. But that something is made known from outside through apparitions and dreams is plainly not a matter of revelation but of anger. Indeed, it is written in the law that God, angry with Aaron and Miriam, said, “If a prophet arises from among you, through visions and dreams I will make myself known to him; but not in this way as with Moses my servant, because I will speak to him in visible form and not through dreams, as someone will speak to his own friend.” You see how the things of anger come through visions and dreams, whereas those addressed to a friend are mouth to mouth, in visible form, and not through riddles, visions, and dreams as to an enemy.

Translator's notes for section 17.18 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἐν γὰρ τῇ ἐν ἡμῖν ἐκ θεοῦ τεθείσῃ σπερματικῶς....
The four-dot printed gap leaves a noun or additional wording unavailable. Exactly four dots remain, and thing is only generic English grammatical support, not an identification or recovery of the lost content.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν γὰρ τῇ ἐν ἡμῖν ἐκ θεοῦ τεθείσῃ σπερματικῶς....
Rendered as: For in the thing placed within us by God in seed form ....
Exactly four gap dots remain. Thing is generic English nominal support for the surviving article/participle; it does not identify the unavailable noun or restore a specific faculty.

3. Translation choice — Greek: θεοῦ δὲ χειρὶ σκέπεται καὶ ἀποκαλύπτεται
Rendered as: It is covered and uncovered by God’s hand
Preserves the cover/uncover opposition underlying revelation rather than describing only disclosure.

4. Translation choice — Greek: Μωϋσῇ τῷ θεράποντί μου
Rendered as: Moses my servant
θεράπων is an attendant or servant; the wording is retained without importing a different familiar biblical quotation.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν εἴδει
Rendered as: in visible form
εἶδος is appearance or form, fitting the contrast with dream and riddle. Directly is a looser alternative that would obscure the explicit form-language.

SECTION 17.19

If, then, our Jesus also appeared to you through a vision, was made known, and conversed with you, it was as with an adversary, in anger. That is why he spoke through visions and dreams, or even through revelations that come from outside. But can anyone become wise for teaching through an apparition? If you say, “It is possible,” why did the teacher spend an entire year staying with people who were awake and conversing with them? And how shall we even believe you about the very claim that he appeared to you? How did he appear to you, when you think the opposite of his teaching? But if, after being seen and instructed by him for a single hour, you became an apostle, proclaim his words, explain his teachings, love his apostles, and do not fight me, who lived with him. For you have stood against me as an enemy, when I am a solid rock, a foundation of an assembly. If you were not an adversary, you would not, by slandering me, revile the proclamation that comes through me, so that I should not be believed when I say what I myself heard from the Lord while present—that is, as though I had been condemned and were unapproved. Or if you call me “condemned,” you accuse the God who revealed the Messiah to me and attack the one who pronounced me blessed on account of revelation. But if you truly wish to cooperate with the truth, first learn from us what we learned from him, and, becoming a disciple of truth, become our fellow worker.”

Translator's notes for section 17.19 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπ’ ἐκείνου μιᾶς ὥρας ὀφθεὶς καὶ μαθητευθεὶς
Rendered as: after being seen and instructed by him for a single hour
Preserves the passive being seen by him rather than silently reversing it into seeing him. The hour qualifies the short encounter and instruction.

2. Translation choice — Greek: στερεὰν πέτραν ὄντα με, θεμέλιον ἐκκλησίας
Rendered as: when I am a solid rock, a foundation of an assembly
Retains Peter’s self-description as rock/foundation. Church is a conventional alternative for ἐκκλησία, but the Greek does not specify a later institution.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν χριστὸν
Rendered as: the Messiah
Uses the POB title rendering because χριστός here functions independently, not in a personal-name construction.

4. Translation choice — Greek: „κατεγνωσμένον“
Rendered as: “condemned”
Preserves the marked quoted verdict without identifying an unnamed opponent with a historical person not named in this section.

5. Translation choice — Greek: δηλονότι ὡς ἐμοῦ καταγνωσθέντος καὶ ἐμοῦ ἀδοκίμου ὄντος
Rendered as: —that is, as though I had been condemned and were unapproved
δηλονότι introduces an explanatory statement of the alleged grounds for withholding belief. That is preserves its scope outside the supposed condemnation rather than saying that condemnation itself was clear.

6. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τί ὅλῳ ἐνιαυτῷ ἐγρηγορόσιν παραμένων ὡμίλησεν ὁ διδάσκαλος;
Rendered as: why did the teacher spend an entire year staying with people who were awake and conversing with them?
The entire-year duration qualifies the teacher’s staying and conversing, not the duration of the listeners’ wakefulness. Spend an entire year expresses the temporal dative, staying represents παραμένων, and conversing preserves ὡμίλησεν. Awake remains the listeners’ state in contrast with a dream encounter, without a claim of uninterrupted yearlong wakefulness.

SECTION 17.20

Hearing this, Simon said, “Far be it from me to become a disciple either of him or of you. For I am not ignorant of what must be known. What I asked about as though learning was so that I might know whether you can show evidence to be more evident than an apparition. But you spoke as you wished; you did not demonstrate it. And now, tomorrow, I will come and speak with you on the subject of God, whom you insist is the maker, and show that he is not the highest and good. I will also show that your teacher said the same things as I, and expose you as not having understood.” After saying this, he went out, unwilling to hear an answer to the matters he had proposed.

Translator's notes for section 17.20 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὀπτασίας ἐνάργειαν ἐναργεστέραν δεῖξαι
Rendered as: show evidence to be more evident than an apparition
Evidence/evident preserves the visible repetition of ἐνάργεια/ἐναργεστέρα. Evidence here denotes manifest direct encounter, the direct-perception category contrasted earlier with apparition, not documentary or syllogistic proof. ὀπτασίας is taken as the comparative genitive, than an apparition, because Simon asks whether Peter can establish the superiority of direct encounter. The material possessive alternative takes it with ἐνάργειαν: show more evident manifestation of an apparition, with the comparison left implicit. Neither attachment is a correction to the printed Greek.

2. Translation choice — Greek: μὴ αὐτὸν εἶναι ἀνώτατον καὶ ἀγαθόν
Rendered as: that he is not the highest and good
Preserves the coordinated predicate under the negative without silently splitting it into two independent categorical denials.

3. Translation choice — Greek: σὺ δὲ ὡς ἠθέλησας εἶπες, οὐχ ἔδειξας.
Rendered as: But you spoke as you wished; you did not demonstrate it.
As represents the manner expressed by ὡς, not an object meaning whatever content you wished. The contrasting failure to demonstrate remains explicit.

4. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ τὸν σὸν δὲ διδάσκαλον τὰ αὐτά μοι εἰρηκέναι
Rendered as: I will also show that your teacher said the same things as I
Takes μοι as a dative of comparison with the same things, because Simon proposes to prove the teacher’s agreement with his asserted position against Peter’s interpretation. The same things to me is a material alternative taking μοι as recipient of said; the main rendering does not claim that Simon’s receipt of teaching is grammatically excluded.

HOMILY 18

SECTION 18.1

At dawn, when Peter came forward to converse, Simon spoke first: “As I left yesterday, I promised you that today I would return, debate with you, and show that the one who fashioned the world is not the highest God, but another, who alone is good and has remained unknown until now. To begin, then: do you say that the maker himself is also lawgiver, or not? If he is lawgiver, he is just; and being just, he is not good. If he is not good, Jesus proclaimed another when he said, ‘Do not call me good, for the good one is one, the Father in the heavens.’ This does not agree with the lawgiver’s being both just and good.” Peter said, “First tell us: on account of what actions does the good one seem to you good, and on account of what actions the just one just? In this way we can aim our arguments at the target.” Simon said, “You tell me first: what do you think goodness is? Or justice, too?”

Translator's notes for section 18.1 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: δίκαιος δὲ ὢν ἀγαθὸς οὐκ ἔστιν
Rendered as: being just, he is not good
Retains Simon’s opposition of justice and goodness as his claim, not the translator’s conclusion.

2. Translation choice — Greek: κατὰ σκοποῦ τοὺς λόγους πέμπωμεν
Rendered as: aim our arguments at the target
Preserves the aiming/target image.

3. Translation choice — Greek: Σὺ πρῶτον εἰπὲ τί σοι δοκεῖ τὸ ἀγαθόν; ἢ καὶ τὸ δίκαιον;
Rendered as: You tell me first: what do you think goodness is? Or justice, too?
The substantival good and just are rendered as goodness and justice. Or ... too preserves the second question’s disjunctive and additive ἢ καί rather than replacing both questions with one and-linked list.

SECTION 18.2

Peter said, “So that I do not spend time in a more contentious debate, rightly demanding that you answer my questions, I will give the answers as you wish, although I was the one who asked. I say that the one who provides is good, as I see the maker himself doing when he provides the sun to good and evil people and rain to the righteous and unrighteous.” Simon said, “This is most unjust: he provides the same things to the righteous and unrighteous.” Peter said, “Then you tell us from now on how he would act to be good.” Simon said, “You must say.” Peter said, “I will. If, by providing the same things to the good and righteous and also to the evil and unrighteous, he is according to you not even just, and if, by providing good things to the good and bad things to the bad, you would reasonably call him just, what further course of action could he take, if not this way: providing temporary things to the evil, in case they change, and eternal things to the good, provided they remain? Thus, in providing for all but granting favors to different recipients, his justice is good and all the more patient in this respect, if he forgives the sins of sinners who repent and also promises eternal life to those who have acted well. But in judging at the end and assigning to each what is deserved, he is just. If, then, these matters rightly stand this way, acknowledge it; but if they do not seem right to you, refute them.”

Translator's notes for section 18.2 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἐγώ φημι ἀγαθὸν εἶναι τὸν παρεκτικόν
Rendered as: I say that the one who provides is good
The articular τὸν παρεκτικόν is the accusative subject of εἶναι; ἀγαθόν predicates goodness of that provider. The English retains that direction rather than defining “the good person” as the provider. “Generous” is a contextual alternative for παρεκτικός, but the main text keeps providing explicit, as illustrated by the maker’s provision of sun and rain in the rest of the sentence.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἁμαρτωλοῖς μὲν μετανοοῦσιν χαρίζεται τὰ ἁμαρτήματα
Rendered as: he forgives the sins of sinners who repent
The complete μετανοοῦσιν denotes the sinners’ moral-spiritual response in this forgiveness context. “Who repent” follows the October 13 contextual policy, superseding the former mandatory reorientation gloss. It expresses a changed disposition toward wrongdoing, not merely sadness or a new opinion, without requiring proof of already completed reform or supplying an unprinted Godward phrase. The participle is distinct from the encompassing if, which remains separately retained for printed εἰ; forgiveness is not removed or made unconditional.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ζωὴν αἰώνιον ὑπογράφει
Rendered as: promises eternal life
ὑπογράφω can pledge, prescribe, or outline. Promises fits the positive undertaking to those who act well, without claiming automatic possession already.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς σοὶ δοκεῖ αὐτὸς ὢν ἐπυθόμην ποιήσομαι τὰς· ἀποκρίσεις.
Rendered as: I will give the answers as you wish, although I was the one who asked.
The supplied construction juxtaposes participial ὢν with finite ἐπυθόμην irregularly. The English reads this contextually as Peter answering despite having himself asked. A relative ὃς in place of printed ὢν would support a smoother clause but would be conjectural; it is not substituted. The supplied stop between article and noun in τὰς· ἀποκρίσεις is a print punctuation feature, not an alleged OCR defect.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ μὲν πᾶσιν παρέχειν, διαφόροις δὲ χαρίζεσθαι
Rendered as: in providing for all but granting favors to different recipients
διαφόροις is taken as a dative of recipients, contrasting everyone with differentiated beneficiaries. It can also mean distinguished or worthy recipients; the main text leaves the difference unspecified. The previous different-gifts rendering would require an instrumental interpretation, by differing gifts, rather than an accusative object; that is a material alternative but the recipient reading is more direct with χαρίζεσθαι.

6. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ μακρόθυμον ταύτη μᾶλλον, εἰ ἁμαρτωλοῖς μὲν μετανοοῦσιν χαρίζεται τὰ ἁμαρτήματα, εὖ πράξασιν δὲ καὶ ζωὴν αἰώνιον ὑπογράφει.
Rendered as: and all the more patient in this respect, if he forgives the sins of sinners who repent and also promises eternal life to those who have acted well.
If preserves εἰ governing the argument through both forgiveness and the promise of life. The participle “who repent” is distinct from that condition; the sentence is not changed into an unconditional assertion by a colon. The contextual repentance gloss does not change the participants or the relation among response, forgiveness, and eternal life.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἐὰν ἄρα μεταβάλλωνται
Rendered as: in case they change
μεταβάλλω is a distinct change expression, not μετανοέω. The moral context permits a change of conduct, but the existing “change” is retained instead of homogenizing this distinct verb into “repent” or adding a Godward formula.

SECTION 18.3

Simon said, “I have said it once: every lawgiver, looking toward what is just, is just.” Peter said, “If it belongs to goodness not to lay down a law, and to justice to lay one down, even in this way the maker is both good and just: good because, from Adam’s time until Moses, he does not appear to have laid down the law in writing; and from Moses down to the present times, as it is written, he is also just.” Simon said, “Show from your teacher’s statements that it belongs to the same one to be good and just. For it seems impossible to me that the lawgiver, being good, is himself also just.” Peter said, “Listen to how the good itself is also just. Our teacher himself, when the Pharisee said, ‘What must I do to inherit eternal life?’ first said, ‘Do not call me good, for the good one is one, the Father in the heavens.’ Immediately afterward he added, ‘But if you wish to enter life, keep the commandments.’ When the man said, ‘Which ones?’ he directed him to those of the law. Had he been indicating someone else as good, he would not have referred him to the commandments of the just one. I myself also acknowledge that what is just is one thing and what is good another; but you do not know that being good and just belong to the same one. For he is good in being patient now with those who repent and receiving them; and he is just when, in judging, he assigns to each what is deserved.”

Translator's notes for section 18.3 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἐγγράφως οὐ φαίνεται τεθεικὼς τὸν νόμον
Rendered as: he does not appear to have laid down the law in writing
Retains the in-writing qualification and appears, not an absolute claim that there was no divine instruction before Moses.

2. Translation choice — Greek: Φαρισαίῳ
Rendered as: the Pharisee
Preserves the source’s identification of the questioner rather than harmonizing it to a different designation in a familiar Gospel account.

3. Translation choice — Greek: μετανοοῦσι
Rendered as: those who repent
The complete participle concerns the people whom God patiently receives, not a change in God himself. The context supports the moral-spiritual response, so “those who repent” follows the October 13 contextual policy. This is not reduced to regret alone, and no unprinted intensifier or “toward God” phrase is inserted.

SECTION 18.4

Simon said, “How, then, when the maker was known—the one who formed Adam and was known to the righteous according to the law, and furthermore to the righteous and unrighteous and the whole world—does your teacher, coming after all those people, say, ‘No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father and those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him’? He would not have said these things unless he were announcing a certain Father who is in secrecy, whom the law also calls Most High, from whom no good or evil utterance has been heard, as Jeremiah too testifies in the Lamentations. In accordance with the number of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt, who are seventy, and marking out the nations’ boundaries by seventy languages, this one gave the Hebrews as a portion to his Son, who is also called Lord and ordered heaven and earth, and appointed him God of gods. By gods I mean those who have received the other portions of the nations. Laws therefore issued from all the gods just mentioned to their own portions, namely the remaining nations; likewise the law established among the Hebrews issued from the Son, the Lord of all. It was determined to be this way so that if someone takes refuge in someone’s law, he becomes part of the portion of the one whose law he has undertaken to practice. No one knew the Most High Father who is in secrecy, just as no one knew of this one’s Son that he is Son. Indeed, you, assigning to the Son the distinctive attributes of the secret Most High, do not know that he is Son, being Father of the Jesus whom you call Messiah.”

Translator's notes for section 18.4 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν ἀπορρήτοις
Rendered as: in secrecy
The expression can mean among unrevealed mysteries or in the secret realm. In secrecy preserves the hidden status without inventing a named location.

2. Translation choice — Greek: κατὰ ἀριθμὸν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ
Rendered as: In accordance with the number of the sons of Israel
Retains Israel, not another textual witness’s sons of God or angels; the explicit count seventy remains.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ αὐτοῦ υἱῷ τῷ καὶ „κυρίῳ“ λεγομένῳ
Rendered as: to his Son, who is also called Lord
Retains Simon’s distinction between the Most High and his Son, who is the maker in this proposal, not the translator’s own theological identification.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ καθ’ ὑμᾶς λεγομένου χριστοῦ
Rendered as: the Jesus whom you call Messiah
χριστός is a disputed independent title attributed by Simon to the other party’s Jesus, so Messiah preserves the title’s force.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὅστις κατὰ ἀριθμὸν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ, οἳ εἰσῆλθον εἰς Αἴγυπτον (οἵ εἰσιν ἑβδομήκοντα), καὶ πρὸς τὰ ὅρια τῶν ἐθνῶν περιγράψας γλώσσαις ἑβδομήκοντα
Rendered as: In accordance with the number of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt, who are seventy, and marking out the nations’ boundaries by seventy languages
The object of περιγράψας is implicit. The English takes the boundaries named in πρὸς τὰ ὅρια as the contextual object of marking out, not as a direct Greek accusative object outside the preposition. A more formally separated alternative is having marked out divisions by seventy languages in accordance with that number and in relation to the nations’ boundaries. Both number and boundary expressions constrain the delineation; no additional printed noun is claimed.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ πάντων κυρίου
Rendered as: from the Son, the Lord of all
Takes the second genitive phrase appositionally, since the Son was already explicitly called Lord in this proposal. From the Son of the Lord of all is a material alternative attaching the second genitive as the Son’s parent; the main text does not claim the appositional grouping is uniquely settled.

7. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν ἐν ἀπορρήτοις ὕψιστον πατέρα ὄντα, ὡς οὐδὲ τὸν τούτου υἱὸν ὅτι υἱός ἐστιν.
Rendered as: No one knew the Most High Father who is in secrecy, just as no one knew of this one’s Son that he is Son.
The main text reads Father attributively as the identification of the hidden Most High, whose inaccessible status and unheard voice Simon has described. A material alternative takes πατέρα ὄντα predicatively: No one knew that the Most High who is in secrecy is Father, just as no one knew that his Son is Son. That alternative aligns the two clauses as failures to recognize paternal and filial identity rather than knowledge of a person; the main reading is retained contextually, not claimed as unique.

SECTION 18.5

After Simon said these things, Peter said to him, “Can you call that very one to witness that you believe this—not the one you now say is in secrecy, but the one you believe in without acknowledging him? For you talk nonsense by defining one thing in place of another. Therefore, if you call him to witness that you believe what you say, I will answer you; but if you stand debating with me things you do not believe, you force me to strike at emptiness.” Simon said, “I heard from one of your disciples ....” Peter said, “Do not bear false witness.” Simon said, “Do not abuse me, you utterly rash man.” Peter said, “Until you name the person who said it, you are a liar.” Simon said, “Suppose that I invented these things, or even heard them from someone else: answer me about them. For if they cannot be overturned, I have learned that this is the truth.” Peter said, “If it is a human fabrication, I will not answer it. But if you have been gripped by the supposition that it is true, acknowledge this very thing to me, and I myself also have something to say about it.” Simon said, “Once for all, I think it is so. If you have anything to say about these things, answer.”

Translator's notes for section 18.5 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: Παρὰ τινὸς τῶν σῶν μαθητῶν ἀκήκοα . . . .
Exactly four printed dots remain; the missing report is not reconstructed.

2. Translation choice — Greek: διαμαρτύρασθαι
Rendered as: call ... to witness
The demand invokes the one actually believed in as witness, not a request for a merely informal reassurance.

3. Translation choice — Greek: κατὰ κενοῦ με παίειν
Rendered as: strike at emptiness
Retains the striking-at-a-void metaphor.

4. Translation choice — Greek: Παρὰ τινὸς τῶν σῶν μαθητῶν ἀκήκοα . . . .
Rendered as: I heard from one of your disciples ....
Exactly four dots remain for the printed gap; the alleged disclosure’s missing content is not restored.

5. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ δὲ ὑπονοίᾳ αὐτοῦ κεχράτησαι ὡς ἀληθοῦς
Rendered as: But if you have been gripped by the supposition that it is true
The selected reading has κεχράτησαι, interpreted contextually as passive holding or gripping. Regular κεκράτησαι is only a possible spelling regularization, not substituted or described as verified text. The English clarifies that the supposition concerns the account’s truth, while preserving the printed construction and its uncertainty.

SECTION 18.6

Peter said, “If this is so, you act with the greatest impiety. For if it belongs to the Son who ordered heaven and earth to reveal his Father who is in secret to whomever he wishes, you, as I said, act with the greatest impiety by revealing to those to whom he did not reveal.” Simon said, “But he himself wants me to reveal.” Peter said, “You do not understand what I say, Simon. Yet listen and understand. Saying, ‘To those to whom the Son wishes he will reveal,’ does not mean that someone learns such a thing by teaching, but only by revelation. Revelation is what lies secretly in all human hearts, covered, being uncovered without a voice expressing his will. Thus one comes to know not by being taught, but by understanding. Yet the one who has understood is not permitted to demonstrate this to another, since he himself was not taught; nor can he reveal it, since he himself is not the Son—unless he says that he himself is the Son. But you are not the standing Son. For if you were Son, you would certainly know those worthy of such revelation. But you do not know. For if you knew, you would do the things done by those who know.”

Translator's notes for section 18.6 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἄνευ φωνῆς τῆς αὐτοῦ βουλῆς ἀποκαλυπτόμενον
Rendered as: being uncovered without a voice expressing his will
The genitive τῆς αὐτοῦ βουλῆς is attached to voice, a voice of his will, expressed readably as a voice expressing his will. It is not assigned independent instrumental force as by his will, for which the supplied genitive gives no established grammatical support. Nonvocal disclosure remains explicit.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ ἑστὼς υἱός
Rendered as: the standing Son
Keeps the standing epithet and Son together, rather than replacing them with a later named title or deleting the unusual description.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν ἐν ἀπορρήτοις αὐτοῦ πατέρα
Rendered as: his Father who is in secret
The secrecy phrase is attributive inside the Father noun phrase, not the manner in which the Son reveals him. Who is in secret makes this attachment explicit without specifying a named hidden realm.

SECTION 18.7

Simon said, “I admit I did not understand how you mean, ‘You would do the things done by those who know.’” Peter said, “If you did not understand, you also cannot know each person’s mind. And if you do not know, you also do not know those worthy of revelation. If you do not know, you are not Son; but the Son knows, and therefore reveals to those he wishes as being worthy.” Simon said, “Let me not deceive: I know those who are worthy, and I am not Son. Yet I did not understand what this is, ‘He reveals to those he wishes,’ as you say. I said that I did not understand not because I did not know, but because I knew that those present did not understand, so that you would state it more clearly and those for whose sake we also conduct the discussion might understand.” Peter said, “I cannot state it more clearly. Since you have understood it, explain it yourself.” Simon said, “I am not obliged to state your views.” Peter said, “It seems to me, Simon, that you do not understand it and are unwilling to admit it, lest, being caught in ignorance, you be exposed as not being the standing Son. For this is what you hint at, even if you do not wish to say it plainly. Thus I know your intentions from your hints, being a disciple of a true prophet, not a prophet. But you, though you do not understand even what is plainly said, wish to call yourself Son, standing against us.” Simon said, “I will remove every excuse from you. I admit that I did not understand what this is: ‘And to those to whom the Son wishes, he reveals.’ So state it more clearly.”

Translator's notes for section 18.7 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ ἑστὼς υἱός
Rendered as: the standing Son
Retains the epithet tied to Simon’s alleged claim; it is not identified with an external historical person.

2. Translation choice — Greek: προφήτου ἀληθοῦς μαθητὴς ὤν, οὐ προφήτης
Rendered as: being a disciple of a true prophet, not a prophet
Preserves Peter’s explicit denial of being a prophet in this statement, rather than harmonizing it to a later title.

3. Translation choice — Greek: Μὴ ἀπατῶ·
Rendered as: Let me not deceive:
ἀπατῶ is first-person singular, compatible with a first-person subjunctive here; let me not deceive preserves that person and the negative. The possible interrogative indicative alternative is Am I deceiving?, expecting a negative answer. The edition’s printed stop fits the chosen noninterrogative construction, but does not settle the form’s mood. No second-person imperative or replacement Greek is introduced.

SECTION 18.8

Peter said, “Since you have admitted, even if only for appearances, that you do not understand it, answer what I ask you, and you will learn. Tell me: do you say that the Son, whoever he may be, is just, or not?” Simon said, “Most just.” Peter said, “If he is just, why does he not reveal to all, but to those he wishes?” Simon said, “Because, being just, he wishes to reveal to those who are worthy.” Peter said, “Then must he not know each person’s mind so that he may reveal to the worthy?” Simon said, “It must certainly be so.” Peter said, “Then he alone was reasonably appointed to reveal, since he alone knows each person’s mind—not you, who cannot even understand the things we say.”

Translator's notes for section 18.8 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: κἂν σχήματι
Rendered as: even if only for appearances
σχήματι can indicate outward form or pretense; even formally is a less interpretive alternative. The admission is treated skeptically, not accepted as sincere without qualification.

SECTION 18.9

After Peter said this, praise arose from the crowds. Simon, thoroughly exposed, blushed in shame, rubbed his forehead, and said, “But they call me a magician, defeated by Peter, and also caught in argument. Yet if someone is caught in argument and taken unawares, he does not thereby have the truth within him defeated; for the weakness of its defender is not the truth of the defeated party. Nevertheless I tell you that I judged everyone present worthy to know the Father who is in secret. Therefore, when I reveal him to them publicly, they should not be angry with me out of envy, since I wish to do them good.”

Translator's notes for section 18.9 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: συλλογιζόμενον
Rendered as: caught in argument
The form can mean reasoning or being brought under a syllogistic argument. The context of defeat and being taken unawares favors being caught in argument; reasoning is a material alternative.

2. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἡ ἀσθένεια τοῦ ἐκδικοῦντος ἀλήθειά ἐστιν τοῦ νικωμένου
Rendered as: the weakness of its defender is not the truth of the defeated party
Retains the compact distinction between a weak defender and the truth he defends rather than rewriting it as truth’s weakness.

3. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ αὐτοῖς διὰ φθόνον ἐμοὶ τῷ εὐεργετεῖν αὐτοὺς θέλοντι χαλεπαίνειν
Rendered as: they should not be angry with me out of envy, since I wish to do them good
Takes αὐτοῖς as the persons for whom getting angry is inappropriate, leaving the grammatical third-person reference intact instead of silently changing it to you, Peter.

4. Translation choice — Greek: γνῶναι τὸν ἐν ἀπορρήτοις πατέρα
Rendered as: to know the Father who is in secret
The secrecy phrase describes the Father, not a secret manner of knowing. This distinction fits Simon’s immediately following public disclosure and agrees with the attributive rendering in 18.6.

SECTION 18.10

Peter said, “Since you have spoken in this way to please the crowds present, I will speak not to please them, but truthfully. Tell me: how do you know that everyone present is worthy, when not even one agreed with you as you disclosed it? For their praising me against you is not the act of people agreeing with you, but with me, to whom they also assigned praise as someone who had spoken rightly. But since God, being just, judges each person’s mind, he would not have wished what you say is true to be given to those on the right through the left. By the same reasoning, someone who receives anything from a thief is himself liable. Therefore, for this reason, he did not wish them to receive what you bring, but rather through the Son appointed to reveal. For who can reasonably reveal the Father except the Son alone, since he knows who is worthy of such revelation? Thus this cannot be taught or learned by teaching, but must be revealed by an inexpressible hand to the one worthy to know it.”

Translator's notes for section 18.10 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τῆς ἀριστερᾶς τοῖς δεξιοῖς
Rendered as: to those on the right through the left
Retains the right/left opposition without identifying unprinted named camps or persons.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἀφράστῳ χειρὶ
Rendered as: by an inexpressible hand
Retains the hand image, not merely a generic divine act.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τίνι γὰρ εὔλογόν ἐστιν ἀποκαλύπτειν τὸν πατέρα ἢ υἱῷ μόνῳ διὰ τὸ εἰδέναι τῆς τοιαύτης ἀποκαλύψεως τὸν ἄξιον;
Rendered as: For who can reasonably reveal the Father except the Son alone, since he knows who is worthy of such revelation?
τίνι and υἱῷ identify the person for whom revealing is appropriate, thus the revealer. The Son’s preceding appointment and knowledge of worthy recipients confirm this role. The English does not make him the recipient by saying to whom the Father is revealed.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἀλλ’ ἐπειδὴ ὁ θεὸς δίκαιος ὢν βραβεύει τὸν ἑκάστου νοῦν, ὃ φῆς ἀληθὲς εἶναι, οὐκ ἂν ἐβουλήθη διὰ τῆς ἀριστερᾶς τοῖς δεξιοῖς τοῦτο δοθῆναι
Rendered as: But since God, being just, judges each person’s mind, he would not have wished what you say is true to be given to those on the right through the left.
Takes ὃ φῆς ἀληθὲς εἶναι as a fronted relative resumed by τοῦτο: the purported truth Simon brings. The subsequent what is brought by you supports this attachment. Alternatively it is parenthetical, which you say is true, modifying the claim that God judges each mind. The printed commas allow both; the revised main text prefers the resumed object without changing the Greek.

SECTION 18.11

Simon said, “For a combatant, using his own weapons contributes greatly to victory. For what someone loves he can also genuinely defend, and what is genuinely defended possesses no ordinary strength. Therefore from now on I will set out what I really think. I say that there is a certain power in secrecy, unknown to everyone, even to the maker himself—as Jesus himself also said, without knowing what he uttered; for sometimes, through much talking, someone hits upon the truth without knowing what he says. I am also speaking about this statement he made: ‘No one knew the Father.’” Peter said, “No longer claim to know his teachings.” Simon said, “I do not claim to believe his teachings; I am debating with you about the things he happened to get right.” Peter said, “So as not to give you an excuse to flee, I will discuss with you as you wish. Nevertheless I call everyone to witness that you do not believe even the argument you have now stated. For I know what you think. And so that you do not think I am lying, I will hint at your own views, so that you may see you are conversing with someone who knows.”

Translator's notes for section 18.11 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ὃ γὰρ φιλεῖ τις
Rendered as: what someone loves
The object can be a position or cause, not necessarily a person; this introduces the own-weapons metaphor.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ ἐπιτευχθέντα αὐτῷ
Rendered as: the things he happened to get right
Preserves Simon’s disparaging account of accidental truth rather than endorsing his claim as a narrator’s assessment.

3. Translation choice — Greek: λέγω δὲ καὶ περὶ τούτου οὗ εἴρηκεν „οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν πατέρα“.
Rendered as: I am also speaking about this statement he made: No one knew the Father
The main rendering takes τούτου as this statement and οὗ as a relative attracted into the antecedent's genitive case, referring to what he uttered. The surrounding discussion of Jesus' words and the quotation supplying their content favor that reading. A material personal alternative is I am also speaking about this one of whom he said, No one knew the Father, potentially linking the Father to the previously mentioned unknown power. The main text does not claim that this statement rather than a personal referent is uniquely established.

SECTION 18.12

“We, Simon, do not say that two angels were sent from the great power, also called the sovereign power, one to create a world and the other to lay down the law. Nor do we say that each came to the things he had made and announced himself as their original author. Nor do we speak of the standing one who will stand as an adversary. Learn how you disbelieve even this hypothesis. The power you say is in secrecy is full of ignorance, for it did not foreknow the ingratitude of the angels it sent.” While Peter was saying this, Simon became very angry and interrupted him, saying, “Why do you babble, you bold man, most reckless of all, plainly disclosing the secrets before uninstructed crowds?” Peter said, “Why do you begrudge the benefit given to the hearers present?” Simon said, “Then do you acknowledge that such knowledge is a benefit?” Peter said, “I do: for once falsehood is known, it gives the benefit of not falling into it through ignorance.” Simon said, “It seems to me that you cannot answer what I put before you. I mean that your teacher too says that there is a certain Father in secrecy.”

Translator's notes for section 18.12 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: οὐδὲ ὁ ἑστὼς στησόμενος ἀντικείμενος.
The nominal clause leaves its finite verbal relation implicit. The main text carries the preceding denial of doctrinal assertion forward; a direct nominal assertion, nor is the standing one going to stand as an adversary, is another grouping. Every surviving element remains.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς μεγάλης δυνάμεως, ἔτι τε καὶ τῆς κυρίας λεγομένης
Rendered as: the great power, also called the sovereign power
κυρίας can qualify power as sovereign, ruling, or mistress-like; sovereign power gives its authority sense without adding a separate named deity.

3. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδὲ ὁ ἑστὼς στησόμενος ἀντικείμενος.
Rendered as: Nor do we speak of the standing one who will stand as an adversary.
The nominal clause is extremely compressed. The main rendering carries do we speak from the preceding repeated denial and preserves standing, future standing, and adversary without supplying a named identity. Nor is the standing one going to stand as an adversary is another possible grouping.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἀτέχνως τὰ ἀπόρρητα
Rendered as: plainly disclosing the secrets
ἀτέχνως here means plainly or without qualification, not necessarily in an unskilled manner.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τολμηρὲ καὶ πάντων προπετέστατε
Rendered as: you bold man, most reckless of all
Preserves both bold and the explicit superlative comparison with all (πάντων), not merely the intensifier utterly.

SECTION 18.13
