Peter said, “I will answer what you want, concerning ‘No one knew the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father and those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.’ First, I am amazed how, when this statement has countless interpretations, you chose the more dangerous part, saying that the statement referred to ignorance on the part of the maker and everyone made by him. For in the first place the statement can have been addressed to all the Jews who supposed David to be the Messiah’s father—with the Messiah himself being the son—and had not recognized him as Son of God. Therefore it was appropriately said, ‘No one knew the Father,’ since everyone named David instead of God. He added, ‘Nor does anyone know the Son,’ because they did not know that he was Son. Saying, ‘Those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him,’ was also rightly said, for the Son who has existed from the beginning alone was appointed to reveal to those he wishes. Thus Adam, the first formed, can have been not ignorant of him; nor can Enoch, who pleased him, fail to know; nor can righteous Noah fail to understand; nor can Abraham the friend fail to comprehend; nor can Isaac have failed to understand; nor can Jacob who wrestled have failed to believe; nor can he have remained unrevealed to all the worthy among the people.”

Translator's notes for section 18.13 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: καὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς ἐν τῷ λαῷ ἀξίοις μὴ ἀποκεκαλύφθαι
The final coordination has μὴ but no newly repeated οὐχ. The English carries the previous negative modal scope, nor can ... unrevealed, rather than adding a new printed negation. A clause-local reading would instead yield and not revealed. The modal/negative scope across the entire list is explained in the lexical note on Enoch, Noah, and Abraham.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ ἐπικινδυνότερον ἐξελέξω μέρος
Rendered as: you chose the more dangerous part
Retains the comparative, not the unsupported superlative most dangerous.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς ἀγνωσίαν τοῦ δημιουργοῦ καὶ τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ πάντων
Rendered as: ignorance on the part of the maker and everyone made by him
The genitives are taken as subjective: maker and created ones are ignorant of the secret Father, as in Simon’s argument. Ignorance of the maker is an objective-genitive alternative, but fits the immediately preceding exchange less well.

4. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς ἐν τῷ λαῷ ἀξίοις μὴ ἀποκεκαλύφθαι
Rendered as: nor can he have remained unrevealed to all the worthy among the people
The final clause is read under the negative modal scope carried from the preceding οὐχ ... μὴ clauses. Its μὴ is retained in unrevealed and the carried denial in nor can. A clause-local reading, and not to have been revealed, remains possible but is less consonant with the preceding argument.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς πατέρα νομίζοντας εἶναι χριστοῦ τὸν Δαυὶδ — καὶ αὐτὸν δὲ τὸν χριστὸν υἱὸν ὄντα — καὶ υἱὸν θεοῦ μὴ ἐγνωκέναι.
Rendered as: who supposed David to be the Messiah’s father—with the Messiah himself being the son—and had not recognized him as Son of God
The printed parenthesis is kept outside the failure-to-recognize phrase and can continue the supposed Davidic father-son relation. It could instead affirm the Messiah’s sonship parenthetically. A broader attachment, taking their failure as not recognizing him as Son and as Son of God, is a material alternative, but the parenthetical punctuation favors keeping the explicit Son-of-God denial as the failed recognition.

6. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδὲ Ἐνὼχ ὁ εὐαρεστήσας μὴ εἰδέναι οὔτε Νῶε ὁ δίκαιος μὴ ἐπίστασθαι οὔτε Ἀβραὰμ ὁ φίλος μὴ συνιέναι
Rendered as: nor can Enoch ... fail to know; nor can righteous Noah fail to understand; nor can Abraham ... fail to comprehend
The governing δύναται is carried through the list, with οὐδέ/οὔτε denying the modal possibility of each negative-infinitive failure. This gives the explicit nor can ... fail construction. Another reading coordinates the negative infinitival complements under a positive possibility—can be not ignorant, can be not without knowledge—without the same emphasis on exclusion of ignorance. The first Adam clause has only the negative infinitive and is kept as a positive possibility of nonignorance; the later coordinated negatives are made explicit rather than flattened.

7. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδὲ τὸν υἱόν τις οἶδεν, εἰ μὴ ὁ πατὴρ καὶ οἷς ἂν βούληται ὁ υἱὸς ἀποκαλύψαι
Rendered as: nor does anyone know the Son except the Father and those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him
The object of reveal is unexpressed in Greek. In both quotation occurrences the English him supplies the Father, chosen from the surrounding discussion of the Son revealing the Father, including 18.10. The placement after the exception about knowing the Son also permits the Son or knowledge of his identity as the object of revelation. The Father is therefore an explicitly disclosed contextual choice, not a uniquely printed object; the quotation is not rearranged to match another witness.

SECTION 18.14

But if, as you say, he is to be revealed to everyone now through Jesus for the sake of knowing him, how do you not call it most unjust that those men did not know him—seven pillars of the world who were able to please the most just God—while now so many from the nations, impious in every way, know him? Were those men not deemed worthy to know the one better than all? And how is what is not just good? Unless by good you wish to mean not the one who benefits those who have acted justly, but the one who loves the unrighteous even if they do not believe, revealing to them also the secrets that he was unwilling to reveal to the righteous. Such conduct belongs neither to a good nor to a just being, but to one who hates the reverent. Are you perhaps the standing one, Simon, who dares to say these things, which have never been spoken in this way?

Translator's notes for section 18.14 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἑπτὰ στύλους ὑπάρξαντας κόσμῳ
Rendered as: seven pillars of the world
Preserves the stated seven without supplying an unprinted list of names.

2. Translation choice — Greek: μήτι σὺ εἶ, Σίμων, ὁ ἑστώς
Rendered as: Are you perhaps the standing one, Simon
Retains the standing epithet and interrogative challenge, not a translator’s identification of Simon.

3. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ δὲ (ὡς φῄς) ἔσται διὰ τὸ εἰδέναι διὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ νῦν πᾶσιν ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι:
Rendered as: But if, as you say, he is to be revealed to everyone now through Jesus for the sake of knowing him
Is to be retains future ἔσται while now retains νῦν. The main text construes διὰ τὸ εἰδέναι purposively, for the sake of knowing, with him supplied as the contextual object, the previously discussed Father. The causal alternative is because of knowing; the clause does not state whose prior knowledge would ground disclosure on that attachment. No claim is added that the revealed one was already known to everyone.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οὗτοι παντὸς κρείττονος γνῶναι οὐ κατηξιώθησαν;
Rendered as: Were those men not deemed worthy to know the one better than all?
The context concerns knowing the proposed highest Father, favoring a personal referent superior to all and παντός as the comparison of κρείττονος. Taking παντός with substantival κρείττονος gives the broader alternative Were these not deemed worthy to know anything superior? The genitive superior object is construed with deemed worthy/knowing in this compressed phrase; the personal interpretation is not claimed as unique.

5. Translation choice — Greek: μήτι σὺ εἶ, Σίμων, ὁ ἑστώς, ὁ ταῦτα οὕτως μήποτε ῥηθέντα εἰπεῖν ἀποθρασυνόμενος;
Rendered as: Are you perhaps the standing one, Simon, who dares to say these things, which have never been spoken in this way?
The things never spoken in this way are the object of Simon’s audacious saying. The phrase does not state that Simon himself claims they were previously spoken; the English does not introduce that unsupported reported-speech proposition.

SECTION 18.15

Indignant at this, Simon said, “I accuse your teacher, who said, ‘I give thanks to you, Lord of heaven and earth, because the things that were hidden from the wise you revealed to nursing infants.’” Peter said, “That is not how the statement was spoken. But first I will speak as though it had been said as you supposed. Even if our Lord had said, ‘The things that were hidden from the wise, these the Father revealed to infants,’ he would not even in this way have been understood to indicate a God and Father other than the one who created the world. For the hidden things he spoke of can belong to the maker himself, since Isaiah also said, ‘I will open my mouth in parables and pour out things hidden from the foundation of the world.’ Do you therefore acknowledge the prophet who was not ignorant of the hidden things that Jesus says were concealed from the wise but revealed to infants? How, then, was the maker ignorant when his prophet Isaiah was not ignorant? But our Jesus in fact did not say, ‘The things that were hidden,’ but spoke what seems harsher; for he said, ‘You revealed them to nursing infants.’ But saying, ‘You hid,’ refers to things once known to them. For the key of the kingdom of the heavens lay with them, that is, knowledge of the secrets.”

Translator's notes for section 18.15 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἔγνω σμένων
The formerly selected fragment was σμέων, yielding ἔγνω σμέων; independently blind-checked print evidence now reads the physical line-start fragment σμένων, correcting the omitted ν. The print still divides ἔγνω / σμένων without a hyphen. The English tests their combined perfect-passive participial reading, not a uniquely certified analysis or replacement Greek. The blind receipt describes the initial ε diacritic as tentatively smooth breathing plus acute, less distinct than the letters, while the following fragment has acute on ε; this anomalous accent/division is preserved as a disclosed print feature. No original letters beyond the independently verified ν are invented.

2. Greek: τὸ δὲ εἰπεῖν „ἀπέκρυψας“
The current selected text reads ἀπέκρυψας, rendered You hid. The blind fragment-check response’s incidental full-line transcription instead reports ἀπεκάλυψας at this quote position. The authorized curation only verifies σμένων, so that incidental quote reading is not adopted or silently substituted here. The discrepancy has been referred to the parent for a separate direct print-word check; this candidate follows the supplied selected Greek rather than certifying the incidental reading.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐξομολογοῦμαί σοι
Rendered as: I give thanks to you
The verb can express acknowledging, praising, or confessing; thanksgiving fits the address to the Lord for revelation, without adding a distinct confession of sins.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἴπερ καὶ εἰρήκει
Rendered as: Even if our Lord had said
Retains the hypothetical concession and its relation to the following denial of a different God, rather than presenting the proposed wording as Peter’s admission of the actual quotation.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ καὶ τὸν Ἠσαίαν εἰπεῖν
Rendered as: since Isaiah also said
Preserves the source’s attribution to Isaiah, not an imported correction from another biblical witness.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ποτε ἔγνω σμένων αὐτοῖς.
Rendered as: refers to things once known to them
Interprets the physical ἔγνω / σμένων fragments together as a perfect passive participial expression, known, with the hidden things as its contextual antecedent and the wise as the recipients of prior knowledge. The verified fragment supplies the ν previously omitted in transcription; no further Greek letters are added. Joining the printed letter sequence for interpretation gives the participial sense associated with ἐγνωσμένων, while the initial accent and physical word division remain anomalous and are disclosed, not silently normalized. As of things once known to them is a more formally elliptical English alternative to refers to things once known to them.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τουτέστιν ἡ γνῶσις τῶν ἀπορρήτων.
Rendered as: that is, knowledge of the secrets
Retains the author’s explicit equation of key with knowledge of secrets, without adding an independently named esoteric system.

SECTION 18.16

And do not say, “He acted impiously toward the wise by hiding these things from them.” Far be it from us to suppose this. For he did not act impiously. Rather, because they hid the knowledge of the kingdom and neither entered themselves nor allowed those who wished to enter, for this reason, in accordance with justice, just as they themselves hid the ways from those who wished, so the secrets were also hidden from them. This was so that what they had done might happen likewise to them, and with the measure they measured, it might be measured to them equally. For the worthy person is owed knowledge of what he does not know; but from the unworthy person it is taken away, even if he seems to possess it and is wise in other matters, and given to the worthy, even if in the duration of their discipleship they are infants.

Translator's notes for section 18.16 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: κἂν ἐν τοῖς χρόνοις τῆς μαθητείας ὦσιν νήπιοι
Rendered as: even if in the duration of their discipleship they are infants
Infants here is explicitly qualified by time in discipleship, not necessarily literal nursing children. The metaphor is retained rather than silently harmonizing all infant-language.

SECTION 18.17

If someone says, “Nothing was hidden from the sons of Israel, because it is written, ‘Nothing escaped you, Israel; for do not say, Jacob, “The way was hidden from me,”’” one must understand that the matters important to the kingdom were hidden from them, but the way leading into the kingdom, which is a manner of life, was not hidden. This is why he also says, “For do not say that the way was hidden from me.” The way is the manner of life, since Moses too says, “Look, I have set before your face the way of life and the way of death.” In agreement the teacher said, “Enter through the narrow and constricted way, through which you will enter life.” Elsewhere, when someone asked, “What must I do to inherit eternal life?” he pointed out the law’s commandments.

Translator's notes for section 18.17 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἥτις ἐστὶν πολιτεία
Rendered as: which is a manner of life
πολιτεία here is conduct or way of living, not a political constitution.

2. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τῆς στενῆς καὶ τεθλιμμένης ὁδοῦ
Rendered as: through the narrow and constricted way
Retains way as quoted here, not an imported gate from another witness.

SECTION 18.18

From Isaiah’s saying in God’s person, “But Israel did not know me, and the people did not understand me,” it does not follow that Isaiah too was hinting at a God other than the known maker. Rather, through a different riddle he called the known one unknown, because the people, ignorant of the known God’s just disposition, sinned and did not suppose that they would be judged by the good God. Therefore, after saying, “But Israel did not know me, and the people did not understand me,” he added, “Woe, sinful nation, people full of sins.” For, as I said, through ignorance of his justice they were without fear and became full of sins, supposing him only good, in the sense that he would not pursue their sins.

Translator's notes for section 18.18 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν διάθεσιν τὴν δικαίαν
Rendered as: just disposition
Retains the disposition/character sense; the argument concerns ignorance of justice, not ignorance that any deity exists.

2. Translation choice — Greek: μόνον ἀγαθὸν
Rendered as: only good
Keeps the restrictive only, which is central to the polemic against separating goodness from judgment.

SECTION 18.19

Some sinned in this way from the supposition that, because of his goodness, he does not judge; others from the opposite view. For, supposing the statements of the scriptures against God to be true, although they are unjust and false, they did not know his true divinity and power. Therefore, supposing that he is ignorant, delights in murders, lets the wicked off through gifts of sacrifices, and also deceives, lies, and does everything unjust, they themselves, thinking they had acted like God, insisted while sinning that they were acting reverently. Therefore they were immovable toward what is better, and when admonished did not turn back. For they had no fear, considering themselves made like God through such actions.

Translator's notes for section 18.19 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὰς γὰρ κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν γραφῶν φωνάς, ἀδίκους οὔσας καὶ ψευδεῖς
Rendered as: the statements of the scriptures against God ... although they are unjust and false
Preserves the historical speaker’s explicit criticism of certain scriptural statements. It is neither softened nor presented as the translator’s own verdict about scripture.

2. Translation choice — Greek: οὐκ ἐπεστρέφοντο
Rendered as: did not turn back
Retains the turning verb distinct from μετανοέω/reorient.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ τῆς διὰ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἀκρίτου ὑπολήψεως
Rendered as: from the supposition that, because of his goodness, he does not judge
The main text understands a supposition of God’s non-judging character, because 18.18 explicitly links presumed goodness with absence of pursuit of sins and judgment. Alternatively ἀκρίτου qualifies ὑπολήψεως: from the uncritical or unexamined supposition prompted by his goodness. On that attachment the adjective characterizes the supposition, not God’s judging activity. Neither reading is treated as a source defect.

4. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτοὶ ὡς ὅμοια θεοῦ ποιήσαντες, ἁμαρτάνοντες ἰσχυρίζοντο εὐσεβεῖν
Rendered as: they themselves, thinking they had acted like God, insisted while sinning that they were acting reverently
ὡς presents the alleged imitation from their viewpoint, not a fact affirmed by the narrator, who just called the accusations about God false. Had acted retains the retrospective aorist participle, while thinking makes their rationale explicit.

SECTION 18.20

One might reasonably say that the words, “No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father,” were addressed to those who supposed him to be like this. And rightly so. For had they known, they would not have sinned by believing books really written against God for testing. Elsewhere too, wishing to show them more clearly the cause of their error, he says, “This is why you are deceived: you do not know the true things in the scriptures, and for this reason you are also ignorant of God’s power.” Therefore every person who wants to be saved must become, as the teacher said, a judge of the books written for testing. For he said this: “Become approved money changers.” Money changers are needed because the counterfeit is also mixed in with the genuine.

Translator's notes for section 18.20 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ ἀληθῆ τῶν γραφῶν
Rendered as: the true things in the scriptures
Preserves the distinction within the scriptures asserted by the author; it is not replaced by simply the scriptures.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς πειρασμὸν
Rendered as: for testing
πειρασμός can mean testing or temptation. The argument treats problematic books as a test of discernment; the temptation alternative remains possible.

3. Translation choice — Greek: γίνεσθε τραπεζῖται δόκιμοι
Rendered as: Become approved money changers
Retains the money-changing analogy and the approved/genuine versus counterfeit contrast.

SECTION 18.21

After Peter said these things, Simon pretended to be shocked at what had been said about the scriptures and, as though alarmed, said, “Far be it from me and those who love me to listen to your statements. Until I knew that you held these views about the scriptures, I put up with you and conversed; but now I withdraw. I ought, however, to have withdrawn at the beginning, because I heard you say, ‘I believe no one who says anything against the one who created the world: neither angels nor prophets, neither scriptures nor priests, neither teachers nor anyone else, even if someone performs signs and wonders, even if he visibly flashes in the air or reveals through visions or dreams.’ Who, then, can persuade you, whether rightly or wrongly, to think anything other than what you have decided, when you remain so firmly and immovably in your own knowledge?”

Translator's notes for section 18.21 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: προσποιησάμενος ἐκπεπλῆχθαι
Rendered as: pretended to be shocked
The narrator explicitly presents the shock as pretense, rather than leaving its sincerity open.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν ἀέρι ἐπιφανῶς ἀστράπτῃ
Rendered as: visibly flashes in the air
Retains the vivid flashing and airborne manifestation, not a generic vision.

SECTION 18.22

As Simon said this and was about to go out, Peter said, “Hear this further thing from me, then go wherever you wish.” Simon turned and remained, and Peter said, “I know how you were astounded then when you heard me say, ‘Whoever says anything against the God who created the world, I do not believe him.’ Now hear something greater than this. If the God who created the world really were in character such as the scriptures describe him, and even if in some other way he were incomparably evil, beyond what either the scriptures could say or anyone else could even conceive, I would nevertheless not stop revering him alone and doing his will. For I want you to know and be persuaded that the person who has no affection for his own maker can never have it for another either. If he does have it for another, he has it contrary to nature and does not know that he has from evil the love of the unjust, since he cannot even keep that love firm. And if there really is someone else above the maker, being good he will receive me all the more because I love my own Father; but he will not receive you, knowing that you abandoned your maker by nature—I do not say father—for a greater hope, without concern for what is reasonable. Thus, if you find someone superior even to him, he knows that you will abandon him too someday, especially since he has not become your father, when you have abandoned even your true father.

Translator's notes for section 18.22 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: ἐὰν τῷ ὄντι ὁ τὸν κόσμον κτίσας θεὸς τὴν γνώμην τοιοῦτος ὢν τυγχάνῃ
Rendered as: If the God who created the world really were in character such as ...
The description is explicitly hypothetical. The severe conditional is preserved, not rewritten as an assertion that the maker is evil.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ πονηροῦ τὸν τῶν ἀδίκων ἔρωτα ἔχων
Rendered as: he has from evil the love of the unjust
From evil adopts the impersonal reading of πονηροῦ, since the immediate context does not identify a personal evil agent. From an evil one or the evil one is grammatically possible but is not asserted through imported theology. Love of the unjust may be love characteristic of unjust people or love directed toward them; the main phrase retains that ambiguity.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν φύσει σου ποιητὴν (οὐ γὰρ λέγω πατέρα)
Rendered as: your maker by nature—I do not say father
Preserves Peter’s pointed change from father to maker in addressing Simon rather than harmonizing all parent-language.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οὕτως εἰ καὶ αὐτοῦ κρείττονα εὑρήσεις
Rendered as: Thus, if you find someone superior even to him
Superior retains broader comparative κρείττονα without specifying the basis of superiority. Better or stronger are material alternatives, but the argument about changing allegiances does not require strength alone.

SECTION 18.23

But you will say, “He knows that no one else is above him, and for this reason he cannot be abandoned.” Then thanks are due to there being no other! Yet he knows the disposition of your mind to be ready for ingratitude. If, knowing you to be ungrateful, he receives you, but knowing me to be grateful does not admit me, according to your account he is irrational, not acting reasonably. Thus, Simon, you are a subordinate of evil without knowing it.” Simon replied, “Then tell us: from where has evil grown?” Peter said, “Since today you already moved to go out and said that from now on you would not listen to me as a blasphemer, if you wish to learn, come tomorrow and I will explain. I will also allow you to examine me as you wish, without contentiousness.” Simon said, “I will do as seems good to me.” After saying this, he went away. None of those who had entered with him went out with him; instead, falling at Peter’s feet, they asked to obtain forgiveness for having been attached to Simon and to be received as they repented. Peter welcomed both those feeling regret and the other crowds, laid his hands on them, praying and healing the afflicted among them. Thus, as he dismissed them, he instructed them to hurry at dawn. After saying this, he went inside with his companions and did the customary things in preparation for the rest that pressed upon them, since evening had arrived.

Translator's notes for section 18.23 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: χάρις οὖν τῷ μὴ εἶναι
Rendered as: Then thanks are due to there being no other
Preserves the ironic thanks and the existential absence, not a moral endorsement of Simon’s fidelity.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἀποδεχθῆναι μετανοοῦντας
Rendered as: to be received as they repented
μετανοοῦντας describes a moral-spiritual response in the request for forgiveness after association with Simon, so “as they repented” follows the October 13 contextual policy. Their repentance accompanies the request for reception; the translation adds neither a completed-reform requirement nor an unprinted Godward destination.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τοὺς μεταμελομένους
Rendered as: those feeling regret
Keeps μεταμέλομαι’s regret or remorse sense distinct from the preceding μετανοέω, rendered repent in its moral-spiritual context. The two surviving source expressions are not homogenized as repentance simply because they describe the same people.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ εἰωθότα πρὸς τὴν ἐπείγουσαν ἡσυχίαν ἐποίησεν
Rendered as: did the customary things in preparation for the rest that pressed upon them
The customary practices are not enumerated here; neither a meal nor a particular prayer is invented.

HOMILY 19

SECTION 19.1

On the next day Peter came forward rather early in the morning. Seeing Simon waiting for him with many others, he greeted the crowd and began to speak with them. But the moment he began, Simon interrupted and said, “Set aside these long preliminaries of yours and answer me as I question you concerning the matter at hand. For I perceive—as I know from what I have heard from the beginning...—that your sole aim is to use every device to demonstrate that the Creator himself alone is a blameless God, and that, in your resolve, you have so great a longing to insist on this that you even dare to call false certain passages of the writings that plainly accuse him. For this reason, I have resolved today to prove that it is impossible for him, being the creator of everything, to be blameless. I can begin the proof now, provided you answer what I ask you.”

Translator's notes for section 19.1 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς ἐπακηκοὼς... ἐπίσταμαι
The selected edition prints exactly three dots between ἐπακηκοὼς and ἐπίσταμαι, apparently marking unavailable wording or a printed break in the construction. The translation retains exactly three dots and supplies no restoration.

2. Greek: καὶ τοσοῦτον προαίρεσιν πόθον ἔχοντα διισχυρίζεσθαι, ὡς καὶ ἐνίας τῶν γραφῶν περικοπὰς σαφῶς καταλεγούσας αὐτοῦ τολμᾶν ψευδεῖς λέγειν
The attachment of ἔχοντα is uncertain. The main text takes it as referring back to Peter in συννοῶ σε, so that Peter has the longing to insist and consequently dares to call passages false. It could formally modify τὸν δημιουργόν, yielding a sense such as ‘to show the Creator ... as having such a longing to insist,’ although that makes the following shift to Peter as the understood subject of τολμᾶν less direct. A looser construal making the Creator’s longing the content of Peter’s insistence would require διισχυρίζεσθαι to function separately rather than directly completing πόθον. No change to the supplied Greek is proposed.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὀρθριαίτερον
Rendered as: rather early in the morning
The comparative adverb indicates an earlier-than-usual or notably early time.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὸ προκείμενον πυνθανομένῳ μοι ἀπόκριναι
Rendered as: answer me as I question you concerning the matter at hand
The rendering preserves both the subject under discussion and Simon’s demand that Peter answer his question.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πάσῃ μηχανῇ
Rendered as: to use every device
μηχανή here denotes a contrivance, method, or strategic means, with Simon’s accusatory force retained.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν δημιουργὸν αὐτὸν δεῖξαι μόνον ἄμεμπτον εἶναι θεὸν
Rendered as: to demonstrate that the Creator himself alone is a blameless God
μόνον is taken as singling out the Creator as the one who is a blameless God; it could alternatively be attached more closely to the predicate.

7. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ τοσοῦτον προαίρεσιν πόθον ἔχοντα διισχυρίζεσθαι, ὡς καὶ ἐνίας τῶν γραφῶν περικοπὰς σαφῶς καταλεγούσας αὐτοῦ τολμᾶν ψευδεῖς λέγειν
Rendered as: and that, in your resolve, you have so great a longing to insist on this that you even dare to call false certain passages of the writings that plainly accuse him
ἔχοντα is taken as resuming σε and therefore referring to Peter, while διισχυρίζεσθαι completes πόθον: Peter longs to insist on his claim. προαίρεσιν is understood as an accusative of respect, ‘in respect of resolve.’ This keeps Peter as the subject of the linked longing, insistence, and daring.

8. Translation choice — Greek: περικοπὰς σαφῶς καταλεγούσας αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: passages of the writings that plainly accuse him
The personal genitive αὐτοῦ and Simon’s polemical context support the hostile sense ‘speak against’ or ‘accuse,’ though a more neutral rendering such as ‘give an account concerning him’ is lexically possible.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἐάν γε
Rendered as: provided
The particle γε strengthens the stated condition for beginning the proof.

SECTION 19.2

“Do you say that there is a ruler of wickedness, or not? For if you say there is not, I can prove from many things, including statements of your teacher, that there is. But if you reasonably acknowledge that the evil one exists, I will carry the argument forward in due sequence.” Peter replied, “It is impossible for me to deny the voice of my teacher. I therefore acknowledge that the evil one exists, because the teacher who spoke truth in everything often said that he exists. For example, he acknowledges that the one who conversed with him for forty days had tested him. Somewhere else, too, I know that he said, ‘If Satan drives Satan out, he has become divided against himself. How, then, can his kingdom stand?’ He also made it clear that he had seen the evil one fall like lightning from heaven. Elsewhere he said, ‘The one who sowed the evil seed is the devil.’ And again, ‘Do not give the evil one an opportunity.’ In giving counsel he also said, ‘Let your yes be yes and your no, no; anything beyond these comes from the evil one.’ And in the prayer he handed down we have the words, ‘Rescue us from the evil one.’ Somewhere else, too, he promised to say to those who act impiously, ‘Go away into the outer darkness, which the Father prepared for the devil and his angels.’ So that I do not prolong the argument excessively, I know that my teacher often said that the evil one exists. Therefore I too agree that he exists. Now, if you have something to say as the next step, as you promised, say it.”

Translator's notes for section 19.2 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: κακίας ἡγεμόνα
Rendered as: a ruler of wickedness
ἡγεμών denotes a leader or ruler; the phrase presents a personal power presiding over wickedness.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ πολλῶν καὶ τῶν τοῦ διδασκάλου σου
Rendered as: from many things, including statements of your teacher
The nouns governed by τῶν are implicit; ‘statements’ supplies the contextual sense without treating the teacher himself as evidence.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπομένως ποιήσω τὸν λόγον
Rendered as: I will carry the argument forward in due sequence
ἐπομένως indicates a logically consequent or orderly next stage.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τεσσαράκοντα ἡμέρας διαλεχθέντα πεπειρακέναι αὐτόν
Rendered as: the one who conversed with him for forty days had tested him
The accusative participle supplies the unexpressed subject of πεπειρακέναι, while αὐτόν is its object. Context favors the evil one as the tester and the teacher as the one tested, although neither referent is named within the clause.

5. Translation choice — Greek: μὴ δότε πρόφασιν τῷ πονηρῷ
Rendered as: Do not give the evil one an opportunity
πρόφασις can mean a pretext, occasion, or opportunity; ‘opportunity’ suits something granted to the evil one.

6. Translation choice — Greek: εἰπεῖν ὑπέσχετο
Rendered as: he promised to say
ὑπέσχετο ordinarily means ‘promised.’ The rendering is not harmonized to a familiar Gospel saying or softened to ‘threatened.’

7. Translation choice — Greek: λοιπὸν εἴ τι ἔχεις ἐπομένως λέγειν
Rendered as: Now, if you have something to say as the next step
λοιπόν and ἐπομένως together mark the next consequence in Simon’s proposed argument.

SECTION 19.3

Simon said, “Since, then, you have reasonably acknowledged that the evil one exists, tell us from the writings how he came to be—if indeed he came to be—and by whom and why.” Peter replied, “Pardon me, Simon, for not daring to say what has not been written. If you say that it has been written, show it. But if, since it has not been written, you too are unable to show it, why do we put ourselves in danger by making declarations about things not recorded? Or have we not believed that we will be judged, not only for what we do but also for what we say in belief, and is that why we speak more boldly about God?” Simon, understanding that this had been aimed at his recklessness, said, “Leave me to take the risk, but do not use what you call blasphemy as a pretext for retreat. For I perceive that you want to draw back so that you may escape being refuted before the crowds: at one time on the ground that you fear hearing blasphemies, and at another on the ground that, since it has not been written how, by whom, and why the evil one came to be, one must not dare to say more than Scripture. Therefore, as a reverent man, you confirm this alone: that he exists. But in devising these tactics you deceive yourself, not knowing that if it is blasphemy to investigate the evil one precisely, the responsibility lies with me, the accuser, not with you, the one defending God. And if the matter under investigation is unwritten and for that reason you do not wish to investigate it, there are certain adequate paths capable of demonstrating the matters under investigation no less than writings can. For example, is it not necessary that the evil one—whom you too say exists—be either originated or unoriginated?”

Translator's notes for section 19.3 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: Ἐπεὶ οὖν εὐγνωμονήσας ὡμολόγησ[ας] εἶναι τὸν πονηρόν, ἀπὸ γραφῶν ἡ[μῖν] λέγε τὸ πῶς γέγονεν (εἴπερ γέγο[νε]) καὶ ὑπὸ τίνος καὶ διὰ τί. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Σ[ύγ]γνωθί μοι, Σίμων, μὴ τολμῶντι εἰπεῖν [ἃ] μὴ γέγραπται.
The selected, image-checked text contains square-bracketed sequences within several words and around ἃ. The translation follows the complete forms explicitly supplied by the selected text and adds no further restoration.

2. Greek: ὁτὲ μὲν ὡς δεδιὼς βλασ[φημί]ας ἀκοῦσαι, ὁτὲ δὲ (ἐπεὶ μὴ γέ[γρα]πται πῶς καὶ ὑπὸ τίνος καὶ διὰ τί [γέ]γονεν ὁ πονηρός)
The selected text again marks parts of words with square brackets. The translation follows the supplied completed forms βλασφημίας, γέγραπται, and γέγονεν without inventing additional wording.

3. Greek: ὅτι μὴ, χρὴ πλεῖον τῆς γραφῆς τολμᾶν λέγειν
The printed comma after μὴ disrupts the contextually expected construction. The translation provisionally attaches μὴ to χρὴ, yielding ‘one must not dare,’ while preserving every supplied word.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εὐγνωμονήσας
Rendered as: reasonably
The participle commends Peter as having acted with good sense or fairness in making the admission.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ πῶς γέγονεν (εἴπερ γέγο[νε])
Rendered as: how he came to be—if indeed he came to be
The parenthetical qualification leaves open the possibility that the evil one did not originate.

6. Translation choice — Greek: περὶ ὧν πιστεύοντες λαλοῦμεν
Rendered as: for what we say in belief
πιστεύοντες may mean ‘while believing’ or ‘as matters of belief’; the chosen wording preserves the connection between belief and speech.

7. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τὴν ἀπόνοιαν αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: aimed at his recklessness
ἀπόνοια can denote folly, desperation, or reckless audacity. Simon understands Peter’s warning as directed at his own conduct.

8. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν ἐπὶ τῶν ὄχλων ἔλεγχον
Rendered as: being refuted before the crowds
ἔλεγχος can denote refutation, exposure, or censure; the public debate favors ‘refuted.’

9. Translation choice — Greek: περὶ πονηροῦ ἀκριβοῦν
Rendered as: to investigate the evil one precisely
ἀκριβόω here means to ascertain exact details. ‘Give a precise account of the evil one’ is also possible.

10. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ αἰτία περὶ ἐμὲ τὸν κατήγορον τυγχάνει, οὐ περὶ σὲ τὸν συνηγοροῦντα τῷ θεῷ
Rendered as: the responsibility lies with me, the accuser, not with you, the one defending God
The legal contrast between an accuser and an advocate is preserved.

11. Translation choice — Greek: ἢ γενητὸν εἶναι ἢ ἀγένητον
Rendered as: be either originated or unoriginated
The pair concerns whether the evil one came into being. ‘Created or uncreated’ is possible but could narrow γενητός prematurely to deliberate creation.

SECTION 19.4

Peter said, “It is necessary.” Simon replied, “Therefore, if he is originated, he came into being through God himself, who made everything: either begotten like a living creature, or projected as substance and coming about outside through mixture. For if the matter from which he came to be was outside him, whether animate or inanimate, he came to be either through God himself or from himself, or even arose from things that do not exist; he belongs to the class of things that are relative to something, or he always existed. Since, then, all the paths toward discovering him have, as I think, been distinguished here, it is necessary that he be discoverable by traveling one of them. One seeking an origin must therefore travel each path and, upon finding the responsible party, understand that he is subject to blame. Is that not so? What do you think?”

Translator's notes for section 19.4 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: [εἰ γὰρ] ἐκτὸς ἦν αὐτοῦ ἡ ὕλη ἔμψυχος [οὖσα] ἢ ἄψυχος, ὅθεν γέγονεν, ἢ δι’ αὐτοῦ [τοῦ] θεοῦ ἢ ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἢ καὶ ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων [συμ]βέβηκεν
The selected text explicitly marks εἰ γάρ, οὖσα, τοῦ, and part of συμβέβηκεν with square brackets. The translation follows these supplied readings without adding an independent restoration.

2. Greek: ἢ δι’ αὐτοῦ [τοῦ] θεοῦ ἢ ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἢ καὶ ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων [συμ]βέβηκεν, τῶν πρὸς τὶ ἐστὶν ἢ αἰεὶ ἦν
The sequence is syntactically compressed. The main text carries the evil one forward as the implied subject of γέγονεν, συμβέβηκεν, ἐστίν, and ἦν because ὅθεν γέγονεν resumes the surrounding inquiry into how the evil one originated. Alternatively, ἡ ὕλη may remain the subject or controlling topic: the clauses would then concern the origin and status of the matter from which the evil one arose—whether that matter came through God, from itself, or from nonbeing, whether it belongs among relative or dependent things, or whether it always existed. No alteration of the supplied Greek is proposed.

3. Greek: ἐκτὸς ἦν αὐτοῦ ἡ ὕλη
The referent of αὐτοῦ may be God, as the sequence most naturally suggests, or the evil one. The translation retains the pronoun ‘him’ rather than resolving it explicitly.

4. Greek: π[ά]σης
The selected text prints the alpha of πάσης within square brackets. The translation follows the supplied completed word and supplies no additional restoration.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ζῷον γεννηθεὶς
Rendered as: begotten like a living creature
The comparison presents ordinary animal generation as one possible mode of origin.

6. Translation choice — Greek: οὐσιωδῶς προβληθεὶς
Rendered as: projected as substance
The philosophical language describes a projection or emanation in respect of substance; ‘emanated substantially’ is a viable alternative.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἔξω τῇ κράσει συμβεβηκώς
Rendered as: coming about outside through mixture
κρᾶσις denotes mixing or blending, while συμβαίνω can describe coming together or coming about. The precise cosmological mechanism remains compressed in the Greek.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ ὕλη ἔμψυχος [οὖσα] ἢ ἄψυχος
Rendered as: the matter ... whether animate or inanimate
ἔμψυχος and ἄψυχος distinguish matter possessing life or soul from lifeless matter.

9. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν πρὸς τὶ ἐστὶν
Rendered as: he belongs to the class of things that are relative to something
The phrase uses the philosophical category of relatives, things whose identity is stated in relation to something else. Under the alternative syntactic grouping, it describes the matter rather than the evil one.

10. Translation choice — Greek: π[ά]σης οὖν ὁδοῦ (ὡς οἶμαι) ἐνταῦθα διῃρημένης
Rendered as: all the paths ... have, as I think, been distinguished here
διαιρέω suggests an exhaustive division or differentiation of possible avenues of inquiry.

11. Translation choice — Greek: εὑρόντα τὸν αἴτιον ὑπὸ μέμψιν αὐτὸν εἶναι νοεῖν
Rendered as: upon finding the responsible party, understand that he is subject to blame
αὐτόν is taken as referring to the responsible cause or agent just found. It could grammatically be heard as referring back to the evil one, but the argument seeks whom to blame for his origin.

SECTION 19.5

Peter said, “It seems to me that if he is shown to have come into being through God, the one who made him should not yet be subject to blame, for perhaps his usefulness might prove more necessary than everything else. But if he should even be shown not to have come into being, but to have existed always, neither in this case is the Creator blameworthy, since he is superior to all things: even if he has been unable to put an end to a beginning that has no beginning because he lacks the nature required to do so; or if, though able, he does not abolish him, having judged it unjust to impose an end on one who received no beginning, and making allowance for one who is evil by nature because he cannot become anything else, even if he should have the desire to become something else. But if, while wanting to make him good, he were unable, even so he is good, because he wants to but cannot. And in the very respect in which he is powerless, he is the most powerful of all, because the possibility is left to no one else. But if there is someone else who is able and yet does not put matters right, then, in the respect in which he is able but does not put matters right, he stands acknowledged as evil, since he does not stop him, as though taking pleasure in the things done by him. But if that other cannot do so either, better is the one who, besides being unable, ‘does not hesitate’ to benefit us as far as possible.”

Translator's notes for section 19.5 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: Ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ, ἐὰν· ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ φανῇ γεγονὼς
The printed punctuation after ἐὰν interrupts the conditional phrase. The translation provisionally reads the condition continuously with ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ while altering no Greek wording.

2. Greek: εἰ καὶ ἀνάρχῳ ἀρχῇ τέλος [ἐπιθ]εῖναι διὰ τὸ μὴ φύσιν ἔχειν οὐ δεδύ[νητ]αι, ἢ δυνατὸς ὢν οὐκ ἀναιρεῖ αὐ[τόν], ἄδικον κρίνας ἀρχὴν μὴ εἰλη[φ]ότι τέλος ἐπιθεῖναι
The selected text marks portions of ἐπιθεῖναι, δεδύνηται, αὐτόν, and εἰληφότι with square brackets. The translation follows the completed forms explicitly supplied by the selected text and makes no additional restoration.

3. Translation choice — Greek: μήπως τὸ χρήσιμον αὐτοῦ πάντων ἀναγκαιότερον εὑρεθείη
Rendered as: for perhaps his usefulness might prove more necessary than everything else
μήπως introduces a cautious possibility here. It can also have the preventive force ‘lest his usefulness prove,’ but Peter’s argument depends on withholding blame because such usefulness may be discovered.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς αἰεὶ ὢν
Rendered as: to have existed always
The phrase explains what it would mean for the evil one not to have come into being.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἀνάρχῳ ἀρχῇ
Rendered as: a beginning that has no beginning
The deliberately paradoxical repetition of ἀρχή is preserved. ‘Beginningless principle’ is a more technical alternative.

6. Translation choice — Greek: διὰ τὸ μὴ φύσιν ἔχειν
Rendered as: because he lacks the nature required to do so
The implicit subject is taken as the Creator, explaining his inability to end the beginningless being. It is also possible to take the subject as the beginningless being or principle: ‘because it has no such nature.’

7. Translation choice — Greek: κακῷ πεφυκότι συγγνῶναι
Rendered as: making allowance for one who is evil by nature
πεφυκότι presents evil as the being’s natural condition, while συγγνῶναι denotes pardon or allowance. The infinitive is construed with the decision not to destroy him; alternatively, it may remain under ἄδικον κρίνας, producing ‘judging it unjust ... to pardon one who is evil by nature.’

8. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ εἰ τοῦ γενέσθαι τὸ ἐπιθυμεῖν ἔχοι
Rendered as: even if he should have the desire to become something else
The complement ‘something else’ is carried forward from the immediately preceding clause; the Greek literally speaks of possessing the desire to become.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἀγαθὸν ποιῆσαι θέλων
Rendered as: while wanting to make him good
ἀγαθόν is taken predicatively of the evil one. An alternative is ‘wanting to do something good,’ but the preceding question of whether the evil one can become otherwise favors the chosen rendering.

10. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν ᾧ ἀδυνατεῖ πάντων ἐστὶ δυνατώτατος
Rendered as: in the very respect in which he is powerless, he is the most powerful of all
The paradoxical juxtaposition of inability and supreme power is preserved rather than explained away.

11. Translation choice — Greek: μὴ κατορθῶν
Rendered as: does not put matters right
κατορθόω can mean to succeed, act rightly, or set something right. The argument concerns an able agent who fails to correct the evil situation.

12. Translation choice — Greek: κρείττων ὁ πρὸς τῷ ἀδυνατεῖν κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμᾶς εὐεργετεῖν ‚οὐκ ὀκνῶν.‘
Rendered as: better is the one who, besides being unable, ‘does not hesitate’ to benefit us as far as possible
πρὸς τῷ with the infinitive means ‘in addition to,’ and κατὰ τὸ δυνατόν limits the beneficence to what is possible. The selected text’s quotation marks around οὐκ ὀκνῶν are represented by inner quotation marks.

SECTION 19.6

And Simon said, “When I have discussed with you each of the points I proposed and shown you who is responsible for evil, then I will also answer what you have said and demonstrate that the God whom you call blameless is liable to blame.”

And Peter said, “Since, from what you have been saying from the beginning, I perceive that you are intent on nothing other than subjecting God to blame as the leader of evil, I have resolved to accompany you along every path you wish and show that God is beyond all blame.”

And Simon said, “You say these things as one who loves the one you have taken to be God, but you are not speaking the truth.”

And Peter said, “But you, as an evil man who hates the God you have failed to know, let loose blasphemous words.”

And Simon said, “Remember that you compared me to a leader of evil.”

And Peter said, “I confess that I lied when I compared you to the evil one, for I was compelled to do so because I could not find anyone equal to you or even worse than you. That is why I compared you to the evil one, for you prove to be much more wicked than even the leader of evil. No one can show that the evil one has spoken against God, but all of us who are present can attest that you boldly denounce him.”

And Simon said, “One who seeks the truth owes it to no one to concede anything contrary to what is. Otherwise, why does he seek at all? What then? Could I not likewise, setting aside an exact investigation of the facts, spend all my time praising a God whom I do not know?”

Translator's notes for section 19.6 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς κακίας τὸν αἴτ[ιον]
Rendered as: who is responsible for evil
The masculine substantive αἴτιος can identify the responsible agent or cause. The personal wording suits the ensuing inquiry into the leader of evil.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς κακίας ἡγεμόνα τὸν θεὸν ὑποβάλλειν μέμψει
Rendered as: subjecting God to blame as the leader of evil
ὑποβάλλειν μέμψει depicts placing or exposing someone under censure, while ὡς κακίας ἡγεμόνα states the alleged basis for that censure.

3. Translation choice — Greek: θεὸν ὃν νενόμικας
Rendered as: the one you have taken to be God
The perfect of νομίζω presents Peter as having regarded or supposed this one to be God. “The God in whom you have believed” is possible but less directly reflects the verb’s evaluative sense.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν γὰρ [πο]νηρὸν οὐδεὶς κατειπόντα θεοῦ δεῖξαι δύναται
Rendered as: No one can show that the evil one has spoken against God
καταλέγω here means speak against, denounce, or malign. The rendering does not import the broader claim that the evil one never otherwise opposes God.

5. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδὲν οὐδενὶ ὀφείλει παρὰ τὸ ὂν χαρίζεσθαι
Rendered as: owes it to no one to concede anything contrary to what is
χαρίζεσθαι can mean grant a favor or make a concession, and παρὰ τὸ ὄν contrasts such favor with reality as it is.

6. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ἐγὼ οὐ δύναμαι, παρεὶς ἀκριβοῦν τὰ πράγματα, εἰς ἐγκώμιον οὗ μὴ ἐπίσταμαι θεοῦ τὸν πάντα μου δαπανᾶν χρόνον;
Rendered as: Could I not likewise, setting aside an exact investigation of the facts, spend all my time praising a God whom I do not know?
The printed question is taken as a sarcastic question about what Simon could do instead of investigating. οὗ μὴ ἐπίσταμαι θεοῦ is understood as an attracted relative construction referring to the unknown God.

SECTION 19.7

And Peter said, “You are not blessed enough to praise him, nor indeed are you able to do this good thing, for then you would be full of him. For this is what our teacher, who does not lie, said: ‘A mouth speaks from the heart’s abundance.’ Therefore you, overflowing with an evil purpose because of ignorance, speak against the only good God, without yet suffering what your daring words deserve. If you suppose there will be no judgment, perhaps you actually think there is no God. Therefore, because you fail to recognize such great patience on his part, you drive him still further toward desperate action.”

And Simon said, “Do not hope to cow me with fear so that I refrain from seeking from you what is true in the examples. I long so greatly for truth that, for its sake, I would not hesitate to undertake even the risk. But concerning the points I proposed to you at the beginning—if indeed you have anything to say—speak now.”

Translator's notes for section 19.7 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: Οὔτε τοσοῦτον εἶ μακάριος αὐτὸν ὑμνεῖν
Rendered as: You are not blessed enough to praise him
τοσοῦτον with the infinitive expresses the degree required for praising God, not merely the quantity of praise.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ περισσεύματος καρδίας στόμα λαλεῖ
Rendered as: A mouth speaks from the heart’s abundance
The rendering follows the wording supplied here rather than harmonizing it with a familiar canonical form; the Greek has neither a definite article before “mouth” nor an added possessive.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὅθεν σὺ περισσευόμενος προαιρέσει κακῇ ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ καταλέγεις τοῦ μόνου ἀγαθοῦ θεοῦ
Rendered as: Therefore you, overflowing with an evil purpose because of ignorance, speak against the only good God
προαίρεσις denotes a chosen disposition, purpose, or moral intention. The causal expression ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ is attached to that evil purpose; it could instead qualify the act of speaking against God.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὅθεν τῆς τοσαύτ[ης] αὐτοῦ μακροθυμίας οὐκ ἀντιλαμβανόμενος ἐπὶ πλεῖον πρὸς ἀπόνοιαν αὐτὸν ἐκτείνεις
Rendered as: Therefore, because you fail to recognize such great patience on his part, you drive him still further toward desperate action
The masculine αὐτόν most directly refers to God, making him the object of ἐκτείνεις. ἀπόνοια can denote desperation, recklessness, or drastic resolve. An alternative contextual interpretation is “you extend yourself still further into recklessness,” but that requires taking αὐτόν reflexively or loosely.

5. Translation choice — Greek: φόβῳ δυσωπήσειν με μὴ ζητεῖν σοι τῶν παραδειγμάτων τὰ ἀληθῆ
Rendered as: cow me with fear so that I refrain from seeking from you what is true in the examples
δυσωπέω can mean shame, overawe, or intimidate. The infinitive with μή states the result Simon rejects, while σοι marks Peter as the person from whom the truth is sought.

6. Translation choice — Greek: εἴγε εἰπεῖν ἔχεις
Rendered as: if indeed you have anything to say
The idiom concerns having something available to say, not merely possessing the physical ability to speak.

SECTION 19.8

And Peter said, “Since you force us to dare to speak as people who have accurately discovered God’s methods—and this though we are humans unable to ascertain precisely even the methods of those like ourselves—then, at least for the sake of those standing by, I will discuss what you wish instead of maintaining the most reverent silence. I agree with you that there is a certain leader of evil, about whose origin Scripture did not dare to say either something true or something false. Nevertheless, let us explore together, from many angles, how he came to be—if indeed he came to be—and let us choose from among the apparent possibilities the one that speaks more reverently. For this is securely inferred from what is probable: first, that one should accord God the more reverent account, especially in this way, when all suspicions have been cleared away and another adequate and safer supposition is available. Nevertheless, even before the investigation I promise you that every path of inquiry can show him alone—God—to be beyond blame.”

Translator's notes for section 19.8 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἐπεὶ ἐκ τῶν εἰκότων λαμβάνεται τοῦτο βεβαίως, ὃ μὲν ὅτι θεῷ τὸ εὐφημότερον δοῦναι πρέπει, ταύτῃ μᾶλλον πασῶν ὑπονοιῶν καθαρθεισῶν καὶ ἄλλης ἱκανῆς καὶ ἀκινδυνοτέρας παρακειμένης ὑποψίας
The supplied, image-checked wording is syntactically compressed, especially at ὃ μὲν ὅτι, and no balancing δέ follows μὲν. The translation takes the clause as introducing a first or principal consideration: that the more reverent account should be accorded to God when a sufficient and safer supposition is available. Alternatively, ὃ μὲν may begin an unfinished first reason. No alteration to the selected reading is assumed.

2. Translation choice — Greek: τὰς τοῦ θεοῦ τέχνας ἀκριβῶς ἐφευρόντας λέγειν
Rendered as: to speak as people who have accurately discovered God’s methods
τέχναι can denote arts, devices, designs, or methods. The participle is represented as describing the capacity in which they would presume to speak; a more strictly temporal rendering would be “to speak after accurately discovering God’s methods.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: [οὗ] τὴν γένεσιν ἡ γραφὴ οὔτε ἀληθὲς [οὔ]τε ψευδὲς εἰπεῖν ἐτόλμησεν
Rendered as: about whose origin Scripture did not dare to say either something true or something false
The paired negatives portray Scripture as making neither kind of pronouncement about the origin. The wording is preserved rather than simplified to “Scripture says nothing.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν δοκούντων τὸ εὐφημότερον ἑλώμεθα
Rendered as: let us choose from among the apparent possibilities the one that speaks more reverently
τὰ δοκοῦντα may mean apparent possibilities or proposed opinions. εὐφημότερον is comparative and favors the account that speaks more auspiciously or reverently of God.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ τῶν εἰκότων λαμβάνεται τοῦτο βεβαίως
Rendered as: this is securely inferred from what is probable
εἰκότα are probable considerations rather than certainties. The source’s juxtaposition of probability with secure inference is retained.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἄμεμπτον αὐτὸν μόνον δύναται δεῖξαι τὸν θεόν
Rendered as: can show him alone—God—to be beyond blame
μόνον is taken with αὐτόν, identifying God alone as blameless. It could instead be attached adverbially to δύναται, yielding “can only show God to be blameless.”

SECTION 19.9

Nevertheless, as you said, if the evil one is something that came into being, then either he came to be as a living creature, or was put forth in substance by God, or was compounded externally; or his choice resulted from the compounding, or it happened to arise without compounding and without God’s counsel. Or he came to be from things that did not exist, or by God from what exists nowhere in any way; or else outside God there was either lifeless or animate matter from which he came to be; or he fashioned himself; or he came into being by God; or he is one of the things that exist in relation to something else; or he always existed. For we cannot say that he does not exist, since we agreed together that he exists.

And Simon said, “You have divided all the paths concerning him well—the main question about him. It is now my part, after scrutinizing the division, to show you that the Creator is liable to blame; but your task is to prove, as you promised, that he is beyond all blame. I wonder whether you will be able to do so. First, if the evil one came into being from God as a living creature, he consequently possesses the same evil as the one who put him forth.”

And Peter said, “Not necessarily. For we see many among human beings who are good yet have fathered bad children, others who are bad yet have had good children, still others who are bad yet produce good offspring, and others who are good yet have become parents of both bad and good children. Thus the first man who was created fathered the unrighteous Cain and the righteous Abel.”

In response Simon said, “You act foolishly by discussing God while using human examples.”

And Peter said, “Then tell us about God without using human examples, while still making it possible for what you say to be understood. But you will not be able to do so.”

Translator's notes for section 19.9 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ γενητός ἐστιν
Rendered as: if the evil one is something that came into being
γενητός can mean generated, originated, or created. The broader wording avoids deciding in advance which mode of origination the ensuing alternatives support.

2. Translation choice — Greek: οὐσιωδῶς ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ προβέβληται
Rendered as: was put forth in substance by God
προβάλλω can describe putting forth or emanation, and οὐσιωδῶς indicates that this occurs with respect to substance. The antecedent of αὐτοῦ is understood contextually as God.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἔξω κέκραται
Rendered as: was compounded externally
κεράννυμι denotes mixing or compounding. ἔξω may mean externally or outside God; the Greek does not explicitly state the reference point here.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἢ ἐκτ[ὸς] ἦν θεοῦ ἢ ὕλη ἄψυχος οὖσα ἢ ἔμψυχος ὅθεν γέγονεν
Rendered as: or else outside God there was either lifeless or animate matter from which he came to be
The rendering takes ἐκτὸς θεοῦ with the existence of matter and treats ἄψυχος and ἔμψυχος as alternatives describing that matter. It is also possible to divide the sequence as “or he was outside God; or there was lifeless or animate matter from which he came to be.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἢ τῶν πρὸς τὶ ἐστὶν
Rendered as: or he is one of the things that exist in relation to something else
τὰ πρός τι is philosophical language for relative or relational entities—things defined through a relation to something else.

6. Translation choice — Greek: Καλῶς πάσας αὐτοῦ τὰς ὁδοὺς διεῖλες, τὸ κεφάλαιον αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: You have divided all the paths concerning him well—the main question about him
τὸ κεφάλαιον may denote a heading, summary, chief point, or principal question. The punctuation leaves its exact attachment compressed, so the translation treats it as an appositional summary of the division.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς αὐτῆς τοῦ προβάλλοντος κακίας τυγχάνει
Rendered as: he consequently possesses the same evil as the one who put him forth
The subject remains the evil one, while τοῦ προβάλλοντος identifies the producer whose evil Simon infers from the offspring’s nature.

SECTION 19.10

For instance, what were you saying at the outset? That if the evil one came into being from God, being of the same substance as God, then God too is evil. But when I showed from the very example you yourself supplied that bad people come from good people and good people from bad people, you did not accept it, saying that the example was human. Therefore I in turn do not now accept that God has been begotten, because begetting belongs to human beings, not to God. But neither can God be good or evil, just or unjust, nor indeed prudent, a living creature, or anything else that can belong to human beings, for such qualities belong to human beings. And if, when investigating God, we must not ascribe to him the good qualities belonging to human beings, there is nothing left to conceive, say, or investigate except this alone: his purpose, which he himself permitted us to understand, so that, when judged, we may be without excuse concerning the things that, although we knew them, we did not keep.

Translator's notes for section 19.10 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἀνθρώ- .πινον
The supplied reading interrupts a single expected adjective with a hyphen, whitespace, and a period. The context and the surviving letters indicate ἀνθρώπινον, “human.” This is treated as an apparent typographical interruption in the selected print, not as a lacuna or missing content.

2. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ ἐκ θεοῦ ὁ πονηρὸς γεγένηται, τῆς αὐτῆς αὐτῷ ὢν οὐσίας, καὶ πονηρός ἐστιν
Rendered as: if the evil one came into being from God, being of the same substance as God, then God too is evil
The subject of the final ἐστιν is implicit. Taking it as God avoids the tautology that the evil one is evil and matches Peter’s summary of Simon’s attempt to blame the Creator. A formally possible but contextually weaker rendering is “then he too is evil.”

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐ[ξ οὗ]περ αὐτὸς ἔδωκας παραδείγματο[ς]
Rendered as: from the very example you yourself supplied
The emphatic οὗπερ and αὐτός attribute the example to Simon, even though Peter developed its comparison in the preceding exchange.

4. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδὲ τὸ γεγεννῆσθαι θεὸν παραδέχομαι
Rendered as: I in turn do not now accept that God has been begotten
The perfect passive infinitive presents God as having undergone generation. The surprising assertion is retained as part of Peter’s reductio rather than changed into “God begets.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: οὔτε μὴν φρόνιμος ἢ ζῷον
Rendered as: nor indeed prudent, a living creature
φρόνιμος means prudent, sensible, or practically wise. ζῷον is rendered broadly as “a living creature,” preserving Peter’s analogy with human predicates.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ τῆς προαιρέσεως αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: his purpose
προαίρεσις can mean choice, intention, purpose, or moral disposition. Here it refers to the divine purpose made knowable for human accountability.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ὅπως κρινόμενοι ἀναπολόγητοι ὦμεν περὶ ὧν γνόντες οὐκ ἐφυλάξαμεν
Rendered as: so that, when judged, we may be without excuse concerning the things that, although we knew them, we did not keep
ἀναπολόγητοι means without a defense or excuse, and φυλάσσω here concerns observing or keeping what was known.

SECTION 19.11

When Simon heard this, he said, “You will not pressure me into keeping silent about his essence and investigating only his purpose. For it is possible both to think and to speak about his essence—I mean, starting from the good qualities belonging to human beings. For example, being alive and being dead belong to a human being, but to God belongs not being dead, but being alive—and being alive eternally. Again, human beings can be evil or good, but to God belongs being incomparably good. And, so that I may not prolong the argument at length, the better of the qualities belonging to human beings belong eternally to God.”

Peter said, “Tell me, Simon: does it belong to human beings to beget evil and good people and to do evil and good things?”

Simon said, “It does.”

Peter said, “Since you have spoken this way, the better of the qualities belonging to human beings must be assigned to God. Since human beings beget evil and good people, God can beget only good people; and since human beings do evil and good things, he himself delights in doing only good things. Thus, concerning God, either it is possible not to speak of the qualities belonging to human beings and to remain silent, or it is reasonable to assign to him the better of the good qualities belonging to human beings. In this way, he alone is the cause of all good things.”

Translator's notes for section 19.11 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: Οὐ δυσωπήσεις με περὶ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτοῦ σιωπή[σαν]τα περὶ τῆς προαιρέσεως αὐτοῦ [ζη]τεῖν μόνης.
Rendered as: You will not pressure me into keeping silent about his essence and investigating only his purpose.
The future with οὐ is taken as Simon’s negative declaration of refusal, fitting his ensuing claim that God’s essence can be discussed. The aorist participle σιωπήσαντα is rendered as attendant action coordinated in English with ζητεῖν. A temporally stricter alternative is “You will not pressure me, after I have kept silent about his essence, to investigate only his purpose,” while interrogative punctuation is grammatically possible but less suitable to the argumentative context.

2. Translation choice — Greek: περὶ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: about his essence
οὐσία denotes God’s being or essence here, whereas the plural οὐσίαι in the next section denotes elemental substances.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ ζῆν καὶ τὸ τεθνάναι
Rendered as: being alive and being dead
The perfect infinitive τεθνάναι denotes the state of having died or being dead, not merely the process of dying.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν προσόντων ἀνθρώποις τὰ κρείττονα
Rendered as: the better of the qualities belonging to human beings
προσόντα denotes attributes or qualities that belong to someone, and κρείττονα selects those regarded as superior.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ δὲ θεῷ τὸ ἀσυγκρίτῳ ἀγαθῷ εἶναι
Rendered as: to God belongs being incomparably good
ἀσυγκρίτῳ may describe the good as incomparable or convey the adverbial sense “incomparably”; the latter produces natural English without changing the claim.

6. Translation choice — Greek: οὕτως π[ερὶ θεοῦ] ἢ οὐ τὰ ἀνθρώποις προσόντα λέγειν καὶ σιωπᾶν ἔστιν ἢ τῶν ἀνθρώποις προσόντων κα[λῶν] εὖλογόν ἐστιν ἀπονέμειν αὐτῷ τὰ κ[ρείτ]τονα
Rendered as: Thus, concerning God, either it is possible not to speak of the qualities belonging to human beings and to remain silent, or it is reasonable to assign to him the better of the good qualities belonging to human beings
The rendering lets ἔστιν govern the coordinated infinitives and takes οὐ directly with λέγειν. If οὐ is instead given wider scope, the first member could be read “it is not possible to speak of the qualities belonging to human beings and remain silent,” but that produces a less fitting contrast with the second alternative.

SECTION 19.12

Simon said, “Then, if God is responsible only for good things, what remains to be understood except that some other principle produced evil, or perhaps it is ungenerated?” Peter said, “Neither did some other power produce the evil one, nor is evil ungenerated, as I will show at the end. For now my task is to demonstrate, as I promised at the beginning, that God is blameless in every way. We have granted, then, that God possesses the better things that belong to human beings incomparably. Therefore it is also possible for him to be the one who sends forth the four substances—I mean the hot and the cold, the moist and the dry. These, being primary, simple, and unmixed, have an appetite for neither side. But, sent forth by God and mixed outside, they can become a living being with a choice to destroy evil people. Thus, though everything has been produced from him, the evil one neither comes from elsewhere nor has received his wickedness from God himself, who made everything. Wickedness cannot exist with him, because the substances, being neutral, were separated out and sent forth from him. When, outside, they were mixed by his skill at his will, the desire for the destruction of evil people occurred. But the wickedness that occurred cannot destroy good people, even if it should wish to, for by law it has authority against those who sin. So, not knowing each person’s character, he gains experience against them, and, having exposed them, punishes them.” Simon said, “Since God is capable of mixing the elements and making mixtures for what he wishes, for whatever choices he wishes to arise, why did he not make each person’s constitution inclined to choose good things?”

Translator's notes for section 19.12 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: κ[αὶ ὁ Σ[ί]μων
The supplied selected-edition text has an unmatched opening bracket after κ and a nested bracketed ί. “Simon said” and the conjunction are translated from the supplied letters, but this note preserves the unusual bracket form. It is not silently normalized, claimed as an OCR error, or used to invent any missing words. The other square brackets in this passage supply portions of words as printed, rather than dot-count gaps.

2. Translation choice — Greek: προβολέα
Rendered as: the one who sends forth
The noun describes an emitter or producer by projection; “emanator” is a technical alternative. The main text retains sending-forth language, not a claim that the passage explicitly teaches creation from nothing.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ κρείττονα ἀσυγκρίτως ἔχει
Rendered as: possesses the better things ... incomparably
The statement concerns superior qualities among those attributed to humans. “Possesses incomparably superior qualities” is a more idiomatic alternative, but the main text preserves the comparative and the separate adverb.

4. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς οὐδέτερον ἔχει τὴν ὄρε[ξιν]
Rendered as: have an appetite for neither side
The two sides can be understood as good and evil in the argument; neither is inserted as a newly printed noun.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πεφιλοκρινημέναι
Rendered as: were separated out
The unusual perfect participle conveys distinction or separation of the substances in this argument. “Carefully distinguished” is possible, but a claim of affectionate separation is not imposed merely from the compound’s form.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν κατ’ αὐτῶν λαμβάνει [ἐμ]πειρίαν καὶ διελέγξας τιμωρεῖ
Rendered as: he gains experience against them, and, having exposed them, punishes them
The hostile κατ’ αὐτῶν is retained. Contextually this can be rendered “he tests them and, after proving their wrongdoing, punishes them”; the main text does not add a specific trial method or identify the implicit object of exposure more narrowly than the people concerned.

7. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς ἃ βούλεται πρὸς ἃς βούλεται γενέσθαι προαι[ρέ]σεις
Rendered as: for what he wishes, for whatever choices he wishes to arise
Both overlapping purpose/relative phrases are represented, not reduced to a single clause. The second feminine relative anticipates the plural choices.

SECTION 19.13

Peter said, “Our present task is to show how the evil one came to be—if indeed he has come to be—and by whom. As for whether this happened without blame, when I have completed the argument now before us, I will then show how and why he came to be, and I will establish that the one who made him is blameless. Nevertheless, we said that the four substances were put forth by God, and thus, by the intention of the one who combined them, the choice of evil things arose just as he wished. For if it had arisen contrary to his purpose, or from some other substance or even some other cause, God’s plan would not have been secure, since rulers of evil might continually arise against his will and wage war against his designs. But it is impossible for matters to be this way. For no living being—and especially one fit to rule—can come into being by accident, since everything that comes into being must come into being through someone.”

Translator's notes for section 19.13 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ δὲ εἰ ἀμέμπτως
Rendered as: As for whether this happened without blame
The expression is elliptical, with the preceding coming-to-be understood. “Whether he came to be blamelessly” is formally possible, but the continuation shows that the issue is whether blame attaches to the maker.

2. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ οὕτως βουλῇ τοῦ συγκρίναντος συμβέβηκεν ὡς ἠθέλησεν ἡ τῶν κακῶν προαίρεσις
Rendered as: and thus, by the intention of the one who combined them, the choice of evil things arose just as he wished
The neuter sense of κακῶν gives the source-transparent “evil things,” with the genitive dependent on προαίρεσις. Alternatively, κακῶν may be masculine and refer to evil people; in light of the preceding purpose of destroying them, the phrase may evoke a purpose concerning evil people, but an explicitly oppositional relationship such as “against” is not expressed by the genitive itself.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ τῆς [βουλῆ]ς βέβαιον
Rendered as: God’s plan would not have been secure
Literally, the phrase is “the firmness of the plan.” The rendering expresses the plan’s settled reliability; God is supplied as the contextual possessor.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἢ καὶ προφάσεως
Rendered as: or even some other cause
πρόφασις can denote a cause, occasion, alleged reason, or pretext. “Cause” fits the argument about an independent basis for the evil one’s emergence.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἡγεμόνες αἰεὶ κακίας
Rendered as: rulers of evil might continually arise
κακίας may identify what these rulers govern or embody. “Leaders in wickedness” is another possible rendering.

6. Translation choice — Greek: οὐδὲν γὰρ ζῷον καὶ ταῦτα ἡ[γε]μονικὸν
Rendered as: no living being—and especially one fit to rule—
καὶ ταῦτα emphasizes an additional noteworthy circumstance: the being is not merely alive but ruling or fitted to command.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκ συμβεβηκότος
Rendered as: by accident
The phrase denotes coming about incidentally or as a mere chance occurrence, in contrast with production by an agent.

SECTION 19.14

Simon said, “What then? Does matter, being coeternal and equal in power with him, put forth rulers against him as an enemy, rulers who hinder his designs?”

Peter said, “If matter is eternal, it is not anyone’s enemy. For what exists forever is also incapable of suffering; and being incapable of suffering, it is blessed; and being blessed, it cannot become receptive to enmity, since, by its eternal constitution, it has no fear of being deprived of anything. Why, rather, does matter not love the Creator, since it is seen bringing forth fruits as food for all those generated by him? And why has it not feared him as the stronger, as it acknowledges by trembling through earthquakes and as, while surging in great waves, it very quickly obeyed the Teacher, who was sailing and commanded calm, and became quiet? What then? Did the demons not come out while both fearing and honoring him? And did not others, first pleading to enter pigs, make their request, since they did not have authority even to enter pigs without his consent?”

Translator's notes for section 19.14 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: εἰσελθεῖν’
The selected edition prints an apostrophe after the infinitive. It is retained in the source quotation as a confirmed editorial or typographic feature but contributes no separately recoverable lexical content to the English and is not treated as evidence for restored letters.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ ὕλη αὐτῷ σύγχρονος οὖσα καὶ ἰσοδύναμος
Rendered as: matter, being coeternal and equal in power with him
σύγχρονος here describes simultaneous eternal existence with God, while ἰσοδύναμος asserts equality of power.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπαθές
Rendered as: incapable of suffering
ἀπαθής can mean unaffected, impassible, or incapable of suffering. The argument connects it with freedom from deprivation and fear, so the fuller reader-facing expression is used.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἀιδίῳ κτίσει στερηθῆναί τινος μὴ πεφοβημένη
Rendered as: since, by its eternal constitution, it has no fear of being deprived of anything
The dative ἀιδίῳ κτίσει has uncertain force. The main rendering understands it causally or instrumentally as matter’s eternal constitution; “in eternal creation” or “as an eternal created thing” are formally conceivable but contextually difficult.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πῶς δ’ οὐχ ὡς κρείττονα πεφόβηται, ὡς καὶ διὰ τῶν σεισμῶν τρέμουσα ὁμολογεῖ καὶ ὡς μεγάλα κυματουμένη τῷ διδασκάλῳ πλέοντι καὶ γαλήνην ἐπιτάξαντι τάχιστα πεισθεῖσα ἡσύχασε;
Rendered as: And why has it not feared him as the stronger, as it acknowledges by trembling through earthquakes and as, while surging in great waves, it very quickly obeyed the Teacher, who was sailing and commanded calm, and became quiet?
Both evidentiary clauses remain attached to the rhetorical question about matter’s fear of the stronger. The dative participles πλέοντι and ἐπιτάξαντι describe the Teacher whom matter obeyed.

6. Translation choice — Greek: μετὰ τοῦ φοβεῖσθαι καὶ προτιμᾶν
Rendered as: while both fearing and honoring him
προτιμάω can mean prefer, esteem highly, or honor. The Teacher is the implied object of both infinitives.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἄλλοι δὲ εἰς χοίρους εἰσελθεῖν πρότερον παρακαλοῦντες ἠξίουν
