Rendered as: And did not others, first pleading to enter pigs, make their request
The participle παρακαλοῦντες and finite verb ἠξίουν express distinct but closely related acts. The translation retains both the prior pleading and the ensuing request rather than collapsing them into one verb.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς μηδὲ τοῦ εἰς χοίρους εἰσελθεῖν’ ἄνευ τῆς αὐτοῦ συγχωρήσεως ἐξουσίαν ἔχοντες
Rendered as: since they did not have authority even to enter pigs without his consent
ὡς introduces the basis implied by their request, and συγχώρησις here denotes permission or consent.

SECTION 19.15

Simon said, “What then? Does that which is lifeless have the natural capacity to produce bad and good things?” Peter said, “On this account it is neither good nor bad, because it does not act by choice, being lifeless and insensible. Therefore here too one can discern how, though lifeless, it brings forth living things, and though insensible, it appears to fashion skillfully formed shapes of both animals and plants.” Simon said, “What then? If God himself animated it, is he not himself the cause of the bad things it brings forth?” Peter said, “If God animated it according to his own will, his spirit works on it, and there is no longer anything hostile to God, equal in power to him, or impossible for him, because everything he brings about comes about as he wills. But you will say, ‘He himself is the cause of evil, if he himself works bad things through it.’ What, then, will you call the bad things? Venomous creeping creatures and deadly herbs, or demons, or also some other things capable of troubling human beings? These—the ..... fine things—would not have existed if the human being had not sinned, on account of which death entered. For while the human being was ......, the venom of creeping creatures was not at work, nor the effects of bad herbs; disturbances by demons did not occur, nor did any other affliction have the natural capacity to attach itself to him. But through sin he fell away from being immortal and has, as I said, become susceptible to every affliction. But if you say, ‘Why, then, did human nature originally come into being susceptible to death?’ I tell you: because of freedom of choice. For if we were not susceptible to death, as immortals we could not be punished for a sin committed with freedom of choice. Thus, because of a somewhat greater immunity to suffering, even if we were bad by choice, justice too would be weakened, since those with bad choices could not be punished because of immunity to suffering.”

Translator's notes for section 19.15 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ὧν αὕτη τίκτει κακῶν
The former selected transcription read ὢν, being, but the independently blind-checked print crop now reads ὧν with rough breathing and circumflex. This is a documented print-transcription correction, not a grammatical conjecture. The blind receipt notes that the breathing/circumflex strokes are crowded and partly merged, with the breathing contour less distinct; that ink uncertainty remains disclosed. The main text uses the selected relative reading and does not certify each crowded stroke as perfectly clear.

2. Greek: τὰ ..... λεπτὰ
The selected edition prints exactly five dots before λεπτά. Exactly five remain in English, without filling the lost qualification or substituting a complete reconstructed phrase. Fine is a rendering of the surviving adjective, with subtle, thin, or small as lexical alternatives.

3. Greek: θάνατος παρεισῆλθε...... γὰρ ὄντος τοῦ ἀνθρώπου
The selected edition prints exactly six dots between death entered and for ... the human being being. Exactly six remain in English, moved to the open complement position after was to keep the surviving being-clause readable without identifying its missing qualification. No immortal or other adjective is restored from the later explicit immortality statement. An alternative retaining the physical interruption order is death entered ...... For while the human being existed, but that bare existential English risks obscuring the missing state. The main reading makes the unresolved state visible, not recovered.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ ἄψυχος οὖσα φύσιν ἔχει ἐμφύειν τὰ κακὰ καὶ τὰ ἀγαθά;
Rendered as: Does that which is lifeless have the natural capacity to produce bad and good things?
The feminine subject is not independently named in this supplied section, so that which is lifeless preserves it without introducing an unprinted matter noun. φύσιν ἔχει expresses a natural capacity or constitution, distinct from moral choice. Produce renders engender or cause to grow.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἄψυχος οὖσα ἔμψυχα προβάλλει
Rendered as: though lifeless, it brings forth living things
Preserves the repeated lifeless/living contrast; literally without soul versus things possessing soul or animate things. The main text does not turn absence of sensory life into absence of every productive capacity.

6. Translation choice — Greek: οὐκ αὐτὸς αἴτιός ἐστιν ὧν αὕτη τίκτει κακῶν;
Rendered as: is he not himself the cause of the bad things it brings forth?
The corrected ὧν is a genitive plural relative linking the bad things to what it produces, with its genitive attracted to κακῶν governed by cause of. It is not the participle being. Cause preserves the causal claim, rather than replacing it with a conclusion about guilt.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ αὐτοῦ πνεῦμα αὐτὴν ἐργάζεται
Rendered as: his spirit works on it
God’s spirit is the expressed agent working on the previously lifeless subject. The clause is conditional on God having animated it according to his will; it is not an independently asserted account of how every bad thing arises.

8. Translation choice — Greek: οὐκέτι τῷ θεῷ ἐχθρόν τι ἐστιν ἢ ἰσοδύναμον ἢ ἀδύνατον
Rendered as: there is no longer anything hostile to God, equal in power to him, or impossible for him
The dative God is understood with the coordinated predicates: hostile to him, equal in power to him, or impossible for him. Impossible represents a limit on capability, not moral opposition; the subsequent everything as he wills supports this reading. Powerless is another lexical sense of ἀδύνατον if read as an intrinsic predicate of the thing, but would not give the same shared-dative argument.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἅπερ τὰ ..... λεπτὰ οὐκ ἂν ἦν
Rendered as: These—the ..... fine things—would not have existed
Exactly five printed dots remain before fine. λεπτά can mean fine, subtle, thin, or small; fine here is not a commendation of moral goodness. The gap prevents identifying any missing qualification or more precise category; none is restored.

10. Translation choice — Greek: οὗ εἵνεκεν θάνατος παρεισῆλθε...... γὰρ ὄντος τοῦ ἀνθρώπου
Rendered as: on account of which death entered. For while the human being was ......
On account of which takes the preceding sin event as the causal antecedent, supported by through sin later in the section. On whose account, referring to the human being, is another possible relative attachment. The six-dot gap is retained as the unspecified state associated with the ensuing being-clause; English places the visible gap after was rather than restoring an adjective or any lost words before the Greek γάρ.

11. Translation choice — Greek: φύσιν εἶχε
Rendered as: have the natural capacity
As in the opening question, φύσιν ἔχει concerns natural capacity, not choice or intention. The main text keeps the claim that afflictions did not have capacity to attach to him, rather than saying only that they happened not to do so.

12. Translation choice — Greek: Διὰ τὸ αὐτεξούσιον.
Rendered as: because of freedom of choice
αὐτεξούσιον is being in one’s own power or self-determination, here the reason susceptibility to death permits accountability. The distinction between freely chosen sin and mere natural production remains.

13. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ οὕτως διὰ τὸ ἀπαθὲς πλεῖόν τι, κἂν τῇ προαιρέσει ἦμεν κακοί, ἡ καὶ δικαιοσύνη ἐξησθένει
Rendered as: Thus, because of a somewhat greater immunity to suffering, even if we were bad by choice, justice too would be weakened
The main text attaches πλεῖόν τι to immunity to suffering, preferring its immediate placement after τὸ ἀπαθές within the cause phrase, before the intervening even-if clause. The preceding contrast between hypothesized immortals and death-susceptible beings supports reading a greater degree of immunity. The indefinite τι is represented by somewhat. A materially different attachment takes πλεῖόν τι adverbially with ἐξησθένει across the intervening clause: Thus, because of immunity to suffering, even if we were bad by choice, justice too would be weakened somewhat more. That reading places the degree on weakening justice rather than on immunity. The printed comma does not uniquely settle the attachment. Something more in the immunity to suffering is a more literal version of the main attachment, not a substitute for disclosing this adverbial alternative; no additional agency, privilege, or restored Greek is asserted.

SECTION 19.16

In response, Simon said, “What else do I still have to say about the evil one except that God made him out of what did not exist? On this account the maker is evil: he made what did not exist come to exist, even though he could have made him good, since the being brought into existence possessed no nature of his own for choosing evil.”

Peter said, “Making him out of what did not exist, with a power of choice, is like the argument we stated earlier: by making his constitution such that he delights in evils, the maker himself appears responsible for what came into being. Since, then, both have a single solution, we will later discuss why he made him delight in the destruction of evil people.”

Simon said, “If he also made the angels with freedom of action, but the evil one departed from being righteous, why has he also been honored with rule? Through the honor he has given him, the one who honored him appears to delight in evils.”

Peter said, “If God appointed him, after he had rebelled, to rule over those like himself, ordering him to inflict punishment on sinners according to law, he is not unjust. But if the objection is that he honored him after he had rebelled, the one who honored him foresaw what was useful: both that the honor is temporary and that it is just for evil people to be ruled by an evil one and to be punished by him when they sin.”

Translator's notes for section 19.16 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ τὸν γενόμενον μηδὲν πρὸς κακίας προαίρεσιν ἰδίαν κεκτῆσθαι φύσιν
Rendered as: since the being brought into existence possessed no nature of his own for choosing evil
The articular infinitive supplies the ground for Simon’s assertion. μηδέν is taken with the possession of an independent nature, not as a restoration of the earlier phrase ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων. “Had no independent nature disposing him to choose evil” is a contextual alternative, but “disposing” is not made explicit in the Greek.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τὸ χαίρειν αὐτὸν κακοῖς τὴν κρᾶσιν ποιήσας
Rendered as: by making his constitution such that he delights in evils
κρᾶσις is the mixture or constitution of a being. “Temperament” would make the phrase more exclusively psychological. κακοῖς can mean evils or evil people; the following explicit reference to the destruction of evil people is rendered separately rather than supplied here.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπ’ ὀλέθρου κακῶν
Rendered as: in the destruction of evil people
The genitive κακῶν is read as personal, in light of the subsequent punishment of sinners. “In the destruction of evils” remains grammatically possible.

4. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτεξουσίους
Rendered as: with freedom of action
The adjective denotes having authority over oneself. “Self-determining” or “with free choice” are possible; the wording avoids importing a later fully developed doctrine of free will.

SECTION 19.17

Simon said, “Could it be that he has always existed and thus overturns sole rule, with another power also ruling alongside it—the power associated with matter?”

Peter said, “If they differ in their substances, they also differ in their powers, and the stronger rules the weaker. But if they are of the same substance, then they are equal in power and alike good or evil. Yet they plainly are not equal in power, for matter was brought by the maker into whatever form of a world he wished. And surely one cannot say that it always existed as a substance, not as matter serving as God’s storehouse. For one cannot say, ‘There was ..... when God had no possessions.’ Rather, he was always its sole ruler. Therefore also eternal [μο........]; and on this assumption it could properly be spoken of, with both the ruler and the [........́.ου] existing.”

Simon said, “What, then? Did the evil one make himself? And is God good in this way: knowing that he would exist for evil, he did not destroy him as he came into being, when, being incomplete, he could have been destroyed? For if he came about suddenly, and fully developed at that, this is why he wages war against the maker, having suddenly become equal to him in power.”

Translator's notes for section 19.17 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: Ἦν ..... ὅτε ἀκτήμων ἦν ὁ θεός
The edition prints a five-dot gap after “There was.” It is retained as exactly five dots. The missing content is not restored. “God had no possessions” renders the surviving ἀκτήμων, which can also mean propertyless.

2. Greek: διὸ καὶ ἀίδιος μο ........
The surviving fragment μο precedes an eight-dot printed gap. The English retains the fragment in Greek beside exactly eight dots, without completing it as “sole rule,” “monarchy,” or any other word. The preceding “eternal” translates surviving ἀίδιος; the incomplete syntax remains visible.

3. Greek: ὄντος καὶ τοῦ ἄρχοντος καὶ τοῦ ........́.ου
The final incomplete word consists of eight dots, an accent, one further dot, and ου. Its nine dots, accent and surviving ending are retained literally inside brackets. The construction introduces both the ruler and a second entity; the second entity is not identified by an invented restoration. The antecedent of “it could properly be spoken of” is affected by the earlier gap.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ τῆς μοναρχίας
Rendered as: sole rule
The argument concerns the sole sovereignty of God, not a human political monarchy. “Single sovereignty” is another defensible rendering.

5. Translation choice — Greek: οὐσία οὖσα, οὐχ ὕλη ὡς θεοῦ ταμεῖον
Rendered as: as a substance, not as matter serving as God’s storehouse
The negative contrast is retained. οὐσία may mean essence or independently existing substance; the main text keeps the lexical distinction from ὕλη, matter. “Treasury” is an alternative for ταμεῖον.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἐξαίφνης συμβέβηκε καὶ ταῦτα τέλειος
Rendered as: he came about suddenly, and fully developed at that
συμβέβηκε presents coming about as an occurrence, without explicitly identifying a creator. τέλειος contrasts with ἀτελής, incomplete, earlier in the sentence.

SECTION 19.18

Peter said, “You are saying impossible things. For even while he was coming into being little by little, he could have chosen to destroy him as an enemy himself. And, knowing beforehand that he would become not good, he would not have allowed it unless he knew that his coming into being would serve his own use. Nor was he capable of suddenly coming into being fully developed by himself, for someone who did not yet exist could not fashion himself. Nor can anything that has substance come into being out of what does not exist. And one could not rightly say that something that has come into being is equal in power to what always exists.”

Simon said, “Is it perhaps, then, one of the things that are relative, and is it evil in this way? It is bad, for example, as water is to fire, but good for ground that is untimely thirsty. Iron likewise is good for farming but bad for murders; desire, too, is not bad for marriage but is harmful for adultery. So also killing is bad, but good for the killer in relation to what he has planned. And greed is bad, but pleasant for the greedy person. Everything of this sort follows this pattern. By this argument, neither is evil evil, nor is good good, for each produces the other. Is it really the case that what seems to be done evilly brings delight to the doer but punishment to the sufferer? And if it seems unjust for someone who has loved himself to enjoy himself as much as possible, and because of this to suffer grievously at the hands of a righteous judge for having loved himself, to whom does it not appear unjust?”

Translator's notes for section 19.18 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: καὶ εἰ ἄδικον δοκεῖ τὸ ἑαυτὸν ἀγαπήσαντα. εὐφραίνειν ὡς δυνατόν ἐστι· καὶ διὰ τοῦτο χαλεπὰ πείσεσθαι ὑπὸ δικαίου δικαστοῦ περὶ τοῦ ἑαυτὸν ἠγαπηκέναι, τίνι οὐκ ἄδικον φαίνεται;
The wording has a difficult scope for the first “unjust”: the articular infinitive and subsequent infinitive can gather the self-pleasuring and its punishment into a single stated situation. The main text retains both occurrences of “unjust” and the positive “loved himself” rather than supplying a missing negation or turning the opening adjective into “just.” Another reading would take the initial description of injustice as Simon’s concession before his challenge about punishment. The supplied punctuation after ἀγαπήσαντα is not treated as a completed sentence.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ἐχθρὸν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ προαιρέσει ἀνελεῖν ἠδύνατο
Rendered as: he could have chosen to destroy him as an enemy himself
God remains the understood subject of ἠδύνατο. προαιρέσει specifies choice, and ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ is represented reflexively as personal agency, “himself.” Another attachment is “as an enemy brought into being by him”; the Greek arrangement does not make the attachment entirely unambiguous.

3. Translation choice — Greek: οὔτε ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων γενέσθαι τί οὐσίαν ἔχει δύναται
Rendered as: Nor can anything that has substance come into being out of what does not exist
The supplied Greek has finite ἔχει (“it has”) beside δύναται (“can”), not a participle meaning “having” and not an expressed relative pronoun. I understand οὐσίαν ἔχει as a loose or parenthetic predication about the indefinite τί, “anything”: “nor can anything—it has substance—come into being out of what does not exist.” The main text integrates that predication into readable attributive English, “anything that has substance,” because the argument is discussing whether an existing being could arise from nonexistence. This is an English syntactic unpacking, not a change of the Greek to ἔχον or the insertion of a relative pronoun. A material alternative is to retain the parenthetic linkage, “Nor can anything—it has substance—come into being out of what does not exist.” That reading can assert substance of the particular posited being rather than limit the denial to a class of things that have substance. The Greek does not uniquely settle this linkage or scope. The negation and the supplied finite ἔχει are retained; the sentence is not harmonized with earlier competing claims about creation from nonexistence.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν· πρὸς τί
Rendered as: one of the things that are relative
πρός τι is the category of what is relative to something else; the supplied punctuation does not require a separate English clause. The following examples explicitly compare different effects on different recipients.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ ἀκαίρως διψώσῃ γῇ
Rendered as: ground that is untimely thirsty
ἀκαίρως marks untimeliness or being out of season. “Ground thirsty at the wrong time” is an alternative; the adverb is not dropped as though the text merely said dry ground.

6. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς δὲ μοιχείαν χαλεπή
Rendered as: but is harmful for adultery
χαλεπή characterizes desire as difficult, harsh, or harmful in its adulterous use. “Troublesome” is possible but could understate the evaluative contrast.

7. Translation choice — Greek: μήτιγε τὸ δοκοῦν κακῶς γίνεσθαι εὐφραίνει μὲν τὸν ποιοῦντα, κολάζει δὲ τὸν πάσχοντα;
Rendered as: Is it really the case that what seems to be done evilly brings delight to the doer but punishment to the sufferer?
μήτιγε ordinarily introduces a doubtful question or one leaning toward a negative answer. “Is it really the case that” preserves that questioning or doubtful force without changing the surviving proposition or making a flat assertion. Simon’s immediately preceding examples of pleasure for a wrongdoer and harm to a recipient also make an affirmative-leaning rhetorical interpretation contextually possible: “Does not what seems to be done evilly bring delight to the doer but punishment to the sufferer?” That alternative would solicit agreement with the relative-effects argument. The main text prefers the less leading doubtful wording because the question’s particle does not uniquely support the affirmative expectation; it does not claim that Simon’s intended answer is uniquely determined.

SECTION 19.19

Peter said, “One must discipline oneself through self-control whenever desire wants to rush toward another person’s harm, knowing that the evil one can destroy evil people, having received authority against them from the beginning. And so this is evil for those who have done evil. But that their souls remain under punishment after their destruction—this is indeed grievous, with someone rightly saying that the previously wrongly defined [one] is correct. For this reason, as I said, one must refuse to wrong someone else for the sake of a brief pleasure, so as not to bring oneself into everlasting punishment for the sake of a little pleasure.”

Simon said, “Is it perhaps, then, that there is nothing evil or good by nature, but the difference is a matter of law and custom ..̓̀.? Among Persians, marrying mothers, sisters, and daughters is a distinctive practice, whereas among others it is forbidden as something most grievous. Thus, since evils have not been defined for everyone, one cannot expect judgment from God.”

Peter said, “You cannot establish this. For it is apparent to everyone that having intercourse with mothers is abhorrent, even if Persians, who are one part of the whole, do not recognize the lawlessness of their abhorrent practice because of bad custom. So too Britons openly have intercourse in front of everyone and feel no shame. Others eat human flesh and do not feel disgust, and others eat dogs’ flesh; still others do things that cannot be spoken of. Thus one must not make judgments by a perception that custom has diverted from what is natural. For being murdered is evil, even if not everyone says that no one wants to experience it himself; and, in the case of theft, no one takes pleasure in his own punishment. So even if in any one case it is acknowledged that there are sins, we must necessarily and rightly also expect a third judgment concerning those sins.”

After Peter said this, Simon replied, “This is how matters concerning the evil one seem to you; tell me.”

Translator's notes for section 19.19 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: τοῦτο ὄντως εἶναι χαλεπὸν δικαίως τὸν κακῶς προδιωρισμένον ὀρθῶς ἔχειν εἰπόντος
The construction can be read as a genitive absolute, εἰπόντος, with its speaker unexpressed: “with someone rightly saying.” δικαίως qualifies the saying; the accusative masculine τὸν κακῶς προδιωρισμένον is then the subject of the reported infinitive ὀρθῶς ἔχειν, “is correct” or “is in a right condition.” This analysis accounts for the surviving forms without emending the Greek or identifying an unexpressed speaker. The main text retains the unspecified masculine referent as “[one].” It could denote a person or being previously wrongly characterized; alternatively, with λόγον understood, it could mean a previously badly defined argument or account that is said to hold good. The Greek here does not name that referent or establish the speaker’s identity. “Wrongly defined” preserves κακῶς with προδιωρισμένον rather than changing it to “defined as evil.” The earlier concern was whether an intelligible grammatical construction could be supported at all; the implied-subject genitive-absolute analysis supplies one. The remaining referent and attachment uncertainty is disclosed rather than resolved by invention, so it is not treated here as an unreadable-source or missing-clause block. This remains a candidate interpretation requiring independent review.

2. Greek: καὶ ἔθει ..̓̀.
The selected edition has two dots, accent marks, and a third dot after “custom.” The three dots and intervening marks are retained exactly as a printed gap; no conjunction or missing argument is supplied.

3. Greek: χαλεπώτ[ατον ἀπη]γόρευται
The square brackets mark supplied letters within words, not a dot-count lacuna. The supplied Greek is translated as printed (“forbidden as something most grievous”), and no additional conjectural letters are supplied.

4. Greek: κἂν οὖν ἑνὸς οὐδήποτε ὁμολογουμένου εἶναι ἁμαρτήματα
The construction is compressed: ἑνός is singular, while ἁμαρτήματα is plural, and οὐδήποτε is unusual in this position. “In any one case it is acknowledged that there are sins” takes ἑνός as one acknowledged instance and retains the plural sins. An alternative is “even if a single person anywhere acknowledges that there are sins.” The conclusion does not require specifying which referent of ἑνός is intended.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ ἐγκρατείᾳ
Rendered as: through self-control
The dative specifies the means of disciplining oneself. “Restraint” is another direct rendering.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀιδίῳ περιβαλεῖν κολάσει
Rendered as: bring oneself into everlasting punishment
ἀΐδιος explicitly conveys everlasting or eternal duration; the wording does not substitute “age-long,” and κολάσει is rendered punishment without making an additional claim about its purpose.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἴδιον τὸ γαμεῖν μητέρας, ἀδελφάς, θυγατέρας
Rendered as: marrying mothers, sisters, and daughters is a distinctive practice
ἴδιον means peculiar or distinctive to the people named. The main text translates the ancient speaker’s assertion without independently endorsing the historical ethnographic claim or adding erotic description.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς καὶ Βρεττανοὶ ἐμφανῶς ἐπὶ πάντων κοινωνοῦσι
Rendered as: So too Britons openly have intercourse in front of everyone
κοινωνοῦσι expresses sharing or participation, here in the sexual context established by the preceding example of intercourse and the absence of shame. The main text therefore makes the sexual activity explicit as “have intercourse,” not ordinary unspecified sharing. The verb can also emphasize communal sexual sharing rather than simply engaging in intercourse; “share in sexual relations” is a material alternative. No particular wives or partners are named, and none is supplied. This renders the ancient speaker’s assertion without independently endorsing its ethnographic accuracy.

9. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ἕτεροι κυνῶν
Rendered as: and others eat dogs’ flesh
The preceding σάρκας…ἐσθίουσι supplies the ellipsis; κυνῶν is the genitive “of dogs.”

10. Translation choice — Greek: τρίτην κρίσιν
Rendered as: a third judgment
The selected source expressly has τρίτην, “third.” No change to “future judgment” or other conjectural reading is made, although the enumeration is not explained in this passage.

11. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ γὰρ τὸ φονευθῆναι κακόν ἐστι, κἂν μὴ πάντες λέγωσιν ὅτι μηδεὶς αὐτοπαθεῖν θέλει
Rendered as: For being murdered is evil, even if not everyone says that no one wants to experience it himself
The main text takes ὅτι as a content-clause marker after λέγωσιν: “say that.” Its immediate position after the verb of saying supports this ordinary linkage. On that analysis, the claim that no one wants to suffer murder is the content of a statement that is not universally made; Peter’s assertion that being murdered is evil precedes the concession. A material alternative takes ὅτι causally and attaches it to the assertion about murder’s evil: “For being murdered is evil, even if not everyone says so, because no one wants to undergo it himself.” On the causal reading Peter himself expressly gives the unwillingness to suffer murder as the justification for calling murder evil, while the concession concerns whether everyone acknowledges that evil. The following appeal to aversion to theft’s personal consequences makes that causal reading contextually plausible. The main content-clause reading is not claimed as uniquely settled, and neither reading changes the surviving negations.

12. Translation choice — Greek: Οὕτως σοι δοκεῖ τὰ κατὰ τὸν πονηρὸν εἶναι, εἰπέ μοι.
Rendered as: This is how matters concerning the evil one seem to you; tell me.
The main text follows the supplied edition’s comma between the opening clause and the imperative and its final full stop: Simon states how Peter views the matter before requesting further explanation. An unmarked interrogative reading is also possible in Greek, particularly beside “tell me”: “Is this how matters concerning the evil one seem to you? Tell me.” That alternative asks Peter to confirm his view rather than first stating it. The punctuation is treated as a printed editorial feature, not an OCR error; neither the speaker’s referents nor the request’s unstated object are invented.

13. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ κλοπῇ οὐδεὶς ἐπὶ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ κολάσει ἥδεται.
Rendered as: and, in the case of theft, no one takes pleasure in his own punishment
The main text connects ἐπὶ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ κολάσει directly to ἥδεται as the occasion or object of pleasure: no one enjoys his own punishment. κλοπῇ supplies the setting, “in the case of theft,” without identifying the person as thief or victim. κόλασις ordinarily denotes punishment or chastisement, but the neighboring assertion that no one wishes to suffer murder makes a contextual alternative important: “and no one takes pleasure in his own suffering through theft,” with κλοπῇ specifying the means of the suffering. The source does not explicitly settle whether this is a penalty associated with theft or the suffering theft inflicts. A further grammatically possible attachment makes κλοπῇ itself the object of pleasure, “no one takes pleasure in theft when it means his own punishment”; that is less transparent to the explicit ἐπί-phrase and is not adopted in the revised main text. No person is uniquely identified and no causal or conditional consequence is added to the main wording.

SECTION 19.20

Peter said, “We remember that our Lord and teacher gave us this command: ‘Keep the mysteries for me and for the sons of my house.’ That is also why ‘he explained to his own disciples in private’ the mysteries of the kingdom of the heavens. But to tell the secret things to you, who fight against us and scrutinize nothing other than what is ours .... (whether true or false), is to act impiously. Yet, so that some of those standing here may not suppose that I am devising a pretext because I am unable to answer what you have said, I will speak, first asking you: if there were no suffering pain, what would the evil one still be?”

Simon said, “Nothing.”

Peter said, “Is evil, then, suffering pain and dying?”

Simon said, “It seems so.”

Peter said, “Then evil does not always exist; indeed, it cannot have existence. For suffering pain and dying are among the things that happen, neither of which occurs when sound health is present. For what is suffering pain other than something being out of harmony? And what is death other than the separation of a soul from a body? Thus there is no suffering pain when harmony exists. For dying is not even among things that have existence at all, because death is nothing, as I said, other than the separation of a soul from a body. When this occurs, the body, being naturally without perception, dissolves, but the soul, possessing perception, exists alive. Hence, when harmony exists, there is no suffering pain, no dying; nor indeed are there deadly plants, venomous creeping creatures, or anything else of this sort whose outcome is death. Hence, when immortality prevails, it will become apparent that everything has come into being with good reason. And this will indeed be so when the human being becomes immortal because of righteousness, with the Messiah’s peaceful kingdom prevailing, when his constitution too is well-balanced, so that not sharp ........ impulses; and his knowledge is also unerring, so that he may not [π.......] any of the evils as good; and he will be in pain, so that he may not be mortal.”

Translator's notes for section 19.20 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: τὰ ἡμέτερα .... (εἴτε ἀληθῆ ὄντα εἴτε ψευδῆ)
The four-dot gap after “what is ours” is preserved as exactly four dots. The source’s parenthetical true/false alternatives are retained; no missing purpose or verb is reconstructed.

2. Greek: ἵνα μὴ ὀξείας........ ὁρμάς
The printed eight-dot gap is preserved as exactly eight dots. The surviving words are rendered as the visibly incomplete “so that not sharp ........ impulses.” No verb such as “experience,” “have,” or “feel” is invented for the missing text.

3. Greek: ἵνα μή τι τῶν κακῶν ὡς ἀγαθὸν π....... τε ἀλγῶν ἔσται, ἵνα μὴ θνητὸς ᾖ
The partial π and seven-dot gap are retained literally, with no conjectural verb. The surviving τε ἀλγῶν ἔσται is positive: “and he will be in pain.” The main text does not silently add “not” to harmonize it with surrounding claims of freedom from pain. The final “so that he may not be mortal” is retained. The loss could affect the attachment or scope of the surviving clauses; no claim is made to recover that lost syntax.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ μυστήρια ἐμοὶ καὶ τοῖς υἱοῖς τοῦ οἴκου μου φυλάξατε
Rendered as: Keep the mysteries for me and for the sons of my house
The dative recipients are retained as “for,” rather than converting the phrase into an unexpressed prohibition. “Preserve” is another rendering of φυλάξατε.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς τῶν οὐρανῶν βασιλείας
Rendered as: of the kingdom of the heavens
The plural οὐρανῶν is retained without substituting an explanatory circumlocution such as God’s rule.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ μὴ ἀλγεῖν
Rendered as: no suffering pain
ἀλγεῖν concerns pain or suffering; “no suffering pain” preserves the experiential act rather than making it identical by definition with every moral evil. The subsequent ὁ πονηρός is rendered personally as “the evil one,” while τὸ πονηρόν is the abstract “evil.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν συμβαινόντων
Rendered as: among the things that happen
This contrasts occurrences or events with τὰ ὑπαρκτά, things that have existence. “Accidents” has a possible technical philosophical sense but is less accessible and could mislead in ordinary English.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ αἰσθητὴ οὖσα ζῶσα ὑπάρχει
Rendered as: but the soul, possessing perception, exists alive
αἰσθητή normally can denote perceptible, but here it contrasts the body’s ἀναίσθητον and supports a sense of having sensation. “Being perceptible” is the lexical alternative and is preserved here rather than treated as impossible.

9. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς τοῦ χριστοῦ εἰρηνικῆς ἐπικρατούσης βασιλείας
Rendered as: with the Messiah’s peaceful kingdom prevailing
χριστοῦ is an independent title, so “Messiah” follows the supplied POB policy. The possessive and the adjective peaceful are retained.

10. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ κρᾶσις εὔκρατός ἐστιν
Rendered as: his constitution too is well-balanced
The cognate words describe a well-mixed bodily constitution. The rendering is consistent with constitution for κρᾶσις in 19.16.

11. Translation choice — Greek: ὅθεν ἀθανασίας ἐπικρατούσης εὐλόγως πάντα γεγονότα φανήσεται
Rendered as: Hence, when immortality prevails, it will become apparent that everything has come into being with good reason
The main text takes εὐλόγως (“with good reason,” “reasonably”) with γεγονότα (“having come into being”): immortality will make apparent the rationale of things that have come into being. This is supported contextually by the argument’s discussion of the usefulness and eventual suitability of created things, not uniquely established by word order. A material alternative attaches εὐλόγως to φανήσεται: “Hence, when immortality prevails, it will reasonably appear that everything has come into being.” On that reading the reasonableness concerns the appearance or inference rather than directly characterizing the rationale of coming into being. Both are grammatically available; the note preserves the alternative without asserting that the main attachment is the only possible one.

SECTION 19.21

Simon said, “You have said these things correctly. Yet in the present world, does it not seem to you that a human being is susceptible to every passion? I mean desire, anger, grief, and such things.” Peter said, “These too belong to the things that happen, not to the things that always exist. They will now be found to occur usefully for the soul. For desire has been made to occur in the living being by the one who made everything well, so that, led by it into intercourse, it may multiply humanity. From humanity a multitude of chosen better people arises, suitable for eternal life. But without desire no one would have undertaken intercourse with a woman; as it is, under the pretext of pleasure, as though gratifying himself, the human being does that one’s will. Yet if someone uses desire for lawful marriage, he does not act impiously. If he rushes toward adultery, he acts impiously and for this reason is punished, because he used badly what was established well. Likewise, anger has received from God the nature of being kindled within us, so that we may be drawn by it to resist sins. Yet someone who uses it without measure does wrong, while one who uses it as deserved accomplishes what is just. We are also susceptible to grief, so that we may have sympathy at the death of those close to us—a wife, children, brothers, parents, friends, or others. For if we did not have the capacity to share suffering, we would be inhuman. All the other things likewise will be found to be fitting, if the reason why they came into being is understood.”

Translator's notes for section 19.21 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν·συμβαινόντων
Rendered as: the things that happen
Occurrences are contrasted with things existing always; “accidents” in a technical philosophical sense is possible but misleading without explanation.

2. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς κοινωνίαν
Rendered as: into intercourse
The immediate purpose of multiplying humanity supports the sexual sense of participation or sharing here. The text adds no sexual detail or named partners beyond the ensuing woman and lawful marriage.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πλῆθος ἐκλογῆς κρειττόνων
Rendered as: a multitude of chosen better people
The compact genitives can alternatively mean “a multitude from which better people are selected.” The main text takes ἐκλογῆς as characterizing the resultant multitude by selection, retaining κρειττόνων as the selected better people; it does not uniquely settle how the selection is made.

4. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς ἄμυναν ἁμαρτημάτων
Rendered as: to resist sins
ἄμυνα can mean defense against or requital of offenses. The main text takes the first, while “to punish offenses” is a material alternative in view of the ensuing measured use of anger.

5. Translation choice — Greek: κατ’ ἀξίαν
Rendered as: as deserved
The term can indicate proportional worth or due measure; the main text does not make every expression of anger just.

6. Translation choice — Greek: οἰκείων, γυναικὸς ἢ τέκνων ἢ ἀδελ-. φῶν ἢ γονέων ἢ φίλων ἢ ἄλλων τινῶν
Rendered as: those close to us—a wife, children, brothers, parents, friends, or others
οἰκεῖοι can mean household members, relatives, or people close to someone. Friends and other people in the ensuing list support the broader relational sense, avoiding an added household-membership restriction. The printed word division ἀδελ-. φῶν is represented as the intact word “brothers”; the single dot with a hyphen is not treated as a multi-dot lacuna or recovered missing word.

SECTION 19.22

Simon said, “Why, then, do people also die before their time, and why do recurring illnesses arise? Moreover, why are there demons, madness, and sufferings of every kind, capable of inflicting great punishment?” Peter said, “Because people devote everything of their own to pleasure, have intercourse without observing the proper times, and thus the depositing of seed, offered at the wrong time, naturally grows countless evils. They should have reasoned that, just as a suitable time for planting and sowing has been appointed, so days requiring observance have been assigned for intercourse. Hence someone who had learned from the tradition of Moses, reproaching the people for sins, called them sons of lunar new moons and sabbaths. At the beginning of the world people were also long-lived and free of illness. But when, through neglect, they abandoned the observance, from that time sons in succession, because of ignorance, ..... having intercourse when they should not, place their own children under countless sufferings. Hence also our [..... αλος], concerning the person disabled from birth who received sight from him, [ἔξετα .............. εν] this man or his parents, he was born blind, answered, ‘Neither did this man sin in any way, nor his parents, but so that through him the power of God might be revealed,’ healing the sins of ignorance. And indeed such things happen because of ignorance: that is, not knowing when one should have intercourse with one’s wife, whether she is clean from menstruation. Yet the sufferings you mentioned come from ignorance; they are not, however, brought about by the evil one. Moreover, give me someone who does not sin, and receive someone who does not suffer; and besides not suffering, you will find him able to heal others as well. Moses, for example, through reverence for God continued without suffering throughout his whole life, and by prayers healed the Egyptians who suffered because of sins.”

Translator's notes for section 19.22 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: υἱοὶ ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ ..... μὴ δεῖν κοινωνοῦντες
The five-dot printed gap is retained exactly. The sentence stays visibly incomplete at the link between the sons, ignorance, and intercourse that should not take place; no missing connective or argument is restored.

2. Greek: ὅθεν καὶ ..... αλος ἡμῶν
The five-dot gap and surviving αλος are retained literally as [..... αλος]. The partial word is not completed to a title or person’s name.

3. Greek: ἔξετα .............. εν οὗτος ἢ οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ τυφλὸς ἐγεννήθη
The surviving ἔξετα and εν flank a fourteen-dot printed gap, all retained literally as [ἔξετα .............. εν]. The subsequent surviving “this man or his parents” and “he was born blind” are represented as incomplete syntax, not joined by a restored question about sin from an external biblical text. No lost words are recovered.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπαρατηρήτως κοινωνοῦσι
Rendered as: have intercourse without observing the proper times
The following planting analogy and days to observe specify the context of observance; “without precaution” is less specific. This is the ancient speaker’s explanation, not independent medical advice.

5. Translation choice — Greek: περιοδικαὶ νόσοι
Rendered as: recurring illnesses
The adjective denotes periodic or cyclical occurrence, not a specific diagnosis.

6. Translation choice — Greek: δαίμονες καὶ μανίαι
Rendered as: demons, madness
The historical categories are retained, not collapsed into a modern psychiatric equivalence.

7. Translation choice — Greek: υἱοὺς νεομηνιῶν τῶν κατὰ σελήνην καὶ σαββάτων
Rendered as: sons of lunar new moons and sabbaths
The source explicitly connects the days with the sons in its argument. No prophet’s name or external quotation is supplied.

8. Translation choice — Greek: οὔτε οὗτός τι ἥμαρτεν οὔτε οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ
Rendered as: Neither did this man sin in any way, nor his parents
This rendering follows the wording of this author’s quotation, without importing differently worded biblical translations.

9. Translation choice — Greek: εἰ καθαρὰ ἐξ ἀφέδρου τυγχάνει
Rendered as: whether she is clean from menstruation
The purity category is the speaker’s, not an added biological assertion. “Whether she has become clean after menstruation” is another contextual rendering.

10. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς ἀγνοίας ἰωμένη τὰ ἁμαρτήματα
Rendered as: healing the sins of ignorance
The feminine participle can agree with δύναμις, power, in the quotation; its action is not assigned to a uniquely named person by the English.

11. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ πρὸς τὸ μὴ πάσχειν καὶ ἄλλους αὐτὸν θεραπεῦσαι δυνάμενος εὕρῃς.
Rendered as: and besides not suffering, you will find him able to heal others as well
The supplied δυνάμενος is nominative, not accusative δυνάμενον. The main English understands the healing ability as predicated of αὐτόν, the sinless person found, despite that case mismatch; the immediately following example of Moses’ freedom from suffering and healing others supports this contextual construal. A material alternative attaches the nominative participle to the addressed person: “and besides not suffering, you, being able to heal others as well, may find him.” That changes the possessor of healing ability. The supplied spelling and case are retained, not silently normalized or characterized as an OCR error. The English choice is not claimed as the uniquely regular grammatical reading.

SECTION 19.23

Simon said, “Let these things be so. Does the inequality among people not seem most unjust to you? For one is poor and another rich; one is ill and ..... is healthy; and there are countless such things in human life.” Peter said, “Do you not see, Simon, that again you are sending your arguments beyond the aim? For while we are discussing the evil one, you have turned aside and introduced an argument about what seem to be anomalies. Yet I will speak to this too. The world is an instrument made with skill, so that the female may eternally bear righteous, eternal sons for the male who is to come. But reverent people could not be brought to completion here unless there were people in need whom they might assist. Likewise, this is also why there are sick people whom they might care for. And the following matters contain this same rationale.” Simon said, “Then the lowly have suffered misfortune: they themselves suffer hardship so that righteous people may be brought to completion.” Peter said, “If their lowliness were eternal, it would be the greatest misfortune. But people’s low conditions and high conditions occur in accordance with their allotted lot. Anyone whose lot does not please him can make use of an appeal and, pleading his case according to law, change his life through it.” Simon said, “What is this lot and appeal?” Peter said, “That is the explanation belonging to another discussion. But if you permit it, we can show you how, being born anew, changing your birth-destiny, and living according to law, you will obtain eternal salvation.”

Translator's notes for section 19.23 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ὃς μὲν νοσεῖ καὶ ..... ὑγιαίνει
The five-dot gap is preserved exactly between illness and being healthy. The subject for the latter verb is missing from the surviving sequence and is not filled by an invented “another.”

2. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ ἐσομένῳ ἄρρενι αἰωνίως ἡ θήλεια τίκτῃ δικαίους αἰωνίους υἱούς
Rendered as: the female may eternally bear righteous, eternal sons for the male who is to come
The symbolic male and female are not identified as God, the world, the Messiah, or any specific persons not named in this clause. The main text attaches αἰωνίως to bearing, preserving continual or eternal generation; it can alternatively qualify the male’s future existence: “for the male who will exist eternally.” The sons’ explicit adjective αἰωνίους is retained separately.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῷ κλήρῳ
Rendered as: their allotted lot
κλῆρος denotes an allotted portion, not necessarily chance or an already specified astrological mechanism. Its precise explanation is deferred by Peter himself.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκκλήτῳ χρησάμενον καὶ νομίμως διαδικασάμενον αὐτὸν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ ὑπαλλάξαι βίον
Rendered as: make use of an appeal and, pleading his case according to law, change his life through it
The legal appeal and adjudication imagery is preserved. ἔκκλητος can refer to an appeal or an appellate authority; accordingly ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ can mean “through it” or “by him,” the agent handling the appeal. The main text does not identify a particular tribunal or human judge.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν γένεσιν ὑπαλλάξας
Rendered as: changing your birth-destiny
γένεσις can mean birth or origin; with allotted conditions and rebirth here, birth-destiny keeps both associations visible. “Changing your birth” is the more literal alternative, while “changing your natal fate” is more specifically astrological.

SECTION 19.24

When Simon heard these things, he said, “Do not suppose that, because in examining each topic I agreed, I was proceeding to another topic because I was fully convinced. I was providing you [ἀλ.....νοίας] of being persuaded, so that you would move to another topic, in order that, having learned all your [......... νοίας], I might condemn you without guessing. But [πεπληροφορημε ............]. Now allow me three days, and I will come and show that you know nothing.” After Simon said this and was about to leave, my father said, “Simon, hear a few words from me, and then go as you please. I remember that at the beginning, before the inquiry, having not yet tested me, you leveled preconceived judgments against me. But now, after hearing the discussion continuously, recognizing Peter’s superiority, and now granting him truthfulness, what do I seem to you? Someone who knows how to judge rightly, or not? For if you say that I judged rightly but do not agree, you appear prejudiced, unwilling even after acknowledgment to agree to defeat. But if I did not rightly declare Peter superior in the inquiry, persuade us how we judged incorrectly—or do not stop debating with him before everyone. For, each time being defeated and agreeing, and, if you have a sense of shame, being condemned by all the hearers in place of a most severe punishment and behaving disgracefully, you will suffer pain in your own soul through conscience. For we have seen your defeat in action, but have heard your words of promise. In the end, then, I do not think you will come to the inquiry as you promised; rather, to appear unashamed, you have promised as you leave to return.”

Translator's notes for section 19.24 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἀλ.....νοίας σοι τοῦ πείθεσθαι παρεῖχον
The incomplete ἀλ.....νοίας, with exactly five dots, is retained literally. The main text translates the surviving giving and being-persuaded wording but does not complete this word as “signs,” “pretenses,” or any other conjecture.

2. Greek: πάσας ......... νοίας σου
The nine-dot gap and surviving νοίας are retained literally. The feminine plural “all” and possessive “your” are translated, without recovering the missing word.

3. Greek: ἀλλὰ πεπληροφορημε ............
The surviving partial participial stem and twelve-dot gap are retained literally after “But.” The stem relates to full assurance, but its lost completion and syntactic continuation are not restored, and no claim that Simon is now convinced is invented.

4. Translation choice — Greek: προλήψεις μου κατέφερες
Rendered as: you leveled preconceived judgments against me
The genitive refers to judgments concerning the father, not necessarily the father’s own prejudices. “You cast down my preconceptions” is a grammatical alternative, but the following reminder of Simon’s failure to test the speaker favors accusations about him.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἀντὶ μεγίστης τιμωρίας
Rendered as: in place of a most severe punishment
The preposition can convey a replacement or an equivalent penalty. The condemnation is not made a separate physical punishment.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν δὲ ἐπαγγελλόμενόν σου λόγον
Rendered as: but have heard your words of promise
The participle ἐπαγγελλόμενον is understood as promise-making or professing, describing the speech that has actually been heard. δέ contrasts those words of promise with the defeat already seen in action; the following prediction that Simon will not return reinforces that distinction. A possible alternative treats λόγον as the substantive argument Simon promises to present, “your promised argument,” but the main text avoids suggesting that this future argument has already been delivered. The singular λόγος is expressed collectively as “words,” not as several distinct unprinted promises.

7. Translation choice — Greek: μὴ αἰδεῖσθαι
Rendered as: to appear unashamed
This can indicate not being ashamed or not losing face. It does not assert that Simon lacks every moral sense of shame.

SECTION 19.25

When Simon heard this, he ground his teeth in anger and went away silently. Since a considerable part of the day still remained, Peter laid hands on the large crowd for healing and dismissed them, then went indoors with his closest companions and sat down. One of the followers, named Sophonias, said, “Blessed, Peter, is the God who chose you and filled you with wisdom for the sake of those of good judgment. For you truly discussed with Simon impressively and without resentment. We ask you also to discuss evil things with us, hoping you will disclose the account concerning him more candidly to us—and not at this very hour, but tomorrow, if you please. For we make allowance for your weariness from the inquiry.” Peter said, “I want you to know that someone who does something with pleasure is refreshed by the very exertions, whereas someone who does not do what he wishes is greatly wearied by the rest itself. So you grant me great rest by making me discuss what I enjoy.” Yet, content with his willingness and making allowance for his exertions, we asked that the postponement be until night, as was his custom, for speech to be directed to the [γνησι.....]. And, having partaken of salt, to sleep [........πημεν].

Translator's notes for section 19.25 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: πρὸς τοὺς γνησι..... λέγεσθαι
The five-dot gap after γνησι is preserved literally. The surviving πρὸς τοὺς is translated as “to the” and the surviving λέγεσθαι is taken passively as speech being directed or spoken. The stem γνησι points toward genuineness or close association, but its completion is not supplied. Missing wording could affect the infinitive’s construction or even contain a lost compound prefix, so “to converse with the ...” is a contextual alternative, not a recovered reading. The main text nominalizes the surviving speaking verb as “speech” to give readable English without inventing the content of speech. No lost words have been recovered.

2. Greek: εἰς ὕπνον........πημεν
The eight-dot gap and surviving ending πημεν are retained as [........πημεν] after “to sleep.” A conventional narrative formula could suggest a verb such as “turned,” but it is not restored from analogy or another passage.

3. Greek: τοῖς καμάτοις συγγόντες
The selected, image-checked source prints συγγόντες. The usual aorist participle of συγγιγνώσκω would be συγγνόντες, but that is only a proposed normalization, not the supplied form. “Making allowance for his exertions” is a contextual construal supported by the earlier συγγινώσκομεν γάρ σοι διὰ τοὺς ἐκ τῆς ζητήσεως καμάτους, “we make allowance for your weariness from the inquiry.” The unusual spelling remains in the selected source and is disclosed rather than silently replaced or labelled an OCR error. No missing print-verification evidence is alleged.

4. Translation choice — Greek: περὶ πονηρῶν
Rendered as: about evil things
The selected text has a plural, while the following περὶ αὐτοῦ is singular. “About evil people” or “evil ones” is an alternative for the plural; the main text retains that plural-to-singular shift rather than silently regularizing both to “the evil one.”

5. Translation choice — Greek: γνησιώτερόν
Rendered as: more candidly
The comparative can mean more genuinely, sincerely, or intimately. The context requests a fuller disclosure to close associates, not a claim that Peter’s prior argument was false.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀνεξικάκως
Rendered as: without resentment
The adverb conveys patient endurance of ill-treatment. “Forbearingly” is a concise alternative, less accessible in modern English.

7. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὴν νύκτα
Rendered as: until night
The main text relates the temporal phrase to the requested postponement. Another attachment lets it describe making allowance for his exertions into the night; the surrounding account of his custom supports night as the deferred discussion time.

HOMILY 20

SECTION 20.1

During the night, he rose, woke us, and sat down as usual. He said, “Ask me about whatever you wish.” Sophonias was the first to begin with him: “Since we desire to learn, explain to us how the account concerning the evil one truly stands.” Peter said, “I have indeed already made it clear through the discussion with Simon, but because the things concerning him were stated together with other points, the matter was not brought to light very clearly. For many points that seem equal in force to the truth give most people some knowledge of the truth itself. Therefore, if I now tell you what I had then told Simon among many points, do not suppose that you have been honored equally with him.” Sophonias said, “You speak rightly. For if you now separate it out for us from the many points stated then, you will make the actual truth clearer.”

Translator's notes for section 20.1 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: πονηροῦ
Rendered as: the evil one
The adjective is substantival and contextually denotes the personal evil ruler discussed in the following sections; “evil” as an abstraction is a possible broader alternative.

2. Translation choice — Greek: κεφαλαίοις
Rendered as: points
The word denotes principal points, headings, or topics in an argument.

3. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτῷ
Rendered as: with him
In the warning about equal honor, the pronoun most naturally refers to Simon. A reference to the subject matter is less consistent with Sophonias’s reply.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἀφορίζεις
Rendered as: separate it out
The verb means to distinguish or set apart; its unstated object is contextually the matter under discussion.

SECTION 20.2

Peter said, “Hear, therefore, the truth about the ordering concerning the evil one. God defined two kingdoms and constituted two ages. He decided that the present world was to be given to the evil one because it is small and passes away quickly, but he promised to give the coming age to the good one, since it is great and eternal. He therefore made the human being self-determining, with the capacity to incline toward whatever actions he wishes. His body is three-part and has its origin from the female, for it has desire, anger, grief, and the things that follow these. The spirit—though itself not third in origin but three-part—has its origin from the male and is receptive to reasoning, knowledge, fear, and the things that follow these. Each of the two triads has one root, so that the human being is from two compounds, female and male. For this reason two ways were also set before him, that of law and that of lawlessness. Two kingdoms were also defined: one called the kingdom of the heavens, and the other the kingdom of those now reigning upon the earth. Moreover, two kings were appointed. One is appointed by law to reign over the present and temporary world, and he was blended so as to delight in the destruction of the wicked. The other, himself also being king of the age that is to come, loves the whole human race. Unable in the present circumstances to have freedom to speak openly ..... as, while trying to conceal who he is, he counsels what is beneficial.”

Translator's notes for section 20.2 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: δυνάμενος .....
The selected edition prints a lacuna of exactly five dots after this word. Its content is unavailable, no restoration has been supplied, and all five dots are retained in the English.

2. Greek: ὧς
The circumflexed form is difficult in this construction and may be an accentual error for the conjunction ὡς. The translation adopts that contextually defensible comparison while disclosing the proposed correction.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἁρμονίας
Rendered as: ordering
The noun can denote an arrangement, composition, or harmonious ordering. “Ordering” suits the ensuing account of paired ages, kingdoms, rulers, and elemental mixtures.

4. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτεξούσιον
Rendered as: self-determining
The term describes possessing authority over one’s own choices, not unlimited power.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τριτογενὲς
Rendered as: third in origin
The contrast distinguishes being third-generated or third in derivation from being three-part. “Third-born” is a more literal alternative.

6. Translation choice — Greek: φυραμάτων
Rendered as: compounds
The word evokes kneaded masses or mixtures and supports the author’s composite anthropology.

7. Translation choice — Greek: χειροτονεῖται
Rendered as: is appointed
The verb denotes selection or appointment; the accompanying reference to law presents the rule as authorized.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἐκράθη
Rendered as: was blended
The compositional force is retained because the following section explains the rulers through elemental blending.

9. Translation choice — Greek: παρρησίαν
Rendered as: freedom to speak openly
The noun can mean boldness, freedom of speech, or openness. The following effort to remain concealed favors open speech or action.

10. Translation choice — Greek: λανθάνειν
Rendered as: to conceal
The infinitive describes escaping notice. Here it is understood as concealing the king’s identity; “to remain unnoticed” is also possible.

SECTION 20.3

“Of these two ..... compels the other, at God’s command. Each person has authority ........... by which to obey whichever of them he wishes, for the purpose of doing good or evil. If someone chooses to do good things, he becomes the possession of the good king who is to come. But if someone should do base things, he becomes an instrument of the present evil one. Through sin, the latter has received authority over him by a just judgment; and, wishing to do so even before the coming age, he delights in punishing him in the present life and, as one gratifying his own desire, carries out God’s will. The other was created to delight in exercising authority over righteous people. When he finds a righteous person, he rejoices greatly, saving him by eternal life; and he too, as one gratifying himself, offers God thanks for them. Every unjust person may be saved after regretting his course, and every righteous man may incur punishment for a final sin. But these two rulers are God’s swift hands, desiring to act beforehand in accomplishing his will. That this is so is also stated in the law in the person of God: ‘I will kill and make alive; I will strike, and I too will heal.’ For he truly kills and gives life. He kills through the left hand, that is, through the evil one who was blended so as to delight in the affliction of the impious. But he saves and benefits through the right hand, that is, through the good one who was created to delight in benefiting and saving the righteous. These have their substances not from outside God, for there is no other first principle. Yet they were not brought forth by God as living beings, for then they would have shared his disposition. Nor did they arise accidentally, having come into being spontaneously contrary to his purpose, since then the greatest part of his power would have been abolished. Rather, the four primary elements were brought forth from God: hot and cold, wet and dry. Thus he is indeed the father of every substance ..... disposition being what comes after the blending; for when they were blended outside, choice was born as their offspring. At the end of the present world, therefore, the evil one, after serving God blamelessly, can, since he is not of a single substance, become good when recomposed away from persistence in evil. For even now he does nothing evil, although he is evil, since he has lawfully received authority to inflict suffering.”

Translator's notes for section 20.3 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: τούτων .....
The selected edition prints a lacuna of exactly five dots after this word, where the grammatical subject or other governing wording may have stood. No subject has been restored, and all five dots remain explicit in the English.

2. Greek: ἔχει...........
The selected edition prints a lacuna of exactly eleven dots after this word. The following relative form may depend on an antecedent in the lost wording, but no missing content has been supplied, and all eleven dots are retained in the English.

3. Greek: οὐσίας .....
The selected edition prints a lacuna of exactly five dots after this word, between the statement about God as father of every substance and the phrase about disposition. No connective or missing claim has been supplied, and all five dots remain explicit.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὥ
Rendered as: by which
The form is taken as a dative relative whose antecedent may have stood in the preceding lacuna. An erroneous or incomplete construction is also possible.

5. Translation choice — Greek: κτῆμα
Rendered as: possession
The word denotes something acquired or owned and presents the person as belonging to the coming good king.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπηρέτημα
Rendered as: instrument
The formation denotes something that serves or ministers. “Servant” is possible, but “instrument” preserves its contrast with “possession.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ὡς ἰδίᾳ χαριζόμενος ἐπιθυμίᾳ
Rendered as: and, as one gratifying his own desire
The construction with ὡς presents the action under the description of gratifying his own desire while he fulfills God’s will. “As though gratifying his own desire” is also possible, but need not imply that the gratification is unreal.

8. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ αὐτὸς δὲ ὡς ἑαυτῷ χαριζόμενος
Rendered as: and he too, as one gratifying himself
This parallel ὡς construction characterizes the good ruler’s action as self-gratification. The alternative “as though gratifying himself” is possible but does not necessarily deny actual gratification.

9. Translation choice — Greek: μεταμεληθέντι
Rendered as: after regretting his course
The verb can denote regret, reconsideration, or a change of mind. The context entails departure from injustice, but the distinct Greek terminology is preserved rather than homogenized.

10. Translation choice — Greek: τελευταίας
Rendered as: final
The adjective may describe one last sin or a sin committed at the end of life; the rendering leaves both temporal nuances possible.

11. Translation choice — Greek: χεῖρές
Rendered as: hands
The author’s bodily image for the two rulers is preserved rather than reduced to “agents.”

12. Translation choice — Greek: προλαμβάνειν
Rendered as: to act beforehand
The verb conveys anticipation or acting in advance; the rulers perform divine punishment or benefit before final judgment.

13. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ μὴν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ὡς ζῷα προεβλήθησαν (ὁμόδοξοι γὰρ αὐτῷ ἦσαν)
Rendered as: Yet they were not brought forth by God as living beings, for then they would have shared his disposition.
The main text takes the parenthetical imperfect indicative as the consequence implied by the preceding denial: if they had been brought forth as living beings, they would have shared God’s disposition. Greek supplies neither ἄν nor an explicit conditional protasis, however, so a direct indicative assertion remains possible: “for they were of the same mind as him.”

14. Translation choice — Greek: ἔξω
Rendered as: outside
The adverb is retained without an invented object. It may mean outside God or externally to the original divine bringing-forth.

15. Translation choice — Greek: μετασυγκριθεὶς
Rendered as: when recomposed away from
The participle denotes recomposition or alteration by mixture. The following genitive is taken as separation from persistence in evil; alternatively, that genitive may characterize a hypothetical single substance fixed in evil.

16. Translation choice — Greek: κακουχεῖν
Rendered as: to inflict suffering
The verb describes subjecting others to hardship or maltreatment; the author presents that activity as lawfully authorized punishment.

SECTION 20.4

After Peter said these things, Micaiah, who was also one of the followers, asked, “From where, then, does human sinning come?” Peter said, “It comes from not knowing that, when judgment has taken place concerning the things they do wrongly, they are certain to be punished. Consequently, although they possess desire for the continuation of life—as I said on another occasion—they satisfy it indiscriminately, through the corruption of half-mature boys or through some other pandering sin. Because they do not know that they are judged, as I said before, their lack of fear drives them to satisfy desire unlawfully. Thus God is not evil, for he established desire well so that there might be continuation of life. Rather, they themselves are most impious, since they have used what is good in desire badly. The same reasoning may also be applied to anger: someone who uses it justly, as is permitted, acts piously, but one who goes beyond the proper measure and takes judgment upon himself acts impiously.”

Translator's notes for section 20.4 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: [σεως γε]
These letters are printed in square brackets within the expression about judgment. The translation follows the resulting selected-edition reading while disclosing its editorially marked status.

2. Greek: [πον]
These letters are printed in square brackets to complete the verb translated “I said.” The translation follows that marked reading.

3. Greek: [εἰς]
The preposition is printed in square brackets. The translation follows the selected edition’s marked construction without claiming recovery of independently verified wording.

4. Greek: [ιπεπείρων]
Most of the adjective is printed in square brackets, and the resulting full printed form is unusual beside the expected form ἡμιπεπείρων. The contextual meaning “half-mature” is defensible, but the marked letters remain editorially uncertain.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ἁμαρτάνειν
Rendered as: human sinning
The infinitive denotes committing wrong or sin; the question asks for its source.

6. Translation choice — Greek: διαδοχὴν
Rendered as: continuation
The term refers to succession or perpetuation, here the continuation of human life through generation.

7. Translation choice — Greek: πληροφοροῦσιν
Rendered as: they satisfy it
Here the verb describes bringing desire to fulfillment rather than intellectual assurance.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἤμ[ιπεπείρων]
Rendered as: half-mature
The editorially marked adjective portrays the boys as only partly mature, literally half-ripened.

9. Translation choice — Greek: κολακευούσῃ
Rendered as: pandering
The participle portrays the sin as flattering or catering to desire; “enticing” is another possible rendering.

10. Translation choice — Greek: καλῷ
Rendered as: what is good
The wording distinguishes desire’s good divinely assigned function from its wrongful human use.

11. Translation choice — Greek: ἑαυτῷ τὴν κρίσιν λαβὼν
Rendered as: takes judgment upon himself
The phrase may mean that the person takes judgment into his own hands by assuming authority to judge or punish, which fits the discussion of exceeding the proper use of anger. It may instead mean that he incurs or receives judgment for himself, which fits the preceding emphasis on being judged and punished. The English intentionally leaves both readings available.

SECTION 20.5

Sophonias spoke again: “Your patience, my lord Peter, grants us boldness to ask you questions on many points for the sake of precision. Therefore, taking courage, we conduct the examination in every way. I remember, then, that yesterday, while Simon was engaged in inquiry with you, he said that if the evil one was generated from God, it follows that he shares the same substance as the one who brought him forth and ought to have been good, not evil. You answered that this does not necessarily follow, since many evil people are born from good people. In the same way, two individuals unlike each other were born from Adam, one of whom was evil and the other good. When Simon objected that you had used human examples, you answered that by this reasoning one should not accept that God begets either, for this too is a human example. But I, Sophonias, accept that God begets; I do not accept that he begets evil, even if good people among human beings beget evil ones. And do not suppose that I irrationally ascribe to God some things pertaining to human beings but not others, because I concede begetting to him but do not ascribe to him the begetting of what is unlike him. Human beings naturally beget sons whose dispositions are unlike their own for the following reason: because they are composed of four parts, their bodies change in different ways according to different alterations; and in a human body, as the distinctive quality of the alteration at each particular time increases or decreases, it disrupts the proportionate mixture. Because the compounds do not always remain the same, the seeds are secreted at different times with different mixtures, and dispositions, whether good or evil, follow them in accordance with the mixture at that time. But in God’s case no such thing can be conceived, for since he is unchangeable and always existent, wh...... he might wish to bring forth, it is altogether necessary that what is brought forth by him should likewise ...... in every respect in relation to the one who begot it—I mean both substance and disposition. But if anyone should wish to call even him changeable, I do not know how he can also call him immortal.”

Translator's notes for section 20.5 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ὅπ......
The selected edition preserves only the fragment ὅπ before a lacuna of exactly six dots. The English represents the incomplete fragment as “wh......” and does not complete it as “whatever,” “whenever,” or another conjecture.

2. Greek: ὡσαύτως ......
The selected edition prints a lacuna of exactly six dots after this word, where wording governing the comparison with the begetter is unavailable. The English retains all six dots and does not supply a verb such as “resemble.”

3. Greek: [δὲ θελήσ]
These letters are printed in square brackets, completing the conditional expression. The translation follows that marked reading without proposing additional text.

4. Translation choice — Greek: μακροθυμία
Rendered as: patience
The noun denotes forbearance or patience, here Peter’s willingness to endure extensive questioning.

5. Translation choice — Greek: παρρησίαν
Rendered as: boldness
Here the noun denotes confidence or freedom to question Peter openly.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀκολούθως
Rendered as: it follows
The adverb marks Simon’s inference that what comes from God must share God’s substance and goodness.

7. Translation choice — Greek: προβαλόντι
Rendered as: the one who brought him forth
The participle describes derivation or production without requiring the more technical English term “emanated.”

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἀνόμοιοί
Rendered as: unlike each other
The contrast between the evil and good sons favors mutual dissimilarity, though the phrase could instead mean that both differed from Adam in some respect.

9. Translation choice — Greek: διαφερόντων
Rendered as: pertaining to
In context the participle concerns features found among or associated with human beings. “Things in which human beings differ” is grammatically possible but fits the argument less well.

10. Translation choice — Greek: τροπὰς
Rendered as: alterations
The term denotes changes or turnings, possibly including seasonal or elemental variations.

11. Translation choice — Greek: ἴδιον
Rendered as: distinctive quality
The phrase denotes the quality or component proper to a particular bodily alteration, likely one of the elemental qualities.

12. Translation choice — Greek: ἀποκρίνονται
Rendered as: are secreted
The verb has the physiological sense of being separated or secreted in the discussion of bodily seed.

13. Translation choice — Greek: ἄτρεπτον
Rendered as: unchangeable
The adjective directly contrasts God with the changing bodily mixtures described immediately beforehand.

14. Translation choice — Greek: γνώμην
Rendered as: disposition
Here the noun denotes disposition, purpose, or cast of mind. “Opinion” is possible but too narrow for the contrast between good and evil offspring.

SECTION 20.6

When Peter heard these things, he became thoughtful for a little while and said, “I do not think anyone can discuss the evil one without doing the will of the evil one himself. Consequently, knowing this very thing, I do not know what I shall do—whether I shall remain silent or speak. If I were to remain silent, I would incur ridicule among the multitude, because, though professing to proclaim truth, I am ignorant of the discourse concerning evil. But if I were to speak, I fear that perhaps God is not pleased for evil to be investigated, but only good. Nevertheless, for you too, in response to Saphonius’s argument, I will make my own views clearer.

“I too agree that not everything belonging to human beings should be attributed to God. For example, human beings, since they do not have transformable bodies, do not transform themselves, but have a nature that is altered over time by changes. God, however, is not like this, for by his innate spirit and through an ineffable power, the body becomes whatever kind he wishes. And this is more readily believable than even that the air, having received such a nature from him, is transformed into dew by the incorporeal mind that permeates it and, when condensed, becomes water; water, when solidified, becomes stones and earth; and stones, when struck together, kindle fire. To such an extent, through alteration and transformation, the air, after first becoming water, ended in fire through these transformations, and what was wet was changed into the opposite nature.

“What then? Did God not also transform Moses’s staff into a living creature, making it a snake, which he transformed back again into a staff? And through that very staff which had been transformed, he changed the water of the Nile into blood, which he also transformed back again into water. Moreover, by an inbreathing of breath he transformed the human being, who was dust, into flesh, and transformed him back again into dust.
