And was not Moses, though himself flesh, transformed into an exceedingly great light, so that the sons of Israel were unable to look directly at him? Much more, therefore, is God supremely able to transform himself into whatever he wishes.”

Translator's notes for section 20.6 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: λίθοι.δὲ
The confirmed print places a period between λίθοι and δὲ without a following space, although the words continue the coordinated description. The translation treats δὲ as continuing the sentence, but that interpretation of the printed punctuation remains provisional.

2. Translation choice — Greek: περὶ πονηροῦ διαλεγόμενον μὴ αὐτοῦ τοῦ πονηροῦ τὸ θέλημα ποιεῖν
Rendered as: discuss the evil one without doing the will of the evil one himself
The repeated substantival πονηρός is rendered personally as “the evil one.” The broader alternative “discuss evil without doing the will of evil itself” remains grammatically possible.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ σώματα τρεπτὰ
Rendered as: transformable bodies
The adjective describes bodies as capable of being changed or transformed.

4. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ταύτῃ μᾶλλον ἔστι πιστεῦσαι, ἢ καὶ ὁ ἀὴρ
Rendered as: And this is more readily believable than even that the air
The rendering preserves the comparison signaled by μᾶλλον ... ἢ rather than replacing ἢ with a causal conjunction. The resulting comparison is contextually difficult. A disjunctive reading, “or even the air,” is possible for ἢ καί, but μᾶλλον favors the comparative construction.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τοῦ αὐτὸν διήκοντος ἀσωμάτου νοῦ
Rendered as: the incorporeal mind that permeates it
The participle depicts the incorporeal mind as extending throughout the air.

6. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς μέγιστον ἐτράπη φῶς
Rendered as: was transformed into an exceedingly great light
The wording describes transformation into light, not merely an act of shining.

SECTION 20.7

But perhaps one of you has thought that someone can be made into something else by another, but cannot himself transform himself into whatever he wishes, and that changing belongs to one who grows old and has to die .....; but this should not be thought of immortals. For did not angels, ageless ...... and of fiery substance, change into flesh, and those with Abraham who were ..........., whose feet people also washed as though those beings were humans of the same substance? An angel also wrestled with Jacob, who was a human, turning into flesh so that he could come into bodily contact with him. And, having wrestled, he likewise turned back to his own nature when he wished. Having now changed into fire, he did not burn Jacob's broad tendon, but inflamed it and made him lame. One who cannot become something else when he wishes is mortal, being subject to his own nature. But one who can become what he wishes when he wishes, mastering nature itself and returning to youth, is immortal. Therefore, all the more, God's power transforms the body's substance into whatever he wishes whenever he wishes, and brings forth something of the same substance with no transformation present, but not of equal power. For the one who brings it forth can also bring about its turning back toward himself into another substance. But the one brought forth, being also a child of the transformation from that one, cannot become anything else without the will of the one who brought it forth, unless that one wishes.

Translator's notes for section 20.7 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἀποθανεῖν ..... ἔχοντος
The selected edition prints five dots. The English preserves exactly five dots, without recovering or supplying the unavailable content.

2. Greek: ἀγήρως ...... καὶ πυρώδους
The selected edition prints six dots after the ageless expression. The English preserves exactly six dots and translates the surviving fiery-substance description, without restoring the missing link.

3. Greek: Ἀβραὰμ ........... σθέντες
The selected edition prints eleven dots followed by the surviving ending σθέντες. The English preserves exactly eleven dots, with only generic passive were representing the surviving inflection. The ending's unavailable lexical stem is not restored, and no complete original wording is claimed.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἀποθανεῖν ..... ἔχοντος
Rendered as: has to die .....
The infinitive with having is read as the prospect or necessity of dying in the context of aging and mortality. The five-dot gap remains a gap; no lost adverb, noun, or other completion is supplied. A capacity-to-die emphasis is a material alternative to has to die.

5. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ οἱ παρὰ τῷ Ἀβραὰμ ........... σθέντες
Rendered as: and those with Abraham who were ...........
The eleven-dot gap conceals the participle's lexical stem. Only its surviving passive plural ending licenses generic were in the English; no specific action such as appearing, dining, or being received is restored. The Abraham phrase and the following feet-washing clause are both retained.

6. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ὁμῶς παλαίσας
Rendered as: And, having wrestled, he likewise
The supplied ὁμῶς is taken in its alike or likewise sense rather than silently normalized to the adversative accent ὅμως. A contextual nevertheless interpretation remains possible but is not imposed.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τὸ πλατὺ νεῦρον οὐκ ἔκαυσε μέν, ἔφλεξε δέ
Rendered as: he did not burn ... the broad tendon, but inflamed it
Both the broad tendon and the contrast between the two fire verbs are retained. Scorched is a material alternative for the second verb; inflamed makes the distinction intelligible without adding an otherwise unexpressed severing or consuming of the tendon.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ὁμοούσιον μὴ παρούσῃ τροπῇ προβάλλει, ἰσοδύναμον δὲ οὔ
Rendered as: brings forth something of the same substance with no transformation present, but not of equal power
Same substance and equal power are explicitly distinguished. The participial phrase states the absence of a present transformation; its exact relation to the bringing forth is left broad rather than expanded into a specific material mechanism.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ μὲν προβάλλων καὶ εἰς ἑτέραν πάλιν οὐσίαν ἐφ’ ἑαυτὸν τραπέντα δύναται
Rendered as: the one who brings it forth can also bring about its turning back toward himself into another substance
The ability verb is elliptical, with the surrounding transformation account supplying the action and the accusative participle supplying the thing turned. The main text reads the turn as belonging to the brought-forth thing, with back toward himself referring to its producer. A material alternative understands the producer's own return to another substance through a loose shift of construction; the accusative participle more directly supports the object-oriented main reading. No specific additional power or physical procedure is supplied.

10. Translation choice — Greek: ὧν καὶ τοὺς πόδας ὡς ὁμοουσίων ἀνθρώπων ἄνθρωποι ἔνιψαν
Rendered as: whose feet people also washed as though those beings were humans of the same substance
Also explicitly represents the καί within this feet-washing clause, separately from the earlier and those with Abraham representing καὶ οἱ. Even their feet were washed is a viable emphatic reading of this particle; the additive main rendering retains the surviving wording without supplying content within the eleven-dot gap.

SECTION 20.8

When Peter had said these things, Micaiah, who was himself one of the companions following him, said, “I too would like to learn from you whether, just as the evil one came into being, so also the good one came into being. If they came into being in the same way, they seem to me to be brothers.”

Peter replied, “They did not come into being in the same way, if indeed you remember what I said at the beginning: the fourfold substance of the evil one’s body, having been carefully differentiated by God, was brought forth; but when that substance had been mixed externally according to the will of the one who brought it forth, the disposition that delights in evils arose in connection with the mixture. Thus one should understand that the fourfold substance brought forth from God is God’s child and itself exists eternally, whereas the disposition that delights in evils arose afterward as an accidental feature of the substance mixed externally by him. Thus it was neither begotten by God nor by anyone else; neither was it brought forth by him, nor did it come forth spontaneously, nor did it always exist, as the substance did before the commingling. Rather, in accordance with God’s will, it occurred accidentally in the external mixing. We have said many times that this must be so.

“But the good one, having been begotten from God’s most beautiful transformation and not having occurred accidentally through an external mixing, is truly a son. Nevertheless, since these things are unwritten and have been made credible by conjectures, let the ....... not be confirmed as certainly being so. Otherwise, the mind, as though it had certainly grasped ...........es, ceases from searching. And remember those instructions of mine too: such things must not be told to .......n, but to those who have proved most trustworthy after testing. Nor should such things be asserted lightly even among yourselves, and you ought not dare to speak as though you had precisely established the discovery of secret things. Rather, you should remain silent and only ponder them. For in speaking, the one who utters them may perhaps sin as one who does not know, and will incur punishment for having dared—even to himself—to utter things honored by silence.”

Translator's notes for section 20.8 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: μὴ πάντως ἡ ....... οὕτως ἔχειν βεβαιούσθω
The selected edition prints a seven-dot lacuna after the feminine article ἡ. The missing subject cannot be recovered from the supplied wording, so all seven dots are retained without restoration.

2. Greek: ὁ νοῦς ὡς πάντως προειληφὼς ........... ες τοῦ ζητεῖν παύεται
The selected edition prints an eleven-dot lacuna followed by the surviving fragment ες. The translation retains the eleven dots and represents the fragment as “es”; no complete word is conjectured.

3. Greek: ὅτι τὰ τοιαῦτα .......ν οὐ δεῖ λέγειν
The selected edition prints a seven-dot lacuna before the surviving final ν. The translation retains all seven dots and represents the surviving fragment as “n” without restoring the missing word.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τετραγενὴς
Rendered as: fourfold
The adjective describes the substance as constituted in fourfold fashion; “four-element” is a possible cosmological interpretation.

5. Translation choice — Greek: πεφιλοκρινημένη
Rendered as: having been carefully differentiated
The verb denotes careful discrimination or separation. “Carefully selected” is possible, but the surrounding mixture terminology favors differentiation.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἔξω δὲ αὐτῆς κατὰ τὴν τοῦ προβαλόντος βουλὴν κραθείσης πρὸς τὴν κρᾶσιν ἡ κακοῖς χαίρουσα προαίρεσις
Rendered as: but when that substance had been mixed externally according to the will of the one who brought it forth, the disposition that delights in evils arose in connection with the mixture
αὐτῆς is taken as the subject of the genitive absolute and as referring to the already mentioned fourfold substance; ἔξω describes its external mixing. Alternatively, ἔξω αὐτῆς may mean “outside it,” with an unexpressed subject of κραθείσης, but that reading would imply an additional constituent not explicitly named here.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ συμβεβηκυῖα κακοῖς χαίρουσα προαίρεσις ἐπεγένετο
Rendered as: the disposition that delights in evils arose afterward as an accidental feature
The wording distinguishes the contingent disposition from the underlying substance and states that it arose subsequently.

8. Translation choice — Greek: στοχασμοῖς πεπιστωμένα
Rendered as: made credible by conjectures
The phrase refers to reasoned conjectures or inferences rather than certain demonstrations.

9. Translation choice — Greek: οὐχ ὡς ἔχων
Rendered as: as one who does not know
The phrase literally describes the speaker as not possessing something, with knowledge or secure understanding supplied from context. “As one who does not possess it” is a more formal alternative.

10. Translation choice — Greek: τὰ σιγῇ τετιμημένα
Rendered as: things honored by silence
The expression presents silence as the honor properly accorded to secret matters.

SECTION 20.9

When Peter had said these things, a certain Lazarus, himself one of the followers, said, “Tell us how the reconciliation is possible: how can it be reasonable for the evil one, who was appointed by a righteous God to be the punisher of those who acted impiously, later to be sent with his angels and the sinners into the lower darkness? For I remember that the Teacher himself said this too.”

Peter said, “I too acknowledge that the evil one does nothing evil in this respect, insofar as he carries out the law given to him. Although he has an evil disposition, nevertheless, because of his fear of God, he does nothing unjustly. But because he slanders teachers of truth as a snare for the undiscerning, this same being is also called the Slanderer.

“As for our truthful Teacher’s saying that he and his angels would depart with the deceived sinners into the lower darkness, it has an explanation like this. The evil one, having been allotted a constitution that delights in darkness, descends with his fellow-servant angels into the darkness of Tartarus and takes pleasure in it, for darkness is congenial to fire. But human souls, being drops of pure light, are drunk in together by a substance of alien fire; and since they do not have a nature capable of dying, they are punished according to their deserts.

“But if the ruler of wickedness, being a human being, is not sent into the darkness because he does not delight in it, then this constitution of his that delights in evils can be recombined into the good one’s disposition, and thus, as good, he will be judged to coexist. This is all the more so because, although he had been allotted a constitution that delights in evils, on account of his fear of God he did nothing contrary to what seemed right to God’s law. And surely, when the high priest Aaron’s staff became a snake and was transformed back again into a staff, Scripture mystically foreshadowed this with reference to the recombination of the evil one’s transformation, which will take place later and which is yet to be.”

Translator's notes for section 20.9 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: γενησομένην τῆς τροπῆς μετασύγκρισιν μυστηριωδῶς ἡ γραφὴ ἐσομένην
Both γενησομένην and ἐσομένην appear to describe the feminine μετασύγκρισιν, producing a redundant and syntactically awkward pair of future expressions. The confirmed printed wording is represented by “which will take place later and which is yet to be” rather than emended.

2. Translation choice — Greek: Τὴν συμφωνίαν ἡμῖν εἰπὲ
Rendered as: Tell us how the reconciliation is possible
συμφωνία denotes agreement or consistency; Lazarus asks how the apparently conflicting claims can be reconciled. “Tell us the consistency” is a more formal alternative.

3. Translation choice — Greek: διαβάλλων δὲ διδασκάλους ἀληθείας εἰς ἐνέδραν τῶν ἀκρίτων
Rendered as: But because he slanders teachers of truth as a snare for the undiscerning
The genitive τῶν ἀκρίτων is read objectively: the slandering of the teachers serves to ensnare the undiscerning. It can instead be read subjectively, yielding “into an ambush laid by the undiscerning against the teachers,” which would make the undiscerning responsible for the ambush rather than its targets.

4. Translation choice — Greek: διάβολος
Rendered as: Slanderer
This preserves the explicit association with the preceding act of slandering. The conventional title “Devil” is an alternative.

5. Translation choice — Greek: κρᾶσιν
Rendered as: constitution
The noun literally denotes a mixture but here refers to the being’s composite constitution.

6. Translation choice — Greek: συμπινόμεναι
Rendered as: are drunk in together
The passive participle preserves the drinking image applied to drops of pure light being taken into alien fire.

7. Translation choice — Greek: μετασυγκριθῆναι εἰς ἀγαθοῦ προαίρεσιν
Rendered as: be recombined into the good one’s disposition
The genitive ἀγαθοῦ is taken substantivally as “of the good one.” A qualitative reading, “into a disposition toward good,” is contextually possible but less directly reflects the genitive construction.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἀγαθὸς συνεῖναι κριθήσεται
Rendered as: as good, he will be judged to coexist
ἀγαθός is taken predicatively of the ruler of wickedness. Alternatively, it may be substantival—“the good one will be judged to coexist”—though the companion with whom he coexists would remain implicit.

9. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ μήτιγε
Rendered as: And surely
The rendering takes the particle as an emphatic transition introducing the scriptural confirmation that follows. Its force is not certain: a tentative “And perhaps” and the scalar “Not to mention that” are also defensible, and the confirmed printed punctuation does not decide among them.

SECTION 20.10

After Lazarus, Joseph—himself also one of the followers—said, “Correctly, everything sa.....; and grant me this too, since I wish to learn: why, for everyone, from the same words ......... some are persuaded, while others refuse to believe?”

Peter said, “The words are not incantations, so that anyone who hears must necessarily believe. Rather, the fact that some are persuaded and others are not intelligently demonstrates freedom of choice.”

We all blessed him who had said these things.

Translator's notes for section 20.10 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: Ὀρθῶς πάντα εἴρ.....
The selected edition prints a five-dot lacuna after the surviving beginning εἴρ. That beginning is recognizable as part of a saying-verb, but the unavailable ending could determine person, voice, and other grammatical information. The fragmentary English “sa.....” preserves the five dots without supplying those unavailable features.

2. Greek: διὰ τί πᾶσι τῶν αὐτῶν λόγων ......... οἱ μὲν πείθονται
The selected edition prints a nine-dot lacuna between λόγων and οἱ. The surviving syntax remains incomplete; all nine dots are retained, and no missing verb or participle is restored.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπῳδαί
Rendered as: incantations
The noun denotes charms or magical spells intended to compel an effect, contrasting with freely given belief.

4. Translation choice — Greek: πάντως
Rendered as: necessarily
The adverb expresses the inevitability that would characterize an incantation’s effect.

5. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτεξούσιον
Rendered as: freedom of choice
The term denotes self-determination or freedom of agency.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπειθοῦσι
Rendered as: refuse to believe
The verb can express disbelief, resistance, or disobedience; the immediate contrast with being persuaded favors “refuse to believe.”

7. Translation choice — Greek: ταῦτα εἰπόντα οἱ πάντες εὐλογήσαμεν
Rendered as: We all blessed him who had said these things
The accusative participle εἰπόντα describes the object of εὐλογήσαμεν. Peter is its contextual referent; the construction is not an unexpressed object followed by a temporal participle.

SECTION 20.11

Just as a meal was about to be served to us, someone slipped in and said, “Appion the Many-Victor has just arrived from Antioch with Annoubion and is staying as Simon’s guest.” When our father heard this, he rejoiced and said to Peter, “If you permit me, I will go greet Appion and Annoubion, who have been my friends from earliest youth. Perhaps I may persuade Annoubion to debate Clement about nativity.” Peter said, “I permit it, and I commend you for fulfilling the duties of friendship. But consider how, by God’s providence, everything conducive to your full assurance is converging from every direction and producing the fitting harmony. I say this because Annoubion’s arrival has proved advantageous to you.” Our father replied, “I truly see that this is so.” After saying this, he went to Simon.

Translator's notes for section 20.11 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: Ἀππίων ὁ πλειστονίκης
Rendered as: Appion the Many-Victor
πλειστονίκης is treated as an epithet denoting numerous victories rather than silently transliterated as another personal name.

2. Translation choice — Greek: περὶ γενέσεως
Rendered as: about nativity
In this debate setting γένεσις concerns birth or nativity, particularly as a subject of astrological determinism; “birth” or “genesis” remains possible more generally.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπαινῶ τὰ φίλων σε πληροῦντα μέρη
Rendered as: I commend you for fulfilling the duties of friendship
The idiom describes performing the part or duties belonging to friends; the English avoids reproducing the awkward literal image of “parts.”

4. Translation choice — Greek: πανταχόθεν συντρέχει τὰ πρὸς τὴν σὴν πληροφορίαν οἰκείαν ἀποτελοῦντα τὴν ἁρμονίαν
Rendered as: everything conducive to your full assurance is converging from every direction and producing the fitting harmony
οἰκείαν is taken with τὴν ἁρμονίαν as “fitting”; attachment to πληροφορίαν, yielding something like “your own assurance,” is also grammatically possible.

SECTION 20.12

As for us who were with Peter, we spent the whole night asking questions one after another, remaining awake because of the pleasure and joy produced by what was being said. When the night was already beginning somehow to brighten, Peter looked at me and my brothers and said, “I am perplexed about what your father decided.” While he was saying this, our father arrived there and found Peter discussing him with us. Seeing Peter disheartened, he greeted him and explained why he had slept outside. We stared at him in astonishment, seeing Simon’s appearance but hearing the voice of our father Faustus. As we recoiled from him and regarded him with loathing, our father was astounded at being treated so harshly and hostilely by us. Only Peter, who saw his natural form, said to us, “Why do you push your father away in disgust?” We and our mother replied, “To us this man looks like Simon, though he has our father’s voice.” Peter said, “For you, only his unbewitched voice is recognizable; but to my unbewitched eyes his appearance too is visible as it really is: he is not Simon but Faustus, your father.” Then, looking directly at our father too, he said, “......... appearance of yours is not visible to them, but Simon’s—the most impious man’s—is; and to us .........”

Translator's notes for section 20.12 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ......... όν σου εἶδος αὐτοῖς οὐ φαίνεται, ἀλλὰ Σίμωνος τοῦ ἀσεβεστάτου καὶ ἡμῖν .........
The selected edition prints two lacunae of nine dots each. After the first gap, only όν survives, either as an isolated form or as the ending of a lost word, and it cannot receive a secure independent English rendering. Both nine-dot gaps remain explicit, and no restoration of either gap or of the broken construction is supplied.

2. Translation choice — Greek: νήφοντες ἐνυκτερεύσαμεν
Rendered as: we spent the whole night ... remaining awake
Here νήφω concerns wakeful alertness during the night rather than literal abstinence from intoxication; “remaining clear-minded” is possible but less closely fitted to the overnight setting.

3. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ ἀθυμοῦντα ἰδὼν προσαγορεύσας ἀπελογήσατο
Rendered as: Seeing Peter disheartened, he greeted him and explained
The unexpressed person seen as disheartened is taken to be Peter, whom the arriving father has just found discussing him. Reference to another participant is formally possible but less natural in context.

4. Translation choice — Greek: μόνος δὲ Πέτρος τὴν κατὰ φύσιν αὐτοῦ ὁρῶν μορφὴν
Rendered as: Only Peter, who saw his natural form
κατὰ φύσιν identifies the form belonging to Faustus’s real nature, in contrast to the magically imposed appearance.

5. Translation choice — Greek: Ὑμῖν μὲν ἡ ἀμάγευτος αὐτοῦ φωνὴ μόνη γνώριμός ἐστιν, ἐμοῦ δὲ τοῖς ἀμαγεύτοις ὀφθαλμοῖς
Rendered as: For you, only his unbewitched voice is recognizable; but to my unbewitched eyes
ἀμάγευτος is rendered as freedom from magical alteration or deception, preserving the repetition applied first to the voice and then to Peter’s eyes.

SECTION 20.13

While Peter was discussing these things, one of the advance party came in from Antioch ..........., saying to Peter, “My master, I want you to know that Simon, publicly performing many wonders in Antioch and calling you a magician and a sorcerer, prepared them for such hatred that everyone longed, upon your coming into the city there, to take a taste of your very flesh. Therefore we, the advance party, together with our brothers whom you had placed with Simon, seeing the city roaring loudly against you, secretly gathered in the same place and considered what we should do. While we were at a loss, Cornelius the centurion arrived, sent by Caesar to the governor of the province—the one whom the Lord healed in Caesarea when he was possessed by a demon. We secretly sent for Cornelius, and he learned from us the reason for our despondency. When asked to help, he most eagerly promised to frighten Simon and drive him away, provided we assisted him in his undertaking. When we readily promised to do everything, he said, ‘While I, through many friends, secretly spread word around that I have come to arrest him, and claim that I am searching for him—since Caesar, having killed many magicians and learned what concerns him, sent me to search for him, so that he may punish him as he did the magicians before him—let your people who are with him also report back, as though they have heard secretly from somewhere that I was sent to arrest him. Perhaps, hearing this, he will be frightened and flee.’ Since, then, we had thought of doing something else, it nevertheless happened this way. For, having heard many of the outsiders telling him privately, doing him great favors, and also our insiders who had been planted there, and as though he had received advice from his own people, he decided to withdraw. So he fled Antioch with Athenodorus and has come here, as we have heard. Therefore we advise you not yet to set foot in that city, until we see whether, in his absence, they will be able to forget the slander against you.”

Translator's notes for section 20.13 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀντιοχείας ........... λέγων Πέτρῳ
The selected edition prints an eleven-dot gap between Antioch and the participle “saying.” Exactly eleven dots remain in the main English. No missing participle, arrival formula, or other lost word is restored from another edition.

2. Greek: πάντα ἄνθρωπον εἰς τὴν ἐκεῖ ἐπιδημήσαντος τῶν σαρκῶν
This passage uses the human-authorized, independently image-checked Greek prefix proposed by F. Wieseler, Adnotationes criticae, 1859, printed page 326 / PDF page 347. The former selected Lagarde prefix is preserved exactly here: πάντα ἄνθρωπον τῶν ἐκεῖ ἐπιδημησάντων σαρκῶν. The selected prefix is: πάντα ἄνθρωπον εἰς τὴν ἐκεῖ ἐπιδημήσαντος τῶν σαρκῶν. Wieseler’s printed proposal is followed by cett.; ONLY the explicitly verified Greek prefix was adopted, not an invented expansion of that abbreviation. The remaining αὐτῶν ἀπογεύσασθαί σου is unchanged from Lagarde. Wieseler also proposes τῇ ἐκεῖ as an alternative to the destination construction; it is noted as another editorial proposal, not silently selected. These are scholarly conjectures, not new manuscript collations or recovery of a uniquely established original. The prior candidate could not securely link the uncurated plural-participle/flesh sequence; the present interpretation is reassessed on the documented changed prefix and the articular flesh phrase, with the remaining attachments disclosed rather than invented. Fresh independent review must judge the entire construction.

3. Greek: φυγαδεύειν αὐτόν. ἐάν γε αὐτοῦ τῷ ἐγχειρήματι ὑπουργήσωμεν.
The English attaches the condition “provided we assisted him” to Cornelius’s promise despite the selected edition’s full stop before ἐάν. The Greek punctuation is not changed or labelled an OCR error; no missing words are restored.

4. Greek: κολάσῃ. καὶ οἱ ὑμέτεροι οἱ συνόντες αὐτῷ
The English continues the initial genitive-absolute circumstance of spreading an announcement into the later imperative asking their people to report back, despite the printed stop after κολάσῃ. This makes the relation explicit without supplying a new main verb to the initial clause or deleting the source period. An alternative presentation can leave the earlier circumstance as a marked sentence fragment before the command; the continuous English is preferred because the later imperative supplies the action coordinated with Cornelius’s proposed announcement.

5. Greek: ὑπολῆσαι
The verified Lagarde print has the eight-letter sigma-form ὑπολῆσαι, with circumflex, and it is retained unchanged. Independently checked primary lexical evidence is E.A. Sophocles, Greek Lexicon of the Roman and Byzantine Periods, 1900, printed page 1121 / PDF page 1147: under ὑπο-λανθάνω = λανθάνω it explicitly cites “Clementin. 461 A ὑπολῆσαι, to forget.” The accent in the lexicon’s quoted form remains uncertain in the independent image reading, possibly circumflex or acute (ὑπολήσαι); that uncertainty does not alter the independently verified Lagarde accent or the sigma. The lexicon attests an interpretation of this unusual form but does not establish ordinary classical morphology. The expected cessation-form comparison ὑπολῆξαι would be hypothetical and is NOT adopted; no Greek emendation or identification with ὑπολήγω is made. The supplied evidence request, response, and receipt hashes bind the supporting dictionary check in the generation packet. Fresh independent translation review is still required.

6. Greek: περικομποῦντος
The selected word is Wieseler’s independently image-verified critical proposal, printed page 327 / PDF page 348: περικομποῦντος. The former selected Lagarde word is retained exactly here as provenance: περισκοποῦντος. The change is editorial and conjectural, not a newly verified manuscript reading. It replaces the looking-around/examining sense with announcing-around, permitting the perfect infinitive to express the announced arrival. No other wording or printed punctuation is silently altered, and independent source-and-translation review remains required.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τις τῶν προόδων
Rendered as: one of the advance party
The noun identifies those who go ahead. “One of those who had gone ahead” is a less collective alternative. A military role or formal title is not added.

8. Translation choice — Greek: μάγον σε ὀνομάζων καὶ γόητα
Rendered as: calling you a magician and a sorcerer
Both accusations are retained. γόης can mean a conjurer, sorcerer, or deceiving charlatan; the magical context supports “sorcerer,” without independently confirming either accusation as true.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς γλίχεσθαι πάντα ἄνθρωπον εἰς τὴν ἐκεῖ ἐπιδημήσαντος τῶν σαρκῶν αὐτῶν ἀπογεύσασθαί σου.
Rendered as: everyone longed, upon your coming into the city there, to take a taste of your very flesh
The current selected prefix has singular genitive ἐπιδημήσαντος, understood circumstantially with the addressee Peter as the visitor identified by the later σου. The nominal “your coming” preserves the aorist participle’s completed-arrival perspective without asserting that the future arrival has already happened. The feminine τὴν has an implicit location, naturally the city discussed here and explicitly named later; the English supplies “city,” but no Greek noun is restored or inserted. The now articular τῶν σαρκῶν αὐτῶν permits postposed αὐτῶν to agree with σαρκῶν intensively, “the flesh itself,” not as the possessive “their flesh.” The unchanged σου supplies Peter as possessor; English “your very flesh” represents that reading. The English repeats “your” to identify both the visitor and flesh-owner as the same addressed man; it does not claim that two Greek pronouns are printed or that both syntactic links are uniquely settled. A possessive reading of αὐτῶν, “their flesh,” remains formally possible but leaves its relation to σου difficult in this context. This is a candidate analysis of the curated whole construction, not acceptance inferred merely from the existence of a critical proposal.

10. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν ὑπὸ σοῦ τῷ Σίμωνι ὑποβεβλημένων ἀδελφῶν ἡμῶν
Rendered as: our brothers whom you had placed with Simon
The placement is done by Peter, expressed through ὑπὸ σοῦ, and involves the community’s brothers with Simon. ὑποβάλλω here can imply covertly planting or introducing them, as the later insiders description suggests. No additional act of conversion or betrayal is supplied.

11. Translation choice — Greek: ὃν ἐν Καισαρείᾳ δαιμονῶντα ἰάσατο ὁ κύριος
Rendered as: the one whom the Lord healed in Caesarea when he was possessed by a demon
The masculine relative can refer to the immediately preceding provincial governor, or reach back to Cornelius. The English “the one” leaves that personal referent unassigned rather than uniquely choosing either man. δαιμονῶντα is rendered in the author’s demonic category, not converted into a modern diagnosis.

12. Translation choice — Greek: Ἐμοῦ διὰ πολλῶν φίλων κρύφα εἰς σύλληψιν αὐτοῦ ἐληλυθέναι περικομποῦντος καὶ ζητεῖν αὐτὸν φάσκοντος
Rendered as: While I, through many friends, secretly spread word around that I have come to arrest him, and claim that I am searching for him
The selected περικομποῦντος is Wieseler’s explicitly printed editorial proposal, meaning proclaiming or spreading a claim around; it is not the former περισκοποῦντος, looking around or examining. The perfect infinitive ἐληλυθέναι now supplies the content of that announcement, “that I have come,” with εἰς σύλληψιν expressing its stated purpose. The accompanying φάσκοντος gives the claim that Cornelius is searching for Simon. The main text connects the genitive-absolute circumstance with the later imperative asking their people to report back; the printed intervening stop is separately disclosed. The words are Cornelius’s proposed announcement in the reported plan, not independent confirmation of an actual arrest order.

13. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπεὶ τοίνυν ἕτερόν τι ποιεῖν ἐπενοήσαμεν, ὅμως οὕτως ἐγένετο
Rendered as: Since, then, we had thought of doing something else, it nevertheless happened this way
Both the opening ἐπεί and the contrasting ὅμως are preserved, without changing the printed conjunction to a different Greek word. A more idiomatic contextual interpretation is “Although we had thought of doing something else, it nevertheless happened this way”; that shifts ἐπεί toward a concessive English link rather than its causal “since,” and is not uniquely established.

14. Translation choice — Greek: εἰς τὰ μεγάλα αὐτῷ χαριζομένων
Rendered as: doing him great favors
The source’s great-favor language is retained as describing the outside informants’ service to Simon. Unlike a different reading with ὡς, the selected εἰς phrase is not automatically translated “as though” doing favors.

15. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς κατὰ σοῦ διαβολῆς ἐκείνου ἀπόντος ὑπολῆσαι δυνήσονται
Rendered as: whether, in his absence, they will be able to forget the slander against you
The plural subject of δυνήσονται is the people of the city under discussion; the slander is the genitive object of forgetting, not a nominative subject that itself subsides. The unchanged sigma-form ὑπολῆσαι is interpreted through Sophocles’s directly cited lexical evidence under ὑπολανθάνω, “forget,” rather than the cessation lemma ὑπολήγω. This is a fresh rendering of the supplied Greek using a dictionary gloss, not an adaptation of an older English passage translation.

SECTION 20.14

When the advance messenger had reported these things, Peter looked directly at our father and said, “Do you hear, Faustus? Your transformation was brought about by Simon the magician, as is now evident. Thinking that Caesar was seeking him for harm, he fled in fear, placing his own form upon you so that, when you died, grief would come upon your children.” Hearing this, our father wept and lamented, saying, “You have judged correctly, Peter. Annoubion ...... of mine, because he loved me, cryptically disclosed the plot, and I did not believe.........., since I deserved to suffer.”

Translator's notes for section 20.14 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: Καίσαρος γὰρ νομίσας ἐπὶ κακῷ αὐτὸν ζητεῖν
The edition prints the genitive Καίσαρος, although the contextual reading takes Caesar as the subject of ζητεῖν, for which the accusative Καίσαρα would ordinarily be expected in this infinitival construction after νομίσας. Καίσαρα is only a proposed grammatical regularization; the translation retains the contextually defensible interpretation without claiming that the regularization is printed.

2. Greek: Ἀννουβίων ...... μού με φιλῶν
The selected edition prints a six-dot lacuna before μού. The surviving “of mine” indicates a lost description or relationship, but its wording cannot be recovered. All six dots remain explicit, and no description is restored.

3. Greek: καὶ οὐκ ἐπίστευ.........., ἐπειδὴ τοῦ παθεῖν ἤμην ἄξιος
The selected edition prints ten dots immediately after the surviving verbal stem ἐπίστευ-. The precise verbal ending and any following words are unavailable; the ten-dot gap is retained without supplying an object or other lost content.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ Σίμωνος τοῦ μάγου ἡ μεταμόρφωσίς σου γέγονεν
Rendered as: Your transformation was brought about by Simon the magician
The construction presents Simon as the agent responsible for Faustus’s altered appearance.

5. Translation choice — Greek: Καίσαρος γὰρ νομίσας ἐπὶ κακῷ αὐτὸν ζητεῖν
Rendered as: Thinking that Caesar was seeking him for harm
ἐπὶ κακῷ indicates harmful or punitive intent without specifying the precise punishment. The contextual interpretation of Caesar as the seeker is retained despite the printed case irregularity disclosed in source_issues.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἑαυτοῦ σοὶ περιθεὶς μορφήν
Rendered as: placing his own form upon you
The concrete image of putting Simon’s appearance around or upon Faustus is retained rather than reduced to simple resemblance.

7. Translation choice — Greek: μυστηριωδῶς τὴν ἐπιβουλὴν ἐξέφηγε
Rendered as: cryptically disclosed the plot
μυστηριωδῶς indicates an indirect, mysterious, or cryptic disclosure; ἐπιβουλή is a hostile plot or design.

8. Translation choice — Greek: καὶ οὐκ ἐπίστευ.........., ἐπειδὴ τοῦ παθεῖν ἤμην ἄξιος
Rendered as: and I did not believe.........., since I deserved to suffer
The first-person speaker and the following first-person ἤμην support “I,” but the precise ending of ἐπίστευ- and any further lost wording remain unavailable. The English does not supply an object of belief.

9. Translation choice — Greek: με φιλῶν
Rendered as: because he loved me
The main rendering takes φιλέω as affection and the present participle causally: his affection motivates the confidential warning. This is supported by 20.11, where Faustus calls Annoubion and Appion friends from his earliest age, and by Annoubion’s disclosure of the hostile plot here. The materially different while kissing me is also viable: φιλέω can denote kissing, and the participle may describe an accompanying action rather than its cause. The main text does not claim that affection is the only lexical sense or that a concomitant kiss is excluded.

SECTION 20.15

After our father said this, not long afterward ....... to us, reporting Simon’s flight to us and that he had set out for Judea that very night. He found our father beating himself and saying with lamentation, “Alas, wretch that I am! Though I heard that he was a magician, miserable man that I am, I refused to believe it. After being recognized by my wife and children for a single day, I quickly returned to my former calamity of being unknown.” Our mother, lamenting, kept tearing out her hair, while we groaned in distress over our father’s alteration, unable to understand what on earth it was. When Annoubion heard and saw these things, he stood open-mouthed. Before everyone, Peter said to us children, “Believe me: this is Faustus, your father. I therefore command you to pay him the regard due to a father, for God will provide some occasion through which, after stripping off Simon’s form, he will plainly reveal your father’s form again.” After saying this to us, he looked at our father and said, “I permitted you to greet Appion and Annoubion because you acknowledge that they have been your friends since childhood, not to associate with Simon the magician.”

Translator's notes for section 20.15 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: μετ᾽ οὐ πολὺ ....... πρὸς ἡμᾶς τὴν Σίμωνος ἡμῖν δηλῶν φυγὴν
The selected edition prints a seven-dot lacuna after “not long afterward.” The missing subject and finite expression governing “to us” are unavailable. All seven dots remain explicit, and the arriving reporter is not identified.

2. Translation choice — Greek: εὗρε δὲ τὸν πατέρα ἡμῶν κοπτόμενον
Rendered as: He found our father beating himself
κόπτομαι can describe striking oneself as an embodied act of mourning; the accompanying lament supports retaining that concrete action.

3. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς μίαν ἡμέραν ἐπιγνωσθεὶς συμβίῳ καὶ τέκνοις
Rendered as: After being recognized by my wife and children for a single day
ἐπιγινώσκω here concerns recognition of identity, while σύμβιος denotes one’s spouse or life-partner; the context identifies Faustus’s wife.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν προτέραν τῆς ἀγνοίας ἦλθον συμφοράν
Rendered as: I returned to my former calamity of being unknown
ἀγνοία is understood contextually as his family’s failure to recognize him, not merely as intellectual ignorance.

5. Translation choice — Greek: Ἀννουβίων δὲ ταῦτα ἀκούων καὶ ὁρῶν ἀχανὴς ἔστη
Rendered as: When Annoubion heard and saw these things, he stood open-mouthed
ἀχανής preserves the visible image of standing open-mouthed in stunned astonishment; “stood aghast” or “stood dumbfounded” conveys the reaction but not the image as directly.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς πατρὶ προσέχειν
Rendered as: to pay him the regard due to a father
προσέχειν calls for attention, adherence, or care toward Faustus in his paternal identity; “attend to him as a father” is more literal but less idiomatic.

7. Translation choice — Greek: δι᾽ ἧς τὴν Σίμωνος ἀποδυσάμενος μορφὴν τὴν τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν προδήλως ἀναδείξει πάλιν
Rendered as: through which, after stripping off Simon’s form, he will plainly reveal your father’s form again
The main rendering takes Faustus as the understood subject of “stripping off” and “revealing,” since the middle image naturally depicts him shedding Simon’s form. The nearest explicit subject is God, so taking God as the agent of the removal and revelation is grammatically possible, though less natural with the stripping image.

SECTION 20.16

And the father said, “I sinned; I confess it.” Annoubion said, “I too, together with him, ask you to pardon a noble and good old man who was deceived, for the unfortunate man has become the plaything of the notorious fellow. Still, I will tell you how it happened. This good old man came to greet us. At that very hour, all of us who were present there happened to be listening together to Simon, who wanted to flee that night because he had heard that certain men were coming from somewhere, here to Laodicea, under a royal order to search for him. When Faustus entered, Simon, revealing what was in his own mind, spoke to us as follows: ‘When he arrives, have him share salt with you. I will prepare an ointment so that, after dining, taking it, and anointing his own face, he may appear to everyone to have my form. But you, having first been anointed by me with the juices of a certain plant, will not be deceived by his strange form; to everyone else, however, Faustus will appear to be Simon.’”

Translator's notes for section 20.16 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: παίγνιον γὰρ γέγονεν ὁ δυστυχὴς τοῦ περιβοήτου
Rendered as: the unfortunate man has become the plaything of the notorious fellow
Preserves the image of Faustus as another person’s plaything and the substantival force of περιβοήτου without inserting Simon’s name.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἀκηκοὼς ἐπιδημήσειν ποθέν τινας ἐνταῦθα τῇ Λαοδικείᾳ
Rendered as: because he had heard that certain men were coming from somewhere, here to Laodicea
ποθέν means “from somewhere,” while ἐνταῦθα and τῇ Λαοδικείᾳ locate their expected arrival.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τὸν ἴδιον θυμὸν φήσας
Rendered as: revealing what was in his own mind
θυμός can refer to an inward impulse, disposition, intention, or anger. The ensuing disclosure favors the broader contextual rendering without excluding its forceful emotional nuance.

4. Translation choice — Greek: Ἁλῶν αὐτὸν ἐλθόντα συμμετασχεῖν ὑμῖν ποιήσατε
Rendered as: When he arrives, have him share salt with you
Ἁλῶν is defensibly the genitive plural of ἅλς, “salt,” as the object of συμμετασχεῖν. Sharing salt depicts participation in the meal; no correction to the printed reading is required.

5. Translation choice — Greek: μύρον τι
Rendered as: an ointment
μύρον denotes perfumed oil or ointment, and the subsequent anointing supports “ointment.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: δειπνήσας καὶ ἀναλαβὼν τὸ ἴδιον χρίσας πρόσωπον
Rendered as: after dining, taking it, and anointing his own face
The ointment is understood as the object taken, while τὸ ἴδιον ... πρόσωπον is read together despite the intervening participle.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς ξένης αὐτοῦ μορφῆς
Rendered as: his strange form
ξένης describes the transformed appearance as strange, foreign, or unfamiliar to the observers.

SECTION 20.17

While he was setting these things forth, I said, “What benefit do you now gain from such a scheme?” Simon said, “First, those who are searching for me will seize him and then cease their search against me. And even if he should be killed by the royal hand, his children—who abandoned me, prosphygont........., and are working together—will experience the greatest grief.”

“For now, Peter, I confess the truth to you: I was afraid of the .........stō—to disclose this. But Simon did not even give us time to speak privately ..........mōn to him; as for Simon’s evil counsel—it appeared. At any rate, in the middle of the night Simon got up and fled toward Judea, escorted by both Appion and Athenodorus. I then pretended that my body was unwell so that, by remaining behind after they had left, I might make him return at once to his own home, in case he might be able to escape notice while hiding among you, lest he be seized as Simon by those searching for Simon and die under the royal wrath. I therefore sent him away to you at an unseasonable hour, and out of concern for him I came by night both to see him and to leave very quickly, before those who sent....................., having returned.”

Then, looking at us, he said, “I, Annoubion, see your father’s true form, being one who has been anointed by Simon himself—I gave this account beforehand—so that the true form of Faustus might appear to my eyes. Being utterly astounded, therefore, I marvel at Simon’s magic: though you are standing here, you do not recognize your own father.” As the father, the mother, and we ourselves wept over the misfortune common to us all, Annoubion also sympathized with us and shed tears.

Translator's notes for section 20.17 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: οἵτινες ἐμὲ καταλιπόντες προσφυγόντ......... συνεργοῦσι
The selected edition prints nine dots after the surviving incomplete form προσφυγόντ. Its lexical stem suggests seeking or taking refuge, but its completion and the missing intervening wording are unavailable. The translation retains the transliterated fragment and exactly nine dots without restoration.

2. Greek: ἐφοβούμην τὸν .........στω τοῦτο μηνύειν
The selected edition prints nine dots between the accusative article τὸν and the incomplete surviving fragment στω. The gap prevents determination of their relationship to one another and to μηνύειν. The translation therefore preserves the article, gap, and fragment without identifying the missing person or changing τὸν.

3. Greek: ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ καιρὸν ἡμῖν ὁ Σίμων ἐδίδου πρὸς τὸ ἰδιάζειν .......... μῶν αὐτῷ τὴν ἐκ τοῦ Σίμωνος κακὴν ἐφάνη βουλήν
Ten printed dots interrupt the sentence and are followed by the incomplete fragment μῶν. The surviving accusative phrase τὴν ... κακὴν ... βουλήν does not straightforwardly function as the subject of ἐφάνη. The English presents the wording as an anacoluthic, detached fragment rather than silently changing the accusative to a nominative; the missing connection remains unavailable.

4. Greek: πρὶν τοὺς πέμψαντας ..................... ἐπανελθών
The selected edition prints twenty-one dots. The lost material prevents determination of how τοὺς πέμψαντας and the nominative participle ἐπανελθών were connected. The exact gap and surviving syntactic fragments are retained without restoration.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπὸ βασιλικῆς χειρὸς ἀναιρεθείη
Rendered as: should be killed by the royal hand
Preserves the source’s personifying image of the royal hand rather than reducing it to an abstract governmental authority.

6. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν ἐπὶ Ἰουδαίαν ἐποιεῖτο φυγήν
Rendered as: fled toward Judea
ἐπί with the accusative marks the direction of Simon’s flight.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ἐπανελθεῖν
Rendered as: return at once to his own home
The idiom can refer to one’s home, possessions, affairs, or people. Faustus’s return to his family makes “home” contextually suitable, though the expression itself is broader.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἀωρίας
Rendered as: at an unseasonable hour
The adverbial genitive denotes action at an unusually late, early, or otherwise inconvenient hour.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἐναλειψάμενος ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Σίμωνος ὢν προδιηγησάμην
Rendered as: being one who has been anointed by Simon himself—I gave this account beforehand
ὢν is translated as a nominative participle agreeing with the speaker. προδιηγησάμην is treated parenthetically; alternatively, the participles may be attached differently within the interrupted sentence.

10. Translation choice — Greek: ὅτι ἑστῶτες τὸν ὑμέτερον οὐ γνωρίζετε πατέρα
Rendered as: though you are standing here, you do not recognize your own father
The participle ἑστῶτες is retained and understood concessively; a more mechanically circumstantial rendering would be “standing here, you do not recognize.”

SECTION 20.18

Then Peter promised us that our father’s form would be restored. He said to him, “You have heard, Faustus, about our circumstances. Therefore, when the deceptive form laid upon you becomes useful to us and you assist us in the matters we command, then I too will restore your true form to you, after you have first done what I tell you.”

The father said, “Anything that is possible for me I will do with the greatest eagerness; only restore my form to my own people.” Peter answered, “You yourself heard with your own ears from my advance messengers, who came from Antioch and said that Simon had been there and had vehemently incited the crowds against me, calling me a magician, a murderer, a deceiver, and a sorcerer—to such an extent that everyone there longs to taste my flesh. You will therefore do as I say: leave Clement with me and go ahead of us to Antioch with your wife and also with your sons Faustinus and Faustinianus. Certain others will accompany you as well, whom I judge capable of serving my purpose.”

Translator's notes for section 20.18 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Translation choice — Greek: τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς μορφῆς τὴν ἀποκατάστασιν
Rendered as: that our father’s form would be restored
ἀποκατάστασις denotes restoration to a former condition, here explicitly the father’s appearance.

2. Translation choice — Greek: ἡ περικειμένη σοι πλάνος μορφὴ
Rendered as: the deceptive form laid upon you
περίκειμαι presents the form as something placed around or upon Faustus, while πλάνος characterizes it as deceptive.

3. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν προόδων μου
Rendered as: my advance messengers
The substantival plural refers to people sent ahead of Peter; “forerunners” is another possible rendering.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν ἐμῶν ἀπογεύσασθαι σαρκῶν
Rendered as: to taste my flesh
Preserves the violent bodily image rather than generalizing it as a desire merely to kill Peter; the Greek uses the plural σαρκῶν.

5. Translation choice — Greek: προαγαγὼν ἡμᾶς εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν
Rendered as: go ahead of us to Antioch
The following narrative has Faustus reach Antioch before Peter and later notify him. Formally, προάγω with an object can also mean “lead us onward.”

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπουργῆσαι τῷ ἐμῷ θελήματι
Rendered as: serving my purpose
θέλημα denotes Peter’s will or intended purpose here, and ὑπουργέω denotes rendering practical assistance.

SECTION 20.19

“With these people, in Antioch ....... while you appear as Simon, publicly proclaim your own meta........: ‘I, Simon, proclaim these things to you. I confess: unjustly I katapseu........ is a deceiver, not a murderer, not a sorcerer, nor is he any of the vile things I previously went so far as to say about him while driven by anger. I beg you—I myself, who brought upon him the hatred among you—stop hating him. For he is a true apostle of the true prophet sent by God for the salvation of the world. Therefore I myself also advise you to obey him concerning what he proclaims, since your entire city will be utterly destroyed. I want you to know the reason why I have confessed these things to you. This very night, angels of God were severely scourging me, the impious man, as an enemy of the herald of truth. Therefore I appeal to you: even if I myself should come on another occasion and speak while making an attempt against Peter, do not accept me. For I confess openly to you: I am a magician, I am a deceiver, I am a sorcerer. For perhaps it is possible through repentance to put away the sins previously committed by me.’”

Translator's notes for section 20.19 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: μετὰ τούτων ἐν τῇ Ἀντιοχείᾳ ....... ἐν ὅσῳ
The selected edition prints seven dots after Ἀντιοχείᾳ. The unavailable predicate or connective has not been restored, and the translation retains exactly seven dots.

2. Greek: δημοσίᾳ κήρυξον τὴν σεαυτοῦ μετα ........
Only the incomplete fragment μετα survives before the eight printed dots. Its identity, completion, and meaning are unavailable. The main text retains “meta” followed by exactly eight dots, not a restored “repentance,” “change,” “reorientation,” or another completed noun. The later complete μετανοίᾳ is translated independently by context; neither the updated terminology policy nor that later noun recovers the lost completion here.

3. Greek: ὁμολογῶ ἀδίκως καταψεύ ........ ἔστι πλάνος, οὐ μιαιφόνος, οὐ γόης
The selected edition prints eight dots after the incomplete verbal form καταψεύ. Its completion, object, and any further words are unavailable, so the fragment is transliterated and the gap remains explicit. The surviving clause is ἔστι πλάνος, without a printed negation; the translation therefore preserves “is a deceiver.” Any qualification or negation that might once have stood in the gap has not been restored.

4. Translation choice — Greek: ἐν ὅσῳ ὡς Σίμων φαίνῃ
Rendered as: while you appear as Simon
ἐν ὅσῳ gives the period during which Faustus visibly bears Simon’s form.

5. Translation choice — Greek: οὐ μιαιφόνος
Rendered as: not a murderer
μιαιφόνος evokes bloodshed and blood-pollution and functions here as an accusation of murderous violence.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὅσα ποτὲ φαῦλα περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγων ἔφθανον
Rendered as: any of the vile things I previously went so far as to say about him
φθάνω with the participle can convey previously or anticipatorily doing something, or going so far as to do it. “Previously hastened to say” is also possible.

7. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτὸς ἐγὼ ὁ τοῦ πρὸς ὑμᾶς μίσους αἴτιος αὐτῷ γεγονώς
Rendered as: I myself, who brought upon him the hatred among you
The context favors taking πρὸς ὑμᾶς as locating the hatred among or in relation to the listeners and αὐτῷ as marking Peter as the affected person. A more directional reading, “the hatred toward you,” is grammatically possible, but its relationship to αὐτῷ would remain uncertain.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ἄγγελοί με τοῦ θεοῦ τὸν ἀσεβῆ ὡς ἐχθρὸν ὄντα τῷ τῆς ἀληθείας κήρυκι δεινῶς ἐμαστίγουν
Rendered as: angels of God were severely scourging me, the impious man
Retains the appositional accusation τὸν ἀσεβῆ and the continuing force of the imperfect verb.

9. Translation choice — Greek: μετανοίᾳ
Rendered as: through repentance
The complete noun μετανοίᾳ appears in a confession of wrongdoing and the prospect of putting away previously committed sins. That context supports “repentance” under the October 13 contextual policy, a moral-spiritual change rather than mere sadness or a new opinion. No destination or intensifier is inserted, and the speculative “perhaps it is possible” remains intact. This complete noun does not license restoring the earlier incomplete μετα........ fragment.

10. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπολῦσαι τὰ προπεπραγμένα μοι ἁμαρτήματα
Rendered as: to put away the sins previously committed by me
ἀπολύω can mean release, dismiss, or put away. The construction permits a nuance of either removing the sins or obtaining release from them.

SECTION 20.20

As Peter was giving these instructions, the father said, “I know what you want, so do not weary yourself. For when I get there, I will take no less care to say what ought to be said about you.” Peter again instructed him, “When you perceive that the city has turned from its hatred and now desires to see us, send word and inform me, and we will catch up with you there. When I arrive there, on that very day I will drive away your alien form and make your own form appear unmistakably to your people and to everyone else.”

After saying this, he arranged for the sons, my brothers, to accompany him, and he commanded our mother Mattidia and some of the more loyal people to go with him. But the mother regarded going with him reluctantly. “For I appear to be an adulteress while consorting with Simon’s form. If I am indeed compelled to go with him, it is impossible to recline on the same couch with him. And I do not know whether I will be persuaded even to go with him.”

When she hesitated to leave, Annoubion encouraged her and said, “Believe me and Peter, and also the very voice, that .... is your husband, whom I love no less than you do. And I myself, for him, sym.........” When Annoubion had said this, the mother promised to go with him.

Translator's notes for section 20.20 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: αὐτῇ δὲ τῇ φωνῇ ὅτι .... ἐστὶν ὁ σὸς σύμβιος
The selected edition prints four dots where wording identifying the husband would be expected. The context may suggest a demonstrative, but no restoration has been supplied; the translation retains exactly four dots.

2. Greek: καὶ αὐτὸς αὐτῷ συμ.........
The edition preserves καὶ αὐτός, the dative αὐτῷ, and only the incomplete prefix συμ- before nine printed dots. The missing verb, its tense, and the resulting claim are unavailable; the prefix could belong to a compound expressing accompaniment, assistance, sympathy, agreement, or another relationship. The translation retains “I myself,” represents αὐτῷ provisionally as “for him,” and leaves “sym” followed by exactly nine dots without inventing a predicate.

3. Translation choice — Greek: διὸ μὴ κάμνε
Rendered as: so do not weary yourself
κάμνω can mean grow weary or exert oneself laboriously; the father indicates that Peter need not labor over further explanation.

4. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν πόλιν μεταβαλομένην τοῦ μίσους
Rendered as: the city has turned from its hatred
The genitive τοῦ μίσους is taken as the state from which the city changes. “Changed with respect to its hatred” is also grammatically possible but less directly contrasts with its new desire to see Peter.

5. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτόθι ἐπικαταληψόμεθά σε
Rendered as: we will catch up with you there
ἐπικαταλαμβάνω here denotes overtaking or joining Faustus after he has gone ahead.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἀπλανῶς φαίνεσθαι
Rendered as: appear unmistakably
The adverb means without deception or mistake, reversing the deceptive appearance imposed by Simon.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τῶν γνησιωτέρων τινὰς
Rendered as: some of the more loyal people
The substantival comparative can describe more genuine, trustworthy, or devoted associates. “More genuine ones” is a more formally transparent alternative.

8. Translation choice — Greek: Μοιχὰς γὰρ εἶναι δοκῶ τῇ Σίμωνος συνοῦσα μορφῇ
Rendered as: For I appear to be an adulteress while consorting with Simon’s form
δοκῶ may mean “I appear” or “I consider myself.” The context emphasizes the adulterous appearance created by accompanying someone who visibly bears Simon’s form.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτῆς κλίνης συγκατακλιθήσεσθαι
Rendered as: to recline on the same couch with him
κλίνη may denote a couch or bed; the literal posture is retained while the marital implication remains contextual.

10. Translation choice — Greek: ὃν οὐκ ἔλαττόν σου ἀγαπῶ
Rendered as: whom I love no less than you do
The reassurance favors comparing Annoubion’s love for the husband with Mattidia’s love for him. The elliptical comparison can alternatively mean “whom I love no less than I love you.”

SECTION 20.21

But Peter ......... diōtata, God orders our affairs. For we have Annoubion with us .......... ogon. For when we are staying in Antioch, this man will thereafter discuss nativity with us more sincerely, as a friend. And so, when the father set out by night for nearby Antioch with those whom Peter had instructed, together with Annoubion, at dawn the next day, before Peter went out for the discussion, Appion and Athenodorus returned to Laodicea, having sent Simon ahead, seeking the father. For after coming to you that very evening, he was no longer seen by his own people. The nine printed dots mark unavailable wording after “Peter” and before the surviving fragment διώτατα, apparently the end of an incomplete word or expression. 2. Greek: Ἀννουβίων .......... όγον
The ten printed dots mark unavailable wording after Annoubion and before the surviving fragment όγον, apparently the end of an incomplete word. The exact gap is retained and the fragment is transliterated; its interpretation remains provisional, and no completion has been supplied.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ὁ θεὸς τὰ πράγματα ἡμῶν οἰκονομεῖ

4. Translation choice — Greek: περὶ γενέσεως τοῦ λοιποῦ

In the context of Annoubion and astrological discussion, γένεσις concerns birth or nativity, while τοῦ λοιποῦ means thereafter or henceforth.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς φίλος γνησιώτερον
Rendered as: more sincerely, as a friend

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπανῆλθον εἰς τὴν Λαοδίκειαν τὸν Σίμωνα προπέμψαντες Ἀππίων καὶ Ἀθηνόδωρος ἐπιζητοῦντες τὸν πατέρα

The participle ἐπιζητοῦντες presents their seeking in connection with their return; the rendering does not add a separate onset or subsequent beginning of the search.

7. Translation choice — Greek: τί δόξαν αὐτῷ
Rendered as: what came over him
Literally “what seemed good to him,” the phrase idiomatically refers to what entered his mind or prompted his conduct.

8. Translation choice — Greek: δακρύων καὶ κοπτόμενος
Rendered as: weeping and beating himself
κόπτομαι can depict striking oneself as an expression of grief; the bodily image is retained.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ἐπὶ θάλασσαν ὥρμησε
Rendered as: rushed off as though toward the sea
ὡς qualifies the reported direction and does not state that he reached or entered the sea.

SECTION 20.22

On hearing this, Appion and those with him wailed and beat themselves, saying, “Why did you not receive him?” And just as Athenodorus was about to say to me, “It was Faustus, your father,” Appion forestalled him and said, “We learned from someone that Simon, after finding him, sent him away ............................... the truth, Faustus himself having begged him, because he did not wish to see that his own sons had become Jews. When we heard this, we came for this reason, seeking him. But since he is not here, the person who told us appears to have spoken truthfully. As, therefore, we heard it from him, so we have told you.” But I, Clement, understood Peter’s purpose: he wanted to plant in them the suspicion that he was going to look for the old man among them, so that they would become afraid and flee. I therefore joined in his plan and said to Appion, “Listen, my dearest Appion. We were eager to give him, as our father, the things we regarded as good. But if he himself did not wish to receive them and, on the contrary, was disgusted with us and fled—I will say something rather harsh—we do not care about him either.” When I said this, they left, taking offense as though at cruelty, and (as we learned the next day) of us ......., they set out in Simon’s tracks for Judea.

Translator's notes for section 20.22 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἐξώρμησε ............................... τὰ ἀληθῆ
The thirty-one printed dots mark unavailable wording connecting ἐξώρμησε with τὰ ἀληθῆ. The exact gap is retained, and no missing action, negation, or speech has been restored.

2. Greek: ἡμῶν ....... κατ’ ἴχνη Σίμωνος
The seven printed dots mark unavailable wording that governed or completed the genitive ἡμῶν. The resulting fragment is preserved in its source order without conjecturally supplying its syntactic relation.

3. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπολολύξαντες ἐκόψαντο
Rendered as: wailed and beat themselves
The verbs portray loud lamentation and bodily striking in grief, so both actions are retained.

4. Translation choice — Greek: εὑρὼν αὐτὸν ὁ Σίμων ἐξώρμησε
Rendered as: Simon, after finding him, sent him away
ἐξορμάω may be intransitive, “set out,” or causative, “send out.” Taking αὐτόν as also supplying the object of ἐξώρμησε supports the causative rendering, though the following lacuna prevents certainty and the intransitive alternative remains possible.

5. Translation choice — Greek: ὑπόνοιαν αὐτοῖς ἐνσπεῖραι
Rendered as: to plant in them the suspicion
The image of sowing or planting suspicion is preserved.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς τὸν γέροντα ζητεῖν μέλλων παρ’ αὐτοῖς
Rendered as: that he was going to look for the old man among them
παρ’ αὐτοῖς has the dative and directly allows a locative or associative sense: “among them,” “at their place,” or “in their keeping.” Context could construe looking for someone in their keeping as demanding him from them, but the main rendering preserves the more source-transparent locative construction.

7. Translation choice — Greek: συνέδραμον αὐτοῦ τῷ βουλήματι
Rendered as: I therefore joined in his plan
The expression literally describes running together with his purpose and contextually means cooperating with or furthering the plan.

8. Translation choice — Greek: βδελυξάμενος ἡμᾶς ἔφυγε
Rendered as: was disgusted with us and fled
βδελύσσομαι expresses abhorrence or revulsion, stronger than simple dislike.

9. Translation choice — Greek: ὡς ἐπ’ ὠμότητι δυσχεράναντες
Rendered as: taking offense as though at cruelty
ὡς presents cruelty as their construal of Clement’s words rather than an unqualified judgment by the narrator.

SECTION 20.23

Nevertheless, after ten days had passed, ......... from Antioch, from the father, reporting to us how the father, dēmo........., by denouncing his appearance and speaking well of Peter, had moved the entire city of the Antiochenes into longing. He also reported that, as a result, everyone desired to see him, but that some, angry with him as though he were Simon because of their surpassing affection for Peter, even wanted to lay hands on Faustus as though he were Simon; and that therefore Faustus, fearing that he might be killed, had sent to ask Peter to come immediately, so that Peter might reach him while he was still alive and make a timely appearance before the city while its longing for him was at its height. When Peter heard this, he gathered a great many people for assembly, appointed one of his followers as bishop, baptized and healed, and, after remaining three days in Laodicea, hastened to set out for nearby Antioch.

Translator's notes for section 20.23 (not part of the ancient text):

1. Greek: ἡμερῶν δέκα διελθουσῶν ......... ἐκ τῆς Ἀντιοχείας παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ἀγγελῶν ἡμῖν
The nine printed dots mark unavailable wording after the genitive absolute and before the phrase beginning ἐκ τῆς Ἀντιοχείας. The missing wording apparently included main-clause material, potentially a subject and finite verb, with ἀγγελῶν describing the reporting mission. The exact gap is retained without inventing a messenger or finite verb.

2. Greek: δημο......... αὐτοῦ μορφῆς
The nine printed dots follow the surviving fragment δημο and mark unavailable continuation of the word or phrase. The fragment is transliterated and the exact gap retained; its interpretation remains provisional, and no adverb such as “publicly” has been restored.

3. Translation choice — Greek: αὐτοῦ μορφῆς κατηγορῶν
Rendered as: denouncing his appearance
αὐτοῦ may refer to the father’s present appearance, Simon’s appearance, or the person represented by it. The non-reflexive “his” preserves that referential ambiguity.

4. Translation choice — Greek: Πέτρον εὐλογῶν
Rendered as: speaking well of Peter
In this public-speech context εὐλογέω can mean praising or speaking favorably of someone rather than pronouncing a blessing.

5. Translation choice — Greek: τὴν πᾶσαν Ἀντιοχέων πόλιν εἰς πόθον μετέθηκεν
Rendered as: had moved the entire city of the Antiochenes into longing
The rendering preserves the source image of transferring or moving the city into a state of longing.

6. Translation choice — Greek: ἐνίους δὲ καὶ χαλεπαίνοντας αὐτῷ ὡς Σίμωνι διὰ τὴν πρὸς Πέτρον ὑπερβάλλουσαν στοργὴν
Rendered as: some, angry with him as though he were Simon because of their surpassing affection for Peter
The Greek expresses “the surpassing affection for Peter” without an explicit possessor. “Their” takes the affection as belonging to the townspeople and as motivating their anger against the man they took for Simon, which best fits the report that the city longed for Peter. Alternatively, the phrase could refer to the supposed Simon’s conspicuous affection for Peter.

7. Translation choice — Greek: ἐξαυτῆς ἐλθεῖν πέμψαντα ἀξιοῦν· τὸν Πέτρον
Rendered as: had sent to ask Peter to come immediately
τὸν Πέτρον is taken as the delayed object of ἀξιοῦν. Alternatively, it may be read as an anticipatory accusative identifying Peter as the implicit subject of the following purpose clause. The printed punctuation makes the attachment conspicuous, so the main construction remains provisional, though both readings identify Peter as the one asked to come.

8. Translation choice — Greek: ὅπως αὐτὸν ζῶντα ἐπικαταλάβῃ
Rendered as: so that Peter might reach him while he was still alive
ἐπικαταλαμβάνω here means to catch up with or reach someone; ζῶντα describes the endangered Faustus.

9. Translation choice — Greek: τῇ πόλει ἀκμαζούσῃ πόθῳ τῷ πρὸς αὐτὸν
Rendered as: before the city while its longing for him was at its height
The city is portrayed as being at its peak or flourishing in its longing; the pronoun most naturally refers to Peter but remains formally pronominal.

10. Translation choice — Greek: πρὸς τὸ ἐκκλησιάζειν πλείστους συναγαγὼν
Rendered as: he gathered a great many people for assembly
ἐκκλησιάζειν can denote convening or addressing an assembly and need not imply a later formalized church service.

11. Translation choice — Greek: ἐπίσκοπον ἐκ τῶν ἀκολούθων καταστήσας
Rendered as: appointed one of his followers as bishop
ἐπίσκοπος denotes the appointed overseer; “bishop” preserves the narrative’s office term.

End of Pseudo-Clementine Homilies.
